10028-spalding-s-official-baseball-guide:
Spalding's Official Baseball Guide for 1913, edited by John B. Foster and sold for ten cents, served the game's fans and officials. Published by the American Sports Publishing Company in New York, it opens with an introduction on the progress of America's national game.

Inside are the personnel of the National League, the oldest base ball organization, with editorial comment by Foster and records of leagues from Illinois-Missouri to Indiana-Illinois-Iowa and the International League. The guide is a snapshot of organized baseball in 1913, when the modern game was coming of age.
10838-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction opens its thirteenth volume with the number of January 3, 1829, priced at two pence. Its leading engraving shows Bruce Castle, Tottenham, as it appeared in 1686, copied from a print after Wolridge. The text traces the ancient castle to Earl Waltheof, who married Judith, niece of William the Conqueror.

An old brick tower over a deep well, once used as a dairy, marks the site's age. The Mirror's mix of picture and short history aimed at family readers. Modern readers get a neat sample of how the 1820s learned local history, one engraving at a time.
10950-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
A weekly miscellany for general readers, The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, issued this number on Saturday, February 7, 1829, priced twopence. The lead piece describes villas in Regent's Park, including the Marquess of Hertford's villa designed by Decimus Burton, with its six-column portico, Venetian roof, and glass lanterns.

Other items mix history, biography, and anecdote, from Roman villas larger than Versailles to a king returning from chapel at Windsor, watched by crowds from Cheapside. Engravings illustrate the articles. The issue shows early nineteenth-century popular learning: short, varied pieces meant to amuse and instruct a family audience in one sitting.
11112-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction for Saturday, January 10, 1829, opens with Macclesfield Bridge in Regent's Park. Designed by Mr. Morgan, the bridge crosses the canal near Primrose Hill, with cast-iron columns of the Grecian Doric order, arches over canal, towing path, and banks, and ornaments praised by architect Mr. Elmes for lightness, elegance, and originality.

Other items in the number mix travel, history, and anecdote, including a battlefield story of Scotch soldiers cooking beefsteaks in a French cuirass, used as frying pan and dish. The Mirror's short, illustrated pieces aimed to amuse and instruct a family audience for twopence. This number shows early Victorian popular journalism at its most varied.
11322-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated March 7, 1829, this Mirror number leads with Rugby School, founded in Elizabeth's ninth year by Lawrence Sheriff, a London grocer, as a free grammar school for Rugby and Brownsover children. The article traces the school's endowment. from eight acres at Lamb's Conduit Fields worth little at first to a London property that rose sharply in value as the metropolis grew, funding master and almsmen.

The school's rise among classical seminaries is the article's theme, told through deeds, leases, and salaries. Shorter items complete the sheet. For historians of English education, the number preserves a concise, contemporary account of how a provincial grammar school became famous on the back of London land.
11331-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The March 28, 1829 Mirror leads with Guy's Cliff, a mile and a half northeast of Warwick, where the Avon winds through fertile meadows beside rock and wood. Leland's phrase, a home of pleasure, a place meet for the Muses, heads the article, which traces a Saxon oratory. a hermit's cell under Edward III and Henry IV, and Guy of Warwick's retirement after his duel with the Danish Colbrond. Henry V's charmed visit is also recalled.

Felice, Guy's neglected countess, is said to have buried him there. The article blends legend with topography in the Mirror's usual manner. Readers of Warwickshire history will find a compact, romantic account of a site where poetry, chivalry, and landscape meet.
11338-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
This supplementary Mirror number, numbered 373, reviews Scott's Anne of Geierstein, or The Maiden of the Mist, praising the Waverley novels' knowledge of the human heart and mastery of passions. The reviewer argues Scott's free, conversational style strikes feelings and common sense at once, identifying readers with heroes' impulses. That chapter endings work like good stage exits, leaving readers curious for the next scene. Scott's incognito, now removed, has not dimmed his fame.

The review treats Scott as a national author whose popularity may outlive matter-of-fact works. Shorter items accompany it. For Scott scholars, the number preserves a contemporary verdict on a late Waverley novel, admiring but no longer rapturous, as the reviewer admits.
11340-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The May 30, 1829 Mirror leads with Epsom's new race stand, built by the Epsom Grand Stand Association with twenty thousand pounds capital in thousand twenty-pound shares, patronized by Jockey Club stewards. Modeled on Doncaster's stand but larger, it accommodates four to five thousand persons, measures 156 feet wide and 60 deep. A Doric portico, a terrace ten feet above ground, and a magnificent central flight of steps. Temporary accommodation was promised for the spring races beginning June 2.

The article avoids competing with racing lists, offering architecture instead of tips. Shorter items follow. For sporting historians, the number records Epsom's commercial growth, as racing became a business with shareholders, stands, and crowds.
11342-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated January 17, 1829, this Mirror number leads with Prince Rupert's palace in Barbican, a Beech Lane house where the prince lived under Charles II. The article notes Charles's visit, when Cripplegate ringers earned a guinea for a merry peal, and praises Rupert as a man of science: inventor of Prince's Metal. firearm locks, and gunpowder improvements, fellow of the Royal Society, Board of Trade member, and first governor of the Hudson's Bay Company, whose influence founded it.

Rupert's military fame, the writer argues, will fade before his artistic and useful legacy. Shorter items follow. For London historians, the number preserves a lost City house and a reminder that a Civil War cavalier could also be an experimental philosopher.
11343-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated May 9, 1829, this Mirror number leads with Cornwall Terrace in Regent's Park, designed by Decimus Burton and named for the king's ducal title when regent. The article praises its regularity and beauty, with a rusticated ground story, Corinthian stories with fluted shafts and well-proportioned capitals, and a facade of great architectural elegance. Adjoining York Terrace, engraved in number 358, it was among the park's earliest and most admired buildings.

A Cosmopolite column and a concluded piece on the Times newspaper follow, dissecting how readers consume court circulars and money-market news. The terrace piece and the newspaper piece together show the Mirror's range: buildings and media in one sheet. Regent's Park enthusiasts will value the contemporary praise for Burton.
11347-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The May 16, 1829 Mirror leads with Laleham Park, a villa on the Thames between Shepperton and Staines, lately the temporary residence of the young Queen of Portugal. The article describes an elegant villa on forty acres with fine elm timber, laid out under the Earl of Lucan, and a lively, light-haired child queen. nearly the same age as Princess Victoria, who arrived in London the previous October and stayed at Grillon's Hotel before ill health required country air.

Laleham's fame for angling and its transparent shallows complete the picture. The piece is celebrity reporting in 1829 form: a royal child, a pretty house, and a river. Shorter items fill the sheet, but the young queen gives the number its news value.
11348-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The May 2, 1829 Mirror leads with Clarendon House in Piccadilly, the splendid mansion of the Earl of Clarendon facing St. James's Street, on the site of present Grafton Street. Built with stone intended for St. Paul's, it cost fifty thousand pounds and employed three hundred men, and enemies called it Dunkirk House, claiming it was built with money from selling Dunkirk to France. Clarendon himself later apologized for its vanity and expense, which embarrassed his affairs.

George Monck, Duke of Albemarle, later bought the house. The article balances admiration for the pile with the political scandal it caused. Shorter items follow. For Stuart historians, the number preserves a famous house and the envy that helped ruin its builder.
11350-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The June 20, 1829 Mirror leads with Exeter 'Change in the Strand, celebrated for its menagerie and merchandise: wild beasts and cutlery, kangaroos and hosiery, elephants and pins. The article recalls Burleigh's house, where Elizabeth visited her treasurer, becoming a receptacle for beasts upstairs and shopkeepers below, including Clarke the cutler, who amassed a princely fortune. Improvement has now condemned the building, and the beasts move to the King's Mews at Charing Cross.

Two doors east of this world of wonders, the Mirror itself first appeared. A building for public societies is planned for the site. The article is both obituary and memoir, mourning a London curiosity. For city historians, it preserves Exeter 'Change at the moment of its removal.
11361-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The June 27, 1829 Mirror leads with Loch Goil Head in Argyleshire, a small village at the end of Loch Goil. rendered interesting as the residence of Thomas Campbell, author of The Pleasures of Hope. Campbell's château or retreat appears on the left of the engraving, its romantic position probably inspiring many soul-stirring compositions. Nearby stand Carrick Castle, said to be built by Danes, Ben Cruachan at 3,300 feet, Inveraray Castle, Loch Lomond, and Glencoe.

The article sells Argyleshire as Alpine sublimity within Britain, with poetry as its guide. Shorter items follow. For Campbell readers, the number locates the poet in his landscape, showing how literary fame turned a loch-head village into a destination.
11382-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The January 31, 1829 Mirror leads with the Colosseum in Regent's Park, a polygon of sixteen sides, 130 feet in diameter, whose exterior the engraving shows. Each angle bears a double square Doric pilaster supporting an entablature, above which sit a blocking course. attic, and majestic cupola on three receding steps, glazed above and copper below, finished with an immense open circle. The portico, copied from Rome's Pantheon, is praised as among the best Graeco-Doric in the metropolis.

An earlier number guided readers through the interior; this one treats the architecture. The Colosseum housed a vast panorama, and the Mirror's attention shows its novelty. For Regent's Park historians, the number preserves a building now vanished, described while it still astonished visitors.
11390-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The January 24, 1829 Mirror presents villas in Regent's Park, with engravings of Hanover Lodge and Grove House seen from Macclesfield Bridge. Hanover Lodge, residence of Colonel Sir Robert Arbuthnot, offers a handsome portico, a dining room, and drawing rooms sixty feet by eighteen, with nine chambers above and domestic offices complete. Its grounds avoid geometrical formalities, unlike old gardeners who carried square and compasses. Grove House, home of George Bellas Greenough, was designed by Decimus Burton.

The villas exemplify a light, elegant style, unlike southern London's brick monstrosities. Shorter items follow. For Regent's Park enthusiasts, the number pairs two villas in one sheet, showing how the park's domestic architecture complemented its terraces.
11486-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 22 August 1829, priced at twopence, opens at St. Peter's Church, Pimlico. The church stands east of Wilton Place in St. George, Hanover Square. Henry Hakewill designed the Ionic building. It runs east and west as a parallelogram.

A small chancel and vestries extend the east end. A six-column portico fronts the west. Steps lead to three entrances. Columns carry an entablature and pediment. Notes after the main piece turn to insects and cruelty to small creatures. Royal visits get a note as well. The weekly blend stays the same.
11487-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The May 23, 1829 Mirror leads with the Fortune Playhouse in Golden Lane, Barbican, built by actor Edward Alleyn, founder of Dulwich College, in 1599, burnt in 1624, and rebuilt in 1629. A treasure reportedly found digging foundations probably fell to Alleyn, and the name Fortune may derive from it. The spacious brick building showed royal arms in plaster, retained in the engraving even as its lower part became shops, base purposes for a temple of drama.

Ben Jonson and others called Alleyn the first actor of his time, playing leading roles in Shakespeare and Jonson, drawing crowds wherever he performed. Shorter items, including Royal Academy pictures, follow. For theatre historians, the number preserves a Shakespearean playhouse in its decayed, shop-filled state.
11611-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 6 June 1829, priced at twopence, opens at Holland House, Kensington. Sir Walter Cope built it in 1607. Henry Rich, Earl of Holland, gave the house its name. Its form is a half H, and Inigo Jones designed the entrance piers.

Francis Cleyne decorated the gilt room, which keeps its first state. Kensington has housed celebrated men since William the Third. He was the first royal tenant of the palace there. A later piece turns to Old Charing Cross. It was one of Edward the First's memorials to Queen Elinor, later destroyed by Reformers.
11710-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 13 June 1829, priced at twopence, opens at Cumberland Terrace, Regent's Park. The terrace completes the magazine's series of architectural illustrations there. Nash designed the terrace, raised above the road, with a carriage sweep and balustrades.

A garden promenade lies below, level with the road, for residents of the terrace. Centre and wings join by two handsome arches, with Doric columns and a balustrade above. Allegorical figures of seasons, quarters of the globe, and arts and sciences crown the masses. A later piece solves the fate of La Pérouse through the massacre of the Hunter's crew at the Feejee Islands in 1813.
11740-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 4 April 1829, priced at twopence, opens at the tomb of Gower the poet in St. Mary Overy, or St. Saviour, Southwark. Dr. Johnson, the writer notes, dignified Gower as the father of English poetry, so no apology is needed for the memorial.

Three Gothic arches, rich in cinquefoil tracery, roses, and carved work, form the tomb, with trefoil niches behind and a Doric column rising between. Cherubim descend from the interior arches, and foliage crowns the whole. A later piece shows the Hirlas Horn, a piece of plate given at the Denbigh Eisteddfod of 1828 to Dr. Jones, its honorary secretary.
11742-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 25 April 1829, priced at twopence, opens at Sussex Place, Regent's Park, said to be built from Nash's designs, though counted among his least successful works. It was among the earliest terraces in the park, and its contrast with chaster neighbours drew critical pasquinade.

A centre with pediment, two octagonal towers, and wings with four towers each, all topped with cupolas and minarets, make the range. The effect, the writer says, is far from pleasing, though a landscape painter might enjoy its picturesque outlines. Later notes cover Loch Katrine, ten miles long, never freezing, and portrait painting.
12017-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
This volume of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction contains original essays, historical narratives, biographical memoirs, sketches of society, topographical descriptions, novels and tales, anecdotes, and poetry. It opens with a portrait of the late Sir Humphry Davy. Its subtitle promises the spirit of the public journals and discoveries in the arts, for twopenny readers.

The Davy memoir notes that a few days before his marriage he received knighthood from the Prince Regent, the first dignity of that kind the prince conferred. It follows his discoveries relating electricity and chemistry, with Davies Gilbert's speech awarding him a royal medal. Science, biography, and miscellany share the volume in the magazine's familiar mix.
12089-letters-of-travel-1892-1913:
Rudyard Kipling's Letters of Travel, 1892 to 1913, in the Dominions Edition published by Macmillan in London in 1920, gathers travel letters from three sources. From Tideway to Tideway appeared originally in The Times, Letters to the Family in The Morning Post, and Egypt of the Magicians in Nash's Magazine.

Kipling writes as an imperial traveller and reporter, moving between Canada, South Africa, Egypt. Other parts of the empire with a journalist's eye for harbors, railways, soldiers, and settlers. The letters, spanning two decades, show his style hardening from youthful impressionism to the confident, sometimes combative voice of his later public writing.
12213-odd-charges-odd-craft-part-13:
A stranger eating and drinking in the warm tap-room of the Cauliflower meets a withered ancient nursing an empty mug in Odd Charges, a comic tale from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft. The old man blows through a cold churchwarden pipe, waiting for charity.

The stranger, generous with his mug, draws out tales of Bob Pretty and village feuds, including a coat dropped on a head from a window and thanks sent down for kindness. Jacobs lets the tap-room talk wander from poaching to revenge, with each anecdote sharpening the last. The title puns on odd charges: the bills, accusations, and favors that pass between drinkers. The story is a small masterpiece of pub narration.
12477-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated 14 February 1829 and priced at twopence, this number of the Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction opens with an engraving of the interior of the Colosseum. A key explains the print in detail, from its central tower and galleries to its refreshment room, music rooms and the old ball from St. Paul's Cathedral.

That blend of picture, explanation and short reading typifies the weekly miscellany, which mixed literature, science, history and curiosity for a broad audience. Later pages would carry anecdotes, sketches and notices in the same accessible style. The issue is a small window on cheap illustrated print in the 1820s, when a panorama print could teach as well as entertain.
12498-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated 21 March 1829, this Mirror number leads with Chester Terrace, Regent's Park, in a spirited engraving. The range of palatial residences, named from the royal earldom of Chester, stands between the Colosseum and St. Katharine's Church, with the Colosseum's cupola in the distance. Nash, architect of York Terrace, designed it.

Like most of the park's terraces, Chester Terrace presents a noble appearance, the article says, as fine as any similar structure in the park. Short pieces around it keep the weekly mix. The number shows Regency London in print, a new park, new terraces and a public eager to see them pictured.
12897-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated Saturday, February 21, 1829, this Mirror number leads with Warwick Castle, inhabited from its foundation for nearly a thousand years. The town on the Avon, debated as Roman or Saxon in origin, gets its own history before the castle's towers and sieges. Antiquaries Rous and Dugdale supply the learned notes.

Later pages turn to encyclopaedias, tracing the word from the Greek circle of liberal learning to the vast modern works of human knowledge. Short notes and anecdotes fill the rest. The issue shows the weekly's habit of pairing a grand old building with light learning for general readers.
12898-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated Saturday, February 28, 1829, this Mirror number leads with York Terrace in Regent's Park, a splendid range of homes that looks like one unique palace. Entrances at the rear, uniform doors and windows, and undivided gardens give the terrace a princely, little-Versailles air. Its Græco-Italian design, with rusticated piers and round-headed windows, earns praise.

Later pages travel to Mecca, where unpaved streets turn to dust in summer and mud in rain, and no house is thought older than four centuries. The mosque itself, repaired by many sultans, counts as modern. The issue pairs London architecture with foreign travel notes.
12899-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated Saturday, April 18, 1829, this Mirror number opens at Harrow School, founded by John Lyon under Elizabeth with letters patent and a code of rules. The archbishops of Canterbury once kept a residence on the hill. The free grammar school grew from Lyon's small gift of thirty marks a year into one of England's eight great schools.

Later pages turn to South America, where Bolivar leaves his army to Paez and repairs to Angostura as Morillo advances toward the Orinoco. Foreign friends who flew to freedom's aid earn the writer's praise. The issue pairs English school history with stirring news from abroad.
13578-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
A supplementary number of the Mirror of Literature, volume thirteen, number 361, opens with the Naturalist, illustrated by the talipot tree, the glowworm, and the deathwatch magnified. A new Journal of a Naturalist, with the motto plants, trees, and stones we note, earns praise as a delightful volume almost synonymous with this division of the Mirror.

London building follows, with Belgrave Square rising in about four years, houses of the largest size round spacious squares and wide streets, built by gentlemen and tradesmen as a pre-eminent example. A confederate in knavery, needy and outcast, links his destiny with Fitzroy, who lives by plundering the unwary and is hailed as Magnus Apollo. Nature, building, and rogue memoir share the supplement.
13644-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror of Literature for March 14, 1829, opens with the grand entrance to Hyde Park, designed by Decimus Burton. A screen of handsome fluted Ionic columns, three carriage archways, two foot entrances, and a lodge stretch about one hundred and seven feet, with a bold central projection. Lord Burleigh's maxim, that a realm gains more by one year's peace than ten years' war, frames the praise.

A chronological table follows rulers from Cromwell's interregnum, 1648 to 1660, through popes, emperors, and kings of France, Spain, Portugal, Denmark, and beyond. A review of Penelope, or Love's Labour Lost, praises a mixture of satire and fashion without starch or silly affectation. The number mixes architecture, chronology, and novel criticism.
16760-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-2-of-6-:
This slice of Holinshed's Chronicles covers Stephen, earl of Boulogne, from his swift crossing after his uncle Henry died in 1135. Stephen was son of Stephen of Blois and Adela, daughter of William the Conqueror. He seized the realm with help from his brother Theobald. His brother Henry, bishop of Winchester, aided him too. Yet he had sworn to uphold the Empress and her heirs.

The same day he landed, a great winter tempest of thunder and lightning struck, which chroniclers read as a sign of trouble to come. The slice opens the Anarchy in Tudor prose, with side notes naming its sources. Readers who push through the old spelling get a reign that starts in oath-breaking, storm, and civil war.
17320-political-and-literary-essays-1908:
The Earl of Cromer's 1913 set gathers political and literary essays from the Edinburgh Review, Quarterly Review, Nineteenth Century, and Spectator. Topics run from the government of subject races and army reform to free trade, China, Egypt, Disraeli, Russian romance, the Greek anthology, and the future of the classics. Pieces on Wellington, Burma, and Portuguese slavery widen the range.

Cromer writes as an imperial statesman and man of letters, firm in view and clear in prose. His essays show Edwardian Britain debating empire, trade, and culture at full stretch. Historians and essay lovers will find a rich, opinionated volume from a leading voice of its age.
2113-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Carlyle closes the First Silesian War in Book Thirteen, from May 1741 to July 1742, leaving the general European war ablaze all round. The British king, paladin of the Pragmatic Sanction, carries the axis of the world on his shoulder. The Pragmatic Sanction, which secured Maria Theresa's throne, drew Britain into German war.

Carlyle writes of a small gentleman with proud eyes and poor sight, trying to unriddle a waste of diplomacy under pain of death. The volume ends Frederick's first war with a peace that settled Silesia but not Europe. Carlyle's small gentleman is George II, whose German lands pulled him into a continental tangle.
22242-the-youth-s-companion-volume-lii-n:
The Youth's Companion was America's best-loved family weekly for a hundred years. This number, volume 52 number 11, is dated Thursday, March 13, 1879. J. T. Trowbridge, a regular contributor, supplies the lead story. In it a one-eyed hostler leans on a bar and lectures on bears. Let them alone, he says, and they will mostly let you alone. A vicious one turns up now and then.

Stories, poems, household pages, and a children's corner fill the issue. The Companion reached more American homes than any magazine of its century. Mark Twain and a dozen presidents wrote for it. One surviving number shows the wholesome, story-rich mixture that made it a fixture by the fireside.
30186-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
Rossiter Johnson edits volume 13 of The Great Events by Famous Historians, a chronological history told in the words of eminent historians, with brief links by specialists. Charles F. Horne supplies an outline narrative, then Louis Adolphe Thiers tells how John Law promoted the Mississippi Scheme in 1716 and how the South Sea Bubble burst in 1720. Prince Eugene's own account covers the siege and battle of Belgrad in 1717, and Bach lays the foundation of modern music in 1723.

The National Alumni published the volume in 1905, promising a non-sectarian, non-partisan account with thorough indices, bibliographies, chronologies, and courses of reading. Each event reads as a complete narrative, not a summary, so the book suits readers who want history in strong period voices. Later volumes carry the chain forward, but this one stands well on its own.
3089-original-short-stories-volume-13:
Old Judas closes the series in volume thirteen, beside a wild black lake. The opening story surveys a wild lake of stagnant black water, reeds waving in a vast circle, with a grandeur almost religious and an air of sinister desolation. The volume adds The Little Cask, Boitelle, A Widow, The Englishmen of Etretat, Magnetism, A Father's Confession, and A Mother of Monsters. Later tales include An Uncomfortable Bed, A Portrait, The Drunkard, The Wardrobe, The Mountain Pool, A Cremation, Misti, Madame Hermet, and The Magic Couch.

A father's confession tells of a month of horrible anguish and hatred toward a child blocking his path to happiness. The final volume shows Maupassant's full range, from horror to irony.
30954-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Held here is volume thirteen of the Swanston Edition of Robert Louis Stevenson's works, printed in London in 1912. The edition ran to twenty-five volumes, with two thousand and sixty copies printed and two thousand for sale. This volume holds The Wrecker, with a prologue set in the Marquesas and a front showing the back verandah at Vailima.

The yarn opens with a sound commercial education and Roussillon wine, then introduces Mr. Pinkerton, a figure who shapes the hero's fortunes. Chapters follow extremes of fortune, bad luck in Paris, going west, irons in the fire, and faces on the city front. Then comes the wreck of the Flying Scud and the vanishing of its crew. It is a sprawling adventure of business, ships, and mystery, in Stevenson's late, Pacific style.
31288-the-conscript-a-story-of-the-frenc:
Erckmann-Chatrian's The Conscript, in the Scribner translation of 1911, is the French authors' sustained sermon against war. It follows their Madame Thérèse with the tragic story of 1812 and 1813 rather than Napoleon's victories. Its first part follows the grande armée through Alsace toward Moscow and the Beresina, with anxious waiting, rumors of disaster, and a demoralized, straggling retreat.

The second and larger portion follows the fatal campaign that opened doubtfully at Lutzen and Bautzen and ended at Leipsic and the capitulation of Paris. Joseph Bertha, torn from his betrothed and peaceful trade by conscription, tells the story with shrewd, simple reflections that make his fate stand for a generation's.
31289-waterloo-a-sequel-to-the-conscript:
Erckmann-Chatrian's Waterloo, translated from the French and published by Scribner's in New York in 1911 as a sequel to The Conscript of 1813, tells the campaign from a private soldier's standpoint. It describes only what he saw. The introductory note argues that this limit still admits events of the greatest importance and incidents of intense dramatic interest, from the combat at Hougoumont Farm to the Emperor's departure for Paris.

The narrative also pictures France after the first Bourbon restoration, when the unbounded joy at Louis XVIII's return in the spring of 1814 gave way, through the new regime's stupidity. That stupidity prepared the gradual return of Napoleon. As familiar history and historical commentary, the novel shows how a restoration lost a war-weary people.
3246-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-:
This volume of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction dates from the spring of 1829. Number 365, priced at twopence and dated Saturday 11 April 1829, opens with an engraving of Old Somerset House. The editors call it one of the greatest antiquarian treasures they had lately offered readers. The house took its name from Edward Seymour, Duke of Somerset.

The Mirror was a weekly miscellany, mixing pictures, history, and light reading for a popular audience. Each number packed short pieces and engravings into a cheap sheet. This volume preserves that format intact: a window onto what ordinary London readers browsed in 1829, from old buildings to anecdotes, before the age of the illustrated newspaper.
34150-wilson-s-tales-of-the-borders-and-:
Alexander Leighton revised this thirteenth volume of Wilson's Tales of the Borders and of Scotland, published in London and Newcastle in 1885 by Walter Scott, with a glossary. Tales run from The Unknown by John Mackay Wilson and The Trials of Menie Dempster by Leighton to the Professor's Tales, the natural history of idiots, and the Floshend Inn.

Lottery Hall, the dominie and the souter, the dominie's courtship, the souter's wedding, Roseallan's daughter, the two sailors, and the Dream complete the set. The opening tale finds a young Spanish woman in faded silk, faint and weary, bearing an infant on the road to Rothbury in 1785. The volume offers Border tales of mystery and life.
34815-jane-s-all-the-world-s-aircraft-19:
Fred T. Jane set in order this book of all the craft of the air of the world, first put out in 1913. The text here is a reprint of 1969 of that year's book. It came out each year, as its first leaf states. In its first days it was known by a name of ships of the air, not craft. The book thus stands at the dawn of flight, when the ship of the air and the plane shared the sky.

The aim of the book is a full roll of the craft of the air of all lands for its year. Such a roll, made new each year, let a man of the trade or of the press know what flew and where. The reprint of 1969 kept the book of 1913 in the dress of its day, ads and all.
3563-memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volum:
This thirteenth volume of Bourrienne's memoirs covers Napoleon in 1815, the year of his return from Elba and his final fall. Bourrienne writes as a former secretary watching the Hundred Days unfold: the emperor's landing, his march to Paris, and the gathering of armies against him. The Hundred Days read here as a rush of hope followed by a second, harder reckoning.

The narrative carries the excitement of a comeback and the speed of its collapse. Old loyalties revive for a season, then break again at Waterloo and after. Bourrienne gives the view of a man who knew Napoleon's court in its prime and now saw it dissolve. The volume suits readers reaching the end of the long story.
3593-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volum:
This thirteenth volume of Montaigne's Essays gathers chapters thirty two through thirty seven of Book Two. They include a defense of Seneca and Plutarch and the story of Spurina. Other essays treat war according to Julius Caesar, three good women, the most excellent men, and the resemblance of children to their fathers. Montaigne opens by noting how much help Seneca and Plutarch lent to his age and to his book.

The essays show Montaigne reading the ancients as friends and guides, not as distant authorities. He defends them against critics, borrows their tactics, and compares their lives with his own family. The volume suits readers who enjoy classical learning worn lightly, with personal comment at every turn.
3803-file-no-113:
Emile Gaboriau opens this early detective novel with a Paris bank robbery that fills the evening papers. On a February morning in 1866, thieves force an impregnable safe at the bank of Andre Fauvel in the Rue de Provence and take three hundred and fifty thousand francs in notes. Police arrest a clerk, known in the papers only by initials, and the town talks of nothing else for four days.

Then the case deepens, as the papers prove wrong or at least careless, and private passions surface behind the crime. A billiard room quarrel, where Gaston confronts Jules Lazet over a remark about a nobleman's daughter, shows how honor and money tangle. Readers who like the roots of detective fiction will find a tale where the mystery matters less than the human wreckage around it.
47832-perpetua-a-tale-of-nimes-in-a-d-21:
Perpetua, a tale of Nîmes in the year 213, by the Reverend S Baring-Gould, was published by E P Dutton and Company of New York in 1897. The scene is Nemausus, modern Nîmes, in the province of Gallia Narbonensis. Twenty four chapters carry the tale from the Kalends of March to a close named Credo.

The first chapter paints the city on a bright spring day: anemones in bloom, roses budding, tulips in the vineyards, and a cool air from the snowy Alps. A rock amphitheatre and a spring of bottle green water fix the ground. Aemilius, Baudillas the deacon, and the boatmen of the lagoons enter the cast. A manumission, the basilica, and the arena mark the road to a martyr's end.
49341-seattle-car-foundry-company-catalo:
A Seattle car works put out its third trade book in December 1913. The book sells log cars and trucks for the great north woods. A record log fronts it as proof of the cars' strength. That log was cut by the Sunset Timber Company of Raymond. It stood thirteen feet six at the butt in full span.

Nine feet two at the top and twenty-eight feet long, it ran. One car bore that vast load with ease, the book crows. Frame trucks and joined trucks fill the plates in turn. Weights, wood kinds, and prices guide the mill buyer well. Rail and camp men were the book's true guests in trade. Iron and pine rule it.
49422-a-select-collection-of-old-english:
Volume thirteen of A Select Collection of Old English Plays was edited by Carew Hazlitt. Robert Dodsley first published the set in 1744. This fourth edition sorts the plays in date order. Notes from all earlier commentators are kept, with new notes added. The volume opens with A Match at Midnight, a comedy of 1633. It was acted by the Children of the Revels. Its cast list names Sir Marmaduke Many-Minds and a usurer called Bloodhound.

Tim Bloodhound, the usurer's son, opens the play with Sim the clown. Tim runs his father's petty pawns and jokes about their craft. News comes that a rich widow will soon be their stepmother. The comedy promises tricks, matches, and London low life in the old stage manner.
50839-the-chronicles-of-enguerrand-de-mo:
The Chronicles of Enguerrand de Monstrelet open a thirteen volume history of France. Thomas Johnes turned the French work into English prose. Longman and partners issued volume one in London in eighteen hundred ten. The tale runs from fourteen hundred to fourteen hundred sixty seven.

Monstrelet takes up the thread where Froissart laid it down. Cruel civil wars of Orleans and Burgundy fill his first span. Paris and Normandy in English hands, then freed, mark the mid years. Johnes gives the set to John, Duke of Bedford, his friend and lord. That duke’s namesake, regent of France, strides through the tale. Charles the Well-Beloved, crowned at Rheims, heads the first part. A Spanish squire’s challenge to England’s knights stands early here. Great pardons at Rome and a Breton duke’s death fill those pages.
52607-the-chronicles-of-enguerrand-de-mo:
Chronicles of Enguerrand de Monstrelet, volume two of thirteen, is a history of France in the fifteenth century. Thomas Johnes translated the chronicles for this London edition of 1810. Longman and partners printed the set in Paternoster Row that year. The full title promises an account of the cruel civil wars between the houses of Orleans and Burgundy.

The chronicle begins at the year 1400, where that of Froissart finishes, by its title page. It ends at the year 1467, and is continued by others to the year 1516 in the same account. Monstrelet, a Burgundian official, watched the age of Joan of Arc from the other side of the war. Johnes translation, in thirteen volumes, put his day by day record into English hands, where it remains a prime source for the last act of the Hundred Years War.
5287-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
La Fontaine's thirteenth volume opens with St Julian's Prayer, a tale that begins by laughing at charms, philters, secret spells, and prayers. So many place all their cares in such things. The author admits he never believed in them, yet notes that with the fair such words are viewed as sacred virtues, working wonders in love.

Saint Julian's prayer, repeated by Reynold D'Ast, produces a benefit classed as good fortune. The tale that follows turns prayer into comic proof. Readers get a volume in which La Fontaine mocks superstition while granting it a storyteller's power, in verse that is sly rather than scolding.
52911-the-chronicles-of-enguerrand-de-mo:
The Chronicles of Enguerrand de Monstrelet, in Thomas Johnes's translation, fill thirteen volumes; the third was printed in London in 1810. The title promises an account of the cruel civil wars between the houses of Orleans and Burgundy. It covers the English possession of Paris and Normandy, and their expulsion thence. The chronicle begins in 1400, where Froissart leaves off, and ends in 1467, continued by others to 1516.

Contents of this volume open with French captains sent to harass the Armagnacs on the frontiers. Ambassadors go to England, and the duke of Bourbon's children win their liberty. Duke Louis of Bavaria is driven from Paris by the Parisians, and his people robbed. Sieges at Domfront and Bellesme, and the battle of Saint Remy du Plain, fill the year-by-year record of the Hundred Years War.
57582-my-queen-a-weekly-journal-for-youn:
My Queen was a weekly tale sheet for young women at five cents. Issue three is dated October 13, 1900, from Street and Smith. Grace Shirley's tale leads the issue in full. Its name is Marion Marlowe's True Heart, or How a Daughter Forgave. A year's run of the sheet cost two and a half dollars.

The tale starts in a farm house cook room on a cold, grey day. Marion's heart and her power to forgive drive the plot. Home love and past wrongs press on her choice. Such weeklies gave young maids a whole tale each week. Cheap print, warm hearts, and clean ends rule the form.
58083-the-chronicles-of-enguerrand-de-mo:
The Chronicles of Enguerrand de Monstrelet, in Thomas Johnes's translation, run to thirteen volumes printed in London in 1810. The history begins in 1400, where Froissart leaves off, and ends in 1467, continued by others to 1516. This seventh volume carries the wars between the houses of Orleans and Burgundy and the English hold on Paris and Normandy.

Its chapters tell how captains of Sir John de Luxembourg surprised the castle of St Martin and were all taken and slain. Poton de Saintrailles makes his attempts, the lord de Barbasan besieges Anglure, and the Maid of Orleans is condemned and burnt at Rouen. The general council continues at Basil, and the duke of Bar invades Vaudemont. Monstrelet is a chief source for the last phase of the Hundred Years' War.
5915-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
An interpolated novel anchors this Don Quixote portion, chapters thirty-three through forty. Chapter thirty-three relates the novel of the ill-advised curiosity, set in Florence among two gentlemen of wealth, Anselmo and Lothario, friends so great that all called them by a special distinction. Chapter thirty-four continues that novel, chapter thirty-five stages a heroic battle at the inn, and chapter thirty-six adds more curious incidents there.

Chapter thirty-seven continues the story of the famous Princess Micomicona, chapter thirty-eight gives Quixote's curious discourse on arms and letters, and chapters thirty-nine and forty let the captive relate his life. Readers get Cervantes's nesting tales at full stretch, as inn guests tell stories within the story. The part suits readers who enjoy the novel's digressions as much as its knight.
63750-the-story-tellers-magazine-vol-i-n:
The Story Tellers' Magazine, volume one, number two, was published in New York in July 1913 and edited by Richard Wyche. The issue begins a King Arthur series in twelve numbers, opening with Merlin and His Prophecies. It also carries pieces on Beethoven's Moonlight Sonata, Endymion, Saint Christopher, and England's first poet.

Wyche led the national storytelling movement, and the magazine served teachers, librarians, and camp leaders. Articles discuss the image in storytelling, the Uncle Remus stories in the curriculum, storytelling for Camp Fire Girls, and the play spirit in America. Advertisements for Underwood typewriters share the pages. The number preserves a moment when storytelling was a trained profession with its own methods, journals, and summer schools.
63913-the-chronicles-of-enguerrand-de-mo:
The Chronicles of Enguerrand de Monstrelet, volume eight of thirteen, is part of Thomas Johnes's English translation, published in London in 1810. Monstrelet's history begins in the year 1400, where Froissart's finishes, and runs to 1467, continued by others to 1516. Its title promises the cruel civil wars between the houses of Orleans and Burgundy. It also covers the English possession of Paris and Normandy and their expulsion thence.

The eighth volume opens with a Scottish crime. James the First, king of Scotland, is murdered in his bedchamber during the night by his uncle, the earl of Athol. The next chapter brings La Hire, Poton, and other French captains near to taking Rouen, before the English surprise and defeat them. The town of Bruges then rebels against its lord, with great conflict and slaughter.
64948-the-chronicles-of-enguerrand-de-mo:
The Chronicles of Enguerrand de Monstrelet, here in Volume Six of thirteen, is a French medieval history in Thomas Johnes's English translation. The London edition came out in 1810. The chronicle takes up where Froissart ends, in the year 1400, and runs to 1467, with later hands adding years beyond.

Its stated ground is the cruel civil war between the houses of Orleans and Burgundy. It also covers the English hold on Paris and Normandy, and their expulsion at last. The contents of this volume open with the death of Charles the Sixth at the Hôtel Saint Paul and his burial at Saint Denis. A treaty of Meulan follows, and news of the king's death spreads. Monstrelet wrote as a man of his time, and his annals remain a prime French witness to the Hundred Years' War.
65396-the-chronicles-of-enguerrand-de-mo:
The Chronicles of Enguerrand de Monstrelet, volume ten of thirteen, in English by Thomas Johnes, was printed in London in 1810. The chronicle runs from the year 1400, where Froissart leaves off, to 1467, and is continued by others to 1516.

The title promises an account of the cruel civil wars between the houses of Orleans and Burgundy. It adds the holding of Paris and Normandy by the English, and their expulsion thence. Chapter one of this volume treats the king of France countermanding his summons to the duke of Burgundy. The king forbids him to come to Montargis and orders him to send three or four of his nobles to consult with the peers. History fans get France civil war from a near witness, in one middle volume.
65943-a-soldier-s-life-on-the-western-fr:
A Soldier's Life on the Western Frontier in 1813 is a pamphlet of soldiers' letters from the War of 1812. The staff of the Public Library of Fort Wayne and Allen County prepared it in 1953, as one of a historical series. The letters come from the Ohio frontier, where the war in the west dragged on. One is dated at Zanesville, Ohio, on March 28, 1813.

Its writer had last written from Upper Sandusky, sure that something of importance would soon happen. Unfortunately, he says, the war in this quarter is protracted far beyond what he contemplated. Even the best informed people in the army had expected a quicker end. His battalion joins the Petersburg Volunteers and two companies from Pittsburgh, with some three hundred and fifty regulars. This one shows the waiting, marching, and hoping of 1813.
66126-travels-in-nova-scotia-in-the-year:
Travels in Nova Scotia in the Year Nineteen Thirteen is Charles Gilbert Hine's mock-heroic record of a walking and sailing trip along the province's south coast. Issued as Hine's Annual for 1913, the book promises a full, free, and authentic record of perilous adventures and marvelous escapes. Its weather deity is His Most Ungracious Majesty, Jupiter Pluvius the First, whose rain rules the trip.

Hine sailed from Boston on the twelfth of October 1913 aboard the Governor Cobb. His contents promise the manners and customs of the people and the stories and legends of the southern shore, with short excursions into the country's history. Port Latour, Burchtown, Shelburne, and the road to East Jordan anchor the route. The verses of Masefield, hungry for the sea's edge, stand for the book's motto.
70514-the-survey-volume-30-number-7-may-:
The May 17, 1913 issue of the Survey, a journal of social welfare. Its opening feature, under the Common Welfare heading, covers the Pittsburgh school strike. Pittsburgh school affairs stand under a cloud, the editors write. Interested parties stir that cloud for their own ends. One faction fights Senator Oliver politically. Another wants the old ward-board system back.

Charges against Superintendent Heeter came from a housemaid. A court trial acquitted him. A citizens' committee still studies his fitness. Meanwhile the new central board spent heavily on reform. It turned dirty fire-trap schools into decent buildings. The editors argue that most citizens see the improvement since 1911. Scare headlines and children's parades cannot hide it. The issue preserves Progressive Era school politics in detail.
71519-the-survey-volume-30-number-3-apr-:
The Survey filled Volume Thirty, Number Three, dated April 19, 1913, with reform news. The lead piece treats the strike of the Jersey silk workers at Paterson. For seven weeks, 27,000 mill and dye house workers had struck, the piece states. Broad silk weavers rose first against the three and four loom plan.

Ribbon weavers and dye men joined, seeking an eight-hour day and $12 a week. Dye men had worked twelve-hour shifts in damp, hot, foul air. The Industrial Workers of the World led the strike, the report notes. Reform readers gain close, grave facts from a famed labor fight.
72417-the-survey-volume-30-number-2-apr-:
The Survey for April 12, 1913 is one weekly issue of a journal of social work, volume thirty, number two. Its opening section, The Common Welfare, leads with the wake of a great flood. By the end of the past week, Red Cross workers in the flood district reported the relief work well in hand. Out of chaos a careful survey was showing the true size of the rebuilding problem.

That problem does not shrink, the report warns, even as the list of the dead grows shorter in later counts. Large sums will be needed, it is clear. Every message from Red Cross agents stresses the urgent need to keep raising funds, and to redouble the effort. A despatch from the national director at Columbus, just back from a tour of flooded towns with the governor, gives the fullest summary yet.
72425-the-survey-volume-30-number-24-sep:
The hosted text is one weekly issue of The Survey, a magazine of social welfare work, volume 30, number 24, dated September 13, 1913. The issue is headed The Common Welfare. Its lead piece joins a factory fire to a new safety rule.

After the fire at Binghamton, the New York labour board held hearings on the closing in of factory stairs. With the backing of the attorney-general, the board has now set rules. In factories under five floors, the stairs used as exits must be walled in with fire-resisting walls from the basement up. The doors in those walls must shut of themselves. The issue prints the rules in full, as a matter of life and death for factory hands.
73160-the-chronicles-of-enguerrand-de-mo:
Volume nine of The Chronicles of Enguerrand de Monstrelet tells France’s wars in the fourteen hundreds. Thomas Johnes turned the chronicle into English in thirteen volumes. Longman and partners issued the set in London in eighteen hundred ten. Monstrelet takes up the tale where Froissart laid it down.

His span runs from fourteen hundred to fourteen hundred sixty seven. Civil war of Orleans and Burgundy fills the great tale. England’s hold on Paris and Normandy, then its loss, stands here. Chapter one shows the French king call a truce void. Verneuil falls to a miller whom an Englishman had beaten. The Count de Saint Pol takes Nogent and Pont-Audemer next. Dunois wins town after town for the crown in this volume. Saint Lo, Carentan, and Argentan all yield in their turn.
73899-the-survey-volume-30-number-4-apr-:
The Survey, volume thirty, number four, is the issue of April twenty sixth, nineteen thirteen. Survey Associates published the social welfare weekly from East Twenty Second Street, New York. Its common welfare section opens with relief work after the great Ohio floods. Dayton, where the river burst its levees, is the centre of the report.

The aim, the piece says, is full rebuilding of lives, not mere handouts of supplies. Red Cross gifts at Washington reached one million seven hundred fifty thousand dollars. Ohio's own gifts passed six hundred thousand, spent through the Red Cross too. A citizens' committee under John Patterson channels the money in Dayton itself. Four thousand families were registered in the first week after the waters fell. Teachers and local committees help the trained relief agents in the work.
73922-the-survey-volume-30-number-5-may-:
The Survey, a journal of social work, devoted its number of May 3, 1913, volume thirty, number five, to the common welfare. Its lead article reports the spread of the survey idea across America. A hundred and more cities in thirty-four states, it says, have asked for surveys or advice since the Department of Surveys and Exhibits of the Russell Sage Foundation organized the previous October.

The article explains what a community survey is: a democratic effort to advance the well-being of the whole community. It is shouldered by representatives of all its interests, with chambers of commerce now backing the work. Quick pathfinder surveys diagnose a city's condition and point to the lines a longer study should follow. Timing, financing, and trained leadership decide which requests the department answers, and half-ready cities are told to wait.
73983-the-chronicles-of-enguerrand-de-mo:
Enguerrand de Monstrelet chronicles, here volume five of thirteen, were translated by Thomas Johnes and printed in London in eighteen ten. The chronicles run from the year fourteen hundred, where Froissart finishes, to fourteen sixty seven, and are continued by others to fifteen sixteen. Volume five treats the cruel civil wars between Orleans and Burgundy. English possession of Paris and Normandy fills much of the tale.

Chapter one brings Cardinals Orsini and San Marco to France to appease quarrels of princes of the blood royal. A peace made at Montereau is not kept. Chapter two treats King Henry of England conquering towns in Normandy. Chapter three treats Paris taken by the Duke of Burgundy, with Parisians turning to his party. Later chapters show towns and castles submitting to Burgundy. Historians get a near contemporary French record of the Hundred Years War.
75163-the-american-red-cross-magazine-vo:
The American Red Cross Magazine, volume eight number two, is the April print of that aid guilds sheet for nineteen thirteen. It was sent from the guilds chief house in the chief town. Its front vow is to aid in the bar and ease of mans pain in peace and in war. A list of the guilds chiefs stands at the front. The head of the land stands at its head.

Parts give bright views of the guilds work in a war land of the east. Its men fought a gut ill there and fed the cast out. Work in a south land, a blast in a port town, and works and aid in the far east take heads. Aid for a starved land, the red seal drive, first aid drills, and the nurse corps fill the list.
7598-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Part thirteen of The Caxtons turns toward departure, as Pisistratus prepares to leave home. The call cannot be refused: an old sea-roving strain in his blood will have its way, and he must be a soldier or a rover. His family will mourn and miss him, but no chain holds young eagles to the eyrie. Lytton makes the old theme of leaving home fresh again, through a son who must argue his freedom politely.

The argument itself is managed with love and cunning. The young man seeks to insinuate his project into favor with his unsuspecting family through innocent arts. Saint Chrysostom on the priesthood supplies his cover, defending deceit for a good purpose by scriptural examples and calling it good management instead. The part thus joins a son's ambition to a scholar's excuse, and both to affection.
76168-room-13:
Room 13 is a crime novel by Edgar Wallace, published in London in 1924 and dedicated to his friend Sir Emsley Carr. The story opens inside a prison, under a stone archway carved with the Latin words Parcere Subjectis, spare the vanquished.

Johnny Gray, who jokes that the motto means Parky Subjects, pulls a heavy hand-cart up the slope each day beside Lal Morgon and watches the gate-warder's key turn. Wallace lingers on the exercise yard, the church, the raised warders' benches, and the graveyard of released lifers. Thirty-three chapters follow. Wallace wrote thrillers at great speed, and this one starts where many of his criminals end, with a man counting the days inside.
813:
813 is a 1910 Arsène Lupin novel by Maurice Leblanc, in which the gentleman thief must clear his own name. When one of Lupin's victims is found dead in a way that points to him, he insists on leading the police search for the real murderer himself. The hunt that follows is one of the strangest in the series.

The mystery turns on a package of letters once written to Bismarck and on a clock where the number 813 carries a hidden meaning. A reigning emperor is drawn into several journeys in disguise as the case widens. Murders multiply, and Lupin works both sides of the law to reach the truth first.
arxiv-2412-00013:
Yi-Qiao Xu and Bing-Zhao Li introduce a new signal transform that works on Clifford-valued functions, in a 2024 mathematics paper. Time-frequency tools like the Fourier and wavelet transforms struggle with high-dimensional signals that carry direction. Their linear canonical Stockwell transform adds angular, scalable, and localized windows, giving more directional freedom at each scale.

Using operator theory, the authors work out the transform's core properties: an inner product relation, a reconstruction formula that rebuilds the signal, and an interval theorem. Worked examples confirm the formulas behave as claimed. The paper positions the transform as a sharper lens for multi-scale analysis of multi-dimensional signals in engineering and physics.
arxiv-2412-00113:
Kart-Leong Lim, Rahul Dutta, and Mihai Rotaru predict capacitor fields with a boundary aware network in a 2024 paper. Mesh based solvers must rerun from scratch whenever boundary conditions change, and physics informed networks must retrain. Both habits waste time in design loops where boundaries shift often.

Their end to end model takes boundary changes as input, so one trained network answers across conditions. The test problem is a long air filled capacitor. Against a plain neural network and a physics informed one, the new method won clearly under shifting boundaries. It also kept full skill as a forward model. The authors aim the approach at fast electrostatic design studies.
arxiv-2412-00413:
Satoshi Masaki studies in 2024 a system of two linked wave equations of a classic kind used in optics and quantum physics. He asks how small waves behave over very long times. Past work leaned on a special condition that gave the system a guard quantity, a mass like total that holds the waves in check.

Masaki finds a new class of systems that break that condition and so lack the guard quantity. Even so, he proves that small solutions exist for all time. He also shows what shape they settle into in the long run, described by a simpler system of ordinary equations. A key tool is a four fold guard quantity that survives in this class. The result widens the range of wave systems whose long fate is understood.
arxiv-2412-00613:
Xunye Tian and co-authors present a 2024 paper on a basic test in data work. The test asks whether two sets of data come from the same source. Good tests depend on finding a clear way to show the data. Past work split data into a training set and a test set, and learned that view from training data alone.

The authors show that the full set can shape the view, as long as set labels stay hidden. Their method first learns the shape of the data, then trains a model to stress the gaps. In tests, the method beat well-known rivals. It used both the data shape and the group gaps.
arxiv-2412-00913:
Thomas Li and Francisco Barreras present Garden City, a synthetic dataset for mobility research, in this 2024 paper. GPS traces of human movement are widely used, but commercial sets are sparse and error prone. Processing steps can add further errors. With no ground truth, checking those steps is hard.

Their simulator creates fake but realistic travel traces with known true paths. It copies the flaws that cause trouble in real commercial data. Researchers can run their cleaning algorithms on the fake data and compare output with truth. That gives an intermediate check before trusting results on real data. Code is open source, with tutorial notebooks and sample datasets. The sandbox aims to raise the standard of mobility data work.
arxiv-2412-01113:
Keito Kudo and seven co-authors ask when a language model settles on an answer during step by step math reasoning. Some fear the written steps are a story made after a snap call. They trace inner signals while models work through controlled sums.

Models had not fixed the answer when the prompt landed. They built sub answers on the fly as each step was written. Those steps thus push the final answer in a real causal way. The chain can be read as a true trace of inner work, at least for this math kind.
arxiv-2412-01313:
Ofer Aharony, Netanel Barel, and Tal Sheaffer study in 2024 the strings that form inside a class of confining theories. In such theories, particles are bound by a flux string, and a theory of the string itself describes its wobbles. In two space dimensions plus time, some theories have a far lighter mass scale than the string's tension, which changes the physics.

Working at low energies with plain perturbative tools, the authors argue the string's width is set by that light scale, whatever its length, short of extreme cases. They also compute the ground energy of a looped string and how its sound-like waves scatter, at leading order.
arxiv-2412-01713:
Constant Roux, Come Perrot, and Olivier Stasse present a controller for the biped robot Bolt, in a 2024 paper. Their approach pairs a whole-body model predictive controller with a footstep sequencer that plans where each foot lands in real time. The pairing aims at robust walking on two legs. Tests run in simulation rather than on the physical robot.

In those tests, the robot tracks commanded speeds well. It also recovers from pushes and from slips underfoot. On top of the control work, the team give a theoretical sensitivity analysis of the footstep sequencing problem. That analysis explains how sensitive the plan is to its inputs. It deepens the grasp of why the controller behaves as it does.
arxiv-2412-02213:
Liang-Wen Ji and co-authors chart how doping changes a diamond-lattice magnet, in this 2024 paper. The parent material is a sulfur-based spinel whose cobalt atoms sit on a diamond sublattice and order antiferromagnetically at a fairly high temperature. It also has a narrow energy gap, making it a mild insulator. Swapping nickel in for cobalt, step by step, lets the team watch both magnetism and conduction evolve on one map.

At about a third nickel, the material flips from insulator to metal. The magnetic order temperature falls steadily and vanishes near full replacement. In the metallic range a spin-glass-like freezing appears at low temperatures. The finished phase diagram ties these regimes together, giving later studies a reference for this family of frustrated magnets.
arxiv-2412-02313:
Jiamian Hu, Yuanyuan Hong, Yihua Chen, He Wang, and Moriaki Yasuhara release a messy real-world data set for robust machine learning in a paper from 2024. The images show ostracods, tiny crustaceans sorted by genus and species. Over seventy-one thousand expert-labeled specimens include about five and a half percent likely errors. Noise comes in open-set and invented-class flavors, and the classes are wildly imbalanced.

Standard robust methods failed to beat plain training on the raw labels. Simple cross-validation ensembles found bad labels better than dedicated detectors. The authors argue fine-grained, imbalanced noise is an unsolved regime. The data set and protocols are public to push new methods. Taxonomy curation is the motivating application.
arxiv-2412-02613:
Gabriele Giudici and co-authors test whether people can feel the stiffness of far-off objects through a robot hand, in a 2024 study. Remote handling matters in health care and in harsh places where people cannot go. Cameras show shape and place, but they say little about how soft an object is. The team used gloves fitted with motors, plus robot fingertips that can sense touch.

Volunteers squeezed soft objects by remote control, with no view of the objects at all. One feedback mode sent back only the contact force. A second mode also sent back how far the hand had closed. People could tell soft from firm objects by feel alone in both modes. Adding the closing signal seemed to help when two objects felt close in stiffness, the authors report.
arxiv-2412-02813:
Madisen Holbrook and co-authors image the inner structure of a layered crystal in a 2024 paper. The material, known by the short name WSe2, is a semiconductor made of thin sheets. Its band structure, which sets how electrons move, has traits tied to where the center of each electron cloud sits inside the crystal cell.

Using a scanning tunneling microscope, the team mapped where the electron density peaks at two key points in the band structure. At one point the peak sits between atoms, and at the other it sits on the atoms. That split shows the material is a special kind of insulator whose state cannot be smoothly changed into a plain one. The method offers a direct way to read band traits from real-space images.
arxiv-2412-02913: Boudabra, Kroumi, and Smii study whether one known solution to a chance embedding problem stays bounded in twenty twenty-four. The Skorokhod problem asks for a stopping rule that makes a wandering path end with a given spread of values. Gross gave a solution for the flat, two dimensional case. The team asks if that solution can run off without bound. They show it stays bounded when the target spread meets some mild rules. The short note settles the size question for this classic construction under those stated conditions.
arxiv-2412-03113:
Rei Murakami settles cases of a geometric equation under a symmetry assumption in a 2024 paper. The complex Hessian quotient equation is a hard partial differential equation from complex geometry. A conjecture tied whether it can be solved to a numerical condition on the data behind it.

Working under Calabi symmetry, Murakami proves that it does ensure a solution exists. A new conjecture is then proposed about special representative functions in a given cohomology class, and confirmed under the same symmetry or when the class is semiample. This cuts a hard problem down to one where sharp criteria can be proved, marking ground for the general case. The proof holds in this case alone, and the full case stays open.
arxiv-2412-03213:
Guangda Liu and four co-authors compress the memory cache of language models without throwing context away. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Long documents swell the key-value cache and slow replies. Older compression drops tokens for good, losing facts. Page-based recall keeps tokens but groups them by position alone. Meaning-based grouping is the missing piece.

Their ClusterKV groups tokens into semantic clusters. Recall then fetches whole clusters when later steps need them. Algorithms and systems work make the clustering fast enough to use. Accuracy holds up better than with eviction or page schemes. Long-document question answering is a prime use case. Complex reasoning over long context also benefits. The cache shrinks while the past stays reachable.
arxiv-2412-03313:
Chifan Leung studies symmetry groups attached to iterated polynomial maps, in this 2024 math paper. Repeating a map builds a tree of preimages, and the Galois group that shuffles that tree is called arboreal. Whether such groups can be non-abelian, meaning order matters in their operations, is a subtle question in dynamics and number theory.

Leung proves a non-abelian result for certain maps whose Julia set, the chaotic boundary of the iteration, is not real at an archimedean place. The paper also asks which polynomials over the real numbers have a fully real Julia set. Finally, it shows that some Lattès maps, built from doubling points on an elliptic curve, have non-abelian arboreal Galois groups. The results serve readers in arithmetic dynamics.
arxiv-2412-03413:
Andrea Asperti leads a team of nine on this paper from two thousand twenty-four. It rebuilds sea surface temperatures where clouds blind the satellites, with deep learning in place of the old interpolation math.

The team works from night images of the MODIS Aqua sensor. A U-net fills the clouded patches while leaving the clear reads untouched. That care for the known values sets the method apart. Its best build halves the root mean square error of the standard gap-filling products. Such maps feed weather and climate work, where a hole over a warm current can skew the whole read. The study is a clean case of a learned fill that beats the classic craft.
arxiv-2412-03513:
Kuei-Chun Kao teaches a famous image-text model new depth by distilling knowledge from a large language model into it. CLIP aligns pictures and captions, but its encoders skim shallow features from both. His 2024 paper presents Knowledge-CLIP, trained with a distillation scheme based on Llama 2. Three objectives work together: the text encoder is trained to mirror the teacher's richer embeddings; concept learning assigns soft concept labels; and contrastive learning keeps the image-text alignment sharp.

A teacher that has read the world can lend its concepts to a model that only saw captions. Soft concepts, graded rather than binary, carry nuance a label list cannot. The author works solo on a widely used foundation model. Gains here ripple into every search, tagging, and zero-shot tool built on CLIP. The paper is a recipe for upgrading a standard part.
arxiv-2412-03613:
Safaa Habib and Romain Veltz study waves that travel through networks of nerve cells held in check by inhibition, in a 2024 mathematics paper. Neural field equations describe how activity spreads across a sheet of brain tissue. Waves in such systems can speed up, slow down, or break into patterned pulses. The authors build both proofs and computer tools for a special class of waves whose shape is modulated as they move.

First, they prove that these traveling waves hold up under small disturbances, and that a small set of nearby behaviours captures how they can change form. They also work out the waves' spectral properties and give schemes to compute them. Applied to a model where inhibition stabilises the network, the methods reveal folding, rhythm-born, and combined change points in the pulses. The pulses also snake and wind as one timing dial turns.
arxiv-2412-04013:
Miklós Rásonyi presents a Fourier based method from 2024 for bounding how fast distributions converge in total variation distance. Total variation distance gives a strong way to judge closeness between probability laws. Rates in that distance are often hard to obtain from weaker forms of convergence alone.

The method links total variation rates to metrics tied to weak convergence. Three areas show how the bounds can be used in practice. They are Malliavin calculus, normal approximation, and stochastic dynamical systems with memory. Readers in probability get a compact tool with clear use cases, rather than a long catalogue of cases. The short format keeps the focus on the method itself and where it applies.
arxiv-2412-04113:
Erlend Storvik and Carina Bringedal take a mixed model to its sharp edge in a 2024 paper. Their model joins a phase field, which paints two stuffs and the wall between them, with the laws of flow in porous rock. As the wall thins to a line, what laws survive?

By matched layer sums, each side keeps its own flow laws with its own stuff marks. Shift and pore push run smooth across the line, while fluid share and stress must balance there. The wall pull bends with its curve, fed by flow and stretch. A test run shows the wall crawl as the sums foretell. Rock teams gain the sharp form of a soft model.
arxiv-2412-04213:
Shuhao Ma and co-authors predict muscle forces from electrical signals on the skin, without needing labeled training data. Fast computer models of muscle would help the study of human movement, but physics-based models run slowly, and data-driven models need labels that are hard to collect. The team's method embeds physics inside a neural network to guide learning.

A forward dynamics model based on the classic Hill muscle model sits inside the network as an added loss term. That term steers the network toward outputs the physics allows. Tests on the wrist joints of six healthy subjects showed force predictions as accurate as, or better than, methods trained with labels. The system also recovered each person's muscle-tendon parameters accurately. The authors present the approach as a way to get labeled-data quality from unlabeled signals, with personalization built in.
arxiv-2412-04513:
Faizuddin Ahmed, Ahmad Al-Badawi, İzzet Sakallı, and Abdelmalek Bouzenada ring BTZ black holes inside two modified gravity theories. They listen to the quasinormal modes. Their 2024 paper compares f(R) gravity and Ricci-Inverse gravity. The two are cousins. They share spacetime shapes but differ in their cosmological constants. The authors derive wave equations for massless holes and for spinning ones. They trace the effective potential as mass and theory parameters change.

Heavier holes and larger values raise that barrier. That holds perturbations in more tightly and shifts stability. A generalized uncertainty principle then corrects the Hawking radiation picture. Its marks may show in mode decay rates. The survey ends with null and timelike geodesics. Wave data may one day grade these claims.
arxiv-2412-04713:
Yuichiro Kitajima examined in 2024 a claimed trade-off between two strange quantum effects. One test probes whether distant particles share linked fates; another probes whether a measurement's context changes its result. A received idea, the monogamy relation, held that a state could break at most one of the two test bounds.

Kitajima reviews the surprise result that breaks that idea: with the right measurement choices, one state can break both bounds at once. Many such setups turn out to exist. The link between the two effects is richer than the old trade-off allowed, and foundations of quantum theory must make room for it.
arxiv-2412-04813:
Lihao Zhang, Xiaoyu Wang, Qi Li, Haibo Xie, Liangliang Zhang, Lei Zhang, Jie Pan, Yingchun Cheng, and Zhe Wang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It studies CrOCl, a thin layered crystal whose atoms line up in stripes and act as an antiferromagnet.

The team built tunnel junctions from one and two layers of the crystal and tracked how their resistance shifts in a magnetic field. At low voltage the resistance change is positive once the crystal flips phase, but at higher voltage it turns negative. The authors tie the flip to extra electric dipoles in the first phase, backed by theory. The result points to a way to steer spin devices with voltage, saving energy.
arxiv-2412-05013:
Thomas Sievers and Nele Russwinkel reported a project in 2024 on a social robot for public offices. The project, run with Kiel City Council, asked if a human-like robot could give information in a town hall. It also asked what skills such a robot would need when it meets the public.

The team built a test use case, listed the skills the robot should have, and ran early trials. Users liked the robot far more than a tablet with a web page. Its speech, gestures, and shifts in posture helped. The authors also propose linking the robot to a model of human thought to improve its dialogue.
arxiv-2412-05113:
Jozef Strečka, Fadwa Benabdallah, and Mohammed Daoud show how a magnetic field can turn a pair of atomic chains into a good channel for quantum teleportation. The channel is built from two spin chains, each made of linked trimers, and the cargo is an entangled two-qubit state sent through two paired links. The authors check the transfer by comparing the entanglement going in and coming out, and by computing teleportation fidelity across temperatures and field strengths.

A moderate field sharply improves performance. The field drives the chains from an antiferromagnetic phase into a ferrimagnetic one, which supports a fully entangled channel. The authors name a real copper compound with this chain structure as an experimental candidate, estimating the scheme could work at temperatures up to 40 kelvin and fields up to 80 tesla.
arxiv-2412-05313:
Ahmed Jaafar and co-authors set a test for home robots that must learn long tasks from few tries in a 2024 paper. A useful home robot must fetch and carry across rooms and floors, yet most learned ways drink data by the tank.

Their test, named with the Greek letter lambda, scores how well a model learns from a lean set of runs. People drove the robot through near six hundred tasks by hand, which keeps the runs true to life and fit to replay. On the test, end-to-end learning did poorly even with a head start of past training. A split way, which pairs big base models with a planner, did far better on far less data. The team posts the set for the field.
arxiv-2412-05713:
Anthony Pietz, Karin John, and Uwe Thiele model why bacterial films spread more slowly on soft surfaces than on stiff ones. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Bacteria settle on surfaces and grow into dense colonies wrapped in a self-made polymer skin. On soft gels, that spread can stall.

Their model treats the film as a thin fluid layer that drinks in solvent by osmosis. Growth of new cell mass feeds the spread. On a soft base, the surface dents under the film, and that dent cuts the inflow at the film's edge. With less inflow, the edge creeps or stops, based on how fast mass grows. Simple scaling rules link softness to the push that drives the drink-in. The model matches the broad range of spread speeds seen on gels in the lab.
arxiv-2412-06013:
Baturin and six co-authors model how hydrogen ionizes inside the Sun, a process that sets key properties of solar plasma. Hydrogen is the Sun's main ingredient, and its ionization digs a deep, lopsided dip in a basic sound-speed related quantity across almost the whole convection zone. The tricky part is counting hydrogen's excited states, which depends on a partition function with a cut-off tail that must come from quantum mechanics in plasma.

The team ran their solar simulation with two rival formulas for that function, one older and one newer. The newer one shifts ionization to higher temperatures, and the resulting profiles twist around each other like ropes. The choice also moves the helium ionization feature. Because the two elements' signals are tangled, the authors argue the Sun itself can test which atomic model is right.
arxiv-2412-06213:
Das weighs ultralight axions as the dark matter behind an oddly deep radio signal from the cosmic dawn, in a 2024 paper. The axion is a guessed particle that could solve two puzzles at once: the missing mass of the cosmos and a symmetry riddle in particle physics. Telescopes saw the 21-centimeter line from the first star era dip far deeper than models allow. Something cooled the young gas, or heated the background light.

Ultralight axion-like particles, once they settle into a shared condensate, could chill the gas by touch. The same particles, bent by early black holes or magnetic fields, could flip into photons and warm the radio background instead. Das runs both plays at once across the dawn ages. Together they cancel a side effect, an excess of neutrino-like species, that cooling alone would leave. The paper frames axions as a live, testable cause of the signal.
arxiv-2412-06513:
