Umang Bhaskar and Yeshwant Pandit study fair division in a setting drawn as a graph, in two thousand twenty-four. People are points on the graph, and goods are the lines joining them. A good has value only for the two people at its ends. The goal is a split that no one envies once any single good is removed.

Earlier work proved such a split exists when each pair of people shares at most one good. The pair extend that result to graphs where pairs can share many goods. They prove the split exists, and can be found fast, for several graph types. These include two-sided graphs, tree-like graphs, and graphs with long shortest cycles.
arxiv-2412-06613:
Chun-Peng Chang, Alain Pagani, and Didier Stricker tackle a weak spot of multimodal language models: naming the right object in a crowded 3D scene. Their 2024 paper notes that such models write fine captions but give vague directions. When a target sits among look alike distractors, a robot partner needs exact, space aware wording to guide a person.

The task, called contextual object localization and disambiguation, demands that instructions single out the target alone, a stricter bar than standard 3D captioning. The authors propose simple methods that sharpen a model's spatial focus. Scores rose on standard text similarity metrics, and a 3D grounding model confirmed better spatial grasp. The gains matter as these models join robots that work beside people.
arxiv-2412-06813:
Min Zhang and co-authors build a finite element method for magnetohydrodynamics that keeps its fields honest by construction. Simulating hot, electrically conducting fluid coupled to temperature is a staple of fusion and metallurgy, and small leaks in divergence, the no-monopole rule for magnetism, rot long simulations. Their hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin scheme is arranged so velocity and magnetic field stay exactly divergence-free everywhere.

The method allows any polynomial order and treats velocity, field, pressures, and temperature at matched degrees. The authors prove the discrete system has exactly one solution and that errors shrink at the best possible rate as the mesh refines. Numerical runs confirm the theory. Robustness under the thermal coupling, the usual spoiler, is the design's selling point.
arxiv-2412-07013:
Rohit Hegde extends the Heisenberg model of magnetism by letting electrons move, and uncovers an asymmetry between the two kinds of charge carriers, in this 2024 paper. The classic Heisenberg model freezes electrons in place and keeps only their spins. Hegde adds a kinetic term that commutes with the Hubbard interaction, a combination that enriches the spectrum without interference between the parts.

One payoff is exact: textbook linear spin wave theory lands cleanly inside the time-dependent Hartree-Fock framework, as localized behavior emerges from moving electrons. The embedding works for every spin-half model and should extend to multi-orbital systems. Away from half filling, the motion of doubly occupied sites and empty sites can be tuned separately, and that differential tuning skews ordering and fluctuations. Hegde argues kinetic couplings deserve equal billing with band parameters when modeling asymmetric behavior near the Mott insulator.
arxiv-2412-07113:
Dongjun Kim and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on a small set of parameters inside language models that seems to carry their coding skill. Brains park skills in set regions; the team asked whether models do the same for programming. They call the suspected region the Coding Spot.

They located the region and then altered just those parameters. Coding test scores swung sharply, while skills outside coding stayed mostly intact. The split held across the tasks they tried. If skills really live in pockets like this, tuning a model for one trade may not require touching the rest. The paper opens a path to surgical, skill-by-skill model edits.
arxiv-2412-07213:
Weizhen Bian and co-authors present a personal literature manager in 2024. Researchers face a flood of papers, with uneven quality and search terms that often miss their mark. Their system aims to match papers to each user's real interests and past habits.

A language model bot turns plain questions into proper academic terms over several rounds of examples. A probability model then filters papers by explicit needs and past behavior. Recommendations, one-line summaries, and word cloud views round out the tool. The authors pitch it as a precise, tailored aid for literature work.
arxiv-2412-07313:
Ioannis Sarridis and co-authors introduce FaceX, a tool to explain face attribute classifiers, in a 2024 paper. The catalog creator field mixes in affiliations and emails, so the head byline governs. Standard explanation tools work image by image, which forces slow manual checks to judge a model's overall behavior.

FaceX sums model activity over nineteen set face regions, such as hair, ears, and skin, across a whole test set. It also shows the image patches with the most impact for each region. Tests on four benchmarks, with and without planted bias, show the tool spots bias and tracks fixes well. It gives auditors a summary view that single image tools lack.
arxiv-2412-08013:
Himangshu Sekhar Sarma and Subhradip Ghosh compute what happens when a ferroelectric layer grips a magnetic one in a paper from 2024. Two-dimensional stacks promise memory that switches with voltage, not current. Pairing a 2D ferromagnet with a 2D ferroelectric is the recipe. MXenes and dichalcogenides supply tunable building blocks.

Their stack joins vanadium diselenide with a scandium carbide oxide. Density functional calculations map the coupled ground states. Flipping the electric layer's polarization drags the magnetic layer's behavior with it. Bilayer and trilayer forms were both tested. Such magneto-electric coupling is the working heart of low-power memory. Theory flags the stack as worth growing in a lab.
arxiv-2412-08513:
Kristoffer Wickstrøm, Thea Brüsch, Michael Kampffmeyer, and Robert Jenssen improve how explanation tools report their own certainty, in a research paper from 2024. These tools highlight which pixels drive a model's view of an image. Knowing whether a pixel is surely important matters for trust, but older tools only show how much scores vary.

Their method, REPEAT, runs an explanation tool many times and treats each pixel as a coin flip between important and not. That yields a direct estimate of importance plus a certainty score. In their tests, the certainty scores were easier to read than older measures and better at flagging images unlike the training data.
arxiv-2412-08713:
Joris Koefler, Umut Oktem, Shruti Paranjape, Jaroslav Trnka, and Bailee Zacovic probe a deep trait of gravity amplitudes in a 2024 paper. Amplitudes give the odds of particle events in physics. MHV amplitudes are the simplest non-zero class for gravity. Unlike gluon cases, gravity versions lack some known math structures.

The team notes gravity amplitudes have no log-type singular points. They also lack the geometric build that works for gluons. Their numerators hold notable zeros that shape the values. The authors propose that those traits pin each amplitude down in a unique way. They sketch proof steps and give computed checks for set cases. The path may yield a new way to study adjoints.
arxiv-2412-10113:
Antonino Ficarra and Somayeh Moradi write a 2024 algebra paper on sortable shapes and the rings built from them. Their shapes are collections of sets with a sorting property, taken in a strong flag form. From such a shape they build a ring from its top faces, and a second algebra from ideals tied to its layered skeletons.

The authors show both algebras have strong order properties: they are well-behaved domains with a key depth property. They then study when the ring is Gorenstein, a symmetry property, by way of its divisor class group. A final result shows every such shape can be peeled vertex by vertex. That peeling gives a clean test for the depth property of the shapes themselves.
arxiv-2412-10413:
Muhammad Imran, Abdul Wahab Ziaullah, Kai Chen, and Ferda Ofli test how well large language models handle disaster posts in this 2024 paper. During crises, social media carries fast, messy reports that response teams must sort. Older trained models sort them poorly when the event changes.

The team ran six well-known models over posts from many real disasters. The strongest models, both from one commercial family, generalized best across events and information types. Most models struggled with flood posts in particular. Giving examples barely helped, and urgent requests and needs were often missed. Typos and other language quirks also tripped the models. The authors publish full benchmarks for both no-example and few-example settings.
arxiv-2412-10513:
Ana Ozaki, Roberto Confalonieri, Ricardo Guimaraes, and Anders Imenes ask, in a 2024 paper, how well a simple tree can stand in for a black box model. Trees are easy to read, so they can help explain a big model. The hard part is proof: how close is the tree to the real model, and when can it be trusted? The team turns to a frame called PAC, which gives a bound on how wrong a learned rule can be.

They adapt a tree method to earn that bound, then pull trees from BERT-based language models in a case on job bias by sex. The trees show bias tied to jobs in those models. The work gives staff a way to audit a big model with a small, checked, and plain one.
arxiv-2412-10713:
Five researchers design attacks that steer learning agents toward chosen behaviors in a paper from 2024. Safety checks for deep reinforcement learning often track only total reward. An attacker, though, may want a very specific harmful behavior, which reward scores miss. Their method, RAT, first trains an intention policy that matches human preferences. That policy becomes the target the victim agent is pushed to copy.

The attacker also reshapes which states fill the training buffer, making the push more controlled. In robot simulation tasks, RAT beat prior attack methods at inducing target behaviors. Curiously, training against such attacks also produced tougher agents. Tests extended to decision transformer agents on standard control tasks.
arxiv-2412-10913:
Alessio Guerra, Marcello Lepre, and Oktay Karakuş measured extreme opinions on Reddit during the 2023 Israeli-Palestinian conflict, in this 2024 arXiv paper. Online anger can flare with real-world events, but tracking that link needs numbers, not impressions. The team built a word-based scoring method that needs no hand labels.

They gathered over 450,000 posts from four subreddits with different leanings. Their score blends anger, polarity, and subjectivity in each post. Scores spiked around major events, such as hospital and refugee camp bombings and the collapse of a ceasefire. The study also compared how scores moved across communities and which words drove them. The authors note both the promise and the limits of measuring extremeness this way.
arxiv-2412-11013:
Spencer Daugherty extends symmetric function theory to variables that partly commute. Symmetric functions form a classic algebra with rich bases and links to counting. A colored form lets letters from a finite alphabet fail to commute in a controlled way. Inside it, Daugherty defines a new algebra that matches the classic one when the alphabet has one letter.

The new algebra is shown to be a Hopf algebra, with product, coproduct, and antipode spelled out. Its graded dual also generalizes the classic symmetric functions. Seven algebras in this family fit into one diagram joined by Hopf maps. Colored forms of the classic bases are built for both new algebras. A dual basis pair extends the Schur functions, and open questions close the work.
arxiv-2412-11413:
A twelve-author team presents a gentler way to image delicate materials with electron beams, in a 2024 paper. Their tool shines an electron beam on a sample and reads the light it gives off, which reveals traits at very small scales. The catch is that the beam often harms fragile samples before a clean reading is done.

Flat materials only a few atoms thick are especially easy to damage. The team borrowed a sharpening trick from image processing, called pan-sharpening, and applied it to this beam method. Tests showed the trick can give sharp, detailed maps while the beam stays mild. Less damage means truer readings of the sample as it really is. The approach may also help guide beam-based pattern writing for future quantum light devices.
arxiv-2412-12013:
Ole Sönnerborn tightens the math of holonomic quantum gates in this 2024 paper. In this style of quantum computing, gates arise as the computing space is carried around a closed loop. The gate equals the twist picked up along the path.

A known inequality sets a floor on how long that path must be, based only on the gate's own spectrum. It also bounds how fast such a gate can run. Sönnerborn shows that when the space around the computing space is roomy enough, any gate can be run along a shortest path. The result makes the bound exact in that setting, not just a floor.
arxiv-2412-12113:
Sarthak Arora and colleagues mapped pollution vulnerability along the river Ganga in 2024 using satellite data and structured decision methods. Sewage mixed with surface water is a severe hazard in the densely populated basin, where monsoon flooding meets enormous daily flows of untreated wastewater. The team wanted to pinpoint which stretches of a wide riverscape face the greatest risk.

They applied the analytic hierarchy process, a method that weighs many factors into a single score, together with geographic information systems and remote sensing data. Four variants of the method, including network, nested, and fuzzy versions, were used to bound the main model's uncertainty, and composites of all of them defined the final vulnerability picture. Most of the study area scored low in vulnerability, while a small share scored highly or extremely highly vulnerable, marking priority zones.
arxiv-2412-12213:
Amine Mohamed Aboussalah, Xuanze Li, Cheng Chi, and Raj Patel wrote a 2024 paper on a neural network for option pricing that learns from finance theory rather than price data. Most learned pricers fit past market prices, which can bake in errors. Their network, FINN, instead trains on a replication task drawn from dynamic hedging.

By learning to replicate payoffs, the network recovers the fair pricing rule on its own. Classic Black-Scholes prices come out correctly, and basic relations like put-call parity appear without being taught. The method stays stable in varied volatility settings, including ones with no closed form answer. On implied volatility surfaces, FINN landed closer to market values than a standard model fit. The approach extends past the most liquid options.
arxiv-2412-12413:
Albert Senen-Cerda asks how much is lost when quantum measurements are confined to a small subspace, in this 2024 paper. Real instruments cannot always perform the ideal measurement. His test problem: align two fixed quantum states as closely as possible after one of them has been measured, a Procrustes-style task.

He compares the best result using only measurements inside the low-rank subspace where the states live against the best using any measurement at all. The ratio between them, the suboptimality, turns out not to depend on the size of the full space. It grows at most like a polylogarithm of the subspace dimension, a very slow growth. The proof uses random methods, trace inequalities, and norm bounds for special frame decompositions. The message for practice: restricted measurements lose surprisingly little, which can guide cheaper measurement policies.
arxiv-2412-12613:
Victor Koltalo and co-authors scale up pulse energy in a compact laser compression cell by using vortex beams. Their 2024 paper reports on a Herriott type multi-pass cell under forty centimeters long. The beams carry a twist, in the Laguerre-Gaussian family, with orders one to three set by a spatial light modulator that allows fast reconfiguration.

Pulses of 180 femtoseconds and 610 microjoules were compressed to 44 femtoseconds with the highest order beam. Peak power of the ytterbium laser rose from 2.5 to 9.1 gigawatts. Careful measurements showed the output beams stayed spatially uniform, and the vortex charge survived compression intact. The result points to shorter, stronger pulses from a small footprint device.
arxiv-2412-12813:
Guerrero and eight co-authors confirm that the nebula HaTr 5 is a planetary nebula in two thousand twenty-four. HaTr 5 was once tied to the shell of a historic nova from the fifteenth century. That link set a bound used by the hibernation view of cataclysmic variables. Spectra and archive images now test the claim.

The hydrogen glow implies far more ionized mass than a nova can eject. Its spread speed and age also clash with a nova shell. Motions of the nebula and the variable star part ways as well. The pair is a chance overlap on the sky, they conclude.
arxiv-2412-13213:
Four authors wrote a 2024 paper on a software toolkit that joins many sky images into one large mosaic. The toolkit first came out in 2002 and is free for anyone to use. It was built as a set of small parts, so users can fit it into their own work flows with ease.

The paper stresses a growing use in radio work, the study of the sky through radio waves. Uses since 2020 span early tests for a huge new radio array, maps of gas between stars, and hunts for fast radio bursts. The authors show why a flexible, open design has kept the tool in use for over twenty years.
arxiv-2412-13313:
Masha Vlasenko presents lecture notes on congruences and cohomology given at two schools in 2024. The notes teach p-adic methods in the de Rham cohomology of algebraic hypersurfaces. Worked examples carry the ideas, with uses in number theory and combinatorics. The core rests on a paper series with Frits Beukers on objects called Dwork crystals.

Later parts tour uses in physics and arithmetic geometry. The style stays elementary, aimed at students new to the tools. Questions from school participants shaped the final written form. Schools in Trieste and São Paulo hosted the two course runs. The notes aim to open a deep area to a wider set of readers.
arxiv-2412-13713:
Morales, Muñoz, and Tu wrote in twenty twenty-four about why brain maps of smells drift over time. A given odor sparks a pattern of nerve activity in the smell cortex. Over days, that pattern shifts even though the odor stays the same. The cause of this drift was unclear. The team built a realistic computer model of the piriform cortex, a key smell area in mammals.

Their model mixes two kinds of change in nerve links. Slow random shifts over days push patterns to drift. Fast learning during repeated smells pulls patterns back toward stable forms. The model matched recent animal experiments in detail. It offers a clear mechanism for drift and its link to learning. The same idea may apply in other brain regions.
arxiv-2412-14013:
Valeria Banica and Luis Vega survey six years of work on wild, turbulent behavior in a classic wave equation and a linked geometric flow. The equation, the one-dimensional cubic Schrödinger equation, was long set aside in turbulence studies because it can be solved exactly. The linked flow describes how a curve moves along its own normal direction.

Working with others, the authors proved a wide range of complex behavior in these systems. Their results cover the birth of sharp points, growth of wave energy, fractal patterns, and bursts of activity. Some findings confirm what computer simulations had suggested earlier. The survey, written for a special issue, gathers the story in one place for mathematicians.
arxiv-2412-14413:
David Bałut and six co-authors read a sign of deep entanglement in the strange metal state of a famous superconductor, in a paper published in 2024. In ordinary metals, the entanglement measure grows with the square of temperature, as room for scattering grows. Their measure comes from a recent response measurement that showed a scale-free shape in the test crystal. From it they work out the entanglement measure at each temperature.

In the strange metal, the measure grows as temperature falls, then flattens to a fixed floor at zero temperature. That floor is set by both a high cutoff scale and a low shape scale at once. Such a mix of high and low marks a doped Mott state, where weight shifts across scales. The authors close with what this means for slim models of the famous Hubbard framework.
arxiv-2412-14713:
Gravity bends light, and the warping of galaxy shapes lets astronomers weigh the universe and trace its growth. Alba Kalaja and co-authors explore a pairing: weak lensing measured by radio telescopes, matched against lensing of the cosmic microwave background. Radio surveys see mostly star-forming galaxies, which lie farther away on average than optical ones and suffer less dimming by dust.

Using simulations of the Square Kilometre Array telescope and the Simons Observatory, the team shows this pairing pins down the distance spread of radio sources to within about 1 to 10 percent. That fix also sharpens measures of how galaxies trace dark matter. With the full array, the method beats a Euclid-like optical survey, tightening cosmology limits by about 30 percent and the bound on neutrino mass by about 24 percent. The authors present the pairing as groundwork for joint studies of radio and background surveys.
arxiv-2412-14913:
Neha Pathania, Ramniwas Meena, and Subhashish Banerjee track quantum links between two qubits sitting in a squeezed warm bath in a 2024 paper. The bath drains the pair's quantum traits over time, a process called decoherence. The team asks how those traits fade and which knobs protect them.

Four measures of non classical link proved highly sensitive to how the pair couples to the bath as a group. The authors tie those measures to teleportation quality, using top fidelity and its spread as scores. Their map of the trade offs aims to guide quantum sensing and other tasks that must run in noisy settings.
arxiv-2412-15013:
Riccardo Munafò and co-authors published this 2024 paper on finding a heart device in ultrasound scans. The device, called a MitraClip, treats a leaking heart valve and is guided by live 3D scans of the heart. Noise and low contrast in those scans make the small clip hard to see.

The team built an automated pipeline that segments the clip and classifies its state, from fully closed to fully open. A computer model of the clip is then fitted to refine the outline and measure the device. Trained on 196 scans from a heart simulator, the system located the clip with sub-millimeter average error. Better views of the clip could help surgeons place it with more care.
arxiv-2412-15113:
Large language models can learn from examples placed inside the prompt itself, a skill called in-context learning. Thomas F Burns, Tomoki Fukai, and Christopher J Earls note in this 2024 paper that the attention part of such models acts much like older models of linked memory in the brain. Drawing on that link, the team designed a new way for information to flow inside the model.

Their design lets attention heads pass signals straight to each other along a shared stream. In a small two-layer test model, the new setup learned the in-context skill faster than the standard one. The team then tried it in models with eight million and one billion settings, where it also did better. The work offers brain-inspired design hints for future models.
arxiv-2412-15413:
The CMS Collaboration reports rare light-based processes seen in lead-ion collisions at the CERN LHC, in a 2024 paper. The data came from glancing collisions in 2018, where the ions miss each other but their light fields interact. One process turns two photons into an electron pair, known as the Breit-Wheeler process. Another has light scattering off light itself, a faint effect long sought in such collisions.

The pair-production results matched standard theory well and helped sort rival models of the ion's photon flow. For light-by-light scattering, twenty-six candidate events stood against about twelve expected from background. Joined with earlier data, the signal now passes five standard deviations, the bar for a discovery claim. The team also set the tightest limits yet on hypothetical axion-like particles in part of the mass range.
arxiv-2412-15513:
Samantha Alloo and Kaye Morgan present a 2024 paper on stabilizing X-ray image reconstruction. Speckle-based X-ray imaging can yield three kinds of pictures at once: absorption, phase, and dark-field. Their retrieval method rests on an equation whose inversion is numerically shaky. A standard fix adds regularization, but the result swings wildly with the chosen strength, and picking it is slow and subjective.

The pair automates that choice. A related, steadier equation gives a trustworthy phase picture, which serves as ground truth while their algorithm tunes the regularization step by step. On synchrotron data from a four-rod sample, the method recovered clean phase and dark-field images with no hand tuning. The authors expect the trick to help other retrieval schemes with the same instability. It makes their imaging pipeline friendlier for routine use.
arxiv-2412-15613:
Xing-Yu Li and co-authors settle when a class of differential equations can have tidy solutions, in a 2024 paper. The equations link a function with its rates of change, and their weights are sums of exponential terms. The question is which such equations admit solutions that grow at a bounded, finite order.

The authors give a test that is both needed and enough for such solutions to exist. When the test passes, they write down the exact form of every such solution. Each one turns out to be an exponential sum as well. The result answers part of a known open problem in the field. It should guide later work on growth of solutions.
arxiv-2412-15713:
Martin Köhncke and co-authors publish a full data set of load tests on a concrete box girder bridge, built for reuse. The bridge, raised in 1972, still serves and now wears a fixed health watch of one hundred twenty-eight sensors. Full-scale load data on real bridges is rare in the open. This set pairs test loads with the watch's reads, all in one shared file form.

Trucks of known weight parked at set spots and crossed at set speeds, full and empty. Weights were also stacked on the deck in three steps for long, slow tests. Laser tools checked truck place and pass times as a cross-proof. Strain and sag reads repeated cleanly across slow passes. The set can feed model tuning, wear hunts, and odd-change alarms for other bridges.
arxiv-2412-16213:
Tommy Nguyen, Mehmet Ergezer, and Christian Green introduced this 2024 method for attacking 3D scene models. Neural radiance fields build lifelike 3D views from photos and now serve in key applications. Their safety holes are far less studied than those of flat image models. The authors use reinforcement learning to craft poisoned versions of such models.

The crafted noise survives spinning and resizing of the scene, which makes black-box attacks realistic. Tests ran from small objects like bananas to whole lighthouse scenes. Targeted attacks made classifiers call a banana a slug and a truck a cannon with high confidence. The poisoned models can also serve as training fodder to toughen vision systems. Code is public for checking and follow-up work.
arxiv-2412-16513:
Jia-Jie Li, Yu Tian, and Armen Sedrakian test dense matter theories against star data in a 2024 paper. Neutron stars pack more than a sun's mass into a city-sized ball. New measurements from the NICER telescope give tight mass and radius pairs for several pulsars. Those pairs can judge equations of state, the rules that say how ultra-dense matter pushes back.

The team applies Bayesian reasoning to a family of covariant density models with density-dependent couplings. Only basic nuclear particles are included, keeping the test clean. Updated telescope ellipses and other sky constraints narrow the allowed parameter space. A refined description of how couplings change with density sharpens the fit. The work shows which model versions survive the newest data.
arxiv-2412-16613:
David Lacoste and Michele Castellana sped up the Gillespie algorithm in 2024 by running many simulations in parallel inside single variables. The Gillespie method is the exact standard for simulating chemical reactions that jump at random times. Their improvement stores variables as binary words, so each bit lane can carry an independent run at once.

The authors report a large gain in computing yield from that trick. The gain may open the way to simulating systems that are not well mixed, a case the classic method handles poorly at scale. They show the idea on the Frank model, a classic scheme for how one handedness of molecules could win out in early life chemistry. Author order follows the text head, which lists Lacoste first. Readers get a neat bit-level speedup for a workhorse method.
arxiv-2412-16713:
Guy Oldaker and Maria Emelianenko present a family of clustering methods that contains several classic ones as special cases. Clustering sorts data into groups that summarize its shape. Each field has bred its own method, from image cuts to signal analysis.

Their family is indexed by a single dial and shares one minimization strategy. Turning the dial recovers known methods such as k-means and its subspace cousin. The methods stay easy to read and scale to large, high-dimensional data. An added self-tuning mechanism finds structure and settings without expert input. It can also be bolted onto other methods. The unification may end some reinvention across fields. One frame, many tools, is the pitch.
arxiv-2412-16813:
Adak, Lepe, and Rivera build a numerical scheme for the vibration tones of a flowing fluid, the eigenvalues of the Oseen problem. Their 2024 method uses virtual elements, flexible shapes that fit awkward domains, in a nonconforming flavor that keeps the computed flow exactly divergence-free.

Under the standard theory of compact operators, they prove the scheme converges and recover the doubled convergence rate for the spectrum that theory predicts. Eigenfunctions and eigenvalues both come with error bounds. Numerical tests close the paper, checking the scheme's behavior on practice problems. The authors present the method as a clean way to get fluid tones without spurious modes.
arxiv-2412-16913:
Yulan Liu, Shaohua Pan, and Shujun Bi study the stability of best solutions in a class of optimization problems in this 2024 paper. The problems involve matrix constraints that must stay positive semidefinite, a common shape in control and statistics. Tilt stability asks whether a best solution moves only gently when the problem is nudged.

The authors use a second-order subderivative tool to build checks that can be verified point by point. For a linear form of the constraint, they give both a near-matching necessary check and, under a mild condition, an exact two-way check. Earlier work needed strong regularity assumptions that this paper drops. The authors say it is the first such treatment for this problem class.
arxiv-2412-17113:
Benjamin Ellis and co-authors adapt, in a 2024 paper, a popular training optimizer for the shifting conditions of reinforcement learning. In that field, an agent learns by trial and error, and its training targets move as it improves. Tools borrowed from supervised learning, where targets stay fixed, often misbehave in this setting. Workarounds such as target networks have become standard patches.

The authors instead fix the tool itself. They analyze how a jump in gradient size, such as when a target network updates, swells the step size of the Adam optimizer. That swelling can wreck performance. Their variant, Adam-Rel, judges time steps relative to local events rather than one global clock. The aim is steadier updates in a nonstationary world. The paper frames this as adapting the toolchain to reinforcement learning, rather than patching around it.
arxiv-2412-17313:
Evan Johnson argues that a long ecology debate may be unresolvable as posed. His paper, from twenty twenty-four, concerns density dependence, how strongly a population bounces back toward balance. Decades of work have flipped back and forth on the evidence. Johnson gives three reasons to expect lasting doubt.

An economics twin debate on shock effects also refuses to settle, despite deep work. His own tests on a world population database make the core point. The answer hinges almost wholly on which time-series model one picks. Model choice, not data, drives the verdict. A simpler target, a single effective pull-back measure, can still be estimated well.
arxiv-2412-17613:
Lawrence Wang and Stephen Roberts argue instability can be a teacher in a 2024 optimization paper. Textbook gradient descent stays stable only while the learning rate respects the sharpest curvature of the loss, yet real neural networks train happily beyond that edge and generalize better for it.

The authors show the wobble is productive: when updates grow unstable, the landscape's principal directions rotate, steering parameters toward flatter basins that tend to generalize. They prove depth itself guarantees such rotations in any network with more than one layer. Empirically, large learning rates beyond the threshold acted as implicit regularization. Sometimes the optimizer must stumble to explore.
arxiv-2412-17713:
Nicolas Boulanger, Guillaume Lhost and Sylvain Thomée wrote a 2024 note on a partly massless spin-2 field and its links to other fields. In flat space, its partner set matches a known supergravity spectrum around a curved space. The authors sort all ways to deform the free theory while keeping parity. That sorting must yield a consistent gauge structure.

They re-derive a known non-Abelian vertex by a distinct route. Its gauge algebra looks like that of the curved space theory. But the deformation blocks at the next order, they show. Adding more fields gives new vertices yet the same block. Only adding the graviton solves both issues.
arxiv-2412-17913:
Qianli Ma and co-authors report a physics study from 2024 on a crystal with a pattern known as the Shastry-Sutherland lattice. The material holds pairs of spins, called dimers, and the team wanted to know why it shows no magnetic order even at very low heat levels. They tested a sample of a barium, cerium, zinc, and sulfur compound.

Heat and magnet tests showed no order down to a very low point, near 73 millikelvin. A simple dimer model matched the neutron data and the other tests well. The pairs showed strong XY-type links, and their ground state was an entangled state, not the singlet state seen with other links. The authors conclude that the material is a quantum paramagnet made of entangled pairs.
arxiv-2412-18113:
Esteban Andruchow and Eduardo Chiumiento ask when two subspaces of a Hilbert space can share one common complement. A complement fills a space alongside a subspace with no overlap; two subspaces may each have many, yet share none. Their 2024 paper sorts pairs of subspaces into those with a common complement and those without, inside the Grassmann manifold of all subspaces. Viewing subspaces through their projection operators turns the question into operator algebra. The set of pairs with a common complement proves open, and its connected pieces are examined.

Such structure results matter in operator theory, where changing subspaces is a daily move. Knowing the good set is open means small wobbles cannot destroy a shared complement. The authors map the boundary of the bad set as well. Their work gives a clean geometric picture of an algebraic question.
arxiv-2412-18413:
Sushant Kumar Behera and co-authors model how twisted molecules filter electron spin in a 2024 paper. The effect, seen since 1999, lets chiral molecules pass one spin kind more than the other, a gift for spin devices and selective chemistry, yet its engine stays disputed.

The leading guess needs stronger spin orbit coupling than atom level math gives for light atoms. Using a fully relativistic code, the team track how twist imprints on electron state chirality and shifts under an electric field. A transport model then reads spin flow against twist angle. The trends match lab signs but plead for a broader coupling theory.
arxiv-2412-18513:
Tianzhe Xiao and four co-authors show that private graph data can leak from shared training signals in a 2024 paper. In federated learning, clients share model gradients instead of data, but attackers can sometimes rebuild the data from those gradients. Existing attacks target images or text, not the sparse, yes or no structure of graphs such as molecules.

Their attack method adds two parts: one forces the rebuilt graph to stay sparse and discrete, and another fills in common missing substructures. Tests on molecular datasets showed the method reconstructed graph data more accurately than earlier attack techniques. The work warns that federated graph learning, used for things like drug data, needs stronger privacy defenses than it has today.
arxiv-2412-18613:
Tomer Ullman turns the classic illusion test on its head for AI vision models, in a 2024 paper. An illusion splits how a thing is from how it looks, and that split probes the mind's wiring. Models are often asked whether they fall for the same tricks as people. Ullman instead shows them near-illusions: scenes that look like famous tricks but hold no trick at all.

The ducks are just ducks. The crooked lines really are crooked, and the circles differ in size because they truly differ. Many current vision-language models still call these scenes illusions, seeing a gap that is not there. The failure runs deep: models learn to expect trickery in such frames, and report the expectation over the evidence. Ullman ties the slip to wider known faults in these systems. The test set offers a cheap probe of whether a model looks at all.
arxiv-2412-19013:
Sunho Kim, Chunhe Xiong, and Junde Wu extend quantum resource theory to measure advantage relative to a chosen set of weaker states. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-four. Resource theories price features like coherence and entanglement by the edge they give in physical tasks.

The authors define relative superiority over any convex set of resource states. A generalized robustness measure then captures the largest relative edge in telling subchannels apart. They also frame deficiency: how far a state falls short of the best states for the same task. Their geometric measure fits coherence and entanglement and prices the shortfall exactly in some cases. The work broadens what resource measures can say.
arxiv-2412-19313:
Yang-Hui He, Vishnu Jejjala, and Tomás Silva use in 2024 simulated annealing to build brane tilings, the dimer patterns that encode a large class of gauge theories. Hand-building tilings that stay geometrically sound is slow and error-prone. A metaheuristic search could speed discovery a great deal.

Their optimizer hunts for tilings that meet the needed consistency rules. Known examples are recovered, which validates the search. The method also derives a new tiling with twenty-six quantum fields. Each tiling maps to a gauge theory with a toric moduli space. The authors offer the approach as a fresh tool for the string theory toolbox, where computer search can scout patterns for human proof.
arxiv-2412-19713:
Gyanchandani, Oza, and Roy grow a net bit by bit to outline livers in scans in this twenty twenty-four paper. Liver cuts need true 3D maps of the organ and its lumps for safe work. Big fixed nets can cost much and can tune too tight to their drill set.

Inside, their net stacks fresh blocks as it drills, and stops when tight-tune signs show. Its learn curves can bend in ways plain fixed nets can not match. That bend skill helps it read the deep links in 3D ward scan data. Scores on liver map tasks beat plain nets and fixed kin nets in tests. Its growth can be read back through the learned weights, which aids trust.
arxiv-2412-20113:
Jacek Miekisz and Javad Mohamadichamgavi build a game model, in a 2024 paper, to study how time delays affect cooperation. Their model is based on the Snowdrift game, a standard setup where players choose whether to cooperate or not. New offspring first sit in young compartments, then mature into adult groups at rates that depend on their strategy, while deaths keep the total size bounded.

In the matching random birth-death process, the time spent young acts like a delay. The authors find a new effect: when both strategies wait the same average time, cooperators end up more common in the random model than in the matching smooth model. In short, delays favor cooperation when random swings are present, a result that links timing, chance, and social behavior.
arxiv-2501-00013:
Lirong Wu and seven co-authors present RAAD, a setup for designing antibodies without knowing the target epitope in advance, in a two thousand twenty-four computing-and-biology paper. Antibody binding is governed by the complementarity finding regions, whose design remains hard to compute.

Earlier methods handle long regions poorly, assume a given epitope with static interactions, and ignore specificity. RAAD enriches node, edge, and relation features with context and shape information, then models antigen-antibody interaction dynamically to co-design sequences and structures. A new specificity metric and a contrastive constraint push designs toward certain binders. Tests across region types and lengths show strong modeling, making, and tuning results.
arxiv-2501-00413:
Jiale Huang, Xiangjian Qian, and Mingpu Qin present a paper published in 2024 on a hybrid method for simulating quantum matter on classical computers. Matrix product states compress a quantum state efficiently but strain when entanglement grows; Clifford circuits handle huge entanglement and simulate cheaply, yet miss the non-Clifford magic. Their combined method, CAMPS, lets the circuit carry the entanglement it handles best, leaving the matrix state only the remainder.

The authors extend the hybrid to fermions, particles whose antisymmetry usually blocks such tricks, by mapping them to spins. On two standard testbeds, the spinless t-V model and the spinful Hubbard model, accuracy improved markedly over matrix states alone, especially under strong interactions. They offer the method as a sharper tool for many-body fermion problems.
arxiv-2501-00713:
Michael Bennie and five co-authors present a system that writes replies pushing back against hate speech in four languages, in this 2025 paper. Their entry joined a shared task on multilingual counterspeech generation, where low resource languages are the hard test. The model reads the situation around each hateful post before answering.

A simulated annealing search, tuned on multilingual data, shapes replies that stay factually grounded. The system placed first for Basque, second for Italian, and third for both English and Spanish on the task's mix of standard scores and an AI judge. It in fact swept the top three spots for Basque. The authors break down scores in detail and argue context aware generation is the way to scale counterspeech beyond big languages.
arxiv-2501-00813:
Felix Oberbauer and ten co-authors drive tiny magnetic oscillators with light and current at the same time. Spin-transfer torque nano-oscillators suit brain-inspired computing because they are small and energy lean. The team fabricated optimized devices and excited them with AC laser light plus DC bias current. Laser heating set up thermal gradients that made pulsed thermoelectric voltages through the Tunnel Magneto-Seebeck effect.

Magnetic field sweeps showed clean switching between parallel and antiparallel magnetization states in both voltage parts, a trait that suits multistate memory. Millivolt signals in open circuit match CMOS needs. Under bias, spikes tied to Barkhausen jumps and double switching hinted at neural-like spiking behavior.
arxiv-2501-01013:
Ziju Shen and five co-authors rebuild CT volumes from scant data in a 2025 paper. Standard CT scanning costs time and radiation dose. A multi source static scanner grabs sparse views fast, but the data fall short of a full picture. Filling the gaps is an inverse problem.

Their solver grows images through a diffusion generation process. Each generated volume is projected back onto the measured data for consistency. A neural network represents the missing orthogonal part of the volume implicitly. Self supervised training tunes that representation without ground truth scans. Together the stages sample an approximate posterior for the volume. Tests under varied sparse settings confirm the approach works. The method targets faster, lower dose clinical scanning.
arxiv-2501-01613:
Chunyi Zhang, Junfeng Wang, and Tian-Wen Cao compare hot and cold gas inside the Whirlpool galaxy, in a 2025 paper. Cold molecular gas is the raw stock for new stars, while hot gas glows in X-rays after winds and explosions heat it. How the two phases feed and stir each other shapes a galaxy's life.

The team combined deep Chandra X-ray data with millimeter surveys of the galaxy M51, studying patches about a thousand parsecs wide. Hot gas brightness falls off sharply within the inner two kiloparsecs. Links between hot gas glow, infrared light, and star birth shift from the center to the outskirts. Mapping those links shows how star making heats its own fuel supply across a spiral galaxy.
arxiv-2501-01813:
Robotic furniture that moves through a room needs a way to telegraph its intentions, the way a person turning toward a door signals a plan. Nguyen and co-authors explore whether a mobile robotic partition can speak through gesture.

Fifteen experts from several fields joined improvisation sessions, moving a switched-off robotic wall by hand to act out six architectural intentions of varying purpose and urgency. Motion tracking, a movement questionnaire, and discussion produced twenty distinct gestural strategies. Beyond pointing-like and emblem-like gestures known from robot research, the team names a third kind. Architectonic gestures use the furniture's sheer spatial effect, blocking, opening, or looming, to make the message plain. The study is an early step toward adaptive buildings people can read at a glance.
arxiv-2501-02213:
Nguyen Van Thu, writing alone in 2025, studies when a third substance can coat the border between two separated fluids in an ultracold gas. The gas is a Bose-Einstein condensate with three components, where the first two refuse to mix. The third can act like a surfactant, gathering at their interface and possibly wetting it fully, a change known as a wetting transition.

Working within Gross-Pitaevskii theory and taking the first two components as symmetric, Thu derives the nucleation line that marks where wetting begins and draws the phase diagram around it. Solving the linearized equations gives each component's wave shape. A simple formula then estimates the surfactant layer's thickness before wetting sets in. That thickness grows in a straight line against the logarithm of the chemical potential ratio, a neat rule for later experiments.
arxiv-2501-02413:
Dan Suciu, Yisu Remy Wang, and Yihong Zhang laid semantic foundations in 2025 for equality saturation, a program and query optimization method. The method rewrites a program inside a compact graph that holds many versions at once. It is popular in practice, but its theory lagged behind.

The authors define its meaning through tree automata and show a deep link to a classic database chase process. They pin down which chase runs mirror the method, study when the process must stop in three settings, and give a shape test that guarantees stopping. Theory now backs a tool many builders already trust.
arxiv-2501-02513:
Dennis Delali Kwesi Wayo, Leonardo Goliatt, and Darvish Ganji survey how quantum computers built from light have grown from lab demos toward larger, steadier machines. Their 2025 review covers the parts that make, guide, and detect single photons, plus the error control such systems need.

The authors report steady gains on many fronts at once. Coupling of light into chips now passes ninety percent, and top detectors catch more than ninety-eight percent of photons. Error rates have fallen below one in a thousand, and tests with over one hundred photons pass what normal computers can match. The review also covers how machine learning now helps design circuits, and why these steps matter for computing, secure messages, and sensing.
arxiv-2501-03013:
Leonid Yatsenko and co-authors model how light travels through a gas of simple atoms in a 2025 paper. The atoms have just two energy levels, and the stream of photons can change character as it passes, even forming light with quantum traits no classical wave can show.

Their equations track the photon destroying operator itself, which lets them compute how photon pairs correlate in time. That measure reveals antibunching, where photons arrive one by one rather than in clumps. Both sealed and open versions of the atomic system are treated, along with the smearing from atomic motion and detuning of the drive. Predictions match data from a waveguide experiment well. Future work will extend the method to richer systems.
arxiv-2501-03413:
Tassilo Klein and co-authors introduce SALT, a 2025 dataset of linked business tables drawn from a real enterprise planning system. Foundation models shine on text and images, but linked tables with foreign keys trip them up. Business data is exactly that shape, yet research sets from real firms are rare.

SALT curates sales tables whose rows point across tables by key, as in live company software. The set is built to train and test table representation learning, the craft of turning rows into model-ready vectors. By opening authentic enterprise data to researchers, the team hopes to sharpen models for real business tasks. Autocompletion of sales records is the namesake use case. The dataset fills a gap between toy tables and the messy data firms actually keep.
arxiv-2501-03813:
Pulsating stars called RR Lyrae are trusted mile markers for measuring distances in space, but their brightness curves must be known precisely. A team led by K. Baeza-Villagra built a large template library in 2025 from fast, repeated observations with a wide-field camera on a telescope in Chile. The field they watched lies toward the crowded center of the Milky Way.

The library covers two pulsation styles in four color bands, with one hundred thirty-six templates of one style and one hundred forty-four of the other, all public. A new method handles stray bad measurements while the curves are shaped. The authors also study curve traits such as rise time and skewness, and how they link to period and color. The templates will serve a coming giant sky survey.
arxiv-2501-04013:
Avetik Arakelyan and Rafayel Barkhudaryan prove a learning cure for hard equations settles on truth in a 2024 paper. The cure trains a neural web on the equation's own rules, with no solved cases needed. Such webs are used wide, yet proof that their best fits march to the true answer was thin.

For a class of fully bent second-order equations, they show the fit chain nears the one true rough-sense answer. The proof leans on a compare rule that keeps such answers unique. More data thus means more truth, at least here. Users gain ground to trust the cure.
arxiv-2501-04613:
Yuhe Bai tackles the cost of training knowledge graph embeddings in a 2025 paper. A knowledge graph stores facts as linked triples, and embeddings turn its items into number lists that computers can compare. Most training methods ignore the graph's class structure, lose meaning, and cannot scale to very large graphs.

Bai's algorithm uses the class structure, called the ontology, to split the graph into parts by type. Each part can then be trained in parallel, and the splits carry extra meaning into the learned number lists. Early results on several standard test sets look strong. The work aims to make meaning-aware training possible at the scale of the largest real graphs, where facts run into the millions.
arxiv-2501-04813:
Sharareh Alipour, Ermiya Farokhnejad and Tobias Mömke give better approximation algorithms for travelling salesman problems in the semi-streaming model, where a graph must be read in passes with small memory. Their base problem is maximum path cover: a set of vertex-disjoint paths that covers the most edges. Path covers then feed tours for the salesman variants.

For any small error term, their path cover method reaches about two thirds of the best size, up from one half in past work. On that base, the tour for the one-two distance salesman problem reaches a factor near four thirds, and the maximum weight tour reaches near seven twelfths. Each gain improves the best semi-streaming result known before.
arxiv-2501-05013:
Ventura and co-authors study a 2025 set of planetary nebulae in the Large Magellanic Cloud and the stars that made them. A nebula is the shell a dying star sheds, and its dust shows how well the star made dust in its last phase. The team links the shells' gas and dust to the mass and metal mix of each parent star.

Nine nebulae were studied, seven rich in carbon dust and two with silicate dust. For carbon-rich shells, the dust share rose steeply as parent mass grew. Models of star aging and dust growth were joined with light data to draw that link.
arxiv-2501-05513:
The early universe's exploding stars are nearly invisible, yet they record how the first generations of stars lived and died. Coulter and co-authors report in 2025 a likely supernova caught by the Webb telescope in a galaxy seen as it was when the universe was young, at redshift 3.6. The flash, found in a deep survey field, glowed brightly in the ultraviolet at discovery.

Its light curve matches a Type IIP supernova, the kind born from a red supergiant, here of about twenty suns with an unusually strong blast. The host's chemistry is poor in heavy elements, like the local settings where such strong blasts occur. It is the most distant supernova of its class yet pinned with a measured redshift. The authors read it as a hint that such explosions change with cosmic time.
arxiv-2501-05613:
Qi Sun and co-authors study chemistry inside a cryogenic buffer gas cell in 2025, a tool that makes cold beams of molecules for quantum and precision work. Molecules are usually freed by blasting a metal target with a laser in a donor gas. Reactions with a high barrier, such as calcium with hydrogen gas, were thought to be shut off in such cold cells.

The team reacted calcium with three forms of hydrogen gas and found the plain form could act as both reactant and buffer gas, beating its heavier forms. A reaction network model traced the higher yield to fast shaking excitation of the reactant gas. The result gives a sturdy way to make bright cold beams of metal hydrides, molecules wanted for laser cooling and trapping work in physics labs.
arxiv-2501-05713:
Thomas Schurmann wrote a solo physics paper in two thousand twenty-five rethinking an extension of the uncertainty principle. The extended principle adds curvature-scale effects to the usual quantum limit on knowing position and momentum at once. Schurmann recasts it in operational terms: what a real measuring device can pin down.

Position is set by the apparatus, such as a slit of fixed width or a ball of fixed radius. With momentum operators that fit the extended algebra, he proves a sharp lower bound on momentum spread times preparation size. The bound returns to the standard limit when the deformation fades. He extends it to curved spaces in two and three dimensions.
arxiv-2501-06313:
Pascal Gewecke, Jascha Zander, and Roman Schnabel measure the trembling of dark, rough surfaces with laser light whose noise has been squeezed below the usual quantum limit, in a 2025 paper. Squeezed light sharpens sensing, as in gravity-wave detectors, but only if most photons come back. Matte surfaces scatter or soak up light, so the trick seemed closed to them.

Instead of bouncing light off the surface, the team let the beam pass beside it and read the air pressure wave the shaking surface sheds. With squeezing worth ten decibels, the setup matched a plain beam ten times stronger. It resolved an ultrasound ripple of 0.12 millipascals with millimeter detail. The authors see uses where surfaces cannot be touched and light must stay eye-safe.
arxiv-2501-06413:
Demao Kong and Hai-Bo Yu probe dark matter in gas-rich galaxies in twenty twenty-five. Five such galaxies, found with the MeerKAT telescope, show sharply rising rotation curves. Their visible matter is not dominant, so their dark matter halos must be dense inside. The standard halo model fits them only with extreme concentrations.

Those required concentrations sit far above the cosmological median. Self-interacting dark matter offers another account. In its core-collapse phase, halos naturally reach such high inner densities. Halo environment matters too: filament halos match average concentrations, while node halos run denser. The authors suggest these galaxies formed in cosmic nodes of dark matter. Readers get observational signs that dark matter may interact with itself.
arxiv-2501-06813:
Yiheng Xu and four co-authors pick subsets under noise with a method that judges each pick by its worst credible showing. Choosing a small set with the best total effect drives tasks from spreading influence to sparse modeling. In practice the score of any set is measured with error, and greedy or older evolutionary methods either wobble under that noise or burn too much computing. The team's method, PORE, balances two goals at once: a robust score that discounts lucky noise, and a small set size.

That balance lets it find well-shaped solutions while spending its budget wisely, fixing a known waste in a predecessor method. On real data for influence spread and sparse regression, the method clearly beat the greedy rule and both earlier evolutionary rivals. Follow-up tests that removed parts of the design confirmed the robust score does the heavy lifting.
arxiv-2501-07013:
Manuel Bernal-Lecina and four co-authors present a classroom robot that stays in place, in a paper from 2025. Most school robots roll on wheels, which fixes a narrow idea of what a robot can be in class. Their robot, Sthymuli, is static by design and is meant to open new kinds of interaction among robot, students, and teacher.

They build on Thymio II, a well-known school robot platform, so results can be fairly compared with wheeled robots. The paper lays out the constraints and needs that shaped the design. It reports the current state of the build and the work still ahead for classroom trials.
arxiv-2501-07313:
E Zhu and T Preibisch measure X-ray activity in nearby stars in this 2025 paper. Strong X-ray and ultraviolet output from red dwarf stars may threaten planets around them. Fair samples are needed, since active stars are easier to detect and can skew the picture. The team built volume complete samples of three star types.

The samples held 205 M stars, 129 K stars, and 107 G stars near the Sun. X-ray data came from four space telescopes. Detection completeness passed eighty percent for each group. Red dwarfs split into two glow levels, with the later types glowing relatively stronger. Most M stars still fall inside the normal range set by larger stars. The results calm some fears about planet habitability.
arxiv-2501-07513:
Myoung-Woo Yoo and co-authors build a micromagnetic framework for cluster magnetic multipoles, the patterns that capture the symmetry of spin arrangements in magnetic materials. The head title speaks of simulations for these patterns, while the catalog title names a formalism. Their 2025 paper notes that high order forms of them rule how electric and optical effects work in altermagnets and in non-collinear antiferromagnets.

Textures of these patterns have been seen at micrometer scales, but how they act at middle scales was largely unexplored. The framework lets the team study such systems place by place and in numbers, even when the pattern is not uniform. As a test case, the team simulates domain wall motion for magnetic octupoles in a manganese tin compound. It catches how the wall changes shape and gains an emergent inertial mass.
arxiv-2501-07713:
Reza Jalayer and co-authors stress-test AI hand detection for factory robots on scenes unlike its training data, in a 2025 paper. Robots working beside people must spot hands reliably to stay safe, yet models are usually graded only on data resembling their training set. The team built a varied industrial dataset: plain and cluttered backgrounds, tools, zero to four hands, gloves on or off, seen from head-mounted and fixed cameras.

For the harder, out-of-distribution tests they added rare cases like crossed fingers and motion blur from fast hands. An ensemble of two segmentation networks did the outlining, with uncertainty tracked through prediction entropy. Models trained on industrial data beat those trained on everyday data, and all models struggled with the unusual scenes, though industrial training generalized far better. The authors argue that context-matched training data matters as much as model choice for safe collaboration.
arxiv-2501-07813:
Feijie Wu and five co-authors built a routing layer that sends each question to the right specialist agent, in a 2025 paper. Companies keep knowledge in separate stores that cannot be merged, so each store gets its own answering agent. Users then face two failures: they pick the wrong agent, or their question needs facts from several agents at once.

Their framework, RIRS, sums up each agent's store as a point in embedding space. A front server matches the question to the closest agents only, which cuts delay and avoids noisy all-agent broadcasts. For hard questions, the server loops: it gathers partial answers, forms a middle result, and sharpens the question for the next round. Tests showed precise agent picks and strong answers on both single-step and multi-step questions, with no training needed.
arxiv-2501-08113:
Amalia Fodor and Cosmin Crucean work out how W bosons decay and form in the early universe. Their twenty twenty-five paper is set in de Sitter space, a model of fast cosmic expansion. In flat space some of these steps cannot happen at all.

Using first-order methods, the pair compute rates for W bosons breaking into lighter particles. They also find rates for electrons giving off W bosons, a step open only under strong early expansion. The rates turn on particle masses and the Hubble value for expansion. Clean math tools keep the results finite. Readers see how an expanding space changes what particles can do.
arxiv-2501-08613:
Ramya Keerthy Thatikonda and co-authors grade the graders for machine written logic, in a 2025 paper. Tools now turn English claims into formal logic for solver programs, yet few checks tell a right formula from a wrong one. The authors test how well current scoring methods spot planted flaws.

They twisted true formulas in word and symbol ways and watched each score react. A word overlap score overreacted to surface changes. A graph score caught shape changes but missed some symbol swaps. A meaning based score best matched a strong model acting as judge. Mixing scores beat any single one. The study guides builders of logic checking tools.
arxiv-2501-08713: Ohad Drucker and Alexander Rabinovich study in 2025 how to build systems that run forever. The classic Church problem asks for a finite-state system that meets a written spec, and it was solved decades ago. The endless-state version has been touched only a few times, with no full solution. The authors present a systematic study of that harder problem, centered on building winning strategies for a class of parity games that a rich logic can define.
arxiv-2501-09113:
Pablo Peso Parada and co-authors propose a way to personalize speech recognition by shaping training data around each user's own voice conditions, in a paper from 2025. Standard augmentation adds random noise and echo to training speech. Phones that adapt to their owner already recognize speech better.

Their method builds extra training data tuned to the acoustic traits of the end user. Against a strong baseline system, the approach cut word errors by about fourteen percent relative to standard augmentation. It also reached good accuracy faster, needing sixteen to twenty percent less training. The authors present it as a practical step for on device personal speech tools.
arxiv-2501-09413:
Thomas Baker and Jaimie Greasley build a quantum algorithm for the slope of one of matrix algebra's most useful quantities. The logarithm of a determinant appears across physics and computing, and its derivatives yield real physical quantities in statistical models and field theories, as well as matrix inverses themselves. Their 2025 paper extends the quantum gradient algorithm to many variables and aims it at this target.

The payoff is a shortcut to the pseudo-inverse of a sparse operator. Instead of reading out all the entries of the matrix, the method measures one expectation value of a quantum state. In the ideal case its cost grows only with the number of relevant eigenvectors and the square of the target error, and it converges faster than linearly when the matrix is ill-conditioned.
arxiv-2501-09713:
Estibalitz Ruiz Irusta and Juan Miguel Morales make peer power trading fairer across rich and poor members of an energy community, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Direct trades can shut out poorer peers when a manager chases total gain alone. Members are grouped by energy poverty level for the fix.

Trades are reshaped to shrink the largest gap between group trade patterns, with a cap on total loss. A test grid with sixteen hundred peers cut unfairness by up to about seventy percent. Adding a non-profit shared solar plant erased the gap fully in the test. Readers in community energy get a fairness dial with a stated cost.
arxiv-2501-09813: Teodor-George Marchitan, Claudiu Creanga, and Liviu Dinu describe their team's entry in a shared task on spotting machine-generated text across languages, held with the COLING 2025 GenAI workshop. They tried both masked language models and causal models for the binary detection job. Their best model placed first of thirty-six teams on the micro F1 score, at 0.8333, and second on the macro F1 score, at 0.8301. The short paper reports the approach of the Unibuc-NLP team and its standings in the task's first subtask.
arxiv-2501-09913:
Hugo Latapie presents a position paper, published in 2025, proposing a formal test for whether an AI system truly has common sense. The paper is the second in a series on safe and beneficial artificial intelligence. Its litmus test sets tasks that lie beyond the concepts a system already knows, built from minimal prior knowledge rules combined with self referential arguments in the style of Gödel.

Latapie applies the idea to a popular abstract reasoning benchmark and weighs the roles of training data limits and physical or virtual embodiment. He also warns of deceptive hallucination, where stronger systems fabricate smooth answers to hide gaps. Scaling without common sense, he argues, sharpens that risk, while a hard test of novelty could certify safer systems.
arxiv-2501-10013:
Matan Ben-Tov, Daniel Deutch, Nave Frost, and Mahmood Sharif craft realistic attacks on tabular data classifiers in a 2025 paper. Fake rows that fool a model are useless if no real record could ever look like them. Attackers also want maximum effect for minimum effort and change.

Their system mines the hidden rules a database obeys, using leading automatic tools. A tailored attack algorithm first bends rows in feature space to flip the model's call. The system then projects those rows back onto the mined rules so they stay plausible. Tests on three data sets and two network designs show higher success than prior attacks. The fakes also change fewer fields by smaller amounts, which makes them harder to spot.
arxiv-2501-10413:
A team of patrol drones that learns to hunt rogue drones together is the subject of a 2025 arXiv paper by Panayiota Valianti and co-authors. The setting is a sensitive facility under threat, and the patrol must find and keep eyes on several intruders at once, a joint search and track problem.

The team trains the drones with multi agent reinforcement learning, rewarding them for the number of intruders held in track. Wide simulation runs with varied team sizes tested both performance and scale. The authors argue that finding and following the threat deserves as much attention as the better studied jamming step.
arxiv-2501-10513:
Rohit Dwivedula and co-authors present ConfigBot, a system that retunes robots as conditions change. Their 2025 paper notes that service robots juggle tasks like navigation and perception on limited onboard compute. Fixed system settings waste resources or cause unstable behavior when loads shift. Their system profiles running apps and tweaks settings on its own to meet a set performance target.

Tests ran on several real robots, each with its own software stack and needs. Some needs changed with context, like place or task phase. ConfigBot held stability while using resources well across these trials. The authors argue that automatic tuning suits robot fleets in shifting settings. It replaces hand-set configs and over-built hardware margins.
arxiv-2501-11213:
Flowlines carry oil, gas, and water from wellheads to surface equipment, and their failures are studied far less than big pipeline failures. The authors combine map data with machine learning to map that risk. They build their data set from Colorado regulator records, matching locations and extracting shape features.

Several learning methods were tried, including logistic regression, support vector machines, boosted trees, and clustering. Combined ensemble classifiers scored best, especially after a step that compressed the data's dimensions. The analysis highlights which spatial and operating factors track with risk. It also marks high-risk zones where monitoring should focus. The authors argue the approach can improve environmental safety and cut human exposure. They stress that better source data would sharpen the models further.
arxiv-2501-11313:
Zheng Wang and co-authors build new sequence sets in a 2025 arXiv paper. Such sets have a low ambiguity zone, which matters for systems that sense and communicate at once. The team introduces a new class of functions, called locally perfect nonlinear functions.

Using these functions plus interleaving, they build three new classes of sequence sets. The sets cover both periodic and aperiodic cases with flexible parameters. The periodic sets are nearly optimal against a known bound. The aperiodic sets meet the matching bound as well, a first in the literature. The authors also show the sequences in each set are truly distinct.
arxiv-2501-11813:
Julia Falconer, Eibe Frank, Devon Polaschek, and Chaitanya Joshi show how deep learning can extract expert uncertainty from past decisions, in a 2025 paper. A known method infers a prior distribution from records of expert calls. That method had only been shown on table data. Real experts use richer inputs, like images and text. The authors adapt the method with deep learning models. Those models can read the same inputs the experts saw.

The paper surveys model types suited to mimicking expert choices. It then walks through a worked example. The example weighs colon cancer risk. Step by step, it shows how to fit the model and read off uncertainty. The result is a distribution that reflects expert doubt. Such priors can feed later statistical analysis. The aim is to capture judgment that experts cannot easily state as numbers. The approach suits fields where records of decisions are plentiful.
arxiv-2501-12513:
Michael Coopman studies a chance rule on permutations weighted by a count called the major index, in a math paper from 2025. The rule links to a known q form of a classic measure in group theory.

Coopman gives a clean sampling method that draws permutations with just the right odds under that rule. With that sampler in hand, he proves known facts about the linked measure without heavy group theory tools. The same method yields facts about the limit shape of large draws, how often small patterns show up, and the cycle form of the draws.
arxiv-2501-12813:
Julio Sánchez-Cánovas and Manuel Donaire analyze two excited atoms acting as one system. Their paper appeared in 2025. They study how long the pair stays excited, which way it sheds light, and what forces the atoms exert on each other. Exact formulas cover the time evolution, the pattern of emitted light, and the internal forces, both the tidy kind and the lossy kind.

The lossy forces turn out to be nonreciprocal: the push on one atom does not mirror the push on the other. That imbalance leaves a net force that rocks the pair. For two lithium atoms in high orbits, the authors estimate the pair could drift by about 120 nanometers over its lifetime. A force that moves the center of mass from inside is a striking break with everyday mechanics.
arxiv-2501-13413:
Valuyan computes a quantum correction to the Casimir energy in a 2025 solo physics paper. The setting breaks Lorentz symmetry in a scalar field theory. The field sits between two membranes with rough surfaces. Four kinds of boundary conditions are worked through in turn.

Position-dependent counterterms fold the boundaries into renormalization. A box subtraction scheme and a cutoff tame the divergences. Results cover both massive and massless field versions. Several degrees of membrane roughness are compared in the results. The findings stay consistent with theoretical expectations throughout. The work extends Casimir studies to rough, symmetry-breaking settings.
arxiv-2501-14113:
Santosh, Jia, Goroncy, and Grabmair present RELexED in a 2025 arXiv paper. Legal summarization squeezes long documents into short, coherent summaries. Models that read only the source often drift off theme or shift style.

RELexED guides the model with exemplar summaries fetched from other cases. A two-stage selection balances how close exemplars sit to the query against how varied they are among themselves. Scores come from influence functions, and a point process enforces the balance. On two legal datasets, RELexED beat models without exemplars and those picking exemplars by similarity alone.
arxiv-2501-14413:
Hairline cracks in road surfaces warn of bigger failures ahead, but they are painfully hard for software to outline. Blessing Agyei Kyem and co-authors build Context-CrackNet in this 2025 paper, a segmentation network with two added modules for fine detail and wide context.

One module sharpens focus on the crack region, and the other gathers scene-wide cues so faint lines are not lost. Across ten public data sets, the system beat nine strong rivals on overlap scores while staying fast enough for field use. Tests removing each module confirmed both parts earn their place, pointing toward practical, large-scale road monitoring.
arxiv-2501-14613:
Besancon and co-authors summarize, in a 2025 paper, recent progress in a software library for Frank-Wolfe optimization methods. These methods solve constrained optimization problems by moving toward extreme points, and they shine on large scale problems where other methods are costly. The library, written in the Julia language, gathers fast implementations of the leading variants.

The package was built with two purposes. It aims to be the standard toolbox for practitioners who apply these methods. And it offers a modular playground for algorithm designers testing their own variants and building blocks. The paper reviews recent uses of the library in the literature, matching those two purposes. It then benchmarks several variants on important problem classes. Curated experiments show the performance on offer. The authors present the library as shared infrastructure for the optimization community.
arxiv-2501-14713:
James Seale Smith and co-authors present a 2025 machine learning paper on shrinking large language models for small devices. Their method, FlexiGPT, scores each block of the network for importance, cuts the weak ones, and replaces them with shared copies of surviving blocks fitted with small low-rank adapters. Output normalization and a careful starting point help the replacements learn fast.

At thirty and forty percent compression, the trimmed models beat existing pruning methods on nearly every benchmark the authors tried. The same machinery can also grow a small model, lifting its scores across the board with a sliver of extra training and few added parameters. The work offers a two-way tool: compress big models, or stretch small ones.
arxiv-2501-14913:
Ankit Kundu and co-authors show how a thin glassy layer lets quantum emitters flash together across long spans. Their 2025 paper studies emitters tucked inside a slim dielectric film. Guided light modes in the film link the emitters over many wavelengths, far past what open space allows.

Arrays in the film glow as one, both in total and in chosen directions, a shared burst called superradiance. The effect even appears where a plain setting would show none. Layer shape thus steers shared quantum behavior in ways atom setups cannot reach. The work opens paths to many-body light effects in built photonic settings.
arxiv-2501-15013:
Bhattacharya and co-authors present a 2025 theory paper on the top data rates of multi user interference channels. In such channels, many senders share one air space and each receiver hears the rest as noise. Past proofs of the best rates lean on heavy tools and long case lists.

Their route splits each user's stream into sub user parts and leans on a classic entropy power bound. Plain single user Gaussian code books then suffice for the best rates, with no exotic tricks. Only the sub users a receiver truly decodes add constraints, which trims the case load hard. The outcome is a full, finite list of rate mixes under a shared power cap. The frame aims at lean design for cell free nets.
arxiv-2501-15313:
Sheikh Samit Muhaimin and Spyridon Mastorakis ask if a spy on the network can tell what a person is doing in virtual reality, from the traffic of the headset alone. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Virtual sets are now used in schools, fun, and work. Yet their safety and privacy risks are not well mapped. The team takes traffic from twenty-five such apps on a known headset. They seek marks in that traffic, which may be coded, that give away both the app and the act in it, such as grasping a thing, walking, talking, or flying. Their work tests how much a mere flow of packets can bare.
arxiv-2501-15413:
Ramya Iyer, Mustafa Doga Dogan, Maria Larsson, and Takeo Igarashi build a mixed-reality tool that helps home makers design with scrap wood. Scrap piles bind what can be made: each board has its own span, grain, and flaws. Their 2025 tool lets a maker log each real board as a virtual twin in the view of the room. Twins can be moved, stacked, and tried in place, where the piece will stand.
