The detector senses the faint light flash a fast charged particle makes in a clear medium. Two large panels, each one meter square, catch the flashes. Fibers that shift the light color carry the signal out in crossing rows.

Crossing rows give the hit point along both axes of the panel. Computer modeling set the sharpness of the position read at under two millimeters. The device ignores most natural background radiation on its own. Its sense of direction also cuts blur from stray muons. Uses include hidden-structure scans in archaeology and earth science.
arxiv-2503-04313:
Mikhail G Katz recounts the stormy history of infinitesimals, the infinitely small quantities once at the heart of calculus. In the 1700s the thinker d'Alembert branded them chimeras, and critics repeated the charge for two centuries. His 2025 essay follows the idea through its champions and its foes.

Key episodes feature Cauchy, Noël, Poisson, and Riemann, who used tiny quantities in serious work. Reactions from Moigno, Lamarle, and Cantor show how heated the dispute became. The essay ends with Peano and the start of a modern revival. Katz writes for readers curious about how a banned idea survived underground and returned. The piece is a compact tour of a long argument in math.
arxiv-2503-04413:
Hyunwoo Yoo asks whether generative language models can read DNA in a 2025 arXiv paper. Encoder models such as DNABERT already classify DNA well, but decoder-style generative models were little tested on sequences. His test case is antimicrobial resistance genes.

He evaluates how well generative models handle DNA with varied labels. He also tracks what happens when extra text information is added beside the sequence. The models matched or beat encoder results in his tests. Adding text boosted flexibility and accuracy. Code and data are shared in a public repository. The study widens the toolkit for DNA sequence analysis.
arxiv-2503-04513:
Jiageng Zhong and co-authors proposed in 2025 a new workflow for drone mapping with sparse photos. Standard photogrammetry needs heavy overlap between aerial images to build accurate maps. Flights with low overlap break that method and leave gaps. The team's approach leans on monocular depth estimation, which guesses depth from a single image.

Tie points from aerial triangulation anchor the guessed depth to real metric depth. That turns each depth map into a full metric map, giving dense coverage of the scene. Tests used twenty images drawn from a 296-image high-overlap flight. The rebuilt surfaces reached meter-level accuracy but were far more complete than standard results. Areas seen in only one photo, usually lost, were recovered.
arxiv-2503-04813:
Joykirat Singh, Tanmoy Chakraborty, and Akshay Nambi present SPHERE, a 2025 pipeline that helps small language models reason better at math. Small models often fail on multi step problems as early errors snowball. Good training data that show preferred reasoning paths are scarce.

SPHERE lets the model build its own training data in three stages. It generates solution steps, corrects its own errors, and produces varied valid paths to the same answer. Training on that data sharpened reasoning across several math benchmarks, from school level sets to olympiad problems. Some trained models matched or beat a top large model on certain sets. The authors argue self evolution can close much of the gap for small models.
arxiv-2503-04913:
Giddings and a large survey team study galaxy mergers inside a forming supercluster seen as it was long ago, in a 2025 paper. The Hyperion proto-supercluster sits at redshift about 2.5, meaning its light left when the universe was young. Dense regions are thought to speed up galaxy growth, and mergers are one growth path. The team used Hubble Space Telescope imaging plus rich survey data from the COSMOS field.

They measured how often galaxies there have close companions moving at similar speeds, a sign of interaction. Comparing that fraction with the emptier field shows whether crowding boosts mergers. The work feeds into the larger question of how the most massive structures in today's universe were assembled so early.
arxiv-2503-05013:
Jovan Mikić wrote a math paper from 2025 on a triangle of numbers tied to paths on a grid. Each number in the triangle counts paths from one corner to a point that never rise above the main diagonal. A cousin family counts paths that stay below a flatter line. Mikić gives a new formula that builds the triangle's numbers from an alternating sum.

He then proves that this sum can be divided evenly by both the cousin number and a central binomial count. The proof rests on a new class of binomial sums he names M sums. He also gives a fresh reading of a related family of fractions, linking them to a known set of Schröder numbers. The work ties three classic counting families into one frame.
arxiv-2503-05613:
Dong Shu and co-authors present a 2025 survey on sparse autoencoders, a tool for peering inside large language models. These models are powerful but opaque: many features overlap inside a single neuron pattern. A sparse autoencoder teases those tangled features apart into cleaner parts that humans can inspect.

The survey lays out how these tools are built and trained, including recent design gains. It sorts the ways researchers explain the features found, by looking at inputs or at outputs. It also reviews how to judge whether an autoencoder is doing its job well. The final part covers real uses, from understanding model behavior to steering it. The field aims to make model internals legible and safer to control.
arxiv-2503-05913:
Luo and co-authors squeeze the mathematics of vibrating atoms down to a fraction of its size. The force constants that describe how three or four atoms interact in a crystal form enormous tensors, and carrying them makes heat transport calculations crawl. Their tensor learning method finds low-rank stand-ins for these tensors of any order, solving an optimization problem to keep them faithful.

Compression reaches factors of a thousand to ten thousand for the three- and four-body tensors, while scattering rates and thermal conductivity stay accurate. Full conductivity calculations speed up nearly a thousand-fold across five varied materials, from silicon to a monoclinic oxide. The authors say the trick opens the door to strongly anharmonic materials that were previously out of reach.
arxiv-2503-06613:
Stars are born in dense cores inside cold gas clouds, but what chops the cloud into cores is debated. Kousuke Ishihara and co-authors weigh two suspects, gravity and turbulence, in two nearby clouds, the Polaris Flare and Lupus I. They catalog cores in space telescope maps and measure their masses and spacing.

Average core masses came out near a quarter of the Sun's mass in both clouds. Core spacing peaked between 0.1 and 0.2 parsecs, far tighter than gravity alone would set. That spacing instead matches the cloud's sonic scale, the length where turbulence turns quiet. Core densities also followed the statistical shape turbulence predicts. The authors conclude turbulence, not gravity, does the chopping here. Filament breaking showed no clear role.
arxiv-2503-06713:
Rohollah Khoshlahni and co-authors propose in 2025 a cooler way to create tiny magnetic whirlpools called skyrmions. In antiferromagnetic materials, where neighboring spins point opposite ways, these whirlpools could store data. The usual way to make them uses electric currents, which waste heat and limit the materials that work.

The team instead sends sound-like waves across the surface, which strain the material as they pass. That strain twists the spins and can seed a skyrmion with far less heating. Using a standard motion model, they show how the waves reshape skyrmion movement in nickel oxide and cobalt oxide like materials. The method opens a low-energy path for future magnetic devices.
arxiv-2503-06913:
Dohyun Ahn and Taeho Kim study how to pick the safest option under heavy tail risk, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A decision maker has a fixed budget of samples to split among options with unknown loss distributions. The best option is the one with the smallest extreme tail risk, and losses may be heavy-tailed.

The authors propose data-driven sequential sampling rules for this task. The rules aim to maximize the rate at which the chance of a wrong pick falls to zero. They prove their methods beat existing approaches on that measure. Numerical studies back the theory. The work speaks to fields like finance and engineering, where rare but huge losses matter most and cheap sampling is limited.
arxiv-2503-07313:
Missing values in data are rarely missing by pure chance; they cluster by who people are, and that can tilt a model's fairness. Aeysha Bhatti, Trudie Sandrock, and Johané Nienkemper-Swanepoel test that tilt in this 2025 paper. They punched large holes in three standard fairness datasets under three different missingness rules, then repaired the holes with simple fixes like deleting rows or filling averages.

Surprisingly, which rule made the holes mattered little for fairness. Deleting incomplete rows gave the fairest models on average, and random forests were the fairest learner. What often mattered was the pairing of fix and learner. The authors warn that quick, simple repairs carry fairness consequences worth checking.
arxiv-2503-07413:
Language models excel at chat, yet dense picture jobs like outlining objects or marking joints strain text-only answers. Yan Tai and co-authors presented in 2025 REF-VLM, a single framework trained to handle many such visual tasks end to end.

Its core idea splits each task into three named parts: the concept, the decoding type, and the target, marked by clear symbols. The team also built a training set of over one hundred million exchanges spanning twenty-five task types, mixing prompts like points and boxes with outputs like masks and depths. In tests, REF-VLM beat rival models across standard benchmarks, suggesting one referring scheme can unify varied visual work.
arxiv-2503-07513:
Siyuan Song, Jennifer Hu, and Kyle Mahowald test whether language models truly know their own minds, in a 2025 paper. Introspection would be gold: a model that reports its inner knowledge faithfully could be read like a witness. The team probes twenty-one open models in two fields, grammar sense and word prediction. In both, inner knowledge can be measured outright, from the odds the model itself puts on each string.

The test asks whether the model's spoken answers track its own odds better than a twin model's odds would. On the surface, prompted answers score high, as do probability reads. Yet no edge of self-access shows: the answers match a near-twin's inner state as well as the model's own. The authors conclude that fluent self-talk is not self-knowledge, and warn linguists not to grade a model's grammar by its interviews.
arxiv-2503-07613:
Nuzhat Nuari Khan Rivu, Md Kamrujjaman, and Asif Iqbal model the fight against HIV and AIDS in North America against the UNAIDS milestone targets. Their 2025 paper covers the 90-90-90 goals and their stricter 95-95-95 successors. Those targets mean nearly everyone with HIV knowing their status, nearly all of those on therapy, and nearly all of those with the virus suppressed.

The team contrasts chance based stochastic models with fixed deterministic ones. The chance based kind, they argue, mirror real world messiness better. They compute the basic reproduction number to guide interventions and check when the disease free and endemic states are stable. Optimal control methods then seek plans that cut prevalence at the lowest cost. Data came from the official UNAIDS site.
arxiv-2503-07913:
Cold atoms held in light grids near a chip make compact quantum sensors, but the grid must reach the chip's face. Robert Leonard and Spencer Olson describe a beam layout that does exactly that. Three beams strike a reflective chip coating and bounce back through themselves. Their interference builds a phase-stable three-dimensional lattice right up to the surface. The team built the lattice and measured how tightly it holds atoms.

A cooling method then chilled eighty million atoms to about one microkelvin inside the grid. Traps this close to a chip suit portable clocks and field sensors. The design keeps the optics simple while the physics stays near the surface where devices need it.
arxiv-2503-08213:
Models that search text for the right passage to feed a generator work well in English, but Hindi has lacked a search model built for it. Nandakishor M builds one from scratch in 2025, named DeepRAG, starting with more than 2.7 million Hindi text samples. A custom tokenizer was shaped around how Hindi words are built, and the model learned to place related passages near each other.

The new model beat the general multilingual models in use by twenty-three percent in retrieval precision. It also plugs into a common toolkit for building full Hindi question answering systems. The author offers the process as a template for other languages short on tailored tools. Language specific building, the work argues, pays off.
arxiv-2503-08313:
Shile Chen, Jiaxing Zhao, and Pengfei Zhuang calculate, in a 2025 paper, how a strong magnetic field distorts a classic probe of hot nuclear matter. The Drell-Yan process, in which a quark and antiquark annihilate into a lepton pair, reports on the earliest moments of a heavy-ion collision. Those same collisions briefly create the strongest magnetic fields in nature, so the probe and the field cannot be separated.

Working through the photon's decay into quark and lepton pairs inside the field, level by level, the authors find a clear suppression of the process at low and middle pair masses. Their counting is complete in the lower energy region. At higher masses, the widened phase space of the upper levels may instead lift the spectrum. The paper tells experimenters where the magnetic fingerprint should show in their data.
arxiv-2503-08613:
Ipek Efe and co-authors showed a chemistry-based way in 2025 to set the electric polarization inside ferroelectric films, atom layer by atom layer. Oxide links can host phenomena absent in bulk substances, and ferroelectric films are usually controlled by engineering the depolarizing field. This team used a varied lever: the charged sheets inside a layered Aurivillius substance. They tracked the sheets forming in situ during growth.

The findings reveal how those charged bismuth oxide layers polarize their surroundings, producing the group's characteristic antipolar arrangement. The team then used the stacking as an electrostatic setting to create new dipole setups, inserting a multiferroic layer into the form. Lattice chemistry, rather than outer fields, becomes the control knob. For future low-power memory and logic devices built on ferroelectrics, that is a truly new design freedom.
arxiv-2503-09113:
Yonas Tefera and co-authors build health scores for machine bearings that obey real world rules, in a paper from 2025. Plain data driven scores can drift in ways no real bearing would, while pure physics models lack full facts about the system.

Their method bakes three rules into training: scores must fall steadily, stay in a set range, and track signal energy. A constrained autoencoder learned from vibration charts of a standard bearing set. Its wear curves came out smoother and scored better on trend, steadiness, and rule fit than plain rivals. Single rule tests showed which rule drove which gain.
arxiv-2503-09213:
Mohammad Al-Turany and co-authors present a 2025 white paper on software for the next generation of physics experiments. Nuclear, particle, and astroparticle physics face swelling data volumes and complex computing needs. The paper, from the JENA computing effort, argues that software planning must start at the design stage of each experiment.

The report merges views from the three European strategy bodies for these fields. It lays out joint strategies for better software, shared frameworks, and computing infrastructure. Mixed hardware, from standard processors to graphics chips, gets special attention. Career paths for research software specialists are also addressed. The authors aim to align three communities behind common tools. Shared planning should cut duplicated effort across experiments.
arxiv-2503-09513:
Trigger-action gadgets let one smart device set off another, and attackers abuse the chain by faking events to fire devices they do not own. Md Morshed Alam and co-authors build a runtime defense called RESTRAIN in a 2025 paper. Older defenses check event fingerprints offline, while newer online ones lean on guessing the impact of an attack, which limits how widely they generalize.

RESTRAIN sends in defense agents that profile attack actions as they happen. Reinforcement learning then tunes a defense policy fitted to the security needs of that network. The system is platform-independent, working across different trigger-action setups. In experiments, the agent took effective real-time defense action against remote injection attacks. The authors present the approach as a more flexible shield for connected homes and buildings.
arxiv-2503-09713:
Timothée David-Cléris, Guillaume Laibe, and Yona Lapeyre present a fluid simulation code rebuilt to run on thousands of graphics processors at once, in a 2025 paper. The code, Shamrock, simulates astrophysical fluids with the smoothed particle method, a cloud of particles carrying the flow. It borrows the algorithm of the Phantom code and wraps it in a portable framework written for exascale machines.

Its tree structure, which groups nearby particles, rebuilds on the fly with negligible cost, so processors rarely wait on messages. In a uniform-density test with tens of billions of particles, one time step took a few seconds across more than a thousand graphics cards. That is billions of particles per second, with parallel efficiency above ninety percent. The authors pitch Shamrock for the coming generation of supercomputers and the huge cosmic simulations they enable.
arxiv-2503-10113: Shivashankar and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on counting splittings of numbers into parts painted in two colors. One color may only land on parts divisible by a power of five. Two-color partition counts hide arithmetic patterns. The team builds generating functions for these counts along arithmetic progressions of the total. From those formulas they prove an infinite family of Ramanujan-style congruences: the counts vanish modulo growing powers of five at regular intervals. The result extends partition congruence theory into a restricted two-color setting.
arxiv-2503-10313:
Arpan Kanrar, Charlotte Roelants, and Manoj Yadav advance, in a 2025 paper, the theory of skew left braces, an algebra form with two linked operations. Such forms grew out of work on hard equation sets and now stand as a field of their own. The team marks out a subclass where the center-like part and the lower chain of the brace play well with each other. In that class they define a graded form of sameness, called n-isoclinism, built on brace commutator words they set out.

They prove key claims for the first grade that match famed group theory results. Two braces that match in this sense share a common cover and a common host brace. The match also passes to the group built from the brace's two operations. Traits of nilpotency, a measure of how tame the brace is, stay the same under the match.
arxiv-2503-10613:
Advait Gupta, NandaKiran Velaga, Dang Nguyen, and Tianyi Zhou build an agent that edits images in steps while watching cost, in work from twenty twenty-five. Text-to-image models still struggle when edits come in many turns. Each turn can need a chain of tools, and tools vary in price and skill. Blind search for a good chain burns time and money. Language models plan well but judge costs poorly.

Their agent, CoSTA-star, works in three stages to blend both strengths. A language model first draws a tree of subtasks for the edit. That tree trims a large tool graph down to a small subgraph. A star search then finds a cheap, high-grade path through it. A vision model grades each step, and a fail updates tool scores at once. The search can then reroute fast and even switch modes mid-task.
arxiv-2503-10813:
Moffat presents a 2025 theoretical paper on black holes and the puzzles they raise for physics. Standard theory gives black holes a central point where density grows without bound, and it treats horizon formation in conflicting ways for near and far observers. Moffat proposes extending spacetime into complex numbers to address both issues.

He extends the Schwarzschild solution into that domain and uses contour methods to remove the singular point while keeping the main features. A new radial coordinate gives a smooth account of the interior. In this frame, a horizon can form in finite complex time, and information can be traced across it. The author also treats the collapse of a dust sphere in the same frame.
arxiv-2503-11313:
Beatrice Matilde Ferrari and co-authors shape electron beams with light before the beam hits its target, in this 2025 paper. Electron microscopes see detail at the scale of atoms, but shaping the electron wave itself has lagged behind the shaping tools long available for light. The team built a light-based modulator and fitted it into two ultrafast microscopes, ahead of the sample.

Light striking the electrons reworks both their sideways and forward wave traits in a controlled way. By reading the electrons' energy and momentum after the device, the team rebuilt the shaped wave at the sample plane and confirmed the shaping worked. They present the device as a step toward new imaging modes that exploit a sculpted probe, rather than a plain one, in fast electron microscopy.
arxiv-2503-11413:
Niels Pronk, Bowy La Rivière, and Natalia Chepiga map the phases of a frustrated spin chain, in this 2025 paper. The chain holds spin-1 atoms with competing neighbor forces and a single-ion term that favors certain spin states. On one side sits the Haldane phase, a protected state of matter; on the others, two ordered phases.

Two transition lines that bound the Haldane phase merge at a special point with higher symmetry, which the authors match to a known field theory. Past that point, a fresh line marks a deconfined quantum critical change between two orders that cannot coexist. The diagram gives a clean lattice home for that rare kind of transition.
arxiv-2503-11513:
Ziqin Zhou and co-authors build a layered tokenizer for text to video generation in a 2025 paper. A tokenizer squeezes video into tokens a language model can work with. Video is heavy: it spans space and time, repeats a lot, and shifts sharply. Their system stacks codebooks in layers, like classic animation workflows.

Top layers hold broad meaning at high squeeze; lower layers keep fine motion and detail. The scheme encoded eight second clips at about seventy percent fewer bits than rival tokenizers, with like picture quality. Tests probed the trade between squeeze and fidelity. The authors argue that strong semantic tokens make the language model's job simpler.
arxiv-2503-11713:
Juan Carlos Perdomo revisits an old puzzle, in a 2025 preprint, about whether social events can be predicted at all. Predictions about society do not just describe the future. They shape it, by changing what people expect and do. Twentieth-century thinkers such as Merton and Simon treated this loop as a core problem for social science. Perdomo gives the question a modern form using tools from machine learning theory.

He draws on performative prediction, where the forecast changes the data, and on outcome indistinguishability. His main result says accurate prediction of social events is always efficiently possible. That holds no matter how strongly the forecast bends the outcome. Yet he also shows such forecasts are often not what we actually want. The paper closes by weighing what forecasters should aim for instead. It speaks to both social scientists and builders of prediction systems.
arxiv-2503-11813:
Lazaros Souvaitzis, Antti Rantala, and Thorsten Naab simulate what happens when two star clusters merge around massive black holes, in a 2025 astronomy paper. Each cluster in their runs held a black hole of five hundred solar masses. As the clusters combined, the two holes paired into a tight binary that slung stars and smaller black holes around.

Within a hundred million years, about eight hundred stars fled faster than fifty kilometers per second, and some thirty stellar black holes escaped too. Roughly thirty stars were hurled beyond three hundred kilometers per second. Control runs showed the paired holes, not the merger alone, drive the ejections. The remnants kept a gentle spin that would be hard to read as a sign of the hidden holes. The authors expect the hole pairs to merge within the age of the universe, sending out gravitational waves for future detectors.
arxiv-2503-11913:
Aman Gupta, Daniel Prasanth, and Venkat Chandra Gunja show how a fully classical client can use a quantum server in secret, in two thousand twenty-five. Future quantum services will likely pair many weak clients with a few strong servers. The client must hide both its data and its task, even from the server itself.

Their setup joins an older blind computing protocol with a method that prepares starting states from afar. Unlike the older plan, the work does not proceed step by step with the server. They ran the scheme on a public quantum service with worked examples. The authors note that its security was shown in a game-based model, the weakest such model.
arxiv-2503-12013:
Chen Du and co-authors report in 2025 the first clear timing signal from a repeating fast radio burst source. Fast radio bursts are fierce flashes from deep space, and many think a highly magnetic neutron star lies behind them.

The source sent more than twenty eight hundred bursts over forty nine days of watching. On most days no steady rhythm showed up. On two days, though, a period near 1.7 seconds stood out with strong support from tests. The slight growth in the period points to a young magnetar, about forty four years old in spin down terms, with a very strong surface field.
arxiv-2503-12113:
Six researchers wrote a physics paper in two thousand twenty-five on how electrons and lattice vibrations couple in correlated materials. That coupling can seed superconductivity, but its size is usually computed with simple approximations. Near a metal-to-insulator transition, electron density fluctuations grow large and those approximations break down.

Using a dynamical mean-field method, the team studied a doped square-lattice model near the Mott transition. Where the charge response swells at long wavelengths, the coupling to the lattice grows strongly even if the bare coupling is small. The boost feeds back into the electrons and into the pairing force between them.
arxiv-2503-12613:
Rashid Mushkani, Hugo Berard, and Shin Koseki argue that disagreement should guide city design choices. Their 2025 study in Montreal asked thirty-five residents to judge twenty streets. The group included wheelchair users, seniors, LGBTQIA2+ residents, and immigrants. City scores often squash many needs into one number, hiding minority views.

Group gaps were patterned: wheelchair users split most on access and practicality. LGBTQIA2+ residents stressed inclusion and liveliness, while seniors prized security. Talks closed knowledge gaps but not value clashes. The team then built a bargaining method that weighs budgets and reports the worst-off group's outcome too. In a pilot, the bargained plan lifted total and worst-group scores and cut inequality.
arxiv-2503-12813:
Alizadeh and four co-authors forecast epidemics with a hybrid model in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Their network pairs convolutional layers, which read spatial patterns, with memory layers that track time. Two nature-inspired search methods, named for whales and gray wolves, tune the settings. COVID-19 case data from twenty-four countries served as the test bed.

The hybrid beat classic statistical models and a memory network alone. Errors fell by margins the authors report as statistically firm. The tuning step covered learning rates, batch sizes, and training rounds. The authors pitch the frame as a general tool for outbreak planning. It is meant to guide resource allocation in future crises as well as past ones.
arxiv-2503-12913:
Jakob Moderl, Anders Westerkam, Alexander Venus, and Erik Leitinger present a Bayesian method to find and place objects with radar. Their twenty twenty-five paper fuses data from several sensors at once. The method hunts for the few active entries in large dictionaries, where each entry stands for a possible object at set parameters.

The twist is that the dictionary parameters themselves are estimated, not fixed. Group sparsity helps: linked entries rise or fall together. In a multi-radar test, the method kept close objects apart even as their paths crossed, a case where a rival method blurred them. Adding more radars sharpened both detection and position estimates.
arxiv-2503-13113:
Gabriele Sanguin and co-authors use two-level optimization to teach neural networks honest confidence. Modern networks often sound sure when they should not. Their 2025 paper frames training as a bilevel problem, where an inner task fits the data and an outer task tunes how trust is scored. The network thus learns to grade its own calls while it learns the calls themselves.

Trials ran on toy shapes and on a blood alcohol dataset. The rival was isotonic regression, a standard fix applied after training. The bilevel route cut calibration error while keeping accuracy intact. The authors pitch the frame as a built-in cure, not a patch. Better-graded confidence matters wherever software calls feed real choices, from clinics to courts.
arxiv-2503-13313:
Mat Rybak and colleagues use a gravitational lens as a microscope to settle what makes radio-quiet quasars glow at long wavelengths. Candidate sources include star formation, a dust torus, weak jets, and a corona above the accretion disk. Telling them apart needs resolution no millimeter telescope has. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team exploits microlensing: stars in the foreground galaxy magnify the compact parts of a quadruply lensed quasar. Between two observing epochs years apart, the millimeter flux ratios among the images changed strikingly.

The change fits microlensing of a source no bigger than a few dozen astronomical units across. That compactness leaves coronal emission as the likely origin. The millimeter and X-ray brightnesses also follow the classic relation known from stellar coronae. The authors call it the first unambiguous evidence for coronae in radio-quiet quasars.
arxiv-2503-13613:
Zachary Mauri and co-authors present a 2025 method for computing hybrid states of light and matter from first principles. These states, called exciton-polaritons, mix photons with excitons and offer ways to tune how a material behaves. Past models tend to wash out atomic detail and the many body physics that real systems need. The team build their method on a standard equation for paired electron and hole states.

In their frame, the hybrid states emerge from an attractive exchange force between electrons and holes that changes over time. Tests on two materials show that this force shrinks the size of the exciton by a lot and boosts its light signal by about ten times. Results for a third material match measured dispersion curves well. The method also shows how light coupling reshapes both single particle and collective excitations.
arxiv-2503-14113:
Crowds of agents that follow leaders appear in traffic, robotics, and animal groups. Melanie Harms and co-authors study how to steer them with sparse control, acting on few agents rather than all. Starting from a model that tracks every individual, they find conditions for fast stabilisation. Under those conditions a Lyapunov function, an energy-like measure of disorder, decays exponentially for leaders and followers together.

They then extend the analysis to a hybrid model: followers described in bulk by a mean-field equation, leaders still tracked one by one. There they identify how strong the control gain and the interactions must be to stabilise the whole system at a target state. The results show how the sparsity of the control and the coupling strengths jointly decide whether coordinated behaviour emerges. The work gives designers of multi-agent systems concrete conditions to aim for.
arxiv-2503-14313:
Jie Chang, Michael Grabchak, and Jialin Zhang test confidence intervals built on Turing's estimator. Their 2025 paper deals with a classic problem: guessing the chance of outcomes that never showed up in a sample. Turing's method gives such guesses, but the error bars around them need care.

Simulations map how several interval forms behave on small samples. The team gives a rule for picking the right interval for a given sample. They apply the method to authorship, sorting tweets by writer. New theory backs the approach for two common discrete distributions. The work joins computing practice with proofs about the estimator's long-run behaviour in samples.
arxiv-2503-14813:
Zhongyu Ouyang, Chunhui Zhang, Yaning Jia, and Soroush Vosoughi study stability in click prediction for social platforms in a 2025 study. Recommenders judge success by click-through rate, a binary guess about whether a user will tap an item. Real feeds change fast, though, and models chase short-term noise, overfitting passing fads instead of durable patterns of interaction.

The authors argue that scaling the supervision signal acts quietly as a smoothness control on the model, in the style of a Lipschitz regularizer. Steadier models should track genuine user and item dynamics rather than jitter. The insight links a training detail to robustness in fast-moving online environments.
arxiv-2503-14913:
Xiao Chen, Yixin Luo, and Jingrun Chen blend neural networks into the finite element method in a 2025 numerical analysis study. Finite elements are the workhorse for engineering equations, while physics-informed neural networks learn approximate solutions from the equation itself. Their hybrid runs in three steps: train the network, add its solution to the finite element space, then solve finally inside that enriched space.

Enrichment can add or multiply the network's output against standard basis functions. Convergence analysis and tests support the scheme. The blend aims to let a rough neural guess do the hard shaping, leaving the reliable finite element machinery to certify the answer.
arxiv-2503-15313: The Euclid Collaboration presents a paper from its first quick data release in 2025 on how galaxy patterns change with cosmic time. It studies two linked patterns: how the share of passive galaxies varies with crowding, and how galaxy shapes vary with crowding. The work spans the span from redshift one down to a quarter of that value, using the new Euclid survey data.
arxiv-2503-15413:
Torbjörn Lundberg and Leif Lönnblad presented a 2025 model for how particle showers reconnect in the PYTHIA program. Color reconnection affects the final mix of particles after a crash. Past models used only a flat measure of distance in the cross plane.

Their new model uses full distance in space and time between partons to set the chance of a reconnection. It builds on a dipole view and is meant for the Angantyr model of heavy-ion crashes. The authors test its effect in electron, proton, and lead crash systems of many sizes. Their main goal is a fair account of basic particle counts across those systems.
arxiv-2503-15613:
Gavin Lamb and co-authors published this astronomy paper in 2025. It decodes a flicker in gamma-ray burst 211211A, an odd event: a long burst from a merger, not a collapsing star. A precursor flash arrived a second before the main event, carrying a claimed rhythm of about twenty cycles per second.

Taking the rhythm as real, the authors work out what engine could produce it. The pulses demand a relativistic jet and an episodic engine switching on and off at the rhythm's period. For a black hole engine, the wobble fits precession of the inner disk a few gravitational radii out. For a magnetar engine, disk instabilities at tens of kilometers could do it, given strong enough fields. Neither engine can be excluded. The authors lean toward a neutron star and black hole merger remnant, with the rhythm born as the young jet first couples to its disk.
arxiv-2503-15713:
Stokes waves are smooth, repeating waves that travel across deep water, and their stability is a classic math problem. Sergey Dyachenko and Dmitry Pelinovsky studied Euler's equations for such waves in a 2025 paper. They used a change of variables that maps the wavy surface in a cleaner way, then asked when a stable wave starts to turn unstable.

The pair prove that a new unstable mode appears at each peak of the energy curve, as long as wave speed is not also at a peak there. They derive a short form for the new modes and use numbers to show they grow only as steepness rises. The proof matches earlier numeric work.
arxiv-2503-15813: Yi Gao and Kui Wang prove a sharp bound for vibration tones of domains in Gauss space in 2025. The tones are the first nonzero Neumann eigenvalues, which describe how a region rings when its edge is free. Their result bounds the harmonic mean of the first several tones for domains that are symmetric about the origin. The bound is best possible of its kind. It extends an earlier Szegö-Weinberger type result in the same setting, which covered a narrower case.
arxiv-2503-16213:
The ATLAS Collaboration searched in 2025 for heavy neutral leptons, hypothetical long-lived particles that could explain neutrino masses. The search looked for such particles born in the decay of W bosons, using proton collision data from the Large Hadron Collider. Two decay patterns were targeted, one fully leptonic and one mixing a lepton with a pion.

Both patterns would appear as vertices displaced from the collision point, a signature of a long-lived particle. No excess of such events was seen. The null result excludes these particles below a set mass for both major theoretical variants, down to very small mixing with known neutrinos. The analysis sets the terms for future searches of this kind.
arxiv-2503-16313:
Ramis Khasianov wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on bounded analytic functions in the unit disk, a classic topic in complex analysis. The paper derives new inequalities for weighted sums of the coefficients in the power series of such functions. Its methods build on work by Kayumov and Ponnusamy and on Reich's theorem about majorizing subordinate functions.

Sharp estimates are obtained for the area of the image of a smaller disk under functions given by lacunary series, series with many missing terms. Estimates are also proved for the Bohr-Bombieri function of the Hadamard convolution operator, under weaker assumptions on the first coefficient than earlier work required. The differentiation operator serves as a test case showing where the bounds apply.
arxiv-2503-16913:
Lishui Fan and five co-authors present FGIT, a fine-tuning method that helps language models write correct code, in this 2025 paper. Models trained the standard way sometimes produce code that looks right but fails, because training treats every token alike. The slips usually hide in small stretches where a wrong version differs from a right one.

FGIT first compares correct code with near-miss wrong code at line and token level to find those error-sensitive stretches. Training then weights those stretches more heavily, with the weights shifting as training goes on. Across seven models and three benchmarks, the method raised first-try success by about seven percent on average. Some smaller tuned models even beat a closed-source rival, and gains held across many model families, which the authors take as a sign of broad usefulness.
arxiv-2503-17113:
Vittorio Pagni, Sigurd Huber, Michael Epping, and Michael Felderer speed up a way to load classical data into a quantum state, in work from 2025. Loading is a known bottleneck: a list of numbers must be written into the heights of a quantum wave. Their scheme improves a prior one by a square-root factor in time.

Variants cover complex numbers and a dial that sets how much of the work runs in parallel. The qubit count grows gently with list size and the dial. Run time depends on how dense the data are. For random inputs, the team proves a near-minimal mean run time. Tests on radar satellite images suggest real data behave just as well, which could let quantum transforms gain an edge.
arxiv-2503-17213:
Ting Sun and co-authors present PP-DocLayout, a family of models that map the layout of document pages, in a 2025 paper. Layout mapping finds titles, text blocks, tables, and formulas, and it feeds many document tools. Old models struggled with varied formats, messy pages, and the speed needed for huge data sets.

The system spots twenty-three region types across many document kinds. Three sizes are offered. The large model scores highest, at 90.4 percent on a standard overlap measure, and reads a page in about thirteen milliseconds on a test GPU. The small model trades some accuracy for speed on weak hardware, even running on a plain CPU. The authors aim the tool at building training data for document and multimodal AI.
arxiv-2503-17613:
Nicholas Tenev built an economics model in 2025 about why new workplace tools can fail. A manager wants staff to spend real effort testing a new tool before the group decides to adopt it. Checking takes work, and no one wants to be the only one who bothers.

When staff can act together, they may all skip the checking, since firing a whole group at once costs the manager too much. A widely useful tool can make the problem worse, because the gain from skipping grows. Workers may even keep using a tool they know is flawed. Tenev links the logic to the mortgage crisis and to new AI tools.
arxiv-2503-17713:
Benjamin Zhou wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on counting curves in certain geometric spaces at all levels of complexity. Gromov-Witten invariants count curves in a space, sorted by genus, a measure of how many holes the curve's surface has. Zhou works with a pair: a smooth Fano surface and a smooth divisor inside it.

From that pair he builds a bundle space and pulls out higher genus invariants for it. The method leans on a degeneration formula for maps between log spaces. Part of the count is done by a link between refined tropical curve counting and log Gromov-Witten theory. As a bonus, flips of the space yield a blow-up formula for the invariants. When the surface is toric, he also proves an all-genus match between open and closed versions of the count.
arxiv-2503-17813:
Shue Long Chan argues that security bug scores miss a whole dimension: how connected a bug is. The standard scoring system weighs how easy a bug is to exploit against the harm it does. That covers the known facts. It says little about the fog around a bug, where many exploit paths and side effects may lurk.

Chan proposes connectedness, a count of how strongly a bug ties to other entities in a system. Wide ties mean wider possible impact and more doubt about the true score. The short paper makes the case for adding this axis to severity calls.
arxiv-2503-18713:
Sweeping a future collider's beam across the top quark's birth threshold would weigh the quark to within a few MeV, project Matteo Defranchis and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv study. The scan is on the program for the electron positron stage of the planned Future Circular Collider.

Experimental precision could reach about 7 MeV on the mass and 12 on the width, in a clean mass scheme. Theory errors from missing calculation orders run several times larger today, so sharper theory is the bottleneck. The authors also size up a later run above threshold aimed at the top quark's grip on the Higgs field.
arxiv-2503-18813:
Edoardo Debenedetti and nine co-authors present a design that shields language model agents from prompt injection attacks, in a paper from 2025. Agents that read untrusted data can be tricked by hidden instructions inside that data. Model-level fixes have proven brittle, so the team builds safety into the system around the model.

Their layer first pulls the control plan and data paths from the trusted request itself. Untrusted content then cannot steer what the program does next. Capability checks also block private data from leaving through unapproved calls. On a standard agent benchmark, the shielded system solved most tasks while giving provable security.
arxiv-2503-19013:
Joheen Chakraborty and co-authors find pulse bursts in a star-tear event in a 2025 paper. Pulse bursts are soft X-ray flares that recur near huge black holes in small galaxy cores. Near ten hosts were known when the work was done, the team notes.

Their burst host is a star torn by its black hole that also shows rare crown lines. Bursts recur on wild spans, from half a day to a few days per gap. Proof now ties some bursts to fresh flows from such tears, this case the third.
arxiv-2503-19213:
Murong Yue surveys how language model agents answer questions. The survey appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Older QA agents need heavy data and adapt poorly to new settings. Agents built on large language models use the model as a reasoning core. They can also act in outside environments, fetching and checking facts. That mix beats plain pipelines and naive model answers.

The review sorts the field by stage of work. Planning, question understanding, retrieval, and answer generation each get a section. Designs within each stage are compared. Yue then lists open challenges facing these systems. Future directions close the survey. Builders of question-answering tools get a map of current practice. The paper also marks where gains are likeliest next.
arxiv-2503-19313:
Chao Li and Boyu Zhang wrote a 2025 math paper on the shape of stable minimal hypersurfaces inside a space that is topologically a four dimensional sphere. A minimal hypersurface is a sheet that cannot shrink its area with small wiggles, and stable ones resist such shrinking in a stronger sense. The authors build such sheets with simple topology inside certain compact four dimensional spaces with boundary. Those spaces sit inside a smooth space that has the same overall shape as a sphere.

For spaces with positive scalar curvature, they prove a stable sheet exists that is either a three dimensional sphere or a joined sum of simple loop products. That rules out a wide class of more complex shapes in the sheet's basic parts. The results carry over to the topology of black holes in four dimensions. The proof joins tools from geometric measure theory with four dimensional topology.
arxiv-2503-19413: Aritra Bhowmick, Jin-ichi Itoh, and Sachchidanand Prasad prove a stability theorem in differential geometry in a 2025 paper. The cut locus of a point on a curved surface is the set of places where shortest paths from that point stop being shortest. The authors show that if the metric is nudged slightly, in a sense that controls its second derivatives, the cut locus moves only slightly, measured in Hausdorff distance. Along the way they prove the cut time itself depends continuously on the metric.
arxiv-2503-19513:
Franz Waltenberger and co-authors track what happened when Reddit killed its third party apps in a 2025 paper. In mid 2023 the platform forced beloved clients like Apollo to shut, and many predicted an exodus. The team followed alternative app users from January to November 2023 to see who actually left.

About twenty two percent of those users quit Reddit for good. Among users who had publicly threatened to leave, forty five percent followed through. Yet total platform activity showed no visible dent. The authors conclude most users found switching to the official app cheaper than moving platforms entirely. The episode offers a rare real world case for migration research.
arxiv-2503-19613:
Milan Groshev and colleagues field-test OROS, a system that jointly runs 5G networks and teams of mobile robots with an eye on energy. Robots sent outdoors on 5G can offload work to the cloud, yet battery life still caps their missions. OROS coordinates robot navigation and sensing while tuning the cloud services behind them, guided by live feedback.

Trials ran on shop-bought robots over a campus 5G network. By shifting heavy computing to the edge and switching off idle sensors, OROS saved about fifteen percent of robot energy against leading methods. Longer battery life means longer missions and better use of each robot.
arxiv-2503-19813:
Cristian Morasso and co-authors guide the choice of a baseline in AI explanations in a 2025 paper. Some explanation tools compare a model's answer on real input with its answer on a neutral input, called the baseline. Which neutral input one picks can change the whole story the tool tells. A poor pick makes the explanation mislead, even when the model is sound.

The authors argue the baseline should sit on the model's decision edge, where its answer flips. They offer a way to sample that edge and pick a baseline from it. Tests on fake cases and checks with standard tools back the method. Their guidelines aim to cut the guesswork in baseline choice and make explanations more trustworthy.
arxiv-2503-20013:
Simulations of magnetized plasma near black holes usually skip real electrical resistance. They trust the grid itself to supply a stand-in. Michael Grehan and co-authors test whether that trust is earned. They compare four model families, from ideal magnetohydrodynamics to force-free electrodynamics, on two basic behaviors: how current sheets decay, and how magnetic field lines reconnect.

In one dimension, the stand-in resistance in ideal models decays too slowly, spreading subdiffusively. Models with explicit resistance match theory properly. In two dimensions, ideal models reconnect at rates tied to grid resolution, a warning sign. At fine resolution they converge toward the resistive result. The study draws a clear line: numerical resistance is not physical resistance, and some questions can only be asked with the real thing switched on.
arxiv-2503-20413:
Automated proof search builds trees of attempts, but most tools hard-wire how those trees are stored and walked. Kevin Kappelmann presents Zippy, a framework that loosens those choices. It stays independent of the concrete tree shape, the search algorithm, the state handling, and the effects a search may trigger.

Zippy grows from functional programming ideas: zippers for moving through trees, plus arrows, monads, and lenses. The result is a search users can inspect, navigate, customize, and extend rather than merely run. Kappelmann implemented the framework in Isabelle/ML, the metalanguage of a major proof assistant. The 2025 paper targets people who build proof tools, not just use them.
arxiv-2503-20813:
Steven Louis and co-authors wrote this engineering paper in 2025 on magnetic tunnel junctions, tiny stacks whose resistance flips with magnetism. Such parts anchor spintronic memory and brain-like chips. Designers need a circuit model that acts like the real part, not just a rough sketch. The team built one from the physics of the stack and ran it in LTspice, a common circuit simulator.

They checked the model against direct math solutions of the governing equation. The two agreed closely across key acts: resonance, switching by field or by spin push, and steady oscillation. The model takes live fields and voltages as inputs, which suits rich designs. The authors offer it as a fast, true stand-in that lets whole circuits be tested with such junctions inside.
arxiv-2503-21113:
Yang Xu and co-authors send image data through scattering media with a fast optical gate in a 2025 paper. Fog, tissue, and turbid water scramble light, which ruins pictures. Their gate uses a thin indium tin oxide film whose response spikes near a special wavelength band.

Two short pulses mix in the film, and only unscattered, ballistic photons convert to a new color. That filtering keeps the spatial pattern held in brightness or phase with high fidelity. When the scattering churned over time, flicker fell by about a hundredfold. Unlike bulk crystal gates, the sub-micron film keeps fine spatial detail. The demo points toward imaging inside the body and free-space optical links.
arxiv-2503-21413:
The BESIII Collaboration reports first sightings of two particle decays in a 2025 paper from its detector in Beijing. The decays involve heavy charmed baryons, particles that hold a charm quark, breaking into a lighter charmed baryon plus two neutral pions. Seeing a decay for the first time confirms theory and sharpens mass and width values.

Both parent particles are excited states of the same base baryon, at two nearby mass levels. Their decay into two neutral pions is hard to catch, since neutral pions leave faint traces in the detector. First observations of this kind help map the family of charmed baryons. Hundreds of authors share credit, as is normal for a large collider team.
arxiv-2503-21613:
Javier Coronado-Blázquez tests whether large language models can sum up books from memory alone in a 2025 paper. No source text is given to the models. The test uses a varied set of books and several model designs.

Each AI summary is scored against a strong human summary. Every model also grades the work of the others, not just its own. Word overlap and meaning scores add a second check. Results show clear gaps in content and style across models, plus signs that models favor their own style. The study helps show what these models store about books and where memory-based summaries fall short.
arxiv-2503-21713:
Gee and co-authors present a 2025 study on whether winning or losing streaks bend a chess player's next results. Sports lore claims such winner-loser effects are real, but data are usually thin. Online chess offers millions of games to test the claim. The team built a layered Bayesian model that lets each player carry a personal effect size.

Across the whole pool, they found little sign of a shared streak effect. A few single players did show signs in their own records. Streak data twist through time, so the authors checked their model with care. The paper is a cautious verdict: momentum in chess looks personal, not universal.
arxiv-2503-22013:
Charles Maher and Katherine Newhall study unusual network materials in a 2025 paper. Some materials suppress density swings on large scales in a way normal disordered matter does not. Network versions promise to combine that trait with useful physical properties. The question is how much of the trait survives when a point pattern is turned into a network.

They built four kinds of network layouts from both ordinary and special point patterns, in two and three dimensions. None of the layouts kept the full trait of the starting pattern. How much survived depended on the layout chosen and on disorder in the pattern, but not on the beam shape used to render it.
arxiv-2503-22213:
Maltsev studies how contour lines grow in a special class of almost repeating energy landscapes, in a 2025 paper. The landscapes are quasi-periodic potentials with eightfold rotational symmetry, patterns that never quite repeat yet hold a strict hidden order. Such patterns arise in photonics, the science of light-guiding materials, where eightfold designs are prized. The question is how the closed level lines of these potentials expand as they near the percolation threshold, the point where paths first connect across the whole pattern.

Maltsev estimates the scaling indices that govern that growth rate. Those numbers allow a fair comparison between these orderly quasicrystalline landscapes and the random potentials used in many physics models of the plane. The work adds a quantitative handle on how eightfold quasicrystals differ from mere disorder, a distinction that matters when engineers choose patterns for optical devices.
arxiv-2503-22813:
Kaibo Hu surveys the many faces of cohomology in a 2025 paper. Cohomology sorts holes and twists in shapes, a core tool of topology. Hu shows the same ideas now run through much of applied math and science.

Chains of spaces, called complexes, code key facts about a system. They can tell if an equation has a fix, if it is the only one, and if it stays stable. Cases range from solid and fluid flow to Einstein equations and networks. New grid methods that keep the chain shape help make those codes work on a computer.
arxiv-2503-23213:
Diana Bolanos and co-authors build RECALL-MM in 2025, a data set of consumer product recalls meant for risk analysis. Recall records hold lessons about hazards that designers could use earlier, yet they sit underused. The team drew records from the United States product safety database and enriched them with generated material.

The data set pairs recall text with product names and images in one shared space, shown through maps that cluster like products together. Two case studies show designers placing a new idea among past recalls to spot hazards before launch. In a third, a large language model judged hazards from product images alone and often matched the historical record. Gaps also appeared, marking where image only judgment falls short and human review still counts.
arxiv-2503-23413:
Rajesh Kumar and co-authors review what neutron stars teach about dense matter in a 2025 paper. A neutron star packs more than a sun's mass into a ball the size of a city. No lab on Earth can match that crush, so the stars act as a natural test bed.

The review pulls rules from three sides: deep theory, Earth-based tests, and sky data. Lab clues come from atom smash tests and low-energy nuclear work. Sky clues come from star masses, sizes, and waves from star mergers. Set side by side, the clues narrow how stiff dense matter can be. That helps link small-scale nuclear rules to what telescopes see.
arxiv-2503-23713:
Priyanka Gautam and four co-authors speed up the hunt for the best people to seed a rumor, an ad, or a warning in a changing social network, in this 2025 paper. Influence maximization picks a small seed set whose spread reaches the most people. In temporal networks, where friendships and contacts appear and vanish, recomputing seeds from scratch at every moment is ruinously expensive.

The team's predictor pairs a graph neural network, which reads the network's structure, with a bidirectional memory model that reads its history forwards and backwards. Together they nominate candidate seed nodes with about ninety percent accuracy across varied networks. Only the shortlisted candidates then face the expensive spread simulations, cutting the computational bill sharply. Marketers chasing viral reach and officials planning emergency messaging share the same mathematics: find the few mouths from which the message travels farthest, in a network that will not sit still.
arxiv-2503-23913:
Xiaoxuan Wang, Yihe Deng, Mingyu Derek Ma, and Wei Wang propose a weighting trick to help language models train on their own math work, in a paper from 2025. Models can write step-by-step solutions and learn from them, needing only the final answer as a check. Which self-made examples to stress, though, was an open question.

Their method, EAST, weighs each example by the model's uncertainty, read from entropy. A single dial sets how sharply the weights favor unsure cases. On the MATH benchmark, plain self-training gained nothing, while EAST gained about one point. On GSM8K, EAST added one to two points over the plain method. The authors argue that hard, unsure cases teach the model most.
arxiv-2503-24113:
A giant radio telescope now being built will pour out hundreds of petabytes of sky data each year. Giuseppe Tudisco, Fabio Vitello, Eva Sciacca, and Ugo Becciani describe a viewing tool for that flood in a 2025 paper. Their tool, VisIVO, helps astronomers see patterns in huge data cubes.

The tool is moving from a desktop program to a client-server system. Heavy work will run in parallel on computing clusters, while the user steers from a light front end. That shift lets teams open and probe files too large for one machine. The authors frame the move as a must for the new telescope era, where data size outgrows local disks.
arxiv-2503-24213:
Tamás Kriváchy and Martin Kerschbaumer tackle a weak point in tests of quantum nonlocality, in their 2025 paper on the triangle network. In that setup, three parties share quantum states with no outside inputs, and the nonlocal effects are thought to be fragile. Lost photons are the main worry, since missing detections open a loophole that weakens any claim.

Working with special photon states called N00N states, the pair show the opposite of fragility. Even the smallest such state tolerates up to ten percent photon loss in the channels while still certifying nonlocality. Under a fuller noise model, guided by neural network search, the tolerance rises to about fifty percent. They also show the method works with realistic light sources, using the sources' own heralding signals so that no rounds need to be thrown away after the fact. The detection loophole, they argue, can be closed.
arxiv-2504-00013:
Joachim Baumeister and seven co-authors published a paper in 2025 on configuring complex products at industrial scale. Customers increasingly want tailored products, from bikes to machinery, and each order must respect thousands of compatibility rules. The authors offer the field a shared testbed so competing solvers can be compared fairly.

Their COOM suite holds product models written in a dedicated language, sorted into three layers of rising difficulty, each illustrated with a bicycle model and joined by larger scalable examples. A solving workflow based on answer set programming handles the models, and the paper shows how the same suite adapts to other solving paradigms. A common benchmark, the authors argue, is what the configuration community needs to measure real progress.
arxiv-2504-00313:
Zequn Zheng, Hongchao Zhang, and Guangming Zhou decomposed hard tensors with generating math rules in a 2025 paper. Splitting a multi-way data array into a sum of simple rank-one pieces underlies squeezing and signal separation. The middle ranks, between the largest and second-largest dimensions, defeat standard iterative methods, and flattening tricks inherit the same hard case. Symbol-based direct methods exist, yet they demand uniqueness and grow expensive at high rank.

Their two-stage method first solves a generating math rule system, then refines by tuning. Handling even non-unique decompositions as long as rank stays within the largest dimension. The flattening-first workflow common in practice is exactly the regime targeted.
arxiv-2504-00513:
Asma Yamani, Malak Baslyman, and Moataz Ahmed test whether language models can draft user stories for AI systems in this 2025 study. A user story is a short note stating who wants a feature and why. Writing good requirements for AI tools is hard, and few open examples exist because most systems are private and their documents stay closed.

The team fed abstracts from research papers to three language models and collected 1,260 stories drawn from forty-two papers across many fields. They graded the stories with a standard quality frame and also pulled out safety and ethics needs. The models wrote stories that matched varied user needs well. The authors share the full set as a public data set for research and early design work.
arxiv-2504-00713:
Rijun Huang, Qingjun Jin, and Yi Li push a classic model of particle physics to a record depth in 2025. The model, set in two dimensions, describes fermions that interact through direct contact with each other. Its high-energy behavior is hard to pin down because endless extra terms can appear.

A symmetry argument shrinks the set of extra terms that truly matter. The team computed the key running rule, the beta function, for one such term at seven loops of diagrams, confirming it feeds real divergences. Their tricks turned hard integrals into ones a graphical method could solve. No model with spinning particles had passed five loops before.
arxiv-2504-00913:
Joel Dahlin and co-authors study solar flares in this 2025 paper. Flares are sudden bursts on the Sun that turn stored magnetic energy into heat, motion, and fast particles. The team looks at how magnetic fields snap and reconnect in three dimensions during a flare. Their main tool is a set of detailed computer models of an erupting flare.

The models show a sheet of electric current filled with small magnetic loops called plasmoids. The team traces field lines over time and marks where they shorten fast, which signals reconnection. Those events leave spiral marks along the flare ribbons seen on the Sun's surface. The marks match fine detail in real telescope images, which helps read what spacecraft see.
arxiv-2504-01213:
Banafsheh Adami and Nima Karimian build a system that tells real touchless fingerprints from fakes. Their 2025 paper addresses a security gap: contactless fingerprint readers are comfortable, but easier to spoof with printed or molded fakes. Their design joins a transformer-based image network with a memory module that sharpens attention, plus a dynamic filter at its core.

Training mixes real and spoof images across three public data sets. Error rates came out very low, under a tenth of a percent for rejecting real users and near one percent for accepting fakes, beating prior domain adaptation methods. The work targets phone-grade convenience without surrendering the door.
arxiv-2504-02113:
Francesco Giacosa and Martin Rohrmoser examine a surprising break of isospin symmetry in heavy-ion collisions, in a 2025 paper. Isospin is a near-symmetry of the strong force, and it holds well in empty space. A recent experiment, though, found far more charged than neutral kaons when argon and scandium nuclei collided. The authors use a quark recombination approach to build a ratio that should equal one whenever the symmetry holds.

With that yardstick, nucleus-nucleus collisions break the symmetry clearly, at a high level of confidence. Proton-proton data, by contrast, show no such break. The team predicts other boosted ratios in heavy-ion collisions, such as protons to neutrons near 1.2. They also extend the method to incoming antimatter, useful for pion-nucleus studies.
arxiv-2504-02313:
Zhuoran Tan and co-authors build a learning system to catch stealth attacks in supply chains, in this 2025 paper. Modern supply chains mix software, hardware, and digital assets from many sources. Those links create entry points that advanced persistent threats love to use.

Current defenses lean on integrity ledgers or on reading open source code directly. Fast, hidden intrusions can slip past both styles of guard. The team learn from time-stamped graphs that carry provenance records. Sharing the learning across machines keeps large chains manageable. Provenance shows where each asset came from and who touched it. That trail gives the detector context that raw alerts lack.
arxiv-2504-02613:
Asad Mahmood and co-authors design drone-assisted 5G networks that adapt to moving users in this 2025 paper. Drones can serve as flying base stations where ground coverage is weak. Their paths and the network's resources must be planned together. Users move, so the plan has to track them in real time. The team built a lean prediction model for user motion. Users are grouped by a clustering trick to keep the math tractable.

The joint problem aims to lift the worst user's data rate. It is split into three parts: user assignment, 3D path design, and resource shares. The parts are solved in turns with an approximation method. Simulations showed performance close to the ideal bound. Quality of service and computing cost are balanced in the design. The work targets dynamic settings such as events and disaster zones.
arxiv-2504-02713:
Shankha Shubhra Mukherjee and co-authors introduce Web3DB in a 2025 paper on databases owned by their users. Classic databases sit on one firm's servers, which creates privacy risks and a single point of failure. Past attempts at shared control often broke with the table-based tools most firms still use.

Web3DB keeps the familiar table model but spreads control across a network. A chain-based ledger handles fine-grained access rights, and storage itself is shared out. Queries run across nodes under a fair, chance-based pick of who does the work, with chain records to check the result. The system supports SQL-like queries, serves many users at once, and allows open data sharing. The paper lays out the design and a working build.
arxiv-2504-02813:
Timothy De Deyn and co-authors extend, in a 2025 math paper, recent tests that can tell whether a geometric space is smooth by looking at its category of well-behaved sheaves. For plain schemes, two such tests were proved not long ago, using strong generators and bounded structures. Stacks, which carry extra symmetry data, were not covered.

The authors prove stack versions of both tests for wide classes of stacks. A key step shows that smoothness matches a clean equality between two sheaf categories on the stack. Their route also gives a test for when the bounded derived category has a classical generator. That extends known results for rings and schemes to a broader world.
arxiv-2504-03013:
Sela Fried, Toufik Mansour, and Mark Shattuck count strings of symbols by tracking how often neighboring symbols differ by a chosen amount. Such counting problems sit in enumerative combinatorics, where exact formulas replace brute-force listing. A recent permutation problem asked for arrangements avoiding a fixed gap; the authors pose the matching question for words over an alphabet of any size.

For words, only adjacent positions matter, which simplifies the setup. They derive an explicit generating function for the distribution of the gap statistic, valid for every alphabet size and gap. The same machinery then handles set partitions written as growth sequences. Several sequences from the standard encyclopedia are identified along the way.
arxiv-2504-03213:
Aaron Park studies, in a 2025 paper, a hypothetical particle built from eight quarks. The octaquark, as he frames it, joins two baryons and one meson into a single compact object. Exotic multi-quark states have moved from speculation to discovery in recent years, and theory must say which combinations can hold together. Park uses a deliberately simple model of the color-spin force.

First he builds the octaquark's wave function so it respects the Pauli rule, with the real-world breaking of flavor symmetry included. Then, for every allowed set of quantum numbers, he computes the color-spin energy and compares it with the lightest breakup products. Several quantum number choices survive as candidates for compact octaquarks. The paper gives experimenters a short list to hunt for.
arxiv-2504-03313:
Bram de Wilde and co-authors build a tool that makes fake body shapes on demand for virtual medical tests. Such tests let researchers trial scan methods without the cost of real patients or lab models. To be useful, the fake shapes must be steerable toward a chosen patient type, not just random.

Their model codes shapes as smooth fields in a neural network, a form that can change its holes and links with ease, as thyroid shapes do. It learns a code where each dial steers one kind of shape change. Checks on rebuild quality and body plausibility showed sharp shapes with fine control over the changes, fit for targeted virtual trials.
arxiv-2504-03413:
Samapan Bhadury and co-authors derive an exact Wigner function for fermions coupled to a periodic chiral condensate, published in 2025. A Wigner function is a quantum analogue of a phase-space distribution, used to study how particles and spin are distributed. The condensate here, a chiral spiral, varies periodically in space.

Starting from the exact solution of the Dirac equation in that background, they obtain the exact formula for the Wigner function, up to quantum loop corrections. Several coefficients in the result show properties that a standard semiclassical expansion cannot reproduce. The axial vector part of the function is especially useful for studying spin polarization. During a slow change from the periodic potential to a uniform one, the polarization vector is twisted from its original direction, they find.
arxiv-2504-04013:
Xuechun Li and co-authors build a spatially aware model for judging earthquake damage in a 2025 paper. After a quake, responders must sort which hazards struck where: shaking, landslides, liquefaction often overlap. Standard models use one fixed parameter set everywhere, which misreads varied terrain, and sensors alone cannot untangle piled-up hazards. The team's causal Bayesian network instead wires the hazards together with parameters that change by location.

Gaussian processes carry the spatial variation, and normalizing flows shape the hidden variables. Across three real earthquakes, the system beat existing methods by up to thirty-five percent on a standard ranking measure. The authors argue that letting cause and effect bend with the landscape is the key step, and that better maps mean better aimed relief.
arxiv-2504-04413:
Abhishek and Mummidi built a particle model in twenty twenty-five that ties ghost particle mixing to the birth of the matter gap in the cosmos. The model adds a second Higgs pair and two heavy ghost kin that favor such particles. A taste rule with five helper fields shapes the mass grids.

The shape gives a named mixing scheme that fits known lepton masses and mixing. It puts one decay mass far below what tests today can reach. The same frame can grow the matter gap at low energy scales. Tests could one day reach its heavy kin, they note.
arxiv-2504-04513:
Maryam Khanahmadi and Klaus Mølmer propose a way to make exotic quantum states of light and send them down a wire in one stroke, in a 2025 paper. The states they want are non-Gaussian, shaped unlike the smooth bell curve of ordinary laser light. Such states are the fuel of error-proof quantum computing, but they are hard to make on demand. Their scheme pairs two kinds of loss in a superconducting circuit.

One loss is shaped to be nonlinear; the other is the plain leak of light into a waveguide. Together, cheap low-order effects fake a strong high-order one. That trick lets the circuit emit ready-made wave packets of prized states: cat states, grid states, and paired-cat states. The authors name real circuit platforms and settings where the plan should work. The draw is hardware thrift: no extra parts for shaping the output.
arxiv-2504-04613:
Kleanthis Malialis and three co-authors improve learning from endless data streams in a 2025 paper. Stream learning powers monitoring of infrastructure, social media, and recommendations, but streams shift over time, arrive unlabeled, and must be processed fast with little memory. Their method asks a human expert to label only a budgeted selection of examples.

Two paired neural networks train together incrementally, comparing examples in a learned space, while extra synthetic examples are generated in that same space to stretch the labels further. Both the label selection and the augmentation work in the compact latent space, keeping memory small. Simulations showed faster learning or better accuracy than strong current methods. Code and datasets are public.
arxiv-2504-04813:
Chung-Ru Lee and Chin-Rong Lee derive in 2025 how a special class of fermions spreads over energy levels. Fermions are particles that refuse to share a state, but in the class in view, two with opposed spin also cannot share a level. That extra ban changes the gas laws of a dense swarm of such particles.

Working from the grand ensemble of statistical physics, the pair finds a new spread law for the class. Against a free electron gas, the new gas has a higher Fermi energy and higher pressure from crowding. Its response to magnetic fields stays the same as the standard gas, though. The higher pressure lifts the mass cap for white dwarf and neutron stars to 1.6 times the classic value.
arxiv-2504-04913:
James Rodi and Lorenzo Natalucci present a proposed space mission to catch brief flashes of hard X-rays, in a 2025 paper. Such flashes can pair with gravitational waves and neutrino signals. Catching them fast takes wide views of the sky and quick reactions. No mission is yet planned for this work in the next decade, when detectors will find far more events.

The mission, GRINTA, pairs two instruments. A large detector watches a wide sky area for short bursts across a broad energy range. A masked telescope pins down source positions and follows them up. The main goal is joint events seen across many messengers. The tools would also study many other hard X-ray sources. The authors frame the mission as filling a gap in plans for the coming decade.
arxiv-2504-05313:
Yichen Li leads a team of eight authors in 2025 in surveying a young field. It mixes two ideas: recommending the next item from a user's recent history, and training that recommender without gathering private data in one place. Sequential recommendation reads the order of clicks and buys to guess what comes next.

Federated learning lets each user keep their data on their own device while still training a shared model. The survey maps how researchers have combined the two, what designs exist, and where the hard problems sit. As the first systematic map of federated sequential recommendation, it gives newcomers the lay of the land.
arxiv-2504-05513:
Elle Weeks and Eli Tziperman wrote a 2025 paper that questions a settled view of El Nino, the Pacific warming cycle. Fits of a simple recharge oscillator to data keep saying the cycle is damped, kept alive only by weather noise. They test the fitting methods themselves on fake data from both kinds of oscillator.

Both linear and nonlinear fits lean toward the damped verdict even when the truth is self sustained. The bias is built into the method, not the world. So past fits cannot settle the question. A self sustained El Nino stays possible. The paper is a warning about reading nature through a model's favourite answer.
arxiv-2504-05713:
Unnikrishnan Nair and Sunoj rework the standard yardsticks of poverty in this 2025 paper. Most measures of poverty are built on distribution functions, which state the share of people below each income level. The authors instead build the same measures on quantile functions, which run the view the other way, giving the income level at each share of the population.

Recasting the measures in this form yields a fresh method for studying poverty, the authors argue. Some new results fall out that are hard to reach in the older frame. The paper also proposes several flexible quantile models that can enrich the ones now in use. Their worth is shown on real data, so the new frame is tested against actual income records rather than left as pure theory.
arxiv-2504-05913:
Theodor Wulff and three co-authors model what draws the eye in videos in twenty twenty-five. Saliency means which objects stand out to a viewer.
