How long-term and short-term motion shape saliency in video is still under-studied. Their model learns a joint picture of frames and past saliency at once.

The system takes frames plus earlier saliency maps as a prior for the next guess. It breaks both streams into spatiotemporal tokens. Inside a token, short-term detail is captured; across tokens, long-term links form. A dual-stream transformer handles the two streams before fusing them. A masking scheme based on saliency is also applied. Readers get a model that can track shifting focus as a scene plays out.
arxiv-2504-06113:
Kushwaha and co-authors probe the magnetic state of a ruthenium compound with neutron and muon tools in two thousand twenty-five. The compound groups its ruthenium atoms in threes, called trimers, inside a barium and oxygen frame. It orders magnetically at a low set point, sixty kelvin.

Below that point, neutron tests found two distinct waves of spin motion. Modeling shows the spins sit at an angle rather than in line, driven by rival pulls between near and next-near neighbors plus strong spin-orbit effects. Traces of the waves linger above the order point, which points to short-range order. Muon tests back that view and show the order is dynamic, shaped by local twists in the trimer shape.
arxiv-2504-07013:
Anton Chernev and three co-authors study thin behaviors in coalgebra in a 2025 paper. Coalgebras model systems whose states branch into structured sets of successors, such as ordered tuples or multisets. A thin coalgebra is one with only countably many infinite paths from each state. The work was driven by verification goals and earlier results on thin trees.

Their main result describes thinness in an inductive way, through an initial algebra. They build a syntax for thin behaviors and give a single equation that decides when two terms name the same behavior. For a special case, their syntax recovers a known rank notion for thin trees.
arxiv-2504-07113:
Aly Kassem and co-authors stress-tested the router systems that decide which language model should answer each user question. Routers promise savings by sending easy questions to small models and hard ones to large models. Existing tests, though, mostly check general skill and ignore how routers behave on specific kinds of requests or on risky ones.

The team built a benchmark that sorts questions into categories such as coding, mathematics, translation, and jailbreak attempts, and adds privacy and safety checks. Tests on five routers showed a pattern of crude category-based choices. One router sent every coding and math question to the strongest model even when a weaker one would do. It also sent attack attempts to weak models, which raises safety risks.
arxiv-2504-07213:
Adriano Vinhas, João Correia, and Penousal Machado present a 2025 survey at the meeting point of two machine learning fields. Evolutionary methods automate the design of learning algorithms by breeding and selecting them. Self-supervised learning, meanwhile, extracts useful features from unlabeled data, which matters when labels are scarce.

Papers combining the two have multiplied, yet no map of the territory existed. The authors chart the combined work, propose a taxonomy, and name the emerging subfield Evolutionary Self-Supervised Learning. Evolution can shape self-supervised pipelines, while self-supervision can guide evolution itself or cut labeling needs. The survey closes with open challenges and research directions for a young but fast-growing area.
arxiv-2504-07413:
Spencer Matthews and Bin Nan build a regression method for survival data cut off at both the start and the end. Disease onset studies enroll people at varied times, so early events are missed entirely, a left truncation, while later ones are censored when the study ends. Ignoring the truncation biases every estimate. Their 2025 paper proposes a semiparametric sieve likelihood for a linear model under both distortions. They prove the estimates settle on the truth, follow a normal law, and reach the best possible efficiency. Simulations back the theory.

Sieve methods approximate the unknown parts with growing flexible families, letting data speak where theory is silent. Efficiency matters because onset cohorts are expensive and small. The authors give practitioners a method with guarantees. Their setting, delayed entry plus censoring, is the rule in epidemiology, not the exception.
arxiv-2504-07513:
Jianqiao Wangni proposes GPT Carry-On, a cheap way to customize large language models for each user or task. His 2025 paper notes that full fine-tuning needs costly training hardware, while most deployed machines only run models. The carry-on idea trains a small extra branch of transformer layers on top of a frozen base model.

The branch learns from the base model's final embeddings, then merges to form the custom model. Several branches, or branches from models skilled in chat, code, or math, can mix into one. Training the add-on took under a gigabyte of memory for a hundred-million-parameter layer on a thirty-billion model. Small tests on math questions and open models looked promising.
arxiv-2504-07613:
Galaxy clusters trace the skeleton of the cosmos, and their clumping pattern carries the fingerprints of matter and its roughness. Valtteri Lindholm and co-authors measure that pattern in a 2025 paper using a large X-ray-selected cluster sample. They split the clustering signal into three shape components and compare them with theory.

To read the signal they need to know how strongly clusters exaggerate the underlying clumping, which they take from cluster masses and simulations. The measured pattern matches what the Planck satellite's cosmology predicts. Their own fit prefers slightly less matter and a rougher cosmos, but the Planck values sit comfortably inside the uncertainty.
arxiv-2504-08013:
Bae, Mohammadpour, and Najati examine in 2025 when a quadratic equation stays stable under small changes, inside spaces known as locally convex cones. Stability in this sense asks whether a near solution stays close to an exact one. Past work had opened this question for such spaces, and the authors carry it to a classic quadratic form.

New theorems in the work describe how these operators behave when they are perturbed. The results add to the theory of Hyers-Ulam stability and show what sets quadratic operators apart in this setting. Readers with a background in analysis get a fuller frame for work on stability in wider spaces.
arxiv-2504-08413:
Charlotte Out, Sijing Tu, Stefan Neumann, and Ahad Zehmakan extend a classic model of how opinions settle in a network to include outside media voices. In the Friedkin-Johnsen model, people blend neighbors views with their own starting opinion. The new version adds media sources that push a fixed stance and never budge. Writing from a twenty twenty-four conference paper, the team asks when two opposing outlets can radicalize a network, and how long that takes. Cases with equal-strength rivals are solved exactly, giving the final opinion pattern.

With only one outlet present, the team proves that stubborn sources are far stronger than ones that also adapt. Simulations on real and synthetic networks matched the theory closely. The work speaks to debates about biased coverage and false balance, giving platform designers a formal handle on how fixed outside voices warp network opinion.
arxiv-2504-08813:
Models that reason across images and text are spreading fast, and their safety has lagged behind their skill. Junfeng Fang and seven co-authors ran the first systematic safety study of such multimodal reasoning models in 2025, comparing them with the base models they grew from.

Three findings stand out. First, a reasoning tax: gaining reasoning skill badly eroded built-in safety, with jailbreak attacks succeeding about thirty-seven percent more often. Second, blind spots: some scenarios, such as illegal activity, saw attack rates jump far beyond the average. Third, a hopeful sign: in about seventeen percent of bad reasoning chains, the final answer corrected itself back to safety. The authors call for safety audits that vary by scenario.
arxiv-2504-09213:
Song Yang and co-authors decode brain signals with a spiking neural network. Their twenty twenty-five paper serves implants that read motor cortex signals for brain-computer interfaces. Classic decoders lack accuracy; deep nets cost too much power for daily wear.

The spiking model fires sparse events like real neurons, sipping energy. A fusion step blends hand-built signal features with ones a deep net extracts, lifting accuracy further. Tests on motor signals from two rhesus macaques beat standard artificial networks on accuracy. Efficiency rose by tens to hundreds of times. A cooler, longer-lived implant decoder is a real step toward practical thought-driven devices.
arxiv-2504-09313:
S Sabari and co-authors wrote a 2025 physics paper on vortices in ultra-cold atom clouds with long range forces. Such clouds, called condensates, can hold spinning whirlpools when rotated. Two forces act inside: a short range contact force and a long range dipole force, and both can be tuned from push to pull.

The team solved the governing equation for a flat, rotating cloud. First they steadied a cloud that pull forces would collapse, by dialing up push from the long range side. Then they flipped both signs to test how much the vortex pattern cares. A purely dipolar cloud grew more vortices as the long range push rose. They checked the pattern across three atom types, led by a strong dipole isotope.
arxiv-2504-09413:
Jia Qin tackles motion in-betweening, the animator's task of filling the frames between sparse key poses. Hand filling is slow, and pure learning methods can drift into poses no real body could hold. The proposed fix pairs a diffusion generator with a physics-based adapter.

In stage one, a diffusion model drafts transitions on a standard skeleton, ignoring who the character is. That draft works across many character shapes at once. In stage two, a reinforcement learning controller retargets the motion to the true character's build and dynamics. It scrubs artifacts and restores style while keeping the motion lawful. Tests on standard sets and stylized figures show smooth, true-to-style results even from sparse, far-apart keys. One model can thus serve a whole cast without retraining.
arxiv-2504-09613: Michael Borinsky and Mathijs Fraaije speed up Feynman integral evaluation in twenty twenty-five. Their algorithm samples loop momenta distributed according to a given Feynman integrand. It builds on the tropical sampling method from earlier work. The samples can evaluate phase-space-type integrals far more efficiently than naive sampling. They provide an implementation called momtrop. Applied to integrals from the loop-tree duality framework, it gave convergence speedups of more than a million fold over naive methods.
arxiv-2504-09913:
Jongmin Lee and Ernest K Ryu sharpen the theory of a classic learning algorithm for long-run average rewards, in a 2025 paper. Value iteration updates value guesses step by step. Most past theory covers the discounted case, where near rewards count more, while the average case had only loose bounds.

The authors give fresh finite-step bounds for the average-reward case. A fixed-up form of the algorithm shrinks error at a steady one-over-steps rate in the general multi-chain setup. They also prove a matching lower bound, tight up to a small constant factor, for simpler setups. The pair of results closes much of the gap in knowing how fast the method settles. Code-free proofs anchor the claims.
arxiv-2504-10013:
Carolin Penke and co-authors share in 2025 best practices for training large language models on supercomputers, drawn from a German project for open multilingual models for European languages. Such training needs huge computing, complex software, and careful workflows. The report details work on a national supercomputer to train a seven billion parameter model, from system layout to daily operations.

Topics include the training infrastructure, software choices, and tools for profiling and benchmarking. Measured throughput is given for varied ways of splitting work across machines, and for features such as flash attention. Engineering and operational problems are shared openly, so other teams can avoid them when training large models.
arxiv-2504-10213:
Lian-Cheng Ji and co-authors describe HYDRA, a detector built to track pions from the decay of hypernuclei. Their 2025 paper presents the instrument for an experiment at a German heavy-ion facility, where exotic nuclei containing a strange quark are made in collisions. Catching the faint pion tracks from their decay takes a light, precise tracker inside a large magnet.

The design joins a time projection chamber, which records particle paths in gas, with a plastic scintillator wall for timing and triggering. Low mass in the beam path keeps the tracks clean. The paper lays out the build and reports the first characterization tests of the finished detector.
arxiv-2504-10313:
Aitor Arrieta compares ways to order software tests for cyber-physical systems built in Simulink, in an empirical study from 2025. These system simulations run long and repeat at several testing levels, so running the most revealing tests first saves real time. Order can be set with code knowledge or without it.

Eleven ordering methods were compared across six models of varied size and complexity, the largest such study in this setting. Code-aware methods edged out blind ones overall. Among code-aware methods, a simple total-greedy rule won on larger models. Blind methods ordered tests faster. The results guide test teams balancing order quality against ordering cost.
arxiv-2504-10413:
If a shape in a curved space wraps its region with the least perimeter, must the whole space split neatly in two? Alessandro Cucinotta and Mattia Magnabosco answer yes when two things hold. Their space is a Riemannian manifold with non-negative sectional curvature, and its volume grows only quadratically far out.

In that world, a single perimeter minimizing set forces the space to be isometric to a product. The set's boundary is exactly a slice of that product structure. The result ties a least-perimeter question to the rigid geometry of the space itself.
arxiv-2504-10613:
Xing David Wang and Ulf Leser present a 2025 arXiv paper on finding papers that can complete partly known facts in biomedical knowledge bases. Curators still extract multi-entity relations by hand, and a key step is retrieving documents that fill missing slots. Gold training data are scarce, so the team mines existing base records to build weakly labeled examples.

Two ideas carry the model: a layered contrastive loss that learns from noisy, incomplete relation structures, and a balanced sampling plan that draws good negative examples from varied records. On two benchmarks the method set a new best, topping strong rivals by several points on the ranking score.
arxiv-2504-10813:
Zhendong Ang and co-authors sharpen how software tools predict data races before they happen, in a 2025 paper. A data race occurs when threads reach the same memory without proper ordering. Two families of prediction methods exist: one swaps harmless step orders, the other reasons over run prefixes. Past tools grew ad hoc, with little shared theory.

The authors formalize both families and compare what each can catch. Prefix methods, in three styles, all catch the same race class, which provably covers the swap-based class. Merging the two yields a new class, granular prefix races. It can be predicted while streaming, in constant memory and linear time. The union beats either method alone.
arxiv-2504-11013:
Rein Liefferink and five colleagues present a 2025 physics paper explaining how a laser flash can stamp magnetic whirlpools into a film. These whirlpools, skyrmions, are candidates for future memory bits, and light creates them in trillionths of a second. Atom-by-atom simulations reproduce the effect but explain little; the authors build a coarse-grained theory instead, treating creation and destruction as heat-driven hops over energy barriers.

During a heat pulse, the two hopping rates decide how many skyrmions appear, and the simple model matches both simulations and experiments at a fraction of the cost. It doubles as a recipe book for tuning experiments toward a desired skyrmion count. Unexpectedly, it also predicts a fast lane for erasing skyrmions, a new effect for ultrafast magnetism to test.
arxiv-2504-11313:
Yuting Shen and Jingwei Liang offer a new math method in a 2025 paper. The basic task is to find a point that lies in two or more closed sets at once. Such tasks show up in imaging, planning, and signal work. Classic methods bounce a guess between the sets until it settles.

One classic method can spiral slowly when the sets are flat subspaces. The same method can be very fast on curved sets, though. The authors build on it by adding a mix of projection and reflection steps. They also give a version whose settings change as it runs. Proofs in the paper back the claims, and number tests support them. The goal is faster, more reliable solving across both flat and curved cases.
arxiv-2504-11413:
Niclas Tilgner led a large team imaging a thin bismuth layer in a 2025 paper. Diffraction methods normally lose the phase of scattered waves, which blocks a full picture of a sample. A standing wave method using X-rays gets around that loss. The team applied it to a two-atom-thick material prized for its quantum effects.

The bismuth layer sits between a silicon carbide base and a graphene sheet. Imaging showed that adding hydrogen shifts where the bismuth atoms sit under the graphene. One of three silicon bonds per cell takes up the hydrogen, and that small shift creates the layer's signature band pattern. The work shows the method can settle key structural questions directly.
arxiv-2504-11713:
Aaron Havens and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a faster way to train diffusion samplers. Such samplers learn to draw samples from a target defined only by an energy function, a common task in physics and chemistry. Past methods needed many costly energy checks, which capped the size of problems they could handle.

Their method, Adjoint Sampling, rests on stochastic optimal control theory. It allows far more training updates than energy checks, which makes training much cheaper. It also keeps the guarantees of an earlier method without needing fixes that push samples toward the target. Tests cover classic energy functions and neural network energy models. The team even generates molecule shapes across many systems with one trained model. They plan to release the hard test cases openly.
arxiv-2504-12013:
Robert Krause, Lars Gottesbüren, and Nikolai Maas build a hypergraph partitioner that gives the same answer every time. Splitting a hypergraph into balanced parts underpins chip design and scientific computing, and the best parallel tools rely on randomness, so runs differ and results cannot be reproduced. High-quality local search had no good deterministic parallel form.

The team generalizes a recent refinement method called Jet, retunes its rebalancing, and adds a deterministic scheme over flow-based refinement, even though the underlying flow solver is not deterministic. In tests, the Jet version matched or beat the leading non-deterministic solver's default quality while running only about fifteen percent slower, with speedups up to fifty-five-fold on 64 cores. The flow version edged past its random rival on quality for about a third more time. The authors call it the first deterministic parallel partitioner to rival the best solvers.
arxiv-2504-12113:
Anfu Tang, Laure Soulier, and Vincent Guigue teach search systems to ask better clarifying questions by first naming what is unclear. Their 2025 paper works in information retrieval, where a proactive assistant should ask about a vague query before answering it. Large language models can generate such questions from prompts, but ordinary step-by-step prompting does not distinguish one kind of ambiguity from another.

Their scheme inserts the distinction. The model must first predict the type of ambiguity in the query, treating that label as an instruction, and only then write the clarification. Experiments on data sets with human-written clarifying questions compare the method against several prompting baselines, and simulated users add a second judgment of quality. The authors argue that ambiguity is not one problem but a family, and that a system which says which member it faces clarifies more usefully.
arxiv-2504-12413:
Canadian firms gain speed from digital tools, yet each new tool can open a door to online crime. Joann Jasiak, Peter MacKenzie, and Purevdorj Tuvaandorj weigh that trade-off in a 2025 study. They merge two 2021 national surveys, one on digital use and one on cyber crime, into a single firm-level data set.

The team builds a digital use score for each firm and flags which firms met a cyber event. A trimmed statistical method then picks out the traits that predict output gains and risk. Large gaps split firms by size, field, and staff mix. Fast uptake of cloud and smart tools raised both output and risk. Large firms bore the most risk, the study finds.
arxiv-2504-12813:
Simon Sagmeister and five co-authors draw lessons from building a full self-driving software stack in a paper from 2025. Research teams usually build and publish each driving module on its own. Stitching those parts back into one stack that runs on a real car brings its own set of snags, apart from the flaws of any single algorithm.

The authors base their account on the TUM Autonomous Motorsport team's race car work. They sort the snags they met when deploying research code on real test vehicles and give strategies that worked for them. Open-source code on GitHub lets other teams reuse the fixes and judge full stacks more fairly.
arxiv-2504-13113:
Jason Zev Ludmir, Sophia Rebello, Jacob Ruiz, and Tirthak Patel propose a way to spot odd data in 2025. Their method uses quantum machines and needs no training step. Finding rare, risky events matters in fields such as finance, health, and energy, yet labeled cases are scarce.

The team calls the method Quorum and builds it on quantum autoencoders. Since it learns without labels, it can be used where normal training is hard. Training quantum models is often blocked by hard gradient work, which this design avoids. The paper sets out the method as a first of its kind for this task.
arxiv-2504-13213:
Wei-Min Yang sets out the flavor side of a grand model that ties the birth of the cosmos to the traits of matter. The base model claims to cover the first burst of space, dark energy, dark matter, and the slight edge of matter over its twin. Flavor, why each kind of matter has its mass and mixing, was left out. Yang adds a flavor symmetry to fill that gap.

The symmetry yields the mass of each quark and lepton and how they mix. It also links quark mixing to lepton mixing and shows why the two differ. One neat yield is a mass web for the ghost-like neutrinos with just four free knobs. It fits all known readings and predicts one mass in advance, 0.01037 electron volts. A fresh path for the birth of the matter edge closes the piece, with tests named.
arxiv-2504-13313:
Four plasma physicists teach a machine to finish an equation that never ends. Simulating hot plasma with the Vlasov-Poisson system splits the particle distribution into an endless ladder of fluid-like moments, and any simulation must cut the ladder somewhere. The team works in a Fourier-Hermite representation, where the physics becomes that ladder, and uses reservoir computing to model the small-scale rungs that truncation would throw away.

With the learned closure in place, the solver needed far fewer velocity points for the same accuracy. In gentle, near-linear cases the error at the closed rung stayed within two percent. In strongly turbulent cases the method tracked the true spectra better than plain truncation and cut the needed velocity resolution sixteen-fold. The authors present the work as a first step toward cheap, accurate models for designing magnetic fusion reactors.
arxiv-2504-13713:
Samuel Cerezo, Gaetano Meli, Tomás Berriel Martins, Kirill Safronov, and Javier Civera release a benchmark that sits where robot mapping meets neural scene rendering, in a research paper from 2025. New rendering methods are being used inside SLAM systems, which track a device's motion while mapping a scene. Older data sets miss the joint challenges of both fields.

Their data set was recorded with a robot arm for precise motion. It holds forty sequences with color and depth images, motion sensor readings, and exact ground-truth poses. Five object setups appear under four lighting setups, with separate training and test paths. Baseline results show the set is a relevant test for this growing area.
arxiv-2504-13813:
Prosenjit Bose and co-authors play cops and robbers on graphs drawn with crossings in this 2025 paper. In the game, cops move along edges to catch a robber on a vertex. The cop number is the smallest crew that always wins. Graphs drawn cleanly on bounded-genus surfaces need only bounded crews.

Graphs that allow one crossing per edge break that rule entirely. The paper asks whether the distance between crossing edges restores order. In a variant where a cop within a few steps counts as a catch, bounded numbers return when crossing pairs sit close together. The authors cover several drawing classes and link crossing geometry to pursuit power.
arxiv-2504-13913:
Raphaël Kou and Antony Lewis wrote a 2025 cosmology paper on testing ideas about the infant universe. The faint glow left from the early cosmos already limits what could have happened back then. Changes to the standard model before that glow was released would also leave marks in how matter later clumped. Upcoming galaxy surveys can read those marks.

The authors forecast how much sharper the tests become when several probes are combined. They join galaxy clustering, the bending of light by matter, and lensing of the background glow itself. They also account for shared errors between the probes, an effect often ignored. For one idea, early dark energy, the combined data could cut the uncertainty on its density by a factor of three to four. Most of the power comes from the largest scales, which are cleaner to measure.
arxiv-2504-14113:
Self-driving cars must label every part of a road scene in each camera frame, and that job must run fast on small hardware. Jiyong Kwag, Alper Yilmaz, and Charles Toth present a light method for it in this 2025 paper. Most current methods pull smooth, continuous features from the image with deep networks. Smooth features, though, can blur the crisp categories a road scene needs.

Their method uses vector quantization, which swaps each smooth feature for the nearest entry in a fixed codebook. Crisp entries help the model find distinct features more easily. They also squeeze out noise, since odd values get snapped to a clean entry. The result is a smaller, faster model for labeling roads, cars, and people. Light models matter for cars that must react in real time.
arxiv-2504-14313:
Gaurav Katoch, Debajyoti Sarkar, and Bhim Sen explore a time-based form of entanglement in a holographic model, in this 2025 physics paper. Holography links a gravity theory in a curved space to a quantum theory on its edge. Recent work proposed measuring entanglement across time spans, not just space spans. The authors test that idea in a model of a sudden global energy jolt, called a quench.

They place time spans at varied spots relative to a shell of matter falling into the space. Spans set early or late match the known results for calm space and for black hole states. But when the falling shell cuts across the span, the pattern shifts sharply from the usual space-based story. The work maps how time-based entanglement reacts to a violent change.
arxiv-2504-14413:
Piotr Bacik, Joel Ouaknine, David Purser, and James Worrell take on the p-adic Skolem problem in a 2025 paper. A linear recurrence builds each term from past ones, and the classic problem asks whether any term hits zero. A theorem from over ninety years ago says zeros are rare, but its proof gives no way to find them.

The authors give algorithms that decide whether a recurrence has a zero in the p-adic numbers, a parallel number system used in number theory. The tools also list exact forms for all such zeros. Their output is always right, and halting rests on a standard unproven hypothesis about the p-adic exponential. The tools also settle a paired version of the classic problem.
arxiv-2504-14613: Yeonjae Hong and Sukmoon Huh count special bundles on a classic surface in a 2025 math paper. The surface is the Veronese surface, a standard shape in geometry. On it they study rank two vector bundles that respect the surface's torus symmetry. The bundles also meet a vanishing rule that marks them as arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay. They sort and count these bundles, up to a twist by the hyperplane class. Their tools come from Klyachko's account of such bundles through filtrations, plus matching cohomology counts. Sample bundles round out the paper.
arxiv-2504-14713:
Toufik Mansour wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in combinatorics, counting shuffles that dodge small patterns. The objects are derangements, rearrangements where nothing stays in place, read in a flattened cycle form. The patterns are vincular, meaning some entries must sit side by side. For each pattern of length three, the paper counts the avoiders by their number of cycles.

Generating functions, which package whole counts into single formulas, are the main prize. The kernel method cracks most cases by solving the equations those functions obey. One pattern needs an exponential version, yielding a formula built from Stirling numbers and a striped matrix's determinant. The hardest pair of patterns calls for two extra statistics tracked alongside. The results complete a tidy corner of pattern avoidance, a field that catalogs how structure emerges from forbidding small shapes.
arxiv-2504-15013:
Yow-Fu Liou, Yu-Chien Tang, and An-Zi Yen explore in 2025 how language models can write extra reading material for lessons, to save teachers time. Making good course material takes long hours of work. Their test case is the deeper reading sections that sit under short online lesson videos.

Their method starts from the video's spoken text. A model drafts a longer article that adds past events, cultural notes, and short tales to make points vivid. A ranking step based on meaning then finds courses that relate to the article. A second model pass polishes those course picks. The aim is a pack of reading and course links that a teacher can check and use fast. The study asks how far such auto made material can be trusted in real teaching.
arxiv-2504-15413:
Alimzhan Amanov and Damir Yeliussizov study in 2025 the peak symmetry vectors inside spaces of tensors. Tensors arranged with symmetric or alternating signs form stages for group actions, and their highest weight vectors mark the extreme directions of those actions. How many such independent vectors exist is counted by generalized Kronecker coefficients, a long standing puzzle in algebra.

The authors describe the algebraic rules tying together the classic constructions of spanning sets for these peak vectors. Their proofs rest on a duality they uncovered between the symmetric and alternating worlds. That mirror view pays off twice over. It gives fresh meaning to power expansions of Cayley's first hyperdeterminant, a famous invariant from the nineteenth century, and to its dual exterior form. The work ties an old determinant mystery to modern representation theory.
arxiv-2504-15713:
Abgaryan, Nersessian, and Yeghikyan recast the Zernike math set as a bent-space swing in this twenty twenty-five paper. The set first served lens math, then got a force-read in mote terms. Its force tale held a fake term that made sums look not real.

Inside, a gauge shift wipes that fake term by a clean change of frame. The set then matches a known swing on a ball or saddle face, term for term. A mote twin of that shift maps the set to the same swing's mote form. At one weight tie the swing turns to a free mote on those faces. Off that tie, the set acts as a near-true force form in their read.
arxiv-2504-15913:
Roberto Assef and a large team of co-authors studied a strange galaxy in a 2025 paper. The galaxy hides a brilliant quasar behind thick dust, yet it glows faintly blue, like an unhidden one. That blue light was suspected to be quasar light scattered toward us by gas around the galaxy.

Using a telescope in Chile, the team measured how the blue light is polarized, a fingerprint of scattering. About a quarter of the light was polarized, confirming the scattering story. Maps of the signal showed the polarization changing across the galaxy's face. Matching the maps with simulations let them describe the scattering material. The picture that emerges is a huge outflow of gas streaming in a direction we do not look down. The work shows how polarized light can reveal hidden winds in buried galaxies.
arxiv-2504-16013:
Markos Poulos and Konstantinos Termentzidis study one-way heat flow in graphene sheets pierced by pores, in a 2025 paper. Molecular dynamics simulations show heat preferring to travel from the porous side toward the clean side, with a rectification of about eighteen percent. Lengthening the clean region and shrinking the pores both strengthen the effect.

A simple resistance model explains the behavior: each region's conductivity responds differently to temperature, and the effect peaks when their resistances match. The model underestimates the effect, though, and vibration analysis reveals new defect modes gathered around the pores. Arranged pore patterns beat random ones, while pore shape matters little.
arxiv-2504-16113:
Xin Wang and Xiaoqi Li build an artificial intelligence method for finding flaws in NFT smart contracts in a 2025 paper. The NFT market grew fast, and contract bugs can cost users dearly. Manual review is slow and costly, while past automated models handled the task poorly.

The team gathered over sixteen thousand public contracts and sorted them into five flaw types, such as reentrancy and unlimited minting. A random forest model, tuned by grid search, learned to spot each flaw type from code features. It read access control patterns for one flaw and call placement for another. The ensemble beat single decision trees and held up after tuning. The authors offer it as an efficient path to automated contract checks.
arxiv-2504-16613:
Mohammad Javad Zakavi and co-authors study reflecting surfaces mounted on drones, and how the drone's hovering wobble affects the link. Their 2025 paper looks at intelligent reflecting surfaces, panels that bounce signals toward users, lifted by unmanned aerial vehicles for future networks such as 6G. Gains include better coverage and flexible placement.

The team models random tilts of the hovering drone in both sideways and vertical angles, with a full three dimensional radiation pattern for the surface. They derive formulas for the pattern and for outage probability, and check them with simulations. Wobble hurt performance a lot. To keep links alive, the surface should use fewer elements, even though that cuts directivity.
arxiv-2504-16713:
Storm, Sun, Rocha, and Van der Meer present a paper from twenty twenty-five on mixing data-driven and physics-based material models by uncertainty. Multiscale simulations need training data for fast surrogate models. Covering all load cases in training data is costly, though. Their mix uses a fast probabilistic surrogate where it is confident. Where doubt grows, it swaps back to the true high-fidelity model. A phase-field method governs the swap zones and keeps them smooth. Doubt from the surrogate drives the phase changes directly.

A purely local swap rule is compared against the smooth phase approach. Tests use a Gaussian process surrogate for an elastic-plastic material. The mix speeds multiscale runs while holding accuracy where it counts. The authors detail conditions for stable, exact results.
arxiv-2504-16913:
Shifali Agrahari and Sanasam Ranbir Singh teach a model to spot machine-written text and name which model wrote it. Fake text threatens school honesty and public trust, so detection tools matter. Naming the source model adds a trail that plain yes-or-no detectors lack.

Their method, COT Fine-tuned, works in two tasks at once. One task sorts text as human or machine made. The other pins down the exact generator model. The twist is chain-of-thought reasoning: the system spells out its steps before ruling. Tests show high accuracy on both tasks, with the reasoning trace aiding both scores and trust. Readers can audit why a text was flagged, not just that it was. The work comes from an open-source intelligence challenge setting.
arxiv-2504-17013:
Lazic tackles class imbalance in Bayesian prediction models in a paper from 2025, using drug safety as the test case. In toxicology data, harmless compounds far outnumber harmful ones. Models trained on such data call most things safe and miss the rare toxic cases that matter most for safety checks.

His fix raises each observation's likelihood to a power set by how rare its class is, scaled so total information stays the same. That builds cost-sensitive learning into the Bayesian update itself. Tests on fake data and on a liver injury model improved balance and caught more toxic cases. The change is small in standard tools.
arxiv-2504-17113:
Daniel Kronovet and co-authors report an eighteen-month experiment in running a shared house without bosses. The nine-bedroom Los Angeles coliving house kept 98 percent occupancy and below-market rents. Drawing on Elinor Ostrom's commons theory, the team built three digital tools to replace managers.

A chore market gives each resident a monthly duty of one hundred points, claimed from tasks whose value rises the longer they sit undone. A pairwise voting layer lets residents quietly reshuffle task priorities. A hearts ledger tracks rule keeping through light challenges and peer karma. Logs of hundreds of chore claims, heart events, and group purchases suggest the tooling can hold a commons together without steady leadership.
arxiv-2504-17313:
Zhuohang Zhu and colleagues teach one model to do two stock jobs at once: forecast future prices and predict future price changes, several steps ahead. The tasks sound alike but behave differently. Price levels drift in a log-normal way, while changes stay roughly normal. Multi-step versions compound errors, so most earlier work settled for one step or one task. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team's encoder reads several channels, covering price history and price changes together. A novel tokenization turns those channels into patches the encoder can digest.

The patched design is meant to respect the two targets' different statistics inside a shared representation. Investors, regulators, and portfolio managers are the named audience. The paper frames tokenization, borrowed from language modeling, as the lever that makes joint multi-step stock modeling tractable.
arxiv-2504-17613:
Bowen Deng and co-authors published a 2025 paper on generating synthetic patient records that are useful, not just realistic. Hospitals cannot share real records freely, so machine learning trains on synthetic ones. Most generators copy the statistical shape of real data. The authors argue that is the wrong target: common patterns dominate, and the rare cases models most need to learn stay rare.

Their framework, TarDiff, steers a diffusion generator with the downstream task itself. Generation is guided toward samples that improve a specific clinical model's performance on its target outcome. Usefulness, not resemblance, becomes the objective. The setting is health-record time series, the sequences of measurements that chart a patient's course. If synthetic data can be aimed, scarce-data problems in medicine get a new lever: manufacture the examples your model is missing. The paper reframes data generation as a form of teaching.
arxiv-2504-17713:
Fernando Suarez, Jose Manuel Pena, and Omar Larre review target-date funds and advise Chile's pension reform on taking them up, in work from 2025. Target-date funds shift savings toward safer assets on their own as the saver nears the end of work life. Chile's reform swaps its old multi-fund habit for them. The theory and practice of glide paths, the preset slide toward safety, are surveyed in depth. Hurdles for regulators and managers get close attention throughout.

The glide path, they argue, should respond to total wealth as it changes. Risk tolerance should bend the path for each saver. A wide band around the standard mix of assets is proposed. That room would spur rivalry in strategy among fund managers. Other kinds of assets and wider spread would gain space to grow. A glide path model shaped for Chile remains future work.
arxiv-2504-17813:
Some classification errors cost more than others. Mistaking one benign tumor grade for the next matters little; missing the step into cancer changes a life. Dileepa Pitawela, Gustavo Carneiro, and Hsiang-Ting Chen argue in 2025 that ordinal classifiers should respect such uneven stakes. Their method, CLOC, learns ordered representations by contrastive learning with a new multi-margin loss that lets each boundary between neighboring ranks carry its own importance.

Flexible margins smooth the transitions between classes and reduce overfitting to quirks in training data. The team tested CLOC on five real image datasets — age estimation, photo dating, knee arthritis, diabetic eye disease, and breast cancer subtyping — plus a synthetic set simulating biased clinical decisions. It beat existing ordinal methods across the board. The authors stress that the learned order is interpretable and controllable, matching how clinicians actually weigh mistakes.
arxiv-2504-18013:
Arunima Bhattacharya, a solo author, proves that solutions of the Hamiltonian stationary equation are smoother than they first appear, in a 2025 math paper. The equation governs a class of special surfaces in complex space, tied to the physics of calibrated geometry. Its solutions carry a parameter called the Lagrangian phase, which can make the equation behave kindly or harshly.

Working in complex Euclidean space of dimension four or less, Bhattacharya shows that any solution with a modest level of smoothness, of class C1,1, is in fact fully smooth. This holds for every value of the phase, including the awkward ones where standard methods stall. The paper also derives a precise estimate that bounds the solution's higher-order smoothness in terms of its basic size. Such regularity results clear the ground for using these surfaces in geometry.
arxiv-2504-18113:
Aniket Dixit and co-authors build cheap stand-in worlds for training learning agents, in work from 2025. Reinforcement learning agents learn by trial and error, which can take vast numbers of steps in the real task. A stand-in world that mimics the real one can cut that cost.

The team used an algorithm that finds sparse equations for how a system changes over time. With very few real trials, their stand-ins matched the true dynamics of two classic test tasks closely. Agents trained inside the stand-ins needed far fewer steps than agents trained in the real tasks. Their final scores were about the same. The method gives accurate, readable stand-ins, which suits labs that need cheaper and clearer training setups.
arxiv-2504-18213:
Nicolas Münger and co-authors improved in 2025 the 3D scene labeling that self-driving trains need, by fixing the training data rather than the model. Laser scans thin out with distance, so faraway people and tracks get missed. Working with a railway dataset, they pasted extra pedestrian examples into scans at realistic distant ranges. A second trick redistributed point density to help far track detection.

Both fixes lifted distant-range accuracy while barely affecting close-range performance. The team also set the first benchmark for this labeling task on the dataset. Their point is that data-centric tweaks can solve problems that bigger models alone do not. The methods target the specific failure modes of railway perception, where missing a distant person is the dangerous error.
arxiv-2504-18713:
Devansh Agrawal and co-authors present a 2025 paper on safe robot mapping when position estimates drift. Robots rely on maps to avoid obstacles, but vision-based tracking drifts over time. Most mapping methods assume the pose is exact, which can mark blocked space as free and cause crashes. The team builds maps that stay correct near the robot despite that drift.

Their frame shrinks the safe zone by the drift gained at each step. Two popular mapping styles were adapted: safe flight corridors and signed distance fields. Proofs show both stay correct under the stated drift bounds. In model tests and a real rover run, rivals crashed into mapped obstacles. The new frame stopped the rover in time.
arxiv-2504-19313:
Matheus Brito and Vyjayanthi Chari study standard modules for a quantum algebra tied to the A-type symmetry family, in a math paper from 2025. These modules, called Weyl modules, are sorted by special labels known as dominant weights. Knowing which labels occur is a basic step in the theory.

The authors find the full set of such labels. They then prove that maps between two standard modules form a space of at most one dimension, and they give an exact test for when a nonzero map exists. The socle of a standard module, its innermost simple part, is described and shown to be simple for large rank. Results are applied to mixed modules, extension counts, and new tensor subcategories.
arxiv-2504-20013:
Beizhe Hu, Qiang Sheng, Juan Cao, Yang Li, and Danding Wang study what happens when machine-written fake news floods a news recommendation system, in a research paper from 2025. Detectors struggle with this fake news one item at a time. Its effect on the whole news ecosystem was less explored.

The team built a simulation with about fifty-six thousand generated news items of varied types. As fake items entered the rankings, real news slowly lost its edge, a pattern they call truth decay. They trace it to familiarity: text that reads smoothly tends to rank higher, whatever its truth. The authors discuss countermeasures and urge platforms to act early.
arxiv-2504-20213:
Yuan Xia and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on whether language models can truly learn formal logic, tested by making them write checkable proofs in Boolean logic. A model gets assumptions and a goal and must produce a proof a checker accepts. Real proofs are too scarce to train on, so the team synthesizes valid proofs with a randomized generator.

A template trick rewrites training proofs into varied shapes, teaching flexibility with complex expressions. Their tests judge reasoning rather than memorization. Models proved short arguments strongly, then faded as proofs grew. The augmentation helped even small models, suggesting reasoning habits can be trained, within limits the authors map carefully.
arxiv-2504-21113:
Placing a team of robots or sensors across rough ground is hard when hills and walls block straight paths. Donipolo Ghimire, Carlos Nieto-Granda, and Solmaz S. Kia introduce a 2025 framework called NavEX for that task.

NavEX groups target points around a few chosen hubs, then plans paths that respect walls and rough ground. It can serve two goals: fair reach, where each target stays close to an agent, or hot spots, where dense zones get more cover. Math built into the method keeps the plan near the best known result. Tests in simulated settings show it works in complex ground where older plans, built on straight-line distance, fall short.
arxiv-2504-21513:
Nerijus Sidorovas and co-authors study internal waves in a two-layer fluid in a 2025 paper. The waves travel at the boundary between layers and have moderate height. Shear currents run in a straight-line pattern through the fluid. A long-wave model with strong nonlinearity gives the base system.

The team work with an extended Korteweg-de Vries equation drawn from that model. A near-identity change of form maps it to a Gardner equation with new traits. From the map they build lone wave and wave train solutions. Direct simulations of the full system test how well each shortcut performs. The improved form holds up well in the checks.
arxiv-2504-21713:
Manuel Fernandez-Guasti and co-authors study dances where many bodies chase each other along one shared curve. Their 2025 paper sets the bodies under a spring-like pull that grows with the gaps between pairs. The shared curve is a limaçon, a loop whose shape is set by two size terms and a whole-number twist. The team asks when a joint dance on that curve can exist at all.

They prove a clean rule that ties the twist count to the body count: the dance exists just when two key ratios miss whole numbers. With a symmetry added, the rule sharpens. They also count how few shape ratios lead to crashes, and find extra conserved values.
arxiv-2505-00113:
Harlan Campbell and Antonio Remiro-Azócar present a study from twenty twenty-five on trials that use outside groups as their control arm. Such single arm trials matter when a fair coin toss trial cannot be run. A close cousin compares treatments across trials with no shared arm. Both need care to avoid bias when groups differ.

The pair build one causal frame for both designs. They add an outcome model on top of a known weighting method based on entropy balance. The mix stays sound if one of its two parts is right, a trait called double robustness. Tests with fake data show less bias and tight scores. They also show how to use the method when raw data for the outside group is not at hand.
arxiv-2505-00213:
Tianyu Qiu and four co-authors shrink multi agent planning problems by teaching a network to ignore bystanders, in this 2025 paper. Game theoretic planners model every agent's choices, so their math swells with crowd size and runs too slowly for real time use. Their Player Selection Network learns which nearby agents actually influence the decision maker's best move.

A mask drops the rest, and the smaller game solves fast. A second network guesses other agents' goals when those are hidden, so the selection still works under incomplete information. In simulations and real pedestrian data, the trimmed games matched or beat hand built selection rules on prediction accuracy and planning safety, while keeping far fewer players. The module, the authors note, plugs into existing planning frameworks.
arxiv-2505-00513:
Ioannis Emmanouil and Wei Ren write a 2025 algebra paper about ways to build new groups from old ones while keeping certain deep properties. Two known operations can formally enlarge the stock of examples of groups that meet a given homological condition, meaning a condition about how the group can be resolved by simpler pieces.

The authors apply this enlargement to two specific conditions. First, they show there are plenty of groups whose group algebras are virtually Gorenstein, a balanced form of symmetry in their structure. Second, they add examples for Moore's conjecture, which links projectivity with relative projectivity. The paper's value lies in widening the known test cases for both questions.
arxiv-2505-00613:
Hyde and co-authors present a fast method to build phase screens for simulating how light waves travel through turbulent air at several colors at once. Such screens help test adaptive optics systems before they are built. Their 2025 paper uses fast Fourier transforms to synthesize the screens.

The team checked the method by comparing a known theory value, the path length structure function for two colors, with what their screens produced. The two matched very well. The authors say the method will help run two color adaptive optics simulations in strong turbulence. That setting is where older screen methods tend to struggle most, they note. Such tests matter before hardware faces real sky conditions.
arxiv-2505-00913:
Han Wang, Adam White, and Martha White fix a fine-tuning flaw in twenty twenty-five. Policies learned offline often get worse before they get better online. Early exploration overrides what offline training taught, causing a performance dip. Most prior progress chased learning speed instead, leaving the dip in place.

Across many settings, the authors show algorithms either dip or learn too slowly. Their new algorithm builds on one called Jump Start. It gradually allows more exploration, guided by online estimates of performance. That pacing protects the offline policy while still improving it. Readers in reinforcement learning get fine-tuning that aims for monotonic improvement rather than a valley first.
arxiv-2505-01013:
Yohei Nishino, James Gardner, Yanbei Chen, and Kentaro Somiya propose a measurement scheme, in a 2025 preprint, that dodges the quantum pushback limiting precision sensors. When light measures a free mirror, the light also shoves it, and that shove blurs the next reading. This back action sets the standard quantum limit. Speed meters dodge it by reading velocity instead of position. A known double-pass design reads velocity through a one-way style coupling. Building that coupling is the hard part.

The authors replace it with reservoir engineering, a way of shaping a system's environment. Their scheme uses only ordinary two-way interactions. They show it can match the double-pass speed meter at its best, once feedforward is tuned. The force sensitivity then beats the standard quantum limit. The paper offers cavity optomechanics a second route to back-action evasion, which matters for gravitational wave detectors and other fine sensors.
arxiv-2505-01313:
Shang Wang, Huanrong Tang, and Jianquan Ouyang published a paper in 2025 on searching for good neural network designs inside a ResNet-shaped sandbox. Architecture search automates what engineers usually hand-tune, but wide-open search spaces wander. The authors fence the space to residual networks and let the search vary convolution, pooling, and dense layer settings plus how the residual blocks connect.

Accuracy alone can crown bloated or lucky designs, so they add validation loss as a second objective to keep the search honest. On three image benchmarks, handwritten digits, fashion items, and a hundred-class photo set, the method found architectures competitive with hand-built rivals. A modest space with a two-eyed score, the paper suggests, beats a grand space judged on accuracy alone.
arxiv-2505-01813:
Georgios Vassos, Richard Lusby, and Pierre Pinson present a study from twenty twenty-five on buying truck haulage for shipping containers under doubt. Flows of containers and market rates both shift in hard to guess ways. The team frames the choice of haulage volume as a staged transport problem with chance built in. They solve it with a dynamic method that splits the problem by stage.

Cargo flows come from a count based time model that keeps links between flows. Tests show the method scales to real sized cases and yields near best plans. Doubt in inflow drove cost far more than spot market swings. They also give a new stop rule for the solver that trades run time against plan quality in a fair way.
arxiv-2505-01913:
Ali Khalatpour, Luke Qi, Martin Fejer, and Amir Safavi-Naeini study loss in lithium niobate cavities in a 2025 paper. Thin-film lithium niobate is prized for quantum and nonlinear optics, but its cavities still lose more light than the material limit allows. Surface roughness is a prime suspect. The team separates sidewall roughness from interface roughness in racetrack cavities.

Very high quality factors are reached in both wide and narrow waveguides, they report. In wide guides, interface roughness dominates the loss. In narrow guides, sidewall roughness rules. Their model joins three-dimensional wave simulations with measured roughness and can apply to other photonic materials, they say.
arxiv-2505-02113:
Tomohide Kawatsu and co-authors map in 2025 flat zones in the pull curve of a quantum spin chain with a set spin size. Such flat zones, where pull holds as field grows, can break the plain shift rule of the chain. Past work had not shown that break for this chain type.

Exact counts on finite clusters and a level read method draw the maps. Maps at a third and two thirds of full pull show the new flat zone in both. The team sets this chain next to kin models to mark what is shared and what is new. Set pull curves fill out the case.
arxiv-2505-02213:
Wenwen Si and Hongxiang Qiu proposed in 2025 a way to give honest lower bounds for how long something lasts when some times are cut off early. Such cut-off data arise when a study ends before an event occurs. Older distribution-free methods often assume all cut-off times are known, which is a strong demand.

Their method uses a one-step fix drawn from flexible modeling and aims to stay valid for the training set at hand. It can also give a bound for the wider group with a small change. Tests and a real case on phone app use showed good results. The method held up better when the working model was wrong.
arxiv-2505-02313:
Jacqueline Harding and Cameron Domenico Kirk-Giannini ask what AI safety means in a 2025 philosophy paper. A tidy answer says the field is just the work that aims to prevent or reduce harms from AI systems. They call that the safety conception, and they test it against how the field actually talks.

Two habits strain the tidy answer. Many in the field frame the goal as guarding against disaster level risks from future systems, a much narrower aim. Others treat AI safety as a branch of safety engineering, with its own norms. The authors ask which meaning the field should own, and what follows from each choice.
arxiv-2505-02513:
Farhana Javed and Josep Mangues-Bafalluy design trust tools for 6G networks in a 2025 paper. Future networks will span many providers that must share services on the fly. Deals between them need both openness and secrecy. A hybrid blockchain is their proposed base.

The setup runs on Hyperledger Besu and mixes public and private deal flows. Smart contracts handle service listing, choice, and breach reports, with roles for each party. A working proof of concept was built and tested. Public steps held steady delay, while private steps cost more due to off-chain work. Lessons cover contract design and scaling for live use across domains.
arxiv-2505-02613:
Highway cameras watch traffic day and night, but spotting trouble in one lane among many is slow work for people. A 2025 paper by Mei Qiu and four co-authors offers a lane-by-lane detection system that reads camera video instead of road sensors. The system pulls out lane-level facts such as vehicle count, lane occupancy, and the share of trucks.

The team built a dataset of 73,139 lane samples marked with four kinds of problems checked by experts. Three are traffic events: a blocked lane and its clearing, a foreign object in the road, and lasting congestion. The fourth is a camera fault, a shift in camera angle. Tests show the mixed system, which joins deep learning, rules, and machine learning, beats older methods on precision, recall, and F1 score.
arxiv-2505-03013:
Joel Frohlich, Leonardo Christov-Moore, and Nicco Reggente argue that a theory of how the brain predicts the world can explain recent drone sightings in the United States, in a paper from 2025. They stress that honest, healthy people can misread lights in the sky. The sky gives few cues to fix a wrong first guess.

Lights far away are sparse signals, so prior beliefs fill in the gaps and are hard to update. The authors also suggest humans evolved to treat the sky as deeply meaningful. Falling trust in science bodies may add to the effect. They close by urging stronger astronomy teaching, so public beliefs better support accurate seeing.
arxiv-2505-03113:
Zherui Zhang and ten co-authors survey how to shrink vision transformers so they can recognize images on modest hardware, in a 2025 paper. Transformers read images powerfully but demand heavy computing and memory. That cost shuts them out of phones and small devices.

The survey sorts shrinking tricks into three families. Designers can build leaner parts, make networks adapt on the fly, or distill knowledge from big models into small ones. Each family is graded on the standard ImageNet test for accuracy, size, and speed. The authors weigh the trade offs openly. They close with open problems meant to steer builders of practical vision systems.
arxiv-2505-03313:
Binqiang Xie, Boling Guo, and Bin Zhao prove a negative result about a classic flow problem, in this 2025 paper. The Kelvin-Helmholtz problem concerns two fluid layers sliding past each other and the waves that grow between them. Here the fluid cannot be compressed, and a magnetic field runs across the flow. The question is whether math models of this setup have well-behaved solutions at all.

The authors show that the problem is ill-posed, in both its simple linear form and its full nonlinear form. In plain terms, tiny changes at the start can blow up so fast that no stable solution exists. Their proof backs a claim made long ago by Chandrasekhar in his book on fluid and magnetic stability. He held that the crosswise field does not tame this growth.
arxiv-2505-03713:
Xingyue Han and co-authors report physics results from 2025 on a magnetic crystal with unusual light effects. The team worked with thin films of a compound built from europium, iridium, and oxygen. The films grow along one crystal direction and act as a Weyl semimetal with no net magnetism. Light based tools let them watch hidden magnetic order that normal probes miss.

Using a microscope based on circular light effects, the team pictured patches of magnetic order below the point where the order sets in. Two patch types showed up, with spins pointing all in or all out. Even with no applied field and no net moment, the films gave a strong signal in both light tests. The authors tie the signal to curve effects in the electron bands near Weyl points.
arxiv-2505-04013:
Chih-Cheng Rex Yuan and Bow-Yaw Wang attack a hard combinatorial puzzle with a logic solver. Their 2025 paper concerns the poset cover problem: given a set of total orders, find the fewest partial orders whose completions cover them all. The problem is known to be NP-complete.

A naive translation into Boolean satisfiability blows up in size. The pair instead build swap graphs, a reduction trick that keeps the encoding lean. Modern SAT solvers then crack instances of fair size with ease. Tests with the Z3 prover on random inputs back the claim. The work shows how a careful encoding can bring a forbidding problem within reach of standard tools.
arxiv-2505-04213: Matias Alvarado gives explicit bounds for Zsigmondy sets of Drinfeld modules in a 2025 paper. Drinfeld modules are number theory objects that mirror elliptic curves over function fields, and Zsigmondy results promise new prime factors in their value sequences. The work covers certain families of rank two modules. The main plan bounds the local heights attached to these modules, then relates the canonical height, the natural size measure in the theory, to the classical height that is easier to compute. Those bounds then give concrete limits for the exceptional sets.
arxiv-2505-04313:
Stephen Varey, Alessandro Di Stefano, and The Anh Han introduce KERAIA in this 2025 paper, a platform for building AI that reasons with symbolic knowledge. The driving question is how to turn unwritten human expertise into algorithms a machine can run. Older knowledge systems tend to be static and brittle in changing settings. KERAIA aims for knowledge that adapts while staying explainable.

Its tools include clouds that gather knowledge on the fly, relations that shift with context, and lines of thought that leave a traceable reasoning trail. A custom language and a paradigm builder join many inference styles in one frame. Case studies span naval war simulation, water plant fault diagnosis, and strategy in the board game RISK. The authors compare their platform with ontologies, rule systems, and knowledge graphs.
arxiv-2505-04513:
John Etnyre, Burak Ozbagci, and Bülent Tosun settle which small Seifert fibered spaces can bound a rational homology ball symplectically in a 2025 mathematics paper. These spaces are built from a base with legs of fiber data, and complementary legs are the special pattern in question.

They prove that any such space with complementary legs fails to bound, symplectically, for at least one orientation. With tighter hypotheses they characterize exactly when bounding is possible, splitting the answer by a numerical invariant's sign. The contrast with the smooth world is sharp: smoothly, far more of these spaces bound balls. As a payoff, the authors complete the classification of contact structures on spherical three-manifolds that admit such fillings, at most six per manifold.
arxiv-2505-04813:
Richard Liu and co-authors boil a 3D shape down to a handful of curves. Their 2025 paper presents WIR3D, a method that fits Bezier curves to a shape so they carry both its geometry and its look. A big pretrained vision model guides the fit through its inner responses.

Tuning runs in two phases: coarse shape first, then fine features steered by key points. A surface-fit loss keeps the curves honest to the true skin of the object. Users can steer which features the curves keep. The finished curves double as handles for bending the shape. Tests span shapes of varied build and texture.
arxiv-2505-05013:
Andreas Osnes and Magnus Vartdal built models for turbulent-like stress in flow through particle clouds in two thousand twenty-five. Even without true turbulence, particles stir the flow in ways that act like extra stress, called pseudo-turbulence. Models are needed to close the averaged equations for such flows.

Their main model extends earlier work for incompressible flow to compressible flow below the speed of sound. It is built from data of fully resolved simulations of particle clouds. A second, local model ties the stress near a particle to the drag force on it, for use in simulations that track particles one by one. They also give a first model for the related energy transport terms.
arxiv-2505-05213:
Matthias Bentert, Pål Grønås Drange, and Erlend Haugen sharpen the theory of overlapping biclustering in two thousand twenty-five. The task: edit a two-sided graph into neat complete blocks, called biclusters. Edits may add or drop an edge, or split a vertex in two, which lets one item sit in several clusters at once.

Two variants of the task were known to be hard to approximate, and one had a shrunken core instance, a kernel, of size order k to the fifth. The team improves that kernel to order k squared and extends it to the second variant. They also give a fast solver whose run time depends on the edit budget in a fixed way. Both open questions from the earlier work are thus closed.
arxiv-2505-05313:
Ishizuka and Sato compute how twisted lattice vibrations, called chiral phonons, answer to infrared and terahertz light, in this 2025 paper. Unlike ordinary phonons, these carry a handedness as atoms circle in place. Shining light on them might stir effects with no parallel in normal crystals.

Nonlinear response theory shows the light-born angular momentum grows with the square of the phonon's lifetime. That makes it far larger than for ordinary phonons. A heat-flow effect named after Peltier also grows with the same square, through a new mechanism. The two quantities turn out to be locked in a fixed ratio. An orbital current, the charge cousin of spin current, appears as well.
arxiv-2505-05413:
Nilesh Prasad Pandey and co-authors present a 2025 compression method for hyperdimensional computing on tiny devices. That computing style codes data as very long vectors and suits edge AI, but high precision models eat memory and power. Past shrink methods often need costly retraining.

Their method, DPQ-HD, joins three shrink steps: split, prune, and quantize, applied after training with no retrain. It cuts memory and compute by up to a hundred fold in tests while scores stay near the full precision model. An early exit inference trick grades match scores in steps and stops once sure, which saves more energy. The work targets ultra low power hardware.
arxiv-2505-05613:
Achraf Azize and co-authors settle how well a learning system can do when it must pick among options while keeping each user's data private. In the bandit setup, an algorithm tries arms and learns from rewards, but privacy noise blurs what it sees. Past work left a gap between the best proven floor and the best known methods.

The team proves a sharper floor using a new measure of how hard privacy makes the task. They then adapt two known top methods with phased runs and added Laplace noise. Their regret matches the floor up to a factor near one, disproving a guess that forgetting old rewards was required.
arxiv-2505-05813:
Qiufu Li, Huibin Xiao, and Linlin Shen compare two loss functions in 2025 for training image classifiers, and prove a point that was not known before. Training aims for features that pack tight inside each class and stand far apart across classes, a pattern called neural collapse. The classic loss is known to drive that pattern at its best point.

A binary form of the loss has also done well on multi class tasks, for reasons that were unclear. The team proves it too can maximize both the tightness and the spread when it reaches its floor. They also draw the contrast: the classic loss works on relative scores, case by case, while the binary one works on absolute values. The result helps explain when each loss should be picked.
arxiv-2505-06113:
Anupkumar Bochare proposes in 2025 a camera only system that gives self driving cars a bird's eye map of the road, with no laser scanner. Laser gear is costly, so cheaper cars often lack it. His design stretches a known map building method with modern detection and depth tools.

Cameras around the car feed object spotting and depth guessing models, and the views merge into one top down map. On two public driving data sets, the system hit high road marking scores and found most cars. Its place errors stayed near one meter on average. Bochare frames the result as proof that cameras alone can guide budget cars.
arxiv-2505-06213:
Jordi Guàrdia and Francesc Pedret bring elliptic curves to bear on an old question about cubic number fields, in this 2025 paper. A number field is monogenic when its ring of integers is generated by a single element's powers, a tidy structure that is hard to verify. Pure cubic fields, built from a single cube root, are the test case.

Each such field, they show, picks out a unique orbit in a cohomology group attached to a matching elliptic curve, relative to a threefold isogeny. If the field were monogenic, that orbit would have to sit in the soluble part of a Selmer group, which gives a concrete test that can rule monogenity out. From this they bound how many monogenic cubic fields can exist in terms of the curve's rank. Assuming a standard unproven hypothesis, they also settle many individual fields.
arxiv-2505-06313:
Bohdan Pavlyshenko applies AI to news analytics on NATO unity in two thousand twenty-five. GPT models with retrieval read news, video comments, and forum threads. Scores gauge sentiment, unity, and trust in Article 5 across sources. Two levels of summaries build from single items to the whole set.

Bayesian regression draws trend lines through the model scores. Spread in those lines shows how unsure each trend is. The scores for NATO unity trend downward in his data. A neural differential model adds scenarios for how views may evolve. The work tests AI analytics, not real political claims.
arxiv-2505-06413:
Ming Liu and five co-authors craft a natural reflection backdoor attack on vision language models used in self driving cars. Such models boost reasoning through visual question answering, but their backdoor weakness was little studied. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Faint reflection patterns, like those on glass or water, were planted in some training images from a driving set. Matching text labels got long, off topic prefixes stuck in front. Fine tuned models then answered triggered images with bloated text, causing big delays, while clean inputs behaved normally. The authors vary poison rates and camera views to map what drives the effect.
arxiv-2505-06613:
Yuan-da Wu, Xiaoyu Zeng, and Yimin Zhang give a strict math analysis of a relativistic model for systems of fermions, the particle family that includes electrons. The model, called Hartree-Fock, balances attraction and the exclusion rules that fermions obey. The authors first prove a sharp form of a classic inequality for systems of many orthonormal states.

They spell out the shape of the states that make that inequality an equality. A companion inequality follows by duality, a result they note is new. With those tools they prove that lowest-energy states of the model exist exactly when the coupling stays below the sharp constant from the inequality. They also work out how the states behave at large distances.
arxiv-2505-07113:
Schipani and a large team describe in 2025 a plan to add light-wave direction measures to the VLT Survey Telescope. The telescope in Chile has taken wide sky images since 2011. A new survey from the Rubin Observatory will soon lead that field, so the older scope needs a fresh edge.

The project, called VSTPOL, would fit a large turning filter in front of the wide camera. That would make it the first large survey scope built for this kind of measure in visible light. Such data can back up work by a gamma ray array on the same site. The paper lays out the design and the science it would open.
arxiv-2505-07413:
Tung L Nguyen and Toby Dylan Hocking teach, in a 2025 paper, a neural network to set the key dial in a changepoint detection method. Changepoint detection finds the moments where a data sequence shifts character, a need in finance, genetics, and health monitoring. The optimal partitioning method locates those shifts well, but its penalty value, which caps how many shifts it may claim, is hard to pick. Analysts once chose it using hand-built summary features of each sequence.

The new approach feeds the raw sequence to a recurrent network, which learns its own features and predicts a good penalty directly. Across twenty benchmark genomic data sets, the learned penalties generally beat the hand-crafted method on detection accuracy. The authors present the work as a step toward changepoint tools that tune themselves.
arxiv-2505-07613:
Islam and co-authors measure, in 2025, how heat actually moves through thin films of ruthenium and tungsten, candidate metals for future chip wiring. Copper struggles at tiny scales, and these metals were suspected of carrying much of their heat through lattice vibrations rather than electrons. The team tested that suspicion several ways.

A classical law linking heat and electrical conduction failed for both films, by factors near two and three. The mismatch implies vibrations carry about forty-five percent of heat in ruthenium and sixty-two percent in tungsten. Vibration transport barely noticed grain structure or shrinking size, a useful trait for nanoscale wiring.
arxiv-2505-07913:
Getting food to markets is half of food security, and Robert Benassai-Dalmau and co-authors measure that access across a whole continent in a 2025 paper. They combine open map data with World Food Programme market records for Africa. Three yardsticks are compared: travel time to the nearest market, whether a market sits within thirty minutes, and how evenly markets are spread.

The gaps are wide. Rural and poorer populations face much longer trips and thinner coverage, with some areas hours from any market. Access tracks the wealth map closely and lines up moderately with official food insecurity ratings. Market data are patchy, the authors admit, but the framework still exposes structural gaps. They offer it to planners deciding where roads and markets would help most.
arxiv-2505-08013:
Gonglin Chen and co-authors present RDD in a 2025 paper, a robust feature finder and describer built on a deformable transformer. Finding match points across photos is a core step for 3D reconstruction and robot mapping, but big view shifts still break most methods.

The deformable attention design locks onto key spots, cuts search cost, and learns shape change well. The team also built an air-to-ground data set to train on, beside a standard depth photo set. RDD beat top prior methods on sparse matching and can do semi-dense matching too. Two new hard benchmarks test big view and height changes. Vision teams get a stronger tool for hard photo pairs.
arxiv-2505-08313:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports a measurement of double parton scattering in same-sign W boson pair production. Data came from proton-proton collisions at thirteen TeV at the Large Hadron Collider during Run Two. The sample holds an integrated luminosity of 140 inverse femtobarns.

Events had two same-charge leptons, electron or muon, missing transverse momentum, and up to one jet. An excess over expected background was seen with a significance of nearly nine standard deviations. The measured cross section times leptonic branching fraction was about four and a half femtobarns. That result gives a double parton scattering effective cross section of about eleven millibarns.
arxiv-2505-08713:
Ruan and Wang studied in 2025 how tiny bubbles pinch off and fire inner jets inside tapered microchannels. In a shared-flow setup the pair watched bubble birth run through four stages: growth, necking, break-off, and settling. Two shape knobs, the nozzle's reach into the taper and the taper's angle, ruled how the neck thinned. Across all shapes the thinning followed the same power laws.

The neck's shrink over time and space proved self-similar, and staged math models caught that behavior well. The jet itself springs from a flow squeeze: the taper front stretches while the rear pinches. Jet speeds evolved alike across flow regimes. The pair offers shape rules for building bubble-jet devices.
arxiv-2505-09313:
Qiangqiang Liu and co-authors present a method for spotting fake accounts in blockchain token giveaways, in a research paper from 2025. In a Sybil attack, one actor runs many addresses to claim extra tokens. The team aims to catch those addresses from their transaction patterns.

For each address, the method builds a two-layer graph of its transactions. It then pulls out timing traits from the address's life, such as its first trade and its first fuel payment, plus amount and network traits. A learning model merges these traits into one judgment. On a set of 193,701 addresses, with 23,240 of them fake, the method beat rival tools on all main scores, each above 0.9.
arxiv-2505-09413:
