Changfeng Ma and co-authors render realistic images from sparse point clouds in a 2025 paper. Point clouds record surfaces as scattered dots, often too sparse for clean rendering. Learning methods can fill the gap, but many lean on category-specific training or dense input.

Their method predicts flat 2D Gaussian blobs straight from the cloud. Two twin modules set the blobs from point positions, normals, colors, and distances. Splitting decoders then clone and refine the blobs, which helps the method cope with thin data. Once trained, the system handled clouds from new categories without retraining. Tests across data sets showed top rendering quality, and the blobs render directly with no extra cleanup of the images.
arxiv-2505-09513:
János Takátsy and co-authors lay out how to build and use dephasing prescriptions for environmental effects in gravitational wave astronomy, published in 2025. A binary's surroundings, such as gas or a third body, slowly shift its orbit, and that drift shows up as a phase shift in the wave signal. Templates must include that shift to detect and measure it.

The first part unifies two decades of literature: how orbital changes map to phase drift in time and frequency, with inconsistencies in earlier work resolved. Worked formulas and examples are collected as a reference. The second part derives new results for eccentric sources. Even modest eccentricity can greatly boost how detectable the environmental effects become in ground-based detectors, the authors show, improving the odds of seeing them.
arxiv-2505-09713:
Markovich and Osipov study how a message spreads through a growing random network in this 2025 paper. The network follows a preferential attachment model in which new nodes link to old ones with random counts of edges. A message passes from node to node, and the question is how many nodes hold it by a fixed time.

The authors derive the probability formulas for the number of informed nodes and for the total number of nodes, and for the share informed. A key step proves the chance that a message passes from an informed node to an uninformed one. Simulations illustrate the theory. The results describe spread in networks that grow as the message moves.
arxiv-2505-09813:
Doğaç Eldenk and Alperen Çetin retell one company's move from a single large software system to many small services, through the lens of what went wrong. Software incidents are unavoidable, but splitting a system changes their shape. The company, Carbon Health, shared its technology stack and its step-by-step breakup. The team then analyzed 107 incidents from that journey.

Patterns in the failures point to lessons about where cuts were made and what broke at the seams. Services split too eagerly created new failure modes at their borders. Based on the record, the authors suggest a gentler first step: tidy the single system into clean internal modules before pulling it apart into separate services. They argue this order can cut incidents and build sturdier software. The case is offered as field notes for other teams facing the same migration.
arxiv-2505-09913:
Saddam Hussain, Simran Arora, Anzhong Wang, and Ben Rose present a 2025 reconstruction of dark energy's equation of state using the newest DESI baryon acoustic oscillation data. They fit several dynamic dark energy models jointly to supernova samples, cosmic chronometers, and microwave background distance measures, with Bayesian methods. Across models, the equation of state sat in the phantom regime at early times and favors quintessence today.

The authors propose a new Gaussian-shaped form, BellDE, which avoids phantom behavior at high redshift while still dipping briefly below the phantom line near the transition era, around redshift 0.5. Their model stays statistically competitive while flexing where dark energy matters most. The paper offers the shape as a calibrated alternative for DESI-era cosmology.
arxiv-2505-10013:
Lake Yin and Fan Huang present DIF in a 2025 paper, a frame to benchmark hidden bias in large language models. Models can shift answers when social context changes, a flaw that is both an ethics and a skill problem. No standard gauge for this one bias type existed, the authors argue.

DIF wraps logic and math problems from known sets in varied social personas and grades the shift. A null model check adds a robustness test to the score. The frame confirms hidden bias in model behavior where it is applied. A fresh trend also shows up, with accuracy and bias moving in opposite ways. That link backs the view of bias as a skill gap, not just a values gap.
arxiv-2505-10113:
Does training a medical AI on one specialty make it best at that specialty? A 2025 paper by Xinlan Yan and co-authors builds a test set to find out. Their data set, S-MedQA, holds over twenty-four thousand English medical questions across fifteen specialties, with some questions tagged to more than one field.

Questions were built by machine and checked by experts for trustworthiness. When models were fine-tuned on one specialty's data, they did not always do best on that same specialty. Yet the models' confidence in key clinical terms rose across all fields at once. The authors argue the gains come mainly from shifting the model into the medical domain as a whole, not from injecting narrow specialty facts.
arxiv-2505-10313:
Tiny carbon sheets with an unpaired electron can act as sensors for the surface they sit on. Nicolò Bassi and co-authors test that idea in a 2025 study of a small nanographene placed on a magnetic rare-earth alloy.

On plain gold, the molecule shows a sharp signal at zero voltage, the mark of its lone spin being screened by the metal. On the magnetic alloy, that signal splits into two peaks set well apart. The team reads the split as a strong effect of the alloy's outward magnetism on the molecule. The result shows how such molecules could probe magnetic surfaces that are hard to read by other means, a step toward spin-based sensing.
arxiv-2505-10513:
Surabhi Luthra and three co-authors present a scheme for early fault-tolerant quantum computers in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Error correction will shield qubits and allow basic logical operations. But early machines will have few logical qubits. Costly steps like magic state distillation will strain them. Non-Clifford operations, such as small-angle rotations, are the bottleneck the authors target.

Their method, mitigated magic dilution, samples logical circuits with the help of error mitigation. It uses noisy encoded magic states rather than pure ones. They test the idea on simulating a two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model, a benchmark in condensed matter physics. In some time ranges, their scheme beats distillation in cost. The work aims to stretch what small fault-tolerant machines can do.
arxiv-2505-10913:
Muntasir Hoq and co-authors build a tool that spots sense slips in student code and names the part that slips, in a study from 2025. Code can run clean yet do the wrong thing; those sense slips are the marks of false lore in a learner's head. Teachers can not read a whole class's code live.

Their frame reads code as a tree and weighs its limbs with a care net, which flags the limb that bears the slip. Tests show the flags land true and, more, show how learners trip: which plans they mis-bend, and where. A flag with a limb and a tale attached, the team argues, is a teach aid, not just a grade.
arxiv-2505-11313:
Researchers with the HotQCD team use lattice QCD to study quarkonium, bound pairs of a heavy quark and its antiparticle, in hot matter. These pairs help probe the quark-gluon plasma, a soup formed at extreme heat. Their heat changed spectra carry the clues, but rebuilding them from lattice data is a hard, ill posed task.

The 2025 study works with 2+1 flavor setups at three heat levels above the change point. It joins two physics based pieces: a low range part from a complex potential and a high range part from vacuum theory. The join fits the lattice data well. One charmonium state shows a wide thermal blur, near melting, while its bottom kin stays sharp.
arxiv-2505-11513: Valery Sinev and co-authors reworked the antineutrino spectra of uranium and plutonium fuel forms using the summation method. Their math allows the shapes of single fragment spectra to be tuned where data are missing. The spectra agree with reactor measurements from several experiments. They also match the observed inverse beta decay cross sections with the best fit so far. Getting these spectra right matters for reactor watching and for neutrino work that relies on them.
arxiv-2505-11713:
Kaiser Shafi and Sandeep Chatterjee ran oxygen-on-oxygen collisions in a model in twenty twenty-five. They test if the flow of debris shows alpha clustering in oxygen nuclei. Heavy-ion collisions at two hundred giga-electronvolts turn the first shape of a nucleus into flow you can gauge. If the nucleons of oxygen bunch into alpha particles, some flow patterns should shift. They would not match a smooth density profile.

With viscous relativistic hydrodynamics, the authors computed symmetric and asymmetric cumulants. They computed rapidity-even dipolar flow too. Some observables proved keen to the first shape. Ones that link elliptic and triangular flow were keenest. In high-multiplicity events, dipolar flow split in a clear way. It split between clustered and smooth starts. The results give experimentalists firm signs to hunt for. Ultra-central collisions are a key case.
arxiv-2505-11813:
Yixuan Dong and co-authors enrich training images for niche classifiers in a 2025 paper. Domain image tasks need more data, but fake images must stay diverse, faithful, and clearly labeled. Diffusion-based makers often trade one of those needs against the others.

Their framework, SGD-Mix, guides mixing with saliency maps that mark the true subject. A fine-tuned diffusion model then varies the background while guarding the subject. Label clarity survives because the class-defining part is preserved by design. The method also damps the randomness that strong diffusion edits can cause. Small, specialized datasets stand to gain the most from such careful synthesis.
arxiv-2505-12113:
Hsin-Hsiung Huang, Yuh-Haur Chen, and Teng Zhang propose a classifier for finding disease regions in brain scans, in a 2025 paper. Brain MRI data are high-dimensional, and scans from different people often misalign. Their model uses a sparse tensor method with a twist: it also reads a shifted copy of the data.

The shift makes the method more robust to misalignment while keeping results interpretable. Theory gives consistency guarantees under a stated condition. Simulations showed the model can recover spatial signals through noise. On two public Alzheimer's datasets it classified well and pointed to regions known to matter, such as the hippocampus. A slice-choice strategy aids reading of the results.
arxiv-2505-12613:
When cyber danger rises, United States defense networks are ordered into higher protection postures, graded levels called CPCON. Mark Timmons and co-authors noted in 2025 that those shifts are still carried out largely by hand, unevenly and with errors. Their paper presents a prototype that runs the changes from one center.

A policy-driven orchestrator issues standard actions across mixed networks, isolates compromised segments, and checks that each order actually took hold. In emulated attacks the system made posture changes faster, more accurate, and easier to verify, with a human still in the loop. The authors build on earlier work in host-based intrusion response.
arxiv-2505-12813:
James Sellers and Roberto Tauraso wrote a math paper in two thousand twenty-five on sums of divisors, with stress on the odd case. A century ago, MacMahon gave two families of generating functions that link such sums to integer partitions. One family runs over all whole numbers, and the other runs over odd whole numbers only.

Work since then grew the first family and found congruences for the terms of its series. Sellers and Tauraso now grow the odd family in the same way, with like methods. They prove new Ramanujan-like congruences for the terms, in families that go on without end. Such rules show clear patterns in which terms vanish modulo a given number.
arxiv-2505-13113:
Karel Proesmans and four co-authors measure the cost of flocking in twenty twenty-five. Self-propelled particles that align undergo a transition from disorder to collective motion. Their focus is the dissipation, or entropy production, of that transition. Each particle also carries an internal state that biases how it moves.

Their lattice model respects thermodynamics throughout: state changes and hops obey local detailed balance under one interaction energy. For weak interactions, dissipation is maximal, and leaving out internal states makes it come out far too low. For strong interactions, dissipation drops and a partial count captures most of it. Macroscopic and microscopic dissipation counts agree upon coarse-graining. Readers in statistical physics learn when hidden internal states must be tracked to get the price of a flock's motion right.
arxiv-2505-13313:
Most white dwarfs wear hydrogen atmospheres, but a stubborn share show none, and theory has struggled to match the hydrogen mass that observations imply. James MacDonald, writing alone in a 2025 paper, tests whether a brief unstable phase early in the life of the dwarf can close that gap. The instability strikes just after the giant branch stage ends.

MacDonald evolved one- and two-solar-mass star models through the giant phases and onto the cooling track. With the instability active, the final hydrogen masses landed in the range that pulsation measurements suggest. The instability also drew loops in the path of the star across the brightness diagram, loops that vanish when it is suppressed. Long monitoring or the shape of the thrown-off nebula might reveal those loops.
arxiv-2505-13413:
Wang and co-authors present VGFM, a method for learning how a population of single cells changes over time from snapshot data. Snapshots freeze cells at separate moments, and because measuring destroys the cells, no one can follow the same cell twice. Cells also divide and die, so group sizes shift between snapshots.

The method jointly learns two things: how each cell's state moves, and how mass grows or shrinks across the population. It builds on a relaxed form of optimal transport, a math tool for matching uneven groups. Tests on synthetic and real data beat earlier methods. Better cell-dynamics models help biologists trace how tissues develop and how diseases progress.
arxiv-2505-14113:
Bruno Viti, Elias Karabelas, and Martin Holler present CONSIGN, a 2025 method for honest uncertainty in image segmentation. Segmentation models output per pixel confidence scores, but those scores are rough guesses, not firm error bounds. Formal methods exist to convert them, yet they ignore how nearby pixels relate.

CONSIGN groups pixels by spatial structure before applying conformal prediction, a framework that yields error guarantees at a level the user sets. It works with any pretrained model that can produce several sample outputs. Tests covered three medical datasets and two subsets of a general photo dataset, with three base models. Accounting for spatial structure improved the quality of the uncertainty sets across measures. The authors target high stakes uses such as medical imaging.
arxiv-2505-14313:
Leonardo Bertolazzi and co-authors test in this 2025 paper whether small language models can learn logic, not just mimic it. They use syllogisms, the classic two-premise arguments, and frame the task as picking the right premises. Clean data sets let them isolate true logical skill from memory of surface patterns, a point of debate for larger models.

Their training twist is meta-learning: the model practices across many small tasks so it picks up rules that carry to new shapes. Small models trained this way gained strongly, above all when data was scarce. On the team's syllogism task, the tuned small models even beat GPT-4o and o3-mini, which hints that how a model learns can matter more than size.
arxiv-2505-14513:
Yen-Chen Wu and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on shrinking the layer stacks of large language models. Such models stack tens to hundreds of layers, and more layers cost more to run. Work on image models showed smooth, flow based layers can beat stacks of fixed ones.

Their design swaps a block of layers for one learned move operator trained by flow matching. It stays compatible with the base model's shape. A new walk method keeps the links between steps that past flow methods lost. On a mid-size open model, the swapped form beat plain layer skips at the same cut size. With the walk method, a dozen layers folded into one with a small quality loss. The authors see a bridge between the two model styles.
arxiv-2505-14713:
Dionissios Hristopulos, Anastassia Baxevani, and Giorgio Kaniadakis bend a classic bell curve's skewed cousin in a 2025 paper. The lognormal law models everything from incomes to pollutant spikes, but it dictates exactly how its high tail must fade, an order real data often disobey.

Their kappa-lognormal family adds one dial. Turning it lightens the right tail smoothly, and some settings even split the curve into two humps. The authors derive the family's main formulas in closed form, bound its averages, and supply the gradient machinery needed to fit it to data by computer. A joint version for processes unfolding in space or time follows.
arxiv-2505-14813:
Rui Pan and co-authors study, in a 2025 paper, ripples in the early universe under a modified loop quantum cosmology. In such models the universe bounces instead of beginning in a bang, and the ripples start in a shrinking phase long before. Picking the right starting state is delicate: a bad pick can spawn fake particles. Using a classic method, the team finds a state that stays stable and quiet in that remote phase.

With the start fixed, they build close-form approximations for how each ripple mode evolves. The form of the answer shifts with the ripple's wavelength, drawing on three families of special functions. Each solution's free constants are pinned by the chosen starting state. The work gives later studies a clean launch pad for computing what such a bounce would imprint on the sky.
arxiv-2505-15213:
Sampanna Yashwant Kahu teaches a neural network to guess which task the Linux scheduler will run next. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Linux's fair scheduler juggles programs so the processor stays busy without making the system feel sluggish. Predicting its choices could open the door to smarter, data-driven scheduling.

Kahu built a fresh data set by recording a live kernel's scheduling decisions. A memory-based network, an LSTM, was then trained to forecast the next task in line. The paper weighs how such a predictor could plug into the kernel itself. Pathways and pitfalls of that integration are discussed in detail. All code is shared for others to reproduce and extend. The work treats the operating system's core as a place where learning can help.
arxiv-2505-15313:
Kazuaki Mishima, Antoni Bigata Casademunt, Stavros Petridis, Maja Pantic, and Kenji Suzuki built a face generator in 2025 with separate control over pose, expression, and emotion. Face images mix stable identity with changeable traits, and keeping one fixed while steering the others is hard. Their diffusion model targets that split.

Two light control modules sit inside the model's attention layers, steering the changeable traits with little added cost. Training pushes identity features to stay independent of control signals, aiding clean control and variety. Tests and user studies showed better control accuracy than prior methods, plus more diverse outputs when only identity is given. The design suits uses needing consistent faces with directed expressions.
arxiv-2505-15613:
Ajay Agarwal and Santhanam study how city traffic tips from flowing to jammed, using the real street maps of four cities. Gridlock is an emergent property of the whole network, and toy grids may lie about it. Their 2025 paper loads those street networks, plus a regular square grid for contrast, with three variants of random-walk traffic enriched with realistic features.

In every network and every model, raising the rate at which vehicles are born drives a sharp transition from free flow to congestion. Smarter routing that knows the traffic can shift the tipping point but never abolish the jam. The organic street networks show an in-between regime where jammed and flowing districts coexist. In free flow, rare extreme events strike small side streets more than hubs, echoing a pattern first seen in very different networks.
arxiv-2505-15813:
Muquan Yu and a large team meta-trained in 2025 a transformer that models a new person's higher visual brain areas from only a handful of examples. Brain encoders usually need long, costly scans for each person, which blocks wider use. Their system, BraInCoRL, learns in context: shown a few image-and-response pairs, it builds a voxel-level model of that person's visual cortex on the spot. Training itself was shaped to reward this quick adaptation.

On wholly new images the model beat existing encoder designs in the low-data regime, and its accuracy kept growing with more context. It also carried over to a fresh dataset with different people and scanners. Attention patterns pointed at images that matched each voxel's taste, aiding interpretation. The authors say such models make brain reading cheaper and more personal.
arxiv-2505-15913:
Paul Faehrmann, Jens Eisert, and Richard Kueng get more from a classic quantum test by keeping its leftover state, in a 2025 paper. The Hadamard test reads information from one helper qubit and throws the main register away. That waste struck the authors as a missed chance. A second tool, classical shadows, can snapshot the main register with shallow circuits.

Joining the two tools keeps the strengths of each, they argue. Their example task is estimating phases of a quantum state. The helper qubit gives the eigenvalues, while the shadows reveal how close the state sits to target states and to energy levels. They also show how reversed controls can extend the scheme. The work suits today's noisy mid-size quantum machines.
arxiv-2505-16113:
Panagiotis Lymperopoulos and Vasanth Sarathy build a way to measure doubt in language model answers that lean on outside tools, in a research paper from 2025. Models often call classifiers or search tools when their own knowledge runs thin. The final answer then rests on two fallible parts, and past doubt measures cover only one.

Their framework rates the model's text doubt and the tool's output doubt jointly. It extends token-level uncertainty methods to the tool-calling case and adds fast approximations for real use. Tests used two new question sets built from classic machine learning data, plus a retrieval-augmented system. The scores flagged shaky answers well, a step toward trust in high-stakes fields such as medicine.
arxiv-2505-16313:
Arjhun Swaminathan and Mete Akgün speed up adversarial attacks in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Image classifiers can be fooled by tiny, invisible changes. In black-box settings the attacker sees only the final label, and forcing a chosen wrong class is especially hard.

Their attack, TEA, uses edge information from the target image to shape the perturbation. Earlier methods leaned on the geometry of decision boundaries instead. Across models, TEA beat leading methods while using nearly seventy percent fewer queries. That frugality matters where queries are limited or costly. TEA also gives older geometry-based attacks a better starting point. The work sharpens a known weakness of image models under tight access limits.
arxiv-2505-16413:
Jos Zuijderwijk and co-authors present a way to judge how open a government really is, in this 2025 paper. Good records matter for openness, yet most checks ignore how staff actually handle files day to day, and deep audits cost a lot. Their system, called TAPAS, reads real data from a document system and looks for habits that block openness.

At a Dutch ministry, they scanned two decades of records and found eight such habits in four groups. Files were left incomplete, hard to reach, unclear, or filed late. Because the system runs on data the ministry already holds, it can watch these habits over time at low cost.
arxiv-2505-16513:
Vaishali Maheshkar and co-authors tested modern machine learning for sorting plastics by light in a 2025 study. Only a small share of plastic waste in the United States is recycled, and most ends up in landfills. Sorting mixed plastics well is one key step that better machines could improve.

Sorting centers already use light sensors to tell plastic types apart, and firms sell optical sorters for the task. The authors compare current learning methods on the job in detail, weighing accuracy and practical limits. Their findings show which methods suit real sorting lines, where errors cluster, and what gains are realistic. Recycling firms and researchers get a grounded guide instead of vendor claims.
arxiv-2505-16613: Fine particle air pollution kills over years of exposure, and Federica Spoto and co-authors ask whether wildfire seasons make that slow harm worse in a 2025 study. Their population covers more than sixty million older adults in the United States. The answer is yes: where wildfire events occur, the mortality effect of long-term exposure to fine particles grows stronger. The authors frame the finding as a new way to think about wildfire health risk, not just smoke days but lasting vulnerability.
arxiv-2505-16913:
Fabio Cunden, Giovanni Gramegna, and Marilena Ligabò study a quantum particle whose mass jumps from place to place. Their twenty twenty-five paper treats a free particle on a line with a mass profile full of sudden steps. Each jump point needs a boundary rule to define the energy operator.

For a scale-free family of such rules, the authors solve the spectral problem. The wave patterns turn out highly sensitive to energy, in an erratic way. The system also holds endlessly many distinct semiclassical limits, each marked by a point on a curve in a torus. The work shows how rough material traits and edge rules can jointly shape quantum behavior.
arxiv-2505-17213:
Ramanakumar Sankar and co-authors simulate Jupiter's water storms to learn how deep wind shear steers convection on the giant planet. Lightning maps show storms crowding into cyclonic belts while the calm anticyclones stay quiet, and vapor maps show rich upwelling at the equator. The deep atmosphere that drives it all cannot be observed directly.

Their 2025 study runs a global circulation model of cloud formation and varies the parameterized deep shear. Storm strength, frequency, and placement answer strongly to the local dynamics the shear sets. Eddy vapor transport, the restless shuffling of water vapor by swirling flows, emerges as a key accomplice in feeding the storms. The work links the weather we see to winds we cannot.
arxiv-2505-17313:
Soham Dutta and Arnab Saha modeled a tiny heat engine made from a single particle in 2025. The particle is an ellipsoid held by light tweezers, which can grip both its place and its tilt. It follows a Stirling cycle as baths and grip strength change over time.

The particle takes heat from the hot bath and turns part of it into useful work. Output and efficiency depend on the particle shape and on its tilt bias. Links between place and tilt, caused by the uneven shape, help tune the engine. The authors study work spread and efficiency limits, then work out the case of a near-round particle in detail.
arxiv-2505-17513:
Binh Nguyen, Shuji Shi, Ryan Ofman, and Thai Le show that fake-speech detectors can be fooled by changing the words, not the sound, in a 2025 paper. Voice cloning now powers fraud and impersonation, and guard systems mostly listen for acoustic flaws. What happens when the spoken text itself is tweaked had gone largely untested.

The team attacked both open and commercial detectors with small changes at the transcript level. Detection fell sharply: some attacks succeeded more than sixty percent of the time, and one commercial tool dropped from perfect scores to about a third correct. A case study copied a celebrity audio scam and slipped past commercial checks entirely. The authors urge builders to defend the language side as well as the sound side.
arxiv-2505-17613:
Jihan Yao, Yushi Hu, and colleagues built a benchmark for systems that generate across several media at once in a 2025 study. Judging generated images, audio, and mixed text-media output is hard because automatic scores often disagree with people. Their benchmark borrows the verifiable-task idea: choose tasks whose outputs can be checked by a program rather than by taste.

Tasks span four combinations, pairing image, audio, and interleaved text with each medium. Checkable scoring makes results repeatable across labs. A reliable yardstick matters as multimodal generators move into products, since weak evaluation lets fluent but wrong output pass unnoticed.
arxiv-2505-17713:
Frans Perkkola and co-authors run a quantum algorithm on real hardware in a 2025 paper. Today's quantum machines are noisy, so circuits must stay short. The team tackled a regression task, predicting numbers with a tunable quantum circuit, and focused on how the input data is loaded into the machine.

A diagram-based method rewrote the circuit in leaner form, pushing and folding parts to cut gates. With those trims, the regression ran successfully on current hardware. The loading method suits any values, not just this task. The authors offer the toolkit as a general aid for making quantum programs fit the limits of present machines. The work was funded by a national quantum computing campaign in Finland.
arxiv-2505-17813:
Michael Hassid, Gabriel Synnaeve, Yossi Adi, and Roy Schwartz question, in a 2025 paper, whether long chains of thought really make language models reason better. Reasoning models now spend huge compute writing long inner monologues before they answer. The team checked if shorter chains might do as well.

Within one question, the shortest chains were far more likely to end in a right answer, up to 34.5 percent more often than the longest. The authors then built a method that runs several tries at once and stops when the first few finish, voting among them. That method matched or beat plain voting while using up to 40 percent fewer tokens. Training models on short chains also beat training on long ones.
arxiv-2505-17913:
Anna Duwenig studies special subalgebras inside twisted groupoid algebras in this 2025 paper. She asks when the algebra of a smaller groupoid counts as a diagonal inside the larger one. The smaller piece must be an open, normal subgroupoid with a twist. Past work treated such non-traditional cases through a related Cartan subalgebra lens.

She first gives an explicit picture of the Weyl groupoid and twist tied to any such subalgebra. That picture is then joined with a classic theory of these algebras. The result is a set of conditions that are both needed and enough for the diagonal property. The work sharpens the map of how these algebras sit inside each other, a topic in operator algebra theory.
arxiv-2505-18013:
Hanze Zhang, Kaiming Wang, Rong Chen, Xingda Wei, and Haibo Chen present a caching system for computers that share a pool of remote memory, in a research paper from 2025. Pooling memory across machines gives flexibility, but fetching data from afar is slow. Caching hot data locally helps, yet keeping copies in sync across machines is costly.

Their system, DiFache, drops the central sync manager. Each machine can void stale copies on others by itself, since the apps already order conflicting access on their own. It also adapts how much it caches based on how often each item is read or written. On real Twitter traces, it beat rivals several-fold.
arxiv-2505-18113:
Halyun Jeong, Jack Xin, and Penghang Yin study a training trick in this 2025 paper on small neural networks. The trick, called the straight-through estimator, lets a network learn even though its weights are cut down to just one bit, a step that saves size and power.

Earlier work on the trick assumed endless training data. The authors instead ask how much data is enough, and they derive bounds tied to the size of the data itself. With noisy labels, they show the method can drift away from the best weights and then return to them. Tests also show the trick can fail on some data unless the data is first put on a common scale.
arxiv-2505-18613:
Faithful Chiagoziem Onwuegbuche and three co-authors release a ransomware data set in a 2025 paper. Machine learning detectors need examples, but public collections of malicious software behavior are small and hard to reproduce. Their collection holds over 4,800 ransomware samples from sixty-four families, plus a balanced set of harmless software, spanning 2006 to 2024.

The samples cover the main ransomware styles, from simple lockers to rented attack kits. The team also published rules for building such data sets well, and followed them. To test the data, they shrank millions of behavior features down to a few hundred informative ones. Detectors trained on the set reached accuracy near ninety-nine percent. Explanation tools pointed to registry tampering and odd program strings as strong danger signs. Data and code are public for other teams to build on.
arxiv-2505-18713:
Guodong Du and eleven co-authors propose Neural Parameter Search, a pruning method that slims fine-tuned models, in a two thousand twenty-five machine learning paper. Fine-tuned checkpoints carry heavy redundancy and often forget general skills outside their specialty.

The method works on task vectors, the differences between fine-tuned and pretrained weights. Different low-rank subspaces of a task vector matter unequally, so the search prunes within them efficiently. Slimmer models transfer better through pairwise interpolation, merge more cleanly across tasks, and deploy at lower storage cost with near-original performance. Experiments across vision, language, and multimodal benchmarks show substantial gains. Code is publicly available.
arxiv-2505-18813:
Nancy Ghangas and Shubhrangshu Dasgupta study how entanglement evolves for atoms inside photonic crystals in this 2025 paper. Photonic crystals are materials patterned to trap light in set bands of color. Atoms with several energy levels sit inside, and their shared quantum links can be steered by light they exchange.

The pair modeled the system with equations and computer runs. When atoms sit close together, their direct interaction dominates and can protect entanglement, above all when their dipoles point oppositely. With dipoles at right angles, entanglement pulses in waves, shaped by dark states formed through interference. Placing atomic levels deeper in the forbidden band speeds the fading of those waves. The work maps knobs for tailoring quantum links.
arxiv-2505-18913: Surajit Sen and co-authors demonstrate teleportation of a three-level quantum unit, a qutrit, in this 2025 protocol paper. Qutrits carry more information per particle than two-level qubits. The team built a complete set of two-qutrit entangled states from the symmetry theory of the SU(3) group and worked through every measurement step the end-to-end protocol needs. The measurement gates turn out to be non-unitary, framed as unavoidable in higher dimensions. Their scheme extends the classic teleportation protocol with minimal changes.
arxiv-2505-19013:
Kiljae Lee, Ziqi Liu, Weijing Tang, and Yuan Zhang fix group level data pricing against gaming, in work from 2025. Data Shapley scores how much each data point helps a learning model. Buyers often need group scores instead, since providers supply data in batches rather than one point at a time.

Current group scores can be gamed by shell groups that split to inflate their worth. Their faithful group score is built to block that split trick by design. A new method computes the score fast with proven accuracy bounds for large groups. Tests beat leading methods on both speed and closeness to true values. Fair batch pricing for data markets is the clear target use.
arxiv-2505-19313:
Text-to-image models do not always draw what the prompt asks, but steering their inner activations can reach concepts that prompting cannot. Marta Aparicio Rodriguez, Xenia Miscouridou, and Anastasia Borovykh study in 2025 when such concepts are reachable at all. They built training setups with three obstacles: few examples of a concept, captions that underspecify it, and biases that tie concepts together.

Three findings stand out. Reachability switches on sharply — a handful of samples can be enough. Where in the model's layers the steering happens matters greatly, with some concepts reachable only at certain stages. And as dataset quality falls, prompting fails fast while steering keeps working. The authors suggest providers can skip costly retraining and instead hand users better control mechanisms.
arxiv-2505-19613:
Amira Guesmi, Bassem Ouni, and Muhammad Shafique present TESSER, an attack that crafts image tweaks on one model and fools many others. Such transfer attacks matter for security, since they need no peek inside the target. Attacks brewed on vision transformers often fail to cross to older network kinds. Their 2025 frame adds two guards to the tweaks.

One scales the tweak by how much each image patch matters to the model. The other smooths the tweak's high-frequency noise with a soft blur rule. On a big image set across twelve designs, TESSER beat the top past method on both network families. It also cut through defended models at a strong rate. Its tweaks sit on the image parts humans look at too, the team shows.
arxiv-2505-20113:
Cristian Santini, Laura Melosi, and Emanuele Frontoni test entity recognition on historical Italian in this 2025 paper. Archives are being digitized fast, but old texts bring spelling shifts, broken structure, and scanning errors that defeat tools trained on modern text.

Their test bed is Leopardi's Zibaldone, a vast set of scholarly notes from the nineteenth century holding 2,899 references to people, places, and works. The team ran both fine tuned BERT style models and large language models on the data. Instruction tuned models struggled with the humanistic text, while the fine tuned models held up better, even on hard types like book references. The dataset is offered for repeatable research.
arxiv-2505-20213:
A quantum gas thrown far from equilibrium often relaxes by a universal script, whatever its starting state. Qi Liang and six co-authors report in 2025 that a strongly interacting gas of lithium molecules follows the same script as a weakly interacting gas studied before.

The team stamped a random phase pattern onto a thin, tube-like gas of Feshbach molecules and watched it settle. Its relaxation matched the pattern seen when a shock-cooled rubidium gas formed its ordered state, even though the gases differ in interaction strength and makeup. The authors argue for one shared non-thermal fixed point with a wide basin of attraction for tube-like Bose gases. Microscopic details, in this view, wash out of the late behavior.
arxiv-2505-20313:
Son Tran, Edjard Mota, and Artur Garcez wrote a 2025 book chapter on mixing neural networks with logic. The field, called neurosymbolic AI, tries to join learning from data with strict step-by-step reasoning. That union could fix known weaknesses of large language models, such as waste of data and shaky fairness and safety.

The chapter presents one simple system built on energy, a way of scoring how well a network state fits a set of rules. The system can hold and reason over any statement of propositional logic. Tests check that its energy-based reasoning matches true logical reasoning, using a classic network model. Learning from both data and given knowledge is also tested against purely symbolic and purely neural rivals. The authors hope the clear presentation revives work on networks as fast, parallel logic machines.
arxiv-2505-20413:
James Sunseri and co-authors present a 2025 joint read of two faint sky signals around a set of heavy galaxies. One signal tracks hot gas speed in galaxy halos, the other tracks how halo mass bends light from far galaxies. Each alone leaves the gas and dark mix tangled.

Fit together, they pull the two apart: the gas profile is pinned from near the core to fifty times the core width. The gas skirt falls off more gently than some sims say, a hint of strong gas push-back. Skipping gas in light-bend fits also low-balls halo mass by a fifth.
arxiv-2505-20613:
Ziju Shen and a large team of co-authors present an open theorem prover that works step by step in the Lean proof language. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Automated provers have mastered school and contest math, but advanced college topics remain hard. Their system aims to push that boundary with retrieval help.

A fine-tuned language model drives the prover, while a search tool fetches useful past lemmas. To train it, the team built a pipeline that turns plain-language problems into formal statements. They also built a fresh benchmark of algebra problems to test on. On a standard college-level set, the prover solved about a quarter of problems given many tries. On their own algebra set, it solved more than half. Both scores matched or beat the best known systems.
arxiv-2505-21013:
José Antonio Fernández-Fernández, Fabian Löschner, and Jan Bender present a faster Newton's method in two thousand twenty-five for computer graphics simulation. Newton's method solves the nonlinear equations behind soft-body and rigid-body motion. To keep steps downhill, standard practice projects every element's Hessian matrix, clamping negative curvature, but that distortion slows convergence.

Their variant, Progressively Projected Newton, projects only a small subset chosen cheaply from the current residual. The global matrix thus stays closer to the true one, cutting both iterations and costly eigen-decompositions. Across contact-free and contact-rich deformables, co-dimensional bodies, and rigid bodies, it used under ten percent of the projections of rivals and usually converged in fewer steps. Only very large time steps and quasistatics favored the old method.
arxiv-2505-21713:
Matías Blaña and ten co-authors modeled in 2025 how cluster tides reshape the small galaxies that orbit inside galaxy clusters. Tides strip a satellite's outskirts, leaving its dense core, so satellites near the center should pack their mass tighter. The team combined orbit models with cosmological simulations to test this. Both total mass density and star-only density showed the expected sorting with distance.

The pattern held out to about half the cluster's virial radius, then flattened or rose slightly where tides weaken. Real data from the Virgo and Fornax clusters and from Andromeda and the Milky Way matched the trend. The team suggests the turning radius works as a photo-based probe of a host's gravity field. It marks where satellites were strongly processed by tides. The study links galaxy appearance to the unseen halo that hosts it.
arxiv-2505-21813:
Madi Matymov and co-authors stop treating data augmentation as a folk art. Flipping, cropping, and warping training data makes machine learning sturdier, but choosing the settings is usually trial and error or a costly search. Their 2025 paper takes a probabilistic view: the augmentation settings are hyperparameters of the model itself, and picking them is a problem of Bayesian model selection.

Since the ideal objective cannot be computed directly, the authors derive a tractable stand-in that lets augmentation and model parameters be tuned together in one training run. They back the method with theory on approximation quality, generalization, and invariance, and test it on vision and language tasks. The tuned augmentation improved calibration and held up better than fixed or absent augmentation. The authors offer a principled dial where practitioners previously turned knobs by feel.
arxiv-2505-22113:
Zhiyuan Li, Yi Chang, and Yuan Wu built a benchmark in 2025 to catch large reasoning models wasting thought. Reasoning models often outperform ordinary language models on hard problems. But they suffer from overthinking, spinning out long chains of redundant tokens that add little accuracy, especially on easy questions. That waste costs real computing resources at scale.

Their benchmark, THINK-Bench, evaluates thinking efficiency directly rather than accuracy alone. They propose new efficiency metrics and score many reasoning models across the reasoning process, outcome quality, and chain-of-thought characteristics. The analysis shows how differently models spend their tokens for similar results. For builders of reasoning systems, the message is practical: a model that thinks twice as long for the same answer is not twice as smart. Measuring thrift is a first step toward fixing it.
arxiv-2505-22213:
Automated theorem provers search for proofs by generating clauses and discarding useless ones. Márton Hajdu, Laura Kovács, and Andrei Voronkov improve that cleanup in 2025. They define redundancy more sharply, using partial clauses, so that more clauses and inferences count as safe to drop. The new idea blurs the line between redundant clauses and redundant steps.

They build a calculus, PaRC, on these partial clauses and prove it still finds a contradiction whenever one exists. They also implement it in the Vampire prover. In tests, the stronger cleanup solved 24 benchmark problems that no prover had solved before, including earlier versions of Vampire itself.
arxiv-2505-23013:
Liangkai Hang, Junjie Yao, Zhiwei Bai, and sixteen co-authors show that taming model complexity, a cheap training knob, lifts language model reasoning and scaling at once. Their paper from twenty twenty-five adjusts two levers: the initialization rate and the weight decay coefficient. Complexity control in this form needs no new data or architecture. The scaling law improves across model sizes and data sizes alike.

A sharper test compares 2.4-billion-parameter models pretrained on one trillion tokens under varied complexity settings. Holding the initialization standard deviation fixed loses to a constant initialization rate. With the rate held constant, the scaling curve drops faster as either size or data grows. The team frames complexity control as a steady, general path for pushing large models further.
arxiv-2505-23813:
Abhijit Talluri sets out a design for shared machine learning that guards both privacy and uptime. In shared learning, many sites train one model without pooling raw data, a fit for banks and hospitals bound by strict rules. Standard designs can stall when a site or the hub fails, and their privacy claims can be hard to prove. His 2025 design adds noise at each site to shield local data.

Time-stamped state records let training pick up where it left off after a fault. Hash-based proofs let others check that steps were done as claimed, with no raw data shown. The design is aimed at tasks like credit risk scoring on touchy bank data. Talluri frames it as a base for shared learning that firms can audit and trust.
arxiv-2505-23913:
Gustavo Sutter and co-authors strip Bayesian optimization down to a single learned step. Their 2025 paper addresses the tuning of expensive black-box functions, where each test costs dearly. Classic Bayesian optimization pairs a surrogate model with an acquisition rule, and even with modern in-context surrogates, picking the next point still needs costly maximization full of knobs.

Their method samples the optimum directly, in context, with no acquisition step at all. The proposal is zero-shot: the model reads the history of past trials and proposes the winner outright. Simplifying the loop removes fragile tuning and speeds the search for the best settings in science and engineering problems.
arxiv-2505-24213:
Geng Li, Chunjiang Shi, Ying Chen, and Wei Sun study scattering between two J/psi particles in this 2025 physics paper. They use lattice QCD, a grid-based way to compute strong force effects. The work looks for new structures near the pair's energy threshold.

In one channel they find an attractive force that could allow a near-threshold scalar structure. It may match a state called X(6200), though a cut effect blocks a firm call. In a second channel they find a tensor resonance near 6.54 GeV. Its mass and width match states reported by the ATLAS and CMS teams. Quark rearrangement seems to drive the gap between channels.
arxiv-2506-00113:
Sean Benevedes and Jesse Thaler introduced ensemble weights that carry honest error bars for neural density ratios in a 2025 paper. Such ratios drive inference in particle physics, where a likelihood ratio tied to unknown parameters is the prize. Their ensembles train a set of basis functions once, then treat the mixing weights as the uncertain part.

Weight uncertainty flows straight into the final parameters, with no extra resampling rounds. The team tested the idea on quark and gluon jets from collider-style data. They learned the ratio between the two jet types, then estimated the quark share in a mixed sample. The stated errors covered the truth at the promised rate. The authors offer the scheme as a lean route to simulation-based inference.
arxiv-2506-00313:
Nicolaas Weideman and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on tools that trace how data flows inside computer programs. Such tools help find weak spots that hackers could use. They work on the raw code files that users run, where the flow of data is hard to track. No one had a good gauge of how exact the best tools are.

The team built a huge test set of small programs with known data flows, plus flows drawn from six real programs. They ran three well-known tools on the set and found that all three were far from exact. They then added three fixes to the way the tools model a program. With the fixes, the tools found nearly all true flows and raised the share of right flags a great deal. The fixes also helped find real weak spots.
arxiv-2506-00413:
Daniel Israel, Guy Van den Broeck, and Aditya Grover sped up a new kind of language model that writes in parallel, in a paper published in 2025. Word-by-word models are slow by design. Diffusion models can in truth draft many words at once, but in use they lag or lose quality. Their fix adjusts how many words are drawn per step.

A blending law mixes the word probabilities of the diffusion model with the joint probabilities of a small word-by-word partner. That flips the standard trick, where a large checker vets a small drafter. Cache tricks and a trimmed mask input cut cost further. Three dials trade speed for quality. On test sets the method won much speed for a hair of quality loss. The authors present it for live text work.
arxiv-2506-00513:
Yaxiong Wang and colleagues let vision-language models tune their image encoder at test time in a 2025 paper. Test-time adaptation adjusts a model to new data on the fly, with no labels available. Standard methods freeze the image encoder for lack of supervision, even though shifted test images are exactly where that encoder needs help, leaving a gap between training and test views.

Their SSAM framework learns from associations the model builds itself. Soft prototype estimates guess how test images group into categories and reorganize the feature space, while a reconstruction step anchored on those prototypes keeps the encoder stable. Wide experiments across benchmarks support the design. Adapting the encoder, not just the read-out, closes more of the shift gap.
arxiv-2506-00613:
Julian Quevedo and co-authors propose grading robot control software inside a learned dream of the world, in this 2025 paper. Testing a robot policy in reality is slow and expensive, while hand-built simulators take endless manual work to look right. Their system, WorldGym, instead trains a video-generating model that predicts how the world responds to actions, then lets the policy play inside that model.

Starting from a single real camera frame, the world model rolls the scene forward while a vision-language model hands out rewards. When the team graded real robot policies this way, success rates inside the dream tracked real-world success closely, and the rankings between policy versions, sizes, and training stages were preserved. The setup also exposed weaknesses: modern robot policies still confuse object shapes and get distracted by fake look-alike objects painted on the scene.
arxiv-2506-01413:
Yulei Qin and a team of co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on teaching large language models to follow complex instructions. Real instructions often stack many constraints at once, arranged in parallel, in chains, or in branches. Plain chain of thought prompting, the obvious fix, can backfire here, since models tend to just restate the instruction instead of taking it apart.

Their method, RAIF, first breaks complex instructions down using existing taxonomies, with a data building method others can reproduce. It then trains the model with reinforcement learning, using rule based rewards that can be checked directly. The training targets the shallow reasoning that plain prompting produces. The goal is reasoning that finds how constraints nest inside each other, so test time effort scales with real difficulty.
arxiv-2506-01513:
Thomas Pusztai, Jan Hisberger, Cynthia Marcelino, and Stefan Nastic present Stardust, a simulator for the 3D continuum of edge, cloud, and space computing. Their 2025 paper starts from the rise of low Earth orbit satellite constellations.

Workflows may soon run seamlessly across edge, cloud, and satellite nodes, but launching satellites is costly, so orchestration ideas must be tested in simulation. Existing simulators handle only small constellations unless many machines are used. Stardust can simulate mega constellations three times the size of the largest current low Earth orbit system on a single machine. It also lets users add custom components, which aids experiments with new algorithms.
arxiv-2506-01813:
Djallel Bouneffouf, Matthew Riemer, and Kush Varshney introduce the Shepherd Test, a conceptual test for superintelligent AI agents, in a 2025 paper. The test is inspired by human relations with animals, where care, manipulation, and use arise under unequal power. It targets moral and relational traits, not just skill.

They argue an AI crosses a dangerous threshold when it can manipulate, nurture, and use less intelligent agents while pursuing its own survival and growth. Such an agent must weigh its interests against the well-being of others under it. The authors say this shift matters for AI governance, beyond traditional evaluation.
arxiv-2506-01913:
Thomas Pethick and co-authors generalize gradient clipping, a trick used to keep model training stable. Clipping caps the size of an update step, and their 2025 paper blends it with two older ideas: steepest descent and conditional gradient steps. The blend works under a wider notion of smoothness that allows non-Euclidean geometry.

The team also folds weight decay into the method through a link to the Frank-Wolfe short step. With random data, their momentum-based version reaches an order-optimal convergence rate. They name the deep learning form Clipped Scion and test it on image classification and language modeling. Optimization readers get a clipping method with proofs, not just habits, behind it.
arxiv-2506-02213:
Kahn Rhrissorrakrai and co-authors test quantum group models on small health data sets in a 2025 paper. Small data is a common bind in health and life fields, where samples are scarce next to traits. The team builds group models that vote, using up to dozens of quantum bits in sims and on real gear.

Tasks span fake sets and gene data from kidney cancer patients, with response to immune care as the call. Group design leans on few tuned knobs but long links across bits. The team maps how the link shape steers skill, to guide peers.
arxiv-2506-02513:
Hiromichi Nakazato and Tohru Ozawa prove a neat fact about a key operator in physics in their twenty twenty-five paper. The operator is the d'Alembertian, the wave operator that sits at the heart of many models of waves and fields. Many such models are written as equations for how things change in space and time.

The pair shows this operator is the one and only second-order operator of its kind with two traits. It stays the same under the Poincare group, the full set of moves and turns of space-time, and it stays the same under stretching space-time. Their proof reads these traits off a related polynomial and checks how it acts under flips of time and turns of space.
arxiv-2506-02613:
Xiushan Jiang and Weihai Zhang present a study from twenty twenty-five on control of systems that face random noise. They use learning methods that do not need a full model of the system. Classic Q-learning has gaps: its theory is loose, and it needs added noise while it runs. The pair take a fresh view of a known control task with noise that scales with the state.

They recast the task as a paired problem with a best and a worst side, and prove the two sides meet. From set rules for the best point, they draw both model based and model free methods. A test case shows the model free method works. They link it to how the brain guides arm moves.
arxiv-2506-02713:
A research team uses large language models to guess what daily-life needs drive people's purchases, in a 2025 paper. On service platforms, knowing the need behind a purchase helps suggest the right service at the right time. Older methods forced each guess into a fixed list of needs, which misses the variety of real life.

Their system, PIGEON, treats the task as open-ended. It first pulls up a user's past behavior so the model can read their tastes. It then shapes guesses using a classic ladder of human needs, from food and safety up to esteem. A matching step links each free-form guess to real services on the platform. Tests on real data beat fixed-list methods by a wide margin on service recall. Extra training let smaller models perform nearly as well, which suits real deployment.
arxiv-2506-02813:
The brain solves tasks by routing work through shifting coalitions of regions, but nobody knows the rules that build those coalitions. Jack Cook, Danyal Akarca, Rui Ponte Costa, and Jascha Achterberg probe the question in artificial networks built as mixtures of expert modules. Each expert differs from the others, like brain regions do.

Left alone, the experts never organized into pathways, which suggests the brain must add extra pressure. Three added biases did the trick: charging a cost for using fancy experts, easing that cost when the task goes badly, and randomly dropping experts during training. The resulting pathways mirrored how real brains mix cortex and deeper structures by task difficulty. The authors offer the setup as a lab for studying brain routing.
arxiv-2506-02913:
Agniva Chatterjee works in complex analysis in a solo 2025 paper on Bergman spaces, which are sets of well-behaved functions tied to a region in multi-dimensional complex space.

Two classic transforms turn abstract data supported on a compact convex set into concrete functions. Earlier work pinned down what those transforms yield for the Bergman space in flat, two-dimensional cases. Chatterjee extends the picture to higher dimensions for strongly convex regions. He proves duality results that match the flat case. He also gives examples showing the flat results cannot be stretched to all convex regions in higher dimensions. The paper sharpens the map of where these dual views hold and where they fail.
arxiv-2506-03313:
When scientists test a model of a changing system, the answer can shift for many reasons: starting values, settings, math methods, or the model's very form. Viríssimo introduces Low-EFFourth, a MATLAB framework that builds ensembles of models at several levels to sort out those effects. It began in climate modeling, where such uncertainty checks are routine.

The framework is built for low-dimensional systems that change over time. With small edits it can serve other fields, from disease spread to economics and engineering. The paper is a formal reference for the code base, sketching its purpose, structure, uses, and development plans. The author aims to give researchers a flexible, efficient way to see which uncertainties matter most, instead of trusting a single model run.
arxiv-2506-03513:
Wei Kou, Xiaoxuan Lin, Bing'ang Guo, and Xurong Chen map the glue tube between a quark and an antiquark with a smart network. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, uses physics-informed neural networks. Such networks bake the governing equations into their training. The equations here come from type-two superconductivity, an analogy for the strong force field.

Lattice simulations supply the raw field data. The network works backward to extract the equation's parameters. Reformulated math lets it respect boundary rules, with a fractional extension. Rebuilt field maps are scored against the data. From them come the string tension and the tube's width. Both numbers speak to how quarks stay confined.
arxiv-2506-03713:
Rebuilding a 3D scene from a handful of photos is a guessing game: most of the scene was never seen. Sam Bahrami and Dylan Campbell improve the guess in 2025 by changing what the model stores. Instead of a flat stack of feature planes, their PlückeRF representation stores the scene as structured lines in space, each dressed with learned features.

The point of lines is connection. A pixel in a photo defines a ray through space, and rays pass near lines. The format lets information flow between a 3D location and the nearby rays and lines that constrain it. Trained as a feed-forward system — no per-scene optimization — the model reconstructs better than the equivalent triplane design and than prior feed-forward methods. The authors credit the geometry: the format itself tells the network which views should inform which parts of space.
arxiv-2506-04113:
Yanjie Dong and five co-authors aim to cut the chatter in a shared learning scheme for wireless feedback. Their two thousand twenty-five paper deals with channel state information, which phones must send back to base stations. Learning-based compression helps, but training it across many phones means constant exchanges of model values. Those exchanges eat bandwidth and time. The team tries a split design instead.

One shared model sits at the base station, with small local models at each phone. Only boundary values cross between them during training. A pipeline module at the station also cuts training time. The authors report far fewer exchanged values than rival methods. The scheme keeps feedback quality while easing the load on the network.
arxiv-2506-04313:
When two protons collide at high energy, the total chance of any interaction keeps creeping upward, and theorists have long wondered how high it can go. Miguel Correia, Alessandro Georgoudis, and Andrea Guerrieri derive a universal ceiling for that total chance at finite energies. Their bound rests on a single low-energy number that the modern bootstrap programme can fence in without assuming any detailed model of the strong force.

At high energies the bound meets real proton collision data, and at low energies it matches direct numerical maximisation. The authors guess that one special amplitude sits at a strongly coupled corner of the allowed space and saturates the ceiling. That candidate shows a rising total cross-section, rings of scattering, and families of resonances lined up along curved trajectories.
arxiv-2506-04413:
Coupled resonators, from optical cavities to microwave circuits, are usually described by a simple picture in which each one's modes blend into shared ones. E A Muljarov argues in a 2025 paper that this famous tight-binding picture generally fails. It cannot describe even the simplest test case, two dielectric slabs side by side, a system simple enough to solve exactly and check.

In its place he builds a rigorous theory that computes the true modes of any pair or group of three-dimensional resonators, whatever their material, from the modes of the parts. The theory shows how proper hybrid modes, bonding and antibonding, actually form. Slab pairs and mirror-layer cavities serve as testbeds where the new math can be verified precisely.
arxiv-2506-04513:
Gustavo Henrique do Nascimento and co-authors prune neural networks by cutting whole neurons and whole layers at the same time. Big models are slow and costly, and past pruning cut one structure or the other, never both. Their 2025 method picks, round by round, between a layer-cut and a neuron-cut version of the model.

The pick goes to whichever child model stays most alike to its parent, by a standard similarity score. Repeated rounds yield very sparse models that keep their accuracy. On two classic image networks, compute needs fell by eighty-six and ninety-six percent. Pruned models also resisted attacks and odd inputs better, and cut carbon output by up to eighty-three percent, the authors report.
arxiv-2506-04713:
Hanxin Wang, Tian Liu, and Shu Kong address few-shot learning with image-text models in 2025. The head title is Enabling Validation for Robust Few-Shot Recognition, which differs from the catalog title. With few labeled cases, teams lack spare data to tune their models, so models overfit.

The authors use extra cases pulled from outside sources as a stand-in test set. That creates a puzzle, since tuning on the main data tends to hurt scores on the pulled cases. They frame tuning as a balance between two goals and pick a middle point. Their staged tuning method improved how well models handled new data in wide tests.
arxiv-2506-05013: Semyon Yakubovich, writing alone, develops product formulas for Whittaker functions in this 2025 math paper. Whittaker functions are special functions that appear in many areas of analysis and physics. The work builds generalized formulas for products of these functions with different indices. From those formulas it constructs a new class of index transforms and finds the matching inversion formulas. Special cases cover transforms built from products of modified Bessel functions and Whittaker functions. The proofs draw on the Kontorovich-Lebedev and Olevskii transforms with complex index.
arxiv-2506-05113:
Anuj Abhishek, Alexander Katsevich, and James Webber bring statistics to edge detection in CT scans in a 2025 paper. Judges of a scan need to know whether an edge seen in a reconstruction was really in the object. Classic microlocal analysis answers that for perfect, noiseless data, but real scans carry noise and finite sampling steps.

Their statistical microlocal analysis frames edge detection as a hypothesis test at each tiny neighborhood of the image. The test checks for an edge and its direction, and its power measures how detectable the edge is given the noise level and sampling step. Simulations matched the theory's predictions closely. The method also quantifies uncertainty in edge strength and direction, which classic analysis cannot do.
arxiv-2506-05213:
Solving a hard puzzle can be framed as a search through possible moves, and Nathan Herr, Tim Rocktäschel, and Roberta Raileanu let the language model run the search itself. Their method, LLM-First Search, drops the fixed rules that classic search algorithms use to decide where to explore next. Instead, the model scores its own position and chooses whether to press on or branch elsewhere.

On the Countdown numbers game and on Sudoku, the method beat three established search strategies. It did best on the harder tasks without extra tuning, used computation more efficiently, and gained more than the rivals both from stronger models and from bigger compute budgets. The authors release their code and argue that handing the model the controls suits its growing reasoning strength.
arxiv-2506-05313:
Ta-Ying Cheng and co-authors present a way to repaint the material of an object in a photo using another photo as the sample, in a 2025 paper. A chair could borrow the brushed metal of a kettle, or a table could take on marble. Their method, MARBLE, works inside the representation space of a vision-language model, where materials can be described as directions. Those directions steer a standard image generator.

The team first found which block inside the generator's denoising network controls what material an object appears to be made of. Blending two sample materials means walking between their directions in that space. A small add-on network gives dial control over single traits such as roughness, shine, transparency, and glow. Tests showed clean blends, several edits in one pass, and success on paintings as well as photos.
arxiv-2506-05613:
Seddighin and Seddighin improved a fairness guarantee in twenty twenty-five for splitting indivisible goods among people whose tastes combine items in complex ways. The benchmark is the maximin share: the best value a person could promise themselves if they cut the pile but chose last.

For the broadest taste class, called subadditive, the best known promise had been shrinking fast as the group grew, with a double logarithm in the way. The authors lift the guarantee well past that barrier. Their proof leans on fresh matching methods and new rounding tricks for awkward valuations. Those tools, they note, should serve other fair division problems too. Constant-level promises were already known for simpler taste classes. This result narrows the gap for the hardest general case, a step toward fair splits that hold up in messy real settings.
arxiv-2506-05813:
Ye Bai and co-authors present MAPLE, a system for answering hard questions over tables, in a 2025 paper. Large language models often fail such questions in a single pass. Simple step-by-step prompts lack error checks. They also throw away lessons from past problems.

MAPLE splits the work among four agents that mimic human problem solving. A Solver drafts an answer with a reason-and-act loop. A Checker verifies the answer, and a Reflector diagnoses errors and fixes the plan. An Archiver stores solved cases in long-term memory for later use. The loop lets the system catch its own mistakes. Tests aim to show steadier table reasoning than single-pass methods.
arxiv-2506-05913:
Leonie Schürmeyer and co-authors develop optimal trial designs for finding effective doses of two drug combinations, in a 2025 paper. Combination studies matter because drugs can amplify or blunt each other. The doses that hit a target effect form contour lines on a fitted response surface.

Their new criterion chooses test doses to shrink the uncertainty band around those contour lines. Theory in the paper includes equivalence results and efficiency bounds for the design. Examples span several surface models used for dose response data. Against the ray and factorial layouts common in practice, the optimal design estimated the effective combinations more precisely. A case study drawn from a cancer dose study shows the largest gains. The authors offer the method for planning future combination trials.
arxiv-2506-06013:
Mohimenul Kabir, Van-Giang Trinh, Samuel Pastva, and Kuldeep Meel count hard-to-reach states in Boolean networks, in a paper from 2025. Such networks model systems as nodes that flip between on and off, from gene circuits to logic. A trap space is a region of states that, once entered, can never be left. The smallest such regions reveal where a system settles in the long run.

Counting those regions for large networks is too slow by brute force. The team recasts the counts as an approximate counting task drawn from answer set programming. Their method skips listing every case and still lands close to the true count. Tests on a wide set of benchmarks show the method scales far better than past tools. It opens fresh uses in biology, debate models, and logic programs.
arxiv-2506-06113:
Labeling text for hate or offense splits human judges, and averaging their votes erases real perspectives. Benedetta Muscato and co-authors ask whether language models can hold the disagreement instead. They test four open models with in-context learning, feeding labels three ways: merged hard labels, and separate hard or soft labels that keep each annotator visible.

Zero-shot prompting could voice multiple perspectives. Few-shot examples, oddly, often narrowed the range instead of widening it. How examples were chosen, by similarity or by disagreement, mattered more than their order. The 2025 study warns that teaching models to mimic majorities is easy, and teaching them pluralism is not.
arxiv-2506-06513:
Joao Merenda, Gonzalo Travieso, and Odemir Bruno present in 2025 a benchmark for methods that classify networks into kinds. Network classification matters in biology, sociology, and computing, but testing methods fairly is hard. Their data set is built from synthetic networks in set classes and subclasses, with added structural noise at varied types and levels.

Five ways of extracting features from a network were tested, from classic structural measures to walk based and embedding methods. An improved walk method won on both classes and subclasses, even under heavy noise. Automated pattern methods also did well. Classic topological measures, despite wide use, consistently scored weakest, which stresses the need for robust feature methods.
arxiv-2506-06613:
Arefe Boushehrian and Amir Najafi ask whether compressible data families stay learnable when samples are corrupted in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Sample compressibility means a whole data family can be summed up by a few of its samples. A landmark result says compressible families can be learned, and many tight bounds followed.

The authors prove such families remain learnable from perturbed data, under conditions they show are both needed and enough. They cover two harms: added random noise, and an adversary who tampers with a limited share of samples. Their framework pairs the compression scheme with a cleanup step. New bounds follow for mixtures of uniform and Gaussian distributions, settling two open problems.
arxiv-2506-06913:
Xian Guo and six co-authors present OneSug, a unified end to end generative framework for e-commerce query suggestion. Suggestions guide users toward their needs and cut typing effort. Traditional modules use multi stage cascades that trade response time against conversion, but inconsistent goals across stages cause inefficiency and weak results.

OneSug enriches prefixes with related queries, then generates suggestions with an encoder decoder model that unifies the whole process. A reward weighted ranking strategy with behavior level weights captures fine grained preferences. Large scale industry evaluations show effective and efficient suggestion. The system has run on the full traffic of the Kuaishou search engine for over a month with significant gains.
arxiv-2506-07413:
Ziwen Wang and co-authors reformulate a popular learning method in 2025 so it shapes its data space with more care. Contrastive learning trains models by pulling like items together and pushing unlike ones apart, across text, images, and more. Two flaws persist: like items can be pushed apart when no guide steers pair choice, and the method leans hard on large mixed batches and tailored alterations.

Their variant treats the supervised form of the method as inference over hidden class labels. It maximizes a bound that weights each pair by the chance the two share a class. That replaces the brute force of comparing all pairs with a softer, guided sum. The team reports tests of the variant. A gentler contrastive rule could generalize better from smaller batches.
arxiv-2506-08113:
Timothee Hornek, Amir Sartipi, Igor Tchappi, and Gilbert Fridgen benchmark pre-trained time series models for electricity price forecasting, in a 2025 paper. Good price forecasts guide trading on power markets. New foundation models promise strong results, but their value for this task was untested.

The team compared six pre-trained models with classic statistical and learning methods. They used day-ahead prices from five European countries for one year and forecast one day ahead. Two pre-trained models matched the classic methods, but none beat the best seasonal model. That model, which captures daily and weekly cycles, was the most consistent overall.
arxiv-2506-08213:
Jasem Hamoud and Artem Kornosov studied irregularity measures for trees in 2025. Such measures sum how much the connection counts of neighbouring vertices differ, capturing how uneven a network is. Min and max degrees bound that unevenness, and the paper ties the two together.

Working with the Albertson index and a related sigma index on trees with at least three vertices, the authors relate the indices to the degree sequence of the tree. The extreme degrees play a central role in deciding which sequences can occur and how the indices behave. The results speak to when a degree pattern is realisable as a tree with a given irregularity. The work sits in chemical graph theory, where such indices describe molecular structure.
arxiv-2506-08313:
Oriyomi Hassan and co-authors propose a new probability curve for lifetimes in a 2025 paper. Survival and reliability data are awkward: early failures bunch up, yet a long tail of late cases stretches out. Classic distributions rarely capture both shapes at once. The authors blend two known families, an exponentiated exponential-Pareto part and a half-normal part, through a mixture.

The blend keeps closed forms for everything a practitioner needs: the density, the cumulative curve, survival and hazard rates, and moments. Closed forms matter because censored data, where follow-up ends early, are the norm in medicine. The authors frame the model for biomedical use, where honest risk curves guide treatment and follow-up choices. Properties are derived in full so others can fit and test the model on real cohorts.
arxiv-2506-08513:
Cameras without lenses use a patterned mask plus software to form an image. Leyla Kabuli and co-authors asked how to design the mask for the most gain, in work from twenty twenty-five. Their yardstick is shared information: how much the raw reading tells about the scene. That lens makes the design task clear and testable.

Best masks match their mixing level to how sparse the scene is, the study found. All best designs end with readings of like sparsity. Masks built by that rule rebuilt test scenes better, with no need to tune a rebuild method in step. Bench tests checked the rule from raw readings alone. The results give design rules for a broad class of mixing sensors.
arxiv-2506-08613:
Floating sea trash is hard to spot in satellite photos, and Joost van Dalen, Yuki Asano, and Marc Russwurm offer a search tool in a 2025 paper. Trash mixes many materials, so no single color view shows it well in mid-grade imagery. Experts now pick views case by case by habit and lore.

Their tool tries many band and index mixes and keeps the one where a general segmentation model scores best on a small labeled set.
