Qi He, Peiran Yu, Ziyi Chen, and Heng Huang revisit why shuffled gradient training converges, dropping an assumption the theory usually leans on. Shuffling methods, which sweep data in random order each round, are fast in practice. Their proofs, though, typically demand Lipschitz smoothness, a leash on how fast gradients can change, which common models violate.

Counterexamples first show the assumption failing in the wild. Then the team's step-size scheme restores the best known convergence rates without it. The guarantees cover nonconvex, strongly convex, and plain convex losses, under both random and arbitrary shuffles, needing only bounded variance. Simulations confirm the rates are not just ink.
arxiv-2507-09313:
Yueqian Wang and co-authors published this study in 2025. It benchmarks video language models on proactive interaction: speaking up at the right moment, not just when asked. In proactive chat, a system watching a video must choose its own response times. That timing choice breaks classic grading, which reads only the words. The team built ProactiveVideoQA, the first bench for this skill, and PAUC, a score that folds response timing into quality.

Many baseline systems were run on the bench, and a user study checked human taste. PAUC agreed with people's preferences better than text-only metrics. The authors argue timing is part of helpfulness, not a side detail. A model that answers late can be right and useless at once. Their tools give this young research area a shared yardstick.
arxiv-2507-09513:
Yanchen Wang and co-authors, working with the International Brain Laboratory, present BEAST, a system that learns animal behavior from unlabeled video. Neuroscientists film animals constantly, but turning footage into measurements usually needs hand-labeled training data for every new setup. BEAST pretrains a vision transformer for each experiment using two self-teaching tricks: filling in masked parts of frames, and telling apart moments in time.

One pretrained backbone then serves many jobs. It extracts behavior features that track neural activity, finds body poses, and cuts continuous action into segments, for single animals and groups alike. Tests across several species showed clear gains over specialized models. The authors offer BEAST as a general workhorse for labs where labeled video is the bottleneck, letting the same footage teach the model that will analyze it.
arxiv-2507-09613:
Giovanni Geraci and nine co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv tutorial marking twenty-five years of Wi-Fi. The name is unchanged, but today's technology shares little with the first generation beyond branding. Rather than marching generation by generation from Wi-Fi 1 to the coming Wi-Fi 8, the authors organize the story by the mechanisms that moved it.

They cover spectrum politics and coexistence with other users, then the physical layer tricks that multiplied data rates more than a thousandfold. Medium access control grew from a simple take-turns scheme to frame aggregation and wideband access. Later sections trace multi-user transmission, energy saving for battery devices, seamless bonding of three frequency bands, and access points that coordinate with each other. An appendix looks past the current standard to millimeter-wave operation, sensing, security, and machine learning. It is a reference history for engineers and the curious alike.
arxiv-2507-09913:
Kawasaki and Campbell write a pencil and paper model for the faint bonding pull felt through graphene in twenty twenty-five. In remote epitaxy, a crystal film grows aligned to a base hidden under graphene sheets. Past work used heavy computer slabs and plain charge maps as stand ins. Their model uses a classic pair potential with two fade factors.

One factor covers the extra gap, the other the screening by graphene's free charges. For most bases, the pull lands at a few to tens of milli electron volts. That rivals graphene's own weak grip, so the two must be read together. Extra graphene layers nearly kill the pull, they show.
arxiv-2507-10013:
Tom Kouwenhoven, Kiana Shahrasbi, and Tessa Verhoef wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It re-tests the bouba-kiki effect, where people link soft words like bouba to round shapes and spiky words like kiki to jagged ones, in vision-language models.

Two builds of CLIP are probed: one with a ResNet eye, one with a Vision Transformer. One test scores the models' picks by probability, as in human trials. A second uses Grad-CAM to see where each model looks when it pairs a word with a shape. Neither build shows the effect in a steady way. The ResNet build leans round, but both fall well short of human scores on the same task. The models' inner codes, the team finds, do not yet blend sight and sound as people do.
arxiv-2507-10413:
Gabriel Rocha asks whether a famous impossibility result in computing survives even when the machines get magical help. The consensus problem asks scattered processes, talking out of sync, to agree on one value. A classic theorem says no certain method can promise both agreement and an eventual answer if even one process can fail. Rocha argues the barrier stands even when computation is stretched by oracles, idealized helpers that answer hard questions instantly.

He then borrows tools from the study of complex systems, where order appears from many simple parts. Viewed that way, inconsistency itself may be an emergent feature of agreeing systems as they shift phases. Turning to logics that tolerate contradiction without exploding, he argues the emergent danger there is not inconsistency but triviality, where everything becomes provable. He closes by sketching consensus methods that could reason in such logics.
arxiv-2507-10513:
Kruse, Griston, and Wilcox surveyed how quantum mechanics is taught to advanced undergraduates across the United States in twenty twenty-five. The subject is famously hard, and courses differ widely. Some start with spin systems, others with wavefunctions and the Schrödinger equation, and textbooks vary in coverage.

Seventy-six instructors described their courses, methods, and topic coverage. Traditional lecture was the most common approach, but many used interactive lectures or other non-traditional methods, plus tools like clicker questions. Many taught single-semester courses covering about as much as first-semester courses in two-semester sequences, though with more variability. Comparing the two starting approaches showed large overlap, with differences on only a few topics. The authors offer the portrait to guide future teaching research and course design.
arxiv-2507-10613:
Zhengyu Chen and co-authors explain why language model gains slow as training scales up in a 2025 paper. Classic scaling laws promise steady gains from bigger models and more data. In practice, recent gains have tapered, a pattern dubbed sub-scaling.

Tests across more than four hundred models point to two culprits. Packed, redundant data yields less fresh signal per token, so returns fade. Poor splits of compute between model size and data also waste effort. The team offers a revised law that fits the slow regime better. Data quality and variety, they argue, now matter as much as raw scale.
arxiv-2507-10813:
Justin M Kasowski, Apurv Varshney, and Michael Beyeler test ways to simplify scenes for bionic vision. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. A bionic eye turns camera input into patterns of electric pulses, with very low detail. Showing all key things at once can swamp the user in a busy scene.

In a virtual city, sighted users do a wayfinding task under a simulated bionic view. One method marks all key object kinds at once. An other cycles through kinds over time, to cut clutter. Both beat a plain edge view. The first lifts the odds of success, while the second lifts the odds of a path with no crashes. Each has its own trade-off.
arxiv-2507-10913:
Shuangyao Huang, Haibo Zhang, and Zhiyi Huang teach drone swarms, in a 2025 preprint, to dodge each other and obstacles with help from image processing ideas. Collision avoidance for many drones at once usually needs heavy message sharing and tricky credit assignment. Their reinforcement learning framework borrows a trick from contour maps. Obstacles are treated as peaks on a two-dimensional field. Flight paths follow contours, and contours never cross peaks or each other, so collisions are avoided by construction. The routes also come out smooth and cheap in energy.

Because agents barely interact during learning, training scales to large swarms. Where contours fail or vanish, intensive training lets the drones adapt anyway. Wide experiments compare the framework against leading multi-agent learning methods. The authors report that domain knowledge, poured into the reward, does work that generic algorithms must learn the hard way.
arxiv-2507-11213:
Rongsheng Li and a large team of co-authors probe a honeycomb magnet in 2025 with terahertz light in strong fields. The material is a candidate for a quantum spin liquid, a rare state of matter. Its exact spin model is still debated.

They used a twin-free single crystal to watch spin excitations as temperature and field changed. At zero field, a sharp spin wave appeared in the ordered state. A field turned the waves into a broad continuum before the spins aligned. Strong differences between two crystal axes demand a highly directional spin model.
arxiv-2507-11313:
Elodie Maignant, Tim Conrad, and Christoph von Tycowicz rebuild cellular family trees in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Single-cell sequencing samples cells from a process as it develops, and trajectory inference orders them by progression. When the process is differentiation, the order should get back a differentiation tree. Sequencing gives gene expression levels and RNA velocity, a vector calling how expression will change, forming as one a vector field in space.

Joining up the velocity field traces each cell's expression path, from its stage to its read stage. The team holds that these root-to-cell curves lay the differentiation tree faithfully in Euclidean space. With varifold distances, measures to compare curves, they set a similarity between cells and prove it near-matches the shortest-path distance in an isomorphic copy of the tree. The result gives trajectory inference a firmer math base for a used method style.
arxiv-2507-11813:
Shaniya Jarrett, Kelly Holley-Bockelmann, and Robert Scherrer ask whether black hole mergers trace the universe's large-scale structure in this 2025 paper. A future space mission, LISA, will hear low-frequency gravitational waves from space. Massive black hole pairs merging are among its richest sources. If mergers cluster like galaxies do, LISA could map cosmic structure on its own. The team tested that idea inside a large universe simulation. They compared the clustering pattern of mergers with that of galaxies.

A standard two-point measure captured how strongly each set clumps. The comparison shows how faithful a tracer the mergers are. An independent map of structure would cross-check telescope surveys. It could also reveal biases in how mergers follow matter. The work is simulation-based, ahead of the mission's launch. Its results guide what LISA data could say about cosmology.
arxiv-2507-11913:
Zhu and co-authors send pictures by meaning rather than by pixels in this 2025 paper on wireless communication. Networks strain under image traffic, so the team describes each image as a scene graph of objects and relations. Users share probability graphs that capture which relations usually occur together, letting sender and receiver agree on what is predictable.

A two-stage method strips out relations the receiver can guess, and the receiver rebuilds them from the shared graph. A multi-round extension comes with theory for its performance. Simulations showed higher throughput and good agreement in meaning between sent and rebuilt images. The authors argue high-level semantics can ease congestion without losing what pictures convey.
arxiv-2507-12013:
Siddhant Dutta and co-authors automate the design of quantum tensor networks in a paper from 2025. Quantum architecture search seeks the best circuit layout for a task without hand design. Their framework uses reinforcement learning with a staged curriculum.

Agents start with shallow, simple circuits and face harder ones step by step. Four classic learning methods were matched against quantum-enhanced versions of the same methods. All were boosted by a replay system that revisits the most useful past tries. The setup targets variational circuits, whose settings are tuned during training. Staged learning should help agents stay stable as circuits grow. The work aids tools that design quantum software on their own.
arxiv-2507-12313:
A self-propelled particle that runs and tumbles through a fluid which thickens under shear behaves unlike its textbook cousins. Subhanker Howlader, Sayantan Mondal, and Prasenjit Das study that motion in this 2025 paper, in one dimension, with no thermal noise. The medium's resistance grows steeply with speed, and a flipping two-state force drives the particle.

Starting from the governing probability equation, the authors derive the steady-state velocity distribution in closed form, plus a formula for how fast the particle spreads. As the flipping rate varies, the distribution passes through several sharp transitions, which they locate exactly. Computer checks match the theory, and the transitions survive a change in how the thickening is modeled.
arxiv-2507-12513:
Kun Cheng, Tao Han, Matthew Low, and Tong Arthur Wu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It lays out how to rebuild the full quantum state of a pair made of a meson and its antimatter twin, a task called quantum tomography.

Pairs formed in collider events hold rich quantum links in their flavor states. The authors give a step-by-step way to build the pair's density matrix in Bloch form at a chosen time. They argue that two of the four known systems are the best picks, thanks to how their flavors swing and decay. Doing this well can shed light on how the pairs are made, how their links fade, and whether new sources of CP breach hide in the data.
arxiv-2507-12913:
Five researchers propose using split forms of uncertainty to choose how an artificial intelligence system should explain itself, in a 2025 paper. As models grow more complex, their reasons grow harder to read, which weakens trust. Uncertainty comes in two kinds: one from noisy data and one from the model's own gaps in learning. The team argues each kind calls for a different style of explanation.

When the model's own uncertainty runs high, its explanations should be distrusted or rejected outright, and the gap itself becomes a kind of explanation. When data noise dominates, the choice between listing key factors and showing what-if cases should follow the noise level. Tests on both classic and deep learning setups showed the approach made explanations sturdier and easier to reach. The authors frame it as a path toward AI people can trust more.
arxiv-2507-13313:
Chao Feng and co-authors released in 2025 a dataset for catching intrusions in crowdsensing systems without centralizing data. Internet of Things crowdsensing gathers data from many devices, and malware inside them is a live threat. Decentralized federated learning lets devices train a shared detector while keeping raw data local. The dataset records behavior from clean devices and from eight malware attacks.

Over twenty-one million raw records came from system calls, file activity, resource use, kernel events, and network traffic. Grouped into thirty-second windows, they became about 342,000 training records. Experiments compared plain machine learning, centralized federated learning, and the decentralized variant across node counts and layouts. The decentralized approach held its own and usually beat the centralized one. The authors offer the data as a base for securing device crowds.
arxiv-2507-13713:
Kazuhiro Ito and four co-authors study monodromy operators for hyper-Kähler varieties over p-adic fields. These operators act on cohomology and connect with a known Lie algebra built from the second cohomology. A conjecture links how nilpotent the operators are on higher cohomology to their behaviour on the second, much like Nagai's conjecture for degenerations over a disk.

The team verifies this arithmetic form for varieties of the four known deformation types. Their route also brings a new method to study such varieties over p-adic fields through Sen's theory. Both kinds of operators are treated in the argument.
arxiv-2507-13913:
Matous Volf and Jakub Simko tackle automatic labeling of political texts in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Sorting writing by political leaning, and telling political text from non-political text, sounds simple, but models trained on one source often fail on another.

The authors survey existing datasets and models and find a pattern of narrow, siloed solutions. To fix it, they merged twelve datasets for leaning classification and built a new politicalness dataset by extending eighteen others with the missing label. Benchmarking both old and new models with leave-one-out designs, they trained versions that generalize better across sources. The work gives researchers a broader test bed for a task that feeds media analysis and content moderation.
arxiv-2507-14013:
Ji-Yan Wu and five co-authors built a deep learning system in twenty twenty-five to spot nutrient deficiencies in plant leaves from multispectral images. Early detection lets farmers fix fertilizer, disease, and stress problems before yields suffer. Their plants were grown under controlled nutrient stress so symptoms could be labeled reliably.

The system enhances the YOLOv5 detector with a transformer attention head and feeds it nine-channel multispectral input. Self-attention helps it catch faint, scattered symptoms. Against the baseline model, it improved overlap scores by about twelve percent on average. It proved especially good at hard symptoms like chlorosis, the yellowing of starved leaves, and pigment buildup. The authors pitch the approach as a step toward sharper plant phenotyping for precision agriculture.
arxiv-2507-14313:
John Campbell constructs a basis that turns a partition algebra into an algebra of a monoid, in a paper from 2025. The catalog lists no creator, but the head gives Campbell as the author. Partition algebras are built from diagrams that show how sets are split and joined.

A twisted version of such a structure was known, but no basis gave the plain, untwisted form. Campbell builds the wanted basis from a known matrix unit construction and from known links between tableaux and partition diagrams. A product rule for the basis is given in explicit diagram terms. The work covers the well behaved case where the algebra splits into simple blocks.
arxiv-2507-14813:
Sanjay Singapuram, Ronald Dreslinski, and Nishil Talati speed up pattern hunts in time-stamped networks in a 2025 paper. Such networks model ties that change over time, from money flows to social posts. Finding small repeat patterns in them serves fraud hunts and attack watch, but each ask is now run alone.

Their frame, called Mayura, mines many patterns at once by sharing the work where patterns overlap. A tree sorts kin patterns so shared search paths run once, not per ask. Tests show the shared hunt cuts waste a great deal. The work suits banks and guards alike.
arxiv-2507-15313:
Abhishek Krishnamoorthy and co-authors grow a tree tool for a broad class of pattern words. Base words in the class trace a line of odd slope and split in neat ways. A fresh broad form spans words on three or more signs, built by swap rules. Some traits of the base class carry to the broad form, and some fail. Their 2025 study asks which words keep the neat split trait.

A tree of such words, grown by set rules, serves as the test bed. Words on the tree that split into small kin of their own class form the prized sub-class. More tree-based claims sort the broad words by their traits. The work gives word-math scholars a clean grip on a class that had been loose.
arxiv-2507-15613:
Andrii Balashov, Olena Ponomarova, and Xiaohua Zhai wrote a 2025 paper on attacks that trick company AI assistants into leaking secrets. Tools like Microsoft 365 Copilot answer questions using private company data. An attacker cannot ask for secrets directly, so they chain many harmless-looking questions together instead.

Each small answer reveals a little, and the pieces add up to confidential information. The authors call this a multi-stage prompt inference attack. They built realistic attack scenarios, including indirect prompt injection, and developed a formal threat model for them. Their analysis uses probability and optimization tools to show when such attacks can succeed. The work gives security teams a way to test defenses before real attackers do.
arxiv-2507-15913:
Renato Neves, José Proença, and Juliana Souza build a programming language for systems that mix steady change with chance. Their 2025 paper covers systems like adaptive cruise control, random walks over time, and particles that collide as they drift. Such systems need a language where both motion and chance can be reasoned about with care.

Their language extends a classic simple loop language with commands for both parts. They give it two meanings: one based on step-by-step running, and one based on math objects. A theorem then proves the two meanings match. They also built a working interpreter for the language. The result gives programmers a firmer base for checking hybrid software.
arxiv-2507-16313:
Kyle Broder, Anton Iliashenko, and Jesse Madnick present a 2025 math paper extending two classic ideas from complex geometry to a wider setting. The ideas, hyperbolicity and the Schwarz lemma, govern how rigid curved spaces can be. The wider setting is calibrated geometry, where a chosen form picks out special surfaces.

The authors define two grades of hyperbolicity for such spaces and build a measuring tool for the stronger one. They prove the stronger grade implies the weaker, with examples where the reverse fails. For flat model cases, they list exactly which domains pass. They also prove a Schwarz type bound for a class of surface maps into any calibrated space.
arxiv-2507-16513:
Krebbekx, Tóth, and Das extended a graphical method in twenty twenty-five for checking the stability of nonlinear feedback systems. Scaled relative graphs draw a system's input-output behavior as a picture in the frequency domain, turning hard proofs into shape checks. Past work handled only square systems, where inputs and outputs match in number.

Real systems are often non-square, with more sensors than controls or the reverse. The authors embed such operators into a shared space while keeping the true input size, which avoids overly cautious results. They prove rules for joining systems and bounds on gain and stability for the whole loop. Formulas cover common building blocks, and examples show the gain over older approaches. The work targets control design for systems written in a standard fractional form.
arxiv-2507-16713:
Kaixian Qu and co-authors present a robot system that learns planning from its own experience, in a 2025 paper. Language models plan robot tasks well in words, but they do not know a given robot's body or limits. Their system, PragmaBot, uses a vision-language model as both brain and eye. The robot judges outcomes by sight and reflects on failures.

Reflections go into a short-term memory for fast fixes during a task. After each task, lessons are summed into a long-term memory. New plans draw on that memory through a search step. In four hard tasks, success rose from about one third to over four fifths with reflection. Across twelve real scenes, long-term memory lifted success from about one fifth to four fifths. The gains held on tasks the robot had not seen before.
arxiv-2507-16813:
Dong Liang and co-authors present HOComp, a method for pasting an object into a photo of a person, in this 2025 paper. Simple pasting often breaks when the person must interact with the object, as in holding or lifting. Their method first asks a large multimodal model to find the interaction zone and name the action, then guides the person's pose step by step.

A second part guards looks: the object's shape and texture, and the person's appearance, must stay faithful to the inputs. The team also built the first dataset for this task. On it, HOComp beat rival methods in both scores and human judgment.
arxiv-2507-16913:
Mark Costantini and co-authors present a leaner way to map the inner structure of the proton for use at the Large Hadron Collider, in a 2025 paper. The maps, called parton distribution functions, give the odds of finding each kind of quark or gluon at each energy share. Their uncertainty must be pinned down with care, and the rigorous Bayesian route is slow.

The team's idea is to write each map as a short sum of chosen basis shapes, drawn from a squeezed-down version of a neural network's space. Few numbers then define a map, so Bayesian sampling runs fast. The size of the basis can be dialed up or down, which makes overfitting and underfitting visible and lets model choice follow clear rules. They test the method on synthetic scattering data with repeated closure checks, aiming at full global fits next.
arxiv-2507-17013:
Tobias Weber and co-authors wrote this software paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, to present laplax, a Python package for Laplace approximations in the JAX framework. The Laplace approximation is a fast way to estimate uncertainty in a neural network's weights, which unlocks Bayesian tools like model choice by Occam's razor.

The package is built in a modular, purely functional style with few outside dependencies. That design makes it easy to swap parts in and out for experiments. The authors aim it at researchers working on Bayesian neural networks and uncertainty estimates for deep learning. Rapid prototyping is the stated goal, along with better Laplace methods themselves. The paper is a tool announcement: it describes what the package does and how it is put together, rather than reporting a benchmark race.
arxiv-2507-17113:
The authors test a core rule of space distance math in a 2025 paper. The rule ties shine distance to span distance for far objects. Break it, and new physics may lurk. Their test pairs young star cloud gauges with sound wave marks from two sky surveys. Four forms of a drift dial let the rule bend with time. A neural net rebuilds spans sans model picks to match the sets.

No form broke the rule past the soft trust line. Two-wave and three-wave marks agreed with each seam. Star clouds reach past the span of burst-star gauges, which gives the test long arms. The authors read the null as a back for the stock space frame. Their net path may serve next tests.
arxiv-2507-17213:
Anamika Pandey and T Raja Sekhar solve a two-dimensional flow problem for a gas with no pressure, where matter can pile into infinitely thin sheets. With three constant starting states, the pressureless Euler equations produce tangled wave meetings. A delta shock can form, carrying mass and energy concentrated on a moving line.

Using generalized characteristic analysis, the authors derive nine distinct solution patterns. Some echo the Mach reflection known from aerodynamics, and in some a vacuum region opens where the gas vanishes entirely. Computer simulations with a central upwind scheme match the theory closely. The work maps the full menu of outcomes for this stripped-down model of gas motion.
arxiv-2507-17313:
Peng Cheng studies radiation near a black hole horizon in a 2025 paper, under a head title on scattering radiation emitted near that horizon. The radiation in view can be seen as part of the Hawking spectrum, the faint glow a black hole is predicted to emit. Cheng prepares outgoing light states just outside the horizon of a Schwarzschild black hole.

As the source point nears the horizon, gravitational redshift pushes the radiation toward zero frequency in the outside frame. After passage through the curved space potential, Cheng derives the leading soft response in a region of weak curvature. He formulates a scattering probability that stays safe from infrared problems. The response also links to electromagnetic memory far away, giving a partial fingerprint of the source.
arxiv-2507-17413:
Rongfu Liu, Alessandro Sonnenfeld, Carlo Nipoti, and Rui Li probe, in 2025 work, how old, red galaxies grow late in life, by reading their star-packed cores. Their gauge is the star mass and its slope inside a fixed ring near each core. Mergers are the prime suspect for late growth, so the pair of gauges can test that tale.

A sky survey gave the gauges for many such galaxies across a span of look-back time. No clear drift showed in the gauge link, and the team caps how fast it could shift. Toy runs of merged galaxies then set a cap on how much mass dry mergers could add in that span: about a tenth. A longer time span should let the test bite, they say.
arxiv-2507-17513:
Nazar Buzun and three colleagues present HOTA, a Hamiltonian take on optimal transport, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. At its core, this field moves probability mass from one spread to the next at the least cost. Generative models use it to guide flows of mass. Most of them take space to be flat, in the Euclidean sense.

Real data often lives on curved manifolds, where those flat-space claims fail. HOTA takes on the dual dynamical transport task head-on, through Kantorovich potentials. Its Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman form does away with the need to model the density in full. The method can even cope with cost functions that are not smooth. On standard benchmarks and on custom datasets with such rough costs, HOTA beat all baselines. It won on both how fit the paths were and how close to best they came.
arxiv-2507-17613:
Xiaoxue Chen and co-authors rebuild real scenes in 3D so they can be relit and re-rendered, in a 2025 paper. Their system, InvRGB+L, works from one drive-through record of camera images plus LiDAR scans. Camera-only methods often misjudge surface materials when light shifts around.

LiDAR brings its own glow data, taken with active light in a band apart from daylight. The team built a physics model for that LiDAR shading and tied camera and LiDAR material reads together. The model can render fresh views in both modes, shift a scene to night, and drop in moving objects. Results beat prior top methods on city scenes. Such tools serve driving simulators and digital twins of real streets.
arxiv-2507-17813: Adrien Martina classifies mass deformations of supersymmetric Yang-Mills matrix models in a 2025 paper. These matrix models are toy versions of gauge theory used to probe quantum gravity and string ideas. Martina sorts every deformation that keeps supersymmetry intact, across dimensions three, four, six, and ten. In ten dimensions, the polarized IKKT model is the only option. In four dimensions, two massive models avoid the sign problem that blocks computer studies. Those two stand out as strong candidates for numerical work on non-perturbative physics.
arxiv-2507-17913:
Elizaveta Iarovikova and Andrey Kupavskii wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It settles how large a family of spanning trees can be when each pair of trees in the family must share at least a fixed count of edges.

A spanning tree here is a set of edges that links all corners of a complete graph with no loops. A family with the shared-edge trait is called t-intersecting. For all large graphs and all sound values of the shared count, the authors find the exact top size of such a family. Complete results of this kind are rare, the authors note. The paper gives a full answer for trees where past work had only parts.
arxiv-2507-18113:
Junyong Jiang and colleagues attacked reinforcement learning agents without touching their world in a 2025 paper. Agents in robotics and driving learn policies that adversaries would love to nudge into bad choices. Older attacks rewrite the environment or the policy itself, which real attackers often cannot do. Here, other agents already in the scene behave so as to lure the target into poor actions.

A language model drafts adversarial reward signals tuned to the target's weaknesses, refined by an iterative optimization loop. A second algorithm finds the critical states where a bad choice hurts overall performance most, so effort concentrates there. Across varied test environments the method beat prior attacks. Defenders must now watch fellow agents, not just sensors.
arxiv-2507-18413:
Enrico Santi, Fabio Tardivo, Agostino Dovier, and Andrea Formisano present a 2025 GPU version of a solver step for table constraints. Such constraints list the allowed value sets for a group of variables, and they can stand in for any other constraint. Real cases can hold thousands of rows, which swamp plain processors.

The team ported the top propagation method, Compact-Table, to graphics chips and built it into a live solver. That move taps the chips' huge parallel power for the row checks. Tests on a set of hard cases check how the GPU form fares against the standard one.
arxiv-2507-19013:
Ankit Kumar and Panagiotis Manolios give the first machine-checked proof that a popular messaging protocol behaves as promised. Their 2025 paper concerns Floodsub, a peer-to-peer publish-subscribe system where nodes join and leave freely and pass each new message to all neighbors but the sender.

To state what correct means, they define a stripped-down specification, Broadcastsub, which hides wiring and subscriptions and keeps only the delivery promise. The proof shows every run of Floodsub matches the specification, using a method called well-founded simulation that reasons locally about states and their successors. The authors note it is the first mechanized refinement proof for a real-world pubsub protocol.
arxiv-2507-19113:
Liliana Pasquale and three co-authors report a trial of language models for writing software requirements in a paper from 2025. In an IT consulting firm, analysts build a formal design document from scattered notes, emails, and product sketches, a slow and fragmented task. The team fed models a summary of source material plus document templates and asked for draft sections and user stories.

Three top models were compared with human analysts on correctness and quality. The models sped up drafting and made documents more uniform. Quality hinged on the inputs, and human revision was still needed. The authors favor a pairing: models draft, analysts oversee.
arxiv-2507-19313:
John Campbell, Giuseppe De Laurentis, and Keith Ellis present a physics calculation from 2025 on how three Higgs bosons can be made at once. The paper works out, in full analytic form, the leading one-loop amplitude for gluon fusion into three Higgs particles. The result keeps the full effect of the heavy quark running in the loop.

Making three Higgs bosons at once would test how the Higgs field interacts with itself, a central goal for current and future colliders. The authors use finite-field methods and partial fractions to reach a short, compact formula. Their form of the result runs more than ten times faster than older numerical tools. That speed makes the process far easier to include in studies of collider data.
arxiv-2507-19613:
Samantha Wu and Daichi Tsuna model the late radio glow of exploding stars that shed mass to a partner in this 2025 paper. Many supernovae crash into gas the star lost before dying, and the crash shines in radio years later. In close binaries, a star can hand mass to its companion and puff out a shell in the process.

Their models show lower-mass stripped stars leave a detached shell, while heavier ones leave a steady wind. The crash of the blast into that gas makes radio light as bright as the brightest late glows seen in hydrogen-poor supernovae. Early-time wiggles need extra touches, like sped-up gas or an uneven shell. The work links late radio data to binary history.
arxiv-2507-20013:
Baturay Yilmaz and Esra Erdem build a generator for hard stable roommates benchmark problems with many solutions. The roommates problem pairs people so no two would rather switch. Fair variants that maximize total satisfaction are hard to solve.

Random generators often yield no stable matching at all. When matchings exist, they are often few and easy to list. Listing then makes the fair variant simple in practice. The new algorithm targets instances rich in stable matchings. In such cases fair solutions resist simple enumeration. That hardness makes them honest tests for solvers. The study supplies tougher benchmarks for matching research. It helps separate real solver strength from easy cases.
arxiv-2507-20313:
Emily Adlam argues that modern spacetime physics unsettles old accounts of laws and possibility, yet also offers new tools. Her 2025 paper works in the philosophy of physics. She focuses on relational observables, quantities defined by relations inside a system rather than by an outside frame, as used in general relativity and quantum gravity research.

Adlam suggests the internal view used in partial and complete observables, and in quantum reference frames, can show how non-modal facts arise from modal ones. That supports a form of modal ontic structural realism, where structure and possibility come first. Philosophers of science get a bridge between technical work on observables and classic puzzles about lawhood.
arxiv-2507-20513:
Shiva Sinaei, Chuanjun Zheng, Kaan Akşit, and Daisuke Iwai speed up optical design, in a paper published in 2025. Ray tracing follows light through each surface of a lens system in turn, which is accurate but slow. Their method, Ray2Ray, trains a neural network to jump straight from incoming rays to outgoing rays for a whole system.

They trained the network on nine store-bought optical systems. Its predicted rays landed within about a micron of the true position and a hundredth of a degree in angle. That is close enough for many design checks, at a fraction of the computing cost. The authors present neural stand-ins as a practical shortcut for lens designers, with full tracing kept for final checks.
arxiv-2507-20713:
Z Z Alisultanov and A Kudlis study disorder in layered materials in a 2025 physics paper. The materials in focus can sit in a special protected state, or in a plain state, based on their inner structure. Random jumps between layers, called off diagonal disorder, blur that picture and add states inside the energy gap.

A single flaw creates a trapped state whose energy crosses the gap middle in the plain phase but never in the protected phase. That crossing works as a local sign of which phase the material is in. Two math routes agree on state counts across four regimes. Strong disorder can close the gap, yet one phase stays robust.
arxiv-2507-21013:
García Talavera and seven co-authors probe the superconducting state of a platinum-lead compound with a needle-sharp microscope at near-zero temperatures. The material, PtPb4, turns superconducting below about 3 kelvin. The team measured how many electronic states sit at each energy inside the superconducting gap.

The gap measured 0.48 milli-electron volts, matching classic theory closely. Oddly, patches of the surface kept superconducting signs in fields far above the bulk limit, and a few spots showed a gap even above the transition temperature. The authors discuss how structural defects might explain these stubborn regions. The material's kinship with a surface-state compound adds interest to the findings.
arxiv-2507-21413:
Kai Ma and Tong Li wrote this 2025 physics paper on a proposed hunt for new physics using light striking light. When two light beams cross, they can scatter off each other through quantum effects in empty space. The team proposes hitting a photon beam with a strong laser pulse and reading the scatter with care.

They compute the standard rate of this scatter from full quantum formulas. Then they add the effects of two rival ideas: a classic nonlinear theory of the field, and a family of light particles called axion-like particles. The standard signal should be within reach of near-future tests with modest running time. The authors chart how sharply such a setup could probe the settings of each rival idea, giving experimenters a fresh low-energy window on both.
arxiv-2507-21513:
Kenneth Li and co-authors ask in 2025 what it should mean to say a neural network has learned a world model. The phrase is used loosely in machine learning talk, which makes claims hard to test. The authors offer a set of exact criteria meant to give the term a working meaning that labs can share.

Their focus is on whether a network holds an inner picture of a hidden state space of the world, leaving action effects for later work. The criteria build on probing methods that read out what a network's inner signals encode. A key extra is a set of checks that such a picture is not just a trivial echo of the data or task. The paper aims to turn a slogan into a claim that experiments can confirm or refute.
arxiv-2507-21613:
Zihao Mi and Zhan Wang introduce a new way to describe how energy is spread inside jets of particles, in a 2025 physics paper. Jets spray out when high-energy collisions shatter protons, and their inner pattern reveals the forces at work. Their measure records energy landing at one chosen angle from the jet's axis.

The authors work out the math that splits this measure into parts that can each be computed, using an effective theory built for such problems. They tame the large correction terms that usually spoil predictions, and show the cleaned-up measure depends mainly on the jet's own scale. That makes it a sharp probe of how gluons split inside jets, a process that is hard to extract by other means. Final predictions are compared with a standard event simulator.
arxiv-2507-21913:
Chunzhi Xiang and co-authors make a fast algorithm faster still by teaching it about walls. The fast multipole method computes long-range interactions in particle systems in linear time, but the classic version assumes open space. Their 2025 paper treats the Laplace equation in a half-plane whose edge carries Robin boundary conditions, the kind that mix a field's value with its slope.

The new work rests on an expansion theory for the reaction part of the Green's function, the echo the wall sends back. A Fourier transform puts that echo into an integral form, from which the team derives far-field approximations and the shifting operators the algorithm needs. The tree of sources is built from the real charges and their mirror images together. The authors prove the method converges exponentially, like its free-space parent, and confirm the linear scaling in numerical tests.
arxiv-2507-22213:
Yetukuri and Khan study how online shops can rewrite a shopper's search words to match what the shopper truly wants. Short typed searches often hide the real goal. Their 2025 work builds a data pipeline that mines large logs of past searches for signs of intent.

The pipeline uses both clear clicks and quiet cues, such as what a shopper views or buys. Models trained on this rich data learn to rewrite searches based on intent, not just on word match. Tests across several product groups show gains in the share of good results near the top. The authors offer the setup as a base for later work. Gains were judged with measures that reward putting the right products high in results.
arxiv-2507-22613:
Yann Dreze, Muting Hao and Luca di Mare present a faster way to simulate conjugate heat transfer in their 2025 arXiv paper. Such simulations couple fluid flow with heat conduction in a solid, and the solid's slow thermal time scales make unsteady cases costly to run.

Their method describes the solid's temperature field with eigenfunctions of the heat conduction equation, paired with a fine local solution near the interface. The split lets them speed up the slowest thermal modes on purpose. One-dimensional checks and scale-resolving tests show up to a fourfold cut in the time needed to reach steady conditions, with little extra cost or error.
arxiv-2507-22813:
A neural network can be secretly trained to misbehave when it sees one hidden trigger pattern, a backdoor that owners may never spot. Hossein Mirzaei and co-authors offer a way to rebuild that trigger in a 2025 paper, without any training data on hand. Their tool guides a picture-making model with the suspect network itself, steering each draft toward what the network treats as the trigger.

Older hunts roam the full pixel space and often return noise that merely fools the network once. By searching inside the picture maker's own smooth space, the new tool finds patterns tied to the backdoor itself. On shared test sets it sorted clean models from rigged ones far better than rivals. For groups that buy or download models, the method is a stronger safety check before real use.
arxiv-2507-23113:
Yangxinyu Xie and three co-authors tackle AI use in school writing in a 2025 arXiv paper. Teachers want to allow helpful AI edits yet catch misuse, but today's detectors flag innocent students too often and lean against some groups. Hidden marks in AI text, called watermarks, give firm odds, yet no one had tried them for class work with mixed levels of allowed help.

The team adds a checking method that keeps false flags in check across varied classes. They test essays from native and non-native English writers, with seven levels of AI help, from grammar fixes to added content. The setup spans several models and mark schemes, and it gives schools hard numbers for fair rules on AI help.
arxiv-2507-23213:
A number Lescot attached to a ring, built from the Bass series of its modules, might in principle run off to infinity, and he asked whether it always stays finite. Srikanth Iyengar, Sarasij Maitra, and Tim Tribone answer for many new families of rings in 2025.

Lescot had settled the question for Gorenstein and Golod rings. The new insight ties his invariant to the map from ordinary cohomology to stable cohomology, which lets multiplicative structure do the work. Where that map behaves, finiteness follows. The paper widens the known territory considerably while leaving the general question open, a typical shape for progress in commutative algebra.
arxiv-2507-23313:
Alfio Ferrara and co-authors ask how text-to-image models split a picture into content and style. Classic computer vision treats the two as separate, yet diffusion models get no such lesson during training. Using Rembrandt as a test case, the team studied a transformer-based image model as it painted from written prompts.

They read cross-attention heatmaps, which show which prompt words steer which pixels. Words naming things mostly shaped the regions holding those objects. Words naming a style mostly touched the background and surface texture. The split varied with the prompt and style requested, but its presence hints that the models pick up the content-style divide on their own. The team shares code, data, and a tool for viewing the maps.
arxiv-2507-23513:
Nikolaev and co-authors use synchrotron light as a measuring tool for blazed diffraction gratings, in a 2025 optics paper. At grazing incidence, a single scattering pattern captures both the sharp diffraction orders and the soft diffuse scatter from the grating surface. The team evaluated how each part of the pattern responds to the grating's structure, checking the method against microscope data.

Diffraction proved sensitive to the average groove profile, while diffuse scatter tracked the roughness of the reflective surface. Simulations with several exact solvers and a simpler theory backed the readings. The authors commend synchrotron measurements to the optics community as precision metrology for modern elements.
arxiv-2507-23613:
Francis Appiah and co-authors present a solver for wave problems at many frequencies in a 2025 paper. The Helmholtz equation governs steady waves in sound, light, and other fields. Solving it again for each frequency and each source wastes effort when many answers are needed.

Their method extends an approach that filters a related wave equation over time. One wave solve, paired with several filters, yields answers for all frequencies at once. A standard speedup method makes the iteration converge faster. The scheme can run with few time steps per wave period and keeps costs in line with grid size. Tests show accurate results at high order in space.
arxiv-2507-23713:
Zhangting Chen, Dimitrios Konstantinides, and Charalampos Passalidis derive formulas for the chance that an insurer's total claims crash through a rare barrier, in a 2025 paper. Insurance risk models add up claims over time while investments grow or shrink the reserve. Rare, huge aggregate losses are what sink firms, so their probability needs sharp estimates.

The claims here arrive as vectors — several lines of business at once — with heavy, subexponential tails and tangled dependence between them. The authors give asymptotic estimates on both finite and endless horizons, for varied investment price paths. Two new dependence structures join the toolkit, and even the one-line case gains fresh results. Actuaries pricing extreme risk get theory that fits messy reality better.
arxiv-2508-00413:
Junyu Chen and six co-authors upgrade the compression stage of image generators to make training converge faster, in a 2025 paper. Wider latent channels improve reconstruction sharpness. They also slow the diffusion model's learning badly. That trade-off caps quality for high-resolution generation. Two fixes attack the slowdown from different sides.

First, the latent space is trained into a set order. Early channels carry object structure, later ones fine detail. Second, extra training goals focus on those structure channels. The diffusion model then locks onto content sooner. On a standard benchmark at high resolution, quality beat the prior version. Generation also ran four times faster in their setup. Code is public for builders of latent diffusion systems. Higher compression ratios become practical with the change.
arxiv-2508-00513:
Yiming Xu and co-authors present CMUCL, an end to end method to spot odd nodes in graphs whose nodes carry raw text. Such text attributed graphs show up in high risk fields, where anomaly hunting matters. Older pipelines encode the text apart from the graph task, so the features may miss what counts for spotting oddballs.

Their 2025 method trains text and graph encoders together, using contrast tasks that cross the two modes and work within each. Those tasks run at several scales to pull out anomaly linked signals. A scoring step then mines mismatch to grade each node. The team also releases eight data sets built for this task.
arxiv-2508-00613:
Benedikt Maderbacher and Roderick Bloem present a method that builds reactive software once, for whole families of settings at once, in a 2025 paper. Such systems must answer their surroundings endlessly, and each setting value could demand a fresh build. Their method instead synthesizes a program with the setting left as a dial.

The loop starts by building concrete systems for a few small settings. It then generalizes them into one parameterized program and drafts a proof: an invariant plus a ranking function. Failed proofs hand back a setting worth adding to the first step. Tests cover literature examples stretched with parameters plus fresh problems.
arxiv-2508-00913:
Mohammadi, Wu, and Gilitschenski pretrained event cameras with time in mind in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Event cameras report only brightness changes, pixel by pixel, leaving long-term context to the model. Earlier self-supervised methods borrowed image tricks and ignored that long history. Their framework, TESPEC, pretrains on long event sequences instead.

The model learns by reconstructing a target video built from accumulated events. That pseudo-grayscale footage carries scene meaning while resisting noise and motion blur. Rebuilding it forces the network to reason over long stretches of time. Recurrent models, previously held back by weak pretraining, benefit most. Downstream tests in detection, segmentation, and depth estimation reached state-of-the-art results.
arxiv-2508-01013:
Arjun Manoj and co-authors compare tunable frameworks for multi-fidelity optimization in a 2025 paper. Design problems often allow cheap rough tests and costly exact ones. A good method blends both, using the cheap runs to scout and the dear ones sparingly. The team worked with Gaussian process surrogates, models that guess outcomes and their uncertainty.

They add a proximity-based rule that picks which fidelity to run next without a separate scoring function per level. They also extend a confidence-bound strategy to the multi-fidelity setting. Benchmarks against rival strategies weighed accuracy, hunger for costly runs, and ease of tuning. The proximity rule gave steady control over costly usage while keeping convergence brisk. Test cases included chemical kinetics models, among them dynamic catalysis for ammonia production.
arxiv-2508-01113: Deschamps, Maier, and Stalljohann wrote a 2025 paper settling a conjecture about magnetic motion on energy surfaces. The systems pair geodesic flow with a magnetic field. The question, dating to 1998, asks when energy surfaces fail to be of contact type. The authors build, on any closed space, a huge family of systems of strong geodesic type. Each carries a closed magnetic orbit, trivial in homology, on every energy level, with negative action below a named threshold. Critical values come out in closed form, proving the conjecture for this class.
arxiv-2508-01413:
Jixia Li and co-authors measure the beam shape of a radio telescope in 2025. The Tianlai array uses three large fixed curved reflectors on the ground. Such dishes are too big for indoor test chambers, so their beam must be mapped another way.

A small drone carried a signal source high above the array in its far field. The team read the array's own signals as the drone flew, and corrected for the source antenna's own shape. Beam maps along both axes were built for a band of radio waves. Checks against bright sky sources and simulations backed the method's accuracy.
arxiv-2508-01613:
Marco Castelli and Arpan Kanrar answer two open questions about solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation by studying one map attached to each solution. The equation sits behind knot theory and quantum groups, and its set-sized solutions carry a squaring map whose cycle structure shapes what can be built. Two researchers had asked whether unsplittable solutions exist whose squaring map is a swap, or a three-cycle. Their 2025 paper widens the question to cycles of any prime length.

Under two common conditions, a permutation group that is nilpotent, or a solution whose size is a prime power, the answer is no: such solutions must split apart. The paper also gives splitting criteria in this setting. Latin solutions, the most rigid kind, behave even more stiffly. The authors frame the result as a map of where indecomposable examples can and cannot hide.
arxiv-2508-01813:
Zhe Zhang and co-authors give a full polarization analysis for electron positron collisions that produce a J/psi particle decaying into a baryon and an antibaryon. Their 2025 paper works in the helicity formalism, listing all allowed helicity amplitudes for both steps and how they transform under parity and CP operations. Beam polarization is taken into account throughout.

All eight independent polarization components of the produced J/psi can be nonzero, they show. A polarization transfer matrix then tracks how that polarization passes into the decay products. Joint angular distributions are derived for hadronic and radiative decay models. A worked case gives error estimates for probing CP violation in a mixed baryon pair.
arxiv-2508-01913:
Kamal Al-Sabahi and Yousuf Khamis Al Mabsali propose a new system for checking authorship in academic publishing in a 2025 paper. Journals face gift authorship, names added without consent, unclear roles, and hidden conflicts of interest. Current ID systems tell researchers apart but do not enforce consent or verify who did what.

Their design uses self-sovereign identity tools. Each author holds a digital ID and signed credentials that record identity and contributions. A blockchain registry stores consent and peer-review records so they cannot be quietly changed. Privacy math called zero-knowledge proofs can flag conflicts without exposing private details. A survey of researchers, editors, and reviewers suggested the scheme would raise trust in publishing. The authors present it as a step toward a more open and accountable system.
arxiv-2508-02113:
Yihang Huang and co-authors scrub lens flare out of photos with a sequence model built for the job. Flare, the streaks and ghosts thrown by bright lights inside a lens, tangles with the scene behind it. Earlier removers often leave patches that clash with their surroundings. DeflareMamba leans on state space models, which scan an image efficiently while holding long-range context.

Its hierarchy samples pixels at varied strides to bind distant regions together, while locally enhanced blocks guard fine detail. Both scattering and reflective flares yield to the treatment, and untouched regions keep their natural look. Cleaned photos also helped object recognition and image-text matching downstream. The authors release the code for a task state space models had not touched before.
arxiv-2508-02213:
Black holes ring with faint flickers called quasi-periodic oscillations, and their rates encode the space near the hole. Bidyut Hazarika and two co-authors use those flickers in 2025 to test a modified theory of gravity joined with a nonlinear form of electromagnetism. They track how two knobs of the theory shift the orbits of gas circling a charged black hole.

Raising one knob steadily moved the innermost stable orbit and the flicker rates away from the classic charged hole's values. Three models of where flickers arise were fitted to data from holes of many sizes. A sampling method then pinned down the ranges the data allow for the theory's knobs. The authors say the flickers give a workable test of the theory.
arxiv-2508-02413:
Antrea Christou and Cogan Shimizu present a 2025 tool for browsing knowledge graphs with help from their schemas. Such graphs hold vast labeled links, which makes them hard to roam and grasp. The same strain shows up when users try to view such data or find items in it. A schema, when present, states how links may run, and the tool leans on that extra knowledge.

The InK Browser gives split views: a schema map, lists by type, neighbor views, and map views where place data exist. Its views come as modules, so each one gives a fresh angle on the same graph. A grown user survey tests whether such flexible views ease the hunt through graph data for a range of uses.
arxiv-2508-02513:
Tanja Baeumel and co-authors probe how language models do arithmetic inside, in a paper from 2025. Recent work shows models store numbers digit by digit, not as whole values. This study hunts the actual circuits behind that scheme. The question is whether set neuron groups handle each digit place.

Feature importance scores and causal interventions pinned down the circuits. Units, tens, and hundreds each had their own module of MLP neurons. The pattern held across model sizes. It also held whether numbers were tokenized as one chunk or digit by digit. Arithmetic inside these models is thus compositional, built from place-wise parts. Knowing the parts makes the black box a little more legible.
arxiv-2508-02613:
Martin Ladecký and co-authors fix a slow solver for smooth, high contrast data in a 2025 paper. Fast Fourier solvers are strong tools for periodic cell problems in multiscale modeling. On regular grids they beat classic methods. But when material traits vary smoothly with sharp contrast, their convergence drags badly.

Their Green-Jacobi preconditioner upgrades the standard Green version while keeping near linearithmic cost. Paired with a conjugate gradient method, it cuts iteration counts a lot in elasticity tests, they report. The gain matters for fracture models, topology design, and adaptive grid solvers, all of which create smooth trait changes.
arxiv-2508-02813:
Remco van der Hofstad and co-authors tackle a pure-math question in a 2025 paper on random graphs. They study configuration models, where each node gets a set number of stubs that pair up into edges, and each edge carries a weight from some field.

Their main result concerns the rank of the graph's adjacency matrix as the graph grows huge. The scaled rank settles to a limit that does not depend on the chosen weights or even on the field they come from. To prove it, the team adapted a method that explores graph components step by step and turns the count into fixed-point equations. The proof links random-graph structure to clean algebra.
arxiv-2508-03313:
Libo Zhang, Xinyu Yi, and Feng Xu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It tracks full body motion in real time from the motion and pressure sensors in a phone and a smartwatch, a pairing found in daily gear.

Sparse sensors make pose hard to read, and most past sets show flat ground only. BaroPoser is the first to add barometric reads, which track height change as a person climbs or dips. That cue sharpens both pose and travel over rough ground. A local thigh frame splits local limb moves from whole-body travel, which aids learning. Tests on public sets and live takes beat the best motion-only methods on the same gear.
arxiv-2508-03413:
Akshay Madhav Deshmukh surveys attacks and privacy risks in smart cars and vehicle networks, in a paper from 2025. Modern cars are rolling computers linked by wireless ties to each other and to road systems. Those links support smart transport, but they also open doors to attack. Moving vehicles make guarding the network harder than in fixed setups.

The survey maps the main network designs used between vehicles. It then traces how car security has grown as models gained more software. Attacks are sorted by type, each paired with its known defenses and a worked example. Privacy risks get their own pass, since cars broadcast where they go. The paper closes with the open problems that designers still face. It serves as a map for builders of safer car networks.
arxiv-2508-03613:
Yong Lin and co-authors present Goedel-Prover-V2, a family of open models for formal theorem proving, in a 2025 paper. Three ideas drive the gains. Training data grows in steps of rising difficulty, so the model masters harder theorems in stages. A compiler feedback loop lets the model fix its own proofs. And merging checkpoints restores variety lost late in training.

The small eight billion parameter model scored 84.6 percent on a standard test set, beating a rival over eighty times its size. The flagship scored up to 90.4 percent with self correction on. On a hard contest set it solved 86 problems, taking first place among open models at the time.
arxiv-2508-03713:
Minsuk Chang and co-authors link chart-reading skill to eye movement in a 2025 study. People differ in how well they read charts, and those gaps shape what a chart tells them. The team ran a study with 235 people who took three chart skill tests. Eye tracking showed clear gaps between strong and weak readers.

Strong readers kept a tight focus on the key parts of a chart. Weaker readers roamed more and locked on less. From these patterns the team built two models. One predicts where a viewer will look, given their skill level. The other works in reverse, guessing skill from a single gaze map with 86 percent accuracy in under a minute. Both point toward charts tuned to each reader.
arxiv-2508-03813:
Song He, Canxin Shi, Yichao Tang, and Yao-Qi Zhang uncover, in a 2025 preprint, a hidden symmetry in the squared scattering amplitudes of a three-dimensional gauge theory. The theory, known as ABJM, is a cousin of the maximally symmetric four-dimensional one. The authors define squared amplitudes for it in the planar limit, mirroring a known construction. One generating function then packs the integrands for every particle count and loop order with a fixed sum of the two. It turns out to be unchanged under swapping any of its parts, a secret permutation symmetry.

Written through that symmetry, the function becomes a blend of simple graph types, checked for all cases up to the tested totals. Graph rules guessed from the pattern let the team bootstrap the next case outright. New tree and loop results fall out. The authors suspect one bipartite correlator underlies all squared amplitudes here.
arxiv-2508-04113:
Solar cells lose much of the light that hits them, and thin films can trap more of it. Le Tri Dat and Nguyen Duy Vy study a copper tin sulfide layer, a light absorber, sandwiched with nanometer-thin metallic films of gold, silver, copper, and aluminum. Using Maxwell's equations for fields crossing the stacked layers, they compute how much light the absorber keeps at each wavelength and thickness.

The stack's optical cavity effect lifts absorption sharply, with the best designs reaching about 60 percent in the reported range. The authors identify the thickness windows for the outer layers that harvest the most thermal energy from light. They present the results as guidance for choosing layer thicknesses in solar cells and other light-harvesting devices.
arxiv-2508-04213:
Alessia Pisu and co-authors automate the maps that organize science itself. Their 2025 paper presents Sci-OG, a method for building ontologies of research topics from paper collections, work long done by hand and quickly outdated.

The pipeline runs in three steps: pull candidate topics from papers, classify how topic pairs relate, then refine the result into a structured ontology. Its core pairs an encoder language model with features drawn from how topics appear across the literature. On over twenty-one thousand hand-labeled topic triples it beat fine-tuned rivals and large-model baselines, reaching the best F1 score. A trial run extended a computer science ontology into cybersecurity. The authors pitch the tool for keeping literature maps current.
arxiv-2508-04413:
Galaxies and their central black holes grow together, but the ones that stray from the shared size line may reveal the rules. Wenlin Ma, Weiguang Cui, Romeel Davé, Daniel Anglés-Alcázar, and Hong Guo study the strays in the SIMBA simulation in a 2025 paper. The simulated size line matches the observed one well. Scatter around it is measured against the middle value for each galaxy.

Stray direction links to cold gas, star birth, color, and how the black hole feeds. Two feeding modes split the work by era and galaxy size. Tracking family trees of the strays suggests a story: early galaxies seed holes early, then jet feedback starves their growth.
arxiv-2508-04913:
Santosh Chapagain, Shah Muhammad Hamdi, and Soukaina Filali Boubrahimi explore in 2025 transformer models for detecting hate speech online. Hate posts can cause real social and physical harm, and social platforms host huge volumes of them. Older deep learning models face limits with long text and parallel training.

They use a meta-collection of thirty-six data sets with more than a million social media samples. Several transformer models were tested, including BERT and GPT-2 variants. A fine-tuned ELECTRA model scored best. Error analysis shows ongoing trouble with sarcasm, coded language, and noisy labels in the data.
arxiv-2508-05613:
Haitao Hong and co-authors fix a flaw in how language models learn by trial in a 2025 paper. Two kinds of judges score their tries: fixed rules, which are exact but stiff, and learned judges, which bend but can be gamed. Each kind fails in its own way.

Their frame trains the actor and the judge side by side. Rule scores, sharp when an answer is plain right, anchor the judge as it learns. The judge, in turn, grows more supple where rules are mute. This paired growth aims to block gaming while it keeps the range of true praise. Model teams gain a sturdier loop for teaching hard thought.
arxiv-2508-05713:
Takehiko Mori studies abstract dynamical systems on discrete spaces and their links to operator algebras, in work from 2025. A famous example is the Collatz map, which sends numbers through a simple rule whose long-term behaviour is still unproven. Mori focuses on maps that satisfy a bounded condition on countable sets of points.

When a map meets the bounded condition plus a separating condition, the system's minimality matches the irreducibility of an associated algebra of operators. For a general map, Mori studies the sets it leaves invariant and builds an order-preserving link to subspaces tied to the algebra. A further uniqueness condition turns that link into an exact match. The results give a symbolic way to represent such systems and connect them with topological dynamics.
arxiv-2508-06013: Yiheng Ye and Spencer Gessner rebuild the cross-wise profile of electron bunches at a test facility in 2025, using a scan method akin to medical tomography. Their short report centres on a hard case: two bunches stacked on top of each other, each with its own profile. A single sweep of a focusing magnet, read the right way, teases the two apart. As the team tuned the charge, the play of charges took charge of the motion in ways they had not forecast.
arxiv-2508-06313:
Heavy robot arms that run on electric drives need models that stay true under load. Amir Hossein Barjini and co-authors present such a model and controller in a 2025 paper. Their arm uses electric linear actuators, whose behavior mixes mechanics, motors, and heat in hard-to-formula ways.

A stand-in model blends physics with a neural net trained on a real test rig. That model feeds a layered controller that turns force and speed goals into actuator commands, with a proof that the system stays stable. In simulations the arm tracks paths within less than a centimeter. Tests on a one-joint rig under fake loads confirm the control works in hardware, not just in code.
arxiv-2508-06413:
Victor Vanpeene and co-authors film a battery anode at work, in four dimensions and at nano scale, in a 2025 paper. The anode blends silicon and graphite, a high-capacity mix whose swelling and cracking shorten cell life. Their tool is live X-ray holo-tomography at a synchrotron, paired with a method that tracks how each speck of the material moves between frames. One formation cycle gets watched.

The film sorts what truly drives local action. Fast diffusion channels rule, balancing the depth bias set by slow ion and electron travel. Particle shape, seat in the layer, nearness to silicon clusters, wetting by the liquid, and strain each play a part, but not equal parts. The team ranks the factors on one scale of sway. That ranking, they say, hands makers a practical order of attack: fix the channels first.
arxiv-2508-06613:
Jenny Calahan, Karin Öberg, and Alice Booth model how harsh starlight from neighbors reshapes the chemistry of planet-forming disks. Their 2025 paper notes that most young stars with such disks sit in clusters like the Orion Nebula. Strong ultraviolet light there is the norm, not the exception.

Heat from the light breaks molecules and warms the disk, so the zone where gases freeze into ice shrinks. Past one Earth-orbit radius, the air grows richer in water, hydroxyl, and loose atoms. Hydrocarbons near the star stay largely untouched even under extreme fields. Deeper layers gain simple gas molecules as breakdown products sink. Planets born in such glare draw on a reset mix of gas and ice.
arxiv-2508-06713:
A new family of magnets promises spin-based electronics, but its neat magnetic order may spontaneously go wavy. Changhee Lee, Nico Hackner, and Brydon examine that risk in this 2025 paper. These odd-parity antiferromagnets split electron spins in a pattern that needs tidy, commensurate order to work. A whole class of crystals with doubled unit cells could host them.

The team shows the same symmetries that allow the prized pattern also allow a term favoring waves — patterns that drift out of step with the crystal. Magnetism with a wandering period follows, whatever its microscopic cause. Magnets with higher-wave patterns are prone too, above all when electrons roam freely. Device hopes must reckon with this built-in instability.
arxiv-2508-06813:
Hogan and co-authors teach big language models in 2025 to code in Q, a niche language of high finance. General models shine in common languages but starve in rare ones with little web text. The team built a puzzle-style test set for Q, graded the top frontier models on it, then trained their own line.

Training ran in stages: broad reading, guided practice, then reward-based polish, across five model sizes from the same open family. Their best hit fifty-nine percent on the test, beating the top frontier model by nearly thirty points, they report. Even the smallest beat a leading commercial model. The full recipe is open source, a template for other rare tongues of code.
arxiv-2508-07013:
Yufan Zhou, Jingyi Li, Wenkang Xu, and An Liu sharpen a sensing method that recovers sparse signals from few samples. Their 2025 paper treats super-resolution compressive sensing, used in wireless sensing where target positions rarely fall on a neat grid. Off-grid targets blur the recovery, and older methods lean hard on hand-set knobs.

Their framework alternates between two jobs at two speeds. At the slow pace, it estimates the sparse signal with a Bayesian method whose prior pushes hard for sparsity, then refines the grid points that carry the energy. The grid polish runs faster, using a classic optimizer to nudge positions to super-resolved accuracy at low cost. Applied to channel extrapolation, the scheme beat baseline methods in simulations. The design aims at robust recovery when targets sit close together.
arxiv-2508-07113:
Herivelto Borges and Lucas Reis sort the leanest value sets a sum can take in a 2025 paper. The sums live on a field with a set count of parts, and the lean ones hit as few marks as their grade can let.

What sets of marks can such a lean sum take? The pair names the full clan of sets that can show, for sets of more than two marks. Flat blocks of the field are a root kind, and the pair lists all lean sums that land on them. A claim then names all lean sums for any such set. The claim is proved for small fields and for wide sets, with fresh proof for the fourth rung. The same claim solves a clan of bent lines whole, the pair shows.
arxiv-2508-07513:
Emre Kurtoğlu and Mohammad Mahbubur Rahman compare three ways of estimating where a radar echo comes from, in a simulated automotive setting. Frequency-modulated continuous-wave radar, the car industry standard, sweeps its transmit frequency in a ramp. Mixing the echo back down yields a beat tone whose spectrum reveals range and speed. Resolving two targets close in angle is the harder problem this project takes on.

A virtual antenna array supplies the spatial samples for the simulated seventy-seven gigahertz system. Plain spectral estimation is fastest but resolves angles poorly. Two super-resolution methods, a classic subspace technique and compressed sensing, sharpen the picture considerably. The project report, with code released, reads as a compact benchmark of the speed-resolution trade. For safety functions that must split adjacent road users, resolution wins the argument.
arxiv-2508-07613:
Zhengrui Xu and co-authors automate how recommender systems blend goals in a 2025 paper. Feeds rank posts by mixing many aims, like clicks and watch time. Hand-shaped curves and hand-set weights do that mixing today, at high labor cost and with uneven trade-offs.

Their frame learns smooth, always-rising blend curves with a special network, then lets a light model set personal weights per user. A balance strategy adjusts task weights during training to stay near the best trade-off front. Tests on two public sets and live trials showed strong gains. The method drops hand tuning while keeping ranks consistent.
arxiv-2508-07813:
Zhao Liu and co-authors map the ground states of a thin Fermi gas with a split spin landscape, in work from 2025. The gas pairs in the plain wave style, but a d-wave magnetic split, called altermagnetism, tilts the field. The team works the phase map with pen-and-paper math inside a mean-field frame.

Four phases appear: a classic paired fluid, a plain metal, a nodal fluid with special topological surfaces, and a drifting pair state with net motion. Both odd phases spring from the magnetic split alone, in a model with one band and no net magnetism. The authors offer the map as a test bench and a lab guide.
arxiv-2508-08013:
Mohamad Assaad, Zeinab Nehme, and Merouane Debbah design two communication-light federated learning methods for wireless networks, in a 2025 paper. Federated learning trains models across edge devices without moving their data, but the training traffic can swamp a wireless link. Their methods send single numbers instead of long vectors, and let many users transmit at once.

One method estimates gradients from two probes, with no gradient math at the device. The other computes gradients directly. Both fold channel knowledge into the learning itself, so no extra resources go to measuring the channel, and devices need not stay in sync. The authors prove convergence for both and bound their performance.
arxiv-2508-08113:
Yinpei Dai and co-authors give robot control policies a simple visual hint: drawn-on aiming lines. Their method, AimBot, overlays shooting lines and a scope reticle onto the robot's camera views. The overlays are computed from depth data, camera positions, and the gripper's pose, so they show where the gripper sits relative to objects. The drawing costs under a millisecond and needs no change to the learning model, since the policy sees augmented images.

Across visuomotor policies, in simulation and on real robots, the cues consistently improved performance. Policies struggle to infer spatial relations from raw pixels, and an explicit drawn cue relieves that burden. The trick is deliberately low-tech: no new sensors, no bigger networks. It suggests that some robot failures are perception-presentation problems, fixable by showing the model the geometry it needs in a form it can read.
arxiv-2508-08813:
Efren Mesino-Espinosa and Alejandro Velez-Santiago study in 2025 a hard class of equations that mix effects inside a region with effects on its edge. Their model uses fractional forms of a nonlinear operator, which let distant points sway each other. The edge rule adds its own fractional terms, so the two parts must be solved as one.

The pair prove that the model has just one weak solution and that it stays bounded across the whole region. They also bound how much the solution can shift when the input data shift, and they prove a rule for comparing two solutions. A final result gives a version of a classic alternative theorem for this nonlinear setting.
arxiv-2508-09013:
Km Rubi and co-authors steer quantum interference with a voltage dial in an oxide sandwich, in a 2025 paper. At the boundary between two insulating oxides, a sheet of electrons can flow with high mobility.
