Their sample's electrical resistance wiggled with magnetic field in a steady rhythm — not the usual high-field pattern, but a low-field one surviving to ten degrees above absolute zero.

The rhythm's fading with heat and field marks quantum paths dephasing. Raising the electron density with a gate voltage shrank both the wiggle's size and its tempo, then erased it entirely. A voltage switch for interference points toward oxide devices that compute with electron waves, tuned on the fly.
arxiv-2508-09113:
Mark Turiansky, John Lyons, and Noam Bernstein show how machine learning can speed up the prediction of light spectra from defects in solids, in a paper from 2025. Defects give gemstones their color and can emit single photons for quantum networks. Their light patterns depend on how atoms vibrate, which is costly to compute for large cells.

The team uses learned atomic potentials in place of direct physics calculations, with little loss of accuracy. Routine data from standard calculations proved enough to tune the models. The speed gain allows the use of higher-grade theory for sharper spectra. Results matched both direct calculations and experiments for several defects. Fine details were resolved in the spectrum of a known quantum defect in silicon.
arxiv-2508-09413:
Xiaorong Zou extends a trigonometric interpolation method so it can solve a class of problems that mix derivatives and integrals in two dimensions. Trigonometric interpolation was of late adapted to non-periodic functions and to ordinary differential equations. Integro-differential problems of Fredholm type are harder, with kernels that may even be singular.

The improved algorithm approximates functions on a two-dimensional grid. Its accuracy stays tied to how smooth the target is, as tests with numbers confirm. Put to work on second-order Fredholm problems, it converges fast with just a moderate grid. It handles singular kernels and general boundary conditions. The design extends to Volterra problems and to ones of higher order. Tests across types of boundary condition all did quite well.
arxiv-2508-09713:
Rahul Hemrajani tests language models on legal work in India in a 2025 paper. Courts and firms wonder whether these models can handle core lawyer tasks. Hemrajani set up a survey experiment in the Indian setting. Models including GPT, Claude, and Llama each produced work on tasks such as spotting issues, drafting, giving advice, doing research, and reasoning through problems.

A junior lawyer produced matching work for comparison. Advanced law students graded all outputs, blind to source, on helpfulness, accuracy, and completeness. The models excelled at drafting and issue spotting, often matching or beating the human work. They stumbled on specialist research, inventing sources and stating false law. Hemrajani concludes the tools can assist lawyers, but human judgment stays essential for fine reasoning and exact law.
arxiv-2508-09813:
Saikat Chakraborty and co-authors test a quiet assumption in cosmology. A universe expanding almost like the standard Lambda CDM model, they note, is often assumed to run on near constant dark energy. They compare the motion based view of expansion with the force based view of what drives it.

Their 2025 study builds two explicit example models and checks both views in each. The two views do not match, they find. An almost standard expansion history instead fits an almost unified dark fluid, a single stuff that plays both dark roles. Since real data never give the exact standard marker, they question whether Lambda CDM is the best standard model.
arxiv-2508-10713:
Murat Temiz and Vemund Bakken build a graphics-chip frame to fake how antennas act, as a source of training data for learning tools. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Learning tools can find the best antenna designs, but they are hungry for data. Each fake run on classic tools takes long, so big training sets are hard to make. The team takes an open-source wave faking tool and runs it on graphics chips. Their frame can turn out vast sets of antenna runs at speed. They check its output against a paid tool's results. The aim is a cheap well of data for design by machine.
arxiv-2508-10813:
Philippe Balbiani and Tinko Tinchev study when modal logic questions can be settled by computer in this 2025 paper. Modal logic reasons about necessity and possibility. The definability problem asks whether a class of frames, the structures logic runs on, can be pinned down by a formula.

Their focus is Euclidean modal logics, whose frames obey a reachability rule borrowed from geometry. They sort out exactly which of these logics give a definability problem that no algorithm can decide. The result draws a clean line between tame and wild cases. Logicians gain a map of where computation must stop.
arxiv-2508-11313:
Weijia Liu and co-authors present a method for finding the moment in a video that matches a written query, in a 2025 paper. Standard methods read every clip in the video, including ones the query has nothing to do with. Those stray clips blur the match between words and pictures and make training harder.

Their network works in two stages: clean first, then search. One module uses the query text to flag and mask clips that do not fit, and a second module feeds back a rebuilt query to sharpen the cleaning during training. The search then runs on the cleaned video alone. On two standard test sets the method beat prior systems on every measure. The authors add that the clean-first pattern can be bolted onto other search models to lift their scores.
arxiv-2508-12013:
Surajit Das and Aleksei Eliseev present a 2025 study on predicting which students use ChatGPT for their assignments. The rise of chatbots has changed how students work and raised hard questions about honest effort. Most past research was based on opinion, not on measured student behavior.

The authors surveyed 388 university students, mostly in Russia, and built a prediction model from their answers. Study habits, subject tastes, and attitudes toward AI were the strongest signals. The model sorted users from non-users with about eighty percent accuracy. A finer model of use levels reached about sixty-five percent. Students who often used the tool to learn new concepts showed signs of over-reliance, which the authors flag as a risk for schools.
arxiv-2508-12113:
Juan Migliore and Uwe Nagel study a special ideal tied to arrangements of flat hyperplanes in space. An arrangement is called free when its Jacobian ideal has a tidy algebraic shape. A long-standing guess by Terao says freeness depends only on how the planes cross.

The authors define a trimmed version of the ideal, built from its thickest parts, which is always even in dimension. They invent a leftover ideal with surprisingly simple traits, then use liaison theory to climb back to the trimmed ideal. Under mild conditions, they show that key numerical data of the ideal follow from the crossing pattern alone. They also bound a global measure of singularities.
arxiv-2508-12513:
Matt Dallas, a solo author writing in 2025, gives a proof for a faster root-finding method. The method speeds up Newton-type steps for solving hard equations. Two key cases are the classic Newton method and a damped variant used when steps go astray.

Dallas shows that with a guard step in place, the sped-up method still settles near a root. It settles faster than the plain method in a star-shaped region near the root. The guard can also sense when the base method is already very fast and tone the extra step down. Tests on known benchmark problems back the claims.
arxiv-2508-12613:
Fluids are often modeled as particles in cells, and Romanik and co-authors study a version of that model that can be solved exactly, in a 2025 theory paper. Their cells may hold any number of particles. Particles attract each other weakly across the whole system yet repel when they share a cell, a tug of war the authors build into the math.

Starting from an exact formula for the model's partition function, the team extracts pressure, density, and the equation of state in closed form. The model shows a ladder of sudden phase changes, each ending at its own critical point, and the authors locate the first five. Entropy dips sharply when cells hold whole numbers of particles, echoing odd density behavior seen in water-like models. A closed formula for that entropy is among the results.
arxiv-2508-12913:
Himanshu Shekhar, Ashutosh Dheer, Santosh Kumar, and Sukumar study eigenvalue patterns in layered networks with random matrix tools, in a paper from 2025. Layered networks, like social plus contact layers, have block-structured connection tables. How their spectra shift as layers couple was not fully mapped.

After scaling blocks to equal variance, they compare spectra across coupling strengths. A crossover model for two layers captures the smooth move from two independent spectra to one merged spectrum. They also test the frame on protein atom networks from crystal structures. Universal fluctuation patterns persist across layouts, which supports random matrix tools for real networks.
arxiv-2508-13213:
Adamo Cerioli, Edward Lee, and Vito Servedio compared how chess engines and human grandmasters handle strategic tension in 2025. Strong play means balancing immediate chances against long-term plans, keeping many pieces in charged interaction without collapsing. The authors built a network-based measure of that tension from piece-to-piece relationships on the board, then applied it to games by elite engines and top humans.

They find engines sustain substantially higher tension for much longer than grandmasters do. For engines, total tension grows with the algorithm's complexity, while for humans it rises steadily with playing strength, and longer time controls let humans carry more tension. The contrast is systematic: leading engines tolerate dense, interlocked positions balancing attack and defense for extended stretches, whereas human players deliberately simplify and limit complexity. The authors draw lessons about how artificial and biological decision makers manage competing demands.
arxiv-2508-13713:
Ali Abdari, Alex Falcon, and Giuseppe Serra present a 2025 paper on searching virtual museums about farming with plain language. Educational material floods online, and metaverse spaces could organize it into explorable exhibits. But finding the right virtual museum for a query is hard, and training data was scarce.

The team built a dataset of 457 agricultural virtual museums, each with text descriptions. Their hierarchical vision-language model represents each museum at several levels and retrieves matches for natural language queries. It reached about sixty-two percent top-one accuracy and a mean reciprocal rank of 0.78. It also improved results on older benchmarks by up to six points of top-one accuracy. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2508-13913:
Xiong Liu and Wenhua Wang study bounds for operator groups on weak Hardy spaces, in a mathematics paper from 2025. The spaces are built from a non-negative self-adjoint operator and a broad class of function spaces. Such spaces help treat equations where classic tools fall short, but their structure needs care.

The authors give atomic and molecular splits for the weak Hardy space. They then prove bounds for Schrödinger groups with fractional powers of the operator. Under a further bound on the operator, they also bound its imaginary powers. The bounds grow in a controlled way with the time factor. The results extend harmonic analysis to wider settings.
arxiv-2508-14013:
Yang Xiao and co-authors design a faster way to make a knowledge graph model forget selected data. Rules such as the right to be forgotten push firms to strip training data and its effects from models. Full retraining costs too much, but graphs resist easy unlearning because their facts hang together by meaning.

Their 2025 paper defines an influence function for graph unlearning and estimates how parameters shift when data is removed. A Taylor expansion frames the change, while Fisher matrices and zeroth-order methods dodge the costly derivative steps. Tests show the method beats leading graph unlearning baselines on both speed and quality, a gain that grows on large graphs.
arxiv-2508-14113:
Factory cameras that watch workers' gestures raise privacy fears when footage pools in one place, so training on site is the safer route. Vinit Hegiste, Vidit Goyal, Tatjana Legler, and Martin Ruskowski build that route in a 2025 paper. Five workers performed eight upper-body gestures for a pose-based dataset. A pose model turned video into skeleton points, keeping faces out of the data. Four training styles were compared.

Federated training, where sites share model updates but not data, beat central training on the shared test. An ensemble of site models did better still. On a brand-new worker, the federated gains grew far larger. The authors pitch the setup for privacy-aware factory assistance.
arxiv-2508-14213:
Yabo Li and Aditi Mitra study exotic symmetries in moving systems in 2025. Some symmetries cannot be undone, a trait that reshapes how they guard quantum states. The team asks how these symmetries act when a system is driven out of balance. They use one known symmetry as their test case.

They track both steady driving and timed pulses that repeat in cycles. Edge modes tied to the symmetry show up in each case. With disorder added, energy levels split only under very strong mixing that grows with system size. The work shows these symmetries leave clear marks on dynamics, not just on still states.
arxiv-2508-14313:
Can Jin, Yang Zhou, Qixin Zhang, and a wider team wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It unifies two ways of making language models reason better at test time: learning from rewards, and searching with a step-by-step scorekeeper.

Reward-based training is unstable and data-hungry, while fixed scorekeepers need costly step labels and can be gamed. The authors' framework, AIRL-S, learns the scorekeeper from reference solutions by adversarial inverse reinforcement learning. The same learned scorekeeper then serves as the training signal and as the guide during search. Across eight benchmarks in math, science, and code, the trained model gained about nine points over its base and matched a leading commercial model. The paper also shows the scorekeeper transfers to other generators and search methods.
arxiv-2508-14413:
Samarth Gupta and three co-authors challenged in 2025 the belief that diffusion models need about a thousand noise steps to train well. With a carefully chosen noise schedule, a model trained on roughly 32 latent states matched the quality of one trained on a thousand. The team then pushed the idea to its limit. A single latent state, fully disentangled in time, still produced good samples when several such models were combined.

The disentangled design trains faster and can be split across machines, since each state is learned on its own. Measured convergence sped up four to six times across metrics and two datasets. The authors argue the many-step habit of the field is wasteful. Their results open cheaper training for image generators. The work also reframes how the reverse process needs to behave.
arxiv-2508-14513:
Irea Mosquera-Lois and Aron Walsh study in 2025 how missing atoms behave in a crystal used for light detectors and solar cells. In this lead chloride perovskite, missing chlorine atoms are the main defect, and they trap charge in a way that harms performance. Their energy levels swing with heat, which breaks models that assume a frozen crystal at zero degrees.

Exact quantum math for moving atoms is too costly to run directly. The team instead trained a machine learning force field on many tasks to stand in for it. With that tool they tracked the defect at room temperature. The optical level swung widely as the soft crystal flexed, yet the swings averaged out to the pattern that plain defect thermodynamics predicts. The result rescues a simple theory for a moving, warm crystal.
arxiv-2508-14613:
Daniel Willimetz and Lukáš Grajciar tackle a trust problem in materials computing: a model can give a crisp number and still be guessing far outside what it was taught. Their 2025 paper offers a way to flag those risky guesses. The flag comes from how crowded the training data is near the case at hand, measured with a nearest-neighbor method in a squeezed-down map of the data.

The method runs on graphics chips, so it scales to very large data sets. It needs no retraining and works with many kinds of models, which saves the cost of running model teams for comparison. Across case studies that varied in chemistry, model type, and target property, the flag matched team-based doubt well. It marked the odd cases where trust should drop. The authors offer it as a practical guard for lab use.
arxiv-2508-14813:
Jian He, Sven Karbach, and Asma Khedher price options on forward contracts in models where whole price curves move at once, in a 2025 paper. In energy and interest-rate markets, traders deal in forward curves, not single prices. The authors treat the curve as an infinite-dimensional object driven by a stochastic volatility process.

They analyze two model families. One is Gaussian, steered by a matrix-valued noise process. The other adds jumps whose size depends on the current state, extending a classic framework. For both, they find conditions guaranteeing that the needed averages exist, then derive semi-closed pricing formulas for plain call and put options using Fourier methods. The point is practicality: even with infinitely many risk factors, prices tied to specific maturities and the curve's shape can still be computed. That matters for markets where term structure risk is the whole game.
arxiv-2508-14913:
Israel Abebe Azime and co-authors present a framework to localize math word problems across cultures in this 2025 paper. Models solve math well in English but lag in low resource languages. Test sets made by plain translation keep English names, organizations, and money. That hides the true difficulty of native context problems.

Their framework uses language models to rebuild problems with native entities. Names, institutions, and currencies are swapped for local equivalents at low cost. Experiments show translated tests can misstate multilingual math ability. Proper localization gives a fairer score. The method also reduced English centered bias in the resulting datasets. It offers a cheap path to culturally grounded benchmarks for many languages.
arxiv-2508-15013:
Nadav Amir, Stas Tiomkin, and Angela Langdon propose in 2025 a fresh account of how purposeful behavior arises in minds and machines. Standard theory splits an agent's world model into two parts: a description of what is, and a reward function saying what is good.

The authors argue the two parts may not be separate at all. Instead, descriptions and values could grow together out of an agent's goals, each shaping the other as the agent develops. They give this idea its first computational form. If right, the view changes how researchers build agents that act with intent.
arxiv-2508-15213:
Language models can be taught a specialty by letting them pick what they lack, in a 2025 paper by Bolei He and co-authors. General models stumble in fields like medicine, law, and finance, while fetching documents at question time adds noise and delay, and full retraining is costly.

Their framework, Select2Know, has the model judge its own gaps and pull only the knowledge worth internalizing, through selective fine-tuning. Learning is staged like human study: grasp the concepts first, then practice reasoning, with generated practice data and a reinforcement step to sharpen the second stage. On medical, legal, and financial tests, the method beat rivals and matched models pretrained on the whole domain, at far lower cost.
arxiv-2508-15413:
Pixi Kang and co-authors teach wearable activity trackers to adapt to each wearer with just a few examples, in a 2025 paper. Activity recognition models usually fail on new users because bodies move differently. Their framework first learns a general movement representation across many users. Then, directly on the device, it fine-tunes light classifier layers from a handful of labeled samples from the new wearer.

The team ran the system on an energy-sipping RISC-V microcontroller chip. Across three benchmarks covering gym exercise, hand gestures, and ultrasound gestures, adaptation lifted accuracy by about four, seventeen, and four percentage points. The gains came with minimal computing and memory cost. The authors release the framework openly. They argue on-device few-shot learning makes wearables both personal and practical without cloud help.
arxiv-2508-15513:
Kreider and a large team model light production in inorganic scintillators in two thousand twenty-five. Such crystals flash when radiation hits them and serve as detectors. They have lately tracked decays of exotic nuclei in place of silicon. Right use needs a firm grasp of how the light forms.

Their frame grows from classic Birks and Meyer-Murray work. It covers heavy ion beams across a broad energy range. For heavy fast ions, delta electrons make most of the light. Tests on a common crystal match data on output and quenching. The model will guide future exotic nuclei work.
arxiv-2508-15613:
Ivo Ivanov and Carsten Markgraf gave a fast method in 2025 for aligning two three dimensional point clouds when the rotation axis is known. Alignment must be robust, since most points can be wrong matches in hard cases.

A least squares form that truncates large errors can cope with very high outlier rates, but finding its true best solution is a hard search. Their solver uses a new convex shortcut and a pruning method to speed up branch and bound search. It aligns clouds of one hundred points to proven best in under half a second, about a hundred times faster than a leading rival on this task. Tests on tricky crafted cases back the claim.
arxiv-2508-15713:
Kumar Gaurav and Ishan Sharma model, in a 2025 paper, how landslides reshape small rocky bodies in space. Rubble asteroids spin and shed loose surface soil, and slides can shift both shape and spin. The pair limit their study to slides that spread evenly around the body's axis.

Their model averages slide depth while tracking spin, changing shape, uneven gravity, and soil loss to space. Sunlight pressure on the body also enters the spin math. Runs on real asteroids show how surface soil moves in practice. Over a body's life, impact-triggered slides push soil toward the equator. That flow stops the body from splitting by spin and quickly builds the top shapes seen on many near-Earth asteroids. Slides may thus explain a common asteroid form.
arxiv-2508-15913:
Bachmann, Du, Fraas, and Wessel study a smoothing tool for quantum spin systems and put it to several uses. The tool averages a system's motion over time with a bell-shaped weight, called a Gaussian filter. Earlier work used weights that decay more slowly to keep spectral facts exact. Their 2025 paper accepts small spectral errors in exchange for much tighter locality, meaning each smoothed quantity depends only on nearby spins.

Concrete uses include a gentle method for morphing one system into another, bounds on how fast correlations fade with distance, and stability results away from defects. The authors also apply the tool to the quantum Hall effect, a benchmark problem in the field. They present the filter as a flexible bridge between dynamics and locality.
arxiv-2508-16013:
Pietro Bernardelle and co-authors test how fake personas can bend the political leanings of language models. Models now work in politically tender settings, so their drift matters. The team used a standard sixty-two statement compass test as their probe.

Seven open models, from small to very large, answered under two hundred thousand synthetic personas. More than two hundred sixty million replies were logged. Larger models covered a wider spread of leanings when personas hinted softly. Direct priming toward one corner moved every model that way, as intended. Cues also varied by topic theme. The scale of the study makes the patterns hard to dismiss. It warns deployers that a persona prompt is also a political dial.
arxiv-2508-16413:
Daniele Parlato and co-authors use a precision measure to read the behavior of an open quantum system, in this 2025 paper. Their testbed is the spin-boson model, a single spin soaked in a bath of vibrations. They compute quantum Fisher information, a measure of how sharply a state responds to change, with exact numerical methods.

As the spin-bath link grows, one part of the measure tracks entanglement growth and flags a phase change. Time-based parts reveal memory effects in the bath and a shift from ringing to dull response at a known point. The measure stayed sturdy under noise, which suits it for quantum sensing.
arxiv-2508-16813:
Bingrong Huang and co-authors find how large random cusp forms can grow in a 2025 math paper. Cusp forms are wave-like functions tied to the modular group, a key group in number theory. The team study a random pick of such forms of large weight. They ask how big the top value of a form tends to be.

On a fixed patch of the modular surface, the mean top value grows like the square root of the log of the weight. That rate matches what experts had guessed. The top value also hugs its median tight, with gaps that shrink fast. Near the cusp, the thin end of the surface, the tale flips: the mean top value grows like the fourth root of the weight, up to a log factor. The work pins down both rates with proof.
arxiv-2508-17013:
The-Anh Vu-Le, Tandy Warnow, and six co-authors cluster network data by pulling out dense knots. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, presents DSC-Flow-Iter. The method lifts out tightly linked groups one by one. It leaves many nodes ungrouped, yet its groups are rarely wrong.

That care makes it a good partner for modularity methods, which group broadly but sloppily. The team builds an ensemble that merges both styles of output. On many fake networks with known groups, the blend beats each part alone. It also beats other standard tools. The work is aimed at fields like biology, where networks are large and truth is partly known.
arxiv-2508-17313:
Alexander Alban, Fu-Hsuan Ho, and Justin Ko revisit a proof in 2025 about a model of a disordered system, a system with a random energy for each state. Models of this kind serve physics, where they mimic glasses and other tangled matter. The team wants the long run value of a quantity called the free energy.

They build an enriched model that sits between the base model and a known layered scheme. The proof uses a method that turns the problem into a flow equation of a known type. In the weak link case, where states are only loosely tied, the answer takes a classic closed form. That answer does not depend on the exact tie pattern, a fact the paper confirms. Outside that case, the method breaks down, and the authors give an example to show the edge of their result.
arxiv-2508-17613:
Abd Hamid, Shapiai, and Lai build a model that forecasts Alzheimer's test scores from brain scans in twenty twenty-five. The test, ADAS-Cog, has a total score plus thirteen part scores for distinct thinking skills. Most past models forecast only the total. Their model, based on a vision transformer, forecasts all scores at once from a starting scan.

They weigh the loss on each part score by how much it drives the total. The best weights split by patient group. Strong weights helped most for patients with mild impairment and mixed scan patterns. Mild weights worked better for healthy adults. Even weights wasted the key part scores, they argue. The design stays readable to clinicians.
arxiv-2508-18013:
Manuel Barusco and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on teaching medical image tools to learn over time without forgetting. Such tools learn from normal scans alone and flag scans that look off, a task where spotting the odd region matters. In clinics, the stream of scans shifts as machines and patients change. A tool trained once can then fade.

The team adapted a known tool, named PatchCore, to a step-by-step learning mode. New kinds of scan arrive in stages, and the tool updates while it guards what it learned before. They tested it on a real medical image set with marks at both the image and pixel level. The adapted tool matched versions trained for one task alone. It forgot less than one percent of its past skill. The team calls this a first proof that step-wise learning fits this corner of medical imaging.
arxiv-2508-18113:
Farkhad Akimov and co-authors present an AI agent that does data science end to end in this 2025 paper. Leaders need clear answers from data fast, yet classic analysis takes days. Their agent takes raw data in and hands back plain findings and advice within minutes.

A team of sub-agents splits the work: cleaning data, testing claims, checking results, and writing in plain words. Each writes its own code and weighs cause links. The lead agent forms testable claims first, checks their weight, then builds forecast models on what holds up. It also flags when more data is needed. The authors frame the tool as a bridge from proof to action.
arxiv-2508-18213:
Ayce Idil Aytekin and co-authors present a method to rebuild hand held objects in 3D from one photo in this 2025 paper. The hand itself gives strong clues about the object shape and pose. Past methods needed heavy post processing or gave poor geometry. Their approach builds the shape during a diffusion generation process.

An inpainted guess of the object look conditions the model. During generation, guidance steers the result toward a plausible hand object fit. Surface direction, depth, outline, and joint positions all supply checks. Distance field supervision plus contact rules stop the hand and object from overlapping. The output is a coherent, physically sensible reconstruction. Such tools could serve robotics, virtual reality, and motion capture from plain photos.
arxiv-2508-18413:
David Zoltowski, Skyler Wu, Xavier Gonzalez, Leo Kozachkov, and Scott Linderman find a way, in a 2025 preprint, to run a core sampling method in parallel. Markov chain Monte Carlo builds long chains of samples to model uncertainty. The method is a workhorse of Bayesian statistics. But each step depends on the last, so chain length means waiting time. Past speedups ran many chains side by side instead.

The team reframes the whole chain as the answer to a fixed-point problem. A parallel form of Newton's method can then solve for all steps at once. They adapt the trick to three standard samplers, including Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. In tests, hundreds of thousands of samples came from only tens of parallel rounds. Two new low-memory variants cut cost further. Some tasks sped up by more than tenfold over the step-by-step method.
arxiv-2508-18513:
Hospitals sit on data that could speed research, but sharing it risks exposing patients. Wei, Benson, and Capan study that trade-off directly, using records of adults hospitalized between 2013 and 2015 to predict sepsis at admission or during the stay. They first found the groups easiest to re-identify: older adults, frequent patients, and racial minorities, whose rare attribute mixes stand out. Those same groups also matter most for model accuracy.

Three anonymization methods were then scored on protection and on how much the learning models suffered. Simple k-anonymity protected weakly. Two model-based methods did better, and one of them, MO-OBAM, changed precision and recall by only about two percent while shielding identities. The authors give hospitals a practical ranking and stress that privacy tools must guard the most exposed patients without gutting the data's value.
arxiv-2508-18613:
Eichi Takaya and Ryusei Inamori present a pretraining method for medical image AI that feeds on free metadata: the scan type and the body region of each image. Expert labels are scarce in this field, so metadata that sits unused is a cheap training signal. Their 2025 method encodes both facts as a multi label target for each image.

A ResNet-18 encoder was pretrained on a 16,222 image slice of a large radiology set with a weighted contrastive loss. Fine tuning then won on two of three test tasks, knee MRI tears and thyroid nodule calls. A breast task put it second. Frozen encoder tests favored rivals, so the gain needs task tuning.
arxiv-2508-18713:
Noel Jonathan Jobu and Kenji Nishiwaki propose a dark sector model that also gives neutrinos their mass in a 2025 paper. A fourfold symmetry guards new particles, then softens to a twofold one after a field settles. The lightest heavy fermion left stable becomes the dark matter. Neutrino masses arise at one loop from the same setup.

Two fermion types and two inert Higgs partners with opposed charges make the structure work. A Higgs portal links dark matter to normal matter and sets the right relic amount. A natural partner aids joint annihilation in the early universe. Collider measures of Higgs self coupling could test the idea, the authors note.
arxiv-2508-18813:
Jingwei Hu, Dave Zachariah, Torbjörn Wigren, and Petre Stoica designed identification experiments in twenty twenty-five for systems that must stay in closed loop. Many plants cannot be tested open-loop for safety or continuity, so a probing signal is added to a working controller's input. The probe must teach as much as possible while keeping output wiggles inside set limits.

Working with ARMAX models, the authors first analyze when this setup can identify the system and when the limits can be met at all. They then derive a probing signal computable in closed form, recursively, as data arrives. Numerical experiments display the design's properties and effectiveness. The work gives control engineers a principled way to learn about a running system without disturbing it unduly.
arxiv-2508-18913:
Adam Katav, Yair Moshe, and Israel Cohen build a speaker checking framework for very noisy settings in a 2025 paper. Systems that confirm who is speaking often fail when noise is heavy. Cleaning the audio first can help the ear, yet the cleaning may erase the very traits that mark a speaker, a risk that grows with modern generative cleaners.

Their design extracts speaker traits from both the raw noisy audio and the cleaned audio, then joins them in a paired network. The setup is light and works with many existing checkers and cleaners without change. Tests show it beats past options under severe noise. The work suits voice security in call centers, cars, and other loud places.
arxiv-2508-19213:
When a neutrino strikes a nucleus, the debris tells the story, and simulators must predict every fragment. Joshua Isaacson and co-authors extend a leading event simulator, Achilles, to cover single pion production in full detail. The interaction vertex uses a state-of-the-art coupled-channels model with realistic descriptions of the struck nucleus. The escaping pion then rattles through the leftover nucleus in a simulated cascade.

Every piece of the chain uses consistent physics, from the first strike to pion absorption. The team validates against pion scattering data and against electron and neutrino measurements from major experiments. Neutrino oscillation programs live or die by such simulations: the signal is a handful of particles, and misunderstanding one pion can bend the inferred physics.
arxiv-2508-19613:
Chenzhi Liu and co-authors build ALSA, a way to guess how well a trained model will score on new, unlabeled data from a shifted world. Users rarely know that accuracy until labels arrive. Older guesses lean on the model's own confidence scores, which squash rich signals, or on data similarity, which is costly and narrow.

ALSA works in logit space, the raw scores before squashing. The team shows those scores bunch and spread in ways that track true accuracy. Learnable anchor points in that space, each with its own influence curve, read the pattern. Across vision, language, and graph tests, ALSA beat both confidence- and similarity-based rivals.
arxiv-2508-20013:
Lotte Gross and co-authors build a sorter for fashion products sold across many web shops in a 2025 paper. Each platform names categories its own way, and old taxonomies miss fine distinctions. Their data set holds 271,700 products from forty international fashion platforms.

The system fuses text, image, and joint vision-language features inside a layered classifier. A masking step keeps labels consistent down the category tree. Joint embeddings with late fusion scored best, near ninety-nine percent on the layered measure. A self-supervised cleanup pipeline then found new fine-grained categories, such as shoe subtypes, with clean clusters. Simpler fusion traveled better to unseen platforms, a trade the team weighs for live deployment.
arxiv-2508-20113:
Marcel Ausloos devised in 2025 new ways to rank women's cycling teams across multi-stage races, aiming to capture inequality inside a team. Standard ranking sums the times of a team's best finishers each stage, which hides how much a squad leans on one star. Ausloos adapts classic measures and builds two new ones.

One new gauge, the leadership gap, contrasts the official score with one demanding that riders finish the whole race. The other, competition temperature, borrows entropy to sense how spread the field is. He tests the set on the 2023 Giro d'Italia Donne, Tour de France Femmes, and Vuelta Femenina. The numbers separate squads by strategy and rider depth. Ausloos argues richer rankings help read team tactics.
arxiv-2508-20213:
Boaz Taitler and Omer Ben-Porat model how generative AI changes teamwork when a manager can use it to replace people, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Workers on a shared project can lean on the technology to do more, or to coast. A manager, meanwhile, picks who stays on the team, with the AI filling in for everyone else.

Their math yields sharp warnings. The AI can push workers to give no effort at all, even when the AI is nearly useless. Picking the best team turns out to be a hard computing problem, though the authors give an efficient method for near-linear cases. They also show that dropping a low-value worker can start a cascade that tanks the whole project. Computer trials back up the theory.
arxiv-2508-20313:
López-Valdivia and co-authors measure the chemistry of more than five hundred newborn stars in Orion, in a 2025 paper. Young stars' temperatures, gravities, and element mixes reveal how nurseries seed planets with raw material. Infrared spectra from the APOGEE-2 survey let the team see through the dust that hides these cradles.

Temperatures were set for 548 young stars spanning the Orion complex, from the famous nebula to its scattered associations. For 340 slow spinners, abundances of carbon, magnesium, silicon, potassium, titanium, and iron followed from nineteen atomic lines and model atmospheres. A uniform chemical census across one great nursery anchors studies of how composition varies with birthplace.
arxiv-2508-20413:
Benjamin Coueraud, Vikram Sunkara, and Christof Schutte add a nonlinear conformal rule to the decoder of an autoencoder, to gauge local stretch and compute scalar curvature of the learned shape. Shrinking data to its main factors is key to many tasks. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

An encoder maps data to a low size space, and a decoder maps back. The new rule lets the decoder vary locally and yields a field, the conformal factor, that counts local stretch. The same rule lets the team compute scalar curvature of the learned surface. Tests on a spiral data set and a face photo set show how to read both gauges from the network.
arxiv-2508-20813:
Tao Luo and co-authors teach a foundation vision model to spot tooth decay by mimicking how dentists actually look, in a 2025 paper. Panoramic X-rays are the standard first screen for cavities. Lesions vary in shape and hide in subtle contrast changes. Single-view detectors miss too many of them.

Dentists combine a whole-image scan with tooth-by-tooth inspection. The network copies that dual view. Automated tooth detection crops the local views. Two foundation models pretrain separately on each view, then train together. Screening programs could catch decay before it spreads. Dental AI gains a workflow borrowed from the clinic. The design generalizes to other two-scale inspections.
arxiv-2508-21413:
Yu Zhao and co-authors present a 2025 recheck of six gamma ray bursts once flagged as bent by gravity. A lens between us and a burst should split its flash into twin pulses with the same shape and hue. Claims of such twins carry weight for cosmology, so false ones must be weeded out.

The team ran a full battery on each pair: curve match tests, photon count hardness, burst span, time lag, pulse shape fits, and spectra by time slice and whole. Their rule is strict: one firm clash between the pulses kills the lens claim. All six bursts failed at least one test. The authors conclude none of the six fits a lensing read.
arxiv-2508-21513:
Geri Skenderi gives a 2025 geometric account of why graph based solvers for logic puzzles stall on hard cases. Such solvers turn a logic formula into a graph and learn to judge it. Their scores drop sharply as formulas grow tighter, and no one had a clean reason why.

Skenderi shows that graphs from random formulas are bent in a way that pinches long range links. The pinch worsens as cases harden, and learned messages get squashed as they cross it. Across test sets, the bend strongly tracked both hardness and error. The paper links the flaw to solver design and sketches fixes.
arxiv-2508-21713:
Sonagnon Julien Owolabi, Ibrahim Nonkane, and Joel Tossa write a 2025 note on a tool from algebra called the resultant. The resultant tests when a set of equations shares a common solution. Their focus is on equation sets that stay the same under swapping variables in two groups.

The authors prove a split formula for the resultant of such symmetric systems. The big resultant breaks into smaller ones that are cheaper to compute. They then apply the split to the discriminant of a symmetric polynomial. That quantity also breaks into smaller pieces. The result makes hard symbolic computations more feasible for systems with this kind of symmetry.
arxiv-2509-00013:
Rakshit Poudel, Daya Nidhi Chhatkuli, and Madhav Kafle propose a fix for the center of a Schwarzschild black hole in Anti-de-Sitter space in 2025. In the standard account, the fully stretched form of that spacetime holds a singularity, a point where the math breaks down. The authors propose swapping that point for a tiny de-Sitter patch, a small region of outward-pushing space that does not last.

The swap counts as a deep change to the entangled sector, or to its dual paired state. The authors speculate that the core could shift late-time signals, tame runaway values, and show in how holographic complexity, a gauge of state depth, grows. They also discuss a link to the Page curve puzzle of evaporating holes. The idea is a proposal, not a proven result.
arxiv-2509-00213:
Farhan Fuad Abir, Abigail Elliott Daly, Kyle Anderman, Tolga Ozmen, and Laura J. Brattain build a multimodal model in 2025 to classify phyllodes tumors of the breast. These rare fibroepithelial lesions look much like benign fibroadenomas on scans, so they are hard to classify before surgery. That overlap leads to needless surgical removals.

Their dual-branch network fuses breast ultrasound images with structured clinical data from eighty-one confirmed subjects. Class-aware sampling and subject-stratified cross-validation guard against imbalance and leakage. The fused model beats single-mode baselines at telling benign tumors from borderline or malignant ones. Among six image encoders, ConvNeXt and ResNet18 lead in the fused setting. Sharper pre-surgery calls could spare patients needless operations.
arxiv-2509-00713:
Junghoon Justin Park leads five authors in total, with Huan-Hsin Tseng, Shinjae Yoo, Samuel Yen-Chi Chen, and Jiook Cha, in applying quantum reinforcement learning to Super Mario Bros. Quantum learners promise compact models with vast state spaces, but current noisy quantum hardware limits qubits and adds noise.

Their multi-chip ensemble splits high-dimensional game observations across several small Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks, each on its own circuit, then classically aggregates outputs inside a Double Deep Q-Network. The modular design reduces information loss from dimensionality reduction and remains implementable on near-term hardware. It achieves better performance and learning stability than classical baselines and single-chip quantum models, opening complex environments to quantum agents.
arxiv-2509-00813:
Gyehun Go leads six authors in total, with Satbyul Han, Ahyeon Choi, Eunjin Choi, Juhan Nam, and Jeong Mi Park, in introducing AImoclips, a benchmark for emotion conveyance in text-to-music generation. Systems now create expressive music from natural language prompts, but how faithfully they convey intended emotions has been little studied.

The team selected twelve emotion intents across four quadrants of the valence-arousal space, which maps feelings by pleasantness and intensity, and used six leading systems to generate over one thousand clips. One hundred eleven participants rated perceived valence and arousal on a nine-point scale. Commercial systems skew more pleasant than intended, open-source systems the opposite, high-arousal emotions convey best, and all systems bias toward neutrality.
arxiv-2509-00913:
Disha Shetty leads a team of eight authors on quantum linear solvers for network problems. Network-based linear systems arise naturally from graphs. They connect to many real-world applications. A quantum solver's advantage depends on two scalings. They are the condition number and the sparsity of the graph matrices.

The team analyzes fifty graph families for advantage prospects. Only twenty-one show prospects for exponential advantage with the HHL algorithm. That comparison is against an efficient classical solver. Some families gain prospects with improved algorithms like Childs-Kothari-Somma. The team also introduces a unified graph superfamily. It contains infinitely many good graph families within it. They conjecture rules for judging a family's prospects by eye.
arxiv-2509-01113:
Soft robot hands bend as they grip, which helps them handle people and fragile objects but makes control tricky. Haiyun Zhang, with four co-authors, offers a simpler way to model a soft hand driven by air pressure. Their method treats each bending part as if it were a stiff body on a hinge, a stand-in called a pseudo rigid body model.

To set the model's values, the team uses the logarithmic decrement method, which infers traits from how motion fades over time. On a test hand, their controller tracked position and force far better than a standard PID controller, with much smaller peak errors. The result supports faster, more accurate control of soft hands in real time.
arxiv-2509-01213:
When a model learns new tasks one after another, it often forgets what it knew before, a failure called catastrophic forgetting. Ege Sualp and Mina Rezaei test whether growing a model, training a larger one from a smaller one's progress, can soften that loss. Growth by stacking transformer layers was known to speed training, but its effect on forgetting was unclear.

The pair compared a stacked large model with one trained without growth, across fine-tuning tasks in domain knowledge, reasoning, reading, and bias. Both models gained domain knowledge, yet their retention of reasoning and reading skills diverged in telling ways. Sualp and Rezaei present the study as evidence on when model growth helps continual learning, a key need for language models that must keep learning.
arxiv-2509-01913:
M A Garcia-Marquez, H M Moya-Cessa, I Ramos-Prieto, and F Soto-Eguibar solve a continuity equation in the Madelung-Bohm view of quantum motion. That view rewrites quantum flow in terms of a density and a phase, like a fluid. They assume the phase splits into a space part times a time part plus a time shift. Operator methods then reshape the wave amplitude into a handy form for any starting state.

The reshaped amplitude acts like a squeezed version of the position operator applied to the start. Two cases show the power of the form. In one, no outside potential acts, so motion stems only from the Bohm potential. In the other, the form mimics light spread in waveguide arrays, where even complex values still obey the core equation.
arxiv-2509-02513:
Tuval Danenberg wrote a 2025 solo political science theory paper on how polarisation and issue alignment can grow together under rational learning. Polarisation means views split toward opposite extremes; alignment means one person's views across issues become more consistent with each other.

The model uses Bayesian agents, ideal learners who update beliefs from public signals by the rules of probability. Danenberg characterises which public signals can keep agents polarised on every issue dimension at once. Evidence of alignment itself can push Bayesian agents apart. However, stronger forms of polarisation, beyond marginal beliefs, clash with Bayesian rationality. Whether belief splits become position splits also depends on whether issues can be separated from each other in agents' thinking.
arxiv-2509-02613:
Faruk Alpay and Taylan Alpay present a 2025 mathematical paper building a formal model of an evolving internal state, inspired by the flow of thought. Their state space is a topological space, possibly an infinite-dimensional Banach space, and each trajectory is a continuous path through it.

Ideas from Brouwer's intuitionism treat the sequence of states as a choice sequence, freely unfolding rather than pre-set. The authors prove that evolutions exist and are unique under continuity conditions, using a fixed-point argument. They also show some sets of states cannot carry a classical measure at all. A Tarski-style truth definition for statements about states completes the logical side. The work deliberately avoids category theory while blending classical analysis with intuitionistic views.
arxiv-2509-02813:
Tessa T. Frincke and nine co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper reporting early brightness measurements of 3I/ATLAS, only the third known object visiting the solar system from interstellar space. Observations came from the SOAR telescope in Chile on three July 2025 nights, days after discovery.

Twenty-eight photometric points in a red filter feed the object's growing light curve. No obvious long-term brightness trend appeared. Two apparent brightening events on later nights were tested with contamination, stacking, and aperture experiments. Both turned out to be artefacts of poor seeing and nearby field stars. Reported mean magnitudes for each night give clean reference values. Cometary activity in matching images hides any rotation signal, and activity stayed near discovery levels with no outburst.
arxiv-2509-03313:
Miguel Molina-Hernandez and 3 co-authors extended a radiation chemistry simulator in 2025 to handle FLASH dose rates. FLASH radiotherapy delivers dose at ultra-high rates and seems to spare healthy tissue, an effect researchers are racing to explain. One clue is that radical-radical reactions, where reactive fragments react with each other, speed up under FLASH conditions.

The upgraded GPU-based Monte Carlo tool, gMicroMC, now simulates many pulses in sequence. Water exposed to proton pulses showed a clear threshold in average dose rate. Below it, radicals drained fully between pulses and product yields stayed flat. Above it, reactive species piled up across pulses, raising reaction rates and hydrogen peroxide yields. The buildup between pulses, the authors argue, matters more than interactions between separate particle tracks.
arxiv-2509-03813:
Parth Ashokbhai Shiroya and six co-authors devote a 2025 research paper to classifying indoor surfaces with LiDAR so wireless networks can predict how signals scatter. Millimetre-wave and sub-terahertz links depend on reflections because their signals block so easily. Whether a surface reflects cleanly or scatters diffusely depends on material and roughness.

Their framework sorts surfaces by how specular their reflections are, taking optical reflectivity as a stand-in for electromagnetic behaviour. Over seventy-eight thousand LiDAR points from fifteen materials were divided into patches, letting the system classify from partial views. Patch features capture geometry and intensity, among them elevation angle and intensity ratios. Random forest, gradient boosting, and neural network classifiers are trained and compared. Ensemble tree models give the best balance of accuracy and robustness, confirming LiDAR features capture roughness-driven scattering. Outputs feed scatter-aware maps and digital twins for beam management.
arxiv-2509-03913:
Jiajun Yuan and five co-authors survey STSR, a framework for speech super-resolution, rebuilding wideband speech from low-resolution input in a 2025 research paper. Faithful rebuilding must keep harmonic coherence, the pattern of overtones, and local transients, the sharp attacks that make speech crisp. Diffusion models achieve fidelity but cost too much for many deployments.

Efficient time-domain designs are cheaper, yet they lack frequency views for spectral structure and harmonic alignment. STSR instead works end to end in the MDCT domain, a compressed frequency form of the signal. Its attention mechanism uses layered windowing to gather non-local context, keeping harmonic structure consistent up to forty-eight kilohertz. A sparse-aware regularisation counters the suppression of transient parts that compressed forms cause. Across tests, STSR beats leading baselines in perceived fidelity and in zero-shot reach to unseen conditions, while staying fast enough for real-time restoration.
arxiv-2509-04013:
Testing whether standard benchmark scores for large language models survive simple rewording is what Riccardo Lunardi and three co-authors do in a 2025 research paper. Benchmarks like MMLU present questions in one fixed, standardised wording. Real users phrase the same questions many ways, so a model that only handles the canonical wording is less capable than its score suggests.

The authors generate paraphrases of every question across six common benchmarks, then measure how effectiveness changes for thirty-four leading language models . Model rankings stay relatively stable under paraphrase: the best models mostly remain the best. Absolute scores, however, change and decline significantly, showing the models struggle with linguistic variability. That drop undermines trust in benchmark-based evaluation, since high scores may not reflect robustness to real-world input variation. The authors emphasise robustness-aware benchmarks, designed to measure performance across rewordings, as a better guide to practical deployment.
arxiv-2509-04113:
Sudheer Mishra and one co-author, E Natarajan, develop a numerical method for slow fluid flow problems in a 2025 thesis-style paper. The target is the generalized Oseen equation, which models fluids pushed along by a steady current. Their method is called a virtual element method, since it works on many-sided mesh cells without fixing each cell's inner shape. Equal-order approximations for speed and pressure can turn unstable, so the authors add stabilizing terms built from local projections.

Proofs show the scheme stays stable in a standard energy measure. The same setup also covers the Brinkman and Stokes equations with no extra conditions. Error bounds stay even as diffusion, meaning spreading, gets very small. Computer tests in slow and fast flow regimes back the theory.
arxiv-2509-05013:
Liquidity on a decentralised exchange forms a surface that moves over time and price ticks. Jimmy Risk, lead author with two co-authors, study those dynamics for Uniswap v3 in a 2025 paper. They model liquidity as a time-tick surface and analyse three pools over several sample periods.

Functional principal component analysis and dynamic factor methods reduce the surface to a few interpretable components. For the tightest fee pools, the leading components explain most variation and stay stable, aligning with simple polynomial shapes. Their factor coefficients follow persistent time series patterns with heavy tails and changing volatility, giving a compact statistical picture of automated market maker liquidity.
arxiv-2509-05213:
Federated training of large neural networks struggles when each client's data differ and communication is expensive. Jiaojiao Zhang, lead author with three co-authors, propose FedSub, a subspace algorithm for that setting, in a 2025 machine learning paper. Client drift from heterogeneous data is the other main obstacle they target.

Each client updates only inside a low-dimensional subspace, cutting communication, computation, and memory costs. Low-dimensional dual variables counteract client drift. Their convergence analysis shows how step size and projection choices affect the rate. Experiments demonstrate the efficiency of the design for large-scale federated learning.
arxiv-2509-05513:
First-person video of human hands at work becomes training data for dexterous robots in OpenEgo, a dataset introduced by Ahad Jawaid and Yu Xiang in a 2025 paper. Egocentric video scales well for imitation learning, but older collections lack either precise action labels or detailed hand tracking.

OpenEgo unifies six public datasets into more than a thousand hours of footage. It covers hundreds of manipulation tasks across hundreds of environments. Hand poses are converted to one standard layout, and actions are described with time stamps aligned to the actor's intent. To validate the resource, the authors train language-guided policies that predict hand trajectories. All materials are slated for public release.
arxiv-2509-05613:
Collisions of light atomic nuclei may or may not create droplets of quark-gluon plasma, Lucas Constantin and three co-authors predict in a 2025 nuclear physics paper ahead of a 2025 collider run. Signs of collective behaviour have appeared even in proton collisions, blurring where this exotic matter begins to form.

The team simulates oxygen-oxygen and neon-neon collisions at the Large Hadron Collider with three models. One couples fluid dynamics for the plasma stage to a hadronic transport stage, one runs the transport alone, and one serves as a no-collectivity baseline. Comparing the evolutions on equal footing shows what each ingredient contributes. The predictions target the light-ion run held in July 2025.
arxiv-2509-05913:
Spotting muscle and joint injury risk in athletes from video and body tracking is the aim of a 2025 paper led by Md. Abdur Rahman with five co-authors. Most current tools need controlled settings and a single data type, so they falter at real games and training. The authors combine images with skeletal coordinates in one model, called ViSK-GAT.

Their dataset, MusDis-Sports, pairs pictures with joint coordinates and labels each sample into eight risk grades from the Rapid Entire Body Assessment system. Two new modules refine features within each data type, then align image and skeleton information before judging. Scores passed ninety-three percent across key measures, beating strong standard backbones. The authors pitch the system as a route to earlier, AI-guided interventions in sport.
arxiv-2509-06013: Kalyan Banerjee proves a negative result about cubic threefolds in a 2025 paper: a very general cubic threefold admits no universal codimension-two cycle. Cubic threefolds are three-dimensional shapes cut out by a degree-three equation, a classic testing ground in algebraic geometry. A universal cycle would parametrize all codimension-two cycles at once. Banerjee shows no such object exists for the very general member of the family. He concludes that the threefold is stably irrational, meaning it cannot be made rational even after standard stabilizing tricks.
arxiv-2509-06213:
How would anyone certify that an AI system follows rules it must discover itself? Christo Mathew and six co-authors explore that metrology problem in a 2025 paper. Their testbed is the Game Of Hidden Rules, a puzzle where an agent must infer secret rules to clear a board by sorting pieces into buckets. Only partial observations are available, so rule inference and policy learning must proceed together.

The team trains a transformer-based advantage actor-critic agent under two state representations, one feature-centric and one object-centric. Experiments vary the rules and trial lists to measure transfer and the effect of representation on learning speed. The work frames hidden-rule games as measuring instruments for artificial intelligence itself.
arxiv-2509-06413:
Judging the quality of super-resolved images made by modern generative methods is the challenge summarized in a 2025 paper led by Yixiao Li with thirty co-authors. The VQualA challenge at ICCV 2025 built a dataset of images upscaled by GAN and diffusion methods, whose artifacts differ from classic super-resolution. One hundred eight participants registered; four teams submitted valid final solutions.

The paper describes the dataset, the competing methods, and the results, with the best submissions reaching state-of-the-art quality prediction on the benchmark. The project is public, and the authors aim to standardize how perceptually convincing, but possibly invented, detail in generated super-resolution gets scored.
arxiv-2509-06613:
Electron pairs from heavy-ion collisions are reported by Florian Eisenhut in a solo 2025 conference paper on the ALICE experiment. Dielectrons matter because they escape the hot, dense matter made in such collisions without being reshaped by later hadronic interactions. They offer a direct look at the earliest moments.

Results cover proton-proton collisions taken with the upgraded ALICE detector, plus the status of the lead-lead analysis at a higher collision energy. Eisenhut explains how prompt and non-prompt dielectron spectra are extracted across a wide mass range. The discussion also covers what these measurements could reveal about the Drell-Yan process in a regime where simple theory struggles, and about the first signs of thermal radiation from the hot matter. The paper is a progress report rather than a final measurement.
arxiv-2509-06813:
Wind turbine maintenance logs, written as messy free text, are labeled by language models in a benchmark by Max Malyi and three co-authors in a 2025 energy informatics paper. Cheaper wind power depends on good operations and maintenance data, but unstructured logs resist automated analysis. The authors build a reproducible, open-source benchmarking framework for the classification task.

A diverse suite of proprietary and open-source models is evaluated for reliability, efficiency, and calibration, meaning whether stated confidence matches accuracy. A clear hierarchy emerges, with top models aligning well with a benchmark standard and showing trustworthy confidence. All models agree more when the task is naming a component, an objective call, than when it is interpreting what maintenance action was taken. Since no model is perfectly accurate, the authors recommend a human-in-the-loop setup, with models accelerating and standardizing labeling for human experts.
arxiv-2509-06913:
Massive galaxies that stopped forming stars surprisingly early are counted by Struan D. Stevenson and twenty-four co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. The sample holds two hundred twenty-five quiescent galaxies seen when the universe was young, drawn from the PRIMER and JADES surveys. Only areas with optical coverage in three Hubble filters were used, a restriction the authors show matters for clean, complete samples.

Contamination was checked with JWST spectroscopy, Chandra X-ray imaging, and ALMA observations, coming out modest. Dropping the Hubble data would add star-forming interlopers and lose a fifth of the candidates. Number densities at early times are three times pre-JWST estimates, and most simulations now match the counts at moderate redshift but fall increasingly short earlier. About half the most distant subset shows faint active nuclei, matching recent results.
arxiv-2509-07013:
Sima Najafzadehkhoei and 3 co-authors give a fast way to fit epidemic models to data in a 2025 paper. Agent-based models, which track each person in a fake outbreak, are a key tool for studying how disease spreads. But fitting them to real data takes huge computer time, which hurts when health teams must act fast.

Their method, DeepIMC, learns the link in reverse: from a curve of cases over time, it reads off the traits of the outbreak that made it. A neural net is trained on thousands of fake outbreaks made by agent models, so at use time it can fit fresh data at once, with no new sims. In tests with five thousand varied outbreaks, the method beat a standard Bayesian route on how well it got the true traits back, and its doubt ranges were sharp and well set.
arxiv-2509-07113:
Junfeng Xu and 2 co-authors wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on functions of several complex variables. Complex variables are numbers with real and imaginary parts, and here functions can depend on many of them at once. One tool in the field is the logarithmic derivative, which measures how fast a function grows compared with its own size.

The authors first bound the logarithmic partial derivative for a broad class of such functions, extending older one-variable results to higher dimensions. Next they carry Wiman-Valiron theory, a method for studying growth near a peak point, into several variables. Last, they study how fast solutions of a class of partial differential equations can grow. Each result widens tools that were once limited to a single complex variable.
arxiv-2509-07213:
Finding the exact outline of a breast tumor in ultrasound images is hard when lesions are small or faint. Raja Mallina and 1 co-author present XBusNet in a 2025 research paper. XBusNet is a model that segments, or outlines, lesions by combining images with clinical text. One branch reads the whole image with help from prompts about lesion size and location. A second branch sharpens the edges.

The text prompts describe shape, margin, and standard reporting terms, and the system builds them automatically from stored metadata. No manual clicks are needed. Tested with five-fold cross-validation on a breast lesion dataset, XBusNet beat six strong baselines on standard overlap scores. Small lesions improved the most. Separate tests confirm that global context, edge modeling, and text guidance each add value.
arxiv-2509-07413:
Yuhan Pang and 7 co-authors present a control scheme in 2025 for robots that collect luggage trolleys in airports and warehouses. In their system, mobile manipulators form leader-follower groups, and each base must dock precisely to line trolleys into neat queues. Docking is hard because precision demands are high, surroundings disturb the robot, and the base cannot move sideways.

The scheme, DA-VPC, uses active infrared markers that stay visible across lighting conditions for robust visual guidance. It models the robot's motion limits and camera visibility inside a predictive controller solved by optimization. An extended state observer, a module that estimates hidden disturbances, counteracts pushes while the robot shoves trolleys. Experiments in varied settings show the system docks accurately and stably, supporting fully autonomous trolley fleets.
arxiv-2509-07513:
Charmonium particles, made of a charm quark and its antiquark, act as thermometers inside the hottest matter made on Earth. Ingrid McKibben Lofnes reports recent measurements in 2025 conference proceedings from Quark Matter 2025. Heavy quarks form early in a collision. Charmonia therefore trace the whole life of the quark-gluon plasma. That plasma is the hot, dense medium created in heavy-ion collisions at the Large Hadron Collider.

The proceedings present published results from the ALICE experiment on lead-lead collisions. They cover prompt charmonia and those born later from beauty hadron decays, which reveal how beauty quarks lose energy. A first preliminary result compares two charmonium states at forward rapidity in newer data. Color screening melts some charmonia in the plasma, while recombination builds others back. Comparing the measurements with theory helps physicists tell those competing stories apart.
arxiv-2509-07613:
Fangqi Cheng's 2025 paper, with 2 co-authors, adapts medical vision-language models to diagnose Alzheimer's disease with little data. Medical models often underuse patient metadata, lack clinical knowledge, and are trained on flat 2D image-text pairs at great cost, leaving 3D imaging poorly served. The pipeline instead fine-tunes a 3D CT-based model for 3D MRI, the scan type central to Alzheimer's workups.

Two innovations carry the method. Structured metadata are converted into synthetic reports, enriching the text side so images and words align better. An auxiliary token is trained to predict the MMSE score, a standard clinical measure of cognition tied to disease severity, adding supervision. Lightweight prompt tuning adjusts only small parts of both encoders. The approach aims at accurate diagnosis without the vast datasets medical AI usually demands.
arxiv-2509-08213:
Error bars compress every kind of doubt into one tidy whisker on a chart, and two visualization researchers find that suspicious. Michael Correll and Lane Harrison write a provocation on uncertainty visualization in a 2025 research paper. They argue the error bar rests on a large hidden metaphysics of probability. Other traditions, including religious ones, carve up uncertainty very differently.

Drawing on religious examples, the authors present alternative views of what uncertainty is. Some doubts concern fate, providence, or unknowable will rather than sampling noise. The point is to widen what designers think is worth visualizing. It is also to ask who the audience for an uncertainty display really is. The piece is deliberately provocative. It invites the field to match visual forms to the actual kinds of not-knowing people face.
arxiv-2509-08313:
Thermal glow from the telescope itself is traced and corrected in a 2025 instrumentation paper by Jayke S. Nguyen and 4 co-authors. Mid-infrared imaging from the ground can find older, colder exoplanets that other methods miss. The catch is background: the atmosphere and telescope radiate heat, laying a slowly varying, uneven glow under every image taken with the Keck II telescope.

Understanding where that background originates, in instrument design and in atmospheric conditions, allows its systematic patterns to be modelled and removed. Better photometry in the mid-infrared tightens constraints on exoplanet atmospheres. Ground telescopes cannot escape their own warmth, so characterising the glow precisely is what makes cold-planet imaging from Earth credible at all.
arxiv-2509-08613:
Ke Ma and 4 co-authors improve a model of silicon absorption in the Lyman-alpha forest in a 2025 paper. The forest is a set of absorption lines in distant quasar light, used to study gas between galaxies. Silicon absorption adds a correlated signal that can distort measurements.

Using the Sherwood-Relics simulations, the team finds extra small-scale power that earlier work missed. Their new fitting function allows different line shapes and a changing ratio of silicon to hydrogen absorption. It matches simulated data across a wide range of redshifts. The model matters for future precise tests of dark matter and cosmic gas.
arxiv-2509-08713:
Ziming Luo and 2 co-authors warn about hidden pitfalls in AI scientist systems in a 2025 paper. Such systems run the full research loop, from ideas and experiments to writing papers. Their inner workflow has rarely been examined closely.

Four failure modes are named: poor benchmark choice, data leakage, metric misuse, and post-hoc selection bias. Controlled experiments isolate each mode in two open source systems. Several failures appear, at varied severity, and are easy to miss in a final paper. Access to trace logs and code makes detection far easier. The authors urge venues to require those artifacts with submissions.
arxiv-2509-08913:
Sin-Yu Huang and 1 co-author propose user-oriented image semantic coding in a 2025 paper. Semantic coding sends the meaning of an image rather than every pixel. Users often care about a specific region tied to their intent, which older systems ignore.

A text query from the user guides which features are extracted and sent. The receiver rebuilds an image from those features alone. Large vision-language models, CLIP and LLaVA, support generalization and a loss that scores match to user intent. In zero-shot tests on unseen objects, the method beats prior query aware coding on answer match rate.
arxiv-2509-09413:
Microbes that thrive together in one pond may ignore each other in the next, so a single universal interaction network misleads. Daniel Agyapong and 4 co-authors build an algorithm that respects place and time in a 2025 research paper. Standard co-occurrence methods pool samples from many environments into one snapshot. The team instead studies how microbial associations change across locations and time points.

Their evaluation framework trains and tests models both within one environment and across combined environments. Their proposed algorithm, fuser, keeps each sample group's own signals while sharing information across environments during training. It produces a distinct predictive network per environment rather than one averaged network. Within single environments it matched strong baselines. Across environments it cut test error notably. Ecologists get a tool for asking how communities rewire as conditions change, not just who coexists on average.
arxiv-2509-09813:
Amira Abbas and 5 co-authors design methods to learn sparse quantum Hamiltonians in 2025, judging success by measures a physicist would actually care about. Earlier work often lacked matching lower bounds and graded errors with yardsticks chosen for mathematical ease. Their Hamiltonians involve few Pauli terms, and access comes through watching the system evolve over time.

Two distances anchor the study: one based on telling systems apart through bounded-time motion, another through thermal states at bounded temperatures. Sparse systems with bounded strength can be learned in both settings with modest experiment counts. Fresh lower bounds for the time-based distance nearly match the method's cost, certifying it as close to optimal. Along the way every Pauli coefficient of such a Hamiltonian can be recovered.
arxiv-2509-10013:
Ting-Jung Kuo and 2 co-authors study dome-like metrics on a flat torus that blow up at three marked cone points in a 2025 geometry paper. The cone at the origin opens with angle six pi, while a mirrored pair of points carry angle four pi each, and the whole metric is required to be even. The question is when such a family of spherical metrics can exist at all, and the answer turns out to be written in the torus's own shape.

Existence holds exactly when the torus's Green function possesses a matching pair of nontrivial critical points, and then the cone location and monodromy data are forced. A transformation links this family to a simpler one-cone case. For rhombic tori the authors add a rigidity statement, closing off extra freedom.
arxiv-2509-10113:
Junfeng Xu and 3 co-authors hunt for meromorphic solutions of a special algebraic differential equation in a 2025 complex analysis paper. The equation mixes a polynomial in a function and its derivatives with terms built from a linear combination of those derivatives and a product involving two distinct target values. Questions of which functions can satisfy such a relation sit inside value distribution theory, where normal family ideas often decide what shapes are even possible.

Borrowing exactly that idea, the authors pin down the candidate solutions of their equation. The outcome sharpens and widens earlier findings by Li and Yang and by Xu and collaborators, covering a far larger family in one sweep. For specialists, the paper is a consolidation: scattered special cases collapse into a single broader statement about admissible solutions.
arxiv-2509-10213:
Ming Zhou and six co-authors published this computer security paper in 2025. Their subject is how to fix software flaws on small embedded devices, such as medical equipment, without shutting them down. Such devices have little spare memory or processing power, and they come in many different hardware designs, which makes live patching hard.

The team builds a framework called StackPatch, which prepares patches by rebuilding the saved layout of a running program's stack. It uses exception handling built into common processors to redirect program flow, so the same approach adapts across chip families. In tests on ARM, RISC-V, and Xtensa devices, the group fixed over a hundred known flaws in real-time operating systems, each fix finishing in under 260 processor cycles.
arxiv-2509-10413:
Guojun Tang and seven co-authors map the world of Bitcoin cross-chain bridges in this 2025 survey. Bitcoin has limited scripting. It also lacks built-in ways to work with other chains. That walls it off from wider blockchain finance and multi-chain applications. Bridges are the workaround. The authors sort them into three families. Some simply swap tokens. Others issue pegged assets. A third group passes arbitrary messages between chains.

Each family is graded on several points. Trust assumptions come first. Speed, capital efficiency, and fit with decentralized finance follow. Newer ideas get attention as well. BitVM and recursive sidechains could make interoperation safer and programmable. The survey then turns to the Artificial Intelligence of Things. It sketches bridge uses in energy trading between devices. Health data integration and supply chain automation appear too. The taxonomy is offered as a design foundation.
arxiv-2509-10513:
Mixture-of-experts models switch on only a few specialized sub-networks per input, and Sugyeong Eo with three co-authors improve how those experts specialize in this 2025 study of instruction tuning. Diverse instructions strain the usual routing, where each token is sent to experts with little sense of the whole request.

Their Mixture-of-Clustered-Experts routes in two stages. First, features of the whole sequence steer the input toward an expert group matched to its knowledge needs. Then, inside that group, individual tokens pick their top experts as usual. The design encourages groups to become genuine specialists while keeping fine-grained token routing. Across a broad set of benchmarks, the clustered design consistently beat strong baselines and generalized better, and the authors' analysis points to the routing structure itself as the source of the gains.
arxiv-2509-10713:
Christian Escarrega and 4 co-authors built a low-cost energy manager as an undergraduate design project, reported in this 2025 paper.
