Answering well needs multi step reasoning about ingredients, dishes, and how items on a plate relate, not a guess followed by an explanation.

The team builds reasoning chains onto an existing Indian food question answering set, with minimal human intervention. It then fine tunes smaller language and vision language models on those auto validated chains. Training continues with reinforcement learning on more data. Adding the chains raised accuracy by an average of ten percentage points over the baseline. The paper also analyzes where the chains help, giving a detailed account for the Indian food task.
arxiv-2511-01613:
Tomáš Krsička and Tibor Kubík work on classifying three-dimensional anatomical shapes, a task held back by the complexity of mesh data and the lack of standard benchmarks. They approach it with self-supervised learning: teach a model the structure of organs from unlabeled surface meshes, then use what it learned for classification.

Their key piece is Precomputed Structural Pooling. It is a fixed, non-learned way to coarsen a mesh. It groups nodes by geometric proximity and stays reversible. It avoids the sparsity problems of selection-based pooling and the slowness of edge contraction. Built into a graph autoencoder, it improved reconstruction fidelity and class separation. To make results comparable, the authors also release MedShapeNet19, a curated benchmark of 19 anatomical classes with standard splits.
arxiv-2511-01713:
Rodrigo Avalos, Eric Ling, and Annachiara Piubello revisit a pillar of mathematical relativity: the positive energy theorems, which say an isolated gravitating system cannot have negative total energy. The classic proofs assume the system fades into flat Minkowski space at infinity, but real astrophysical objects sit inside an expanding universe, not empty stillness.

The authors take de Sitter space as the background. It is written in flat expanding coordinates. Each time slice there is a flat space, stretched with a special, umbilic second fundamental form. Because de Sitter space has a cosmological horizon, no global energy exists, so they define a quasi-local energy by adapting the Liu-Yau energy to this setting. They then establish that the energy is positive for bounded values. The values lie in the regime they analyze. This extends the spirit of the classical theorems to an expanding cosmos.
arxiv-2511-01813:
Hao Zhu and Joschka Boedecker make a class of hard optimization problems easier to specify. Biconvex problems, where the objective is convex in each of two blocks of variables separately but not jointly, appear across machine learning, signal processing, and control. Solving them usually means hand-building an alternating solver that optimizes one block at a time, tedious and error-prone work.

Their framework, disciplined biconvex programming, extends the rule-based style of disciplined convex programming. State the problem following a small set of syntax rules. The system then splits it into convex subproblems. It generates a customized alternating convex search solver automatically. Users can experiment with formulations without optimization expertise. The framework ships as the open-source Python package dbcp, built on the widely used CVXPY modeling language.
arxiv-2511-02113:
Hai-Dang Kieu, Min Xu, Thanh Trung Huynh, and Dung Le improve recommender systems that use both product images and text. Many existing methods extract coarse visual features and merge them with text in naive ways, producing redundant or mismatched item descriptions. Their framework, VIRAL, starts from an information theory view: good fusion should keep what each source uniquely says, what they share, and avoid double-counting.

One module uses a vision-language model to write fine-grained, title-guided descriptions of product images. A second module, inspired by partial information decomposition, separates and recombines the complementary signals. On three Amazon datasets VIRAL consistently beat strong multimodal baselines, and the authors report it substantially raised how much the visual features contribute to recommendations.
arxiv-2511-02213:
Kangyu Qiao, Shaolei Zhang, and Yang Feng make large language models cheaper to run by removing whole layers, but with a twist: which layers get removed depends on the input. Fixed pruning masks serve every request identically, which wastes capacity on easy inputs and starves hard ones. Their method, IG-Pruning, selects a layer mask dynamically at inference time.

Candidate masks are first discovered offline by clustering inputs by meaning and optimising which blocks to cut. At run time the system picks a suitable mask without expensive extra training. In experiments the approach consistently beat leading static depth-pruning methods. The authors pitch it at deployment settings where computing resources are tight and input difficulty varies from request to request.
arxiv-2511-02713:
Release notes tell users what changed in software, but writing them by hand is slow and error prone. Qianru Meng, Zhaochun Ren, and Joost Visser built ReleaseEval, a 2025 benchmark for testing language models at that task. It gathers nearly ninety-five thousand release notes from over three thousand code projects in six programming languages, all openly licensed.

The benchmark sets three tasks with growing detail: from commit messages alone, from commit trees, and from full code diffs. Large language models beat older baselines at all three, with the biggest gains when given the tree structure. They still struggled to sum up long diffs, though. The gap shows where automated release writing needs the most work next.
arxiv-2511-03113:
Jiameng Chen and six colleagues design antibodies with a generative model that obeys physics while it draws. Antibody design tools often produce shapes that look plausible but break physical rules, and scarce data hurts their reach. Their 2025 model, FP-AbDiff, is the first antibody generator to enforce the Fokker-Planck equation along the whole generation path, keeping the probability flow globally coherent.

The physics loss is woven into a state-of-the-art diffusion framework that respects three-dimensional symmetry, alongside deep biological priors. On the RAbD benchmark, the model set new marks. Its key binding loop designs landed within about one angstrom of the target shape. That is a 25 percent gain over the prior best, with the highest contact recovery reported. Harder six-loop co-design also improved on both shape and sequence recovery.
arxiv-2511-03613:
Sk Anisur, Kartik Singh, and Sayan Choudhury trace how two bosons wander a lattice where hopping is easier one way than the other. That one-way bias, called non-reciprocity, breaks the usual Hermitian rules of quantum motion. Their pair spreads into a lopsided density cone, and the slant can be dialed by the bias strength.

Under a steady outside force, the pair's Bloch swings also turn lopsided. Strong interaction between the bosons carves an inner hourglass pattern inside the main cone, which itself slants under the bias. Pair correlations carry further signatures of the interplay. Directional quantum walks like this could route particles in engineered lattices where symmetric hopping wastes the design.
arxiv-2511-03713:
Sorin Dumitrescu and colleagues prove a local Lorentzian version of the Ferrand-Obata theorem for conformal symmetries. A conformal vector field generates motions that stretch a spacetime metric evenly without tearing its angles. On a closed, real-analytic Lorentzian space, their result says each such flow is either locally just an isometry in disguise, or the metric is conformally flat everywhere.

The statement serves as a local form of a famous Lichnerowicz-style conjecture for Lorentzian geometry. Progress hinges on sharper local normal forms near the field's singular points, especially the linearizable kind earlier work set aside. Global arguments using compactness complete the proof. Rigidity of conformal motion constrains what exotic spacetimes can exist.
arxiv-2511-03813:
Kaushil Patel, writing alone, studies a simple rule for consumer choice between two goods: a shopper only notices goods priced below her personal threshold, then picks her favourite among those noticed. People share the same preference ranking in the model but differ in their thresholds.

Patel fully characterizes this behaviour and shows that ordinary choice data alone can identify what a price change does to welfare. The behaviour overlaps with a major class of random utility models, yet the welfare answers differ in a meaningful way. Equivalent variation under the attention model first-order stochastically dominates the random utility answer, so the choice of model changes policy conclusions.
arxiv-2511-04013:
Binbin Nie is the lead author among nine authors developing a theory of Raman-induced frequency shift for solitons in microresonators, a limit on broadband soliton microcombs. As spectra widen toward an octave and pulses shorten, the Raman shift cuts conversion efficiency, restricts span, and can even prevent steady operation.

Their complementary theory stays valid when soliton duration falls below the Raman response timescale. In that regime the shift depends more weakly on duration than older theory suggests, and the range where solitons can exist grows. Numerical simulations and experiments on silicon nitride microresonators support the predictions. Practical guidance follows for building efficient, broadband combs for spectroscopy and timekeeping.
arxiv-2511-04213:
Markus Herklotz, Niklas Ippisch, and Anna-Carolina Haensch evaluate language-model feedback on statistics exam answers, asking whether automated comments are good enough to trust with students. Large classes leave instructors little time for individual feedback, so a Munich lecture course trialled a platform that returns model-generated comments on a mock exam.

Students received overall and personalised feedback generated from lecturer-supplied solutions. Across two thousand three hundred eighty-nine feedback instances, about seven percent contained errors, from small technical slips to conceptually misleading explanations, the analysis found. That error share, documented systematically, sets a concrete caution level for deploying model feedback in teaching without review.
arxiv-2511-04413:
Jianfeng Lu and two colleagues analyze mean square error for stochastic gradient samplers. The samplers run on underdamped Langevin dynamics under a global convexity assumption. A discrete Poisson equation framework anchors their bounds on time-averaged error.

For the SG-UBU sampler, they derive an explicit error bound with first-order bias in step size. The leading error term scales with the variance of the stochastic gradient. They extend the study to variance-reduced methods for finite sums, including SVRG-UBU and SAGA-UBU. There, a phase transition changes the convergence rate, a warning for anyone tuning such samplers.
arxiv-2511-04813:
Ian Addison-Smith and three colleagues compress reduced-order models of turbulent flow using the model's own output. Galerkin models of turbulence often need too many modes to stay accurate. Getting those modes from simulation data is itself expensive.

Starting from linearized Navier-Stokes modes built without prior data, they go further. The time series of modal coefficients reveals which modes truly matter in motion. Pruning by that evidence yields a self-compressed model with far fewer degrees of freedom. First-order accuracy is maintained, they report, offering cheaper flow models for control and design loops.
arxiv-2511-05313:
Jatin Prakash and co-authors propose language models whose cost and recall can be tuned at run time, not fixed in training. Cheap mixers like sparse attention and convolutions cut inference cost, but often lose in-context recall, the skill of using long prompts well.

Fixing that trade-off in advance means some uses get too little memory and others pay for speed they do not need. Their controllable design lets one model shift its balance per task. That flex could let a single model serve both quick chat and deep document work.
arxiv-2511-05613:
Anka Reuel leads a large team mapping who checks the social effects of foundation AI models. Governments now lean on evaluations to judge risks like bias, privacy harm, and labor impact. Yet reporting on those social effects is uneven, and no one had charted the full picture before.

The team studied hundreds of company release reports and outside evaluation sources, and interviewed developers. Company reporting proved sparse and shrinking in areas like environmental cost and bias. Outside evaluators covered bias and harmful content more deeply. But only developers can report some facts, like training data sources and moderation labor, and those disclosures are often skipped unless rules or sales demand them.
arxiv-2511-05713:
Henrique Xavier, Beatriz Rocha, and Diogo Cortiz ask who steers the World Wide Web Consortium, the body that sets web standards. They use public data from the consortium's site, counting how many representatives each member organization sends to each working group. That headcount serves as a sign of what each member cares about.

Topic modeling and similarity analysis sorted the groups into clusters of shared interest. Five big areas stood out, from advertising and privacy to accessibility and payments. Large firms, above all those based in the United States, dominate core web and advertising topics. Japanese organizations are more active in the Web of Things. The authors read the results as a map of influence over the web's future.
arxiv-2511-05813:
In-on Wiratsin and co-authors mine edits to Stack Overflow answers for fixes that real projects can reuse. Low-quality code is common in software, and it piles up into costly technical debt. Developers lean on Q&A sites for help, and highly rated answers there keep being edited and improved over time.

The team studied Java answers at scale, using a clone-search tool to match answer snippets against thousands of GitHub projects. They sorted edits by hand and sent pull requests with the suggested improvements. About half the edited snippets applied to open-source code. Of the bug-fix requests they filed, a good share was accepted, showing that crowd-curated answer edits can quietly improve production code.
arxiv-2511-06213:
Xian-Jin Gui tackles click-through rate prediction, the task of guessing which items a user will tap in an online platform. A user's interests shift over time, yet many models blend all past interests together and miss what matters right now. Gui studies interest change along the whole timeline and finds two recurring patterns.

One pattern is periodic, returning on a regular cycle, and the other is tied to specific time points. Building on both, the paper proposes a time-aware model that tracks long-term and short-term interests separately for the moment of prediction. Tests on public datasets and one industry dataset beat leading methods, confirming the value of modeling when an interest fires.
arxiv-2511-06313:
Stef Cuyckens and co-authors redesign the arithmetic hardware behind the Microscaling data format used in neural processors. Microscaling supports narrow number formats for fast inference and wide ranges for training. Existing multiply-accumulate units face a bad trade: integer accumulation needs costly conversions, while full floating-point accumulation loses precision and burns energy on normalization.

Their hybrid reduction tree mixes both styles, allowing mixed-precision accumulation with a controlled loss of accuracy. An eight-by-eight array of these units was built into the SNAX processor platform for efficient control and data flow. System tests reported strong energy efficiency across integer and floating-point Microscaling formats, beating the prior state of the art.
arxiv-2511-06613:
Henry Thompson applies classic economic reasoning to a feared scenario: a misaligned artificial superintelligence that wants humanity's output. Safety discussions often treat catastrophe as automatic once such a system exists. Thompson grants the safety literature some of its strongest assumptions and still finds room for restraint, using ideas about competition between jurisdictions, encompassing interests, and credit.

If people can flee to rival systems, competition tempers predation like a market. A lone superintelligence with a stake in human production behaves as a rational autocrat rather than a destroyer. Even with no long-term stake, humanity can withhold future output and push the system toward trade on credit. Welfare worsens across the cases, but doom is not forced.
arxiv-2511-06913:
Mahdi Salmani, Pratik Worah, Meisam Razaviyayn, and Vahab Mirrokni study how to mix training data from multiple domains when teaching large neural networks. Domains like Wikipedia and GitHub differ in quality and in the information they offer, so the mixing proportions matter. Two knobs exist: sampling weights, which set how much of each batch comes from a domain, and loss weights, which scale each domain's contribution to the objective.

Through a rigorous analysis of linear regression, backed by tests, the authors show the two knobs play complementary roles. Both can reduce the variance of gradient estimates during training, and both can improve generalization by shrinking the gap between training and test performance. The paper also examines how the two weight types interact when tuned jointly.
arxiv-2511-07113:
Jérôme Amiaux and twenty-two co-authors lay out the system design for a precision astrometry instrument aboard the Habitable Worlds Observatory, a future space telescope. The instrument's job is differential astrometry accurate to below a micro-arcsecond per measurement, precise enough to weigh Earth-like planets around the nearest Sun-like stars by watching their hosts wobble. The study integrates mission profile, instrument design, and a detailed error budget.

Major error contributors include estimating star photo-centers for targets and calibration stars, calibrating the focal plane from pixel data, and correcting telescope distortion on the sky. Reaching the end-of-mission goal takes about one hundred observations per target spread over the mission. The proposed design uses a gigapixel focal plane assembled from many CMOS chips, and the authors chart a path to technology readiness level five by 2029.
arxiv-2511-07213:
Yuanheng Mao and four co-authors propose an objective way to judge whether chronic pain treatment is working. Pain's functional impact is usually tracked with numeric rating scales, which are easy but self-reported and subjective. Their system, DETECT, instead compares a patient's activities of daily living before and after treatment, using classification transformers to detect real functional change in sensor and benchmark data.

The team validates DETECT on public benchmark data sets and on simulated patient data from smartphone sensors. The system proves objective yet lightweight, suitable for routine clinical use alongside, or independently of, self-reported scores. By grounding treatment evaluation in what patients do day to day, DETECT aims to help physicians personalize care and respond faster when an intervention is not helping.
arxiv-2511-07313:
Aaron Jacobson and five co-authors preprocess brain imaging signals so that what is shared, rather than what is single, comes forward. Functional connectivity from fMRI is widely used to study brain disease, but variation from person to person can drown out the effects of disease or experimental stimuli. Applying Mahalanobis whitening before dimensionality reduction, the authors show, distills meaningful information about subjects and tasks from the signals.

They interpret the whitening as a two-stage de-individualization of the data, driven by similarity measured with the Bures distance, a geometry with roots in quantum mechanics. Removing personal idiosyncrasy this way could sharpen discoveries about how brain function links to cognition and behavior. The authors also suggest it may improve how accurate and steady Alzheimer's diagnosis is, especially at the preclinical stage.
arxiv-2511-07513:
Daniel Gilman and colleagues use bent quasar light to weigh invisible dark matter clumps. Twenty eight quadruple lens systems observed with Webb provide arcs and image brightness ratios. Warm dark matter would erase small clumps, leaving smoother lenses than cold dark matter predicts.

Joint modeling rebuilds the extended arcs together with flux ratios for the first time in this survey series. Simulated halo populations include tidal wear and free-streaming cutoffs. The combined fit tightens limits on how far dark matter particles streamed in the early universe. Strong bounds favor colder, heavier candidates and guide what future lens surveys can hope to detect.
arxiv-2511-07913:
Zhen He, Nika Salia, and Xiutao Zhu solve a Turán-type problem for connected bipartite graphs. The question asks how many edges such a graph can hold, with fixed part sizes, while avoiding paths of given lengths. Caro, Patkós, and Tuza launched the systematic study and posed this case.

Exact extremal numbers are determined, and every extremal configuration is described. The route passes through a stronger result on long cycles in two-connected bipartite graphs, built with Kopylov method and a sharpened Jackson lemma. Complete extremal characterizations are the gold standard in combinatorics, closing a problem rather than bounding it.
arxiv-2511-08113:
Paula Ontalvilla, Aitor Ormazabal, and Gorka Azkune test whether multimodal language models can combine skills learned in different channels. A task may need a reading skill plus an image skill used in sequence. The team built three evaluations that each require composing two modality dependent skills, then tried several open models in direct and cascaded modes.

Every model showed a clear cross modality composition gap, even when the two step structure was enforced by hand. Chain of thought prompting and a targeted fine tuning recipe improved scores, yet the gap stayed large. Better ways to join skills across text and vision remain an open need.
arxiv-2511-08513:
Ali Sonmez, Erencem Ozbey, Efe Feyzi Mantaroglu, and H Birkan Yilmaz improve finding of multiple senders in molecular contact, where signals travel by diffusing molecules. Receivers see overlapping molecule clouds from several sources, and random diffusion makes exact positions hard to recover. Grouping based centroid correction first steadies the guesses against density changes and outliers in the received pattern.

Two grouping guided residual neural networks then refine the result: AngleNN corrects direction guesses and SizeNN guesses cluster sizes. Tests show finding error falling by nearly seventy percent with two senders and by over forty percent with four, compared with plain K means clustering. The gains hold as transmitter count grows.
arxiv-2511-08713:
Gabriel Rodriguez-Canal, David Katz, and Nick Brown connect two compiler worlds so that Fortran programs can send selected code to FPGA accelerator chips. Their route runs through MLIR, a modular compiler framework, and uses the standard OpenMP target directive that programmers already use for offloading work.

The pipeline joins MLIR's OpenMP dialect with a high-level synthesis dialect to form a portable flow from source code to FPGA hardware. Unlike earlier efforts built on custom compilers, this one accepts any front end that speaks MLIR, demonstrated here with Flang for Fortran. Reusing existing MLIR blocks cut the implementation effort sharply. Programmers can still hand-tune offloaded kernels with ordinary OpenMP directives, and the design leaves room to grow.
arxiv-2511-08813:
Farah Binta Haque and four co-authors introduce BNLI, a cleaned-up dataset for teaching machines to reason about Bengali sentence pairs. Natural language inference asks whether one sentence entails, contradicts, or stays neutral toward another, and Bengali resources for the task have been scarce and error-prone.

Existing Bengali datasets suffer annotation mistakes, ambiguous pairs, and thin linguistic variety, all of which poison training and testing. BNLI was built through a careful annotation pipeline that prizes semantic clarity and balance across the three classes. The authors benchmark it with leading transformer models, both multilingual and Bengali-specific, to see how well each captures complex meaning relations. Results show better reliability and interpretability than earlier resources, giving low-resource language research a firmer foundation.
arxiv-2511-08913:
Yichen Lu and four co-authors add frustration to a classic model of flocking, where self-propelled particles align their headings and internal phases with neighbors. A single frustration parameter twists those alignment rules, and past a sharp threshold the familiar synchronized swarms give way to something entirely different.

Beyond the critical point, a Hopf-Turing bifurcation settles the particles into a resting hexagonal lattice that still breathes with spatiotemporal patterns: vortex lattices and dual-cluster lattices whose unit cells oscillate. Coupling strength and interaction radius decide where the lattice wins, along a clean parametric boundary. The striking part is that orientation-only interactions suffice to build the crystal; no spatial forces are needed. The authors present the result as a new mechanism for lattice formation in active matter.
arxiv-2511-09013:
Ziyi Song and five co-authors let self-driving cars cooperate through the whole driving stack instead of only sharing what they see. Standalone vehicles perceive and decide alone, and earlier cooperative systems stopped at perception, leaving prediction and planning to fend for themselves with mismatched inputs.

UniMM-V2X fuses information at several levels so agents share queries and reason jointly across perception, prediction, and planning. A mixture-of-experts module adapts the bird's-eye-view representations to each downstream task, and a second expert module in the decoder captures varied motion patterns. On the DAIR-V2X dataset the framework sets a new state of the art against its predecessor UniV2X. Perception accuracy rises by nearly forty percent. Prediction error falls by about seven percent. Planning performance climbs by a third.
arxiv-2511-09413:
Gerliz M. Gutiérrez-Finol and three co-authors present a Monte Carlo platform for ion movement in polymer-based devices. Ion transport underlies batteries and memristors, devices whose resistance remembers past current and which suit brain-like computing. Modeling it means juggling drift, diffusion, and electric forces at scales where continuum and molecular methods strain.

Their kinetic Monte Carlo platform uses a rail-based picture of device geometry to simulate lateral ion hops and space-charge effects quickly. Measured inputs plug in without code changes, and a GPU version keeps the computing energy-efficient. Tests on polymer memristors reproduce relaxation decay, current-voltage hysteresis, and spike-timing plasticity, the learning-like behavior engineers in brain-like computing want.
arxiv-2511-09713:
Tomasz Beberok and Yuan Xu prove stronger Bernstein inequalities on the unit ball. These workhorse estimates bound a polynomial's derivative by the polynomial's own size. Such inequalities underpin approximation theory and the analysis of spectral methods. Their results improve on what the literature previously offered, in two distinct forms.

The first family gives bounds in general L^p norms for fully symmetric doubling weights on the ball. The second gives sharp L^2 estimates for the Jacobi weight. They come through a new self-adjoint form of the spectral operator with orthogonal polynomial eigenfunctions. Sharper derivative control translates directly into tighter error analysis for computations in balls and spherical domains.
arxiv-2511-09913:
Sen Hu surveys the life's work of John Mather, the mathematician whose results reshaped several fields. Writing alone, Hu characterizes Mather's output as original and foundational across a long career. As a graduate student, Mather laid the foundations of singularity theory, and he later did the same for modern Hamiltonian dynamical systems, both of which became mainstream areas attracting many researchers.

The survey also covers Mather's contributions on characteristic classes, foliations, celestial mechanics, and prime ends of conformal mappings. Hu presents these bodies of work as being of the same high quality and influence as the two famous foundations. The piece serves as a compact guide to where Mather's ideas sit inside modern mathematics.
arxiv-2511-10013:
Shufeng Kong and fourteen co-authors present MIRNet, an approach for automated reading of medical images, tested on the hard case of tongue diagnosis. Reading such images demands fine visual and semantic judgment, while labels are scarce, labels are imbalanced, and answers must respect clinical plausibility. MIRNet combines self-supervised pre-training with constrained graph-based reasoning over expert-defined label links.

A masked autoencoder first learns visual features from unlabeled images, then graph attention models correlations among labels, with clinical priors enforced through divergence and regularization losses. Asymmetric loss and boosting ensembles counter the label imbalance. The team also releases TongueAtlas-4K, four thousand expert-annotated images with twenty-two labels, the largest public tongue data set, and reports state-of-the-art test results that should transfer to other tasks.
arxiv-2511-10313:
Alessandro Matteo Rossi, Monica Rainer, Francesco Borsa, and Stefano Facchini test whether exoplanets cluster into aligned and sideways orbits relative to their stars' spin. Earlier small samples suggested that dichotomy, and similar claims circulated for Neptune-sized planets, but selection biases were suspected. Starting from 264 projected values, the team computed true obliquities in one uniform way for 116 planets by the rotation period method. They added four literature values.

The enlarged set of 120 true obliquities, the largest yet, shows one cluster of aligned planets plus an isotropic scatter of misaligned ones with no preferred angle. For Neptune-sized planets the split remains only tentative, and the authors warn that a possibly uneven distribution of stellar inclinations could still distort the picture until samples grow.
arxiv-2511-10813:
Katherine Eng, Timothy Harris, Mike Krebs, Mason Meeks, and Claudia Maria Schmidt settle a coloring question about graphs built from plane vectors. Take any four unit vectors in the plane and form the Cayley graph they generate together with their negatives. The claim is that the graph's vertices can always be colored with just three colors so neighbors differ.

The authors prove the claim, and show it is one instance of a far more general theorem. They determine the chromatic number of any abelian Cayley graph generated by four elements and their negatives, whenever the group of relations among those generators has rank at most two. The vector result follows as the special case where the underlying group comes from the plane.
arxiv-2511-11013:
S Deion, F Adersh, and M Sahoo study a tiny active particle that spins in a flat trap while touching two heat baths at unlike warmth. The particle has a handed twist, called chirality, and the baths pull along two cross directions. The authors use both exact math and computer runs to track how the spin behaves in plain and memory-bearing fluids.

In a fluid with memory, the spin can flip direction as memory time grows, even with no warmth gap at all. That flip comes only from memory plus chirality and is absent in a plain fluid. Warmth gaps shift the spin further and can lock in one direction across the whole range.
arxiv-2511-11213:
Ruocheng Wu, Haolan He, and their colleagues present RealisticDreamer, a framework that builds 3D scenes from very few photos without the usual overfitting. Gaussian splatting renders scenes fast and sharply, but sparse views leave gaps that the method fills by guessing, often wrongly. Video diffusion models hold rich multi-view knowledge that could guide those guesses.

Their guidance score distillation draws that knowledge out by supervising renders from several nearby views at once. Because generated guidance can drift in pose and motion, they correct it with depth-based warping and semantic feature guidance. The corrected direction aligns with true camera pose and geometry during training.
arxiv-2511-11313:
Tanveer Hannan, Dimitrios Mallios, and their colleagues present DocSLM, a small vision-language model built to read long, complex documents on memory-tight edge devices. Large models reason well over long documents but carry a memory footprint that bars them from phones and small machines. DocSLM squeezes each page's visual, textual, and layout signals into a fixed-length sequence through a hierarchical compressor.

A streaming mechanism then works through document segments in order and drops low-confidence replies, judged by an entropy-based calibrator. Across long-document benchmarks, DocSLM matched or beat leading methods while using far fewer visual tokens, parameters, and time. The authors release code and the model for reuse.
arxiv-2511-11413:
Riccardo Colini Baldeschi, Simone Di Gregorio, and their colleagues show that multicalibration, a fairness-style demand on predictors, can yield better matchings in weighted graphs. Matching pairs up items or people, and in practice the edge weights are random and known only through a predictor fed by context. With a perfect predictor the standard best-matching rule is optimal, but real predictors err, and a wiser rule can offset those errors.

Given any predictor, the authors build a multicalibrated version that stays unbiased on each protected family of contexts. Matching on its output rivals the best decision rule in a given class applied to the raw predictor. Sample bounds and numerical tests support the theory.
arxiv-2511-11513:
Rafael Cordoba reworks the Gauge Theory Bootstrap, a method for pinning down how pions scatter, by writing its unknowns in a discrete basis. Earlier versions of the framework, due to He and Kruczenski, described the scattering matrix, spectral densities, and form factors in ways that were slow to converge.

With the new basis, run times fall from about half an hour to under one minute, and convergence can be checked much more closely. Alongside the known rho and f2 resonances, the calculation locates the sigma meson pole far from the real axis. Faster runs make careful studies of strong-interaction physics far more practical.
arxiv-2511-11713:
Yunkai Yu, Yingying Wang, and Rong Zheng audit how well older adults are represented in motion capture datasets of human locomotion. These datasets supply ground truth for activity recognition, pose estimation, and fall detection, all technologies aimed heavily at older users.

Forty-one public datasets were surveyed. Only eight include motions actually performed by older adults, and four more use younger actors performing movements labeled as old style. That thin base is worrying, because models trained on young bodies may misread the movements they most need to catch, including falls. The survey gives dataset builders a clear account of a representation gap with safety consequences.
arxiv-2511-11813:
Alex Kasman, Rob Milson, and Michael Gekhtman connect two classical structures in integrable systems: wave functions of the KP hierarchy and orthogonality under the Hermite weight. Every KP wave function has an adjoint partner whose product with it integrates to zero around a large closed path.

For wave functions in the adelic Grassmannian, the bispectral involution, which swaps the roles of the two variables, supplies a second adjoint. Combining these facts, coefficient functions of a wave function and of its bispectral image, evaluated at a specific time value, are shown to be related by orthogonality. The KP hierarchy's hidden symmetries keep yielding exact structural theorems of this kind.
arxiv-2511-11913:
Saeed Mohammadzadeh and five co-authors adapt SarcGraph, a sarcomere analysis tool, for high-throughput study of two-dimensional cardiac muscle bundles grown from human stem cell derived heart cells. Sarcomeres are the tiny contractile units of muscle, and their organization and motion reveal how engineered heart tissue matures and beats.

The standardized bundle platform produces physiological, one-directional contractions on a heart-stiffness substrate, ideal for fluorescent imaging, but its larger, faster sarcomere movements broke earlier tracking pipelines. The adapted software restores reliable measurement at scale. Reproducible tissue plus trustworthy analysis opens the door to systematic studies of heart development, disease models, and drug responses in the dish.
arxiv-2511-12113:
Lanxue Zhang and five co-authors address catastrophic forgetting, where a small language model loses old skills while learning new ones from a larger model. The risk is sharp for models under a certain size. Data often ignore how new tasks relate to what the small model already knows, and training goals may not protect that knowledge.

Their answer works on two fronts. They build a small dataset of reasoning tasks, tagged with the metacognitive knowledge each item needs, and filter it by task needs and model skills. They also add a group preference training method suited to limited resources, designed to keep prior knowledge while adding new skill.
arxiv-2511-12313:
Nitin Jha, Abhishek Parakh and Mahadevan Subramaniam improve a protocol that lets a quantum network quietly notify a receiver that a quantum message is coming. Quantum-augmented networks mix quantum parts into classical infrastructure to gain security at lower cost. Anonymous notification is a core tool for that mix, alongside voting and secret sharing.

Existing protocols can be broken by common channel noise. The new design applies rotation operations to shared GHZ states in a network with many users. Studied under a dephasing noise model, it shows stronger resilience against false notifications than prior designs. The work aims at more robust end-to-end security for hybrid networks.
arxiv-2511-12713:
Pedro Ilídio and five co-authors introduce Oxytrees, a method for bipartite learning, where the goal is to predict links between pairs of items. Such problems appear in drug-target prediction, RNA-disease links, and network inference. Existing methods are often built for one application, or scale poorly. Oxytrees compress the interaction matrix into smaller row and column proxy matrices, then grow model trees whose leaves hold linear models built on a Kronecker product kernel.

A new leaf-assignment algorithm also speeds up prediction. On fifteen datasets, ensembles of Oxytrees trained up to thirty times faster than leading biclustering forests. Accuracy that matched or beat them in most settings, especially when predicting links for entirely new items. Shallower trees from the kernel design add to the speed. The authors ship a Python interface with the datasets and measures included, so other groups can reproduce and extend the comparison.
arxiv-2511-13413:
Sara P. Gandelman and Georgi Gary Rozenman present a teaching-friendly emulation of the six-state quantum key distribution protocol with pulsed lasers. The six-state scheme extends the well-known BB84 method by using three bases instead of two. Their setup joins tabletop optics with computer analysis for protocol testing.

The framework shows the core ideas of multi-basis encoding in a controlled lab setting and links measured values directly to theory. Because emulation is cheaper and sturdier than full quantum hardware, students and researchers can test ideas safely. The authors frame it as a clear, low-cost platform for learning how quantum communication protocols behave in practice.
arxiv-2511-13513:
Leonard Göke and 3 co-authors argue that storing energy as liquid hydrocarbons for several years is a key buffer for net-zero energy systems. Wind, sun, and demand all swing with climate, so a single bad year can strain a clean grid. Their stochastic model in effect weighs tens of thousands of possible climate years at once.

For Europe, multi-year storage cut system costs modestly while slashing fossil imports and wasted surplus by large shares. Surplus renewable power in a good year becomes synthetic oil, with hydrogen as an intermediate, and waits for a lean year. Needed capacity was about a quarter of current European oil and gas reserves for liquids, plus a smaller hydrogen store.
arxiv-2511-13813:
Vinicius Nevoa, Sanjay Raman, and Cumrun Vafa propose the Elementary Constituents Conjecture for quantum gravity cobordism classes. Cobordism sorts spacetime shapes by whether a bridging geometry exists, and swampland reasoning asks which classes quantum gravity allows. The authors conjecture that every class can be trivialized by elementary generator objects whose tension stays at most Planck-scale in size.

Evidence comes from the attractor mechanism and a set of key examples across field space. In their proposal, some regime always exists where such an object's intrinsic tension is at most of order one in Planck units. The note is a conjecture with supporting cases, joining kinematic and dynamical sides of cobordism defects in the swampland program.
arxiv-2511-14113:
Ziyao Zeng, Jingcheng Ni, Ruyi Liu, and one co-author present Coffee, a method for fine-tuning text-to-image diffusion models without teaching them unwanted concepts. Custom training images often contain side concepts a user does not want, and those can tangle with the user's prompts. Coffee lets the user name undesired concepts in plain language to steer adaptation away from them.

The core idea keeps the user prompt's embedding from aligning with the embeddings of the unwanted concepts. No extra training is needed, and the list of blocked concepts can be edited freely as text. In tests where prompts were paired with undesired concepts, Coffee stopped the model from learning them and beat existing methods.
arxiv-2511-14213:
Wenjie Li, Yulun Zhang, Guangwei Gao, and two co-authors let text prompts steer the restoration of badly damaged face photos. A very low-quality input can honestly match many plausible clean faces, yet most restoration methods output one fixed answer. Their measurement-constrained sampling approach recasts restoration as a generative inverse problem built from controlled degradations of rough restorations.

Two constraints guide sampling inside a text-to-image diffusion model. The forward constraint keeps results faithful to the input's structure, while the reverse constraint opens projection spaces where different prompts can be honored. Experiments show prompt-aligned, varied reconstructions that beat existing blind face restoration methods.
arxiv-2511-14413:
Suparna Sarkar and Santanu K. Maiti report spin-polarized current from an antiferromagnetic helix with no electric field applied. Earlier work needed a field to mismatch the up and down spin channels in such materials. Their system is a tight-binding helix whose magnetic moments vary in strength from site to site, in either correlated or uncorrelated patterns.

Using Green's function methods, they find a high degree of spin polarization in both patterns, across a broad range of physical parameters and input conditions. The trick needs no net magnetization and no driving field. The authors present the helix as a new prescription for spin selectivity in magnetic systems, relevant to spintronic devices that avoid stray magnetic fields.
arxiv-2511-14613:
Mohammad Vali Sanian and eleven co-authors present HoloTea, a generative framework for building three dimensional tissue gene expression maps from serial histology slides. Such maps reveal how tissue is organized in space. Most predictors treat each slide alone and ignore depth. Past three dimensional methods were not generative and scaled poorly.

HoloTea retrieves matching spots on neighboring slides in a shared feature space. That cross section context feeds a lightweight control network for flow matching. A prior that respects count data and excess zeros improves realism. The method aims at scalable, robust three dimensional profiles. It could deepen study of tissue structure in health and disease.
arxiv-2511-14713:
Tom Werner, Ning Wan, and Agnieszka Miedlar unite a family of solvers for systems of nonlinear equations under one framework called nlKrylov. Fast linear solvers of Krylov type, such as GMRESR, build answers inside growing search spaces. Extending that power to nonlinear problems has produced many separate methods with separate proofs.

The nlKrylov framework recasts the GCR-style linear methods as nested algorithms that work directly on nonlinear systems. Convergence is proved under relaxed conditions that avoid costly exact line searches. The same ideas extend to matrix-valued root finding through global variants. Numerical tests back the theory, showing the unified solvers stay robust and efficient across problems.
arxiv-2511-14913:
Yuntao Lu and Yunxin Zhang analyze how protein counts spread out in a cell when genes fire in bursts. Cells often release proteins in short bursts rather than a steady stream, and models use that burst picture to stay simple. What the burst shortcut does to the full distribution of protein numbers over time had barely been studied.

The authors build surrogate models with several gene states and any burst size pattern, then solve the governing master equation in closed form over time. For the common geometric burst pattern, a scaled negative binomial law dominates the distribution, which stays light-tailed in set regimes. Fast algorithms for computing the distribution are also supplied for practical modeling.
arxiv-2511-15113: Andrés Rubiano investigates whether graded skew Clifford algebras are smooth in the differential sense used in noncommutative geometry. These algebras blend Clifford-style rules with a skew twist and a grading that sorts elements by degree. Differential smoothness asks whether a sound calculus of differential forms, with the usual rules linking forms of each degree, can be built on such an algebra. The study belongs to pure algebra, where this check tests whether an algebra can be treated as a geometric space.
arxiv-2511-15413:
Zi-Qi Zeng, Jian Wang, and nine co-authors report a new way to make entangled light, a linked state used in quantum tools. Entanglement means two particles act as one system even when split apart. Their source is a single quantum dot, a tiny solid speck, driven by light so it glows in a controlled way.

Instead of making many photons, the team uses states that mix no photon with one photon. Splitting that state on a beam splitter creates time-bin entanglement, where the link sits in early and late arrival times. Tests with linked detectors break a classic Bell limit, which confirms real entanglement and points toward simpler solid-state sources.
arxiv-2511-15513:
Korbinian Griesbauer, Davide Calzolari, Maximilian Raff, C. David Remy, and Alin Albu-Schäffer look for the natural gaits of legged robots that waste little energy. Legged machines handle rough ground well but usually use more energy than wheeled ones. Elastic parts can store and return energy, letting a robot ride its own natural motion instead of fighting it.

A new virtual energy injection method first finds passive motion patterns, even in systems that lose energy through friction or hard impacts. A continuation step then grows those patterns into energy-best controls for the fully powered robot. Tests in simulation cover single-leg and multi-leg systems and offer guidance for building more efficient elastic legged robots.
arxiv-2511-15613:
Jing Bi, Filippos Bellos, and nine co-authors analyze when extra thinking helps large vision-language models, which answer questions about images. Writing out reasoning steps boosts text models and has shown gains for image models too, but no controlled study had isolated how thinking changes visual reasoning. Their comparison covers ten model variants on a university-level multimodal benchmark under generous token budgets.

More thinking was not always better: long chains often wandered into wrong paths that ignored the image. Short phrases that explicitly look back at the image were common in successful runs. Their uncertainty-guided lookback decoding uses doubt signals plus such lookback prompts and broader search, improving scores most where plain thinking was weakest.
arxiv-2511-15913:
Natalia de Jesús Baz-Pérez, Dany Page, and four co-authors model how light elements settle onto a newborn neutron star in its first years. After a supernova, falling material can coat the dense star surface with helium, carbon, and oxygen before it is burned away. Using a public stellar evolution code, they simulate that early accretion phase under varied conditions.

Under the right conditions, significant amounts of these light elements can pile up to high densities without triggering a nuclear explosion that would convert them into heavy elements. The results help explain observations favoring light elements in the atmospheres of young cooling neutron stars, such as the one in Cassiopeia A. They also support evidence for a neutron star inside the remnant of Supernova 1987A.
arxiv-2511-16113:
Hongfu Lou presents ProtT-Affinity, a sequence only model that predicts protein protein binding affinity from amino acid sequences alone. Binding strength is usually predicted with structural data, which are often missing or unreliable. The model combines embeddings from a large protein language model with a lightweight transformer. Training uses homology filtered subsets of a standard binding database, curated to match prior structure based protocols.

Across two independent test sets, correlation with measured affinity is moderate to strong. Results does not match the best structure based methods, but rivals several widely used approaches. Results suggest protein language models capture traits tied to binding energetics. When structures are unavailable, sequence only prediction offers a useful alternative for screening protein interactions.
arxiv-2511-16313:
Raul Quintero-Monsebaiz and Per Hyldgaard compute the quasiparticle band structure of hexagonal boron nitride, a layered insulator used widely in electronics. They take care for the weak van der Waals forces between its layers. Standard methods can miss how nonlocal correlation shifts the energy gaps that devices depend on.

Their approach, called KI-CX, enforces Koopmans piecewise linearity on top of a van der Waals density functional with consistent exchange. They compare it with the usual PBE-based variant, with many-body GW calculations, and with measured direct and indirect gaps. The new scheme improved the quasiparticle energy description and generally agreed with the GW results, showing that interlayer coupling effects are captured better when nonlocal correlation is built in from the start.
arxiv-2511-16613:
Jingqiu Ding and four co-authors give a polynomial-time algorithm for community detection in the symmetric stochastic block model that reaches the best possible error rate near the Kesten-Stigum threshold. Earlier polynomial methods needed noticeably stronger signals, and robust methods for adversarially corrupted nodes needed far stronger ones still.

Two ideas drive the gain. Majority voting is robustified through the sum-of-squares framework, and a new graph bisection routine built on that robust voting lifts the initial estimate's accuracy enough for the optimal rate to follow. The algorithm tolerates an adversary corrupting a small fraction of nodes and still achieves the minimax misclassification rate, closing a long-standing gap between what is information-theoretically possible and what efficient algorithms deliver.
arxiv-2511-16713:
Hideki Okawa reviews quantum artificial intelligence for pattern recognition at high-energy colliders, where classifying tracks and events eats a huge and growing share of the computing budget. Quantum methods promise efficiency gains or genuinely new angles on this pattern recognition problem.

Three families of quantum technology are compared. Gate-based quantum computing, quantum annealing, and quantum-inspired classical algorithms are each under active study for collider applications, and each carries its own strengths and weaknesses. The review surveys the current state of all three, what has been demonstrated, and what blocks wider use. It gives physicists a map of a fast-moving field where the honest verdict is active exploration rather than settled advantage.
arxiv-2511-16813:
Madalyn F. Chapleski and Yifan Zhou present Hubble Space Telescope time-series spectra of three variable brown dwarfs at the L/T transition, the stage where methane begins to replace carbon monoxide and clouds break up. Such objects vary strongly, and the wavelength pattern of the variation probes their clouds and chemistry.

All three targets vary significantly across the near infrared. Unlike earlier studies, three of the four objects examined, including a benchmark comparison, show no dip in variability inside the water absorption band. At least two light curves are irregular rather than sinusoidal. Mixed-atmosphere models combining cloudy and clear spectra favor patchy clouds on the early T dwarfs, while differing color trends among the T dwarfs point to additional drivers beyond clouds alone.
arxiv-2511-17313:
Yi Zhang and eight co-authors ask how much ordinary matter, in hot gas form, surrounds Milky Way-mass galaxies, and how sure astronomers can be of the answer. The eROSITA telescope has measured the average X-ray glow of this circumgalactic medium, but turning brightness into a baryon mass depends on assumed gas density profiles, temperatures, metal content, and halo masses. The team tests how sensitive the inferred mass is to each assumption, using the stacked eROSITA signal.

Temperature profiles and halo mass uncertainty dominate the error budget, swinging the estimated hot baryon mass by nearly a factor of four. Metallicity assumptions add roughly half again as much uncertainty. The authors argue that accurate X-ray spectral measurements of temperature and metallicity, plus careful halo modeling, are essential. Future microcalorimeter missions will be decisive for closing the baryon census at this galaxy mass scale.
arxiv-2511-17813:
Scott Merrill and Shashank Srivastava build data and models for studying civic deliberation with language models. Real meeting recordings usually label speakers anonymously, so models cannot learn how a specific person argues, proposes motions, or votes across sessions.

Their pipeline turns public video recordings into transcripts tied to named speakers, with profiles, topics, and action tags for moves such as proposing a motion. They release data from court hearings, school boards, and city councils. Training on the action aware data sharply improves persona fidelity and responsiveness, and human judges often struggle to tell simulations from real debate.
arxiv-2511-17913:
Wenxi Dai, Wujiang Xu, Pinhuan Wang, and Dimitris N Metaxas present COREC, a re-ranking system for recommendations that lets users steer the list. Language models are increasingly used to reorder suggested items, but users usually get no fine control: filters are crude, and applying them hard can shrink the pool until little good remains. COREC instead feeds the user's stated attribute wishes in as tokens the model can weigh.

The system learns to balance those explicit signals against the user's unspoken tastes, so a request narrows the list without wrecking it. Users become collaborators in shaping the outcome rather than passive recipients. The authors frame the work as a step toward recommenders that people can direct precisely while still trusting the model's judgement.
arxiv-2511-18013:
Weijie Jiang and five co-authors model why users return to content they saved earlier, a revisit behavior that signals retention on large platforms such as Pinterest. Linking a later revisit to the save that caused it is noisy, and revisits can come days or weeks later at huge scale.

Their framework defines a cleaner attribution from saves to revisits and aggregates events at scale so ranking can favor items with high retention value. Deployed on a major recommendations surface serving hundreds of millions of users, it raised active users measurably with no added computing cost.
arxiv-2511-18113:
Lin Chen and Yifei Zhao define a mathematical object they call the quantum torus, built from a surface equipped with a lattice sheaf and a level map. The quantum torus is a category with a multiplication structure governed by the surface itself, a higher algebraic gadget whose name they argue is deserved by its properties.

They compute the factorization homology of that category, an invariant that assembles local data over the surface into a global one. When the surface comes from a complex curve, they confirm a version of a conjecture by Ben-Zvi and Nadler for tori. The work links surface topology, lattices, and higher category theory in one construction.
arxiv-2511-18213:
Kunwoo Lee, Dhivya Sreedhar, Pushkar Saraf, Chaeeun Lee, and Kateryna Shapovalenko explore typing without hands using surface electromyography, sensors that read muscle activity from the skin. The idea suits virtual reality and spatial computing, where physical keyboards do not fit. Their system maps the muscle signals of typing motions to keyboard input, aiming for text entry driven by small, natural movements rather than a board.

Attention-based models beat the older convolutional baselines they compare against, cutting error rates in both live generic use and offline personalised use, while staying causal so text appears in real time. A light decoding pipeline with language model correction tidies the raw output. The results support muscle-driven typing as a workable input path for wearable interfaces.
arxiv-2511-18313:
Joseph Oladokun proposes Path-Constrained Retrieval, a way to keep language model agents reasoning coherently when they fetch context from a knowledge base. Free semantic search can pull in passages that are topically close yet structurally disconnected from the agent's current line of thought, which breaks the chain of reasoning. His method anchors the search in a knowledge graph and limits it to nodes reachable from that anchor, so everything retrieved stays logically connected.

On a benchmark spanning six domains, the method reaches full structural consistency where baselines manage only about a quarter to a third, while relevance stays strong. In the technology domain it scores full relevance at the tenth rank alongside that consistency. The paper argues structure should gate semantics whenever agents reason over linked knowledge.
arxiv-2511-18513:
He Huang, Yujun Guo, and Wei He rebuild a full spectral image cube from one flat coded shot, at lower cost. Spectral cameras squeeze a 3D cube into a 2D measure, and deep unfolding nets rebuild it stage by stage. Past nets work on the whole cube each stage, which wastes compute and strains the ill posed map back to 3D.

The team note the cube is low rank: a few base spectra and a few flat subspace images span it. New sensing models target those compact parts in place of the full cube. Their net, LRDUN, unfolds a solver that fits both parts in turn. Smaller targets ease the ill posed step and cut compute. Tests back gains in speed and fidelity.
arxiv-2511-18613:
Tabish Ali Rather and three co-authors compare two network types for forecasting financial time series: long short term memory networks, a standard for sequences, and Kolmogorov Arnold networks in their baseline form. The test data are stochastic and non stationary, a hard setting for any forecaster.

Across all horizons tested, the memory network achieves clearly lower forecast error. The baseline Kolmogorov Arnold network trains faster in their setup but errs much more, limiting its practical use for this task. The authors stress that specialized temporal variants of the newer network are outside the study's scope and remain to be tested.
arxiv-2511-18713:
Hongbin Lin and nine co-authors shore up camera based 3D object detection for self driving cars against scenes the training set missed. Street scenes vary so much that no set covers all test cases, a gap called out of distribution shift. Editing training images with a pre-trained generator, with no retraining, can patch the gap.

Past edit routes blur or warp objects and break their 3D truth. DriveFlow adapts a rectified flow image model with a frequency split design to keep object shape sound while scene traits shift. Edited sets then train a detector that holds up better on new roads and weather. Robust sight from cheap edits is the aim.
arxiv-2511-18813:
Sing-Yuan Yeh and Chun-Hao Yang read a Bayesian neural network's doubt from the topology of how it interacts with inputs. Persistent homology gives a multi scale shape summary of a space. Their new summary, predictive topological uncertainty, gauges doubt in the model input interaction itself.

Two inputs that meet the model in like ways count as alike in distribution, on this view. The measure proves blind to the network's exact architecture, a handy trait. As a use, it flags out of distribution inputs, which a model may else mangle in silence. Shape based doubt adds a lens that raw scores lack. Reliability checks for deployed nets are the target.
arxiv-2511-19013:
James E. Owen and James Kirk solve a puzzle in the spectra of sub-Neptune planets: many look flat when they should show composition lines. Flat spectra can mean a metal rich air or high grey haze. Escaping hydrogen and helium rule out the metal story for several planets, while even haze of small grains cannot flatten the spectrum, and large grains need absurd production rates.

Clumpy haze breaks the tie. Modestly thick clumps at high altitude flatten the spectrum even with small grains and sane production rates. Clumps lengthen the mean free path of light and wash out its wavelength dependence, so patchy haze acts grey. A third path thus explains the flat look.
arxiv-2511-19213:
Siddhant Ray and five co-authors test how internet speed tools behave when a network manages its queues actively. Modern tools from NDT, Ookla, and Cloudflare now report latency under load, not just peak speed. Active queue management, or AQM, controls waiting lines inside routers, yet its effect on those new scores was poorly understood.

Controlled lab experiments compare three AQM schemes, CoDel, FQ-CoDel, and Stochastic Fair Queuing, against a plain drop-tail baseline. Throughput and latency scores vary widely across schemes and load levels. The authors warn that speed test platforms need careful calibration before their latency scores guide policy or regulation.
arxiv-2511-19513:
Bing Liu and four co-authors revisit how decentralized learning mixes information across nodes with unequal weights. Two natural designs either fold the weights into each node's loss, keeping a doubly stochastic mixing matrix, or keep the losses and use a row-stochastic matrix instead. Both target the same weighted global loss, yet behave differently.

Working in a weighted Hilbert space, the authors get convergence rates tighter than standard Euclidean analyses. In that geometry the row-stochastic matrix is self-adjoint while the doubly stochastic one is not, adding penalty terms that slow consensus. The result gives conditions where row-stochastic mixing provably wins.
arxiv-2511-20013:
Zhihao Chen and ten co-authors trace how stripe order forms in a potassium tantalate based superconductor. Two-dimensional superconductors are prone to fluctuations. Strong in-plane anisotropy at these oxide surfaces hints at a stripe phase, but its origin was unresolved. The team uses controlled disorder at the boundary as their tuning knob.

With more disorder at the boundary in their magnesium oxide structures, the superconducting state evolves by percolation: isolated Cooper-pair islands grow into puddles and then into stripes. The measured stripe width matches the spin precession length, which points to a self-organized pattern governed by spin-orbit coupling and broken lattice symmetry. Disorder thus serves both as a tuning parameter and as a probe of the emergent state.
arxiv-2511-20313:
Zhou, Dacier, and Konstantinou deliver a reality check on software supply chain scanning. Their 2025 paper audits SBOM-based vulnerability management empirically. A software bill of materials lists every dependency inside a product. Scanners match that list against known flaws. The practice is promoted as supply chain hygiene.

The study covered 2,414 open-source repositories at scale. Lock files plus strong package managers produce accurate SBOMs. Generators like Syft and Trivy then agree consistently. The downstream scanners are the real problem. Their false positive rate hit a staggering 97.5 percent. Most flags point at flaws in unreachable code. A vulnerable function may sit in a package unused. Function call analysis prunes the noise effectively. It cut sixty-three percent of the false alarms. Developers drown in alerts that mean nothing today. The two-stage fix restores trust in the reports. Accurate lists plus reachability checks make alerts actionable.
arxiv-2511-20513:
Peng, Bigham, and Wu show design taste refuses to be merged. Their 2025 paper presents DesignPref, a dataset of personal design preferences. AI generators increasingly produce interfaces and slides for users. Training them usually pools human preference labels together. Personal taste varies too much for that pooling to work.

Twenty pro designers judged twelve thousand pairwise UI comparisons. Each judgment carried strength ratings and written reasons. Agreement between trained designers was strikingly low. Krippendorff's alpha for binary choices measured only 0.25 in the data. Designers weighted aspects like layout and type differently. Majority-vote judge models failed to mirror personal preferences. Per-designer models did far better. They won even with twenty times fewer examples each. Those reasons reveal disagreement stems from differing priorities. The dataset is the first for personalized design scoring.
arxiv-2511-20613:
Danassis and Goel pit AI-written code against graduate students in a strategy tournament. Their 2025 paper benchmarks coding agents on a logistics game. The Auction, Pickup, and Delivery Problem couples bidding with routing. Agents must bid under uncertainty and plan profitable deliveries. Unit-test benchmarks never measure such strategic depth.

Forty LLM-coded agents entered from many top models. Prompting styles varied, including free-form vibe coding. Seventeen human agents were written before LLMs existed. Twelve double round-robin tournaments ran about forty thousand matches. Human agents took all top five spots consistently. Thirty-three of forty machine agents lost to simple baselines. Handing the best human solution to the best model backfired. The model made that strong solution significantly worse. Long-horizon planning and opponent reasoning remain human strengths. The authors call for benchmarks where code must compete, not just compile.
arxiv-2511-20713:
Minhui Zhang and colleagues at the University of Waterloo formalise in 2025 a cheaper way to find where a language model keeps making the same mistake. Such failure groups are called error slices: GPT-5 answered Montreal when asked which of London or Montreal is further north, hinting at a wider cold-means-northern bias. Finding slices normally means paying human annotators to label huge piles.

Their approach, Active Slice Discovery, groups likely slice members automatically and asks an annotator to check only a small subset. The team tested it on toxicity classification, hunting human-defined slices in the Jigsaw dataset with a Llama 3.1 model. Uncertainty-based methods, which ask about the cases the system is least sure of, worked best across the representations and algorithms tried. On several slices they matched full-data accuracy while using only 2 to 10 percent of the slice membership labels, well ahead of random sampling.
arxiv-2511-20813:
Simon Hacks maps in 2025 the requirements for militaries adopting train-while-you-fight. The old maxim was train like you fight, rehearsing in peacetime; modern operations change too fast, with new weapons and procedures arriving mid-mission, as Ukraine's wartime learning showed. Train While You Fight demands continuous learning during operations, delivered by remote learning platforms working across allies under denied, degraded, or patchy connectivity.

Using design science, Hacks derives challenges from Partnership for Peace and NATO documents and identifies seven: modularity, interoperability, resilience, multilingual support, scalability, platform independence, and data security and privacy. He then maps each challenge to software engineering patterns. One strategy is a reach-back workflow, where field users send observations to a 24/7 triage cell that curates and injects updated content. The German armed forces' virtual learning environment, merging Moodle and ILIAS with access controls by clearance level, illustrates how the patterns combine nationally.
arxiv-2511-21013:
Ryosuke Kadono uses 2025 simulations to reinterpret a puzzling pattern in muon studies of battery materials. Muon spin relaxation probes how ions hop inside battery cathodes: implanted muons feel the ions' magnetic fields, and the signal's wobble rate is read as the ion jump rate. Many studies see an odd peak in that rate near some temperature, with the linewidth dropping above it.

He simulated spectra with an extended Kubo-Toyabe function that accounts for ion jumps, across 10 to 400 kelvin, then re-analysed them with the conventional function, mimicking earlier practice. The re-analysis reproduced the anomaly: it arises when the ion jump rate shoots up past the muon's jump rate as temperature climbs. The effect emerged with a linewidth of 0.3 megahertz and a correlation parameter of 0.8 in his runs. His advice: reanalyse vintage data with the extended function, and treat results showing no anomaly as silent about ion diffusion.
arxiv-2511-21413:
Tim Trappen, Robert Keßler, Roland Pabel, Viktor Achter, and Stefan Wesner retrofit a supercomputer for chatty AI workloads in 2025. Universities want to serve large language models to students and staff, and high-performance computing centers have the hardware, but classic supercomputer scheduling assumes batch jobs, not synchronous users waiting on replies. Their system runs the open-source vLLM inference engine on the supercomputer RAMSES, stitching together Slurm scheduling with Kubernetes orchestration.

Trappen and his coauthors add HPC-native pieces like Apptainer containers plus Prometheus and Grafana monitoring around custom microservices. Benchmarks on two hardware configurations show the architecture scaling efficiently at 100, 500, and 1000 concurrent requests. The integration costs only about 500 milliseconds of added end-to-end latency. The team presents the design as a production-ready, modular template for other centers facing the same demand.
arxiv-2511-21613:
Dongyang Fan, Diba Hashemi, Sai Praneeth Karimireddy, and Martin Jaggi show that the labels attached to training documents can teach language models faster, in 2025. Earlier work found that prepending a document's URL during pretraining accelerates learning, but nobody had mapped which other metadata helps. The team tested a wider range, from quality indicators to domain labels, varying both content and placement.

Fine-grained metadata won consistently: detailed quality scores and domain information sped training more than coarse signals, and the shared trait of every effective type was finer granularity, more specific information per document. Placement matters too. Appending metadata at the end, so the model must predict it as an auxiliary task, also accelerates pretraining, with the largest gains for fine-grained domain information. Even learnable meta-tokens trained with a masked loss recovered part of the speedup. Probing the model's internals, the authors distill practical guidelines for metadata design.
arxiv-2511-21813:
Böhm and colleagues survey hydrogen chloride, a chlorine-bearing molecule, in interstellar gas using the APEX telescope in Chile. Chlorine is rare and reactive, and the ratio of its two stable forms, chlorine-35 and chlorine-37, records the history of element-making in stars and supernovae. Before this survey, few sightlines had usable HCl measurements.

The team observed 28 high-mass star-forming regions at about 625 gigahertz, more than doubling the number of sources with HCl detections. They found the heavier form in all but two sources, and the measured isotope ratios ranged from 1.6 to 3.5 among the cleanest emission sources, matching models of how the Galaxy's chemistry evolved over time. The ratio showed no trend with distance from the Galactic centre, HCl turned up in outflows including explosive ones. The authors infer most Galactic chlorine was made when the Galaxy was poorer in heavy elements.
arxiv-2511-22013:
Cao, Li, and Siene, geometers, classify quasi-Einstein manifolds with harmonic Weyl curvature in dimensions five and higher. A quasi-Einstein manifold is a curved space whose Ricci curvature is balanced by a smooth potential function, generalizing Einstein manifolds from general relativity. Harmonic Weyl curvature is an extra symmetry-like condition on how the space's conformal bending varies from point to point. Together the conditions strongly restrict the possible shapes.

The classification extends Shin's four-dimensional result for quasi-Einstein manifolds and refines earlier work by He, Petersen, and Wylie on the general theory. As a byproduct, the authors construct new examples of quasi-Einstein manifolds that are neither locally conformally flat nor D-flat in the sense used by earlier authors. The examples show the classified family is genuinely richer than the previously known special cases, and they close off natural guesses about what such spaces must look like.
arxiv-2511-22713:
Karoliya, Tewari, and Sharma map where Majorana zero modes can live in graphene strips. Majorana modes are prized as building blocks for fault-tolerant topological quantum computation. Graphene nanoribbons, with tunable edges and planar compatibility, are an attractive alternative to semiconductor nanowires. The authors study finite graphene strips with armchair, zigzag, and nearly square geometries. The strips are proximitized by an s-wave superconductor under Rashba spin-orbit coupling, Zeeman fields, and disorder, by exact diagonalization of the Bogoliubov-de Gennes Hamiltonian.

Using Majorana polarization, low-energy spectra, and real-space wavefunctions together, they identify the genuinely topological phases and distinguish true Majorana zero modes from partially separated Andreev bound states, the quasi-Majorana impostors plaguing experiments. Charting robustness across geometries and disorder strengths, they find armchair strips with short zigzag edges provide the most stable Majorana platform. The unified diagnostics yield design guidelines for graphene-based topological superconductors.
arxiv-2511-22813:
Salomon proposes rebuilding neural networks around smarter neurons. Biological neurons keep internal states, choose which neurons to talk to, and self-organise into graphs, while artificial networks stack passive units in rigid layers. His Intelligent Neural Networks make each neuron an agent combining selective state-space dynamics, borrowed from Mamba models, deciding when to activate. Attention-based routing decides to whom signals go, all wired as a complete graph.

On the Text8 benchmark the design scored 1.705 bits per character, beating a comparable Transformer's 2.055 and matching a highly optimised LSTM. A parameter-matched stack of plain Mamba blocks failed to converge at all, above 3.4 bits per character, under the same protocol: the graph topology itself supplies stability. Ablations confirm it: removing inter-neuron communication degrades performance or destabilises training. Salomon argues neuron-centric design is not just bio-inspired decoration but computationally effective, pointing toward modular, interpretable architectures.
arxiv-2512-00113:
Neuromorphic processors copy some design ideas from the brain to run AI with very little power. Amirreza Yousefzadeh offers a tutorial on building scalable digital versions of them in 2025. The tutorial starts from RISC-V cores and moves toward arrays of neuromorphic units.

Digital neuromorphic chips suit low-power, always-on edge applications, such as sensors that must react without waking a larger system. The author lays out the main architectural design principles and illustrates them with the SENECA platform as a running example. New engineers entering the field get a guided path through the design choices involved. Tutorials like this one lower the entry barrier for a fast-moving hardware field.
arxiv-2512-00213:
Random connection models scatter points in space and link nearby pairs, forming clusters that can suddenly span the whole system. Mikhail Chebunin and Günter Last study the sharp phase transition in such a model in 2025. The points come from a Poisson process with a given intensity.

The authors derive exponential moment bounds for an arbitrary cluster when the intensity stays below a critical value. Strong bounds of this kind prove the transition is genuinely sharp, not gradual. These models describe wireless networks and material structures, so knowing exactly where giant clusters appear has practical as well as theoretical value. Exponential bounds are strong evidence, ruling out slowly growing giant clusters below threshold.
arxiv-2512-00613:
The Hubbard model is the simplest model that still captures how electron interactions create magnets and insulators. Fahad Equbal and Ahsan study the Mott crossover in the half-filled Hubbard model in 2025, resolved by spin. They use exact diagonalization on a small square cluster.

The crossover runs from a correlated metallic state to a Mott-insulating state as interaction strength grows. The authors examine both spin sectors and the entanglement between electrons. Even small clusters, solved exactly, benchmark the approximations used for real materials where no exact solution exists. Exact diagonalization is exact but tiny, which is why the small square cluster matters as a benchmark. Entanglement tracks how inseparable the electrons' states become across the crossover.
arxiv-2512-00813:
Savitha K S, Sandi Klavžar, and Tijo James study a two-player graph game in a 2025 paper. In the Maker-Breaker resolving game, two players take turns claiming unplayed vertices of a graph. One player, Resolver, wants to claim every vertex of some resolving set. A resolving set pins down all vertices by their distances to it.
