arxiv-2604-10413: Manabe, Shibata, Takamichi, and Aoki carry sign language feeling straight into spoken voice. Turning signs into plain text first drops the non verbal color that signing holds. Their new task, sign to speech prosody transfer, keeps global tone and stress in the spoken result. SignRecGAN trains from single mode sets with no paired sign speech labels, using adversarial training and rebuild losses. Tests show the speech mirrors the signed mood, and the team plans open code.
arxiv-2604-10513: David, Fournier, Limonad, and Mulian fix agent prompts without paying for fresh rollouts. Vague prompts send one agent down split paths with split results. Standard tuning pays twice: once to draft prompts, once to score them. Their SFA pipeline reads old traces, groups node outputs, and ranks meaning traits with a decision tree. Surviving traits enter the prompt as fixes, beating tuned rivals most where rollouts cost most.
arxiv-2604-10613: Arushi and Kumar introduce the first conformal finite-element framework for nonlinear collisional breakage equations. They describe how particles shatter when they hit each other, a process found across science and engineering. Earlier methods struggled in two and three dimensions, where moment sums, stability, and speed all grow harder. Their scheme pairs high-order Lagrange elements with BDF2 time steps and keeps total particle count and volume intact. Tests in one, two, and three dimensions show high accuracy and optimal convergence.
arxiv-2604-10913: Kiriki and three colleagues show that Lyapunov exponents can fail to exist throughout a dense subset of the Newhouse domain of surface maps. For any map in that subset, exponents fail for all points in some open set and every nonzero tangent vector in some open cone. This makes non-existence a persistent phenomenon under robust homoclinic tangencies, not an isolated quirk. The proof builds maps with particular oscillatory return times near a homoclinic tangency, using Newhouse theory and recent work on Lyapunov irregularity.
arxiv-2604-11313: Adhikary explores engineered non-Gaussian coherence as a fuel for quantum batteries. Building on his earlier scheme for generating non-Gaussian states, he tests how coherence in those states can lift battery performance across Gaussian charger profiles under unitary dynamics. Thermal broadening and environmental coupling to the charger are also examined as levers for stable performance under careful thermal management. In plain terms, the work asks whether quantum quirks can store and release energy better. The study is a proof of concept for using thermodynamic resources in quantum energy storage.
arxiv-2604-11813: Dossou-Olory, Andriantiana, Rakotonarivo, and Shozi study a ratio between two counts for a graph. The first counts one-nearly independent vertex subsets; the second is the Merrifield-Simmons index, which counts zero-nearly independent subsets. Building on earlier comparisons of these two quantities, they establish sharp lower and upper bounds for their ratio. Those bounds cover connected graphs, trees, and forests.
arxiv-2604-12513: Yves Ruffenach asks whether a language model can control itself from internal evidence. His model pairs local variational computation with a regulator that holds inner states steady. Checkpoint retention keeps useful past states. A controller uses uncertainty as a live signal, not just an after-the-fact readout. Uncertainty then steers training, retention, and inference-time action. The backbone beats a matched plain rival on language tasks. Its controller stays active with a favorable balance of quality and cost.
arxiv-2604-12613: Michal Czakon and three colleagues compute photon-pair production at next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order in QCD. Two isolated photons at the Large Hadron Collider matter for Higgs studies and new-physics searches. Percent-level theory would sharpen those measurements. This first N3LO calculation tests whether perturbation theory converges. It also shrinks theory error threefold, down to 3 percent. The result paves the way to improved analyses.
arxiv-2604-12813: Xinyue Li and five colleagues split video quality work into perception and calibration. Pretrained multimodal models already sense quality, but tuning them to new scenes costs heavy retraining. DPC-VQA freezes a multimodal model for a base score and adds a light branch for a residual fix. The split avoids full retraining and keeps performance reliable. On user-made and AI-made benchmarks, it matches strong baselines. It uses under 2 percent of standard parameters and stays effective with only 20 percent of labels.
arxiv-2604-13113: Abdullah extends the sigma index, the overall variance of a graph's degree sequence, to fuzzy graphs. She defines the fuzzy sigma index from fuzzy vertex degrees and fuzzy graph size, then proves its basic properties, including sharp lower and upper bounds. She also analyzes how the index behaves under standard fuzzy graph operations, laying a foundation for further work on variance-based topological indices in fuzzy graph theory.
arxiv-2604-13313: Im, Madhwal, and Gupta improve compositional understanding in vision-language models by mining harder contrastive negatives. Their ConcretePlant method targets highly concrete words, whose changes create sharper visual and structural contrasts, and their Cement loss uses a margin to rebalance gradients that easy pairs otherwise dominate. The combined Slipform framework reaches state-of-the-art accuracy across compositional benchmarks and also strengthens general cross-modal retrieval and linear probing.
arxiv-2604-13413: Fang and seven colleagues show that dataset-level metrics hide non-determinism in diffusion language models. Averaging sample quality across runs makes setups with similar total scores look alike, even when single inputs behave very differently. Their fine-grained evaluation tracks sample differences across guidance scale, diffusion steps, Monte Carlo sampling, batch size, and hardware. That spread proves widespread and structured, with code generation far more sensitive than question answering. Their Factor Variance Attribution metric splits observed spread across factor settings.
arxiv-2604-13913: Luo and Zhang prove the Hausdorff dimension of the graph of a random vector-valued Weierstrass function, built from cosine and sine series with random phase shifts. The dimension equals the smaller of two values set by the series' growth and decay rates, holding with probability one. Their result pins down the roughness of a jagged curve whose wiggles repeat at ever finer scales.
arxiv-2604-14113: Tang and colleagues make GUI grounding zoom adaptively instead of uniformly. UI-Zoomer treats both the zoom trigger and the zoom scale as uncertainty problems: a confidence gate blends agreement across random candidates with token-level confidence, firing only when localization is uncertain. An uncertainty-driven crop module then sizes each crop from prediction variance. Gains reach up to 13.4 percent across ScreenSpot-Pro, UI-Vision, and ScreenSpot-v2, with no extra training.
arxiv-2604-14213: Baddis and four colleagues run CUDA codes with Hamilton-Jacobi methods to study shadows of rotating charged Euler-Heisenberg black holes threaded by global monopoles. Shadow shape and energy emission both track the monopole strength, the electric charge, and the spin, while the Euler-Heisenberg nonlinear factor barely moves either. To square theory with Event Horizon Telescope shadow observations, the team uses its CUDA computations to set tight bounds. The bounds cover the monopole factor, the charge, and the spin.
arxiv-2604-14913: Banagl studies equivariant L-classes of Atiyah-Singer-Zagier type for singular spaces. If a finite group acts on a rational homology manifold, the orbit space is again one, but more singular spaces need care. He proves that when the G-space is a Witt pseudomanifold, including all singular complex pure-dimensional varieties, the orbit space is again one. In the compact oriented case this gives Goresky-MacPherson L-classes, and he builds equivariant ones computing the orbit space class through an averaging formula.
arxiv-2604-15013: Koh and four others present DEX-Mouse, a portable calibration-free interface with force feedback, built from off-the-shelf parts under 150 dollars. Dexterous hand manipulation needs large-scale consistent demonstrations, but simulation, video, and glove methods suffer sim-to-real gaps or per-operator calibration. The operator-agnostic design needs no calibration or change, and forearm mounting yields robot-aligned data. In user tests, the attached setup reached 86.67 percent completion and reduced workload versus separated setups. Hardware, software, bill of materials and firmware are open-sourced.
arxiv-2604-15113: Snyder and colleagues present HyperSpace, a modular framework for spatial coding in hyperdimensional vector systems. It splits vector symbolic architectures into plug-in operators. Encoding, binding, and bundling join similarity, cleanup, and regression as separate modules. Tests on two backends show similarity and cleanup dominate run time in spatial tasks, leaving the two systems roughly even end to end. Memory use differs, though, with HRR needing about half the memory of FHRR vectors.
arxiv-2604-15413: Igoshin and seven colleagues adapt the optical theorem, which ties a scatterer's extinction cross section to how strongly it scatters forward, to acoustics. Their method survives real-world limits such as finite sources, weak scattered signals, and imperfect echo-free rooms. On a Helmholtz resonator, it finds one strong resonance near 2000 Hz whose place, height, and shape match full-wave simulations.
arxiv-2604-15513: Chen and three colleagues present Divide and Truncate, a unified scheme coupling multi-physics systems through penetration-free contact handling across rigid bodies, soft volumes, thin shells, rods, and animated objects. Space is split into separate zones, and moves are cut short to stay in their zone, which ensures contact with no penetration. A planar variant restricts only motion toward nearby surfaces, fixing artificial damping and deadlock while staying material- and solver-agnostic.
arxiv-2604-15613: Silva presents Green-ELM, a non-iterative neural design that swaps gradient-based output training for a closed-form analytic solve over fixed random features. Projecting inputs into a high-dimensional random feature space untangles complex class boundaries without backpropagation. With Moore-Penrose, LU, and Cholesky solves, it hits 98.10 percent on MNIST and 86.63 percent on Fashion-MNIST, training 11.6 times faster than an SGD baseline on CPU.
arxiv-2604-15713: Kappelmann and five colleagues study full, lean type tags for rank-one polymorphic lambda terms as used in Isabelle, building on Smolka, Blanchette, and co-workers. They give a full formal spec with proofs, all built in Isabelle/HOL. A human and an LLM agent each draft pen-and-paper proofs on their own, and the agent turns both into Isabelle form, with human hints honing and widening the work.
arxiv-2604-15913: Minotti and Modanese apply the fluctuation-dissipation theorem to Aharonov-Bohm electrodynamics, which unlike Maxwell theory allows local non-conservation of charge. For non-conserved charges at thermal equilibrium, they recover the same spectral energy distribution as Maxwell theory. The electric share of that energy doubles, however, while the magnetic share matches Maxwell, with the excess balanced by a negative term from the Aharonov-Bohm scalar field. For a conductor described by the gamma model, they derive a current correlation spectrum adding violet noise to classical Johnson-Nyquist white noise.
arxiv-2604-16213: Frazier, Damevski, and Pollock study conversational agents for secondary students learning AP Computer Science Principles. Students often turn to web tutorials and question sites, but struggle to find material matched to their task and background. The authors compare general chat agents with custom fixed-response agents built for CSP students, using classroom trials with 45 high school students across six sections, and assess help, effectiveness, and engagement.
arxiv-2604-16313: Wu and ten colleagues present MARA, a framework for answering questions over documents with text and images. Current methods use query-blind document views and a fixed top-k choice of proof. They miss salient content, and fail when relevant proof spreads unevenly. MARA adapts both finding and writing to the query. A region encoder reweights multi-level document views by query fit. A proof controller checks whether proof is enough during writing, and adjusts the choice as needed.
arxiv-2604-16513: Prasad and Mahapatra tackle digitizing piping and instrumentation diagrams, where the field shares one public benchmark of just 12 annotated images. Template generators scatter symbols at random, making graphs unlike real plants and scoring only about a third correct on edge detection. Their SynthPID corpus holds 665 synthetic diagrams whose pipe topology is seeded from real drawings. With a Relationformer, a model trained on SynthPID reached about 64 percent edge accuracy without seeing a real diagram, close to the oracle, though gains flattened beyond roughly 400 images.
arxiv-2604-17113: Amudon, Pandey, and Ganesh study how heat changes the Buneman instability, a plasma instability long studied for its anomalous resistivity. Kinetic calculations show growth rates differing sharply from fluid models, both cold and warm, and from linearized kinetic models. The work recovers the known cube-root dependence of the maximum growth rate, and finds that rate nearly independent of the ion-electron temperature ratio. It also shows ion density lumpiness controlling how beam energy heats the bulk plasma.
arxiv-2604-17213: Ouyang, Liu, and Mallada argue that data-efficient control needs bias from physical law itself, not just smoothness assumptions that demand growing data. For Hamiltonian systems, they exploit symplectic geometry and recurrence on energy level sets to solve target reachability. Their approach pairs recurrence with chain policies, which compose segments from demonstrations into target paths. They give reachability conditions and show data needs depend on geometric and recurrence features of the Hamiltonian rather than state size.
arxiv-2604-17313: Mishra, Varshney, and Sahithi built GuardPhish, a set of 70,015 phishing prompts drawn from real web, email, text, and voice scams, to test open-source language models run offline. Models that spotted phishing intent up to 96 percent of the time still produced usable scam content from the same prompts, with voice attacks succeeding up to 98.5 percent of the time in the worst cases. The authors also trained small filter models on the set that blocked such prompts with strong accuracy without changing the underlying model.
arxiv-2604-17913: Nicoletti and three colleagues build a physics-based model of seismic radiation from water-sediment flows in gravel-bed rivers. It tracks individual particles, computes forces from grain-scale impacts and rolling, and adds broadband turbulence plus vortex shedding in the water column. Synthetic signals travel to receivers through a Rayleigh-wave Green's function, yielding ground-velocity estimates. Applied to a flood in a Tuscan Apennines torrent, the model matches observed frequency bands and separates particle-collision effects from turbulent-flow effects in river seismic noise.
arxiv-2604-18413: Pu, Li, and Chen present a TypeScript parser that speeds code indexing for language-model coding agents. Graph-based indexes preserve call chains that keyword search misses, but existing parsers bottleneck on per-symbol language-server calls. Built on the TypeScript Compiler API, the new parser works directly with compiler trees, semantics, and module resolution. Tests on three open-source TypeScript codebases of up to 1.2 million lines show reliable indexes produced far more efficiently.
arxiv-2604-18613: Napolitano and three colleagues introduce the Lund Plane to Bloch encoding, mapping a clean picture of jet motion into qubits. With it, they build a Quantum Tree-Topology Network holding the Lund tree levels. The QTTN matches large classical designs like LundNet on spin tagging, with decent W boson and top quark scores. It needs three orders fewer knobs. The QTTN beats older methods in the low-data regime and leans less on maker's own shower and hadron-making models. Tested on a 3-qubit SpinQ device.
arxiv-2604-19713: Cavalieri and Fulghesu describe the integral Chow rings for spaces of degree 2 maps from smooth rational curves into projective space. Their account takes the form of a quotient of a polynomial ring in three unknowns. As the target size varies, the relations display rich combinatorial structure, with every nontrivial one captured by two generating functions that are rational functions.
arxiv-2604-20813: Medhanie and Ni bring TrOCR to printed Tigrinya first, in the Ge'ez script. From a pre-trained model, they widen the BPE tokenizer for 230 Ge'ez characters and add Word-Aware Loss Weighting against word-boundary failures from Latin BPE conventions. After adaptation, the TrOCR-Printed variant achieves 0.22 percent Character Error Rate and about 97 percent match accuracy on GLOCR synthetic images. Ablation shows Word-Aware Loss Weighting is the critical piece, cutting CER by two orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2604-20913: Zuo and colleagues present FairyFuse, a CPU inference system for ternary language models whose weights take only minus one, zero, or plus one. It fuses the subcomputations of each layer into one AVX-512 loop of masked additions and subtractions, using no floating-point multiplications at all. Kernel speed rises about 30 times on bandwidth-limited CPUs, and end-to-end it reaches 32.4 tokens each second on one Intel Xeon chip with near-lossless quality.
arxiv-2604-21213: Rishad Shahmurov studies two pinch mechanisms in smooth, swirling Navier-Stokes flow that could drive a finite-time blowup. A signed squeeze balance gives rules for when solutions persist, with a universal factor on the critical diagonal. A sliding shift rule separately hits the endpoint mark, while a pulse train shows end-only control falls short. Together they force any blowup to dodge a whole family of critical detectors.
arxiv-2604-21413: Fabian Wenz, Felix Treutwein, Çagatay Demiralp, and Michael Stonebraker argue that delegating enterprise queries entirely to a frontier language model is the wrong abstraction for messy corporate data. Their RUBICON system instead constrains each source behind a query interface and integrates through a table-centric layer driven by a query processor. On RUBICON-Bench it reaches 100 percent end-to-end accuracy where every agentic baseline scores zero. On SemBench it beats LOTUS and Palimpzest by 14.7 percent accuracy, with about 63 percent lower latency and about 99 percent lower token cost.
arxiv-2604-21513: Giulia Salatino and four colleagues map nonequilibrium states in long-range dissipative systems via jump stats. While Lindblad motion gives steady-state values, path study reveals spatial and time links. On a model with a paramagnetic-to-ferromagnetic shift, they study counting stats of jumps with a Lindbladian approach. They combine cluster mean-field and cumulant sums for short- and long-range links, plus waiting times. Jump links show phase signs and dynamic features across the shift, showing trajectory-resolved signals of collective motion in open systems.
arxiv-2604-22113: Omel'chenko and Laing study ring networks of theta neurons with delayed links, described by new neural field models. They cover spread delays with finite and infinite support, plus signal delays. Even and local bump states stay stable until delay parameters vary, when Hopf splits create traveling waves and breathing bumps. These moving solutions satisfy self-check rules, which the authors solve fast. Tracking waves and repeating solutions as parameters vary shows how delays shape pattern growth in wide theta-neuron networks.
arxiv-2604-22213: Read and four colleagues map the nearby universe with caustic skeleton theory. That theory traces where matter folds into sheets and filaments. Their three-dimensional skeleton matches the observed layout of galaxies around the Coma Cluster and the Pisces-Perseus ridge. It also splits two filament types that look alike but form in different ways. Pisces-Perseus proves dominated by the D4 type, unlike the structure around Coma.
arxiv-2604-22413: Hou and Tang study a failure mode of graph transformers: some tasks need long-range communication, others local interaction. They define distance-misaligned training on a synthetic benchmark: a mismatch between where label information lies and where the model sends communication. They find the preferred distance bias shifts with task locality. An oracle adaptive controller nearly matches the best fixed bias and strongly beats a neutral baseline on mixed and local tasks. A task-agnostic zero-gap controller is weaker, showing adaptation alone is not enough. The control target matters.
arxiv-2604-22513: Protogeros and three colleagues present Cornetto, the first benchmark grading language-model repair of network configurations by function and at scale. Fixing large, linked configurations is risky because a repair can break other parts. Cornetto pairs a generator that synthesizes plausible misconfiguration cases with formal verification checking each proposed fix against ground-truth specs. The released set holds 231 problems across networks of 20 to 754 nodes and varied protocols. Testing 9 leading models, the authors find promise but frequent regressions and fading performance as networks grow.
arxiv-2604-22913: Dittmann and Cantiello add accretion feedback to models of stars in the disks of active galactic nuclei, where gas inflow can reshape stellar structure. Energy released by infalling gas limits how fast stars can accrete, a brake ignored in earlier calculations. Their semi-analytical survey of many disk conditions finds feedback caps accretion, kills runaway growth, and widens the range where stars settle into long-lived equilibria. With gap opening included, feedback also cuts accretion and mass-loss rates sharply, raising equilibrium masses, radii, and luminosities.
arxiv-2604-23113: Liu and nine colleagues tackle detail hallucinations in language models reading long regulatory texts: small errors in thresholds, units, scopes, and conditions that look plausible yet corrupt key facts. They sort the errors into five types and build DetailBench from 172 real and 150 synthetic documents. Their method, DetailDPO, trains on pairs differing in exactly one detail, focusing learning on detail-bearing tokens. Tests on Qwen2.5 and Llama models cut the detail error rate by 42 to 61 percent, with transfer to finance and medicine.
arxiv-2604-23213: Eaves presents minimal seeds, the smallest disturbances that tip the Stokes boundary layer into turbulence. In this oscillating flow above a flat plate, seed paths ride large early linear transient growth, yet only 73 percent of the initial energy sits in the linearly optimal growing mode. The rest drives nonlinear transfer from spanwise- to streamwise-independent structures and covers a timing gap between transient growth's end and the edge state's production phase. The edge state is the saddle point dividing laminar and turbulent basins.
arxiv-2604-23513: Dong and seven colleagues build a language-model driver aid for dense mixed traffic, where timid defaults and misread intentions cause trouble. Their system models scenes in plain concepts, reads both stated and hinted intentions of nearby drivers, and picks moves that are both safe and efficient. Final choices go out as short messages to nearby road users, and simulator tests beat older baselines.
arxiv-2604-23613: Ye establishes convergence guarantees with high probability for random zeroth-order gradient descent, which optimises using only function values rather than gradients. For smooth, strongly convex problems the classic two-query method reaches near-optimality with high probability at a cost that adds only a logarithmic dependence on the confidence level over the average-case bound. A stochastic version under bounded noise needs only modest extra cost for the same reliability.
arxiv-2604-23813: Guo, Shi, Zeng, Hu, Lin, Zhuo, Chen, Gu, and Ma present ShredBench, a benchmark for piecing texts back from shreds. An auto pipeline renders shredded texts from Markdown. It spans four cases and three shred levels, using fresh sources to avoid training-data leaks. Top models handle intact texts well but falter sharply as shredding rises. The gap exposes weak fine-grained cross-modal links.
arxiv-2604-24013: Karim and five colleagues introduce CommFuse, a method that hides the tail latency found in overlap methods for distributed language-model training. It swaps reduce-scatter and all-gather collectives for split peer-to-peer exchanges and interleaves split computation at fine grain. The method works with data-parallel and several tensor-parallel schemes and gives lower latency, better hardware use, and higher throughput in tests.
arxiv-2604-24213: Arrechea, Barceló, and Jannes extend the Harmonic Background Paradigm, in which gravity bends a deeper causality that always contains it in a cone hierarchy. Earlier work covered the idea only in the linear case. Here the authors conjecture its extension to the full nonlinear regime, linking the cone hierarchy to screening, where negative-energy clouds surround but never overcome positive-energy seeds. Ball-shaped matter cases show the idea, and the paper closes with ideas beyond General Relativity.
arxiv-2604-24513: Waldorf builds a full theory of adjusted connections for non-abelian bundle gerbes, structures from higher gauge theory that resisted treatment outside a narrow flat sector. Adjusted structure, an extra layer on the underlying 2-groups, lets his theory sort these connections by an adjusted form of non-abelian differential cohomology. The payoff is a clean, coordinate-free restatement of a lifting theorem linking such gerbe connections to connections on abelian bundle 2-gerbes.
arxiv-2604-24613: Fan, Liao and Ma model nucleon decays into one lepton plus two non-strange mesons. Such decays would probe whether baryon number can change. They correlate two-body and three-body processes within low-energy effective field theory. They do not assume a single operator dominates. Their bounds on 15 three-body modes are tighter. Charged-lepton limits improve by more than three orders of magnitude over Particle Data Group values. Five neutrino modes gain first lower lifetime limits. Two-body constraints also sharpen.
arxiv-2604-24913: Lemaitre and Lessler adapt diffusion models to flu outlooks. Influpaint encodes seasons as images, with pixel intensity for cases. It learns patterns from clinic data and simulated paths. Forecasting becomes making from partial data. It generates lifelike, varied paths with strong scores. In real-time CDC tests across 2023 to 2025, scores rose each season. The best training mix used 30 percent clinic data and 70 percent simulated data.
arxiv-2604-25013: Moreno-Insertis, Priest and Nóbrega-Siverio study singular ambipolar diffusion with 1D Cartesian solutions. They seek answers near null points, characterise eigenmodes, and propose ambipolar-diffusion solver tests for MHD codes. Direct work yields a stagnation flow with flux transfer across three regions. The regions are outer advection, inner ambipolar region, and a deepest Ohmic region. In the last, flux loss occurs at a rate set by advection. Both even and odd eigenmodes appear, with sharp current sheets at the inner nulls. The Bifrost code reproduces eigenmode behaviour.
arxiv-2604-25313: Ju, Wang and Zhang introduce Faithfulness-QA, a 99,094-sample data set built by counterfactual entity substitution for context-faithful RAG models. RAG models often answer from memory rather than context. From SQuAD and TriviaQA, they identify entities and replace them with alternatives from a 76,953-entity bank, manufacturing conflicts between context and parametric memory. Quality filtering ensures 100 percent pass rates across four checks. They release the data set, pipeline and entity bank covering eight categories, as a training resource and benchmark.
arxiv-2604-25513: Luo, Wei and Zhou show that a curved surface in hyperbolic space keeps its positive sectional curvature as it shrinks. It ends as a round point after finite time. That staying power holds for a broad family of shrinking motions, where speed grows in step with the surface's main bending measures and meets set conditions. The family even contains the kth mean curvature motion as one member, so the round point result covers a familiar case too.
arxiv-2604-26013: Dedin Neto and four colleagues constrain neutrino millicharge with supernova time-of-flight data. A millicharged neutrino in magnetic fields feels a small Lorentz-force deflection and a geometric time delay. That delay scales as charge squared over energy squared, like the mass-induced delay. The authors translate supernova mass limits into millicharge limits with a magnetic delay kernel, extending the SN1987A estimate. Bounds run from about 10^-17 e for SN1987A down to the low 10^-19 e range for future bursts, with optimistic combinations nearing 10^-20 e.
arxiv-2604-26613: Wedemeyer, Mitsos, and Dahmen examine a heuristic for robust multi-energy system design that iteratively adds extreme scenarios to the design problem. They show that piecewise-linear inflow-outflow relations, minimum part-loads, and storage complementarity can each break the heuristic when surplus energy cannot be curtailed. With curtailment allowed, storage complementarity stays safe and convex piecewise-linear relations reformulate linearly, but minimum part-loads can still cause failure. In a case study, raising representative scenarios from four to six or eight yields robust designs.
arxiv-2604-26713: Kourliouros, Longo, and Rasmussen study invariant sets of certain nonautonomous differential inclusions, which arise in random and control dynamics and in uncertainty spread. Each one gets a boundary system of differential equations. Its backward unit normal cones lift its fixed sets in one way, becoming fully fixed when the boundary is smooth. They test the method on minimal attractors of linear systems. When the base problem is exponentially stable, one minimal attractor exists for systems whose boundaries are fiber by fiber strictly convex, closed, and smooth.
arxiv-2604-26913: Bresch studies computation of the generalized operator norm and maximizing a Rayleigh quotient, using only forward runs of two linear operators. His method samples search directions evenly from the unit sphere, avoiding tangent-space sampling and access to the metric matrix. Each line search reduces to a 2 by 2 eigenvalue problem on Gram matrices, whose maximizing step has a closed form usually. He proves objective values converge almost surely to the largest eigenvalue, with iterates closing on the leading eigenspace. Tests on Gaussian operators show good convergence barely tied to size.
arxiv-2604-27013: Ahmed and twenty-three colleagues outline the Barcelona Zetascale Lab's pre-silicon checking method for RISC-V chip designs. It joins three platforms: a UVM setup checking RTL function, an FPGA setup for system hardware checks, and a CI/CD flow that builds, deploys, and tests. Run in an industrial loop on large CPU and FPGA hardware, the flow supports growth of hardware and software work. The authors present it as a scalable base for correctness and a key support for European programs such as EPI and DARE.
arxiv-2604-27113: Shetgaonkar and Sharma build a two-host model of disease spread by biting vectors, such as insects that feed on more than one host species. Their model links host diversity, shifting feeding choices, and transmission, showing that host numbers alone cannot predict the outcome. A critical threshold marks whether a shift in feeding choice raises or lowers disease in a focal host, giving a basis for forecasting how control measures change the burden.
arxiv-2604-27613: Lin and three colleagues present AMGenC, a generative inverse design method for amorphous matter that guarantees samples with even charge. Unlike crystals with small unit cells, amorphous matter needs large simulation cells with hundreds to thousands of atoms. Generative design aims to output matter matching desired traits, beating trial and error, but unconstrained element assignments often yield charge-unbalanced matter. AMGenC centers generation on charge balance through element noise, plus a soft per-step projection and a closing discrete projection steering elements to exact balance.
arxiv-2604-27713: Baldwin and Ghanavati present an agentic framework that builds knowledge graphs from AI policy documents and fetches policy-relevant information for answering questions. They build graphs from three AI risk-related policies under two ontology schemas and test five language models on 42 policy questions spanning six reasoning types. Graph augmentation lifts scores across all five models, and an open schema found by models matches or beats the formal ontology. The work links policy documents to answers through structured, retrievable knowledge.
arxiv-2604-27813: Hill builds a block bootstrap max-test that hunts for real predictors when candidates dwarf the sample. The test copes with weakly linked and uneven data, even drifting data, and screens links one by one. By judging only the largest statistic, it skips covariance guessing and re-sampling tricks, dodging cherry-picked predictor choice and post-hoc corrections. Its limit law is tamed by a wild block bootstrap, and it holds size. It spots faint, sparse signals, and Hill tries it on fake data and the VIX gauge.
arxiv-2605-00313:
Guillaume Lambard argues that AI-driven materials discovery is stuck on the wrong target. Computer searches have proposed thousands of candidate structures, yet few can actually be made in a laboratory, a blockage he calls the synthesizability gap. His perspective piece calls for a synthesis-first approach, where the recipe is a primary design variable alongside the structure.

The roadmap rests on three pillars. First, write synthesis procedures as machine-readable protocols. Second, use generative and inverse-design models to propose workable reaction pathways and recipes. Third, close the loop with optimization checked against real experiments and sustainability limits. Lambard also discusses standards and self-driving laboratories, aiming at materials discovery that is reproducible and grounded in how things are truly made.
arxiv-2605-00413:
Hongyan Gao and 5 co-authors fuzz the Rust compiler by asking a language model to complete masked pieces of real, historically buggy programs. Rust is prized for memory and thread safety in critical systems, so its compiler must be trustworthy. Yet Rust's strict syntax means model-generated test programs are usually invalid, and blind generation wastes effort.

Their strategy, clozeMask, mines test code from past compiler bug reports, masks out snippets with particular structures, and has the model fill the blanks. The results stay close to programs that once triggered real bugs, which makes them sharp test material. Their prototype found twenty-seven confirmed bugs across two Rust compilers, ten already fixed by developers. It also beat existing fuzzers on code coverage and bug-finding effectiveness in their experiments.
arxiv-2605-00513:
Ta Thanh Thuy and 8 co-authors introduce ControBench, a benchmark for studying how people argue across ideological divides online. Earlier datasets each miss a piece: some keep the text but not the interaction structure, some model structure without rich meaning, and some lose a stable read on each user's ideology. ControBench combines all three in one resource built from Reddit debates.

The benchmark covers three topics, Trump, abortion, and religion, with thousands of users, posts, and tens of thousands of interactions. Edges between users carry the parent comment being answered, preserving the local shape of an argument. Ideology labels come from users' self-declared flairs, which avoids hand annotation. Mixing across camps is high, as in real debate. Graph networks, pretrained language models, and large language models show distinct performance patterns, especially where ideological boundaries blur.
arxiv-2605-01013:
Ryan and two co-authors model current flow in binary electrolytes where the two ion types carry different valences, a feature that affects reverse electrodialysis cells, batteries, and supercapacitors. Their steady one-dimensional Poisson-Nernst-Planck model imposes constant ionic fluxes and varies them in a general asymmetric electrolyte. Simulations reveal a smooth shift between near-equilibrium and strongly non-equilibrium regimes.

The regimes meet at a valence-dependent middle current where the classical Debye-scale boundary layer vanishes. Asymptotic analysis recovers known limiting results where they apply and gives correct shift results where neither applies. Hidden and explicit solutions are provided for several valence ratios, and a collapsed phase diagram predicts qualitative behavior from charges and fluxes.
arxiv-2605-01313:
Michael Chiwere, Daniel Fortunato, and Grady B Wright look at how weather-style models of shallow water flow on a globe fill in values between grid points. Their model class allows big time steps, but it has long used simple low-order filling while the rest of the model is highly accurate.

The team adds a spectral filling method, which uses smooth wave patterns and so matches the accuracy of the rest of the model. A fast transform keeps the total cost about the same as before. On standard test cases, and over long runs, the new model is more accurate, keeps mass and energy better, and blurs sharp features less. The result suggests global flow models should fill in values at the same high standard they use elsewhere.
arxiv-2605-01513:
Zixi Shao and four co-authors design full-length messenger RNA in one generative pass. A good therapeutic transcript must stay stable inside cells and also translate into protein efficiently, and older tools build it region by region, search at high cost, or retrain for each target.

Their framework, ProMORNA, follows the modern language model recipe. A BART-style model is pre-trained on over six million natural protein-to-message pairs. It is then post-trained in two stages: guided fine-tuning, then multi-objective reinforcement learning that scores each goal on its own scale before blending. In computer tests it pushes past leading baselines on the stability-versus-output frontier. In three lab tests with a reporter gene, its best candidate held activity far longer than the standard benchmark, with a strong edge over the prior best method left as exploratory.
arxiv-2605-01613:
Stefan J Hofmeister follows high-speed solar wind streams on their trip from near the Sun to Earth's orbit, using three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations. Space weather hinges on these streams, yet what a probe measures at one point may not say what the stream itself is doing.

Tracking both the global shape and single plasma parcels, he finds streams do not preserve their parcels. Peak speed, density, or temperature readings do not tag fixed material, so trends built on features can mislead. Speed-based relations link parcels across distances more safely. Where fast wind rams slow wind, compression slows the fast, hurries the slow, and heats both. A boundary layer near the Sun can dominate narrow streams and bias readings low. Sideways flows shuffle mass and flux across latitudes, and the stream's punch at Earth depends strongly on where it is sampled.
arxiv-2605-01913:
Sadia Asif and Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri study why fine-tuning a safety-aligned language model for a new task often weakens its refusal of harmful requests. Earlier work showed safety traits sit in structured patterns inside the model. The authors trace what fine-tuning does to those patterns and find steady drift, warped geometry, and clash between task learning and safety traits.

Based on that account, they propose RefusalGuard, a method that holds safety-related parts of the hidden state stable while letting other directions learn the new task. Tests cover LLaMA, Gemma, and Qwen models on attack sets and normal tasks. RefusalGuard kept attack success near the base aligned models while keeping task performance competitive.
arxiv-2605-02213:
Xuyao Yu, Zijun Gong, and Zhilu Lai design pilot patterns for channel estimation in OFDM systems over channels that vary in both time and frequency. Pilot placement matters for fast-moving uses in 5G-Advanced and 6G, and recent work on related modulation has renewed interest. The authors seek patterns that minimise estimation error under a linear minimum mean square error estimator, on a finite time-frequency grid.

They frame the design as an optimal sensor selection problem and propose two heuristic algorithms. Both start with an initial pattern and refine it by local swaps. One uses convex relaxation with randomised rounding, and the other uses greedy selection. On practical resource block sizes, both beat standard rectangular and diamond lattice patterns.
arxiv-2605-02513:
Edoardo Trombin and five co-authors design a gait planner for lower-limb exoskeletons that must handle more than flat floors. Such devices can help people with movement impairments walk again, but most current systems assume even ground. A useful planner must adapt steps to slopes, stairs, and obstacles in real time, while keeping motion natural and safe for the wearer.

Their method learns a probabilistic model of human gait from a few demonstrations, in both joint and task terms. A camera that senses depth supplies scene data, and the learned path is reshaped as a constrained optimization with set waypoints. Tests in simulation cover flat ground, slopes, stairs, and crossings. Trials on a commercial exoskeleton then check that the method holds up on real hardware.
arxiv-2605-02613:
Gordon J Ross and Isabella Deutsch introduce a new statistical model for events that arrive in bursts, tuned to how message cascades actually unfold. In a standard Hawkes process, every event boosts the rate of later events by the same rule. In a group chat, though, a cascade starter and a later joiner do not play the same role, so equal impact is a poor fit.

Their Ancestor Hawkes process lets an event's influence depend on its origin within a cluster. Applied to data from a nine-person group chat, the model reveals individual response preferences that the standard model misses. Only the sender and the time of each message are used, not its content, so the analysis stays privacy-conscious. The authors point to uses in studying hidden interaction structure and personal notification settings.
arxiv-2605-02713:
Gabriele Bellerino and Angelika Rohde extend limit theory for sums built along stationary Gaussian Markov processes, with an eye on the mixing time. Classic results assume the observation window is far longer than the time a chain needs to forget its start. When that fails, approximation quality is doubtful, even if the chain starts from its steady law, and applied work often sits in exactly that zone.

Working with triangular arrays of such processes, the authors prove quantitative and functional limit theorems when the mixing time is smaller than, comparable to, or larger than the sample size. The main finding is a phase change when the two scales match. New limit processes appear at and before the mixing time, and their links to each other are identified. The work maps a regime classic theory skipped.
arxiv-2605-03013:
Aaron Kleger, Nikolay Gnezdilov, and Rufus Boyack present a small-scale theory of incoherent metals. These are the strange normal state found above the superconducting transition. The state appears in cuprates, heavy-fermion compounds, and twisted bilayer graphene. In that state, electrons do not behave as the tidy quasiparticles of Fermi-liquid theory, and transport has resisted a non-perturbative account for decades.

Their model couples fermions to quantum-critical bosons with spatially random strength, in two dimensions, and is treated without assuming weak coupling. From it they derive a transport formula linking resistivity to quasiparticle lifetime outside the standard Boltzmann frame. The theory also reproduces two known violations: of the usual resistivity ceiling, and of a celebrated bound on the ratio of viscosity to entropy density. Incoherent transport gets a concrete microscopic home.
arxiv-2605-03213:
Javad Forough, Marios Kogias, and Hamed Haddadi survey confidential computing as a hardware shield for AI agents that handle secrets. Agents that plan, call tools, keep memory, and delegate to peers gather credentials and sensitive context across systems no single party controls.

Software-only defenses can be bypassed by a privileged attacker, so the survey maps trusted execution environments as a root of trust. It compares six hardware platforms, builds an agent-focused threat model across five layers, reviews which defenses transfer from single calls, and lists six open problems. No full end-to-end framework for production agents exists yet.
arxiv-2605-03313:
Nawapon Sangsiri and Yufei Tao study distributed learning when clients deliberately distort the gradients they return, a common privacy move. Each reply can stray arbitrarily from the true gradient within a set distance bound, and the server must still learn a convex, smooth function.

They ask two basic questions: how small can the final excess error be, and how many queries suffice to reach a given error? The answers are tight feasibility thresholds for the error gap, plus algorithms that meet those thresholds with proven query counts. The results map the true cost of adversarial gradient noise.
arxiv-2605-03413:
Doojin Baek, Gyubin Lee, Junyeob Baek, Hosung Lee, and Sungjin Ahn propose learning explicit theories of the world from raw observation, rather than only learning to predict what comes next. Human children build internal theories of how things work before mature language, and the authors take that as the model for machine understanding.

Their Neural Theorizer induces latent programs in a learned language of thought and runs them through a shared transition model. Because theories are compositional programs, their parts recombine to explain new phenomena. Experiments show explanation-driven generalization, where observations are understood through the programs that could generate them.
arxiv-2605-03713:
Ruihao Li, Andrew Jacob, Neeraja J. Yadwadkar, and Lizy K. John characterize SPEC CPU2026, the newest version of the standard benchmark suite for processor performance. Although accelerators dominate artificial intelligence work, central processors still run latency-sensitive and everyday services, so benchmark changes matter. The team asks what the new suite changes about architectural conclusions.

They measure the suite on nine recent Intel, AMD, Ampere, and Nvidia platforms. Compared with SPEC CPU2017, the 2026 suite raises instruction volume, memory footprint, and instruction-cache stress. Against datacenter and machine learning suites, it stays a complementary general-purpose benchmark: closer to datacenter frontend pressure than before, yet less vector-heavy than MLPerf and less frontend-extreme than DCPerf.
arxiv-2605-03813: Andrew J. Soto Levins and Ryan Watson introduce and study large homomorphisms on the homotopy Lie coalgebra, a variant of the large homomorphisms earlier defined by Levin. Their work in this algebraic setting yields new cases of a homotopy Lie coalgebra analogue of a conjecture of Quillen, as proposed by Briggs. The paper stays focused on the definition itself and the cases of the conjecture it settles.
arxiv-2605-04013:
Francisco M. Castro-Macías and five co-authors present Conditional Diffusion Sampling. It draws samples from unnormalized multimodal distributions when density checks are limited. Successful approaches build a bridge between a tractable reference law and the target. Parallel tempering is the gold standard. Diffusion-based methods offer a continuous path instead. They cost neural training. The goal is fast, exact sampling.

The authors derive conditional interpolants. These are stochastic processes whose transport follows an exact closed-form differential equation. No neural fit is needed. Starting them is nontrivial. But theory and experiments show its cost shrinks for short diffusion times. Their two-stage method runs parallel tempering to sample the initial distribution. It then transports samples with the exact dynamics. That couples tempering's global search with efficient local transport.
arxiv-2605-04313:
Zhi Xu and Yun Fu introduce a benchmark for testing whether language models can reason about cause and effect when the evidence is messy. Models often confuse correlation with causation, especially when some observations are wrong or irrelevant details are present.

Each test case starts from a known causal graph and adds controlled noise, such as distractors, changed values, hidden common causes, or missing observations. The authors also propose a framework that asks the model to extract variables and build a graph first, then reasons from that structure. Their design separates clean causal logic from coping with noise.
arxiv-2605-04413:
Pengcheng Tan, Jiang Chen, and Dehui Du ask when what-if questions can be answered from data once a common simplifying assumption is dropped. Causal models often assume each mechanism responds in one fixed direction to hidden factors. But in physical contact, the same push can produce opposite responses in different situations.

Their model class keeps a triangular structure. It replaces the one-way rule with two demands: each mechanism can be run backward, and those backward maps obey a matching rule. They prove these conditions are exactly what guarantees that what-if answers can be fully pinned down. They also show that weaker local backward runs are not enough. A neural implementation gains more as the test mechanisms become less monotone.
arxiv-2605-04713:
Alexander Vedernikov studies whether a harmful subject can be removed from an already-trained engagement model without retraining it from scratch. Engagement data sets are organised by subject and often carry noisy, subjective labels, so curators may later decide some subjects should never have been included.

His protocol ranks subjects by a model-dependent harmfulness proxy. It then applies a lightweight approximate unlearning update. It compares the result against an oracle retrained only on the retained subjects. The study uses two public data sets and one fixed recognition platform. It compares baseline, unlearned, and oracle models under the same removal case. That judges how close cheap unlearning gets to the oracle.
arxiv-2605-05113:
Mariia Seleznova asks how long the infinite-width approximation stays trustworthy in recurrent models as sequences grow long. Signal propagation theory usually assumes unlimited width, yet modern recurrent models run at finite width over very long inputs. Seleznova derives exact finite-width formulas for hidden-state signal energies in linear recurrences started from complex Gaussian weights.

Those formulas reveal three regimes set by how depth compares with the square root of width. Below that scale the infinite-width picture holds, near it a new joint scaling limit appears, and far above it finite-width effects dominate. The results pinpoint where standard initialisation schemes such as Glorot start to become unstable.
arxiv-2605-05213:
Sicong Chang and nine co-authors predict chronic rhinosinusitis, a common inflammatory sinus disorder, from routine electronic health records before diagnosis. The condition is hard to spot early because its symptoms overlap with everyday problems such as allergic rhinitis, and its forms vary widely. Earlier studies mostly used single-hospital cohorts, limiting how well their models travel.

Using nationwide longitudinal records from the All of Us Research Program, the team compressed roughly one hundred ten thousand candidate codes into one hundred readable features. Separate models were tuned for six demographic subgroups defined by sex and life stage. The stratified framework beat the best baseline on discrimination, suggesting routine records can support population-level early identification.
arxiv-2605-05313:
Elena Pancino and sixteen co-authors assemble a large catalogue of stellar rotation and binarity in Milky Way open clusters using Gaia's third data release. Rotation shapes how stars evolve and can trace past interactions between stars, but systematic samples across populations only recently became possible. The team gathers member lists for thousands of clusters and enriches them with survey and literature data.

Their catalogue holds tens of thousands of rotationally characterised stars, variables, and binaries, with exotic populations such as blue stragglers hand-picked from cluster diagrams. Among early results are a few hundred new blue stragglers. The resource supports comparative studies of how rotation behaves across cluster ages and stellar populations.
arxiv-2605-05713:
Infrared cameras can photograph the warmth of a breast, but heat blurs as it travels, hiding what a tumor is doing inside. Roni Muslim, Ramacos Fardela, and Tista Artu Indra Kusuma ask how much internal physiology survives at the skin's surface. They simulate a modified Pennes bioheat model on a layered tissue cross-section containing a tumor.

Four idealized blood-flow patterns inside the tumor (uniform, rim-enhanced, dead-core, and directional) produce surface temperature profiles. The authors measure how distinguishable those profiles remain, defining thermal-signature equivalence through an observational tolerance. The analysis bounds what thermography can honestly claim to detect.
arxiv-2605-06113:
Tianci Bu and eight co-authors fix load imbalance across data parallel workers in large language model serving. A model sharded across devices is also replicated across many workers, and each decode step ends at a barrier set by the slowest worker. Even modest persistent imbalance wastes a large share of compute, step after step.

Their routing family, BalanceRoute, assigns incoming requests online within a sub hundred millisecond budget. One variant needs no prediction tools and scores admissions with an F-score that treats safe fills and overflows very differently. A second variant adds a short lookahead and a light termination classifier. Deployed on a 144 chip cluster and tested on production and public traces, the system cut imbalance and raised serving throughput.
arxiv-2605-06413:
Richard Bergna, Stefan Depeweg, and José Miguel Hernández-Lobato work on separating two kinds of uncertainty in Prior-Fitted Networks. These networks learn Bayesian prediction from synthetic tasks, but their output mixes epistemic uncertainty, which more data can reduce, with aleatoric noise, which it cannot. Decisions like active learning need the first kind only.

The authors first show the split cannot be recovered from predictions alone. Because they control the synthetic generator, they can label the true signal and noise for each query and train separate heads for each. Using only epistemic uncertainty for acquisition avoids wasted exploration in noisy settings and improves results.
arxiv-2605-06513:
Andreia F. Silva and six co-authors demonstrate a ductile-to-brittle transition using fudge, a candy of sugar crystals in a water, protein, and fat mixture made by boiling sugar, cream, and butter. How pastes and dense suspensions turn brittle is underexplored despite their wide use. Longer cooking or higher final temperature moves the candy from fluid to ductile solid to brittle fracture.

The authors link the change to a rising share of solid sugar crystals. A calcite particle suspension shows the same sequence as its solid fraction rises from frictional jamming toward random close packing. Simulations show the behavior also depends sensitively on boundary conditions.
arxiv-2605-06713:
Christopher Koch forecasts how agentic AI will industrialize cyber offense between 2026 and 2028, drawing on agency and industry evidence. Agents that plan, call tools, and inspect code change attack economics. The near-term risk, Koch argues, is not instant elite hackers but a compressed attack lifecycle: cheaper reconnaissance, phishing, credential abuse, vulnerability triage, and exploit adaptation for ordinary actors.

Two models organize the forecast, one sorting risk into three channels and one measuring lifecycle compression, with a 2026 Linux kernel incident as a case study in fast privilege escalation. The paper closes with a defense roadmap for large firms and smaller European companies, stressing identity, patch speed, and agent governance now.
arxiv-2605-06913:
Nitya Pandey and seventeen co-authors present YOSO, a pipeline that finds faint moving Solar System objects without brute-force shift-and-stack searches. Traditional methods try many discrete velocities, which is slow and noisy. YOSO instead applies a Gaussian motion filter at the pixel level that amplifies trails across a range of motion rates while suppressing static background and random noise.

On Dark Energy Camera observations it recovered forty-five of seventy-three known objects and found eleven new trans-Neptunian objects plus over two hundred near-Solar-System objects. Rival methods reach slightly fainter sources, but YOSO's false positive rate is extremely low. The authors show scaling paths to the coming LSST survey and other motion-detection domains.
arxiv-2605-07513:
Emile Pierret and three co-authors analyze flow matching, a generative modeling method, in a clean theoretical setting. A Gaussian cloud is transported toward a target made of finitely many points, which mirrors how real systems learn from finite datasets. Because the exact velocity field is known in closed form here, its geometry can be studied without training effects.

They examine the regions that end at each target point under the final flow map. These regions are open and simply connected, and under an extra assumption each is shaped like a unit ball. A four-point example shows they can still be non-convex with curved edges, unlike the cells from optimal transport, with different boundedness and neighbor patterns.
arxiv-2605-07613:
Hongyang Su and five co-authors tackle conversational news recommendation, where suggestions must stay grounded in a fast-changing article pool while users hint at what they want only indirectly. From production dialogues they identify six intent types, five of them implicit, which create a retrieve-first bottleneck for standard retrieval pipelines.

Their system generates intent-driven semantic IDs in a generate-then-match scheme. A language model maps an intent to hierarchical ID prefixes. Those prefixes are fuzzy-matched against the live news pool, guaranteeing grounded picks. A profile-aware reasoning step serves brand-new users from profile data alone. On a large Chinese news platform, their model reported zero hallucination. It matched a GPT-4 hybrid system on top-level accuracy, beat it on finer measures, and cost about one hundred times less.
arxiv-2605-07813:
José Luis Carmona Jiménez studies a special class of spinor fields on Riemannian manifolds, generalized imaginary Spin-c Killing spinors, defined by a twisted parallel-transport equation with an imaginary eigenvalue function. Each such spinor carries a partner vector field, its Dirac current, and the paper's results split depending on whether that current vanishes anywhere.

If the current vanishes somewhere and the dimension is at least three, the manifold must locally match real hyperbolic space in shape, a rigid conclusion. If the current never vanishes, a global account of all manifolds carrying these spinors is obtained. It rests on a completeness condition on the current or on certain leaves. The type I case is finally recast through parallel spinors for a connection with vector torsion.
arxiv-2605-08013:
Haoyang Su and Ying Wen look at agents that work through a command line interface, editing files and running programs step by step. Reinforcement learning can train such agents from task feedback, but two problems remain. The agent sees only part of a large codebase, and a single final reward must be shared across many actions.

For the first problem, the authors add sigma-Reveal, which picks context that fits a fixed token budget at run time. For the second, they propose Action Advantage Assignment, which credits the actions that shaped a long trajectory. Tests use shell-driven information extraction and file editing tasks.
arxiv-2605-08113:
Yaw Osei Adjei tests whether geospatial foundation model embeddings help predict smallholder maize yields across borders in sub-Saharan Africa. Planners need yield forecasts that travel between countries, yet most benchmarks test within one country and overstate how well models generalize.

Using 6,404 field observations from five countries, Adjei compares Prithvi-EO and ViT-Base embeddings with traditional Sentinel-2 spectral features under leave-one-country-out validation. Within-country scores looked moderate, but every feature set failed across borders, with negative R-squared values throughout. Frozen foundation embeddings gave no real advantage, and the author argues that shifting yield distributions, not features, are the main barrier.
arxiv-2605-08413:
K. A. Beyer and a large collaboration measure the sizes of chlorine nuclei with muonic atoms. A negative muon orbits far closer to the nucleus than an electron does. The x-rays it emits encode the nuclear charge radius. They do so with high sensitivity.

The team used a large germanium detector array. The samples were highly enriched and weighed only a few tens of milligrams. They measured the muonic chlorine x-ray energies to eighteen parts per million. Combined with modern atomic and nuclear theory, the data give charge radii for both stable chlorine isotopes. The values are ten times more precise than before. They differ significantly from the previously tabulated ones.
arxiv-2605-08713:
Li and colleagues present REAP, an end to end reinforcement learning method for autonomous parking. Parking still fails in extreme cases such as mechanical and dead end slots, where multi stage methods fall short. End to end methods remove error build up, but imitation learning is limited by data, while reinforcement learning explores poorly.

REAP uses Soft Actor-Critic in an asymmetric learning setup that lifts training efficiency and inference performance. A rule based planner is distilled into the network through behaviour cloning, and a soft collision penalty discourages near obstacle actions. A Real2Sim2Real simulator bridges training and reality: real scenes become digital with 3D Gaussian Splatting, then the model deploys onto vehicles. Trained in the simulator and deployed on real vehicles, REAP parks in varied spaces, including narrow mechanical slots. The work shows end to end reinforcement learning parking works in the hardest slots.
arxiv-2605-08913:
Willy Fitra Hendria logs strange lag spikes when models write text on Apple's graphics back end. Write speed is thought to grow in a smooth way with length. On three model lines, Hendria finds bands where lag jumps up to near twenty one fold. It then drops back at near settings. Set tests place the flaw in the write phase, not the read in phase. Memory strain on its own does not explain it. The flaw is not seen on CPU or on rival graphics stacks.

Key value cache still helps in the main. Its gain falls hard in the bad bands. With cache off, jumps stay in part. Back ends hide modes that coarse tests miss.
arxiv-2605-09113:
Prachi Mishra and three co-authors study codes where certain patterns are not banned outright but must appear at set rates. Ordinary constrained coding forbids patterns completely; weakly constrained codes soften that rule, which suits storage and communication systems with statistical limits.

The authors give a construction, built on Eulerian cycles in graphs, that reaches the best possible rate for such codes. By trimming the codebook they obtain codes that also correct errors, keeping a positive rate while any two codewords differ in many positions. They analyze which rates can be achieved and finish with a practical layered construction whose encoding and decoding both run in polynomial time.
arxiv-2605-09313:
Wu and a colleague present a causal analysis of attention sinks in text-to-image diffusion transformers, testing whether tokens with a lopsided share of attention matter for the model. In autoregressive language models, sinks are assumed to matter a lot, but their role in diffusion transformers was unclear. The team spots the top attention getters at each step and quiets them with paired actions on score and value paths, needing no training.

On 553 GenEval prompts on Stable Diffusion 3, checked on SDXL, removing sinks does not hurt text-image match or preference scores at k equals 1. Only under stronger actions at k at least 10 does HPS-v2 show a metric dependent boundary; CLIP-T stays robust. Shifts in what viewers see when sinks are shut off vary by sink, about 6 times larger than equal budget random masking. This shows a split between trajectory level perturbation and semantic alignment.
arxiv-2605-09413:
Wang and twenty-eight colleagues introduce CEAEval, a context-rich framework for judging whether speech fits its setting in feeling, rather than merely how intense its emotion is. Existing methods mainly rate emotional intensity and miss fit, which hampers reliable judging of speech systems for audiobooks and conversational agents. CEAEval asks whether a sample's feeling matches the intent behind its discourse-level narrative setting.

To support the task, the team builds CEAEval-D, the first speech dataset rich in context with real human Mandarin conversational speech. It gives narrative descriptions plus fifteen dimensions of human notes covering expressive attributes and fit. They also build CEAEval-M, a model combining knowledge distillation, planner-led multi-model teamwork, adaptive audio attention bias, and reinforcement learning. On a human-annotated test set it substantially beats existing speech evaluation and analysis systems.
arxiv-2605-09513:
Anand and five colleagues rethink video point tracking. Matching each point to the next frame works briefly. But small errors pile up under motion, occlusion, and viewpoint change. Their QueST framework treats the things worth tracking as persistent semantic queries. It does not treat them as fleeting point tracks. Each query attends globally over video features at every time step, giving a stable anchor. Light three dimensional grounding keeps trajectories physically plausible.

Tested on long articulated sequences from PartNet Mobility, QueST cut terminal drift sharply. Absolute point error fell by about 68 percent against TAP Net. It also preserved identity better over long horizons than rival trackers. The authors read this as evidence for building semantic monitoring into perception itself. Bolting checks on afterward, they argue, cannot catch drift that never signals failure.
arxiv-2605-09713:
Rajpurohit and three colleagues modeled rare-earth nickelates, oxides whose electric, magnetic, and lattice behavior are tightly tangled. Their three-dimensional model treats charge, spin, orbital shape, and lattice motion on equal footing, with settings drawn from quantum calculations for the nickelate LuNiO3. It maps three competing insulating states governed by electron interactions and couplings to breathing and Jahn-Teller lattice distortions.

When the Jahn-Teller energy on nickel sites with two plus charge beats Hund's exchange rule, a new state appears: charge- and orbital-ordered, yet nonmagnetic. Two electrons share one orbital with opposite spins in that state. Its predicted stability shows magnetic order is not needed for these oxides to switch from metal to insulator, a result that reframes how the transition works.
arxiv-2605-10013:
Monteiro and seven co-authors study a privacy question most work skips: not whether language models can infer personal facts, but how users feel about those inferences and what controls they want. Asking about holidays can reveal income, and asking about medicine can reveal medical history, yet such inferences may expose more than users meant to share. The team built Reflective Layer, a tool that surfaces unstated inferences from users' own ChatGPT histories.

In a mixed-methods study, eighteen regular ChatGPT users judged 215 inferences drawn from their own chats. Against expectations, questions and interest beat worry and concern. Unease centred where guesses felt off the mark or mismatched to expected use. Users were also clearly less comfortable letting advertisers and third-party apps use inferences than platform providers, so acceptability turns on context and transmission, not content alone.
arxiv-2605-10113:
Prodinger, writing alone, counts Motzkin paths with a twist: two kinds of flat step are allowed, but only on odd-numbered levels. Motzkin paths step up, down or flat, never dip below the horizontal axis, and eventually return to it. The sequence A176677 in the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences counts these paths, and the paper shows how to enumerate them, including partial paths that end at a particular level or anywhere.

The tool is the kernel method, which manipulates functional equations for the counting series in a suitable way. The coefficients of A176677 satisfy a holonomic recursion, a recurrence with polynomial coefficients, recently discussed on arXiv. Prodinger shows how that recursion follows in an almost automatic fashion, then swaps the roles of odd and even levels, leaving further flat-step variants to interested readers.
arxiv-2605-10413:
Dana Avramescu and four colleagues develop a light-front Hamiltonian formalism for a high-energy quark traveling through the Glasma, the early, short-lived, strong-color-field stage of a heavy-ion collision. Jets, narrow sprays of hadrons from breaking quarks and gluons, probe the quark-gluon plasma, but little is known about their interaction with the pre-equilibrium Glasma. Their 2026 paper fills that gap.

Truncating the quark Fock space to the single-quark sector, the authors expand the wavefunction in a basis, following time-dependent Basis Light-Front Quantization. Classical Glasma fields act as a time-dependent external potential. The authors compute transverse momentum broadening and the jet quenching parameter, matching classical estimates. They use them for estimates across collision systems. They also study color rotation and its dependence on that scale and gauge choice. The formalism allows improvements, including non-eikonal propagation and parton splittings.
arxiv-2605-10613:
Feliciano Giuseppe Pacifico and five colleagues plant exact fixed points in Neural-ODEs without losing full power. The authors introduce a technique letting Neural-ODEs approximate any velocity fields with fixed points planted in advance. A recipe fits a finite set of points in the base space where the velocity field is exactly zero. Their 2026 paper proves the Neural-ODE keeps full power under any local constraints in the velocity field.

Gradient-based training is strictly constrained inside the assumed class while leaving the power of the Neural-ODE unchanged. The authors give a convenient way of imposing the fixed points and test the method on two classic physical models. Planted fixed points can enhance model clarity. Learning takes place within a clear motion framework where chosen states remain exactly still by design.
arxiv-2605-10713:
Youssef Chaabouni and David Gamarnik study sparse recovery when measurements mix high quality and low quality sources. A few precise readings arrive beside many noisier ones, and the question is how many noisy readings can stand in for one good one.

For information-theoretic recovery they derive a linear trade-off, the price of quality. A blind decoder never pays more than two low-quality samples per high-quality one, while an informed decoder can face an unbounded price. They also show the Lasso algorithm's threshold depends only on average noise, so computation stays robust to mixed quality. Signal-processing teams get the first recovery conditions for this mixed-data regime.
arxiv-2605-11413: Badu and eight colleagues study antiferroelectric ordering in two ferroelectric nematic liquid crystals. The two materials are the single compound DIO and the commercial mixture FNLC919. They measure polarization and mass density modulation against temperature. They find the modulation wavenumber by small-angle X-ray diffraction from a weak accompanying density wave. With Landau theory, the polarization wave is nearly sinusoidal in DIO, while in FNLC919 a sharp drop near the transition signals a soliton-like profile.
arxiv-2605-11513: Guigon, Dixon and Sander study hidden layer distillation for language model pre-training. Most research in this area uses output logits only. Hidden layer distillation promised much for encoders, but its use in decoder pre-training at scale is unexplored. In controlled experiments, Gemma3 3 point 4B taught 123M and 735M students on 168B C4 tokens. There, hidden layer distillation does not consistently beat standard distillation on downstream tasks. Yet it yields a steady perplexity gain over distillation across all shared configurations, suggesting a latent signal exists.
arxiv-2605-11713: Rommel Tchinda Djeudjo, Gourab Kumar Sar, and Timoteo Carletti examine swarmalators, oscillators that sync in both space and phase, under one-sided time delay. Their one-dimensional model puts delay only in self-interaction terms, breaking the symmetry of earlier work. They map states such as async, static phase wave, and active pi, derive stability boundaries, and show that growing delay expands the active pi state.
arxiv-2605-11813: Jinbiao Chen and five colleagues automate a tedious manual task: turning uncertain optimization models into solvable fixed forms. They build AutoRO-Bench, the first dedicated benchmark for this task. They also propose AutoREM, a tuning-free system that grows a textual memory of lessons by reflecting on past failed runs. The memory transfers across base language models without expert knowledge or parameter updates. Experiments show it improved reformulation accuracy and efficiency.
arxiv-2605-12213: Jiazhou Liang and five colleagues present Goal-Mem, reasoning for memory in conversational agents. Chat agents struggle to stay coherent over talks because context is limited, and retrieval often returns weak evidence. Existing methods retrieve by similarity to the user utterance, without reasoning about missing facts. Goal-Mem chains from the user's utterance as a goal, splitting it into subgoals and retrieving memories. It seeks what is missing when subgoals stall. Formalized in Natural Language Logic, it beats nine baselines on two datasets, on multi-hop reasoning and inference.
arxiv-2605-12713: Connerty and Evans advance quantum reservoir computing by making memory capacity controllable through tunable partial-SWAPs. Feedback and recurrent models are the two major validated approaches. Recurrent models use memory and readout qubits to give it fading memory. While tested on hardware and strong on noisy quantum chips, the exact cause behind memory capacity was not fully known or tunable. Their work augments recurrent models, giving designers a knob to tune how much memory it holds.
arxiv-2605-12813: Liang and eight colleagues probe a weak spot of large language models: hallucinations set off by hostile prompts that still read as normal user requests. Their tool, REALISTA, builds a set of valid rewording moves for a prompt and tunes mixes of them in latent space. This joins the reach of continuous attacks with the realism of discrete rewording. In tests it matches or beats prior realistic attacks and cracks large reasoning models where earlier attacks fail.
arxiv-2605-12913: Li and six colleagues revisit Dataset Aggregation, or DAgger, for long-horizon language-model agents, where one early slip can derail a whole run. Supervised fine-tuning gives dense teacher guidance but suffers covariate shift from off-policy data, while reward-based learning avoids that mismatch but gives only sparse feedback. DAgger mixes student and teacher moves turn by turn, easing shift while keeping feedback rich. On SWE-bench Verified it lifts a software-engineering agent by about four points at both 4B and 8B scales.
arxiv-2605-13013: Lim and six co-authors present JEDI, the first online end-to-end latent diffusion world model for model-based reinforcement learning. Pixel diffusion works well but costs heavily, while latent diffusion is cheaper yet weaker and relies on separately trained latents. JEDI learns its latent space directly from the diffusion denoising loss inside a JEPA framework, predicting future latents instead of reconstructing. It matches rivals on Atari100k while using 43% less VRAM and sampling over three times faster.
arxiv-2605-13313: J. de Lucas, J. Lange and M. Krych survey how k-contact geometry can describe field equations that lose energy. Their framework, the k-contact Hamilton-De Donder-Weyl formalism, handles systems where friction or damping drains energy over time. They develop tools for splitting its equations and for checking when the associated equations are hyperbolic or elliptic. They also track how symmetries produce dissipation laws. The paper then gives explicit Hamiltonian descriptions for damped versions of the Klein-Gordon, Burgers, Allen-Cahn and sine-Gordon equations, among others.
arxiv-2605-13413: Christoph Schwerdt studies heat flow on bounded Lipschitz domains, regions with mildly rough edges, under generalised Robin edge conditions. The heat operator is second-order and uniformly elliptic, so it spreads heat in a regular way. His edge conditions allow an operator that can break the rule that solutions stay non-negative. Using Nash's inequality on the Sobolev space H1, he proves ultracontractivity of the solution semigroup, a strong smoothing property that bounds later values by early totals.
arxiv-2605-13513: Rakesh Arora, Tuhina Mukherjee and Arshi Vaishnavi study a weighted eigenvalue problem driven by the logarithmic Laplacian with mixed weights. They prove an endless sequence of Lusternik-Schnirelman values exists, and show the first value is simple, with its function keeping a constant sign in the domain. In contrast, functions for higher values must change sign. As one use, they prove the first value is alone.
arxiv-2605-13813: Lavsen Dahal and three colleagues introduce JANUS, a body-guided dual-stream design for robust CT triage under spread shift. It tunes visual codes on macro-scan priors via body-map Guided Gating. On the MERLIN test set of 5,082 cases, JANUS attains macro-AUROC 0.88 and AUPRC 0.74, beating all copied rivals.
