Their tool is a curveball null model, a shuffle preserving how much each reader marks and each sentence's popularity.

Within single documents, factions are real. Reader pairs agree far beyond the shuffle prediction. The effect is significant in eighty-eight percent of documents. A stricter shuffle preserving which broad regions readers engage still leaves most of the excess, so agreement is finer than shared regions. The second experiment asks whether factions are stable reader traits across documents. There the signal nearly vanishes, and the test only has power for pairs sharing at least four documents. Stability is left unresolved.
arxiv-2606-11713:
Deog Ki Hong revisits a quantum effect in dense matter in this 2026 arXiv paper on theoretical physics. The axial anomaly is a breakdown, forced by quantum mechanics, of a symmetry that classical equations promise to keep. One of its consequences is the chiral magnetic effect: in a magnetic field, an imbalance between left- and right-handed particles drives an electric current along the field.

Hong computes the anomaly explicitly inside dense matter rather than empty space. Through a subtle cancellation between two medium contributions, its form stays as in vacuum, even for massless particles. He then shows the medium supports a persistent, conserved anomalous current carried by the fermions themselves. The current is set by the axial chemical potential, a measure of the handedness imbalance, and reduced by the Fermi velocity. Finally he discusses axion dark matter, which would act as just such an imbalance.
arxiv-2606-11913:
Yuchen Guan and six colleagues compress long videos into neural weights in this 2026 arXiv paper. Understanding hour-long video is hard for vision-language models: content is sparse, and re-encoding the footage for every question is slow. Their proposal treats a video as a Neural Knowledge Representation, a small set of extra network weights that stores its content.

An agent builds this representation once, writing dense descriptions and question-answer pairs about the video and distilling that knowledge into the weights. Afterwards the weights mount onto a frozen vision-language model, which answers queries directly without reloading the video. Video length is thereby decoupled from inference cost, which suits multi-turn questioning. On the LVBench benchmark the method matches state-of-the-art accuracy while cutting end-to-end latency by more than a hundredfold. The authors frame the result as turning video into a portable, reusable knowledge asset.
arxiv-2606-12313:
Bergerhoff and co-authors link two trapped ions into one working segment of a future quantum internet, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A quantum repeater extends entanglement, the linked fate of two quantum memories, across distances where fiber losses would otherwise kill it. A repeater segment entangles two memories through a photonic Bell measurement, a joint check on two photons. Here both memories are calcium ions held in one trap, each emitting a photon. The photons are converted to the telecom C-band, the wavelength window where fibers lose least.

After traveling 220 meters of fiber each, the photons interfere at a central station. The resulting ion-ion entangled state reaches a fidelity of at least sixty-eight percent to the target Bell state. A parity oscillation amplitude of 1.36 backs the measurement. Trapped calcium ions thus look promising for repeater networks and connecting quantum computers.
arxiv-2606-12713:
Aguilera Briones argues that the fight over whether artificial general intelligence has arrived is really a fight about definitions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. An operationalization is a rule for deciding whether a system counts as AGI, and rival rules can return opposite verdicts on the same system. Rather than propose another rule, the author builds DAF-AGI, a framework for judging definitions themselves and the authority behind them.

The framework scores candidate rules on 5 ordinal criteria, meaning graded scales, and adds an audit covering authorship, material interest, certification, outside verification, and revision rights. Applied to 5 measurement families plus a deflationary position, the framework is stress-tested on an arrival claim about current systems. That claim proves certifiable only under a results-based rule. Capability, psychometric, and skill-acquisition approaches do not certify it, and the economic family stays open without evidence that AI takes the place of human labour.
arxiv-2606-13113:
Ayanmanesh Motlaghmofrad and colleagues combine model predictive control with a Lyapunov-checked neural network correction layer for underactuated spacecraft attitude control, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such a craft cannot be steered along 1 axis, so standard control cannot hold its full attitude. Predictive controllers also stay sensitive to inertia uncertainty and unmodelled links. Their design stacks 3 layers to address both problems.

The first layer is a model predictive controller. It plans moves that respect constraints and underactuation, with nominal closed-loop stability under actuator limits. The third is a Lyapunov-based safety layer. It checks the learned correction online and bounds or cuts its influence, keeping the baseline controller's stability. In full runs with reaction wheels, actuator strain, and shocks, Monte Carlo studies show big cuts in steady-state attitude error versus plain predictive control.
arxiv-2606-13213:
Kraus, Huk, and Czado tackle a weakness of vine copulas in this 2026 arXiv paper. A copula is a statistical model that describes how several variables move together. Vine copulas build such models from simple two-variable pieces, which keeps them flexible and practical. They usually rely on a simplifying assumption, meaning each pair's link is treated as fixed whatever the other variables do. When real data break that assumption, the fitted model can go wrong.

The authors propose a calibration step based on noise contrastive estimation, a method that learns by teaching a classifier to tell real data from fake samples. Here the fitted simple model supplies the fake samples, and the classifier yields a correction factor for each real observation. Simulations show the corrections help when the assumption fails and stay near neutral when it holds. Two real data examples show the same practical benefit.
arxiv-2606-13313:
Aubrun explains a breakthrough in sphere packing in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sphere packing asks how densely identical balls can fill space without overlapping. In high dimensions the best density was poorly understood, and lattice packings, where centres sit on a grid-like pattern, are the most tractable case. The text, translated from French Bourbaki seminar notes, presents Boaz Klartag's proof of an improved lower bound on the densest lattice packing. The bound grows with the square of dimension, times the exponential decay.

Klartag's argument uses randomness in two ways. First: a uniformly random lattice has properties that give decent packings. The second is new. It follows the evolution of an ellipsoid, a stretched ball, constrained never to swallow nonzero lattice points. Watching how that ellipsoid wanders yields the factor that lifts the bound. The exposition makes the proof's architecture accessible to a broad audience.
arxiv-2606-13413:
Adans and colleagues connect lattice equations to the Painlevé family in this 2026 arXiv paper. They are nonlinear, and their solutions define special functions, central in mathematical physics. Their symmetric versions carry a hidden action of affine Weyl groups, symmetry groups that organise families. A Volterra-Bogoyavlensky lattice is a system of interacting particles on a lattice with exponential coupling. The authors build a framework using the lattice structure to produce rational solutions of the symmetric Painlevé system.

For the first nontrivial case, they show the Volterra lattice with starting values models the orbits from half-translation operators of the symmetric Painlevé four system. This yields closed forms for all parts in terms of generalised Okamoto polynomials, plus new algebraic recurrences among them. The bridge turns lattice dynamics into a generating machine for the theory.
arxiv-2606-13513:
Zhang and colleagues introduce CloudCons in this 2026 arXiv paper, an end-to-end benchmark for cloud consolidation. Data centres over-provision resources to guarantee reliability, leaving usage low. The forecast-then-optimise approach attacks this by predicting demand and consolidating workloads onto fewer machines. Time series foundation models promise forecasts through zero-shot transfer, learning patterns transferable across workloads. Yet benchmarks score only forecast error, leaving the decision value of a better forecast unverified. A model can win on accuracy and still lose money in consolidation decisions.

CloudCons evaluates forecasting models inside the task. It builds datasets covering workloads from cloud providers. Models are judged by the quality of the decisions they enable, not by error metrics alone. The benchmark bridges a gap between forecast research and operations practice, giving cloud engineers evidence about which models improve usage without endangering service.
arxiv-2606-13613:
Abratenko and the MicroBooNE Collaboration report a first measurement of a rare neutrino interaction in this 2026 arXiv paper. The process is charged-current coherent pion production: a muon neutrino strikes an argon nucleus, which recoils as a whole while a charged pion emerges, leaving the nucleus in its ground state. Below one giga-electronvolt this channel had never been measured on argon. MicroBooNE is a liquid-argon detector at Fermilab that images particle tracks in fine detail.

The process matters because it is a background and a signal in oscillation searches for new neutrino physics. Measuring it on argon, the target of the next generation of flagship detectors, anchors the event models those experiments rely on. The collaboration's analysis isolates the coherent signal from the much larger sea of ordinary neutrino interactions. First measurements of this kind typically carry large uncertainties, but they convert a modelled guess into data.
arxiv-2606-14113:
Keramati, Cao, and co-authors test whether language models can fake student programming mistakes well enough to train teachers and tutors. Authentic error collections accumulate only after long classroom deployment. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses CodeWorkout, over seventy-four thousand real student Java submissions across thirty-seven problems, as ground truth. Five models generated logical errors under three prompting strategies: input-output, chain-of-thought, and self-refinement. Quality was scored on diversity of error patterns and alignment with real mistakes.

All models produced diverse errors, but alignment diverged; Claude Sonnet 4 was most balanced. A blinded expert study with four hundred one annotations found the synthetic errors functionally indistinguishable from authentic ones. A trade-off appeared: problems students struggle on most elicited more diverse but less student-like errors. The generated errors, compilable with one logical fault, form an idealized learner distribution. Still, results support simulated errors in tutoring systems.
arxiv-2606-14313:
Lee and Kim model fields evolving in space and time, acting on each other from afar. Real data arrives at irregular times, at sparse sensors. Long-range, nonlocal coupling compounds this: the integro-differential equations are infinite-dimensional. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes NLBST, a Bayesian model that learns nonlocal coupling yet keeps the math tractable.

The latent field is expanded in a coordinate-based basis. Its weights follow a continuous-time ODE. The learnable operator is a Galerkin projection of that equation, plus a neural ODE residual for extra dynamics. A linear-Gaussian data model allows Kalman-style updates under missing, uneven observations. The basis lets it predict at new sites with no retraining. On synthetic and real-world data, including EPA fine particulate matter measurements, NLBST showed strong forecasts and spatial transfer. Its error bars were well judged, with large gains over baselines in strongly nonlocal, partly seen regimes.
arxiv-2606-14613:
Páez-Velasco proves a Riemannian fundamental theorem for tensor networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Tensor networks compress high-dimensional data and many-body quantum states into linked small tensors. Giving them a Riemannian manifold structure creates a natural home for optimization. A manifold is a smooth geometry with distances and angles.

A central feature is gauge freedom. It is the many equal ways to write the same network. Its characterization is called a fundamental theorem, and it underlies algorithm design. The author studies how this freedom interacts with the Riemannian structure across several families. He uses group actions and Riemannian submersions. Submersions are maps projecting geometry downward while preserving horizontal lengths. He establishes a Riemannian fundamental theorem for the families studied. It clarifies the true shape of the space numerical methods search.
arxiv-2606-14713:
Makarov and Taubkin extract recurring transit schedules from standard timetable data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Transit feeds in the GTFS format list trips by date, but many dates share the same passenger-facing timetable while weekends, holidays, and seasons differ. GTFS never encodes these recurring patterns directly, leaving scheduling and demand models without an explicit object for them.

The authors define a DayType as the complete set of route-pattern trips operating on a date and build a stable extraction method keyed on geographic route patterns. Their comparison framework separates strict timetable differences from small timing shifts and larger service changes. On Japanese and Canadian feeds they found substantial compression, with a median of four nonempty DayTypes per agency, hierarchical nesting between service classes, and country-level differences in how persistently schedules stay disjoint.
arxiv-2606-14913:
Obieke and coauthors tackle long-time prediction of Hamiltonian partial differential equations in a 2026 study. These equations govern waves whose mass, momentum, and energy should stay constant over time. Standard Fourier neural operators learn fast solution maps, but their repeated predictions drift away from those conserved quantities. The team therefore builds structure into the learned operator itself.

Their energy-projection Fourier neural operator pairs a residual update with a projection step that restores the invariants after each step. Tests on the Zakharov-Kuznetsov, Kadomtsev-Petviashvili, and sine-Gordon equations show better long-time stability than a standard operator. Solitons and other wave shapes also move through the domain more accurately, with less phase error. The authors add theory backing the accuracy and stability of the method. Because the projection is an add-on step, it can also attach to other learned models.
arxiv-2606-15013:
Petrlíková and Petricek give the Vega visualization language a formal semantics and type system in a 2026 study. Vega builds interactive charts through reactive data transformations in a streaming dataflow. Its exact behavior is subtle and poorly documented, so typos can yield empty charts and cryptic warnings. The authors model what the system does, then check specifications statically.

Their graph-based operational semantics describes how data updates propagate through the dataflow graph. On top of it, a type system for the transformation language tracks which fields exist at each step. The system is proved sound against the semantics, so accepted specifications avoid invalid field access. Such access is the root cause of the confusing failures the authors document. The resulting checker can catch common real-world Vega errors before runtime. The work joins recent efforts to formalize messy, widely used systems rather than only clean textbook languages.
arxiv-2606-15113:
Bhaumik and coauthors map multi-controlled Toffoli gates onto two-dimensional qubit layouts without losing depth in a 2026 study. The multi-controlled Toffoli gate underpins quantum arithmetic, oracles, and cryptanalysis. Optimal depth decompositions exist for fully connected machines, but real hardware links qubits only to near neighbors. Generic circuit mappers ignore the repeated patterns inside these decompositions.

The authors first give geometric placements that preserve the parallelism of leading decompositions with no added depth. A motif-based packing framework then abstracts each decomposition layer into interaction motifs from basic Toffoli gates. Embedding those motifs without overlap into hardware graphs reveals the smallest layouts that fit. Explicit bounds quantify depth overhead when qubit budgets are tight. The team compares the bounds against routing-aware placement heuristics across many hardware shapes. Experiments confirm which motifs embed cleanly and where overhead becomes unavoidable on restricted layouts.
arxiv-2606-15313:
Wang and coauthors build a speaker de-identification system tuned for dementia speech in a 2026 speech technology paper. De-identification strips who is speaking from a recording while keeping what matters clinically. The trap is that identity and cognitive health cues are entangled in the voice. Removing one aggressively damages the other, which older splitting methods cannot avoid. The authors instead post-train a diffusion voice converter with reinforcement learning. Reward signals from privacy and utility teacher models steer the trade-off.

On two dementia speech benchmarks, the system beat voice conversion baselines. It preserved cognitive utility while protecting speaker privacy better than rivals. The authors also argue naturalness scores alone mislead evaluation. Health-oriented systems need task-specific utility, privacy, and clarity measured together. Because the framework needs only reward signals, it can transfer to other audio domains. Robustness against adaptive re-identification attacks remains future work.
arxiv-2606-15413:
Kon'kov and coauthor study when an isolated singularity of a partial differential inequality can be removed, in a 2026 analysis paper. The solutions live on a punctured ball, a region with its center deleted, and obey a higher-order elliptic inequality with a right side growing in the solution's size. A singularity is removable when the solution extends across the missing point unchanged, so the hole was only apparent.

Earlier work set an integral test, of Keller-Osserman type, under which every solution's singularity is removable. For second-order problems it matches classical results of Brezis and Véron. The present paper derives the matching necessary condition: when the integral test fails, non-removable solutions exist. The removability question is thus settled sharply, showing which growth rates force blow-up at a point and which permit a clean extension.
arxiv-2606-16013:
Sharma and colleagues examine in 2026 why the weights of multiple linear regression can mislead readers. Regression predicts an outcome as a weighted sum of input features, so the weights look like a direct read-out of importance. Trouble starts under multicollinearity, where features move together closely. The fitted weights then swing sharply between similar datasets and can alternate in sign across near-duplicate features.

An eigenmode analysis of the feature correlation matrix explains the failure. Modes with small eigenvalues amplify noise in the weights and create the oscillatory patterns the authors observe. Tests on physics datasets confirm the picture, and a broader check on public datasets shows the effect is not limited to physics. Ridge regularization, which adds a small penalty that shrinks weights, suppresses the unstable modes in the experiments. Even then, the authors warn, shrunken weights still need cautious reading before anyone treats them as physical causes.
arxiv-2606-16113:
Khotanlou and colleagues introduce RecourseBench in 2026, a framework for comparing recourse methods fairly. Recourse methods tell a person what actions would overturn a bad model decision, such as a loan denial. Methods have multiplied, but fair comparison stays elusive. Existing tools are hard to extend, and few check that an added method still matches its published results.

RecourseBench splits the pipeline into five separate layers: Data, Preprocessing, Model, Recourse Method, and Evaluation. Standard interfaces and a registry govern how pieces plug together. A four-tier system grades how faithfully each method is verified. An automated test suite checks every method against its published results before it counts as added. A web interface supports comparison across methods, datasets, and model types. The design aims at strict auditing, so claimed recourse quality can be checked, not just trusted.
arxiv-2606-16313:
Sun and co-authors propose FluidTest in 2026, a human-aligned way to grade self-driving planners on rare, risky scenes. Long-tail scenarios are where planners fail, yet standard metrics saturate among strong systems and free-form human ratings are noisy. FluidTest reframes grading as additional-threat detection. Given a planner's trajectory and an expert driver's reference, it asks whether the planner's path adds unsafe behavior the expert avoided.

Three parts support reliable labels: a pairwise web interface for human annotation, a taxonomy of 32 semantic threats with evidence-grounded decision graphs, and a three-agent verification system that reflects before final calls. On the WOD-E2E benchmark, trained annotators produce consistent labels with the protocol. FluidTest finds additional threats in 65 percent of trajectories from the Poutine planner and 51 percent from RAP, per the report. Even leading planners, it seems, add real risk in most long-tail scenes.
arxiv-2606-16413:
Zhang and co-authors combine augmented reality with a brain-computer interface in 2026 to let users steer a robot arm by gaze and imagined movement. Existing AR brain-robot systems are usually locked to one task, limiting real-world use. This design targets generalist manipulation: eye tracking selects the object, and motor imagery from EEG signals issues the action. Context-aware overlays labeled Place and Use guide the user through each step, inside a shared autonomy framework where the robot handles low-level motion.

A feasibility study ran 18 healthy participants through three multi-step daily activities: drinking, using a drawer, and operating an oven. The interaction style enabled effective sequential task completion, and users rated usability above 70 on the System Usability Scale, a Good rating, per the report. The caveat is real: participants were healthy, not the motor-impaired users the system targets.
arxiv-2606-16613:
Sugiura and co-authors open a coffee economy in 2026 and let language-model agents run it for ninety days, testing whether AI can actually do business. Economic systems are inherently multi-agent: firms must communicate, negotiate, and transact while chasing their own goals over long horizons. Existing benchmarks mostly test one agent in a passive world. CoffeeBench instead assembles two farmers, two roasters, and two retailers, each autonomous, each maximizing cumulative net income while managing cash, inventory, and pricing.

The evaluated model controls one coffee roaster; the remaining firms are fixed reference agents. Across recent open-weight and proprietary models, every model beats a passive do-nothing baseline, and most finish with positive net income. Analysis of agent behavior reveals substantial differences between models in how they communicate, price, and manage stock. The benchmark matters because long-horizon economic competence is exactly what single-task tests cannot measure.
arxiv-2606-16913:
Chen and Sanz-Alonso find the statistical and cost limits of learning operators in a 2026 paper on operator learning. The task is to recover an unknown linear map between function spaces from noisy input-output examples, the pattern behind learning solution maps of differential equations. Wavelet coordinates turn the problem into a huge matrix regression whose structure varies across scales.

The authors establish minimax rates, the best error any method can guarantee, under a Sobolev operator-norm loss. They then build a blockwise least-squares estimator, computed scale by scale, that attains those rates. Estimation difficulty, they find, is uneven across scales. Exploiting that unevenness pays off: assigning scale-adaptive sample sizes, more data where estimation is hard, reaches the optimal total cost among dense least-squares methods. The results give the field matching error and cost floors to judge practical algorithms against.
arxiv-2606-17013:
Borkar explains a classic training pathology of deep networks in a 2026 paper at the border of learning theory and dynamical systems. During training, gradients in some directions shrink toward zero while others blow up, stalling or wrecking learning. Residual connections, which add a layer's input to its output, are known empirically to tame the effect.

The analysis uses multiplicative ergodic theory, the study of long products of random matrices. Gradients through many layers behave like such products, and their growth or decay rates are captured by Liapunov exponents, one per direction. A characterization of these exponents due to Furstenberg and Kifer lets Borkar pin down the spectrum exactly. Adding a residual connection shifts the matrix product toward the identity, and the theory shows exactly how that shift moves the exponents. The payoff is a sharp account of why skip connections stabilize training, replacing folklore with a theorem.
arxiv-2606-17413:
Calle-Saldarriaga and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on measuring carbon dioxide from space. Their method is faster than the standard one, and it states its own error honestly. NASA's OCO-2 satellite infers the gas column from high-resolution spectra. The standard physics-based retrieval is slow, though, and it understates its own errors. The new deep learning framework pays its training cost once, then reads each new spectrum fast.

Real observations lack ground truth, so the team built a detailed simulation set for tests. That set includes realistic forward model errors drawn from earlier calibration work. A multi-branch network reads the spectral bands and produces a spread of plausible values. Two tools shape that spread, and one of them allows skewed shapes. The method beat baselines on point accuracy and gave better-calibrated error bars in the tests.
arxiv-2606-17513:
Vendrell-Gallart, Negarandeh, and Bostanabad present a 2026 arXiv paper on adding trustworthy error bars to neural operators, the fast surrogates that stand in for costly partial differential equation solvers. Plain operators give one deterministic answer, which limits their use where geometry varies and uncertainty matters. Most fixes model doubt about network weights, ignoring the geometry-aware features the operator itself has already learned inside its layers during training on varied shapes.

Their method, REEF-GP, fits a Gaussian process to the frozen operator's residuals, using its own internal embeddings as the kernel's feature space. Spectral-normalised projections, geometry-aware noise, and subset training keep the scheme stable and scalable on unstructured domains. Across five equation benchmarks with changing geometry, accuracy held while uncertainty stayed calibrated at ensemble-beating cost. Doubt also concentrated in physically sensible places such as shock fronts.
arxiv-2606-17613:
Purini, Narwadkar, and Gangadharan present a 2026 arXiv paper showing that traffic forecasting needs far less machinery than the field assumes, little enough to run on a microcontroller. Leading models train graph networks centrally on graphics processors across all sensors, blocking deployment at the roadside. A clue came from shrinking a recent graph-free model's inner width drastically with almost no accuracy loss, suggesting the task needs much less capacity than the models carry in practice.

The replacement is per-sensor ridge regression on periodic features matched to the forecast horizon, updated online by recursive least squares. With only a few hundred parameters per sensor, it took the best error score on most of the standard benchmarks used. The full pipeline, training included, ran on a cheap microcontroller with room to spare. Cold-start training took seconds there and a fifth of a second on a small board computer.
arxiv-2606-18613:
Du and the team present a benchmark for language models working as physician assistants, not physicians, in a 2026 medical AI paper. That assisting role is the plausible near-term clinical role. But it demands skills that must work together, while existing tests measure them separately. They include following a doctor's underspecified requests, talking with patients who describe symptoms in vague terms, and using an electronic health record system that requires precise tool calls.

PhysAssistBench builds scenarios from real MIMIC-IV cases. A multi-agent pipeline turns static records into record-grounded simulated patients, behind a standard FHIR interface. It ships a bilingual test set of nearly thirteen hundred reviewed, doctor-validated turns. Testing leading models, the authors found current systems remain unreliable in this setting. The bottleneck is joining knowledge, communication, and system use together, not fixing any one alone.
arxiv-2606-18713:
Linghu, Dong, and Wang present a neural field whose form is a photonic quantum circuit, in a 2026 scientific machine learning paper. Physics-informed neural fields solve differential equations by fitting a parameterized function to the equation's constraints. They struggle where solutions oscillate. Classical coordinate and Fourier-feature networks poorly preserve phase, frequency, and derivative structure.

In their build, coordinates become trainable optical phases. Multi-photon interference in Fock space mixes them, and photon-number measurements decode the output. The circuit itself is optimized as the form. Across seven benchmarks spanning elliptic, wave, nonlinear dispersive, and inverse problems, the authors find a phase-complexity transition. Classical networks suffice in smooth regimes. But where residual derivatives amplify phase mismatch, the photonic field wins. In the hardest regimes it reached the lowest errors, by up to an order of magnitude, with about a quarter of the trainable parameters.
arxiv-2606-19113:
Anghel and colleagues construct new universal quantum knot invariants in 2026. Knot invariants assign algebraic data to a knot that stays fixed under deformation, letting mathematicians tell knots apart. Universal invariants are the strongest kind, since others can be derived from them. The new family lifts both the semisimple and non-semisimple invariants from the quantum group for sl2 into one object at each level.

For each level, the invariant comes from quantum traces on finite quotients of the generic Verma module over certain quotient rings. When the level is prime, the authors prove this is the maximal invariant the level part of the Verma module can yield. It interpolates between the colored Jones and ADO polynomials at that level. For composite levels the structure is richer. It recovers both polynomial families but may hold extra data neither sequence sees alone.
arxiv-2606-20013:
Atsushi Hori, Takayuki Okuno, and Ellen Fukuda reformulate multi-leader-follower games in 2026 using a regularized Nikaido-Isoda function. Such games stack competition in layers: leaders choose first while anticipating how followers will best respond below. Standard rewrites swap the lower game for its optimality conditions or substitute response functions, but both can demand higher-order derivatives and scale poorly.

The new form approximates the whole game by a single-level differentiable Nash problem with a penalty parameter. It needs no derivative information from the followers' game and assumes no convexity there, widening the class of solvable games. Under a global subanalyticity condition, the authors relate equilibria of the rewrite to equilibria of the original. Hierarchical decision problems in economics and engineering gain a more tractable solver path.
arxiv-2606-20113:
Elroy Galbraith studies when it pays to let a retrieval system search before the user finishes asking. His 2026 paper examines streaming retrieval-augmented generation, where a system guesses the needed query mid-sentence to hide tool latency. Speculation only helps when the right query becomes clear early. Galbraith names that property tool-intent stabilization, the point where a trial query's results settle onto the answer-bearing documents.

Working with the CRAG benchmark of 1,371 questions, he maps how stabilization spreads across queries. He also derives a bound on the share of latency any system could hide, given tool delay and typing cadence. At a realistic operating point, about 74 percent of questions admit latency hiding. A live pipeline met or beat the bound in aggregate, though it cannot forecast single queries. Question type split early from late only weakly. A dense-retriever rerun confirmed the effect is no keyword-matching artifact.
arxiv-2606-20213:
Sara Pucillo reports, for the ALICE Collaboration, a new way of counting strange particles event by event in small collision systems. Her 2026 paper studies strangeness enhancement, the extra production of strange hadrons in heavy-ion collisions, once proposed as a signature of quark-gluon plasma. ALICE had already seen strange-to-pion ratios climb with event multiplicity across every collision system. What remained unclear was the mechanism, hidden inside average yields.

The new measurement gives the full probability distribution for producing a given number of strange hadrons of one species in a single proton-proton event, at 5.02 TeV, covering kaons, Lambdas, Xi, and Omega particles. Counting event by event exposes events with large imbalances between strange and ordinary content, which averages wash out. Comparing the distributions with Monte Carlo generators gives a sharper test bench for production mechanisms.
arxiv-2606-20513:
Anthony Leverrier and Rüdiger Urbanke introduce the Frontier decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes. Their 2026 paper approximates optimal decoding with a pruned dynamic program. Exact decoding tracks logical-coset posterior masses at exponential cost, so practical decoders need a principled shortcut.

Frontier processes error variables in a chosen order, merges prefixes sharing the same residual syndrome and logical label, and keeps only a narrow, scored frontier of candidates. Without pruning, the recursion is exact ordered inference. In code-capacity tests it reaches thresholds close to optimal for the surface and color codes. Under circuit-level noise it achieves state-of-the-art performance with an average retained list under 100 entries for the gross code at a physical error rate of 0.001.
arxiv-2606-20613:
Tabia Tanzin Prama and four colleagues test whether language models judge intimate partner violence differently by the genders involved. Their 2026 paper starts from 475 Reddit posts from r/relationship_advice. Counterfactual variants swap gendered identifiers to create four victim-perpetrator dyads, from female-female to male-male.

Four recent models, GPT-5o, Gemini 3, Llama 4, and Grok 3, evaluate each variant. Holding the story fixed while only genders change exposes whether abuse is perceived differently across configurations. Any disparity matters because people increasingly seek support from these systems in sensitive moments. The audit is designed to reveal where model sympathy is unevenly distributed.
arxiv-2606-20713:
Qingyang Xu proposes FairTutor in a solo 2026 paper on fair access to AI tutoring. Generative tutors give real-time, personal learning support. They also create a new gap. Students with premium services may get clearer explanations and better scaffolding. Students on free tiers may get weaker help. FairTutor is a routing framework meant to close that gap without paying premium prices for every query.

FairTutor combines query analysis, teaching planning, low-cost generation, evaluator critique, and selective escalation to premium models. Xu defines a gap measure for the quality difference between tiers. A new benchmark, TutorAccessEval, spans math, reading, writing, science, and language learning. FairTutor reaches 97.1 percent of premium teaching quality. It also cuts serving cost by 71.6 percent. The result suggests smart routing can protect equity, by saving costly calls for questions where they change the outcome most.
arxiv-2606-21013:
Jingyi Chai and seven colleagues at Shanghai Jiao Tong University introduce an Agentic Time Machine in 2026 for evaluating forecasts of future events. Forecasting matters for elections, policy, and markets. Live evaluation is slow, because the future must arrive. Retrospective replay is fast but usually restricts agents to frozen databases. That loses the realism of live web search. Their infrastructure rebuilds the web state at a chosen past time.

Post-cutoff content is filtered out, so agents cannot peek at outcomes. A planner, solver, and aggregator framework is also proposed. Questions are split into diverse angles. Evidence is gathered in parallel and combined into one forecast. Offline scores under the time machine correlate strongly with live benchmark scores. A fast, honest sandbox could speed forecasting research without contaminating tests with information from after the forecast date.
arxiv-2606-21113:
Vasile Marian, Yong-Bin Kang, and Alexander Buddery present a shareable collection in 2026 of object-centric dataset resources for image generation under limited data. Some uses need extra labeled examples that are hard to collect. Examples include pedestrian analysis, traffic sign checks, and object detection. Synthetic images help most when data preserve object structure, boxes, diversity, and context.

Three resources are standardized: pedestrian scenes from Cityscapes, traffic signs, and potted plants from COCO. Crops and annotations share one format across regimes. Pedestrian scenes include privacy blur and occlusion. Traffic signs are cleaner and high contrast. Plant scenes vary widely in context. Standardized resources let generation methods be compared fairly across difficulty levels, and give small teams training material for object-centric synthesis without assembling private datasets for each new domain.
arxiv-2606-21613:
Bharath Pillai and four colleagues propose a self-checking wildlife monitoring system in 2026 that needs almost no hand-labeled data. Camera traps and acoustic recorders flood conservation programs with data that experts cannot annotate at scale. Their idea uses known species behavior as the validation signal. If a vision pipeline and an acoustic pipeline independently recover the same hourly activity pattern, and both match published behavior, the agreement is unlikely to be an artifact.

The vision side runs zero-shot detection with BioCLIP 2 plus geographic localization from trap images; the acoustic side uses a fine-tuned vocalization classifier. On a breeding herd of Milu deer, both channels reproduced activity rhythms consistent with known deer ecology. The approach suits any species that is both seen and heard with documented habits.
arxiv-2606-21713:
San Dinh, Zichao Wendy Di, and Matt Menickelly speed up X-ray tomography by choosing each next measurement wisely, in 2026. More projections mean sharper reconstructions but also more time, cost, and radiation dose. A rule of thumb says beams aligned with the sample's edges carry the most information, yet finding them normally requires reconstructing the sample first, errors and all.

Their sequential method spots edge-aligned beams directly in the sinogram, the raw measurement data, skipping reconstruction entirely. A scoring rule that weighs exploration against exploitation picks each next set of beams. Images improve while redundancy drops, and the design step stays cheap and immune to reconstruction artifacts. For synchrotron facilities imaging delicate or fast-changing specimens, dose-efficient adaptive scanning stretches scarce beamtime and spares fragile samples.
arxiv-2606-22013:
Abdelfattah and colleagues present Vanguard in 2026, an industrial framework for load testing machine learning model serving systems before they launch. Serving models eats a dominant share of GPU infrastructure, yet capacity planning is often guesswork: under-provisioning causes outages, while over-provisioning wastes expensive hardware. Vanguard estimates serving capacity with an adaptive, feedback-driven search that watches live performance signals as load rises.

Dampening, spike tolerance, and convergence detection help the search settle on the maximum sustainable throughput that still meets service-level objectives. The authors analyze fourteen industrial case studies across recommendation, ranking, vision, and language model classes. Calibrating workloads with recorded real traffic cut estimation error from about thirty percent to between two and six percent. Proper warmup handling improved accuracy by a further 22.2 percent in their measurements. Before Vanguard, many launches were under-provisioned and incident-prone; the paper distils six lessons and architectural guidelines.
arxiv-2606-22413:
Ran Wei and six colleagues, including Jim Woodcock and Simon Foster, address AI-written safety-critical software in this 2026 paper. Vibe coding means accepting code generated by a large language model from a plain-language request, with little review. That speed suits consumer software, but standards such as DO-178C and ISO 26262 demand formal evidence of correctness, which language models cannot supply.

Their pipeline, called Forge, closes the loop between generation and verification using model-driven engineering tools. The model drafts Java code, and automated transformations extract formal versions in three formalisms. Deductive verification, communicating sequential processes refinement, and theorem proving each check the code from a different angle. Every failure returns as a correction prompt that drives the next generation round, while developers never read the formal models. Empirically, the pipeline produced verification evidence of the kind certification standards require for model-generated Java.
arxiv-2606-22513:
Mohammed Rafiq Namiq computes homological invariants of a family of graphs in this 2026 algebra paper. The graphs are co-chordal, meaning their complements are chordal, and the question is when they are sequentially Cohen-Macaulay, a layered algebraic regularity property. The associated edge ideals have graded Betti numbers recording the shape of their algebraic resolutions.

Namiq works through the glued clique complexes of the chordal complements, which decompose into tree-like pieces. From that structure come explicit formulas for the Betti numbers and a complete characterization of the cases. Applications pin down exact invariants for split graphs, threshold graphs, and prime ideal graphs, and classify which of them are Cohen-Macaulay. A closed formula covers nilpotent graphs of products of Artinian chain rings. The zero-divisor graphs modulo n are classified too: they have the property exactly when n is twice a prime or a prime power.
arxiv-2606-22713:
Anas Saleh extracts a readable formula for entanglement entropy in this 2026 physics paper. On Rydberg-atom arrays, the distribution of measured bitstrings is easy to obtain, but the entanglement entropy it constrains is far costlier to compute. Saleh's goal is a closed form a human can apply directly.

He builds a six-term linear formula from quantities derivable from bitstrings. A trained graph neural network guided the feature choice: probing it pinned the prediction to two-point correlations on the boundary between the halves. A search over those boundary quantities then isolated the form. In-distribution, its mean error is about 0.024 nats, several times the network's but with full transparency. Applied unchanged to new distributions, it beat the base network on five of six pools. At larger sizes, frozen coefficients fail, but in a structured way. Refitting per size restores accuracy, and slope scaling laws deploy it without labels.
arxiv-2606-23213:
Dineo Serame, Lionel Tarassenko, and Mauricio Villarroel detect breathing pauses in preterm infants with deep learning in a 2026 paper. Apnoea of prematurity means repeated stops in breathing, a common danger for babies in neonatal intensive care. Bedside monitors alarm on simple rate and oxygen thresholds. Those rules miss short or irregular events and raise many false alarms, tiring staff with non-actionable alerts. The team instead trains networks on the signals hospitals already record: chest impedance, heart tracing, and pulse oximetry light signals.

Serame and colleagues analyze about four hundred thirty hours of recordings from twenty-four preterm infants. Three reviewers annotated the events, giving a labeled set of breathing cessations and non-events. They compare a shallow convolutional network, residual networks, and a ConvNeXt design on a held-out test set. Signal choice mattered more than network depth, with chest impedance models reaching the strongest balanced accuracy.
arxiv-2606-23313:
Guangzhi Sun, Xiao Zhan, and Mark Gales tackle benchmark contamination in language models in a 2026 paper. When test data leaks into training, reported scores inflate and fair comparison breaks. Existing cleanup methods are judged only by total accuracy, which can hide large per-sample changes. Many also need access to a clean model. The authors propose judging cleanup sample by sample, measuring how close each cleaned output sits to a clean model's. On that footing they build a family of methods using ensembles of the contaminated model itself.

Sun and colleagues estimate a per-sample correction from ensemble disagreement, which signals memorization without knowing which samples are tainted. The correction builds a debiased target that removes the inflated probability on correct answers. That target can fix outputs directly or guide retraining to unlearn the contamination.
arxiv-2606-23613:
Smears and Wells build computable error bounds for numerical simulations of mean field games, in a 2026 paper on numerical analysis. Mean field games model strategic behavior across a huge population of players, such as traffic or crowds. Their mathematics couples two equations: one valuing player choices, running backward in time, and one tracking player density, running forward. Finite element methods approximate solutions on a mesh, but users need error guarantees.

The authors prove that the true error, measured in a suitable norm, equals the dual norm of the residual, the amount by which the computed solution fails the equations. From that identity they derive an a posteriori estimator, computed after solving, from residual terms, time jump terms, and stabilization terms. For common stabilizations the extra terms are bounded by the first two, giving a reliable, locally computable estimator.
arxiv-2606-24213:
Zheng and colleagues let the Linux kernel's eBPF programs run closer to native speed, without enlarging the kernel's trusted code. eBPF safely extends kernels for networking, observability, and security. An in-kernel verifier checks every program, then a simple just-in-time compiler translates it. That compiler works instruction by instruction in one pass, to stay trustworthy. It misses optimisations, so eBPF code can run up to twice as slowly as native equivalents.

Bolting optimisations into the kernel itself would need upstream acceptance, long release cycles, and more trusted code per architecture. Kops instead opens an extension interface. Userspace compilers and kernel modules can introduce new native operations into the pipeline safely. The verifier-centred safety story stays intact, while optimisation moves outside the trusted base. Zheng's team presents the interface at a 2026 systems conference. It closes the gap without reopening the safety debate that made eBPF acceptable.
arxiv-2606-24413:
Zamora tells how a Tenerife telescope built for astronomy became a night watchman for Earth orbit. The IAC80 telescope at Teide Observatory has served Europe's space surveillance and tracking since 2015. It tracks the swelling crowd of satellites and debris that threatens working craft. The 2026 account details the telescope and site, the optics in use, and the systems that let it run on its own, across low, medium, and geostationary orbits.

Weight falls on SATRED, the real-time data pipeline. It performs calibration, auto satellite trail detection, and astrometric measurement during observing itself. Trail spotting combines background, contour, and shape work, giving places and brightness for passing objects. Zamora reports the system as a rule gives readings with astrometric precision better than the programme needs. It is research gear reused for running an ever more crowded sky.
arxiv-2606-24813:
Mark Shipton, Amir Boag, and Roee Diamant set out an eight step method for measuring the underwater noise of submerged electric vehicles. Such craft, from robotic submarines to diver propulsion units, emit tonal and modulated sounds from their electric drives. Recording those signatures matters for passive detection and for fault finding. Coastal water fights the measurement: ambient noise and shallow water effects hide the craft's features. Existing noise standards were written for surface ships.

The method covers design of the measurement, checks for cavitation, and choice of frequency bands, plus spectral analysis and subsystem level reading of the data. Corrections for spreading losses then yield source level estimates. Calibrated pass by recordings are combined with craft metadata and noise context. A demonstration uses an A18D autonomous vehicle in coastal water. Drive related tonal groups appear near 5.56, 11.1, and 22.2 kilohertz, with harmonics reaching 105 kilohertz.
arxiv-2606-24913:
Bogdan Djordjević and Nikolay Ivanov introduce and study quantum phase operators for the harmonic oscillator. Phase is a basic observable in quantum theory, yet it resists clean definition, above all in the vacuum state where no phase can be assigned. As photon numbers grow, phase becomes measurable with rising precision, as in strong laser fields. The authors build phase operators tied to the oscillator's excitation level. Their operators turn out to be trace class perturbations of the classical Susskind Glogower operators.

The new operators are studied from both angles. Spectral properties receive detailed treatment. The two phase case, the physically relevant one, motivates the work throughout. Djordjević and Ivanov position their variants against a long literature on the phase problem. That link ties the new operators to the standard ones, so known theory carries over with controlled changes.
arxiv-2606-25013:
Narutatsu Ri, Abhishek Panigrahi, and Sanjeev Arora ask whether the thinking tokens of reasoning models actually deliberate about safety. Mostly, they do not. The intuition says deliberation should help: the model gets space to check an answer against its principles. Across frontier open weight reasoning models from the GPT-OSS, Qwen, Olmo, and Phi families, the refusal or compliance outcome is strongly predictable before any thinking begins. A probe on the first token's hidden state predicts the outcome with about 88 percent balanced accuracy.

Thinking looks more like prefix completion than revision. The outcome rarely changes after the first fifth of the thinking trace. Most deliberation happens when the response distribution is locked to one side. Existing safety interventions push models toward over refusal while suppressing the deliberation signals. Safety behaviour in current reasoning models is far less deliberative than assumed, Ri and colleagues conclude.
arxiv-2606-25113:
Chemotaxis models describe how cells move toward or away from chemical signals. Ahmed Abbas Jaber Al-Furaiji, Ghorbanali Haghighatdoost, and Mustafa Bazghandi apply classical Lie symmetry analysis to a flux limited Keller Segel system in two space dimensions plus time. In this model a cap on the flux changes the behaviour.

The full point symmetry algebra turns out to be small: time and space shifts plus rotations in the plane, nothing more. That smallness is itself the finding, since the flux limit kills the scaling symmetries the classical model enjoys and sharply restricts which symmetric solutions can exist. From an optimal system of one dimensional subalgebras, the authors derive the reduced equations for stationary, translation invariant, radial, travelling wave, and rotating wave solutions. Exact uniform equilibria are pinned down, and integral formulas are given for stationary radial and travelling wave profiles.
arxiv-2606-25313:
Probabilistic computers use flickering bits, called p-bits, to sample and optimise problems mapped onto Ising models, but one chip caps their size. Navid Anjum Aadit leads a team that networked many programmable chips into a single machine holding one million p-bits, reported in 2026. The system flips bits over a trillion times per second while every coupling weight stays in fast local memory. Chips exchange only single bit boundary states during a run, raising a design question about how often that exchange must happen.

Tests on three dimensional spin glasses gave a clean answer: a single timing ratio governs behaviour. Refresh boundaries often enough and the split machine matches a single device reference exactly. Refresh too rarely and solution quality decays in a predictable power law pattern instead. A mean field model reproduced the same trade off, suggesting it is universal.
arxiv-2606-25413:
Pairs of small planets locked near resonance should settle into tidy timing patterns, yet many Kepler systems show timing phases that refuse to damp away. Pin-Gao Gu and Gongjie Li test a suspect in 2026. A stellar companion is wrenching a distant cold Jupiter's orbit through the eccentric Kozai Lidov effect. That effect is a slow exchange between orbital tilt and stretch. Simulations follow resonant super Earth pairs while that outer machinery works on them over millions of years.

The same outer forcing that explains the cold Jupiters' stretched orbits also excited the inner pairs' timing phases. Resonance angles swung wider and, in a significant fraction of simulated systems, broke free into circulation within sixteen million years. Timing phases themselves stayed mostly small. The mechanism offers a route to the restless dynamics seen in young compact systems.
arxiv-2606-25513:
Dark matter might be the visible edge of a whole hidden sector with its own confining force, echoing how quarks bind in ordinary matter. Rao Zhang asks in 2026 whether collider jets of dark particles carry a readable fingerprint of the hidden gauge group behind them. A new simulation framework showers dark quarks and gluons for arbitrary gauge groups, handling the colour bookkeeping with a group theory tagging scheme. Exact three body kinematics keep mass effects sharp, including the dead cone gaps heavy particles carve in their own radiation.

Emission patterns are then drawn on the Lund jet plane, a map of splitting angles and energies, and sorted by a dedicated neural network. Different gauge symmetries separate cleanly in that representation. The discrimination survives aggressive cuts removing the soft details most sensitive to unknown dark hadronisation, and Zhang quantifies how heavy dark gauge bosons shift sensitivity.
arxiv-2606-25813:
Simulating thin gas flows particle by particle drowns weak signals in statistical noise. The slower the flow, the worse the drowning, and the cost explodes. L Teichröb, F Garmirian, and M Pfeiffer advance a variance reduced BGK scheme in 2026 and implement it in PICLas, an open source gas kinetics framework. The method tracks only the deviation from equilibrium, which is where the signal lives. This version adds modified flow estimators and collision operators for stability. Two collision models are shown, the Shakhov model and an ellipsoidal statistical one.

New features join them: adaptive equilibria, variable particle weights, and axisymmetric domains. Benchmarks span synthetic tests and one, two, and axisymmetric dimensions. Against plain BGK runs the new code agrees exactly, as it should. Against an analytical solution for thermal transpiration in a microchannel, it shows the efficiency gains that low signal flows need.
arxiv-2606-26013:
Kheir-eddine Otmani and colleagues improve physics-informed neural networks at their weakest point: shocks. These networks solve partial differential equations by training on the equation itself. Sharp jumps and steep fronts often blur or break the solution. Their G-PINNs framework weights the training loss by location. Gaussian weighting pushes effort toward high-gradient regions during training.

No advance knowledge of the shock is needed. The method finds and tracks moving jumps from the residual pattern alone. Tests use the one-dimensional Burgers equation at very low viscosity. Both standing and moving shocks are included. Errors land near thirteen and fourteen percent for the two cases. A standard network scores forty-five and thirty-three percent on the same tests. The gain comes purely from where training effort is spent. The recipe should transfer to other problems with unknown fronts.
arxiv-2606-26113:
Absos Ali Shaikh and Ananya Tripathi study gradient h-almost Yamabe solitons, self-similar shapes arising from the Yamabe flow. The Yamabe flow deforms a surface or space to even out its scalar curvature. Solitons are the flow's fixed shapes, described by a vector field and a chosen function h. The pair ask when such solitons are trivial, .

Integral inequalities drive the triviality conditions. Sufficient conditions are established on compact manifolds and on complete non-compact ones alike. Scalar curvature estimates follow under square-integrability conditions on the data. The sign behaviour of the function h, which the authors call its signal, plays a decisive role. Results extend and refine earlier work on almost Yamabe solitons. Generalized Yamabe solitons gain a sharper geometric characterization as a result. The study sits in Riemannian geometry, where curvature estimates of this kind classify which shapes a flow can settle into.
arxiv-2606-26213:
Andrew Chen, Ju-Hung Chen, Phurinat Pinyomit, and Alexis Block present RoboTales, a robot that tells stories with sock puppets. The low-cost system animates character-driven tales on a Baxter robot arm. Narration, gestures, and mouth movements run in sync, so puppets seem to speak their parts. Screen-free performance is the point: children get embodied storytelling instead of another display.

Pilot results favour the puppets. Puppet-based telling beat a gesture-only mode on engagement ratings from the HRIES scale. Story recall improved as well. The design is modular and platform-agnostic, so other robot arms can host it. Puppetry has centuries of teaching craft behind it, and social robots bring repeatable, tireless performance. Combining the two offers a fresh channel for child-centred learning spaces. The team positions RoboTales as a step toward deployable storytelling companions rather than a lab curiosity.
arxiv-2606-26413:
Alex Rose, Christopher Jewison, and Jonathan P. How present PRISM, a planner for robots unsure of their exact state. Belief-space planning works with a belief, a probability spread over possible states, instead of one known position. Motion noise and limits on states and controls make guarantees hard. Older planners sample points and link them into roadmaps. Coverage of the belief space often stays patchy, or routes grow costly.

PRISM rests on a new result about controlling state covariance under constraints. Covariance measures how spread out the uncertainty is. The planner splits the job into steering the average state and shrinking that spread. An online step then trims the cost of workable routes. The authors prove full coverage under mild assumptions on start and goal spreads. In hard simulated scenarios, PRISM reached complete coverage where rivals fell short. Its routes also cost less on average, with less variation.
arxiv-2606-26813:
Santanu Mondal and seven colleagues report evidence of powerful outflows from the black hole in a dwarf galaxy. Feeding and feedback by central black holes shape galaxy growth. In small galaxies, though, ultra-fast nuclear outflows were almost unexplored. The team studied Arp 151, a dwarf galaxy, using X-ray data from the NuSTAR telescope and optical data from the MaNGA survey.

The X-ray data hint at a fast outflow moving at a sizable fraction of light speed, at modest statistical confidence. The optical data show a separate galaxy-wide outflow. Their estimated mass loss rates differ greatly between the nuclear and galaxy scales. Comparing the two flows' momentum suggests they are in a momentum-conserving phase. The tentative finding implies dwarf galaxies can also launch ultra-fast outflows, previously seen only in massive galaxies.
arxiv-2606-26913:
L. Belcour of Intel Corporation compresses game textures with a hypernetwork, a network that writes other networks. Neural texture compression stores a material's surface detail as small learned features plus a tiny decoder network. At shading time the decoder rebuilds the texture in real time. Until now, each material needed its own slow optimisation run to find those features and decoder weights.

Belcour trains one hypernetwork to output both at once. Given a new material, it predicts the latent features and the decoder's weights and biases directly. The output space is huge, yet quality matches the per-material reference compressors. Extensions infer several decoders together. Others produce decoders that also perform sharpening the texture as they rebuild it. Per-material optimisation disappears from the pipeline.
arxiv-2606-27413:
Serna-Aguilera and colleagues release GRAFT, a dataset linking gene activity to visible traits in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana. Which genes control which traits is biology's standing question, but existing datasets rarely join expression profiles and trait readings for the same specimens. GRAFT curates exactly that pairing, supporting phenotype prediction and readable graph learning. Graph and hypergraph benchmark tasks come with the release. In the 2026 plant genomics paper, standard regression and explanatory baselines are benchmarked alongside.

A biologically informed hypergraph baseline validates gene-trait links found in the data. The authors describe GRAFT as the first dataset to pair gene information with varied trait data for the same specimens. Public release aims to spur methods that reason over gene data. The genome-to-phenome gap gets a shared measuring stick.
arxiv-2606-27513:
Hilman and Koltai propose a Feedback Network framework linking what people search online to where they go in the real city. Urban research usually studies digital activity and mobility apart, though each shapes the other. Donated data from Budapest residents pairs Google searches with location histories for the same people across four years. In 2026, a radius of gyration, adapted from movement studies, measures spread in both geographic travel and meaning wandering, making the two comparable.

Online exploration proves more concentrated than offline mobility. Digital behaviour runs in narrower, more repetitive interest channels, while physical movement stays diverse. Stable loops connect search and visitation for retail and for business and professional services. The pandemic disrupted spatial routines more strongly than mental wandering, widening the digital-physical gap for a time. A hybrid digital twin of society gains its first working parts.
arxiv-2606-27613:
Dark matter may hide in particles that are never seen directly. Rodrigo Capucha and four colleagues study one hunting ground at the Large Hadron Collider in 2026. The signal is a Higgs boson produced with a top quark and an antitop quark. An invisible mediator particle could appear alongside them. Earlier work covered scalar mediators. This study adds spin-one mediators with vector and axial-vector couplings.

The mediator mass is fixed at five gigaelectronvolts. Simulated proton collisions produce the signal events. Only dileptonic decays of the top pair are used. A kinematic fit reconstructs the event without rebuilding the invisible particle. All major standard-model backgrounds are included. The authors find sensitivity to light spin-one mediators. CP-sensitive angular measures can tell vector, axial-vector, scalar, and pseudoscalar cases apart. Such events could therefore characterise a discovery, not just detect one.
arxiv-2606-27913:
UTe2 is a heavy-fermion material with several field-induced superconducting phases. A metamagnetic transition organises those phases. One sits just below the transition, and another sits above it, seemingly stabilised by it. Theodore Weinberger and fourteen colleagues report steady-field measurements in 2026. Pulsed-field studies dominated earlier work. Torque and extraction magnetometry were used at ambient pressure, and magnetoconductance under pressure.

The steady-field data resolve a complex sub-structure inside the transition. Separate features evolve differently with temperature. That points to distinct contributions from itinerant and localised moments. Some electrons move freely, and others stay put. The itinerant part may connect to a possible spin-density wave state. The team models how Kondo and RKKY interactions evolve. Under pressure, they propose, collapse of magnetic anisotropy enhances spin fluctuations along the hard axis. Those fluctuations are pair-forming in the p-wave channel, and so stabilise the lower phase.
arxiv-2606-28113:
Micromagnetics simulates how magnetisation evolves in ferromagnetic media. The Gauss–Seidel projection method is an efficient, stable scheme for it. Yingxi Miao and Changjian Xie improve it in 2026 with a symmetric variant. The standard method uses a single-sided iteration, using the latest values from a heat-diffusion subproblem. It runs a two-pass iteration instead. Updated information from that stage is fully used. Discrete energy stability is rigorously guaranteed.

Accuracy is retained, first order in time and second order in space. Fast Fourier transforms accelerate the linear systems and stray-field evaluations. Numerical tests cover magnetisation dynamics and domain-wall propagation. The new scheme shows enhanced stability over the standard method. The gain is largest for small damping parameters, where the older method struggles. The strategy extends directly to second-order and efficiency-improved variants, the authors note.
arxiv-2606-28213:
Bang-Xian Han and Deng-Yu Liu ask whether a space's geometry can be detected through optimal transport, the study of cheapest ways to move mass around. Their test uses Wasserstein barycenters, a kind of average of probability distributions, and asks whether a measure of disorder called Boltzmann entropy behaves convexly at those averages.

Han and Liu prove that if a finite-dimensional normed space passes this convexity test for every family of distributions, its norm must come from an inner product, making it a Hilbert space. Every such space passes a famous curvature condition, so their test is strictly sharper. Smooth Finsler manifolds passing the test must likewise have Riemannian tangent spaces. The proof handles flat faces of the unit ball without assuming strict convexity.
arxiv-2606-28313:
Tom Holden-Dye, Max Marvell, Joel Mills, Christopher J. Turner, and Arijeet Pal simulate how operators evolve in quantum systems driven far from equilibrium. Such dynamics explode in complexity, and recent methods cope by truncating the simulation to operators built from few nontrivial pieces, an approach that already works well for many quantities of interest.

Holden-Dye and colleagues propose a leaner cut: truncate by an operator's diameter, the size of the lattice region it touches, rather than its weight. Existing theory for generic circuits makes the rule physically natural. Extensive simulations on the kicked Ising model and the Heisenberg XXZ model show the method stays accurate while running efficiently. It recovers local correlation functions and transport properties, the quantities experiments and theorists most often need.
arxiv-2606-28413:
Hongwei Xu, in a solo paper, asks what kind of machinery a leaderless mesh of artificial agents needs in order to think. Each agent must fold its peers' messages into one internal state, online, as observations arrive at irregular times, on hardware whose weights cannot be retrained. Xu argues the constraints together are far harder than each alone.

From one model of a self-evolving hidden state sampled at random times, Xu derives two necessary conditions. Because the state drifts, the optimal estimator needs an adaptive timescale, and every fixed-gain filter falls short. Because arrivals are clock-free, the estimate must depend on the gap between them, something no gap-blind network achieves at any size. Only continuous-time liquid networks satisfy both at once. Synthetic experiments confirm the separation exactly.
arxiv-2606-28913:
Guo and Zhang study how a network of sensors can estimate a shared parameter when each sensor reports only a yes-or-no threshold reading, and attackers may flip those labels. Nodes exchange information over a graph, and each node's own data may be too weak to identify the parameter alone. That weakness is called non-persistent excitation.

Their distributed recursive projection algorithm spreads information by a diffusion strategy, so nodes borrow strength from neighbours. The team prove almost sure bounds on prediction regret and estimation error without assuming independence, stationarity or Gaussian noise. Under a mild shared excitation condition, every node's estimate becomes consistent even when that node alone is non-exciting. Simulations on a network that is jointly exciting confirm the theory: their algorithm converged, while non-cooperative and tampering-unaware baselines did not.
arxiv-2606-29213:
Singh stress-tests optical character recognition on Devanagari, the script used for Hindi, where systems tuned on English and Chinese have barely been measured. He benchmarks ten systems, from the classical EasyOCR engine to specialised OCR vision-language models and frontier commercial models. Tests span four synthetic degradation conditions and three hundred real printed scans.

On clean rendered text, all ten systems clustered tightly. Under degradation, the specialised OCR models proved most fragile: one produced rare but catastrophic repetition failures, outputs dozens of times too long, wrecking its average despite the best median. On real scans, nine of ten systems collapsed and scores spread across a seventy-six point range. Strong English OCR did not predict Indic skill: one frontier model tied the classical engine, while an open model beat it and neared the leaders. A byte-level post-corrector helped only the engine it was tuned on.
arxiv-2606-29613:
Kim, Babiker, Kim, and Goebel ask whether giving experts distinct roles inside a Mixture-of-Experts model keeps its explanations faithful. Such architectures route work to specialist components, and role-based versions label experts with meanings such as synergy, redundancy, and uniqueness. A labelled role, though, does not guarantee that the model's explanations reflect its real computation.

The team hypothesizes that overlap between experts' internal representations weakens real role separation and degrades attribution-based faithfulness. They add representation-level decorrelation regularization, a training penalty that pushes experts' representations apart. Across several multimodal benchmarks, meaning tests that mix images and text, faithfulness improves on measures of comprehensiveness and sufficiency. Task performance stays intact at the same time. The same trend appears in a standard sparse Mixture-of-Experts baseline without explicit roles. The authors conclude that structural role labels alone are insufficient; separation in representation space does the work.
arxiv-2606-29713:
Yuan and four colleagues present SEVA, an agent that checks whether claims are properly attributed to sources. Hallucination is the top trust problem for language model agents. Fact attribution verifiers stand as the last line of defence. Existing verifiers emit only opaque binary labels. Agents then cannot self-correct, and operators cannot audit the verdict.

SEVA instead emits evidence links, reasoning chains that proceed step by step, calibrated confidence, and a six-category error breakdown with usable fixes. Training it with reinforcement learning is tricky: binary rewards on multi-component output cause advantage collapse, where the learning gradient vanishes. A process reward fixes this by scoring five separate components. A self-evolution loop then refines the agent over rounds, each producing a benchmark specialist rather than a generalist. On the ClearFacts benchmark, the three-billion-parameter version matches a commercial model while producing richer output that stays open to audit.
arxiv-2606-29813:
Zhang leads a nine-author team studying how the antiferromagnet EuAuAs carries current. Their focus is the topological Hall effect, an extra transverse voltage from non-trivial magnetic textures.

Measurements reveal antiferromagnetic transitions below about six kelvin, varying slightly by field direction, plus a field-driven transition. Transport readings show a pronounced topological Hall effect in the ordered state for one field and current geometry. The authors attribute it to finite scalar spin chirality, a measure of how non-coplanar the spins are. Magnetoresistance shows butterfly-shaped hysteresis, likely tied to spin-dependent scattering and domain effects.
arxiv-2606-29913:
Bourne, Gallouët, Mérigot, and Natale study Laguerre tessellations, divisions of space into convex cells described compactly by a set of points plus weights. They are widely used in computational geometry, imaging, and numerical analysis.

The problem is rebuilding a tessellation with prescribed cell volumes from the cells' barycenters, their centres of mass. The authors give the problem a geometric reading through convex order, a way of comparing probability measures by spread. They show the rebuilding can be solved closely by a Wasserstein projection, the closest-point map under an optimal-transport distance, onto the set of dominated measures. The same method fits tessellations to arbitrary centres of mass, demonstrated on microscope images of steel.
arxiv-2606-30013:
Valérie Berthé, Herman Goulet-Ouellet, Toghrul Karimov, Dominique Perrin, and Mihir Vahanwala ask what a simple machine does to a well behaved infinite word. A deterministic finite-state transducer reads an endless input word. It outputs a transformed endless word, symbol by symbol. Which nice properties of the input survive the transformation? The authors answer this preservation question for several classic properties.

The properties include recurrence, being morphic, and having factor frequencies. Recurrence means every block of symbols returns again later. Morphic words grow from repeated substitution rules. The famous Krohn-Rhodes theorem supplies the framework for their proofs. Their techniques come from ergodic theory for symbolic dynamical systems. In that language, the infinite words form shift spaces. The results map exactly which properties transducers always preserve.
arxiv-2606-30213:
Roberto Capistrano-Filho, Juan Muñoz, and José Quintero study whether solitary waves in a higher-order Boussinesq system hold together. Boussinesq systems model surface water waves of small amplitude. Solitary waves travel without changing shape when the system is balanced. Orbital stability asks whether small disturbances stay close to the wave. The system here has Hamiltonian structure and higher-order terms.

Variational methods supply the theoretical analysis. An asymptotic link to generalized fifth-order KdV equations helps too. Stability holds for a broad family of nonlinearities. Both kinds of nonlinearity are covered under scaling assumptions. Numerical simulations then probe the criterion directly. They suggest stable wave velocities span a wider range. Theory may therefore be underestimating the stable window somewhat. The gap invites sharper analysis of it in future work.
arxiv-2606-30313:
Alia Tarek and eight colleagues make brain tumor response assessment inspectable by forcing the model to reason through clinical concepts. Glioblastoma follow-up compares subtle MRI changes against the RANO criteria. Most deep learning predicts response labels straight from image features. Clinicians cannot inspect or correct that black box reasoning. Their model, TRACE, routes predictions through explicit concepts instead.

Baseline and follow-up MRI pairs enter a shared three-dimensional encoder. The model first predicts clinically meaningful root measurements of the tumor. Downstream RANO-derived concepts are then computed deterministically from those measurements. Scan interval and new-lesion facts join as passthrough concepts. Five-fold patient-wise validation runs on the LUMIERE dataset. Four-class performance improves over a plain concept bottleneck baseline. It stays within range of non-interpretable published systems. Correcting a wrong concept can fix the final prediction, experiments show.
arxiv-2606-30513:
Hassan Alhussein builds a cohomology theory for a class of non-associative algebras with a cyclic twist. Cyclic associative algebras obey a symmetric three-factor identity. Products associate and also rotate: the last factor can move to the front. His cohomology restricts Hochschild cochains by a matching condition. That condition comes from the defining rule. The resulting theory sits between two classical ones.

The second cohomology group classifies extensions of the algebra. Extensions by a cyclic bimodule are what it captures. A universal derivation is constructed for the theory. The module of forms is built alongside it. Together they form the full cyclic graded algebra. For trivial coefficients, natural inclusions chain the theories together. Connes' cyclic theory includes into the new one. It includes into Hochschild's in turn. The work extends these methods to this newer algebra class. Shift associative algebras supply the broader family context.
arxiv-2606-30713:
Mikhail Ivanov computes the galaxy power spectrum, the summary of how galaxies cluster by scale, to two-loop order in cosmological perturbation theory. Precision surveys demand models accurate deep into the nonlinear regime, where simple theory fails.
