Their paper shows how to estimate cumulative incidence, the chance of the event by a given time, while handling rival events properly. They work through two published data sets, computing incidence both ways. The Kaplan-Meier figures overshot the true incidence, because they pretend rival-event patients could still have the studied event later. The corrected method counts them as permanently out of the running. The authors addressed the note to clinical researchers, stressing that the choice of method changes reported risks in real studies.
europmc-pmc2584113:
Hulsen, de Vlieg, and Alkema built a web application called BioVenn in 2008 for drawing area-proportional Venn diagrams from biological lists. Genomics projects produce many lists of gene or protein identifiers, and researchers want to see overlaps at a glance. In a proper Venn diagram the circle and overlap sizes match the list sizes, but no existing tool tied that to biological databases.

A user pastes two or three lists and presses submit. The result is a diagram whose areas are proportional to the overlaps. Colours and text size adjust through the page, labels drag into place, and the picture exports as SVG or PNG image files. BioVenn also lists the identifiers in each subset. It links recognised ones to their source databases. It converts between Affymetrix, EntrezGene, and Ensembl identifiers.
europmc-pmc2702413:
Peng and colleagues published a United States study in 2009 on which parts of fine particle pollution send people to hospital. Fine particles are a mix of chemicals from traffic, diesel, wood smoke, and other sources. The question was whether some parts of that mix are more harmful than others.

They used daily hospital and air data from 2000 to 2006 for 119 urban areas and 12 million older adults on Medicare, which is public health cover for older people. Elemental carbon, a soot-like part, was linked to same-day heart admissions. Organic carbon matter was linked to same-day lung admissions, while other parts showed no clear link.
europmc-pmc2772813:
Comas, Homolka, Niemann, and Gagneux tested in 2009 how well standard genotyping methods reconstruct the family tree of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a pathogen with very little DNA diversity. Such monomorphic bacteria are usually typed by mobile or repeated elements: spoligotyping and MIRU-VNTR typing in this case. Using full sequences of eighty-nine genes from a global strain collection as the gold standard, they compared the trees each method produced.

Sequence-based trees were highly consistent and strongly supported, with almost no conflicting signal. Trees from spoligotyping and fifteen-locus MIRU-VNTR clashed with them, distorted by convergent evolution, where unrelated strains gain look-alike patterns. The twenty-four-locus version did better but still missed some lineages, and its power varied by lineage. They advise defining lineages by robust sequence markers and tailoring repeat-based typing to each lineage.
europmc-pmc2777313:
Capra and co-authors introduced in 2009 ConCavity, an algorithm that predicts where small molecules bind on a protein by combining evolutionary conservation with three-dimensional structure. Knowing a protein's functional sites is a key step toward knowing what it does. Earlier methods used sequence or structure alone. Their direct comparison showed the two approaches carry largely complementary information.

ConCavity merges conservation scores with a search for pockets on the protein surface. In large tests on diverse single- and multi-chain structures, it beat existing methods at finding both whole binding pockets and the individual residues that line them. It also reached top performance on catalytic sites and drug binding pockets. Blending the two evidence types, they conclude, improves on either alone and sharpens the link between conservation and function.
europmc-pmc2781113:
Schnoes, Brown, Dodevski, and Babbitt measured in 2009 how often public protein databases mislabel what an enzyme does. Most sequences in these databases were never tested in a lab; computers assign their functions by similarity, and errors can spread. The team audited four major databases using thirty-seven enzyme families with strong experimental records, grouped into six superfamilies.

The hand-curated Swiss-Prot database showed almost no errors. The other databases, including GenBank NR and TrEMBL, averaged error rates from five to sixty-three percent across the superfamilies. In ten families, over eighty percent of entries in some database were wrong. Errors grew in one database between 1993 and 2005, and most came from overpredicting, assigning a specific job the protein does not have. The authors suggest fixes for the systematic causes they found.
europmc-pmc2807913:
Nishimura and colleagues hunted in 2010 for plant proteins that work with ABI1, a brake on signaling by the drought hormone abscisic acid, called ABA. ABA helps plants survive dry spells and keeps seeds dormant. Because backup copies hide many signals from gene studies, the team fished out ABI1's partners directly from Arabidopsis plants.

Nine of the fourteen members of the PYR/PYL/RCAR family, the plant's ABA sensors, bound ABI1 most strongly in living tissue. The grip between one sensor, PYR1, and ABI1 tightened within five minutes of ABA treatment. Plants missing four sensor genes barely closed their leaf pores in response to ABA, hard proof the sensors matter for water saving.
europmc-pmc2826413:
Krebiehl and colleagues showed in 2010 that losing a protein called DJ-1, a rare cause of inherited Parkinson disease, gums up both the cell's power units and its recycling system. DJ-1 was known to guard cells against oxidative stress, meaning damage from reactive oxygen. The team used cells from knockout mice and from human carriers of a faulty DJ-1 version.

Without DJ-1, mitochondria breathed poorly, leaked more reactive oxygen, and changed shape in set ways. Recycling through lysosomes, the cell's digestion sacs, ran slowly at baseline, so defective mitochondria piled up instead of being cleared. A signaling protein called ERK2 was also underactive. The work ties DJ-1 directly to keeping mitochondria sound through steady housekeeping.
europmc-pmc2831913:
Clougherty reviewed the evidence in 2010 on whether air pollution hits male and female lungs differently, and whether the split is social or biological. Studies repeatedly find effects differing by sex, but the pattern is patchy and the reasons tangled: men and women differ in jobs, chores, and hormones, all at once.

Across adult studies, stronger effects more often appeared in women, especially in older groups and in studies using home-based exposure measures. Among children, boys looked more affected early in life and girls later in childhood. The author offers a framework borrowed from gender analysis, which separates social roles from body traits, to help future studies pull the two apart.
europmc-pmc2852313:
Emsley, Lohkamp, Scott, and Cowtan presented Coot in 2010, the graphics program crystallographers use to build and check molecular models by hand. Automated builders can draft a protein chain into an electron-density map, but scientists must inspect, fix, and validate the result interactively, especially at low resolution where errors creep in.

Coot displays atomic models, contoured density maps, and helper objects in a rotatable three-dimensional view built for ease of learning. Its tools cover model building, real-space refinement, and validation checks, with scripting access to nearly everything underneath. The paper surveys the program's features and design choices, including its library foundations, and traces how development has shifted emphasis toward validation as automatic building has improved.
europmc-pmc2855713:
Wang, Henning, and Heber showed in 2010 that two of the most popular lab tests for cell growth quietly misread green tea's star compound. Laboratories reported wildly varying potency for EGCG against cancer cells, and the team suspected the measurement method itself. They compared five assays on prostate and breast cancer cells treated with the compound.

Tests counting DNA or energy molecules agreed closely with direct counting. The dye tests MTT and MTS, which read mitochondrial activity, overestimated surviving cells and made EGCG look about half as potent as it truly was. A different plant compound, apigenin, showed no such distortion. The authors warn that assay choice must match a compound's chemistry when judging botanical extracts.
europmc-pmc2891813:
Oliveira-Ferreira and colleagues overviewed in 2010 the state of malaria in Brazil, a country that cut the disease hugely yet cannot finish it. Annual cases fell from around six million in the early 1940s to about three hundred six thousand registered in 2009. The main mosquito carrier lives across most of the country, but transmission now clings almost entirely to the Amazon Basin.

Disorderly settlement of the Amazon from the 1960s onward pushed cases back up and keeps them there. The milder parasite Plasmodium vivax causes over four fifths of cases and most of the economic burden, while the dangerous falciparum causes most of the rest. Worryingly, vivax has begun producing unusual severe complications in recent years, challenging its benign reputation.
europmc-pmc2930213:
Summers and colleagues reviewed neutrophil kinetics, the birth, movement, and removal of the most common white blood cells, in a 2010 article. Neutrophils kill germs but live only hours in the blood, so the body must replace them at a huge daily rate.

The review covers release from bone marrow, guided in part by signals acting through the CXCR4 receptor, and the split between freely flowing cells and a slower marginated pool. It also covers how aged cells are cleared and how stress or inflammation disturbs the balance. Too much neutrophil activity can injure healthy tissue.
europmc-pmc2936113:
Aggleton and co-authors reviewed the linked pathways between the hippocampus and the front part of the thalamus in 2010. These brain areas connect through several routes, and together they seem central to remembering past events.

Evidence from brain studies, patient work, and electrical tests shows parallel direct and indirect streams, the indirect ones passing through the mammillary bodies. The streams often push activity in opposite directions while staying partly separate. Damage at one site can disturb distant partners across the network. The system matters most for vivid recollection rather than simple feelings of familiarity.
europmc-pmc2936313:
Cole reviewed the biology of human chorionic gonadotropin, better known as hCG, in a 2010 article. The name covers four separate molecules, each made by different cells and each doing distinct work.

Standard hCG from placental tissue supports progesterone output, blood vessel growth in the womb, and quieting of the mother's immune response near the placenta. A sugar-heavy form drives growth and invasion of placental cells during implantation. A free fragment appears in many cancers outside the placenta, while a pituitary form comes from hormone cells in the brain. Each variant gets its own account.
europmc-pmc3000813:
Fiehn and co-authors profiled blood chemicals in obese African-American women with and without type 2 diabetes in a 2010 study. Insulin resistance disturbs the handling of many fuels at once, and mapping that disturbance may expose early markers.

Measuring several hundred fasting metabolites, they extracted components tracking closely with a long-term blood sugar score. Diabetes samples ran high in certain amino acids and their by-products, a hydroxy acid, long-chain fats, and sugar derivatives. Two amino acids climbed steadily with worse sugar control and matched a marker of fuel burning. The pattern hints the cell's central furnace runs inefficiently.
europmc-pmc3017113:
Gao led a large team sequencing two Metarhizium fungi used as living insecticides in a 2011 comparative genome study. One species attacks many insects while its cousin targets only grasshoppers and locusts, a contrast written somewhere in their genes.

The two genomes proved highly aligned in structure, with signs the genus descends from plant-associated fungi. Both devote an unusually large share of genes to secreted proteins, many with no known match. The broad attacker carries expanded families for cutting insect armour, detoxifying, and making toxins, matching its wider menu, while the specialist shows a genome defence trick the generalist lacks.
europmc-pmc3053313:
Izawa and Shadmehr asked in 2011 whether the brain learns movements from two kinds of error at once. One kind is sensory errors, where a movement feels different than predicted. The other is reward errors, where an outcome is worse than hoped. Volunteers adapted their reaching while the quality of visual feedback was varied. The team watched how learning spread to nearby movements and whether predictions themselves changed.

With crisp feedback, learning ran almost entirely on sensory errors. That learning rewrote the brain's predictions and spread broadly to neighboring movements. As feedback grew fuzzy, reward errors took a larger share. Reward driven learning changed the movement just as much, but left predictions untouched and spread only narrowly. The two signatures were so distinct that a person's learning style could be read from them. The work suggests rehabilitation and training should match feedback quality to the learning route they want.
europmc-pmc3156713:
Juliette Stehlé and colleagues recorded every close contact in a French primary school in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. How children mix drives how respiratory infections spread, yet hard numbers were scarce. Pupils and teachers wore radio badges for two days, logging tens of thousands of face-to-face encounters among more than two hundred people.

Each child averaged several hundred contacts a day with dozens of others, totalling nearly three hours of close time, though most single contacts were brief. Contact concentrated inside each class, with children spending about three times longer with classmates than with other classes. The resulting contact matrix, split by class and age, gives disease modellers a realistic alternative to assuming everyone mixes evenly, and helps rank measures such as class closure.
europmc-pmc3228813:
A. P. Jason de Koning and colleagues argued that far more of the human genome is repetitive than textbooks say, in this 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. The standard way to find transposable elements, matching DNA against known element sequences, had credited repeats with about half the genome. Their alternative method hunts for clusters of abundant short fragments related to one another.

The new approach predicted hundreds of millions of additional repetitive bases, pushing the estimate to roughly two-thirds of the genome. Detailed checks on two common element families showed the standard tool misses even moderately long fragments, while the new method stays sensitive down to small pieces. They also identified large amounts of previously unannotated element sequence. The message is that genome annotation needs combined, probability-aware methods.
europmc-pmc3270013:
Ravi Patel and Mukesh Jain introduced the NGS QC Toolkit, software for cleaning next-generation sequencing data, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Modern sequencers pour out enormous datasets, and bad reads can poison every downstream result, so quality control is essential. Fast, efficient tools were needed to handle the volume.

The toolkit is written in Perl as a free, standalone, open-source application. It checks quality and filters for high-grade data. It serves the two dominant platforms of the day, Roche 454 and Illumina machines. Extra utilities convert between sequence formats, trim reads, and compute statistics. Users can set their own thresholds at each step rather than accepting defaults. The authors expect the toolkit to improve the reliability of analyses built on sequencing data across many laboratories.
europmc-pmc3356313:
Agustí and the ECLIPSE investigators asked whether lasting inflammation throughout the body marks out a distinct group of people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The large ECLIPSE cohort followed patients for three years with repeated blood measurements, letting the team separate persistent inflammation from temporary spikes.

Of 1,755 patients, about thirty percent showed no systemic inflammation while sixteen percent stayed inflamed, based on a panel of six blood biomarkers. Despite similar lung damage, the persistently inflamed group died at far higher rates and suffered more exacerbations. The authors identify this as a distinct COPD phenotype that might benefit from targeted anti-inflammatory treatment.
europmc-pmc3418213:
Steinsbekk and co-authors pooled trials in 2012 on group-based self-management education for type 2 diabetes, compared with routine care. Group courses are popular because they cost less and let patients learn from each other. The review gathered twenty-one randomized trials with several thousand participants followed for at least six months.

Blood sugar control improved in the group courses at six months, a year, and two years, and fasting glucose fell too. Knowledge of diabetes and self-management skills rose clearly, and patients felt more empowered early on. Satisfaction and body weight improved at one year, while death rates, blood pressure, and blood fats did not differ. Quality of life results were too mixed to judge. Group teaching, they conclude, earns its place.
europmc-pmc3473013:
Kim and co-authors tested how a high-fat diet stirs inflammation through gut bacteria, in a 2012 PLoS ONE mouse study. Obesity travels with low-grade inflammation, but where that inflammation starts was unknown. Mice ate a high-fat or low-fat diet for eight weeks, and the team tracked gut microbes, gut leakiness, and inflammatory signals in body and colon.

The high-fat diet shifted gut microbes, raised a bacterial toxin called endotoxin in blood and stool, and loosened the gut wall's seals. Mice bred without the toxin sensor TLR4 still gained weight on the diet, but gained far less fat and showed no rise in inflammatory signals. Kim's group concludes the diet drives inflammation by raising endotoxin that acts through that sensor.
europmc-pmc3486913:
Relapsing Clostridium difficile gut infection follows a wrecked gut community, and Trevor D. Lawley with a large team tests a defined bacteria mix as the repair. Their 2012 mouse study uses the epidemic 027/BI strain, which causes chronic, contagious disease and a simplified, unhealthy gut flora that vancomycin cannot fix.

Healthy mouse feces restore a diverse flora and clear the disease. From that model the team builds a mix of just six diverse gut bacteria, including new species. The six restore a health-linked community and clear the 027/BI infection. Defined mixes, the study argues, can displace a harmful gut state without whole-stool transfer, a step toward targeted bacteriotherapy for patients.
europmc-pmc3509513:
Green tea compounds are often credited with fighting cancer, and Guang-Jian Du and six colleagues put ten of them head to head in 2012. They test representative polyphenols, including catechin, epicatechin, gallic acid, and EGCG, on two human colorectal cancer cell lines, HCT-116 and SW-480.

EGCG, short for epigallocatechin gallate, inhibits cancer cell growth most strongly, in a dose-dependent way. It arrests cells in the G1 phase of the cell cycle and pushes them into apoptosis, programmed death. Catechin and epicatechin show no growth inhibition, while gallic acid shows some. Comparing chemical structures against activity, the authors conclude EGCG is the most effective chemopreventive polyphenol in green tea.
europmc-pmc3560213:
Kathrin Benson, Sandra Cramer, and Hans-Joachim Galla reviewed electrical methods for watching cell barriers in Fluids and Barriers of the CNS in 2013. Sheets of epithelial and endothelial cells guard the borders between body compartments, with tight junctions sealing the gaps between cells. Lab models of these barriers need a way to check barrier strength without disturbing the cells or halting the experiment.

Measuring electrical resistance across the cell layer fills that need, and impedance methods extend it further. The review moves from simple resistance meters with two electrode sets to systems that track how resistance changes across frequencies and time. Such readings can flag leaks, follow deliberate opening of a barrier, and watch transport as it happens. Labs studying the blood-brain barrier and gut wall get a practical survey of what each setup can show.
europmc-pmc3570213:
Timothy Levine and colleagues tackled an unknown gene in Bioinformatics in 2013. Changes in that gene, C9orf72, are the most common known cause in families with frontotemporal dementia or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, two nerve diseases that overlap in symptoms and cell damage. Yet no one knew what the gene's protein product actually does inside a cell.

Rather than run bench experiments, the group ran sensitive computer searches comparing the protein's shape and sequence against known families. The match pointed to the DENN family, proteins that switch on Rab-GTPases, the traffic controllers that move cargo between cell compartments. On that basis the authors propose C9orf72 likely helps govern membrane traffic, and suggest renaming it DENNL72. The paper gives later lab work a concrete first hypothesis to test.
europmc-pmc3605113:
Frank Dudbridge, writing alone in PLoS Genetics in 2013, worked out the maths of polygenic risk scores. Such scores add up many small genetic effects into one number per person, built from markers picked in a first study and weighted by their effects there. Scores have proven genetic influence where no single marker stands out, linked related disorders, and fed risk prediction. Sometimes, though, they flop, and no formulas said when to expect success.

From a standard genetics model, Dudbridge derived how power and prediction accuracy depend on the sizes of both samples. They also depend on the share of variance genes explain, the strictness of marker selection, and the weighting scheme. He covered measured traits and case-control disease studies alike. Published successes, the formulas show, were well powered; failures trace to small samples. Useful prediction, he warns, may need samples ten times larger than those at hand.
europmc-pmc3652713:
Counting long-term illness sounds simple until each survey counts it in its own way, Goodman, Posner, Huang, Parekh and Koh warn in a 2013 Preventing Chronic Disease article. Trends point up: more older adults, longer lives, and more people with several conditions at once. Yet clashing definitions block fair counts.

The five authors set out a model for tightening the work, from how a condition is defined to how records are sorted and used. They test the model by running one shared sorting scheme across five national data systems. Recurring marks emerge from the texts they cite: a condition does not end on its own, it comes back, and it lasts months or years. The model is meant for research, policy, program and practice users alike.
europmc-pmc3662313:
A master gene switch may clear the storage jams of a muscle disease, Spampanato and a large team report in a 2013 EMBO Molecular Medicine study. The disease is Pompe disease, where a missing enzyme lets sugar stores pile up in cell waste sacs. The switch, called TFEB in the text, can fire up cell self-eating and push waste sacs to empty at the cell surface.

Raising the switch in a new muscle cell system and in mouse models cut sugar load and sac size. It also sped the handling of self-eating sacs and cleared their build-up. The sacs pushed out bore marks of both waste and self-eating sacs. When self-eating was blocked by gene means, the switch lost nearly all effect. The authors name TFEB a sound target for a disease short on options.
europmc-pmc3688513:
Hangauer and colleagues assembled RNA sequences from human cells and found transcription running far beyond known genes. Their catalogue holds tens of thousands of long non-coding RNAs present at levels of at least one copy per cell, a threshold meant to separate real transcripts from background noise.

These RNAs were not random leakage. Their production was regulated, their sequences showed signs of evolutionary conservation, and they clustered near DNA variants linked to human traits. The authors argue that much of this pervasive transcription is functional biology waiting to be mapped, and they release the catalogue so other groups can test what individual transcripts do.
europmc-pmc3692113:
Zuberi and colleagues update the GeneMANIA prediction server, a web tool that guesses gene function from network data. Given a list of query genes, the server extends it with genes that behave similarly across large genomics and proteomics datasets, and it reports how much each dataset contributed to the prediction.

GeneMANIA also works in reverse. Given one gene of unknown function, it finds the small set of genes most likely to share that function. Enriched Gene Ontology terms among them can hint at the answer. Seven organisms are supported, users can choose which datasets to search, and researchers can upload their own data to fold into the analysis.
europmc-pmc3695013:
Gaser and colleagues applied BrainAGE, a method that estimates the brain's age from a scan, to predicting which patients with mild cognitive impairment would progress to Alzheimer's disease. A brain that looks older than its owner's years signals faster shrinkage and higher risk. The study covered 195 patients, of whom 133 developed Alzheimer's within three years.

BrainAGE predicted conversion with accuracy up to eighty-one percent, beating cognitive test scales, hippocampus volume, and spinal fluid markers. Each extra year of estimated brain age carried about ten percent more risk. The authors highlight that the method is fast, fully automated, and worked across data from many centres, suiting it to screening and monitoring.
europmc-pmc3695513:
Mistry and colleagues stress-tested HMMER3, the main software for finding protein relatives by sequence, against the hand-curated Pfam family database. Profile methods are powerful, but two traps persist: alignments that stretch past the truly related region, and regions in unrelated proteins that converged on similar patterns.

Running the software against more than thirteen thousand curated families, they pinpointed problem cases where one region matched several supposedly unrelated families. Error estimates proved least trustworthy for families with repeating, biased patterns, such as coiled coils. The authors recommend keeping human-curated thresholds in Pfam, especially for the flagged families, rather than trusting automatic cutoffs alone.
europmc-pmc3699713:
Seymour and colleagues report the PICCOLO trial, which tested adding the antibody panitumumab to irinotecan chemotherapy in advanced colorectal cancer that had stopped responding to standard drugs. The trial enrolled patients across sixty British centres, and its main analysis covered 460 people whose tumours had normal KRAS and who had not had EGFR-targeted treatment before.

Survival was no better with the combination. The added drug did delay progression and shrank tumours in more patients, but at the cost of more diarrhoea, skin problems, lethargy, and infections. The authors conclude that adding panitumumab brought no survival gain in this group, and that finer molecular selection is needed to find who benefits from EGFR targeting.
europmc-pmc3737713:
James Herman wrote a solo review in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience in 2013 on how the brain controls adaptation to chronic stress. Stress triggers a hormone chain, the HPA axis, that releases glucocorticoids to shift energy around the body and brain. That response helps at first, but too much of it over time becomes harmful.

A key safeguard is habituation, the fading of the hormone response when the same stressor repeats. It depends in part on feedback from the hormones themselves and on limbic brain sites that regulate stress. Chronic stress can also heighten reactions to new threats. When stress is severe or unpredictable, the axis can fall out of balance for good. Herman links these patterns to the hormone faults and limbic changes seen in depression and PTSD.
europmc-pmc3752613:
Hirotaka Ebina, Naoko Misawa, Yuka Kanemura, and Yoshio Koyanagi reported a study in Scientific Reports in 2013 on using CRISPR/Cas9 against HIV. Drug therapy can hold HIV in check, but the virus hides in a dormant form inside the host genome and can re-emerge. The team asked whether the gene-editing system could disrupt that hidden provirus.

They aimed CRISPR/Cas9 at the virus's control region, the LTR, in T cells carrying dormant or switchable HIV. After stimulation, LTR-driven activity dropped sharply, and sequencing confirmed cuts and mutations at the target sites. The system could also cut internal viral genes out of the host chromosome. The authors suggest CRISPR/Cas9 may become a useful tool toward curing HIV infection.
europmc-pmc3764313:
M. F. Janssen and seven co-authors compared two versions of the EQ-5D health questionnaire in Quality of Life Research in 2013. The EQ-5D describes health in five dimensions. The older version gives each dimension three levels of problems; the newer gives five, which should capture finer differences.

A total of 3,919 people from six countries took both versions, spanning eight patient groups with chronic conditions plus a student group. The five-level version had fewer missing answers and far more distinct health states, 683 against 124. Its ceiling effect fell, meaning fewer people piled up at the top score, and its power to tell groups apart improved. Validity checks against other measures held up. The authors call the five-level system a valid extension of the three-level one.
europmc-pmc3781313:
Janesh Pillay, Tamar Tak, Vera Kamp, and Leo Koenderman wrote a review in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences in 2013 on immune suppression by neutrophils. Neutrophils are front-line cells that kill invading microbes. Newer work shows they can also suppress T cell responses, a role they share with a group called granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells, or G-MDSCs.

The two cell types overlap heavily in surface markers and appearance, and G-MDSCs range from immature to mature forms that suppress by different means. The authors propose that G-MDSCs are best understood as new functional states of neutrophils rather than a separate cell kind. The review sets out the similarities and differences with the aim of clarifying a confusing field and guiding further research.
europmc-pmc3800813:
Bikson and Rahman asked in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2013 why transcranial direct current stimulation, a weak current passed through the scalp, affects some brain circuits more than others. Their review looks for the sources of this selectivity, which matters for using the method safely in treatment and research.

They group the causes into three kinds. The first is the anatomy of the head and brain, which steers where the current flows. The second is activity selectivity, since busy neurons respond differently from quiet ones. The third is input bias, because stimulation shifts the balance of signals a circuit already receives. Together, they argue, these factors explain why one fixed dose can have uneven effects across people and brain areas.
europmc-pmc3842113:
Daniel J. Antoine leads a team in a liver marker study in Hepatology in 2013. Overdose of acetaminophen, a common pain drug, is a top cause of sudden liver failure in Western countries. Standard blood tests can look normal at first hospital visit, even when harm has begun.

The team test a panel of new markers in blood taken at that first visit. One marker is a liver-specific microRNA, one flags cell death, two track how cells die, and one marks power-unit failure in cells. All tied closely to later proof of liver injury. Set against the standard enzyme test, the panel caught injury earlier and with more trust. Early reads could let doctors tailor care to each patient sooner.
europmc-pmc3853013:
Reza M. Salek, Christoph Steinbeck, Mark R. Viant, Royston Goodacre, and Warwick B. Dunn write on reporting rules in GigaScience in 2013. Their field is metabolomics, the study of small molecules in living samples. Naming those molecules right is key, and shared report rules let labs merge and trust each other's data.

Base rules for naming molecules were set years before, yet uptake stayed weak. The authors, from society task groups, push for updates and for journals and data banks to require the rules. One data bank for study deposits gets named as a model. Clear labels for how sure a molecule name is would help most. The piece is a call to action more than a study, aimed at editors and data hosts.
europmc-pmc3858813:
Robert P. Fordham leads a team of co-authors in a stem cell study in Cell Stem Cell in 2013. The gut lining renews itself from stem cells, yet the fetal gut's starter cells were little known. The team grow such cells from human and mouse fetal gut and test their repair power.

The fetal cells form ball-like cultures that can be grown for long spans in a dish. They carry less of a key mature marker and thrive under signals that block adult-type growth cues. A shift in signals coaxes them into mature gut organoids. When placed into an injured mouse colon, the cells patched the lining with proper local cell types. The work points toward patient-matched gut repair grown from starter cells.
europmc-pmc3879213:
Maria S. Robles, Jürgen Cox, and Matthias Mann track daily protein rhythms in mouse liver in PLoS Genetics, with the record dated 2014. Body clocks drive daily waves in gene activity that run metabolism. How far those waves reach the protein level was held back by weak protein counting tools.

Using labeled mice and sharp mass spectrometry, the team counted thousands of liver proteins across two full day cycles. A small share cycled each day. A fifth of the daily-changing proteins cycled with no matching wave in their gene copies, proof that control after the copy stage matters. Many protein waves lagged their gene waves by hours, with lags that shift by time of day. The work redraws how clocks run the liver.
europmc-pmc3922213:
Joseph N. Jarvis, Tihana Bicanic, and a large team study deaths from a fungal brain infection. Their paper appeared in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2014. The infection is cryptococcal meningitis in people with HIV. It is the most common cause of adult meningitis in much of Africa. Even with antifungal drugs, it kills a quarter to nearly half of patients in poorer settings.

The team pooled trial cohorts to reach 501 patients. The patients came from Thailand, South Africa, and other sites. Three factors stood out as signs of early death. The first was how much fungus sat in the spinal fluid at diagnosis. The second was an altered mental state. The third was how fast the infection cleared on treatment. The authors use those signs to point to steps that could raise survival.
europmc-pmc3984213:
Richard T. Burnett and colleagues build a single risk curve for fine particle air pollution in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2014. Counting the global deaths caused by PM2.5, particles fine enough to reach deep into lungs, needs a curve linking exposure to risk across the whole world range. Direct studies run out at the clean levels of rich countries, while many cities breathe far dirtier air. The team integrated risk data from four sources: outdoor air studies, secondhand smoke, household cooking fuels, and active smoking.

The stitched curve covers four adult killers, heart artery disease, stroke, chronic lung disease, and lung cancer, plus chest infections in children under five. Because the same particle dose underlies all four sources, smoking data anchor the curve's high end. The functions were built for the Global Burden of Disease project to price air pollution's toll everywhere.
europmc-pmc3999713:
Alisdair McNeill and ten co-authors test a cough drug as a helper for a faulty enzyme in Parkinson's disease cells, in Brain in 2014. Faults in a gene called GBA are the most common known risk factor for Parkinson's. The gene builds an enzyme, glucosylceramidase, that works in lysosomes, the cell's waste-clearing units.

The team grew skin cells from patients who carried one faulty copy of the gene. Those cells showed low enzyme activity, plus signs of stress in the cell's folding workshop and from harmful oxygen by-products. The drug ambroxol raised enzyme activity and eased the oxygen stress. Ambroxol acts as a chaperone, a helper that steadies the faulty enzyme so more of it reaches the lysosome. The result points to a possible treatment route for patients whose disease links to this gene.
europmc-pmc4005913:
Tobias Großkopf and Orkun S. Soyer review synthetic microbial communities, in Current Opinion in Microbiology in 2014. Natural microbe communities, from oceans to the human gut, hold tens to thousands of species. New sequencing tools map that diversity fast, yet the rules that govern how such groups work stay hard to pin down.

A synthetic community is a small group built by hand from known microbes. It keeps core traits of natural groups, such as exchange of goods between members, but stays simple enough to test and to model. Members can be added, removed, or swapped, so cause and effect come into view. The review weighs what these built systems have shown about interaction and group function, and where their limits lie. Such systems are also gaining use in biotechnology, where a stable, known group can be set to a task.
europmc-pmc4046113:
Radu Stoica and colleagues identify a protein handshake that ties two cell compartments together, in Nature Communications in 2014. The endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria touch over part of the mitochondrial surface. These contacts pass calcium and fats between them and shape many cell tasks. What holds them together was unclear.

The team shows an ER protein, VAPB, binds a mitochondrial partner, PTPIP51, and that the pair acts as a tether. Loosening or tightening the pair changes how much contact forms. A second protein, TDP-43, then enters the story. TDP-43 is tied to motor neurone disease and a form of dementia. In excess it breaks the VAPB partnership, cuts the contacts, and disturbs calcium balance. A kinase that TDP-43 activates helps govern the tether, completing the chain. The work names a fresh mechanism by which TDP-43 may harm neurons.
europmc-pmc4053813:
Derrick E. Wood and Steven L. Salzberg present Kraken, a program that names the microbes in a DNA sample at record speed, in Genome Biology in 2014. Metagenomic studies read all DNA in a sample at once. Sorting millions of short reads by species used to be the slow step, forcing many teams to classify only a slice of their data.

Kraken matches exact short words from each read against a database of known genomes, then assigns the read to the lowest shared ancestor of its matches. The trick is fast enough to classify over four million short reads per minute. That is hundreds of times faster than the standard search tool and an order faster than the quickest abundance estimator, with accuracy to match. The pitch is completeness: studies can label every read they paid to sequence.
europmc-pmc4066613:
Giuseppe Bellelli and colleagues validated the 4AT, a short screening test for delirium in older hospital patients. Their prospective study appeared in Age and Ageing in 2014. Delirium is a sudden, shifting state of inattention and confusion that is common and serious in older inpatients, so a fast routine screen is valuable.

More than two hundred thirty patients aged seventy or older, admitted to a geriatrics ward and a rehabilitation unit, took the 4AT within a day of arrival. A second doctor, blind to the score, made a reference diagnosis within half an hour. Delirium was found in about one patient in eight. The 4AT proved sensitive and specific, and its brevity suits routine practice.
europmc-pmc4132213:
Anouk Middelweerd, Julia S. Mollee, C. Natalie van der Wal, Johannes Brug, and Saskia J. te Velde reviewed smartphone apps that promote physical activity in adults. Their review and content analysis appeared in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity in 2014. App stores held tens of thousands of health and fitness apps, yet their quality was unknown.

Systematic searches of the two main stores yielded sixty-four apps, each rated against a standard list of behaviour change techniques. Apps used five techniques on average, from two to eight. Self-monitoring, feedback on performance, and goal setting were commonest. Motivational interviewing, stress management, and relapse prevention were rare. Paid apps did no better than free ones, and the stores did not differ.
europmc-pmc4147713:
Elizabeth J. Lyons, Zakkoyya H. Lewis, Brian G. Mayrsohn, and Jennifer L. Rowland took stock of the change tricks built into wrist and clip-on step tools. Their study came out in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2014. Tools from brands such as Fitbit add auto feedback and guided steps to the plain step counts of old meters.

The team found thirteen tools for sale and had trained raters use each one for a week or more. They scored the tools on a set list of change tricks, with more checks for tricks shown to work in past pooled work. All tools gave feedback. The span of tricks built in ran wide from brand to brand. The team sees the tools as a way to bring clinic-grade change plans to a mass scale.
europmc-pmc4180313:
Matthias R. Baumgartner and a panel of specialists from twelve European countries and the United States wrote joint guidelines for two rare metabolic diseases in the Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases in 2014. Methylmalonic acidemia and propionic acidemia are inherited faults that let toxic acids build up in the body. Both can kill a newborn or leave survivors with severe brain harm.

The panel graded all available evidence and turned it into shared statements on diagnosis and care. Warning signs are vague, so the guidelines stress fast testing when a baby crashes with acidosis and high ammonia. Long-term care rests on a low-protein diet and carnitine, yet results stay poor for most forms. Kidney failure is a late risk in one disease and heart muscle damage in the other, so follow-up must watch for both.
europmc-pmc4216113:
Marius Ilie, Paul Hofman, and eight co-authors reported a blood warning sign for lung cancer in PLoS ONE in 2014. People with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease carry a high lung cancer risk, but scans find tumours only once they form visible nodules. Tumour cells drifting in the blood might flag danger earlier.

The team filtered blood from 245 people without cancer, 168 of them with the lung disease, hunting for circulating tumour cells. Five patients, all with the lung disease and none of the controls, carried such cells. Yearly scans then found lung nodules in those five patients one to four years later, and surgery confirmed early cancer in each. A year after surgery, none had relapsed. The authors propose these sentinel cells as an early alarm worth testing in larger groups.
europmc-pmc4270213:
Joe Alcock, Carlo C Maley, and C Athena Aktipis ask whether gut microbes steer what we want to eat. Their essay appeared in BioEssays in 2014. Microbes gain when the host eats foods they thrive on, so natural selection may favor microbes that push the host toward those foods.

The authors lay out ways microbes could shape cravings: through reward and fullness signals, mood altering toxins, changed taste receptors, and the vagus nerve that links gut and brain. They also weigh plain host side explanations for cravings. Because diet, probiotics, and other tools can shift gut microbes, the idea points to new ways to tackle obesity and poor eating habits.
europmc-pmc4277013:
An-Na Li and five co-authors survey natural polyphenols, plant compounds found in foods such as fruit, tea, and vegetables. Their review appeared in Nutrients in 2014. Polyphenols draw interest because they can mop up reactive oxygen species, the unstable molecules tied to many long term diseases.

The review covers where polyphenols come from, how they act in the body, and what tests show about their effects on heart disease, cancer, diabetes, and brain disorders. It also treats two weak points: the body absorbs many polyphenols poorly, and high doses may carry risks. Readers get a balanced stocktake of a popular but still unsettled area of nutrition science.
europmc-pmc4285113:
Marie Engelene J Obien, Kosmas Deligkaris, Torsten Bullmann, Douglas J Bakkum, and Urs Frey review microelectrode arrays, grids of tiny sensors that record many neurons at once. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience in 2014. Arrays can both listen to and stimulate cells at many sites, in dishes and in living brains.

Unlike a probe inside one cell, each contact picks up signals from every source near it, so reading the output takes care. The review explains what the signals mean, how new chips pack electronics beside the sensors for sharper recordings, and how the tools reveal both single cell behavior and network patterns. It is a guide for neuroscientists choosing recording methods.
europmc-pmc4299513:
Matthew Scott, Stefan Klumpp, Eduard M Mateescu, and Terence Hwa explain why bacteria obey simple growth laws. Their study appeared in Molecular Systems Biology in 2014. Across many food conditions, one share tracks growth rate in a tidy line. That share is the protein tied up in ribosomes, the cell's factories. The line holds even as thousands of other proteins shift.

The team models how E. coli decides how much ribosome to build. A supply driven feedforward control, tuned to squeeze the most amino acid flow from the food at hand, reproduces the growth laws on its own. The laws thus emerge from the control strategy itself, not from fine molecular details, which is why they hold so broadly.
europmc-pmc4383913:
Simon Forbes and a team of co-authors described COSMIC, the catalogue of cancer mutations, in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. COSMIC collects somatic mutations, changes cancers acquire during life, from the world literature and from genome projects. Release 70, from August 2014, held more than two million coding point mutations across over a million tumor samples, spanning nearly all human genes. Hand curation from almost 20,000 papers gives precise disease and patient detail.

Alongside point mutations, the catalogue holds over six million non-coding mutations, plus gene fusions, genome rearrangements, copy number changes, and expression variants. Cancer genome curation across more than 12,000 genomes adds breadth, exposing unrecognized mutation hotspots and possible drug targets. Each change is mapped to the genome and to its gene, then cross-linked by disease type, making patterns across cancers visible at once.
europmc-pmc4384013:
Allan Davis and co-authors marked ten years of the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. The database began to organize which genes and proteins respond to environmental toxic agents across species. It grew into a resource built on a triad of relationships: chemical to gene, chemical to disease, and gene to disease, all hand-curated from the literature by professional curators using controlled vocabularies. By its tenth year it held 24 million such connections.

The update adds a Pathway View tool that draws the routes connecting chemicals, genes, and diseases. Curation methods were refined, pilot results on chemical effects on traits were reported, and a data set on exposures was in preparation. What began as a prototype is now used to build and test ideas about how environment drives disease.
europmc-pmc4387513:
Marcus Raichle argued that the brain's own ongoing activity, not its responses to tasks, is its main work. His essay ran in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2015. Most brain studies measure reactions to stimuli, which quietly frames the brain as a reflex machine. Raichle notes that the brain spends most of its energy on internal activity. It takes in only a limited stream of sense data, yet keeps a rich organization running at rest, visible in its metabolism and slow rhythms.

He calls this the restless brain. Its intrinsic activity interprets the world, prepares responses, and predicts what will be needed next. Understanding it will require joining brain-systems research with cell and molecular work, since channels, receptors, and energy pathways all shift constantly. The reward he promises is a better account of human behavior, in health and in disease alike.
europmc-pmc4484413:
Abhisek Mitra, Lopa Mishra, and Shulin Li reviewed three linked cell states behind cancer relapse in Oncotarget in 2015. Relapse and spread cause most deaths in advanced cancer, even after surgery or chemotherapy at first succeeds. Persistent cancer stem cells, which resist chemotherapy, are a prime suspect, and drugs against them exist for several cancers, yet recurrence stays common.

Recent work on circulating tumor cells, cancer cells found in patients' blood, shows some carry both stem cell traits and marks of the epithelial-mesenchymal transition, a program that loosens cells for travel. Patients with such cells respond poorly to standard chemotherapy. The transition program may also remodel the tissue around dormant stem cells and wake them. The review maps these links in detail to define the patient group most prone to relapse and to suggest treatments aimed at that biology.
europmc-pmc4499913:
Gennaro D'Amato and a very large panel of co-authors issued a World Allergy Organization statement on weather, climate change, and allergic disease in the World Allergy Organization Journal in 2015. Asthma and hay fever have risen to epidemic levels worldwide. Industry and traffic pollution explain part of the rise, but only broad environmental change can explain the rest, the panel argues, as economies and environments transform across developed and developing countries alike.

Greenhouse gases have already warmed the planet, bringing longer heat waves, temperature swings, more air pollution, fires, droughts, and floods, all of which burden breathing. Pollen seasons lengthen and allergens grow stronger under higher carbon dioxide. The statement reviews how each factor, from thunderstorms to sandstorms, affects asthma and allergy, and calls on health systems and governments to treat climate adaptation as part of allergy care.
europmc-pmc4518313:
June Li leads a twelve-author team uncovering a second route by which platelets are destroyed in a bleeding disorder, in Nature Communications in 2015. In immune thrombocytopenia, the body's own antibodies mark blood platelets for removal, leaving too few to form clots. The textbook route has spleen cells eat marked platelets through Fc receptors.

Antibodies against one platelet protein, GPIbα, often resist that Fc-targeted treatment. Using custom antibodies and patient plasma, the team showed these trigger a different path: platelets lose surface sugars, a process called desialylation, and are then cleared by liver cells instead. Blocking the sugar-cutting enzyme eased the platelet loss in mice, marking both a possible test and a treatment target for stubborn cases.
europmc-pmc4542313:
Thomas McKerrell leads a twelve-author team tracing leukemia-linked mutations in healthy blood, in Cell Reports in 2015. Blood stem cells can pick up cancer-associated mutations and expand into clones without causing disease, a state called clonal hemopoiesis. How common it is, and at what ages, was undermeasured.

The team used ultra-deep sequencing on 15 mutation hot spots in blood DNA from 4,219 people. Clones appeared in 0.8% of people under 60, rising to 19.5% of those aged 90 and over. One gene's mutation, DNMT3A-R882, showed up as early as age 25. Mutations in splicing genes appeared only after 70, which may explain why related blood disorders cluster in old age.
europmc-pmc4590613:
Gyongyi Szabo and Banishree Saha review alcohol's damage to immune defense, in Alcohol Research: Current Reviews in 2015. Even moderate drinking alters immune responses across nearly every cell type of both the fast innate and the learned adaptive arms. Much of the harm stays hidden until a second insult, such as infection or injury, exposes it.

The pattern of drinking flips the effect. A single bout of alcohol damps inflammation, while chronic use speeds it up, fueling liver disease and pancreatitis and reaching many other organs. Chronic exposure also weakens anti-inflammatory signals and degrades antibody and cell-mediated responses alike. The net effect, the authors conclude, is greater vulnerability to bacterial and viral infection and to sterile inflammation.
europmc-pmc4600713:
Working with colleagues, Shi Gu published a 2015 study applying control theory to the brain's structural networks. White matter wiring links brain regions into large circuits that support thought. The authors asked how that wiring shapes the brain's ability to move between mental states. The work appeared in Nature Communications and used network mathematics on brain connectivity data.

Densely connected areas, mostly in the default mode system, made many states easy to reach. Weakly connected areas, mostly in cognitive control systems, helped reach hard states. Areas sitting between network communities, often in attention systems, helped join or separate different systems. The results tie each circuit's wiring pattern to a distinct role in steering brain activity.
europmc-pmc4631113:
In 2015, Yong-Sheng Tong and colleagues' study testing a long non-coding RNA in blood as a marker for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma appeared. Long non-coding RNAs do not build proteins, but tumours release them into the blood, where they stay stable. The team screened ten candidate RNAs linked to this cancer. The work appeared in Molecular Cancer and ran in four stages.

Three RNAs, POU3F3, HNF1A-AS1, and SPRY4-IT1, ran higher in patients than in healthy controls. POU3F3 performed best, with sensitivity of 72.8 percent for detecting the cancer. The RNA in blood came mostly from tumour cells themselves. A simple blood test built on POU3F3 could help find this cancer earlier, when treatment works better.
europmc-pmc4643313:
In 2015, Thorsten Boroviak and colleagues' study profiling gene activity in single embryo lineages to trace naive pluripotency appeared. This flexible stem cell state appears in the early mammalian embryo. The team sequenced RNA from defined cell lineages in mouse embryos from the eight-cell stage onward. The work appeared in Developmental Cell.

They mapped gene modules that mark each developmental state and the patterns that switch naive pluripotency on and off. Stem cells and paused embryos kept nearly the full core circuitry of the natural state. Marmoset monkey embryos used a similar set of pluripotency factors but different signals, including WNT, during early lineage splits. The comparison shows a shared foundation with species-specific wiring on top.
europmc-pmc4678113:
A team led by Sebastian Eustermann published a 2015 study revealing how the protein PARP-1 detects single-strand DNA breaks. Such breaks are the most common DNA damage, and PARP-1 responds within seconds, launching repair signals. Its many flexible domains had blocked structural work. The study appeared in Molecular Cell.

Two zinc finger domains at one end of PARP-1 grip the break, sensing how deformable it is. Their binding drives the remaining domains to fold together step by step, switching on the enzyme domain at the far end. After modifying itself, PARP-1 lets go of the DNA so repair can proceed. The mechanism also explains how PARP-blocking drugs, which kill certain tumour cells, do their work.
europmc-pmc4738713:
Sugimoto, Vago, Teixeira, and Sousa review how annexin A1, a protein switched on by glucocorticoid hormones, helps end inflammation rather than merely suppress it. Neutrophils flood infected or injured tissue first, but if they linger they damage the tissue they came to defend, so their exit must be actively managed.

Annexin A1 and peptides modelled on it cut neutrophil entry into tissue, push spent neutrophils into programmed death, and help macrophages clear the corpses. It also draws in monocytes and reprograms macrophages toward a resolving state that releases calming signals. The authors argue this multi-step control makes annexin A1 a template for a new class of inflammation-resolving drugs.
europmc-pmc4739513:
Vidaurre and five colleagues present a method for catching brain states that last less than a second. Standard tools average brain activity over sliding time windows, which blurs brief, repeated patterns in recordings such as MEG. Their approach models activity as a sequence of discrete states. Each state has its own pattern of power and coupling across brain regions, and no task timings are needed in advance.

Pooling many short visits to the same state lets the method estimate that state's spectrum and coherence cleanly. Demonstrated on MEG data from a voluntary movement task, it picks out fleeting states with distinct connectivity profiles that windowed analyses would smear away.
europmc-pmc4741013:
Frasquilho, Matos, Salonna, and four colleagues review a decade of research on what economic recessions do to mental health. They screen the literature from 2004 to 2014 and keep 101 original studies that link economic factors to measures of mental wellbeing.

The evidence points one way. Recessions, and the hardships that travel with them such as unemployment, falling income, and unmanageable debt, come with poorer mental wellbeing. Rates of common mental disorders, substance problems, and suicidal behaviour all rise. The authors add a caution: most studies are snapshots in time, which limits claims about cause. They close with policy measures that might blunt the damage during downturns.
europmc-pmc4790313:
Andrew D. Wales, Robert H. Davies, and Martin J. Woodward review a side road to antibiotic resistance in Antibiotics in 2015. Germs can gain drug resistance not only from antibiotics. Disinfectants and preservatives, and metals such as copper and zinc fed to livestock, can also train or select for it, a process called co-selection.

The evidence takes several forms. Some defenses shield a germ against many chemical classes at once. Some resistance genes ride together on the same DNA, so guarding against a metal keeps the drug gene too. Whole farm germ communities shift under these pressures, though some gains fade when the pressure lifts. The review weighs how much this matters for germs that pass from livestock to people through food, and what farm practice should change.
europmc-pmc4845013:
Jan Kubanek and five co-authors showed in 2016 that focused ultrasound can change the flow through single ion channels. Ultrasound aimed at the brain can stir neurons in animals and people, but how it does so was unknown. One guess was that sound, a push-like force, opens channels in cell walls that sense stretch. The group tested that guess in frog egg cells fitted with known channels.

Sound at varied strength shifted channel currents by up to about a fifth on average, and the effect reversed when sound stopped. Channel blockers wiped the effect out. Sound thus acts on the channels themselves, a concrete lead for how brain ultrasound works and how it might be tuned for care.
europmc-pmc4877513:
Michael Gejl and co-authors ran a 26-week trial in 2016 of a diabetes drug, liraglutide, in Alzheimer's disease. The drug mimics a gut hormone, GLP-1, which helped in animal models of the disease. Thirty-eight patients were split between drug and placebo, 18 against 20. Brain scans tracked amyloid build-up and sugar use, and a memory scale tracked thinking.

Amyloid rose in both groups alike, so the drug did not slow plaque growth. Brain sugar use fell across regions in the placebo group but held steadier on the drug, hinting at protected brain energy use. Thinking scores add context. A bigger, longer trial would be needed to judge real clinical gain.
europmc-pmc4877813:
Eva M. Klein and co-authors checked the German version of the Perceived Stress Scale in 2016 and set national norms. The ten-item scale asks how stressed life feels and is used worldwide, yet the German form had not been validated. A random community sample of 2,463 people aged 14 to 90, with 1,315 women and 1,148 men, filled it in plus standard mood and life scales.

Scores hung together well and lined up with depression, anxiety, fatigue, delay habits, and lower life satisfaction, as stress should. Two linked factors sat under the items. Norm tables by age and sex now let German studies judge a score against the public. Follow-up over time is the next gap to close.
europmc-pmc4892413:
Vagheesh Narasimhan and co-authors presented BCFtools/RoH in 2016, a tool that finds runs of sameness in sequenced genomes. In such runs, both chromosome copies carry the same letters, often because both descend from one recent ancestor, a state called autozygosity. Older tools used chip data, while sequencing holds far more detail, above all in gene-rich exome reads.

A hidden Markov model, a statistic method that infers hidden states from noisy reads, drives the search. On simulated and 1000 Genomes data, the tool beat older methods in both hit rate and accuracy across error levels. The free tool helps map recessive disease genes and read family history from DNA.
europmc-pmc4939913:
Douglas J. Morrison and Tom Preston review short chain fatty acids, the main products of fiber fermentation in the gut. Their review appeared in Gut Microbes in 2016. Gut bacteria break down carbohydrates people cannot digest. The fatty acids released are the major flow of carbon from food, through microbes, to the host body. Interest rose when receptors tuned to these acids were found on many cell types, which cast them as signals as well as fuel.

The review gathers work on their roles in glucose balance, inflammation, and metabolism in gut, liver, and distant tissues. Effects look broad, touching local gut health and whole body energy handling. The authors caution that well controlled human studies are scarce. Much of the promise rests on animal and cell work. They call for careful human trials to test how much these small molecules really steer metabolic health.
europmc-pmc4971513:
Tina J. Hieken leads a team profiling microbes in breast tissue collected under sterile conditions during surgery. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2016. Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer death among women worldwide. Microbes have been tied to cancer at the stomach, colon, liver, lung, and skin, so the breast was a natural next site. The team sequenced bacterial DNA in tissue from women with cancer and women with benign breast disease.

Breast tissue held a distinct microbiome, unlike breast skin, skin swabs, or mouth swabs. Cancer and benign tissues also differed from each other. Malignant samples were enriched in several low abundance genera, including Fusobacterium, Atopobium, and Lactobacillus. The authors say the shifts are real but small in scale. Whether community change helps cause malignancy or follows it remains open, they note.
europmc-pmc5063913:
Petr Karlovsky and ten co-authors review how food processing affects mycotoxins in Mycotoxin Research. Mycotoxins are poisons made by molds that grow on grain, nuts, and fruit, and legal limits cap them in food worldwide. Good farming and storage cut levels but never erase them, so the review asks what happens downstream, when food is sorted, milled, cooked, or treated to break the toxins down.

Physical removal works best today: hand and machine sorting of grain, nuts, and fruit drops average toxin levels sharply, and milling, steeping, and extrusion cut them further. Chemistry can convert toxins to milder products under heat and strong acid or alkali, and enzymes, including ones from fermentation, can detoxify them too. The authors urge that every new processing method be checked for its toxin effect, and they back enzyme-based detoxification as the line with the largest future promise.
europmc-pmc5066513:
Talisa E. de Carlo, Andre Romano, Nadia K. Waheed, and Jay S. Duker review a new eye imaging method in the International Journal of Retina and Vitreous in 2015. Optical coherence tomography angiography, or OCTA, builds maps of retinal blood flow in seconds without dye, by watching moving blood cells between repeated scans. The review introduces the method, surveys early literature, and sets it against the dye-based standard.

OCTA shows structure and flow together, slices the vessels by depth, and outlines the tiny no-vessel zone at the retina's center with unusual precision. Studies hint at value in macular degeneration, diabetic eye disease, blocked retinal vessels, and glaucoma, and it can reveal abnormal choroid vessels under the retina. Its weaknesses are a small field of view, no view of leakage, and artifacts from blinking or movement. The authors call for clinical trials before it can displace dye angiography.
europmc-pmc5122713:
Jelte M. Wicherts, Coosje L. S. Veldkamp, Hilde E. M. Augusteijn, Marjan Bakker, Robbie C. M. van Aert, and Marcel A. L. M. van Assen catalogued researcher choices in psychology in Frontiers in Psychology in 2016. At every stage of a study, researchers make judgment calls, and bending those calls toward significant results, called p-hacking, inflates false findings.

Their review lists 34 such degrees of freedom across forming hypotheses and designing, running, analyzing, and reporting a study. Each choice can raise the chance of a false positive or exaggerate an effect size, which helps explain why published results often fail to repeat. The authors offer the list as a teaching tool and as a checklist for judging preregistrations and spotting bias risks in studies that were never registered.
europmc-pmc5123813:
Nandan S. Gokhale and a large team of co-authors studied a chemical mark on viral RNA in Cell Host and Microbe in 2016. The mark, called m6A, is added to RNA letters and read by proteins that can boost or destroy the message. They asked what it does during infection by hepatitis C virus and its relatives.

Removing the enzymes that add the mark increased production of infectious virus, while removing a mark-eraser decreased it. Reader proteins moved to the virus's assembly sites during infection, and blocking one spot of marking on the viral genome raised virus output without changing RNA copying. Mapping the mark across dengue, Zika, yellow fever, and West Nile viruses found shared marked regions, making m6A a common control layer for this virus family.
europmc-pmc5127513:
Luca A. Lotta and a large team of co-authors tested whether amino acids in blood cause type 2 diabetes, reporting in PLoS Medicine in 2016. Blood levels of the branched-chain amino acids, leucine, isoleucine, and valine, track strongly with diabetes risk, but that link might not be causal.

Scanning the DNA of 16,596 people, they found five regions that set branched-chain amino acid levels, the strongest near a gene that activates the enzyme which breaks them down. Using gene variants as instruments in up to 47,877 diabetes cases and 267,694 controls, genetically higher levels of each amino acid came with higher diabetes odds, matching ordinary observational studies. Chemical profiles pointed to a slowed breakdown step, supporting a causal role for faulty amino acid handling.
europmc-pmc5210513:
Peter W. Rose and a large RCSB team described updates to the RCSB Protein Data Bank in Nucleic Acids Research in 2017. The bank is the United States data center for the global archive of three-dimensional structures of proteins and other large biological molecules, and it gives the data away free to any user. The update paper reports new tools built around a structural view of biology.

Recent additions include the NGL Viewer, which shows molecules in 3D inside any web browser, faster file downloads, and clearer pages for searching and for single structures. Quality-check information now appears for every entry in the archive. Entries also link outward to gene positions in the human genome, protein changes, and metabolic pathways. Teaching material under PDB-101 was rebuilt as a searchable site with new features, including a digital archive of illustrator Irving Geis.
europmc-pmc5210613:
Yun Zhang and a large team described the Influenza Research Database in Nucleic Acids Research in 2017. Sponsored by the US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, the database is a support center for flu research, meant to speed work on vaccines, tests, and treatments. It pools influenza data from many sources in one free site, with no access limits.

Recent upgrades run on cloud and high-performance computers and let users analyze their own uploaded sequences together with their background data. The site predicts new variant proteins, flags sequence markers tied to traits and predicts their effects, and classifies hemagglutinin, the virus surface protein, by family group. A tool converts between numbering schemes for that protein's subtypes. Links to disease event data were added, along with sections on host factors and antiviral drugs.
europmc-pmc5304413:
Carmen D. Rietdijk, Paula Perez-Pardo, Johan Garssen, Richard J. A. van Wezel, and Aletta D. Kraneveld wrote a review in Frontiers in Neurology in 2017. The review tests a claim about how Parkinson's disease starts. Braak's idea holds that a harmful agent enters through the nose, is swallowed, and reaches the gut. Harm then spreads toward the brain.

The authors weigh lab, animal, and patient studies for and against the claim. Gut and smell problems, spread along the vagus nerve, and cell to cell spread of the protein alpha-synuclein all fit the idea. Still, the staged spread pattern matched only some patients, mainly those with young onset and long illness. The review backs the route but limits the staging claim.
europmc-pmc5316413:
Szymon Juszkiewicz and Ramanujan S. Hegde studied protein quality control in Molecular Cell in 2017. Cells build proteins on ribosomes, small machines that read gene messages. Some messages end in a long run of A letters, which can jam the machine. Jammed machines make cut-off proteins that may harm the cell. A cleanup path must spot the jam and trash the bad product.

The pair found that a protein called ZNF598 starts the cleanup. It tags a small ribosome part, eS10, with ubiquitin at two sites. That tag makes ribosomes halt for good on the A-run messages. Cells that lack ZNF598, or carry ribosomes that cannot take the tag, fail to halt. They read through and add a long lysine tail to the protein instead. Such tails can change where a protein goes and how it dissolves.
europmc-pmc5320013:
Johannes C. Schittny reviewed how the lung grows before and after birth in Cell and Tissue Research in 2017. The lung must build a huge inner surface for gas exchange, fed by a tree of air tubes. Each lung starts as a small pouch off the early gut. From there, growth runs in clear stages that Schittny walks through in order.

First, repeated branching builds all the airways. Next, the airway lining matures and the junction to the gas exchange zone forms. Near the end of that stage, first gas exchange can occur, so babies born early can live. Most of the gas surface comes later, as new walls split air spaces into smaller units. That splitting needs a double layer of fine blood vessels, which later fuses to a single layer. The process runs on into young adult life.
europmc-pmc5421513:
Kuhn and co-authors argue that red blood cells do far more than carry oxygen. Their review appeared in Antioxidants and Redox Signaling. Anemia tracks with grave heart and vessel problems. These include bleeding, clots, stroke, and high blood pressure. The links are strongest in older patients. Raising red cell counts has not reliably fixed the risk. That puzzle points to quality, not just count.

Healthy red cells help control nitric oxide across the body. They also shape redox balance and blood flow traits. They can release active molecules that signal other tissues. When red cells break down or stiffen, those jobs fail. Vessel linings then suffer. The review gathers proof for these extra roles. It also marks what stays speculative. The authors call for studies on red cell function in anemia. Such work could explain why anemia worsens heart disease.
europmc-pmc5457513:
Morland and co-authors identify lactate as a muscle-to-brain signal that grows new brain blood vessels. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Exercise sharpens brain function and delays degeneration. New capillaries in the brain likely help. The growth factor VEGFA drives that sprouting. What first signal links muscle work to brain VEGFA was unknown. The team focused on the lactate receptor HCAR1. It sits richly on cells lining brain vessels.

Mice ran high-intensity intervals for seven weeks. Training ran five days each week. Brain VEGFA protein rose in normal mice. Capillary density rose with it. Knockout mice lacking HCAR1 showed neither change. Lactate injections mimicked the exercise blood levels. They produced the same brain effects in normal mice. Muscle itself told a control story. It showed no vascular HCAR1 expression. It also showed no receptor-dependent vessel change. The receptor completes a muscle-brain circuit.
europmc-pmc5465813:
Panche and co-authors overview flavonoids, a family of plant compounds valued in food and medicine. Their review appeared in the Journal of Nutritional Science. Flavonoids occur in fruits, vegetables, and grains. Bark, tea, and wine carry them as well. Their structures vary widely across the family. Four subgroups organize it. They differ in where they are found. Onions and tea supply most of the flavonols people eat.

Health effects made these compounds famous. Claims lead with protection against oxidation and inflammation. Effects against mutation and cancer are also claimed. The compounds adjust the action of key cell enzymes. Some enzymes face strong blocking from them. Two named targets are xanthine oxidase and cyclo-oxygenase. Links to lower heart disease deaths added research momentum. How they work in the body is still not fully clear. Computer docking studies now predict drug potential. The review closes with directions for future research.
europmc-pmc5483313:
Yohn, Gergues, and Samuels present a review in Molecular Brain on serotonin receptors in depression. Serotonin, also called 5-HT, has long been tied to mood disorders. Drugs that raise serotonin levels are widely prescribed for depression. Yet many patients do not respond to them. The authors review what receptor research adds to older accounts.

The review tests serotonin against three classic accounts of depression. These are the monoamine, neurotrophic, and neurogenic hypotheses. It then examines single receptors, such as 5-HT1A, and their brain circuits. The hippocampus gets special focus as a site of drug action. Gene variants may one day help match patients to drugs, they suggest.
europmc-pmc5624513:
Chan, Stumpf, and Babtie present a network-inference method in Cell Systems. Genes switch each other on and off in webs. Single-cell data can hint at those links, because cells vary. Pairwise statistics miss ties that only show in groups of three.

Their algorithm, PIDC, uses multivariate information theory. It splits shared information among gene triplets. That split exposes direct regulatory links with fewer false ones. On simulated data with known truth, PIDC beat pairwise mutual-information methods. The team also built networks from three real single-cell datasets. They show how context and analysis choices bend the result. Tutorials and open code come with the method. Readers get a sharper tool for turning cell data into testable claims.
europmc-pmc5638113:
Bishop and co-authors report phase two of the CATALISE study. It is a Delphi consensus study on children's language problems. Experts from several countries and professions took part. The panel had 57 members. Phase one set criteria for language disorder. This phase tackles the words used for these problems. Disagreement on terms can block access to services.

Panel members rated statements over two rounds. They saw anonymous ratings and could revise their views. Agreement reached at least 78 percent on 19 of 21 statements. The panel backed Language Disorder for impairing difficulty profiles. Developmental Language Disorder applies when no biomedical cause is known. Risk factors do not rule that label out. It can also occur beside other disorders.
europmc-pmc5689513:
Anselmo and Mitragotri review tiny particles that carry drugs through the body. Their review covers nanoparticle systems given by vein into the blood. Such systems can reach body parts that free drugs cannot. They are among the most studied tools in both lab and clinic.

The authors survey the range of particle types and their strengths. They list systems already approved for patient care and their approved uses. Trials of systems not yet approved get close attention too. The review also covers trials that test approved particles for new uses. Often missed hurdles fill the last part. These span biology, technology, and trial design, and they shape clinical success.
europmc-pmc5820413:
Prame Kumar and co-authors review how neutrophils partner with macrophages. Both cell types guard the body against germs. Working together, they clear infections well. Working out of control, they harm the host instead.

The review traces their teamwork in steady health and in sudden inflammation. It then follows the pair into artery disease from atherosclerosis. A kidney autoimmune disease gets its own section. The gut's odd immune rules close the tour. Fresh views of neutrophil variety frame the whole account. Readers get a joint portrait of two cells that protect and endanger together.
europmc-pmc5866513:
Trincado and co-authors present SUPPA2, a tool for differential splicing analysis. Their article appeared in Genome Biology. Splicing lets one gene yield several transcript forms. RNA sequencing can reveal which forms change between conditions. Older tools demand deep sequencing and much computing time. SUPPA2 aims to work fast and still stay accurate. It also accounts for variation between biological replicates.

The team tested it on real and simulated datasets. They report higher accuracy than rival methods. Gains stood out at low depth and short read lengths. The tool found new splicing events in several test cases. These included events in neuron and blood cell development. Multiple conditions can be compared in one streamlined run.
europmc-pmc5869013:
Ahn and co-authors introduce hBayesDM, an R package for decision-making models. Their article appeared in Computational Psychiatry. Reinforcement learning models can split mental illness into basic parts. They can also link behaviour to brain scan signals. Yet many clinical researchers find the maths hard to adopt.
