The package aims to make such modelling easy and friendly.

It fits models for many learning tasks and social games. Group and individual values are estimated at the same time. Each main step takes a single line of code, the authors say. Outputs include plots and model comparisons. Hidden trial-by-trial values can be pulled out for brain analysis. Little coding knowledge is needed to get started.
europmc-pmc5871013:
Simons and co-authors give a population genetics reading of GWAS findings. Their article appeared in PLoS Biology. Genome-wide studies map variants tied to traits such as height. Why some heritability stays missing was unclear. The team built a model of traits under stabilizing selection. In their model, one trait sits inside a wider trait space. Variants often affect several traits at once.

The model yields simple formulas for genetic architecture. One parameter sums up a strongly selected site's expected effect. The team tested the form on height and body mass data. It fit well, they report. Height studies explain more variance than BMI studies of like size. Most signals trace to mutations near the Out-of-Africa bottleneck.
europmc-pmc5932613:
Kelley and co-authors predict regulatory activity from DNA sequence with neural networks. Their article appeared in Genome Research. Their system reads sequence alone to forecast cell profiles. It predicts epigenetic marks and gene expression by cell type. Convolutional networks spot promoters and distant control elements. The system combines those signals into expression forecasts.

Predictions for variant effects matched known causal variants, they report. Those variants came from human expression studies. The model can suggest how a disease-linked variant acts. That helps narrow which variant in a locus is causal. Noncoding variants drive most trait links found by genome scans. A sequence-only model gives those links a testable story.
europmc-pmc5940313:
Lee and co-authors test how much basal mitophagy in fruit flies depends on Pink1 or parkin. Their study appeared in The Journal of Cell Biology. PINK1 and parkin drive stress-induced mitophagy in cell culture. Both proteins are linked to Parkinson's disease. Their role in everyday, basal mitophagy inside a living animal was unclear. The team built new Drosophila reporter lines to watch it.

The reporters reveal abundant mitophagy in many tissues. Dopaminergic neurons are among them. Loss of PINK1 or parkin left this basal mitophagy largely unchanged, they report. The finding splits routine mitochondrial turnover from the stress response. It also reshapes how the fly can model Parkinson's mechanisms.
europmc-pmc5975413:
Keilwagen and co-authors extend the GeMoMa program to combine RNA-seq data with homology-based gene prediction. Their paper appeared in BMC Bioinformatics. Finding protein-coding genes is central to genome annotation. GeMoMa uses amino acid and intron position conservation between species. The extension can also use RNA-seq evidence when available. Benchmarks covered plants, animals, and fungi.

GeMoMa beat rival tools such as BRAKER1 and MAKER2, they report. It also beat pipelines based on RNA-seq alone. Using several reference organisms helped further. The team applied it to four nematode species and to barley. Current gene annotations may be refined by its predictions, they suggest.
europmc-pmc5991413:
Feng and Stockwell set out unsolved mysteries of how lipid peroxidation causes ferroptosis. Their essay appeared in PLoS Biology. Ferroptosis is a form of cell death driven by membrane damage. It starts when the repair enzyme GPX4 loses activity. Lipid peroxides then build up and kill the cell. The death differs from apoptosis and necrosis in kind. Three big questions remain open, the authors argue.

What drives the peroxidation is still not clear. Where the lethal peroxides sit inside the cell is unknown. How they trigger death is a mystery too. Answers would aid diseases tied to this death route.
europmc-pmc5991813:
Stone and co-authors track state suicide rates in the United States from 1999 to 2016. Their Vital Signs report appeared in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. National suicide rates rose by nearly 30 percent in that span. The team used vital statistics data for all states. A second system covered circumstances in 27 states for 2015. Rates rose in 44 states over the full period.

Twenty-five states saw increases above 30 percent, they report. In 2015, 54 percent of decedents had no known mental health condition. Relationship loss and life stressors were common in both groups. Recent crises hit the no-condition group more often. The authors urge broad public health prevention.
europmc-pmc6008313:
Amabebe and Anumba review the vaginal microenvironment and the physiologic role of Lactobacilli. Their review was published in Frontiers in Medicine. The vagina and its microbes sway conception, pregnancy, and birth timing. They also sway the risk of sex-spread infections. High estrogen states, as in puberty and pregnancy, guard vaginal health. They spur glycogen build-up in vaginal wall cells. Lactobacilli thrive on that glycogen and make lactic acid.

The acid holds vaginal pH low, they explain. The germs and their products form a first defence line. It turns back germs, viruses, fungi, and tiny parasites. The review covers how this balance works in health. It also covers states where the host-germ tie breaks. Harm to reproduction from a stirred germ mix is set out.
europmc-pmc6030513:
Marshall and co-authors test machine learning for finding trial reports. Their article appeared in Research Synthesis Methods. Randomized trials are the gold standard for treatment effects. Yet they form a tiny share of medical papers. Finding them in huge databases takes much manual work.

The team trained models on titles and abstracts. They tested support vector machines and neural networks. An external data set allowed fair comparison with search filters. Machine learning beat standard filters at every sensitivity level. The best model reached an AUROC of 0.987. The authors give cutoffs for two workflows. One suits full systematic reviews, the other rapid answers. Free software lets readers apply the methods in practice.
europmc-pmc6041413:
Martino and co-authors review how cells turn force into function. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Physiology. Cells constantly feel pushes from their surroundings. The matrix around them and neighbor cells supply these cues. Cells must convert such cues into biological responses.

That conversion process is called mechanotransduction. The review traces signals from the cell surface inward. Focal adhesions link matrix contact to the skeleton inside. Tension in that skeleton acts as a second messenger. Shuttle proteins then carry the signal to the nucleus. Gene programs switch on in response. The authors also cover diseases from sensing failures. Heart scarring serves as a leading example. Readers get a molecular map of a basic cell skill.
europmc-pmc6048113:
Hu and co-authors show how root chemicals shape the next plant generation. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Plants change their soil as they grow. Those changes help or hinder later plants. Soil microbes are thought to carry much of that effect.

Maize roots release defensive chemicals called benzoxazinoids. The team found these altered root microbe communities. Next-generation plants grew less in conditioned soil. Their defenses rose, and caterpillars fared worse on them. A breakdown product in soil proved key. Adding it alone reproduced the full effect. It worked by reshaping microbes, not by acting directly. Sterile soil and microbe transfers confirmed the chain. Readers get a clear mechanism for plant-soil feedback.
europmc-pmc6066613:
Lively and Schlichter compare how rat microglia answer different inflammatory triggers. Their research article appeared in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience. Microglia are the brain's own immune cells. Lab studies usually inflame them with bacterial LPS. Real brain damage instead brings cytokines like interferon-gamma and TNF-alpha.

The team exposed cultured rat microglia to each trigger. They tracked nitric oxide, migration, and nearly 100 genes. LPS often drove stronger pro-inflammatory gene activity. It also raised some anti-inflammatory genes. Two resolving cytokines were then tested as brakes. IL-4 worked better after the cytokine trigger. IL-10 proved surprisingly weak after either one. Readers get a caution on modeling brain inflammation in a dish.
europmc-pmc6104813:
Shi and co-authors show how PD-1 guides follicular helper T cells in place and task. Their research article appeared in Immunity. These T cells help B cells mature antibodies. They carry high levels of PD-1. Its job there went beyond simple braking.

Neighboring B cells display PD-1's partner, PD-L1. Contact with it slows the T cells' entry into follicles. PD-1 also steers cells toward the germinal center core. It damps a rival guidance receptor on the way. There, paired contacts sharpen B cell competition. Antibody quality rises as a result. ICOS signals help cells overcome the entry brake. Readers get positioning logic for a famous checkpoint.
europmc-pmc6158913:
Baskaran and co-authors wrote a review in Biomaterials Research on photodynamic therapy and its clinical development. This treatment uses light-sensitive agents, light, and oxygen to kill diseased tissue. Once lit, the agent creates reactive oxygen that destroys tumor cells. The agents are the key to how well it works.

The review traces the agents approved for clinical use and those in trials. Photofrin was an early example. Second-generation agents absorb longer wavelengths, so light reaches deeper tissue. Some were designed to target mitochondria inside cells. The authors survey where each agent is used. Readers get a status report on a treatment that blends drugs, devices, and light.
europmc-pmc6182813:
Thivel and co-authors wrote an article in Frontiers in Public Health clarifying the language of movement and health. Evidence linking too much sitting to poor health keeps growing. Public strategies aim to cut sedentary time and raise activity. Yet researchers still confuse the basic terms.

The authors review the accepted definitions of physical activity, inactivity, and sedentary behavior. They show how the three differ and relate. Attention then turns to work, where most adults spend much of the day sitting. Standing desks are discussed against the energy thresholds that define sedentary time. Clear definitions, they argue, are needed before workplaces can be redesigned well. The piece is a short guide for occupational health.
europmc-pmc6218613:
Ohl and Tenbrock review reactive oxygen species and suppressor immune cells. The cells are called myeloid-derived suppressor cells, or MDSCs. They are immature immune cells that dampen responses. They grow in tumours, infections, and inflammation. The review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology.

These cells both release and face reactive oxygen species. Such species switch on protective paths in the cells. They also set gene programs that shape cell fate. The cells release these species to suppress T cells. That release is a major part of how they work. The authors say targeting this redox control could aid cancer therapy. They also flag roles in infection and autoimmune disease as worth study.
europmc-pmc6310513:
Hunt and co-authors describe the Ensembl variation resources for genome data. The article appeared in Database, the journal of biological databases. Linking DNA variation to traits and disease is a core goal of genomics. Data on variants sit scattered across many sources. Ensembl gathers them into one consistent system.

The team builds pipelines that compare variants with genome annotations. Data are harmonized and served in standard formats. Users can browse them visually or query them by code. Sources cover allele frequencies and disease links. Predicted effects on genes are included too. All tools and data are public. The resource helps labs read a person's genome with context.
europmc-pmc6351513:
Law and co-authors issue joint guidelines for PET imaging of gliomas. Their standards appeared in the European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging. Four expert bodies developed them together. Brain PET increasingly supports MRI in glioma care. The tracers include FDG and labeled amino acids. The named amino acid tracers are MET, FET, and FDOPA.

The document covers the full imaging pathway. It advises when to recommend a scan. It sets standards for performing the scan itself. It then guides reading and reporting the results. Consistent practice should raise image quality everywhere. It should also make reports easier to compare. The authors address doctors in nuclear medicine directly. The standards are version 1.0, open to future updates.
europmc-pmc6355913:
Bellver-Landete and co-authors show microglia build a protective scar after spinal cord injury. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Microglia are the spinal cord's resident immune cells. Their role after injury was often confused with macrophages. The team used special mouse lines and depleting drugs. That let them isolate microglia behavior cleanly.

Microglia multiplied fast in the first two weeks. They gathered around the lesion in a dense rim. There they met incoming white blood cells on one side. Astrocytes formed the scar on the other side. Signals from microglia, including IGF-1, guided that scarring. Removing microglia broke the scar apart. More immune cells flooded in, neurons died, and movement recovery suffered. Extra microglia activity helped the opposite way.
europmc-pmc6358713:
Ramsey and co-authors report a research article in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on the Varroa mite. For fifty years, beekeepers thought this pest drank bee blood, called hemolymph. The team tested that belief with imaging and feeding trials on honey bees.

Mites in fact eat fat body tissue, an organ that stores food and fights germs. They digest the tissue outside their bodies, then take it in. That diet helps explain the wide harm mites cause, beyond the viruses they carry. It also shows why some past mite treatments missed their target. New control methods can now aim at the right feeding process.
europmc-pmc6362613:
Al Tameemi and co-authors present a review in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. The subject is how low oxygen changes the metabolism of cancer cells. Poorly formed blood vessels leave parts of solid tumors short of oxygen for long periods.

The review explains how cells respond by cutting oxidative phosphorylation and altering fat processing. Hypoxia-sensitive transcription factors switch on genes for glycolysis and new blood vessel growth. These changes help tumor cells survive, spread, and resist chemotherapy and radiation. The authors connect each metabolic change to the survival of hypoxic tumors. That link matters for designing drugs against hard-to-treat cancers.
europmc-pmc6372613:
Lobas and co-authors present a sensor study in Nature Communications. ATP is the cell's main energy unit and also a signal between cells. Watching ATP in living tissue needs a sensor that is fast, bright, and picky about its target.

Their sensor joins a glowing green protein to part of a bacterial ATP-making enzyme. It lights up when ATP binds, across the range found in and around cells. It ignores similar molecules and can be aimed at one cell type or spot. Mice and cell tests showed it can track ATP in the cytosol and at the cell surface.
europmc-pmc6376713:
Nyblade and co-authors write about stigma in health facilities, in BMC Medicine. A correspondence article, it draws on a systematic review of work from the past five years. Stigma by health staff can block testing, care, and good outcomes.

The authors assess what programs now know about cutting that stigma. They ask whether one program can tackle stigma for several conditions at once. Shared drivers, like fear and blame, suggest it can. The article names gaps in methods and measurement. It urges clinics to treat stigma reduction as part of quality care.
europmc-pmc6378413:
Palhano-Fontes and co-authors present a randomized placebo-controlled trial in Psychological Medicine. They tested a single dose of ayahuasca, a psychedelic Amazonian brew, in 29 patients with treatment-resistant depression. Depression severity was rated on two standard scales over the following week.

Ayahuasca beat placebo at every check point, and the gap grew over time. By day seven the effect size reached 1.49, a large value. Response rates were 64 percent for ayahuasca versus 27 percent for placebo at day seven. Remission showed the same trend. The authors call it the first controlled trial of a psychedelic in this condition and report good safety in this setting.
europmc-pmc6420413:
Peirce and co-authors describe PsychoPy2 in Behavior Research Methods. PsychoPy is a tool for building behavior experiments with exact timing. It has grown over ten years into a standard for psychology and neuroscience labs.

Users can write experiments in Python or build them with a graphical Builder. Builder lets researchers with little coding still run precise studies. New features include more stimulus types and better hardware timing. The tool also backs open science, with sharing and reproducibility built in. The authors present it as a bridge between ease and control.
europmc-pmc6447513:
Rohaan and co-authors review adoptive cellular therapies, treatments that give cancer patients living immune cells trained or engineered to attack their tumors. Three families are covered: tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes harvested from the tumor, T cells fitted with new receptors, and CAR T cells carrying synthetic chimeric receptors.

The standout success is CD19-directed CAR T therapy in blood cancers, already commercially approved by the FDA when the review appeared. Toxicity receives frank treatment, since these potent cells can harm healthy tissue and trigger severe reactions. Sections on target choice and cell engineering close with where trials worldwide are pushing the approach, especially into solid tumors.
europmc-pmc6462913:
Prakash and Chakrabarti review the shifting global epidemiology of mucormycosis, a fast, vessel-invading fungal infection with high mortality. Incidence is rising worldwide and fastest in Asia, and the susceptible population is changing. Diabetes dominates risk in Asia, while post-tuberculosis disease and chronic kidney failure have emerged as new risk groups there.

Clinical form follows the host: rhino-cerebral disease in diabetes, lung disease in blood cancers and transplant patients, skin disease after trauma in healthy people. Odd forms include kidney-only infection reported from China and India. Rhizopus arrhizus leads worldwide, but Apophysomyces variabilis rules in Asia and Lichtheimia in Europe. Country-level burden studies are the authors' main call.
europmc-pmc6467913:
Chaisson and co-authors assemble the fullest catalog yet of structural variation in human genomes by throwing nearly every sequencing technology at three family trios. Long reads, short reads, strand-specific methods, optical mapping, and many calling algorithms ran in combination, each catching variants the others miss. Short-read studies alone leave most large variants invisible.

Each genome carried 818,054 small insertions and deletions and 27,622 larger structural variants, a three- to sevenfold jump over standard surveys including the 1000 Genomes Project. Inversions averaged 156 per genome, and 58 overlapped regions tied to known microdeletion syndromes. The dataset is offered as a gold standard, with guidance on maximizing sensitivity in future studies.
europmc-pmc6492113:
Caine and co-authors engineer rice that breathes less, and so survives the climate that is coming. Rice feeds billions but drinks heavily and wilts under drought and heat. By overexpressing the epidermal patterning factor OsEPF1 in the high-yielding cultivar IR64, the team produced plants with far fewer stomata, the leaf pores that leak water vapor.

The sparse-pored lines used about 60 percent of the normal water in mid-growth and kept their conductance steady under elevated carbon dioxide. They outlived control plants through drought combined with 40°C heat, while yielding as much or more despite slower photosynthesis in some conditions. Fewer pores, the work argues, is a climate trait worth breeding for.
europmc-pmc6515513:
Cao, Jia and Zhu review two blood markers of heart strain, BNP and NT-proBNP, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Both are released when heart muscle is stretched, and both help doctors diagnose heart failure. The review gives a second use equal weight: the same markers measured after death.

Forensic pathologists cannot run scans or ask about symptoms, so judging the heart of a person who died is hard. Studies show these markers persist in postmortem samples and reflect how the heart worked before death. The authors cover the biology of the markers, what sets their levels, and their test record in both clinics and morgues. They close with open questions and prospects for wider use.
europmc-pmc6568213:
Saunders reviews how engineers tune the tail end of therapeutic antibodies, writing in Frontiers in Immunology. An antibody's grasping arms choose the target, but its hinge and Fc stem decide what happens next. They govern which immune cells get recruited, whether complement is fixed, and how long the molecule survives in the blood.

The review explains how receptors and the complement starter C1q read the Fc, and how small sequence changes or altered sugars can turn those interactions up or down. Some designs sharpen cell killing for cancer work. Others silence effector functions where inflammation would harm, as in autoimmunity. A third family of tweaks grips the recycling receptor FcRn harder, stretching circulation half-life so doses can be smaller or rarer.
europmc-pmc6632213:
Cohen and co-authors present a consensus statement on immunotherapy for head and neck squamous cell cancer. Their guideline appears in the Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer. These cancers kill about 380,000 people each year worldwide. Patients with recurrent or metastatic disease had few options. In 2016 the FDA approved two anti-PD-1 drugs for them. Nivolumab and pembrolizumab followed platinum treatment failure. First-line approval for pembrolizumab came later.

An expert panel from the Society for Immunotherapy of Cancer wrote the guidance. It covers patient selection for checkpoint inhibitors. It addresses treatment sequencing and response monitoring. Managing immune side effects gets detailed attention. So does PD-L1 biomarker testing. The panel limited its scope to FDA-approved drugs.
europmc-pmc6852913:
Wang and co-authors report a study in BMC Cancer on stage IV breast cancer. At this stage the cancer has spread beyond the breast. Where it lands, in bone, lung, liver, or brain, may shape the illness. How features and survival differ by spread site was poorly understood.

The team drew cases diagnosed between 2010 and 2015 from the United States SEER registry. They compared tumour traits across single-site and multi-site spread. Survival was worst for brain spread and best for bone-only disease, with lung and liver in between. Surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy each linked to longer survival in the analysis. The authors say spread site should inform treatment planning.
europmc-pmc6876113:
Di Cesare and co-authors chart childhood obesity worldwide in BMC Medicine. Rates have climbed steeply over recent decades in nearly every region. Children carrying excess weight face mental and social strain now, and higher risk of diseases such as diabetes later. Most will become adults with obesity, since treatment rarely succeeds. World Health Organization member states have pledged no rise in childhood obesity by 2025.

The authors assemble estimates from sources including UNICEF, the WHO, and the World Bank. Obesity was rare almost everywhere in 1975, at about 0.1 percent for girls in sub-Saharan Africa. By 2016 it had become common on every continent. They call for urgent action on food environments.
europmc-pmc6958913:
Li and co-authors review microsatellite instability, a marker oncologists use to guide cancer care. Their review appeared in Cancer Cell International. Microsatellites are short repeated stretches of DNA. When the repair system that fixes copying slips fails, their lengths drift. Tumours with heavy instability respond well to immunotherapy, on recent reports.

Yet patients with such tumours differ widely in immunotherapy benefit, outlook, and chemotherapy sensitivity. The authors explain how instability arises, and how laboratories detect it. They sort tumours into high, low, and stable classes by how much drift is seen. Links with specific cancers, above all colorectal cancer, get close attention. The review aims to give oncologists a clear map of a fast-moving field, and a base for further study.
europmc-pmc6972713:
Pelon and co-authors show that helper cells in lymph nodes help breast cancer spread. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Fibroblasts inside tumours vary, but their variety inside invaded lymph nodes was uncharted. Nodes are the first stop for escaping breast cancer cells, and how many are invaded predicts outcome.

Working from patient samples, the team found four cancer-associated fibroblast types in metastatic nodes. Two muscle-like types, CAF-S1 and CAF-S4, built up there and tracked with invasion. In lab cultures, CAF-S1 pushed cancer cells to move and change shape via two signal routes. CAF-S4, strongly contractile, drove invasion into three-dimensional tissue through NOTCH signalling. Patients rich in these cells at diagnosis, above all CAF-S4, tended to develop distant spread later. Node fibroblasts, the authors say, could serve as a warning marker.
europmc-pmc7022213:
Dudek and co-authors report a brain and behaviour study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. They study the blood-brain barrier, the seal that keeps blood-borne toxins away from brain tissue. Under chronic stress, that seal can leak in a reward region called the nucleus accumbens. Leaks are tied to depression-like behaviour.

The team combined mouse experiments with tests on human samples. Resilient mice kept the seal protein claudin-5 at healthy levels. They showed gene-mark changes at its promoter and lower levels of a repressor, FoxO1. Stressed, vulnerable mice showed raised HDAC1, an enzyme that silences genes. Blocking HDAC1 restored claudin-5 and improved social behaviour in mice. Human depressed samples also showed raised HDAC1, the authors report.
europmc-pmc7054213:
Alexandrov and co-authors catalogue the mutational signatures of human cancer in Nature. Each process that damages DNA leaves a set pattern, or signature, in a cancer's genome. Reading those patterns shows what did the damage. Working within the Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes consortium, the team analysed 84,729,690 somatic mutations, the largest set yet.

The mutations came from 4,645 whole-genome and 19,184 exome sequences spanning most cancer types. The analysis resolved 49 single-base-substitution signatures, 11 doublet-base signatures, 4 clustered signatures, and 17 small insertion-and-deletion signatures. Its scale let the authors split signatures that earlier work had merged, and break some into parts tied to distinct damage or repair routes. Each signature's share of single cancers was measured, linking many to exposures such as tobacco smoke or to broken DNA upkeep. Many signatures still have no known cause.
europmc-pmc7066113:
Wu and co-authors review protection against brain ischemia-reperfusion injury in Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience. When a stroke blocks blood flow, restoring it saves tissue but also triggers its own damage. That reperfusion injury involves oxidative stress, amino acid toxicity, inflammation, and programmed cell death, and it can kill neurons that survived the blockage itself.

Oxidative stress and inflammation feed each other and drive the cascade. During reperfusion, free radicals such as superoxide and hydroxyl radicals, plus nitric oxide, attack cell fats, stoke inflammation, and push cells toward death. Inflammatory factors then tip the balance further and widen the injury. The review surveys neuroprotective therapies aimed at each stage, including natural antioxidants from plants such as ginkgo extracts and polyphenols tested in animals. Its argument is that calming oxidation and inflammation together is the most promising way to limit damage after blood returns.
europmc-pmc7073113:
Wang and co-authors review jasmonic acid in plant stress defence in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Jasmonic acid is a hormone plants make themselves, first identified as a stress signal. Spraying it on plants from outside also regulates their responses. Abiotic stresses such as cold, drought, salt, heavy metals, and harsh light cause large-scale damage to crops.

The review focuses on the signalling pathway jasmonic acid uses against those stresses. At its centre sits a module of repressor and activator proteins, JAZ and MYC, which integrate transcription factors and stress genes. The hormone never acts alone. It works inside a network, cooperating with abscisic acid and ethylene in some settings and opposing salicylic acid in others. Mapping that crosstalk, the authors argue, is the route to understanding plant tolerance as a system rather than a single switch, with uses in breeding hardier crops.
europmc-pmc7092613:
Colizzi, Lasalvia, and Ruggeri argue for a new model of prevention and early care in youth mental health, in the International Journal of Mental Health Systems. Half of all mental disorders start by age 14, the authors note. Young people's needs in this period still go largely unmet despite services built for them.

Care should not rest with mental health professionals alone, they argue. Schools, social bodies, and other health services need to act together in one multidisciplinary, cross-diagnosis framework. Early, broad support could change the path of later illness, since early disturbances account for 45% of the disease burden between ages 0 and 25. The authors say specialists should lead the direction, not carry the whole load.
europmc-pmc7119513:
The CDC COVID-19 Response Team reports early United States figures on underlying health conditions among COVID-19 patients, in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Data cover cases reported from 12 February to 28 March 2020. Of 122,653 reported cases, 7,162 had information on underlying conditions and risk factors.

Among those 7,162 patients, 37.6% had at least one underlying condition or risk factor. The share was far higher among patients admitted to intensive care, at 78%, than among those never hospitalised, at 27%. Diabetes, chronic lung disease, and cardiovascular disease were the most common conditions. Of 184 deaths with full information, 94% occurred in patients with at least one underlying condition. The team calls the findings preliminary.
europmc-pmc7141113:
Pang and co-authors systematically review the early pipeline of rapid tests, vaccines, and treatments for the 2019 novel coronavirus, in the Journal of Clinical Medicine. Policymakers needed to know where to put research money as the outbreak grew. The team searched three major databases plus supplementary sources under standard review rules.

Twenty-seven studies met their criteria. Lab confirmation rested on RT-PCR tests, with a commercial kit from the Beijing Genomic Institute in wide use in China; quick bedside tests and antibody assays did not yet exist. Several vaccine candidates were in development, the likeliest first trial being a synthetic DNA design. Various existing and novel compounds showed lab activity against the virus, and some entered clinical trials.
europmc-pmc7181913:
Tong and co-authors report a family cluster suggesting SARS-CoV-2 can spread before symptoms appear. Their article appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases. The cluster involved two families in Zhoushan, Zhejiang Province, China. It occurred in January 2020. The source was a traveler from Wuhan who seemed well at the time of contact.

Investigators traced each person's contacts, symptoms, and test results. One contact tested positive on January 20 yet had no symptoms. Another family member stayed negative through quarantine. A third developed fever, cough, and muscle aches on January 12. The timeline pointed to spread during the traveler's silent phase. Such early reports shaped how officials viewed isolation rules. They showed symptom checks alone could miss infectious people.
europmc-pmc7225913:
Phillips and co-authors report the ORIOLE trial of targeted radiation for prostate cancer that has spread to a few sites. Their study appeared in JAMA Oncology. The trial enrolled men whose hormone-sensitive cancer had returned with limited metastases. In all, 54 men were randomized. One group received stereotactic ablative radiotherapy, precise high-dose radiation. The other group was simply observed.

The main question was whether radiation improves cancer control. Progression at 6 months was rare in the radiation group, at 1 of 19 men assessed. Treating a handful of spots aims to delay stronger hormone therapy. The oligometastatic idea behind the trial holds that limited spread can still be attacked locally. Results support testing this approach in larger trials. The study marks a shift in how early spread is managed.
europmc-pmc7277113:
Zhang and co-authors follow Chinese college students over time to see how the COVID-19 outbreak affected their mental health, and whether exercise helped. Their longitudinal study appeared in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Sixty-six students answered structured questionnaires during the peak of the outbreak in China.

Rising death counts were tied directly to worse sleep quality. Their effect on negative emotions, stress, and anxiety ran through sleep: poor sleep carried the harm onward. Physical activity, by contrast, directly eased negative emotions. The findings point to two practical levers during an outbreak, protecting sleep and keeping students active, at a time when most mental health attention went to patients and medical staff.
europmc-pmc7338513:
De Biasi and co-authors dissect T cell changes in COVID-19 pneumonia for Nature Communications. The immune system of infected patients is badly impaired, yet the details were unclear. The team profiled T cells and their chemical signals in patients and compared them with healthy controls.

Patients showed shifts across many T cell groups, from naive cells to worn-out, exhausted ones marked by PD1 and CD57. Their most mature T cells divided less well when stimulated. Lymphocytes poured out more inflammatory signals, including TNF, interferon-gamma, and IL-17, and the balance skewed toward the TH17 type. The picture is of an immune system both overactive and aging fast. Such maps may help target immune treatments.
europmc-pmc7347613:
Arra and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications on osteoarthritis. It asks how inflammation helps drive cartilage loss in the joint. The focus is cartilage cells, called chondrocytes, under inflammatory stress. A metabolic shift sits at the center of the work.

The authors show that inflammation switches these cells toward sugar-based energy use. A protein switch called NF-kB drives that change. The shift raises an enzyme, LDHA, which boosts reactive oxygen species in the cell. Those species steady a pro-inflammatory mediator that pushes cartilage breakdown. Blocking this path could slow joint damage, the authors suggest. They name LDHA as a possible drug target. Readers get a clear chain from inflammation to cartilage loss.
europmc-pmc7382213:
Bertozzi and co-authors lay out three regional models for forecasting COVID-19 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Pandemic modeling sat at the center of policy in 2020, yet forecasting a new virus stayed hard. The authors favor deliberately simple models over elaborate ones.

Their three models connect to each other and to a region's case data, letting officials test what distancing does to the curve. The results warn against relaxing non-drug measures while no vaccine or antiviral exists, since spread rebounds. The paper doubles as an accessible framework for generating policy-relevant insight. Readers get a clear look at how modest mathematics can guide big decisions under deep uncertainty.
europmc-pmc7417513:
Wu and co-authors review tumor-associated macrophages, the immune cells that gather inside and around tumors. Their subject is the tumor microenvironment, the mix of cells and signals that shapes how a cancer grows. The review asks whether macrophage groups can be sorted by what they do, not just by where they sit.

The authors sort macrophages into M1-like cells, which attack tumors, and M2-like cells, which help them grow. They show how cell origin, place in the tumor, and flexible cell states blur that split. New tools such as single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial mapping can chart these groups in fine detail. Readers gain a clear frame for macrophage-based cancer care.
europmc-pmc7433213:
Yuan and co-authors review how two cell signal paths, MAPK and AMPK, interact in cancer. The MAPK path is among the best defined in cancer biology. Its overdrive drives over 40% of human cancer cases.

Active MAPK signaling turns on growth genes and blocks AMPK, a key node for cell energy control. That block helps cancer cells bear metabolic stress. New work shows AMPK can push back and tune MAPK by marking RAF and KSR proteins. This two-way talk affects how targeted drugs perform. The authors discuss pairing MAPK blockers with AMPK modulators. Such pairs could form a fresh treatment strategy for cancers driven by this pathway.
europmc-pmc7506513:
Ma and co-authors pool two national aging cohorts to link sleep length with cognitive decline. One cohort is the ELSA in England, the other the CHARLS in China. Together they held 20,065 participants with full baseline data.

The link between sleep and thinking scores formed an inverted U shape. Seven hours a night served as the reference point. People sleeping 4 hours or less scored lower at baseline. So did those sleeping 10 hours or more each night. Both extreme groups also declined faster over 100 000 person-years of follow-up in the pooled analysis. The pattern held in both countries despite cultural gaps. The authors urge watching cognition in older adults who sleep far too little or far too much.
europmc-pmc7532113:
Qian and co-authors review molecular targets in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. The cancer has a poor outlook and high death rate. Gene faults and altered pathways offer points of attack.

One route blocks faulty oncogenes such as KRAS. A second route tries to restore lost tumor suppressors. TP53, CDKN2A and SMAD4 are key examples. A third route exploits faults in genes such as BRCA. Next-generation sequencing can find these faults in patients. Trials such as POLO gave hopeful results. The review also covers cell and antibody therapies. Readers get a structured guide to precision care for this cancer.
europmc-pmc7574913:
Gu and co-authors adapt SARS-CoV-2 to BALB/c mice for vaccine testing. Animal models are vital tools for vaccine work. Wild-type mice cannot be infected by the virus through mouse ACE2.

Passage in mice produced a strain that infects them. The adapted virus caused inflammation and moderate pneumonia. Adaptation hinged on one change in the spike protein. The change was Asn501 to Tyr, called N501Y. It sits in the receptor-binding domain of spike. The model was used to test neutralizing antibodies. A vaccine candidate was also tested in the model. The work gives researchers a small-animal system for SARS-CoV-2 studies and countermeasure checks.
europmc-pmc7595113:
Hamarsheh, Groß, Brummer and Zeiser review immune effects of oncogenic KRAS in cancer. KRAS mutations are among the most common in human cancer. They are also among the hardest to target with drugs.

Mutant KRAS drives steady growth signals in tumor cells. New evidence links it to inflammation that aids tumors. It also shapes talk with the tumor microenvironment. Those effects help tumors escape immune attack. The review covers lab work on KRAS-led immune change. It sets that work beside current clinical trials. Trials target cancers that carry KRAS mutations. Plans to beat immune escape are also discussed. Readers get a link between a classic oncogene and immunity.
europmc-pmc7612013:
Blackledge and Klose review how Polycomb repressive complexes control gene activity in mammals. Precise gene control is basic to cell function and growth. Chromatin and histone marks shape that control deeply.

Two central complexes are PRC1 and PRC2 in the system. Both are vital for normal development in animals. Early knowledge came from simple model organisms. The system has since expanded and diverged in mammals. The review explains how complexes find target sites. Feedback between them builds Polycomb chromatin domains. Those domains then tune transcription at genes. The authors gather new molecular detail in one account. It shows how a chromatin system guides development programs.
europmc-pmc7612213:
Baek and co-authors present a three-track neural network for protein structure prediction, called RoseTTAFold. DeepMind had shown striking accuracy at the CASP14 contest. The team explored related network designs outside that group.

Their network joins three levels of information together. Sequence data form the first track of the model. Distance maps form the second track in the network. Three-dimensional coordinates form the third track there. Accuracy approached DeepMind results at CASP14. The tool solved hard X-ray and cryo-EM modeling cases. It also gave clues on proteins of unknown function. Accurate protein complex models came from sequence alone. The method was shared freely with researchers for wider use.
europmc-pmc7652413:
Zamorano and Grandvaux review ACE2 as the entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2 and its role in related illnesses. Knowing the entry receptor is key to virus behavior. It shapes spread, tissue targets and disease course.

Early evidence pointed to ACE2 for virus entry. The review sums up proof and its limits. Gaps that remain in ACE2 knowledge are named. Expression of ACE2 across tissues is covered in depth. Its role is weighed beside illnesses tied to poor outcomes. Those include hypertension, diabetes and obesity in patients. Heart disease, COPD and smoking status also feature. Possible co-receptors and attachment factors are discussed. Names include neuropilins, heparan sulfate and sialic acids. Alternate receptors such as CD147 are also weighed.
europmc-pmc7698413:
Thi and co-authors review biofilms formed by a hardy hospital germ. The germ is Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which strikes people with weak immunity. It persists in clinics by building biofilms, sheets of cells in self-made slime. These sheets shrug off antibiotics and immune attack.

The review traces the stages of biofilm growth and the signals that guide them. It covers odd features such as cells bursting to share building material. Mixed biofilms with partner germs can even blunt its virulence. The authors cover new ways to detect infection and compile treatments aimed at these biofilms, with their strengths and limits.
europmc-pmc7725513:
The CDC COVID-19 Response Team reports early US data on who fared worst in the outbreak. It covers cases from February 12 to March 16, 2020. By March 16, 4,226 cases had been reported in the United States. The team split outcomes by age: hospital care, intensive care, and death.

Adults aged 65 years or older made up 31% of cases but 80% of deaths. They also accounted for 45% of hospital stays and 53% of intensive care stays. The worst rates sat in those aged 85 years or more. No intensive care stays or deaths were reported at ages 19 or younger. The pattern matched early data from China.
europmc-pmc7737613:
Perdikari and co-authors show how a SARS-CoV-2 protein condenses with RNA into droplets. The nucleocapsid protein wraps the viral genome. Virus cores form inside dynamic cell compartments tied to stress granules. The team tested if this protein splits into liquid-like droplets, a process called phase separation.

Strong droplet forming needed two floppy regions of the protein plus its tail-joining domain. Plain RNA could trigger the process. The protein also entered droplets formed by human RNA-binding proteins, such as TDP-43 and FUS. This may explain how the virus packs its genome and hijacks host proteins for its own copying.
europmc-pmc7779013:
Ochoa and co-authors describe the Open Targets Platform, a free knowledge base that helps researchers pick drug targets. The platform scores evidence that links a target to a disease. Users query it through a web interface, and the code is open source.

The team made 10 releases in two years. Evidence now flows in from 20 data sources. New inputs include CRISPR knockout screens in 300 cancer models from Project Score. Genetic evidence comes from the Open Targets Genetics Portal and UK Biobank. The scoring framework was revised. New content covers side effects seen after marketing, plus target safety and tractability. Interface and backend work improved speed and ease of use.
europmc-pmc7801513:
Chatterjee and co-authors test a blood marker of brain astrocyte damage in older adults at risk of Alzheimer's disease. The marker is glial fibrillary acidic protein, or GFAP. It can be measured in blood samples. The team studied cognitively normal adults aged 65–90 years. Brain amyloid scans split them into low and high load groups.

The high amyloid group held 33 people, and the low group 63. Plasma GFAP was far higher in the high group. The blood amyloid ratio was lower there too. Adding GFAP lifted the sorting accuracy of the test model. The score rose from 0.78 to 0.91. The authors say astrocyte change starts before symptoms appear.
europmc-pmc7852513:
Zavala and co-authors review cancer gaps between racial and ethnic groups in the United States. Unequal cancer rates and outcomes are well proven. They stem from social, money, setting, behavior, and biology factors mixed together. Most large studies, though, drew on people of European origin.

Thin data and few samples from minorities widen the gap. The authors cover breast, prostate, lung, and colon cancers. Gastric, liver, and pancreas cancers add harder cases. Leukemia is included as well. Groups covered include Black, Native, Asian, Pacific Islander, and Latino people. Progress in naming causes has been real. The authors still find wide gaps and urge wider study entry.
europmc-pmc7857413:
Sun and co-authors rebuild SARS-CoV-2 transmission chains in Hunan, China. A minority of sick people cause most infections. How that pattern arises was the puzzle. Records ran up to April 2020.

Detailed tracing let the team separate spread drivers. Long contact time raised the odds of passing the virus on. Close, intimate contact mattered most of all. Most cases passed the virus to no one. A few spread it widely at gatherings or in homes. Control steps can be judged against this picture. Measures that cut long indoor contact should bite hardest. Testing and isolation speed also enter the model.
europmc-pmc7872713:
Abrams presents what the American Medical Association thinks of his electronic reactions method. The item ran in The Dental Register in 1923. It gathers the AMA journal's answers to doctors' queries. The devices named include the oscilloclast and reflexaphore. Inquiries had poured in for some time.

The AMA's view, as printed, was deeply skeptical. His diagnostic claims rested on unproven electric ideas. The journal warned readers against the devices. Abrams reprints the critique under his own name here. The piece is a period record of a famous medical dispute. It shows organized medicine policing the edge of practice.
europmc-pmc7942713:
Moodie presents a study in paleopathology on bone growths in a fossil sabre-tooth cat. The specimens come from the Pleistocene of California. Lesions on the vertebrae look like a human disease called myositis ossificans progressiva. In that disease, bone forms inside muscle and around its tendons. Moodie compares the fossil lesions with similar bone growths in dinosaurs.

Such changes have long been known under the broad heading of myositis ossificans. The medical writing on it is vast, he notes. He restricts himself to the guiding points of that record. The earliest printed reference he cites dates to 1740, a strange case in a boy's back. The paper then weighs how far the fossil growths match the human pattern. It is a study in reading disease across deep time. The comparison spans cats, dinosaurs, and people.
europmc-pmc8123513:
Wiedermann examines low blood albumin as both a warning sign and a driver of infection. Albumin is the blood's workhorse protein, carrying compounds and guarding vessels. When its level falls, infections arrive more easily and hit harder. Sound immune defense, innate and adaptive, needs intact albumin. Oxidized or broken albumin loses its grip on protective lipids. The author builds the case for a causal link, not mere correlation.

Low albumin predicts trouble across viral, bacterial, and fungal infections. It flags risk of hospital-acquired infections, notably C. difficile. In COVID-19 it tracks viral load and lung injury severity. It also distorts how antimicrobial drugs behave in the body. Albumin infusions helped infected cirrhosis patients in randomized trials. Beyond cirrhosis, the evidence stays mostly observational for now. Trials in progress could rewrite ward practice. A cheap blood value may deserve drug-like respect.
europmc-pmc8153313:
Cronin and co-authors examine how dietary fibre shapes the gut microbiota. Fibre intake has fallen as low-fibre Western diets spread. That shift tracks with more gut disease, obesity, and type II diabetes.

The review explains what dietary fibre is and how gut microbes ferment it. Fermentation yields short-chain fatty acids that feed gut health. The authors link fibre to changes in microbe mix and in glucose and lipid control. They also cover metabolic syndrome and insulin resistance. The work gives readers a clear route from diet to microbes to disease risk.
europmc-pmc8240013:
Ossenkoppele and co-authors test tau PET scans as a forecast tool in Alzheimer disease. They asked how well tau imaging predicts mental decline. The study spanned preclinical and prodromal stages of the disease.

It followed 1,431 participants for a mean of 1.9 years. Baseline tau PET predicted change in mental test scores. It beat amyloid PET and MRI volume measures head to head. The edge was clearest in mild impairment and in amyloid-positive healthy people. Tau PET may help time care and select trial patients. The authors call it a promising prognostic tool.
europmc-pmc8287113:
Shorten, Khoshgoftaar, and Furht survey text data augmentation for deep learning. Natural language work is a star use of deep learning. Augmentation makes more training data from what exists.

The survey groups augmentation by its main tricks. Some methods harden local decision bounds. Others lean on brute force, causality, or counterfactual examples. Meaning versus form runs through the choices. The authors list the frameworks built for text so far. They also show how augmented sets can test generalisation. Overfitting stays a core worry that these methods can expose. Test sets built this way can reveal brittle models.
europmc-pmc8397413:
Ross and co-authors take stock of macrophages, immune cells that can drive inflammation or help end it. These cells shift shape and role with ease. The review puts fresh findings together on that plasticity and on non-infectious inflammatory disease.

Much attention goes to allergic and autoimmune disorders. Rheumatoid arthritis serves as a key case. In that disease, pro-inflammatory macrophages build up while calming types stay scarce. The authors also stress how macrophages clear dead immune cells, a step that helps resolve inflammation. Glucocorticoids and other drugs can push macrophages toward repair. Shifting macrophage behavior stays a central treatment goal.
europmc-pmc8444613:
Zhao and co-authors test NAD+ as a guard for the brain in rats with chronic low blood flow. Poor brain blood flow feeds vascular dementia through microglia-driven inflammation. NAD+ had shown anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects in other brain disease models, but not in this one.

Rats with blocked carotid arteries got daily NAD+ shots for 8 weeks. The treatment rescued learning and memory performance. It calmed brain inflammation by shielding mitochondria and cutting reactive oxygen output. Gene scans pointed to the Sirt1 and PGC-1alpha pathway. Cell tests with extra Sirt1 backed the finding. The work ties NAD+ gains to healthier mitochondria in microglia.
europmc-pmc8449013:
Corbett and co-authors find which immune signals match protection from the mRNA-1273 vaccine in primates. Knowing what protection looks like in blood helps judge vaccines without huge trials. The team gave nonhuman primates varied vaccine doses to span a range of responses.

Antibodies against the spike protein tracked with lower virus levels in the airways. Antibodies taken from vaccinated primates protected hamsters on their own. That shows antibodies are a true mechanism of protection, not just a marker. The lower airways needed less antibody for protection than the upper airways. The authors note this gap matters for booster plans aimed at blocking spread.
europmc-pmc8662613:
Cantalapiedra and co-authors describe eggNOG-mapper v2, a tool that labels gene function in huge genomic datasets. Labeling genes by function is a core step in genome work. At metagenomic scale, the task gets slow and hard. Version 2 rebuilds the tool for that scale.

The update refreshes the genome and function databases it draws on. It adds gene prediction straight from raw DNA pieces. It can also predict orthology pairs and find protein domains fast. Output files can be decorated with labels in one pass. The tool runs as a standalone program or as a web service. Tests show it keeps accuracy while handling vast data.
europmc-pmc8690913:
Ji, Wei, and Yang review nanomedicines that pair light-based therapy with cancer immunotherapy. Light therapy can kill tumor cells and trigger immune attack. Yet tumors often suppress immunity and lack strong immune signals. The complex tumor setting also cuts the light therapy's reach.

Smart nanomedicines can tune drug behavior in the body. Some designs reverse low oxygen in tumors, which aids light therapy. Others use tiny frameworks or target parts inside the cell. Combined designs amplify immune responses against the tumor. The review sorts these strategies and their gains. It closes with hurdles the field must clear for clinical use.
europmc-pmc8891013:
Domizio and co-authors trace a DNA-sensing pathway behind harmful interferon responses in COVID-19. Interferons help fight the virus early on. Sustained interferon late in illness, though, tracks with bad outcomes. The suspects here are cGAS and STING. Together they sense loose DNA inside cells. The team profiled skin lesions from COVID-19 patients. They also studied lung tissue and a lung-on-chip model.

Skin profiles showed a STING-driven interferon signature. Macrophages near damaged blood vessel cells drove it. Lung samples with heavy destruction showed the same activity. In the chip model, infection freed mitochondrial DNA in vessel cells. That switch fired STING and killed cells. Blocking STING in mice eased severe lung inflammation. Disease outcomes improved. The authors offer STING as a host-directed drug target.
europmc-pmc8926413:
Nyberg and co-authors compare Omicron and Delta severity in a national cohort in England. Cases were confirmed between late November 2021 and early January 2022. Records linked infection to vaccination, hospital, and death data. The team estimated relative risks for three outcomes. Hospital attendance came first. Hospital admission and death followed. Adjustments covered age, region, ethnicity, and prior infection. Vaccination status was handled with care.

Omicron proved clearly milder than Delta. The adjusted hazard ratio was 0.56 for hospital attendance. It was 0.41 for admission and 0.31 for death. The pattern shifted with age. Children under 10 showed no clear admission advantage. Past infection protected against death for both variants. The authors separate vaccine effects from the variant's own mildness. Their cohort gives one of the firmest early severity reads.
europmc-pmc8967713:
Shitara and co-authors report long-term results from CheckMate 649, a global trial in gastro-oesophageal cancer. Standard chemotherapy alone usually fails within a year. The trial tested nivolumab in two pairings. One arm added it to chemotherapy. Another paired it with ipilimumab, a second checkpoint drug. Chemotherapy alone was the control. The study enrolled 3,185 patients. Of those, 2,031 were randomized across the three arms.

At 24 months of minimum follow-up, nivolumab plus chemotherapy still won. Survival improved in patients with high PD-L1 scores, with a hazard ratio of 0.70. All randomized patients also gained, at 0.79. The ipilimumab pairing missed its significance boundary. No new safety signals appeared. The authors back nivolumab plus chemotherapy as standard first-line care. The cancer type is HER2-negative adenocarcinoma.
europmc-pmc9106713:
Li and co-authors explain cuproptosis, a newly named form of cell death driven by copper. Copper is vital in small amounts but toxic when it builds up inside cells. A recent study found that copper binds directly to lipoylated proteins of the TCA cycle. Those bound proteins then clump and trigger lethal stress.

The account walks through the screens that found the key genes at work. A protein called FDX1 sits upstream and controls the lipoylation step. Loss of iron-sulfur cluster proteins adds to the damage. A mouse model of Wilson's disease showed the same toxic pattern. Readers get a concise guide to a death path distinct from apoptosis and other known forms.
europmc-pmc9158113:
Dalmaijer and co-authors test statistical power for cluster analysis through simulation. Cluster tools find discrete subgroups in data and are now popular in biomedical research. Yet no firm rules exist for working out power before a study runs. The team varied subgroup size, number, separation, and data structure in a systematic way.

Results showed outcomes hinge on large effect sizes or many small effects added up. Sample sizes of 20 per subgroup could suffice when separation was large. Adding more people past that point did not raise power. Fuzzy clustering beat hard clustering for groups that partly overlap. The authors give four practical rules for planning sound cluster studies.
europmc-pmc9252913:
Khoury and co-authors summarize the fifth edition WHO classification for myeloid and histiocytic or dendritic neoplasms. This volume sits inside a single database that catalogues cancers across all organ systems. A companion article covers lymphoid tumors. Diagnosis still rests on multiple clinical and tissue features.

The update refines diagnostic criteria for many disease types. It stresses biomarkers that guide therapy or forecast outcomes. A genetic basis for defining diseases is sought where possible. At the same time, the scheme keeps practical use worldwide in view. The structure runs from lineage to category, family, type, and subtype. The authors call it an evidence-based scheme built to scale with new finds.
europmc-pmc9338613:
Naing and co-authors explain how to size a prevalence study using two free calculators. Picking the right sample size is vital, yet errors in formula and reporting are common. Their tools run in spreadsheet software and in RStudio. That keeps them open to researchers with small budgets.

Four inputs drive the math: confidence level, precision, data variability, and expected loss of participants. The guide shows how each choice changes the final number. The calculators walk users step by step and guard against common slips. They also draft a publication-style report of the result. The authors warn that no single formula fits every study design. Clear reporting, they argue, is part of doing the science right.
europmc-pmc9355713:
Cui and co-authors review quercetin, a plant flavonoid, as a treatment for aging-related disease through the enzyme SIRT1. Quercetin is non-toxic at safe doses and fights oxidation, cell death, and inflammation. SIRT1 helps cells handle stress and slows many aging processes. The pair are studied together across brain, heart, bone, and metabolic disease.

The review maps the signal paths where quercetin acts via SIRT1. These cover oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial repair, and self-cleaning of cells. Diseases include Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, osteoporosis, and diabetes. Delivery by tiny extracellular vesicles is floated as a next step. So is relief of a newer cell-death type, ferroptosis. The authors call SIRT1 a promising shared target. Human dosing proof still lags animal data.
europmc-pmc9364913:
Koenig and co-authors use single-cell methods to map how the human heart changes in failure. They merged cell and nucleus RNA data from 27 healthy donors and 18 people with dilated cardiomyopathy. Fifteen major heart cell types were defined. Age and disease signatures were read cell by cell.

Heart muscle cells converged toward shared disease states. Fibroblasts and immune myeloid cells, by contrast, split into many new states. Vessel lining cells and pericytes shifted their programs without gaining complexity. Heart failure carries lifetime risk of 20 to 45% and five-year death rates near 50%. The map names cell-specific programs that new drugs might target. It is offered as a public resource for heart failure research. Earlier human data sets were too small for this view.
europmc-pmc9569513:
Menon and co-authors review microRNA as a promising drug target in cancer. MicroRNAs are small non-coding RNAs that tune gene output. They bind partner RNAs and block their messages. In cancer, a microRNA can act as a brake or as an accelerator.

Therapy can work in two directions from that split. Teams can block a cancer aiding microRNA. Or they can restore one that holds tumors back. Both routes have shown effect in studies so far. The review covers microRNA creation and normal duties first. It then maps how their control breaks down in cancer. Delivery is the hard part of therapy design. Systems that carry microRNAs into the body get a section. Patents and live clinical trials are summed up at the end. Open hurdles for the field close the account.
europmc-pmc9729113:
Mach and co-authors watch chromosome folding in living cells to test how cohesin and CTCF steer it. Mammal genes often answer to control spots far down the chain. Contacts inside folded domains link those distant partners. How long such contacts last was unknown before this work.

The team imaged chain spots at fine scale in living cells. Contacts inside the domains proved brief and frequent. Sites with facing CTCF anchors met more often. Those meetings also held together for longer spans. Models of chain motion fit the live cell data well. Anchored loops seemed to last around 10 minutes each. The results say long range control rides on passing closeness. Cohesin and CTCF steady a structure that never sits still. That steadiness favors select contacts over random ones.
europmc-pmc9825413:
Sollis and co-authors describe the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog as a knowledge base and submission hub. The Catalog gathers genome-wide association results in standard form. It serves over 200,000 users each year worldwide. Academic, clinical, and industry researchers all draw on it.

Holdings top 45,000 published studies across 5,000 human traits. Over 40,000 full summary statistics sets sit beside them. Content comes from curation and a new author portal. Authors can now deposit results before publication day. Software updates sped up release of those deposits. New data types joined, including sequencing based studies. Gene based and copy number analyses also entered scope. Links tie the Catalog to polygenic score resources. Trait naming was refined for cleaner cross links. The team also pushes for wider population diversity.
europmc-pmc9954613:
Kciuk and co-authors collect evidence on the many anticancer actions of doxorubicin. Doxorubicin is a core part of cancer treatment regimens in wide clinical use. Its exact action routes are still not fully mapped. New work points to broad, varied activity.

The review covers DNA damage and reactive oxygen species production. It also covers apoptosis, senescence, autophagy, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis. Immune effects of the drug are treated as part of its action. Each route is tied to how tumor cells die or stop growing. The authors argue this range explains the drug's lasting place in therapy. Readers get a single account of a classic drug's many modes.
file-no-113:
Gaboriau builds a mystery on a Paris theft in File No. 113, printed in 1867. Emile Gaboriau opens with the evening papers of February 28, 1866. They report a bold robbery at the bank of M. Andre Fauvel. Thieves forced a safe thought to be beyond force and took 350,000 francs in bank notes. A clerk of the bank, named in the papers by initials, was already under arrest.

From that arrest the tale widens. The sampled pages turn to a countess in want of a dowry for her daughter Valentine, and to Andre Fauvel as he hears her tale. He tells her that rank and beauty are a fortune in themselves. Money, marriage, and a clerk's fate hang on the one crime. Gaboriau, a founder of the detective novel, lets the hunt for the thieves carry the secrets of Paris society with it.
frobenius-the-voice-of-africa-1913:
Leo Frobenius led an expedition across the Western Sudan in 1910 to 1912 and told it in The Voice of Africa, published in 1913. The German ethnologist sought the roots of African civilization among Yoruba, Nupe, and Jukun peoples. Sacred art, bronzes, and temples amazed him, and he carried word of them to Europe.

Frobenius argued that Africa held high cultures of great age, a claim Europe resisted hearing. His finds and photographs changed how the West saw African art forever. The book stands as both travel record and manifesto, the voice of a continent speaking through its shrines.
frost-boys-will-1913:
Robert Frost published A Boy's Will in 1913, his first book of poems. Frost was an American farmer and teacher who had moved to England. The poems speak in a young man's voice about nature, love, and finding his own path. Into My Own and Storm Fear are among the best-known pieces.

Many poems pair a plain scene with a quiet doubt or hope. Frost uses traditional forms but a fresh, spoken tone. The book won notice in England and helped launch his career back home. Readers can hear his later themes starting here: work, weather, isolation, and choice. It is a modest and lovely debut.
frus-1861-d113:
Mr. Jones wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 July 1861. The dispatch is document 113 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Jones wrote on the eve of Bull Run, the war's first great battle. His July report is the second of his two papers in this file. Read with his April note, it brackets the season in which the short war became a long one. His two reports, spring and summer, frame the war's first season from one post. One post, two seasons: the frame shows how much the war had changed by July.
frus-1861-d13:
Norman Judd, the American minister to Prussia, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 July 1861. The dispatch is document 13 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Judd was a friend of Lincoln's from Illinois politics, sent to Berlin that spring. Prussia was rising as the strong power of north Germany, and its stance mattered. Judd's reports told Washington how the Berlin court read the American war in its first summer. Berlin watched the war through the lens of its own struggle with Austria and France. Berlin's cool tone suited the Union, which asked no more than strict fairness.
frus-1861-d213:
The State Department sent word to Mr. Marsh on 21 June 1861, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 213 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the opening months of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d113:
Writing home was Charles Francis Adams's duty, and his letter of 31 July 1862 went to Seward. Congress received it as Document 113 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d13:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 4 February 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 13 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d213:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 5 April 1862, in a note printed as Document 213 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons, the British minister in Washington, received it at the legation.

Early April 1862 brought the great battle of Shiloh in Tennessee and the start of the campaign against Richmond. Each swing of the war changed the odds that Europe might step in, so envoys traded paper at a fast rate. A note from this week sits in the file as part of that quick, watchful exchange. Each note was numbered and docketed by clerks, which is why the file reads so evenly.
frus-1862-d313:
On 20 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton another dispatch, printed as Document 313 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Three letters in two days mark the post-battle rush.

Seward wrote on the eve of Lincoln's emancipation announcement, which he had helped shape and knew was coming. The proclamation would give the war a cause that European publics could cheer. His letters to Paris in these days prepared his envoy for the new ground, on which defending the Union also meant defending freedom. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d413:
From Madrid on 9 November 1861, Carl Schurz sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 413 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed to accompany the President's annual message.

Schurz wrote in the weeks when Britain, France, and Spain had just agreed to act together in Mexico, a move that worried Washington deeply. As minister in Madrid he could watch Spanish motives at close range. His reports home fed the Union's effort to keep the European powers separate and neutral. The dispatch is part of the first season of that long campaign, before Schurz left Spain for army service.
frus-1862-d513:
Two days after Pike's latest report was dated, on 8 August 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James Shepherd Pike. It is Document 513 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The crossed dates are the Atlantic mail at work: each man wrote from news the other had not seen. Seward's August orders to The Hague kept up the standing themes of Dutch neutrality and colonial ports. They also kept up the Union's refusal to treat the rebellion as a nation. Pike's replies, arriving a month later, show how those themes landed. The pair of files, order and report interleaved, is the true shape of the record the volume preserves. It is a slow conversation. Two governments carried it on in good faith across an ocean.
frus-1862-d613:
The Danish file opens on 22 January 1862 with this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Bradford R. Wood, the American minister at Copenhagen. It is Document 613 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Denmark was a small maritime kingdom. Its ports and its Sound dues touched Baltic trade. Wood, a New York lawyer, held the post through the war. Seward's opening order set out the Union's case for the Copenhagen court. The Baltic was far from the fighting, but its states' goodwill counted in the general European balance the Department tracked. The letter begins a quiet, regular file in the volume's northern tier.
frus-1862-d713:
Luis Molina wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 September 1862. Molina was Costa Rica's envoy in Washington, a lawyer who had long handled his land's affairs in the United States. The letter is document 713 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Foreign envoys in Washington wrote to Seward on the business between their lands and the United States. For Costa Rica, trade and the transit routes of Central America were never far from the talks. Molina's letter is part of that formal exchange, in which small republics dealt with a great power then fighting for its life. The file that follows shows the talk run both ways.
frus-1863p1-d113:
On 11 March 1863, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the first of three letters to him dated that day in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 113 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Three letters in a day, a week after a batch of twelve, show a desk that never let the London file cool. Seward split his points across the sheets so Adams could use each on its own. This one opens the day's set. It is part of the spring press on Britain, kept up sheet by sheet from Washington.
frus-1863p1-d13:
On 13 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is document 13 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Seward wrote on the day of the battle of Fredericksburg, though its news had not yet reached London.

Letters crossed the Atlantic in about ten days by steamer, so each side wrote in the dark about the other's last moves. Seward's mail set the claims Adams was to press on Britain. They were fair dealing, a tight rein on warships built for the South, and no aid to the rebellion. This letter is one link in that chain of orders.
frus-1863p1-d213:
The mail from London dated 11 June 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 213 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d313:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 3 November 1862. The note is document 313 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Stuart served at the British legation in Washington and handled business with the State Department when the minister himself was away or occupied. His notes form part of the same Anglo-American exchange. It comes from the autumn after Antietam, when Lincoln's first emancipation order had just raised the stakes for Britain. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d413: Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 March 1863. It is document 413 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, among the formal British papers in the Civil War correspondence. Through such notes London lodged protests and guarded its neutral rights against Union measures at sea.
frus-1863p1-d513:
A dispatch dated 14 May 1863 went from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d613:
Document 613, dated 14 August 1863, records a letter from Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the late summer of 1863.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1913:
Wilson's address opens the 1913 volume, and policy fills its circulars. Senator Root repudiates sentiments charged against him on Latin America. A declaration of policy toward Latin America follows.
