The President's peace plan earns its own papers. Brazil terminates its extradition treaty with America. The notice of July 1913 appears in the file. Coffee valorization fills a long Brazilian run.

Japan's grievance dominates the mid-volume exchanges. Bryan sends an aide-memoire to the Japanese embassy. Viscount Chinda's own memorandum stands answered there. Land and citizenship in California drive the dispute. Austria-Hungary arrests naturalized Americans for evading service. The old charge violates the 1871 convention, Washington says. The volume's diplomacy turns defensive. New doctrines meet old treaties.
frus-1919Parisv13:
Volume XIII prints the peace itself. Germany's observations on the conditions open the book. The Allied reply and ultimatum answer them. Then the treaty text runs in full. The League Covenant heads the parts. Borders, the Saar, and Alsace-Lorraine follow. Danzig, Memel, and Schleswig take their sections. Labor clauses close the long list of parts. A separate treaty with Germany, signed in 1921, restores relations. It lets America claim the settlement's rights.

A status table tracks the conference's treaties. A mid-volume passage names the Labor Office's board. Members serve three-year terms under the text. The volume needs no narrative thread. Its documents are the settlement's law. Every later argument starts from these pages.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d113: On November 10, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, and his message is Document 113 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The two leaders wrote almost daily that week, even with a meeting a fortnight ahead, because the plans for two conferences still had loose ends. The record gives the date and the names and no subject. The message survives in the Foreign Relations series' pre-departure papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d13: Roosevelt replied to Churchill on June 28, 1943, and the message stands as Document 13 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The same day produced a Churchill note in return, a sign of how fast the exchange moved that week. The record lists the parties and the date only. In the State Department's published series, the letter belongs to the build-up toward the Quebec talks of August and the summits that closed the year.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d213:
The Joint Staff Planners sent report J.C.S. 600 to the Joint Chiefs of Staff on 11 November 1943. Its subject is airfields for very-long-range B-29 bombers in the China-Burma-India area, tying the question to the decisions taken at the Quebec conference that August.

The planners say B-29s could be ready early in 1944, and that attacks on Japan could start sooner if fields were built in time. They call for at least four fields near Calcutta and five near Chengtu in China, built with British and Chinese help. Their recommendation is that all nine be authorized and finished, as far as possible, by May 1944.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d313:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 410 at Cairo on 25 November 1943, an examination of how weather limits any postponement of Operation Overlord, the cross-Channel invasion of France. It was ammunition in the Anglo-American argument over the invasion's date.

The assault needs a quiet spell of four days with winds of force three or less. Counting ten years of weather, such spells came eighteen times in April and twenty-one in May. They came nineteen times in June, and still seventeen in September. On the assault alone, the operation could slip to September. The build-up after landing needs about three months of workable weather. Tides confine each attempt to two short windows a month, and missing the full-moon window, needed for the air lift, costs twenty-four days.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d413:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent Ambassador Harriman a confidential telegram, numbers 1342 to 1344, from Washington at midnight on 4 December 1943. It reports the uproar in the American press over Moscow's early announcement of the Tehran Conference.

Morning papers in the United States headlined London stories about a Moscow radio broadcast. The broadcast, an official Soviet news agency one for provincial papers, had announced the Tehran meeting. It spoke of talks on the war against Germany and on political questions. Decisions, it said, would be made public later. No word of the conference's end had reached America, and Washington had nothing to announce. Hull says the publication has created a furor. Elmer Davis of the Office of War Information asks the department to learn one thing: whether the broadcast broke any release date the conferees had agreed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d513:
Laurence Steinhardt, the American ambassador in Ankara, reported to Secretary of State Hull on December 9, 1943. Days earlier, Roosevelt and Churchill had met Turkey's President İnönü at Cairo and failed to bring Turkey straight into the war. The State Department printed Steinhardt's message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Steinhardt's post gave him the Turkish view of that refusal: what Ankara feared, what it wanted, and what it might still do. Reports from the man on the spot guided Washington's next steps with a neutral country the Allies badly wanted. For readers, the message continues the Turkish story beyond the conference room doors.
frus-1944-quebec-d113:
An editors' note in the Quebec Conference volume points readers to records from August 1944 about aid to the Polish underground army. That force had risen against the Germans in Warsaw as the Soviet army neared the city. The note lists the published sources where the full documentation on the episode can be found.

The note also records an unresolved detail. President Raczkiewicz of Poland had written to Roosevelt on August 12, and a reply was drafted on August 31. No copy of that reply was ever found in American files. It was sent by pouch to London on September 8. The note shows the volume's editors flagging a gap in the record rather than hiding it.
frus-1944-quebec-d13:
Representatives of the British Chiefs of Staff in Washington prepared this memorandum on July 14, 1944. The British Joint Staff Mission in Washington kept London's military views in front of the American chiefs between conferences. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Staff missions did the alliance's daily military diplomacy: papers exchanged, positions tested, and disputes cooled before they reached the leaders. A July memorandum from the British mission belongs to the preparation of the autumn's great questions, which the Quebec Conference would settle in September. For readers, it shows the professional layer where allied strategy was drafted before it was decided.
frus-1944-quebec-d213:
Hull forwarded two enclosures to Roosevelt on September 11, 1944. One was Ambassador Winant's telegram on the European Advisory Commission. The other was the draft protocol on occupation zones in Germany and the administration of Greater Berlin. Winant reported from London that Ambassador Gousev, chairing the commission, was calling a meeting for Monday afternoon.

Gousev was ready to recommend acceptance of the zones protocol with one gap: the American and British zones left blank, for the two governments to decide themselves. The commission's coming work included control machinery, basic proclamations, and the Austria protocol, where Winant had won agreement for tripartite control with only a small American contingent. Bulgarian armistice terms were in hand, and Hungary's were being formulated.
frus-1945-50-intel-d113:
Hoyt Vandenberg, the new director of central intelligence, wrote to Hoover on 3 July 1946. Vandenberg had taken over the CIG in June, full of plans to make it a real agency. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Vandenberg's arrival changed the group's pace: he wanted the SSU's operations, a bigger budget, and a clear field abroad. His first letters to Hoover opened the sharpest phase of the border war with the FBI. Readers should watch the difference in tone from Souers's careful papers. Where Souers conciliated, Vandenberg pressed. The volume's second half runs on the friction his pressing created, with departments, with the bureau, and with the White House itself.
frus-1945-50-intel-d13:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent a joint memorandum to Secretary of War Henry Stimson and Secretary of the Navy Forrestal on 19 September 1945. It carried the settled view of the nation's top military body. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

When the Joint Chiefs spoke together, the armed services presented one front to the civilians above them. Their memorandum on the eve of the OSS order shows the military claiming its share in whatever intelligence system came next. Readers should weigh the channel: the chiefs wrote to both service secretaries at once, binding Army and Navy to a common line. Much of the volume's later bargaining grows from positions fixed in papers like this.
frus-1945-50-intel-d213:
A memorandum dated 9 May 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Legislative Liaison Division, Central Intelligence Group (Pforzheimer). The reader was the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter). It is document 213 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d313:
A letter from Secretary of Defense Johnson reached Secretary of State Acheson on 7 October 1949. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 313 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. Two years into the CIA's life, the question in these papers is less how to build it than how to fix it.

Between offices that did not answer to each other, a letter was the polite but firm way to press a point. Many of the big fights of these years can be followed letter by letter. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d413:
John Steelman, acting chairman of the National Security Resources Board, wrote to Sidney Souers of the National Security Council on 2 February 1950. The memo is document 413 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Resources Board planned how the nation's farms, plants, and workers would serve in a war. Its place in an intelligence volume shows how wide the word security had grown by 1950. Steelman's memo links war planning at home with the secret work of watching threats abroad. The Board's link to the Council gave its chairman a direct line into war planning at the top.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d113:
Ambassador Winant looked back nearly three years in this personal letter to the President of 28 January 1945. Writing from London, he recalls a Foreign Office meeting where Eden, Maisky, and he first weighed how the three great powers should treat Europe. The letter is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Maisky, the Soviet ambassador, had set out two roads. One divided Europe into eastern and western fields of chief concern. The other had the three nations work as one to destroy fascist rule and rebuild a Europe at peace. His government, he said, chose the second road. Winant traces the Moscow Conference and the European Advisory Commission to those early talks, and his own seat on the commission to Tehran.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d13: Roosevelt answered Churchill on 22 October 1944, the same day the prime minister's message reached him. Filed as document 13 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta, the quick reply shows how fast the two men worked by cable. Their exchanges that fall aligned British and American positions well before the Yalta Conference opened.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d213:
Foreign Minister Bidault gave Hopkins and Caffery France's German terms over lunch in Paris, and Caffery reported them on 30 January 1945. His cable to the Acting Secretary of State is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The talk ran forty-five minutes before the meal.

Bidault set out the stand he and de Gaulle had often given before. All war industry, and near-war industry too, must be wiped out in Germany. A world body should govern the Rhine region, its south held by France alone and its north under mixed control. Germany must be cut down so she can never wage war again. But, Bidault added, he would not like a red flag over Germany to be followed by a black one, the pirate's flag. He also spoke with sympathy of the Security Council voting plan.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d313:
America's Joint Chiefs of Staff met at Floriana, Malta, on the morning of February 1, 1945, and these minutes cover the session. General Kuter opened with a fix to an earlier record: his remarks on British help in the long-range bombing of Japan had been left out. A letter from Sir Charles Portal, Britain's air chief, had since reached General Arnold with Kuter's comments.

Kuter asked that his message be attached to the earlier minutes so the file would be complete, and the chiefs agreed. The detail is small, but it shows how carefully the chiefs guarded the record. Even a missing paragraph could matter when allies compared notes.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d413:
Three staff men did the paperwork for the founding conference in this draft report of February 9, 1945. The subcommittee — Jebb, Gromyko, and Hiss — had been charged a day earlier with two tasks. They were to advise on consulting France and China about the conference decisions. They were also to draft the invitation text.

On consultation, they advised that the United States speak for the three powers to both governments. On the invitation, they attached a draft for the ministers' approval. The report is short and unsigned in feel. Yet it settled the mechanics by which fifty nations would be summoned to San Francisco.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d113:
Churchill cancelled the King's Berlin visit in telegram number 99 to President Truman, sent July 1, 1945. The short message is document 113 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Truman had earlier agreed to Churchill's plan for King George VI to spend a day in Berlin during the conference, lunching and dining with the leaders.

The King has now decided, Churchill writes, that he must visit Ulster during the conference period instead, so Truman's kind telegram on the subject no longer applies. Churchill adds that Truman will no doubt have received the King's invitation to visit Britain. The dropped visit removed a bright social occasion from the Potsdam schedule, though the King's invitation to Truman still stood.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d13:
De Gaulle wants a seat, and Grew's memorandum to the President of May 16, 1945, prepares Truman for the ask. Stettinius had telegraphed that French Foreign Minister Bidault, arriving in Washington the next day, expected to plead strongly for de Gaulle's inclusion. The proposed meeting of Churchill, Stalin, and Truman was the occasion in view. A copy of the Secretary's telegram is enclosed.

Grew suggested how Truman might open the subject when Bidault called. He could refer to a question asked at the press conference the day before. It concerned whether a meeting of the Big Five would take place at San Francisco. He could then cite his reply, as it was interpreted. The memo scripts a delicate refusal in advance.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d213:
Ambassador Harriman reported a hitch in the Soong talks in an extract dated July 12, 1945. The extract is document 213 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. China's foreign minister, T. V. Soong, was in Moscow trying to settle with Stalin the terms tied to Soviet entry into the war against Japan.

Soong suggested to Stalin that he return to Chungking to consult the Generalissimo on the points still at issue. Stalin answered that it was better to reach agreement before he met Truman at Berlin. He wished to settle with the President the date of his entry into the war. The fragment shows the Soviet timetable for joining the Pacific war being tied directly to the Potsdam meeting.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d313:
A farewell call in Budapest gave Schoenfeld one of his darkest reports, sent on July 13, 1945. Valentiny, Hungary's resigning Minister of Justice, came to take his leave. He repeated a warning he had made before: the government did not control its own political police.

The police, Valentiny said, served the Communist Party, and that made them the most dangerous force in Hungarian politics. His successor would fare no better, and repression of non-Communist parties would grow. He hoped America would use its influence for free politics, yet he believed Moscow meant to Sovietize Hungary in full.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d413:
Philip Mosely laid the French zone dispute before Assistant Secretary Dunn in a memorandum written at Babelsberg on July 15, 1945. The European Advisory Commission had completed the draft agreement on the French zone in Germany. Its submission to the four governments, though, was held up by one point: how France's area of occupation in Berlin would be defined.

The American proposal of June 30 simply sent the whole question to the Control Council. It prejudged nothing about whether the French area came from two zones or three. The Soviet proposal of July 11 claimed the Soviet area's greater destruction meant the French area should come from the American and British areas, leaving Moscow's share unchanged.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d513:
Germany's eastern frontier is introduced in a briefing book statement dated July 4, 1945. The inter-divisional committees on Germany and on Russia and Poland, it reports, have recommended a settlement. Germany should be required to cede Upper Silesia, East Prussia, and the portion of Pomerania east of the Kreuz-Dramburg line.

The remainder of German territory east of the Oder, and the territory between the Oder and the Neisse, should remain in German possession. For the summary recommendations that follow, the frontier is divided into six segments, each discussed on its own page. Two underlying studies, the statement notes, tried to analyze the whole problem and frame as reasonable a settlement as its complexity allowed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d613:
Eugene Dooman, a Japan specialist at the State Department, wrote a top secret memo dated July 15, 1945. It is document 613 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Its subject is the occupation and military government of a defeated Japan.

Dooman says the State, War, and Navy departments have agreed a draft stance, now with the Joint Chiefs. Japan's occupation, he argues, should be unified, not split into zones. The United States should also hold the controlling voice on policy there. Allied troops would serve under one commander, an American, with an advisory council of their senior officers. Dooman allows one possible exception to unified rule. Southern Sakhalin and the Kurile Islands, promised to Moscow at Yalta, could be run apart without harm to Japan proper.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1013:
Soviet delegates renewed their claim on the German fleets in this proposal of July 30, 1945. A third of the German surface navy would pass to the Soviet Union. Ships still building or in repair at the surrender are included in that share.

Most of the submarine fleet would be sunk. Boats of the greatest technical interest would be kept and split among the three powers. A third of naval stores, matched by ship class, is also claimed. So is a third of the merchant marine. Transfers would run from August 1 to November 1, 1945, under a Maritime Technical Commission.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1113:
John McCloy, Assistant Secretary of War, sent this message to the War Department on 19 July 1945. McCloy was one of the War Department's top civilian leaders. He had a strong hand in shaping American plans for postwar Germany, and he was with the team at Potsdam.

His message carried the view from the summit back to the Pentagon's leadership in Washington. The War Department ran the army that held Germany, so its chiefs needed word from the talks. A cable of this kind shows the direct line between the men who would rule Germany and the envoys fixing the terms. It is the military half of the peace talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1213:
Patrick Hurley, the American ambassador in China, wrote to the Secretary of State and to Ambassador Harriman in Moscow on 19 July 1945. Hurley dealt with the China file: a Nationalist government at war, a communist rival in the north, and American hopes for a joined front.

Sending one dispatch to both the secretary and the Moscow envoy tied the China and Soviet files together. Soviet moves in Asia bore hard on China's future, as all three men knew. This cable shows that link being worked in practice. It is Washington's China hand writing to its Russia hand, mid-summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1313:
Secretary of War Stimson wrote to the President on 30 July 1945. The letter came in the summit's final days. By then Truman had been fully briefed on the atomic test, and the terms to Japan had gone out with the weapon held behind them.

A war secretary's letter at that hour carried the counsel of the man who had overseen the bomb from its birth. Stimson's advice joined the military and moral weight of the choices ahead. This message is part of the last counsel the president received at Potsdam. It shows the cabinet's elder hand still on the brief at the close.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1413:
Secretary Byrnes answered Ambassador Caffery in Paris on 15 August 1945. The reply came nine days after Caffery's great cluster of cables to the secretary. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Replies from the secretary close the loop that cables open. After reading Caffery's six messages of 6 August, readers reach Byrnes's answer with a sense of what Washington decided to give, refuse, or postpone. The date matters too: 15 August was the day the war against Japan ended. So the reply belongs to the first day of the postwar world. The French file, like everything else, turned a page that day.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-113:
The United States delegation produced this memorandum at Potsdam on July 25, 1945. It is one of several staff memos dated that day in the second Potsdam volume. Such papers moved facts and views around a large team at speed. Some briefed the Secretary of State. Others armed officers heading into committee rooms.

A memo's plain style is the point. Writers skipped ceremony and stated what the reader needed. For later readers, the memo fixes a moment's knowledge inside the delegation. It helps explain why the American side acted as it did in the sessions that followed. The record gains texture from papers never meant to be public.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-13:
A rapporteur's report sums up the foreign ministers' meeting of July 18, 1945, at Potsdam. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. The report lists what the ministers agreed to put before the heads of government that afternoon.

Three subjects were recommended for the afternoon session. First came procedure and machinery for peace negotiations and territorial settlements. Second came the authority of the Control Council for Germany in political questions. Third came Poland, above all the winding up of the London Polish government and the carrying out of the Yalta agreement. On the first subject, the U.S. draft for a Council of Foreign Ministers was approved in principle. A redraft of its third paragraph was also approved. The Soviet team reserved the right to propose a change in the first paragraph.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d713:
Document 713 preserves a text the heads of government approved at Potsdam on July 20, 1945. Approval by Truman, Churchill, and Stalin marked the top level of the conference. Few papers reached that stamp in the first week. The text stands in the second Potsdam volume among the early agreed acts.

An approved text is a fixed point in a moving negotiation. Readers can build around it: what came before, what it settled, what it left. The document shows the leaders acting as a body, not just debating. Such texts became the bricks of the final protocol. Each one narrowed the field of dispute a little more.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d813:
The American team on the Allied Control Commission for Bulgaria wrote to the Joint Chiefs of Staff on July 24, 1945. Document 813 is a military report from Sofia's commission. It carried the team's account to Washington's top soldiers. The paper entered the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A commission's report to the chiefs shows the military line of the occupation story. The team reported its treatment and its findings in formal terms. Readers can set this beside the diplomats' Bulgaria letters. The two channels did not always sing in tune. Their difference teaches how a government sees one place through several eyes at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d913:
The American reparations team in Moscow answered Edwin Pauley's urgent request in this telegram of July 23, 1945. Pauley had asked for 1938 output figures for the Russian zone of Germany. The reply separates factory and mining output from farm output, and gives each as a share of the old Reich.

Industry and mining in the Russian zone produced about 12 billion Reichsmarks, near 31 percent of the Reich total. Farm output came to roughly 6.5 billion, about 48 percent. Land east of the Oder-Neisse gave about 7 percent of industrial and mining output in 1939. The figures leave out the Russian sector of Berlin.
frus-1955-57v13:
Jordan through Yemen fill Volume XIII of the 1955–1957 set, in country order. Jordan leads, with the Templer mission's fallout, General Glubb's firing, and the April 1957 crisis. Aid kept the kingdom afloat in these files.

Saudi Arabia takes the longest run, on aid, the Dhahran lease, and King Saud's February 1957 visit. Syria follows, with ties worsening toward the 1957 crisis. Lebanon, Oman, Kuwait, and Yemen fill shorter runs. The papers show a pro-Western arc under strain from Cairo and from its own streets. Short files on the Gulf states round out the arc.
frus-1958-60v13:
Volume XIII of the 1958–1960 set joins the Arab-Israeli dispute, the United Arab Republic, and North Africa. Israel's arms and aid asks lead, with refugee and Jordan River water fights. Ben Gurion's March 1960 visit closes that block.

Recognition of the United Arab Republic follows, as Egypt and Syria merged. Algeria takes the longest North Africa run, its revolt straining ties with France. Libya, Morocco, and Tunisia close the volume. The files show old levers failing. Each new state or merger forced a fresh count of friends. Tunisia's arms asks close the volume's files here.
frus-1961-63v13:
Western Europe and Canada fill Volume XIII of the 1961–1963 set, the largest of the Kennedy set so far. Integration leads, on the Common Market's pull. NATO follows, with the Multilateral Force in the files.

France, Italy, Portugal, and Spain take country blocks. Britain follows, through the Nassau talks' season. Canada closes the volume. The record shows an alliance rich and restless. Trade walls, nuclear sharing, and de Gaulle's course fill the cables, each ally's price for unity named and argued in turn. The file change of February 1963 marks the sources' own seam.
frus-1964-68v13:
Volume XIII of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964-1968, looks at the Western Europe region as a whole. One long compilation of 339 documents carries the full span of the volume. It deals with the Atlantic alliance, the European Community, and joint defense plans. It also covers trade disputes that cut across borders. Country detail sits in the companion country volume.

The records are memos, cables, and notes of talks with allied leaders. They show U.S. officials reacting to French moves against joint bodies. They track talks on troop levels, nuclear sharing, and money. The volume is the regional half of the series' Western Europe coverage for these years.
frus-1969-76v13:
Volume XIII of the 1969-1976 Foreign Relations series continues the Soviet story from October 1970 to October 1971. The first chapter opens with a meeting between Nixon and Gromyko. Later chapters follow backchannel talks on arms limits, Berlin, and a summit. Kissinger's secret trip to China in July 1971 reshapes the middle of the volume. The final chapter runs from the China announcement to the summit agreement that fall.

Phone talks between Nixon and Kissinger fill many pages. They show the two men weighing Moscow's reaction to the China opening. Arms talks advance in the same months. The volume ends with a Moscow summit set for 1972.
frus-1969-76ve13:
China from 1969 to 1972 fills Volume E-13 of the 1969-1976 Foreign Relations series. Its 175 documents run in one sequence. They follow the first probes between Washington and Beijing after decades of silence. The Pakistan channel, ping-pong diplomacy, and Kissinger's secret trip all appear. The run ends with Nixon's visit and the first steps that followed it. Talk records from the Beijing meetings fill many pages.

A lighter moment in the papers has U.S. staff and Chinese hosts trading jokes about security staff and women's liberation. Beneath it, the records track a careful, staged opening. Each side tests the other on Taiwan and Vietnam.
frus-1977-80v13:
China fills Volume XIII of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1977-1980. Chapters run by period, from November 1976 to January 1981. Early chapters cover the slow start after Mao's death. The June to December 1978 chapter covers the breakthrough to full relations. Later chapters deal with Deng Xiaoping's visit and the first years of normal ties. Taiwan arms sales run through the volume as the hard leftover issue.

State Department papers weigh how to present each arms offer to Taiwan. The aim was to raise the chance that Taipei would accept. The records show trade and strategy growing as formal ties began. The volume ends with the relationship set but still young.
frus-1981-88v13:
Volume XIII of the 1981-1988 series covers the conflict in the South Atlantic, from 1981 to 1984. The first chapter is a prelude, to April 1, 1982. The next covers the search for a negotiated settlement in April 1982, after Argentina seized the Falkland Islands. A third covers the management of the war in May and June. The last covers the postwar years to November 1984. At an April 29 press briefing, officials faced questions on licenses for jet engines for Argentine Skyhawk jets.

The records show Washington torn between two partners, then backing Britain. Shuttle diplomacy fills the April chapter. The volume is the full U.S. record of the Falklands war.
gao-gaoreports-b-297313:
PHT Corporation protested an Army award for gun magazine rounds in GAO decision B-297313, dated December 8, 2005. The winner was Airtronic Services. The goods were M9 magazine cartridges. The buy was set aside for small firms. The firm said past work marks were wrong. It also said the winner's price was too low.

GAO denied the protest. Fit past work meant jobs over 500,000 dollars that showed skill with like goods. The winner had no such past work. The pick lead knew that fact. She still found its wider record backed a mid risk mark. That view fit the call. A firm with no fit past work can still earn a mid mark on a wider record.
gao-gaoreports-b-297413:
Puglia Engineering protested a Coast Guard award for dockside ship work in GAO decision B-297413, dated January 20, 2006. The winner was Todd Pacific Shipyards. The work was upkeep and fix work for ships at dock. The firm hit marks, the price check, and the pick. It said the pick was flawed on its face.

GAO denied the protest. Marks were sound and tests were used in a fair, even way for both bids. The pick lead showed grasp of the strong and weak points of each bid. She weighed tech and price as the call set. That trade-off was sound. A well writ pick that tracks the tests will stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-297800-13:
INDUS Technology protested its cut from a tech services contest in GAO decision B-297800.13, dated June 25, 2007. The buyer was the General Services Administration. The buy was set aside for firms owned by disabled veterans. Bid cover notes set a hold time of 180 days. The call required 350 days at least. It said short bids would be cut.

GAO denied the protest. The cut was sound on the call terms. A hold time is a key term for a wide deal. The call warned of the cut in plain words. Firms that set a short hold time take the risk. The bar was thus fair and the cut stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-311313:
Consolidated Engineering Services, Inc. won its protest. GAO ruled in B-311313 on June 10, 2008. The Social Security Administration sought site care services. The award went to Meridian Management Corporation. The loser fought how past work was scored for each firm. It fought the pick chief's logic as well. The chief had weighed the risk of a shift to a new firm.

GAO sustained the protest. The past-work score drew on points the call did not name. Gaps drawn between firms lacked back in the file. Shift risk was a hush point the call did not list. A chief may not score on points the call keeps mute.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-213:
Oversight of Food Safety Activities, GAO-05-213 of March 30, 2005, maps where four U.S. agencies trip over the same food ground. Agriculture, the Food and Drug Administration, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the National Marine Fisheries Service all guard parts of the food chain. GAO has long called the split a waste of scarce funds.

GAO names the spots where their work overlaps. It tests how far joint deals let them share staff, labs, and data. It asks those who work with the system what they see. Agencies should chase those joint gains harder, the title urges. Full merge plans frame the backdrop.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-313:
Mutual Fund Trading Abuses, GAO-05-313 of April 20, 2005, asks how the stock watch missed a wide fraud under its nose. Fund advisers let pet clients trade fast, past the fund's own stated caps, in the dark. Such market timing raised costs and cut gains for the small holders who played by the rules. A state law chief, not the federal watch, broke the tale in September 2003.

GAO asks why the Securities and Exchange Commission did not spot the abuse in time. It draws the lessons in that miss. It grades the steps the watch has since taken to firm up its fund checks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-413:
Unemployment Insurance, GAO-05-413 of June 24, 2005, asks if jobless aid still leads back to a job. Long job loss runs more apt now than in past years. Swift links to job help count for more. Yet many states now take claims by phone or wire. The walk-in tie that once led a claimant to job aid has thinned.

GAO asks how far the shift to far-off claims has run, state by state. It asks how states tell claimants of their dues and of job help. It asks what states do to speed new work. It asks what is known of who gets such help, and how they fare.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-613:
Fifteen years of Clean Air Act work are tallied in GAO-05-613, a report dated May 27, 2005. The 1990 amendments set EPA hundreds of tasks under three titles. By April 2005 the agency had finished 404 of 452. Of 338 tasks with legal deadlines, 256 were done late. Most ran under 2 years past due, but 94 ran longer. Forty-eight tasks were still open, 45 of them past their dates.

EPA blamed the delays on public input, hard choices among many new duties, and court fights over its rules. Late rules can mean late gains in air quality. Appendices track each title's record task by task.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-813:
Hiring checks for work eligibility are faulted in GAO-05-813, a report issued August 31, 2005. A job draws many people to the United States without papers. Experts say deterrence needs a sound hiring check plus worksite enforcement. GAO studied the paper form employers use for each new hire. It also weighed the priorities and resources of worksite enforcement.

GAO found that fake documents and stolen identities beat the form check too easily. Honest employers struggle to spot fraud. Dishonest ones can hire off-books staff with ease. The long list of accepted documents adds to the problem. A plan to cut that list, proposed in 1998, was still not final. An electronic check pilot shows promise, GAO said, but challenges remain.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1013:
Disaster aid after Katrina and Rita is audited in GAO-06-1013, a report from September 27, 2006. A federal program gives housing units and grant money to disaster victims. The 2005 storms caused damage on an unmatched scale. GAO compared aid for these storms with aid for other recent hurricanes. It described the strain the request volume put on the agency. It tested the program's exposure to fraud.

Headings tell the story. Aid for Katrina and Rita far surpassed aid for the 2003 and 2004 seasons. The agency answered with new approaches, yet known management flaws hindered the work. GAO used sampling, data mining, and undercover work to test for fraud. Its audit and probes reveal room for fraud and abuse in applications and debit card use. Actions are needed to cut such problems in future disasters, it concluded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-13:
Risk-based choices at the Department of Defense are assessed in GAO-06-13, a report dated November 15, 2005. DOD runs costly wars while reshaping its forces and business habits. Money is tight, so GAO has urged a clear framework that weighs threats and risks. In its 2001 strategic plan, DOD promised just such a framework. It would balance priorities against risk over time and track results against goals. GAO checked how far that promise had come.

GAO asked whether DOD had put the framework to work, including in investment choices. It also named the largest hurdles to making the approach stick. The title states the verdict: more action is needed. A framework on paper does not guide budgets by itself. Leaders must use it when they pick between weapons, readiness, and reform. The report shows where DOD's risk talk and its spending choices still part ways.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-313:
Quality control failures at the planned nuclear waste dump fill GAO-06-313, issued March 17, 2006. The Energy Department seeks a license to build the repository at Yucca Mountain in Nevada. In 2004 GAO warned that stubborn quality problems could delay it more. In 2005 the department found staff e-mails hinting at deeper trouble. They suggested records may have been falsified. Quality assurance sets the rules that keep work controlled and sound.

GAO traced the history of the project's quality problems. It checked how the department tracks and fixes them since 2004. It weighed the challenges still ahead. New management tools must spot problems sooner and track fixes better, GAO urged. The department agreed with the advice. Whether the new effort will work, GAO said, is too early to tell. The report shows trust, not just rock, at stake in the license bid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-413:
One new Treasury system was meant to make the government's books add up. Issued April 21, 2006, report GAO-06-413 reviews the Governmentwide Financial Report System. For nine years, weak systems had blocked an opinion on the combined federal statements. The new system would link agency audit figures to the combined report. GAO strongly backs that idea.

GAO judged the Treasury's work to build and install the system. It found a lack of disciplined process in the effort. That flaw puts effective use of the system at risk. The report makes recommendations to cut those risks. Readers see why process discipline matters in a finance system build.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-613:
Federal courthouse rent is examined in GAO-06-613 (June 20, 2006), a report on the rising space costs of the courts. The judiciary pays over $900 million in rent each year to the General Services Administration for court space. That rent goes into a fund that pays to build and repair federal buildings. In December 2004, the judiciary asked for a lasting rent cut of $483 million a year, and the request was denied.

GAO traced how new space, plus rising energy and security costs, pushed rent upward. GAO also found weak tracking of what drove those costs. The report explains why court rent kept climbing as a share of the court budget. It urges better tracking and control of space costs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-713:
Emergency backup plans at federal agencies are reviewed in GAO report GAO-06-713, dated May 11, 2006. Continuity of operations plans keep vital services running during a disaster or attack. Agencies must name alternate facilities and plan for telework when offices cannot be used. The Federal Emergency Management Agency oversees and assesses these capabilities across the executive branch. GAO studied six selected agencies in depth.

GAO found that all six agencies had named alternate facilities and taken steps to ready them. Most had written site preparation and activation plans. Yet none of the agencies followed all of the oversight agency's guidance. None ran all the tests and exercises that applied to them. GAO said planning for alternate sites and telework could improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-813:
Guarding Medicare against bad claims is the subject of GAO-06-813, published on September 6, 2006. GAO has listed Medicare as a high risk program since 1990. The Medicare Integrity Program funds the fight against fraud, waste, and abuse. It safeguards over $300 billion in yearly program payments. The money supports five activities, from claim audits to medical reviews. GAO judged how the agency divides those funds.

GAO found that funding for all five activities had generally grown over time. But the agency's approach to allocating the money had weaknesses. It did not rest on a clear reading of where the risks lie. Coming program changes would also shift what the allocations should be. GAO said the funding approach should be revised. Smarter allocation, GAO argued, would put scrutiny where the dollars are most at risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-113:
Collective protection against chemical and biological attack needs fresh data and clear aims, GAO reports in GAO-07-113, dated January 19, 2007. Such gear gives troops a clean space for group work in tainted zones. Past GAO work found lasting flaws in guarding forces at high-threat sites abroad.

GAO read current threat reports on chemical and biological arms. It asked how far the Defense Department has put such protection at key sites abroad, and on big war assets. It weighed the frame used to rule site policy and rank sites for funds. In the lack of a department list, GAO built its own test to pick key sites.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-213:
Social Security reform plans often lean on general tax revenue, a break with the program's past. GAO studied how clearly that choice is shown in GAO-07-213, issued March 22, 2007. Without reform, scheduled benefits cannot be paid in full in time. The program's actuaries score each reform plan for Congress. GAO reviewed 17 recent scoring memos. It sorted the revenue devices the plans used.

Fourteen of the 17 plans used reallocated general revenue, GAO found. Nine used unlimited transfers to keep the trust fund whole. Other devices included refundable tax credits and estate tax receipts. The key figures sit buried in technical tables, GAO said. That makes plans hard to compare on cost to the wider budget. Solvency of the trust fund alone can mislead readers. GAO urged the actuaries to add a plain summary table to each memo.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-513:
Trust funds meant to carry two Pacific nations past U.S. grant aid may fall short, and GAO-07-513, dated June 15, 2007, runs the numbers. Amended Compacts of Free Association were signed in 2003 with the Federated States of Micronesia and the Republic of the Marshall Islands. From 2004 to 2023, the United States will give an estimated $3.6 billion in combined aid. Grants shrink each year while trust fund deposits grow.

GAO checked how each fund's committee set up, invested, and reported on its fund. Slow choices early on cost the Micronesia fund potential earnings. Yearly reports came late and skipped judging whether the funds can sustain income after 2023. Market swings add risk. Both nations hold options to add income later, but each has limits. The report urges sharper fund management now, while deposits still flow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-713:
Biofuels and the push to grow them fill GAO-07-713, a report GAO released on June 8, 2007. U.S. transport runs almost wholly on oil, a fact that brings cost and pollution risks. Ethanol and biodiesel can take the place of some oil. GAO charted how output, fuel networks, and suitable cars were growing. It listed the blocks in the way. It also judged whether the Energy Department had a joined-up plan for growth.

Output rose fast from 2004 to 2006. Ethanol output went from 3.4 billion to about 4.9 billion gallons. Biodiesel output jumped from 28 million to about 287 million gallons. Still, the two fuels made up just 3 percent of road fuel in 2006. Corn and soybean feed costs keep biofuel prices above oil fuel prices. GAO said the Energy Department lacked a plan that links output, pipelines, pumps, and cars. It urged one, plus a joint review with Treasury of biofuel tax breaks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-913:
Bad payments at Homeland Security are tracked in GAO-07-913, a report dated September 19, 2007. A 2002 law forces agencies to hunt improper payments and report them. The department's reports stayed thin for three straight years. For fiscal year 2006, it skipped risk checks on about $13 billion in payments. Its total disbursements passed $29 billion that year. Two programs were flagged high-risk after review. They cover disaster aid and vendor payments. Recovery of bad payments was the third question.

Without risk checks, the size of the problem stays unknown, GAO said. Grant payments make up over $6 billion of the unchecked sum. Auditors have flagged grant programs as weak before. A fix plan exists, but full compliance will not come in fiscal year 2007. Work to recover bad payments lags as well. GAO urged faster risk assessment across all programs. The department's own reporting should show real error rates. Congress gets a map of the gaps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-113:
Cyber security plans for vital sectors are checked in GAO report GAO-08-113, issued October 31, 2007. Sectors such as health, energy, water, and transport all run on computer systems. In June 2006, the Department of Homeland Security issued a national plan for guarding them. Lead agencies then wrote plans for each sector.

GAO tested each sector plan against set yardsticks. It looked for coverage of cyber assets, weak points, steps to cut risk, and recovery plans. Coverage varied widely from plan to plan. GAO warned that thin plans leave sectors unsure of their own risks. It urged the department to help sectors fill the gaps as plans are updated.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-13:
New mine-hunting gear for the Navy is assessed in GAO report GAO-08-13 (October 12, 2007). The Navy is moving away from dedicated minesweepers. Instead, it plans to place mine countermeasure systems aboard ships with wider missions. The newest host is the Littoral Combat Ship. The shift brings new systems and new ways of fighting mines.

GAO reviewed how far the new systems have come. It also checked how the fleet is taking them up. Program papers and talks with Navy and contractor staff informed the work. The title states the thrust: only by clearing key hurdles can the Navy gain the promised capability.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-313:
In GAO report GAO-08-313, issued February 28, 2008, GAO examines local programs that reconnect youth to education and employment. Disconnected youth are out of school and out of work, and they face higher risks of crime and reliance on public support. GAO studied 39 local programs and spoke with officials from four federal agencies.

The programs differed in funding and structure, but most drew on some federal funds and many had served youth for at least 10 years. Directors credited strong staff, a holistic approach, and program designs that build skills and empower youth. Directors also cited funding limits and grant rules as hurdles. GAO recommended that the Department of Labor help states and workforce boards write contracts that serve youth needing more help while still meeting performance goals. Labor agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-913:
After Hurricanes Katrina, Rita, and Wilma hit the Gulf Coast in 2005, Congress sent tax breaks to rebuild. GAO-08-913, issued in July 2008, tracks how states handed out the four incentives in the Gulf Opportunity Zone Act that state and local governments control. The act covered zones in Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi, Florida, and Texas.

The three hardest-hit states shared large pools: about $14.9 billion in tax-exempt private activity bonds, $323 million in low-income housing credits, $350 million in tax credit bonds, and about $7.9 billion in advance refunding bonds. Florida and Texas got only $3.5 million each in housing credit authority. States steered the incentives to low-income housing and a wide range of private facilities. GAO made no recommendations in this report.
glasgow-virginia-1913:
Ellen Glasgow published Virginia in 1913, opening the great sequence of novels in which she retold her native state's history through fiction. Glasgow, born in Richmond, set out to show what the Southern ideal of womanhood cost the women who lived it. Her heroine shares the state's name.

Virginia Pendleton is raised to be a perfect Southern lady: selfless, gentle, and wholly devoted to husband and children. She sacrifices her mind, her beauty, and finally her health to that ideal. Her husband thrives, grows away from her, and finds her faded devotion a burden. Glasgow's quiet irony builds a devastating case. The novel began her lifelong argument with the sentimental South.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-09-1913:
Volume 9 of Frazer's Golden Bough, third edition, appeared in 1913, titled The Scapegoat. James George Frazer studied the custom of loading a community's sins or evils onto one being and driving it out. Scapegoats could be human, animal, or even objects cast away.

Cases range from ancient Greece and Rome to villages in Asia and Africa in Frazer's own time. He described yearly expulsions of disease and sin, and human scapegoats put to death in some lands. The rite, he argued, let a whole people feel cleansed at one stroke. The volume gathers some of the strangest evidence in the set, and the word scapegoat in daily speech descends from this theme.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-10-1913:
Volume 10 of the third edition of The Golden Bough appeared in 1913, as Balder the Beautiful, Part 1. James George Frazer took his title from Balder, the Norse god whose death all nature mourned. The volume turns to fire festivals, the great theme of the work's close.

Frazer described bonfires at midsummer, Easter, and other seasons across Europe, lit on hills and in village streets. He asked why people leaped through flames, rolled burning wheels, and carried torches around fields. His answer tied the fires to sun magic and the guarding of crops. Part 1 builds the evidence country by country, in the dense, patient style that marks the whole twelve-volume work.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-11-1913:
Volume 11 of Frazer's Golden Bough, third edition, appeared in 1913, completing Balder the Beautiful. James George Frazer closed his argument with fire festivals beyond Europe. He also treated the external soul, the idea that a person's life can rest outside the body.

Tales and rites show souls hidden in trees, beasts, and locks of hair, safe until the hiding place is harmed. Frazer then returned to Nemi, where his whole inquiry began. There the priest was slain by his successor. The circle closes after thousands of pages of matched customs. Whatever readers think of his theory, the gathered lore changed how the world studies myth.
gorky-my-childhood-1913:
My Childhood, the first volume of Maxim Gorky's autobiography, appeared in Russian in 1913 and in English in 1915. Orphaned young, Alexey is taken to his grandparents' house in Nizhny Novgorod. His grandfather rules the dye-works family with beatings, while his grandmother answers hardship with prayer, tales, and warmth.

Uncles fight over the business, fires flare, and the boy learns work and cruelty early. Gorky recalls it all in scenes of startling clarity and color. The book turned his hard youth into a landmark of Russian memoir. It also explains the writer: pity for the beaten, love of story, and a will to learn. Two later volumes continue the life.
hale-history-common-law-1713:
Matthew Hale, a chief justice of England, wrote his History of the Common Law in the late 1600s, and it appeared in 1713, after his death. Hale was famed for his fairness on the bench. His book is the first great historical account of the common law.

Hale traces English law from Saxon and Norman roots through the growth of the courts. He weighs common law against statute and explains how custom gains force. The calm, orderly mind that lawyers admired in Hale runs through the prose. Later giants like Blackstone built on his frame. The book still opens many courses on English legal history.
hallaj-kitab-al-tawasin-massignon-1913:
Mansur al-Hallaj, the wool carder of Baghdad, was crucified in 922 for saying Ana al-Haqq, I am the Truth. His Kitab al-Tawasin is his strangest and densest book, a set of short chapters named for the Arabic letters Ta and Sin. Louis Massignon, who gave his life to Hallaj, edited the Arabic text at Paris in 1913, with French introduction, commentary, and notes. No English version in the public domain exists.

The chapters circle the fall of Iblis, the light of Muhammad before time, and the soul's union with God, in prose like struck sparks. Massignon's notes open the riddles line by line. The edition founded the modern study of Hallaj.
harrison-ancient-art-ritual-1913:
Jane Ellen Harrison published Ancient Art and Ritual in 1913, a short book with large influence. Harrison argues that art is born from ritual. Dance, drama, and image begin as acts done together for urgent needs: rain, food, fertility, and the return of spring. Only later do they become art for contemplation.

She draws on Greek festivals, primitive rites, and modern folk customs. The book is a manifesto of the Cambridge ritualist school. Anthropology and classics both felt its force. Harrison writes with verve and learning in short compass. Readers new to her work should start here. It remade how many thought about the roots of theatre and art.
heath-aristarchus-samos-1913:
Thomas L. Heath published Aristarchus of Samos, the Ancient Copernicus, in 1913. Aristarchus had proposed a sun-centered system in the third century BCE. Heath traces Greek astronomy through this bold pioneer's surviving evidence.

Eighteen centuries before Copernicus, Aristarchus set the earth in motion. His only surviving work measures the sizes and distances of sun and moon. Heath gives its first English translation inside his study. The geometry is ingenious even where the measurements fall short. Other astronomers rejected the moving earth, and Ptolemy's system won instead. Heath's book restored Aristarchus to his proper place in astronomy's history. The sun-centered idea's true birthday sits here. He got the big point right, and the world took note at last.
henderson-fitness-environment-1913:
Lawrence Henderson was a Harvard chemist who studied the chemistry of blood and the balance of acids in the body. His 1913 book The Fitness of the Environment turns a familiar claim around. Life fits its setting, he argues, because the setting itself is strangely fit for life.

Henderson shows how water, air, and carbon suit living tissue in many fine, linked ways. Change those traits a little, and no chemistry of life as we know it could run. His book gave an old teleological idea, that nature shows purpose, a fresh scientific hearing. His argument still turns up wherever fine balance in nature is debated.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum:
Volume thirteen of Thomas Carlyle's Frederick the Great brings the First Silesian War to its close, from May 1741 to July 1742. Prussia had seized Silesia from Austria, and all Europe caught fire around the quarrel. Carlyle gives much of this book to George the Second of Britain, torn between his British ministers and his Hanoverian lands.

George crosses to Hanover, hesitates, half draws his sword, and sheaths it again while French and Prussian armies move. Carlyle mocks the delays yet shows why every choice carried danger. The war ends with Silesia still in Friedrich's hands. Diplomatic paper, camps, and royal indecision make up this crowded middle act.
holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-2-of-6-slice-:
Raphael Holinshed's chronicle gives this slice to King Stephen, earl of Boulogne. Stephen crossed at speed on his uncle Henry's death in 1135. He took the government though sworn to the Empress and her issue. A winter tempest of thunder marked his arrival day, the chronicle notes.

His brother Henry, bishop of Winchester, backed the seizure. The reign dissolves into castle building and private war. Holinshed retails the Norwich charge against the Jews, a child said to be crucified, as the old writers told it. Robert of Gloucester wins Faringdon castle by force in 1145. The slice is the Anarchy in annal form.
husserl-ideen-i-1913:
Husserl published Ideas, the first book of his program for pure phenomenology, in German in 1913. The full title promises an introduction to a science of consciousness and a philosophy built on it. Husserl had already shaken philosophy with his Logical Investigations; the Ideas announced the mature system behind them.

The book's famous method is the epoché, the bracketing of belief in the outer world so that experience itself can be studied cleanly. Husserl describes how consciousness aims at objects and builds a world of meaning from that aiming. The slogan of the school became a return to the things themselves. Few books shaped twentieth-century philosophy more deeply. Continental thought, from existentialism onward, still works in the space the Ideas opened.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-13:
Disease strikes Huronia hard in Volume 13, from 1898, covering 1637 and 1638. Thwaites prints the reports as sickness sweeps town after Huron town. The dying turn in fear and anger toward the black robes.

Many Hurons blame the baptism water for bringing death with it. Priests face threats, closed doors, and grief in every village. Still they baptize the dying and nurse the sick each day. The fathers tell the horror plainly, in their own firsthand words. Tragedy, faith, and blame collide on nearly every page here. Nothing in the telling is softened or held back.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abadia-juan-de-: Juan de la Abadia was a Marano of the fifteenth century. He took part in a plan to subvert the Inquisition in Aragon. When that failed, he joined a plot to kill the inquisitor Pedro Arbues. Arbues was assassinated on September 15, 1485. Juan was caught soon after. The entry gives two accounts of his end. Graetz says he killed himself in prison, while Kayserling says the attempt failed and he was drawn, quartered, and burned.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abd-ul-mejid-21:
Abd-ul-Mejid was sultan of Turkey from 1839 to 1861, and the entry credits him with the new legal standing of Turkish Jews. Two Ottoman charters frame the change. Under the first, of November 3, 1839, Jewish testimony was taken in court, torture was ended, and goods could no longer be seized at will.

The second charter, of February 18, 1856, added equality before the law and in taxes, plus entry to public posts. In 1840 the sultan ordered a fresh trial for Jews accused of ritual murder at Rhodes, and the accused were cleared. That same year he declared by firman that Hebrew books ban the use of blood in rites, and that the charge was a slander. He also named a Jew, Dr. Spitzer, as his own physician.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abin-b-rab-hisd: Abin ben Rab Ḥisda was a Palestinian amora and a disciple of R. Johanan. Some legal views of his are kept in the record. A few notes of his on the sense of Scripture also survive, in the midrashic writing of the age. From those notes it is clear that he had a gift for tongues. He tried to fix the sense of Hebrew words in the Bible by setting them beside like words in kindred languages. The entry cites three midrashic sources for that work of his.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-vita-de:
Italian rabbi Abraham Vita de Cologna was born at Mantua in 1755 and died at Triest in 1832. He was an orator and political leader as well as rabbi of his native city. Mantua sent him to the Parliament of the Napoleonic kingdom of Italy.

In 1806 he went as a deputy to the assembly of notables in Paris. When the Sanhedrin formed in 1807 he became its vice-chairman. In 1808 he joined the French Central Consistory, and later the Consistory of Turin. The entry calls him a man of a transition age: strong for reform, but vague on its aims and means. He left a volume of sermons and essays in defense of the faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-acan-moses-de-z: Moses de Zaragua Açan was a man of Catalonia in the fourteenth century. He is also called Moses Ḥazan. He wrote a rhymed work on chess in the Catalan tongue. He opens with the making of the world. He urges men to praise the Creator by a good life. He backs chess but fights games of chance. Card play, he said, would ruin those who took it up. A copy of his work rests in the Escurial. It was turned into Spanish in 1350.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-accents-in-hebr:
Accents in Hebrew are signs that mark stress on parts of words and lines. Each word has one part spoken with more force than the rest. Lines also rank their words, with some said fast and some with care. In plain English print, word stress goes unmarked. Punctuation does not show all the stops a good reading needs. The Hebrew Bible text works in a richer way.

Its set of signs marks strong and weak stress alike. A reader who knows the signs can chant the holy text in the right way. He need not first work out the grammar or sense. The Hebrew word for accent first means taste. It then means sense or good judgment. That root shows the system's first aim. It marked the pauses that sense demands. The long entry traces the names, the rules, and the past of these signs in depth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-david-bar:
David Baruch Adler was a Danish banker and statesman. He was born at Copenhagen on May 16, 1826. He died there on December 4, 1878. In 1846 he joined a trade house in London. He wed Jenny Raphael there in 1849. In 1850 he came home and joined the bank of D. B. Adler and Company. He worked to shift Jutland's money hub from Hamburg to Copenhagen.

The crash of 1857 put him in a hard spot. In thanks for help in that squeeze, he set up a fund in 1864. It held 20,000 kroner for widows and girls of failed trade men. He backed free trade and helped found its society. He sat in the Danish lower house from 1864 to 1869. Then he sat in the upper house. He held town and court posts as well. Art and trade shows in Denmark also drew his work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aibu-ibu-b-nagg:
Aibu b. Naggari was a Palestinian amora of the fourth generation, in the fourth century. He was a disciple of Hila. He was also a contemporary of Judah b. Pazzi. He reports Halakot for many of his forerunners, and he adds views of his own. Several of his homiletic remarks survive.

One remark builds on a verse in the Psalms. "When he shall be judged, let him be condemned," it says. From this comes a known doctrine: Satan stands ready to accuse a man at his critical hour. The second remark defends David. Scripture seems to say David sat before the Lord, yet sitting in the Temple was barred. Aibu reads the verb as "he settled himself." David, that is, composed himself for prayer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alenu-music-of-: The music of 'Alenu is the traditional tune to which that prayer is chanted. The tune is of fairly late origin. Yet it has the breadth and dignity the words call for. It is built chiefly from its opening phrase, which is repeated several times. Into it is woven a strain from the cantor's lead-in to the 'Amidah. A passing echo of the Kol Nidre melody also appears. The printed version here is plainer than most cantors use. Some swap in a strain from the evening prayers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-algazi-hayyim-b: Hayyim ben Menahem Algazi served as rabbi on Rhodes and at Smyrna. He lived in the seventeenth century. His book gathers notes in the order of the four Turim. A pupil of his brought the book out in 1712. The place of printing was Orthokoi, near Constantinople. Added notes on three Talmud tracts came with the book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alsace-1313:
Alsace is a German land between the Rhine and the Vosges. With Lorraine it forms an imperial land. No sure date marks when Jews first settled there. Learned and rich Jews lived in Strasburg by the late 1100s. Travel notes from 1160 to 1173 prove that much. Old grave stones in Strasburg back the claim.

A law code of about 1200 set duties for Strasburg Jews. A Jews' quarter stood in the city by 1233. The long entry tracks charges, bans, and returns. It gives the place of rabbis under French rule. Their courts judged suits between Jews. Lists of sources close the piece.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-angel-abraham-s: Abraham Angel, surnamed Tshelebi, was a Turkish Talmudist and author of the early nineteenth century. His book Pittuhe Hotam, or Engraving of a Seal, came out at Salonica in 1839. It deals with questions the Talmud leaves undecided, the ones marked to stand unresolved. It also treats passages in the Pentateuch that contain a certain conjunction. The entry is brief and points readers to two standard catalogs of Hebrew books for the record of his work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aronssohn-jacqu:
Jacques Leon Aronssohn, a German physician, was born at Metz on May 2, 1793, and died at Strasburg on September 8, 1861. His father had practiced medicine at the garrison of Pont-a-Mousson. The son went to Strasburg in 1809 to study medicine and took his degree in 1816. He became assistant surgeon at the city hospital in 1823, then went to England to finish his training among leading London doctors.

Back in Strasburg he practiced for twenty-five years and was counted among its ablest doctors. During the cholera of 1832 he organized one of the emergency hospitals. He sat on the central sanitary commission and the board of health, and from 1849 he presided over the Strasbourg medical society. The Legion of Honor came in 1839, along with a title as assistant physician to the king.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashdod-assyrian:
Ashdod stood as the northernmost of the five royal cities of the Philistines. It lay two to three miles from the sea, about halfway between Gaza and Joppa. First Samuel names it first among the Philistine cities and tells how the captured Ark of the Lord was brought there as a trophy. Amos uses Ashdod to stand for all the Philistine cities together.

Judah's claim on the city, in Joshua, is judged merely theoretical. King Uzziah seized it for a time. Its speech is noted in Nehemiah, where the young generation of Jews began to adopt the talk of Ashdod. Judas Maccabaeus seems not to have taken the city itself, but Jonathan destroyed it and burned the old temple of Dagon. Pompey later restored its independence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-askanazy-max-20:
Max Askanazy, a German physician, was born at Stalluponen in East Prussia on February 24, 1865. He studied at the gymnasium and the university of Konigsberg and took his medical degree in 1890. That same year he joined the pathology institute of his own university as an assistant. In 1893 he was admitted to the medical faculty as a lecturer.

His essays treat clinical and post-mortem subjects. One of 1890 takes up nervous loss of hair. One of 1895 studies anemia caused by a tapeworm and the signs in the blood that foretell its course. One of 1897 measures the water in blood and serum across diseases of the circulation, the kidneys, anemia, and fever. The entry lists his papers with care and says little of the man beyond his posts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-auerbach-isaac-: Isaac b. Ḥayyim Auerbach was a Polish rabbi of the first half of the nineteenth century. He served first at Dobria, near Kalisz, and then at Plock. Later he followed his father Ḥayyim as rabbi of Lencziza, in the government of Warsaw. His book "Dibre Ḥayyim," Words of Life, came out at Breslau in 1852. It is a close, pilpul-style study of the Shulḥan 'Aruk and other codes. The volume also holds a treatise by his father and notes by his brother Eliezer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azevedo-moses-c:
Moses Cohen d'Azevedo was haham of London. He was born in Amsterdam about 1720 and died in 1784. He was a son of Daniel Cohen d'Azevedo. In 1761 he followed his father-in-law, Moses Gomez da Mesquitta, as head of the Spanish and Portuguese congregation of London.

Only two sermons of his are credited in print. One marked the accession of George the Third and was preached in December 1760, before his call to London. Both were given in Spanish. They were printed in 1776 with an English rendering, along with prayers for the success of British arms in a fast-day service of that year. His son Daniel served as cantor of the congregation from 1779 to 1812. Of the haham himself, the entry says, a portrait is the only relic left.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bacon-roger-231:
Roger Bacon was an English thinker and scholar of the thirteenth century, born at Ilchester about 1214 and dead about 1294. He studied at Oxford and Paris and became a Franciscan friar about 1250. His wide learning won him the title "doctor mirabilis," while his tools and trials made some suspect magic. His order barred his lectures and kept him under watch in Paris for ten years.

Pope Clement IV asked for his work in 1266, and Bacon then wrote the "Opus Majus," "Opus Minus," and "Opus Tertium" in about eighteen months. The entry stresses his early call to learn Hebrew. It says he urged study of the tongue long before Reuchlin, and that he spoke no ill word of the Jews in all his writing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bally-davicion-:
Davicion Bally was a Rumanian patriot born at Bucharest on Jan. 29, 1809. His family had served princes of Wallachia since his great-grandfather, a banker, helped Nicolas Mavrocordato to the throne in 1716. Bally lost his father at twelve, and a partner cheated the family of nearly all it had. From his father's library he taught himself Rumanian, Greek, French, Italian, German, and Hebrew.

Bally saved Russian stores at Zimnicea in 1829 and won the Order of St. Anne from Czar Nicholas I. He served ten years as cashier of the Bucharest police, unpaid, and helped fund the city's first fire brigade. In 1848 he joined the Revolution and, by declaring it early, saved its leaders from execution. Later he fought a venomous pamphlet against the Jews in 1858 and reformed his Sephardic community's schools and charities. Bitter at fresh persecutions, he left for Jerusalem in August 1882.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baptista-giovan:
Giovanni Salomo Romano Eliano Baptista was a baptized Jew and church writer, born at Alexandria, Egypt. He died in Rome on March 3, 1589. He was a grandson of Elijah Levita, the famed Hebrew grammarian. He traveled widely, knew Latin, Spanish, and Turkish, and taught Hebrew and Arabic in Rome. His elder brother had turned Christian before him and become a priest.

Baptista went to Venice to rebuke that brother and win him back. Instead, he himself converted, declaring himself a Christian in 1551 under the name Giovanni Baptista. He became a Jesuit and wrote a catechism in Hebrew and Arabic. Then he turned on his former people. With two other converts he asked Pope Julius III. to destroy the Talmud as a danger to Christianity. The bull of Aug. 12, 1553 followed, and on Sept. 9, 1553, Talmudic and other Hebrew books were burned in Rome and many Italian cities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bashemath-basma:
Bashemath appears in Genesis under two different family links, and the entry sets both side by side. In one account she is a wife of Esau and daughter of Elon the Hittite. In another list the wife from Elon is called Adah, and Bashemath is a daughter of Ishmael.

The entry notes that the Samaritan text avoids the clash by using the name Mahalath in the second list. It adds a second Bashemath, a daughter of Solomon. She was the wife of Ahimaaz, a royal officer in Naphtali. The entry treats the two accounts as a problem in the text, not as proof of two separate wives.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beck-miksa-de-m:
Miksa Beck was a Hungarian financier born at Bács-Madaras in 1838. His family moved to Budapest in his childhood, and he trained there for business. In 1864 he managed a banking house, and in 1870 he became chief director of a discount bank.

Under Beck's careful lead that bank grew into one of Hungary's most important houses. When a new cabinet took power in 1899, he rose to the bank's presidency. He received the Order of the Iron Crown in 1894 and a noble title the same year. The banking house he first managed, from 1864, was that of J. J. Cohen in the capital.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belin-elijah-be: Elijah ben Moses Belin, the second of that name here, was a German Talmudist who died at Worms on Feb. 26, 1587. He took an active part in the affairs of the Jewish community of that city during his life. A manuscript copy survives of a debate he held in question and answer form with a fellow Worms scholar. That dispute dates from the year 1578 and is set down in part in the Jewish German tongue of the day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benveniste-ben-: Benveniste ben Jacob was one of the officers of the Biḳḳur Ḥolim society of the Spanish synagogue in Venice. He served toward the end of the seventeenth century and was of Spanish descent. His name stands with two others in a set of prayers for the sick and dying used by that society, printed at Venice in 1685. The entry corrects one writer who wrongly gave Benveniste a share in writing those prayers, and points to a catalogue entry for the right account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernard-of-clai:
Bernard of Clairvaux, known as St. Bernard, was a church father born in 1091 near Dijon, in France. He died at Clairvaux on Aug. 20, 1153. A Cistercian monk made abbot, he founded a branch order in his name with 160 houses in his lifetime. He preached the second crusade across France and Germany.

That preaching sparked massacres of Jews in the Rhine valley, and Bernard protested in strong letters. Jews, he held, must not be harmed or destroyed, since they stand as living signs of the Passion. His line set church policy on the Jews for ages after.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beth-peor-3213: Beth-Peor was a place in the Jordan valley. Joshua apportions it to the Reubenites. Deuteronomy sets Israel opposite it. There the Deuteronomic law was promulgated. Hosea's Baal-peor probably means the same place. Eusebius placed it 6 Roman miles from Livias. He set it near Mount Peor. Jerome gave a different distance from Heshbon. No matching site has yet been found. Talmudic references show the place outlived the Second Temple.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-binnui-3313: Binnui is a name borne by several men in Scripture. The entry lists five of them in order. The first was a Levite named in Ezra. The second had taken a foreign wife. A third appears in the same Ezra list. The fourth was Henadad's son. He built part of Jerusalem's wall. He also sealed Nehemiah's covenant. The fifth headed a family returning with Zerubbabel. The entry gives no further detail on any of them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloomfield-zeis: Fanny Bloomfield-Zeisler was an American pianist. She was Maurice Bloomfield's younger sister. She was born at Bielitz on July 16, 1866. Her family settled in Chicago in 1868. Ziehn and Wolfsohn first taught her piano. At ten she played a public concert. At twelve she went to Vienna for Leschetizky. Five years of study followed there. From 1883 to 1893 she toured America widely. She played with all its leading orchestras. In 1893 she triumphed across Europe. Fifty concerts filled her 1895-96 American season.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bondi-mordecai-: Mordecai Marcus Bondi was a German author who lived at Dresden in the first quarter of the nineteenth century. With his brother Simon he wrote Or Ester. That book is a Hebrew dictionary of the Latin words found in the Talmud, Targumim, and Midrashim. Some of his essays also survive in the periodical Jedidja. The entry gives no birth or death dates for him. It lists only those works and the journal pieces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bracelets-3613:
Bracelets are ornaments in ring form for the arm. Hebrews wore them, as did all ancient peoples. Besides adornment, they were worn as guards against demons, much like earrings and amulets.

Women commonly wore bracelets, but men of rank wore them too. Bible passages on war spoil and on Saul's death show that use. Both arms might carry them, and some were coiled like a snake. Three Hebrew words for bracelet occur in the Bible. One seems to mark the wrist band, another the upper arm band. A fourth word may mean small golden balls strung together, worn around the wrist by Arabs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brill-jehiel-37:
Jehiel Brill was a Russian journalist who died in London on Nov. 12, 1886. Sources split on his birth: Zeitlin gives Tultschin in 1836, Fuenn gives British India. He grew up in Jerusalem on strict Orthodox training.

In 1863 Brill founded the Hebrew monthly Ha-Lebanon in Jerusalem. Turkish rulers suppressed it after twelve numbers came out. He revived it in Paris, then in Mayence, where it ran from 1872 to 1881. The paper became the voice of ultra-conservative Jews in those years. Lack of Orthodox support killed it a third time in the end. In 1882 he led eleven farmers from Russia to Palestine for new colonies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bulah-raphael-m: Raphael Moses de Bulah, son of Joseph, was a Palestinian Talmudist and rabbi. He died at Jerusalem on March 23, 1773, where he had served as rabbi and run a Talmudic school. His book on divorce law appeared at Constantinople in 1767. An earlier work of homiletic essays covered the first two books of the Pentateuch. It was printed in 1752. A third work treated the method of the Talmud and again divorce law. The entry gives no birth date or early life for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calatayud-calat:
Calatayud was a city of Aragon with a large Jewish community under Abd al-Rahman the third. A marble tombstone found in 1882 honors a Samuel who died Oct. 9, 919.
