Difference-in-differences models covered over forty thousand participants, about fifteen percent exposed to the program. Exposure cut poverty vulnerability by about three percent and slowed health deterioration. Inpatient use rose about nine percent and out-of-pocket costs fell sharply for both outpatient and inpatient care. Mediation ran through physical examinations and inpatient care. The authors read the extra utilization as released pent-up demand rather than moral hazard.
pmc-10716113:
Urooba Sehar and seven co-authors build a twin-way feel reader for Urdu posts that joins rule flow with a deep net. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. Firms mine posts for views, but word pair counts run weak in real use. A fresh Urdu set was built from video site talks and takes on films, rule, and goods.

Set rules fire feel flow from word to thought by Urdu word links where they can. Where no rule fires, a deep net takes the line. Tests beat five known ways by a span of six to seven marks on the Urdu set.
pmc-10716313:
Saeid Esmaeilian leads a nine-author team reviewing methanol poisoning cases from Iran's pandemic years, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. The aim was to weigh how often brain scans show damage in these patients, and to propose a rule for which patients should be scanned first.

The records covered 306 confirmed patients at two hospitals. Most were men, at about thirty-two years of age on mean. The commonest scan findings were darkened putamen tissue, cerebellar changes, and diffuse brain swelling. Bleeding in the brain was rarer. The patterns in the images tracked blood acidity and consciousness level. They also tracked kidney failure and a range of lab values. The team puts forth criteria for prioritizing scans when patients flood in.
pmc-10716513:
Giorgia Bussu and co-authors test, in a 2023 study, how a burst of sound shifts where babies look next, most of all to faces. Eye tracking let the team watch gaze in a free search task. Babies aged 5 and 10 months heard cues that split by loudness and by type, social or not. Pupil size tracked their arousal, the body's alert state. The team then read how fast each baby turned to a face, and how that changed with age and with the cue just heard.

Loud cues stretched pupils more than soft ones; sound type did not. Older babies turned faster and picked faces more. After loud sounds, the face bias faded fast with repeat views. Pupil size at base and pupil growth each linked to face picks in set ways. The finds back gain theories of arousal in early social sight.
pmc-10717913:
Yan Wang writes a 2023 editorial on how artificial intelligence is reshaping orthopedics, with a focus on progress in Asia. The piece surveys where smart tools now help bone and joint care, from the clinic to the operating room.

AI already assists with diagnosis, treatment planning, and surgical navigation in many hospitals. It also powers forecasts of patient outcomes and watchful follow-up after surgery. Wang highlights advanced work in China as a sign of the field's pace. The editorial weighs what hospitals must build, in data and skill, to use these tools well. It closes with expectations for the next wave of digital orthopedics.
pmc-10718413:
Feike Loots leads a large team in this 2023 study on spotting sepsis risk during a phone call. Out-of-hours GP services triage infection complaints by telephone, and missing early sepsis can be fatal while over-referring floods hospitals. The team linked routine databases for more than 155,000 patients and trained models on the triage information alone.

Age, a home visit rather than a clinic visit, signs of instability, and complaints like malaise, breathlessness, and fever were the strongest predictors. The best simple model discriminated well overall, and machine learning did no better. But a sepsis alert flagging everyone above one percent risk caught most events while being wrong far more often than right. Performance sagged exactly where events clustered, among home-visit patients. The authors conclude the signal is real but not yet sharp enough to guide individual decisions.
pmc-10719113:
Hanqing Liu and co-authors built a brain-wide map of chemical marks on DNA in single cells of the adult mouse. Their 2023 atlas draws on more than one hundred cut regions of the brain. Two lab methods gave both DNA marks and the folded shape of DNA in the same cells.

From hundreds of thousands of cell profiles, the team sorted cells into thousands of groups and hundreds of broader classes. They found millions of DNA stretches where the marks differ by cell type. Maps of where cells sit in the brain matched the mark patterns well. The work also ties folded DNA shape to gene use, and helps predict which gene forms a cell will make.
pmc-10719313:
Yu Muta and co-authors traced a fat-making pathway in 2023 that fuels an aggressive form of colon cancer. This form grows through the serrated route and responds poorly to current targeted drugs. The team found that loss of a protein pair in gut cells frees a switch called SREBP2. That switch ramps up cholesterol production inside the cells.

The extra cholesterol proved vital for early tissue change and for the most aggressive tumor cells, in both mice and human samples. The shift appeared even before tumors formed. Drugs that block cholesterol making hit these tumors hard. The authors propose such blocking as a way to prevent this cancer type.
pmc-10720313:
Gianluca Castelnuovo leads a large team behind a 2023 study plan, the DEMETRA trial, on a phone-based therapy for obesity. Diet and activity plans remain the first line of care, yet many patients drift away from them. A digital therapy aims to keep patients engaged and make care easier to reach.

The plan lays out a multi-center trial with two arms, one using the real app and one a placebo app, with patients kept unaware of which they hold. The app gives tailored support to boost sticking with the program. Weight loss and its upkeep are the key outcomes the trial will judge.
pmc-10720813:
Chuan'an Shen and co-authors describe a faster way to graft skin onto large burns, tested in a 2023 study. The old method lays tiny stamp-sized pieces of a patient's own skin and donor skin one by one, which takes very long. Their new method builds a large sheet of such pieces ahead of time, then lays the whole sheet at once.

The team used the sheet method in 21 operations on 11 patients with deep, wide burns. Grafting took about 0.4 minutes per 100 square centimeters, against about 7.5 minutes for the old way. The sheets took root about as well as hand-laid pieces, near 85 percent against 87 percent. All patients healed and went home, so the faster method opens large burns to a proven repair.
pmc-10725913:
Yi-Jing Cai and nine co-workers wrote a 2023 study on blood ammonia swings in patients with sudden worsening of hepatitis B liver disease. High ammonia drives brain fog and coma in liver failure. Records covered a few hundred patients at one center. Ammonia levels were tracked across the hospital stay.

About one in five died within four weeks. Peak ammonia ran far higher in patients who developed overt brain symptoms. It also ran higher in those who died. After adjusting for other factors, peak level still foresaw both outcomes. Peaks in the first three days were the most ominous. Patients whose ammonia fell within a week fared better.
pmc-10729013:
Ante-Testard and co-authors mapped how fairly HIV testing is spread across sub-Saharan Africa. They pooled household surveys from 25 countries between 2011 and 2019, covering nearly half a million people. They measured testing gaps between rich and poor at national and local levels, separately for women and men. They also checked whether testing levels matched local HIV prevalence.

Inequality varied widely in size and place. Hotspots of unfair access clustered in Western and Central Africa, with a few in the east and south. At the national level, testing matched prevalence everywhere, but at fine local scale the match vanished in about a third of country-sex groups. The authors say programs should be judged locally, not just nationally, so testing reaches the places where need and unfairness overlap.
pmc-10729113:
Laura Salonen, Kristina Alexanderson, and Kristin Farrants chart sick-leave and disability paths among Swedish office staff in a 2023 study. The team used national files for more than a million private-sector white-collar staff, tracked from 2012 to 2018. A sequence method grouped staff who shared like paths of leave days per year.

Five paths stood out. Near nine in ten staff took low or no leave at all. Small groups took leave for body ills, for mental ills, or moved to disability pay. Women, the less schooled, and low earners filled the leave paths more, while men and high earners filled the no-leave ones.
pmc-10731113:
Eva Wölfel and co-authors tested in 2023 whether the bone material of older men with type 2 diabetes is itself weaker, or only rarer. Diabetes raises fracture risk beyond what bone density explains, pointing at the material quality of bone. Most earlier work pressed spongy bone; this study took the dense cortical shell.

In a case-control design, cortical samples from men with and without diabetes were put through fracture resistance testing alongside a battery of matrix measures. The title carries the finding: where the material properties could not be told apart, fracture resistance matched too. The byline is long; the work is framed by its lead author. Readers get a clarifying negative for a real puzzle: in these men, the diabetes fracture risk did not hide in the cortical material itself.
pmc-10733813:
Kim and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-three on where deep brain stimulation acts to ease the slowness of Parkinson's disease. Slowness, or bradykinesia, blends three faults: movements that are small, that fade with repetition, and that lose rhythm. Knowing which fault lives where in the target nucleus could guide personalized therapy.

Fifteen patients did a hand grasping task with stimulation on and off while a motion sensor tracked amplitude and frequency. Raters scored severity blind to the setting. Maps of the stimulated tissue showed amplitude and frequency changes spread as a gradient, partly overlapping, partly distinct. Bigger amplitude gains tracked better clinical scores for both hands. Connectivity maps from a standard brain atlas linked each component to its own network.
pmc-10733913:
Selin Karadirek, a geologist, studied coal from the Soma basin in western Turkey to learn how it formed. Three seams were tested, an upper, a middle, and a lower one. Tests covered the carbon share of each seam, heat-based checks, chemical traces from old life, and the plant parts seen under a scope. Carbon isotope data added a further clue about the source plants and the wetness of the old swamp.

All three seams held type III kerogen, the plant-rich kind that tends to yield gas more than oil. Heat and chemical signs show the coal is not yet mature and sits at sub-bituminous rank. The plant parts were mostly huminite, with small shares of two other groups. The coal is gas-prone but has not reached the heat stage where gas starts to form in real amounts.
pmc-10734013:
Burning methane in pure oxygen, diluted with carbon dioxide, is a route to power with easier carbon capture, but keeping the flame stable is tricky. Mingjian Liao and four co-authors test a design tweak in this 2023 paper. The burner, packed with porous material that soaks up heat, widens along its length.

Computer models of the two-layer burner compared the widening design with a straight tube. The widening shape stretched the stable burning range more than fourfold. Its solid body ran cooler, and its flame sat about two hundred degrees lower, with a small loss in heat recycling efficiency. Carbon monoxide output rose slightly at low power but fell below the straight design at high power. Wall heat loss did not erase the stability gain.
pmc-10734213:
Yuhang Wang and co-authors tracked a night-time air chemical that helps build harmful particles, in a 2023 study. The chemical, the nitrate radical, forms after dark from nitrogen dioxide and ozone. Cleanup drives have cut nitrogen oxides hard, yet an earlier study saw the radical's production rise in China. The team re-checked summer data from 2014 to 2022.

Production did not rise after all, they find, because the balance between the two parent gases kept shifting. Older Beijing readings from 2007, though, warn of a possible surge: as city emissions fall, night air could suddenly favor the radical. The work flags a trap inside well-meant cleanup.
pmc-10735513:
Xiaoling Li, writing alone in 2023, describes research on how host and microbe metabolism interact in disease and aging. Metabolism is a key channel through which the environment, including diet and lifestyle, shapes cell function. When metabolic balance is disturbed, diseases follow and aging speeds up.

The work focuses on a nutrient-sensing pathway built around NAD+ and SIRT1, a protein that depends on it. The abstract outlines a research program rather than a single experiment. Understanding this pathway could reveal how everyday exposures translate into the biology of aging and metabolic disease.
pmc-10735613:
Emily Morris and co-authors asked in 2023 how much of the Black-White memory gap in older Americans runs through stress at three levels of life. Their sample held nearly seventeen thousand adults from a national aging study, followed for six years of memory tests. Stress was read as daily discrimination, neighborhood disorder, and felt standing in society.

Black adults reported more of all three stressors than White adults. Each stressor, on its own, carried part of the link between race and lower starting memory. Together they explained about a tenth of the gap. The groups declined at the same pace afterward. The authors frame the stressors as marks of structural racism that raise dementia risk. They call for work on what shields memory under such strain.
pmc-10735813:
A case study from 2023 looks at help for family caregivers of older patients with dementia in Shanghai, China. In China, few community services exist for such families, so doctors in clinics and hospitals often run teaching programs. Staff at the largest mental health center in Shanghai built one such program and tested its early effects.

Forty caregivers were asked what they lacked, and most said they knew too little about care and treatment. The team then set up weekly talks of ninety minutes, with up to six caregivers at a time. Topics ran from diagnosis and treatment to self care, giving families skills and support close to the clinic.
pmc-10736013:
Andrew Jopson, Chanee Fabius, and Jennifer Wolff study older adults who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid, in work published in two thousand twenty-three. They compare counties with and without managed long-term care. Medicaid pays for much of the help that lets these adults stay at home.

Nearly half of the states have shifted that help into managed plans, hoping for better coordination and fewer needless hospital visits. The authors use a national survey from two thousand fifteen, linked to where each person lived. They focus on four hundred sixty-two people who needed help with daily tasks. They compare health, background, and care experiences across the two kinds of counties. The work fills a gap, since no earlier study had drawn this contrast.
pmc-10736113:
Rafael Samper-Ternent and Lee Jennings introduce a conference panel on priorities based care in a 2023 abstract. Older adults often juggle several long term conditions at once. Care works better when it starts from what each person values most. Hard life experiences shape those values for vulnerable groups in particular.

Four talks make up the panel session described here. One lays out the approach and its gains for patients and families. Another covers rollout inside the veterans health system. Two more cover adapting the approach for Black and Hispanic older adults.
pmc-10736313:
Lillian Hung and co-authors lived alongside older adults in 2023 to learn what it means to share a home with care robots. Two machines were studied: Labrador, a delivery robot that helps with drugs, meals, laundry, and cleaning, and Double, a screen on wheels for video visits. The team used actor-network theory, which treats people, tools, and rooms as linked actors. Talks and field notes were read for themes.

Three themes stood out: the bond with the robot, the robot's own sway, and hard moral points. Life with the machines proved a round of talks and tweaks among users, kin, staff, and the rooms. Far from cold care, the robots sparked fresh kinds of ties, though strain points stayed.
pmc-10736613:
Darlingtina Esiaka, Candidus Nwakasi, and Runcie Chidebe studied cancer risk habits in older Nigerian men in a 2023 paper. Cancer cases and deaths grow in Nigeria, and men are often found at a late, aggressive stage. Risky habits and skipped early checks drive much of that lateness.

The team asked how social conditions, such as schooling, work, and income, shape those habits. They surveyed older men on their traits, checks, and daily risk acts. The links they found help explain why gaps in outcomes persist in Nigeria and the wider region. The work points to where outreach and screening drives should aim first.
pmc-10736713:
Alisa Johnson and co-authors probe in 2023 whether muscle quality helps explain why some older adults with knee osteoarthritis move worse than others. Knee arthritis is a top cause of lost mobility, yet its grip on daily function varies widely by person. Muscle quality, how strong and clean the muscle is rather than just how big, is a suspect gaining ground in aging research.

Their pilot enrolled adults over fifty who met clinical signs of painful knee arthritis. Movement was scored with a short standard battery of tasks. Muscle quality came from ultrasound brightness of the thigh muscle and from strength scaled to body mass. Scores on the movement battery tied to pain, strength, and muscle quality alike. In fitted models, muscle measures explained a large extra share of movement scores beyond pain and strength, after age, sex, and body size were held aside.
pmc-10737013:
Julian Montoro-Rodriguez and Bert Hayslip study what leads grandchildren raised by grandparents to receive mental health care, and what that care does for the grandparents. Published in 2023, the study draws on 239 grandparent caregivers, about a third of whose grandchildren were in counseling. Prior work put service use low among such children, with behavior problems and diagnoses the strongest drivers.

A structural model framed by the Pearlin stress outcome paradigm fit the data well. The child's use of counseling shaped both the grandparent's well-being and the quality of the pair's relationship. The paths ran through different coping resources, notably the grandparent's resilience and social support. Care for the child, the authors imply, is also care for the caregiver.
pmc-10737113:
Lisha Lin and co-authors test blood methylation scores against heart risk factors in older adults, in work from 2023. Methylation marks on DNA can be summed into risk scores for traits like blood pressure. Whether those scores behave the same across ages and habits was unclear.

Scores were built for eight risk factors from past genome-wide studies. Blood data came from nearly four thousand participants in a national aging study, mean age near seventy. Each score tracked its matching risk factor strongly after adjustments. Some links shifted with age, gender, or alcohol use, though. Body mass links grew steeper where scores ran high. The scores may aid early prevention if further validated.
pmc-10737213:
Enna Chen, Claire Growney, and Laura Carstensen report a 2023 study on how thoughts about time shape feelings in daily life. Their work builds on a theory that says goals shift as people feel their time ahead grow short. Older adults, in that view, focus more on the present and on close ties.

The team tracked 190 people aged 18 to 94 for seven days. Phones prompted them five times a day to note their time focus and their mood. Thinking of the past went with worse mood, and thinking of the present went with better mood. Both links were weaker for older adults than for younger ones.
pmc-10737413:
Ad Maulod, Malcolm Ravindran, and Angelique Chan explore a neglected face of loneliness in old age: feeling unneeded, in a 2023 study. Interviews with 44 older Singaporeans traced loneliness across family, friends, work, and community life. Standard accounts stress missing company or feeling left out, but these elders kept returning to lost usefulness.

Being unneeded tied to lost roles, shrinking control, poor health, and dark views of aging itself. In Singapore it also rubs against a merit ethic that ties worth to striving, an idea the state has long promoted. The authors argue that policies against loneliness must restore roles and recognition, not just contact.
pmc-10737513:
Courtney Polenick and co-authors study daily events and mood in couples living with early stage dementia in this 2023 paper. Spouses shape each other well being in later life. Little was known about day to day links in couples where one partner has dementia. The study followed 36 married couples.

Both partners gave brief phone reports each morning and evening for seven days. Reports covered good and bad events that day and current mood. Models separated each person own effect from the partner effect, while accounting for the prior day. More bad events that day meant worse mood for both partners. A partner bad day also raised negative mood the next day. Good events showed their own links to positive mood.
pmc-10738013:
Naheem Noah and Sanchari Das present a 2023 study of safety and privacy on dating apps for older adults. Such apps are now a common way to meet partners, even past age 65. Use means sharing personal data, and older users are prime targets for online attacks.

The authors first scanned 38 past papers on dating app safety. None zeroed in on older adults and dating apps at once. They then audited ten big apps, from Tinder and Bumble to senior aimed services. The audit found weak data habits that put user privacy at risk, with older adults most exposed. The paper ends with clear steps apps should take to guard users.
pmc-10738213:
Alaine Murawski and co-authors build an AI training program to teach negotiation to family caregivers, in a 2023 paper. Caregivers of people with dementia face frequent conflicts as they move through the health system, yet they get little training to settle disputes. The program is called NegotiAge.

Experts made short videos on negotiation skills, and caregivers wrote dialogue from real conflicts. Computer experts fed that dialogue into a platform that builds avatar partners, such as a sibling, an older adult, or a doctor. Caregivers practice in real time and get instant feedback on their tactics. A pilot with twelve caregivers tested the setup and its training flow.
pmc-10738313:
Katie Buys and co-authors examine, in a 2023 study, how social conditions shape depression in older Alabamians, with race-based discrimination under the spotlight. One thousand adults aged sixty-five and over, balanced by race, sex, and rural or urban home, took part in the UAB Study of Aging.

The team separated a verified depression diagnosis from day-to-day depressive symptoms. Experiencing racial discrimination more than doubled the odds of a diagnosis, independent of race and other factors. Life-space mobility and race also predicted diagnosis. Symptoms tracked fear of crime, money strain, and social support instead. The split shows discrimination leaves a clinical mark beyond daily mood.
pmc-10738413:
Ana Alfaro and co-authors measure how often frailty and thinking problems overlap in older adults on dialysis. Their 2023 study draws a diverse sample from a wider project on mind, mood, and mobility. Dialysis patients face high risk on both fronts, yet the overlap was little mapped.

Thirty-five people took part, with an average age near seventy-four. About one fifth spoke Spanish, and the group spanned Asian, Black, and Hispanic backgrounds. Eighty-three percent scored in the impaired range on a standard thinking test. Eighty-six percent were frail or nearly so. Most, sixty-nine percent, carried both burdens at once. The authors urge care plans that treat the pair together, above all for underserved groups.
pmc-10738513:
Maritza Dowling and co-authors study in 2023 how belly fat paths and hormone care act on mind scores in women just past menopause. Early hormone care may blunt some fat linked harms to the brain. The team tests if fat paths split women in a way that tracks mind scores.

Data come from a trial that gave hormone pills, a skin patch form, or a dummy for four years. Two fat paths turned up: a low group that held flat, and a high group that fell after care. The high group scored low on most mind tests at four years and a decade on.
pmc-10738613:
Bilalaga and Almidani studied lung disease, caregiving, and well-being in older United States adults in twenty twenty-three. They used a national sample of adults aged sixty-five and over from the twenty twenty-one National Health and Aging Trends Study. Lung disease meant a reported diagnosis of emphysema, asthma, or chronic bronchitis.

Depression and anxiety came from a standard four-item scale, and social isolation from living situation, contact, and activity answers. Adults with lung disease had notably more depressive symptoms than those without. Anxiety and isolation rates did not differ clearly. Caregivers of adults with lung disease also showed more depressive symptoms, again without clear anxiety or isolation gaps. The authors call for strategies to support the mental health of both groups.
pmc-10739213:
Kat Coschigano and co-authors chart in 2023 who stood as named stand ins for folk in a big blood force trial, and if those stand ins stayed the course. Mind tests in such trials need a close voice who knows the per son's path. Their tales guard a fair read of fade or loss.

Of over nine thou sand in the trial, about eight in ten named such a voice at the start. Wed mates led at half, then grown kids, sibs, kin, and non kin. Nine in ten kept the same voice to the last meet, some five years on. Reach rates by group fill the read.
pmc-10739413:
Caitlan Tighe, Deirdre Quinn, Karley Atchison, and Rachel Bachrach track poor sleep and risky drinking among older women veterans in two thousand twenty-three. Women who served in the military carry high rates of health and mental health strain. Both poor sleep and risky drinking were thought to have risen during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Health record data covered near two hundred forty thousand women aged fifty and older, from two thousand eighteen to two thousand twenty-two. Sleep problem rates rose across age groups, with the highest rates in the fifty to fifty-nine band. Risky drinking followed a like pattern, dipping in some years and rising again by two thousand twenty-one. Few women showed both problems in the same year.
pmc-10739513:
Thomas Fuller-Rowell and co-authors published this 2023 study on whether rich states soften the health shadow of a poor childhood. Parental education predicts adult functional limitations, but whether the surrounding economy bends that gradient was unclear. The team merged the Midlife in the United States study, 10,685 adults, with a century of state economic data. Each person was matched to the mean income of their state during childhood, early adulthood, and prime working years.

In richer states the gradient flattened at every life stage: parental education predicted limitations less strongly. The flattening during prime working years was stronger still for women than for men. The authors read place as a lifelong ingredient in the childhood effect, not just a backdrop, with policy implications for where health inequality is manufactured.
pmc-10740313:
Daniel Boctor and co-authors report a heart valve infection that hid behind negative blood cultures, in this 2023 case report. The culprit bacterium grows slowly and causes a creeping illness. Delay in spotting it let the infection damage the heart over time.

A fifty-one-year-old man arrived with stroke signs. Scans traced the source to his heart, and antibody tests named the bacterium. By then, chronic heart failure had driven severe pressure in his lung arteries. That complication forced a long delay before valve repair surgery. The authors stress that this infection is under-recognized and needs nuanced, patient care.
pmc-10740813:
Vasconcelos and co-authors test whether dietary tryptophan can ease stress in juvenile meagre. Fish in aquaculture face many stressors, and this amino acid is known to soften stress responses. For fifty-six days, the juveniles ate feeds holding half a percent, six-tenths of a percent, or eight-tenths of a percent of it. The team measured growth, blood markers around a brief air exposure stress test, and behavior in anxiety-linked tests.

Survival, growth, and body makeup stayed much the same across the diets. Blood sugar rose after stress in all groups, and one blood marker dipped most in the lowest dose group. The clearest effect was behavioral: in a new tank test, fish on the highest dose froze far less often, signaling lower anxiety. The authors judge tryptophan, especially at the higher dose, a mild but real stress buffer worth further study.
pmc-10742313:
Radiation can change how a cell lives and divides, and those changes differ from cell to cell. Sarah Rudigkeit and Judith Reindl present CeCILE 2.0, a deep learning program that watches single cells in live phase-contrast videos. It finds each cell, sorts it by type, and follows it across generations of division, a volume of tracking no human could score by hand.

From those tracks the program reads out viability, cell cycle progress, and survival, and shows how X-ray exposure shifts each one. It also picks out radiation-specific faults that appear during division. The authors say this is the first tool with a fully joined workflow covering single cells and cell groups together. They offer it as a way to turn mountains of microscope video into firm numbers about how cells answer stress.
pmc-10742513:
Antonio Gidaro and co-authors probe if blood bit sheds tie to age and swell marks in a 2023 pilot study. The sheds come off plate bits and play in clot and swell acts in the body. Past work left their ties to plain marks in sound folk dim and thin.

Sound grown folk join the pilot by free will for the blood draws at hand. Shed counts are set next to a wide list of swell and clot marks. Age is one more mark in the checks run by the team.
pmc-10742713:
Race Creeden and co-authors report a pilot whose brief re-exposure to cabin fumes ended his flying career after he had fully recovered from a first episode. Their 2023 case report concerns aerotoxic syndrome, illness blamed on oil combustion products leaking into aircraft bleed air. The condition is rarely recognized and poorly defined, with its mechanism unsettled.

The 42-year-old pilot first developed duty-limiting symptoms after a fume event, recovered completely, then relapsed on re-exposure and stayed unwell. Judged at risk of sudden incapacitation if exposed again, he was declared medically unqualified for commercial flying, and a disability determination followed. The authors urge clinicians to consider the syndrome in aircrew with odd, episodic thinking or nerve symptoms. Each documented case, they argue, sharpens a fuzzy diagnosis.
pmc-10742813:
Shuqi Xiao, Zhiming Yuan, Yi Huang, and Inês Bártolo review nitric oxide as a candidate treatment for COVID-19. Their review was published in twenty twenty-three. The gas molecule is known to fight microbes and calm inflammation, and it plays a key role in lung blood flow.

The pandemic virus can fail several organs, above all the lungs. The review first sums up how the virus infects, harms, and dodges immunity. It then lays out the case for nitric oxide: direct antiviral action plus anti-inflammatory effects that could slow spread of damage in the body. Limits of the approach are noted as well. The authors present inhaled or delivered nitric oxide as a plausible add-on while specific cures were scarce.
pmc-10743013:
Salmon Likoko and co-authors published a 2023 study of grandparents in South Africa who raise children who have lost both parents. Such caregiving is a large and growing fact of life in the country. It puts the health of the older caregivers at risk.

The team used wave five of a national income dynamics survey. Most caregivers in the sample were aged between twenty-four and thirty-four, and most were Black Africans with a secondary education. Six in ten reported health challenges, with headaches the most common in the past month. Age drove the risk strongly. Caregivers in their late fifties to mid-sixties were nearly nine times as likely to report challenges as the youngest group. Caregivers who were not Black African reported challenges less often. The study maps what puts the health of these caregivers at risk.
pmc-10743113:
Wenzhe Tang and co-authors offer a way to grade the control screens of nuclear power plants in a 2023 paper. Operators read these screens to make calls that carry real risk. Yet screen reviews often ignore how well operators decide, come late in design, and cannot scale to many screens.

Their method uses image entropy, a measure of how much information a picture packs, to score a screen by the load it puts on decisions. It grows out of the team's earlier work on information and choice. They checked the scores against a hands-on trial method and found the cheap method held up. The result is a standard yardstick usable early, late, and across whole fleets of screens.
pmc-10743413:
Senka Blažetić and co-authors examined how mutations in sugar tagging enzymes change calming interneurons in mouse brains, in work published in 2023. The catalog adds one more author than the head byline, so team framing is used. The enzymes finish two major brain gangliosides, and their loss causes cognitive and motor disorders in people.

Mice missing one enzyme showed fewer of all three calcium binding interneuron types across every cortex region checked. The hippocampus and striatum were also examined, along with mice missing a sister enzyme or both. Staining for four markers mapped the cells. The authors tie the missing gangliosides to how these interneurons migrate and mature.
pmc-10744013:
Malena Cohen-Cymberknoh and co-authors track sleep over time in a 2023 study on two lung diseases. Both cystic fibrosis and a related airway disease disturb sleep and lower quality of life for children and adults. Less was known about how sleep complaints change over years, or what new gene based drugs do to sleep.

Sixty seven patients, about half of them children, filled in sleep and life quality surveys at the start and again after four years. Clinic records added health data for each person. The team looked for links between sleep, daily life quality, and health measures, giving families a longer view of sleep in these diseases.
pmc-10744513:
Lizomar Pereira and co-authors propose a bioelectric repair treatment for alcoholic cirrhosis of the liver, in work from twenty twenty-three. Alcoholic liver disease burdens disadvantaged groups heavily worldwide. Drug options for the cirrhosis stage remain limited in effect. The liver regrows well, and that power ties to its bioelectric state. A radio electric asymmetric conveyer aims to restore disrupted cell fields.

Its tissue optimisation reparative protocol targets injured tissue healing speed. The study sets out to test effects on liver function and outcomes. Mechanisms of liver self-repair frame the treatment rationale throughout. Genetic, epigenetic, and environmental drivers of the disease are reviewed. Success would ease both personal and societal costs of cirrhosis. The work positions the device as a candidate worth clinical proof.
pmc-10744813:
Antonio Garcia-Gonzalez and co-authors surveyed in 2023 how fatigue crack growth models handle the small zone of yielded metal at a crack's tip. That plastic zone governs how fast a crack advances under repeated loading. So a model that treats it badly mispredicts the life of aircraft parts, bridges, and pressure vessels. The review set out to compare the ways research staff have woven crack tip plasticity into their growth laws.

The emphasis falls on numeric models, with careful methods looked at beside and test work acknowledged as the needed partner rather than the focus. Each methodology is weighed for its edges and limitations. The authors close by mapping the synergies and the gaps between theory, test, and model. Their aim is to leave model builders with a clear view. That view shows which plasticity treatments are mature and which remain open problems.
pmc-10745913:
Foster and co-authors published a 2023 review of how tuberculosis is diagnosed in children from Papua New Guinea who reach clinics in Australia's Torres Strait Islands. Childhood TB is notoriously hard to confirm: children rarely produce good sputum, and tests miss many cases. Remote clinics lean on scoring systems and desk guides instead. The team audited real practice against those tools.

They reviewed children with suspected TB seen between 2016 and 2019. Sixty-six children qualified, and only seven had bacteria-confirmed disease. Over half were under five years old. The authors compared three diagnostic algorithms, an older score, an aid group's desk guide, and a new World Health Organization algorithm, against what clinicians actually did. The comparison exposes where each rule helps or misleads in a remote setting. The review aims at safer, more consistent decisions for a vulnerable group of young patients.
pmc-10746013:
Wenzhen Wang, Yan Zhu, and co-authors make a three part powder with a simple boil back method and test it on dye waste, in a 2023 study. The powder mixes silver, bismuth, and sulfur. It draws much light, which suits sun driven clean up and light tools.

Best purity came at one set mix of raw parts and one set heat. The grains were small, held heat well, and soaked up light from near ultraviolet to near infrared. In blue dye tests, the powder broke down more than half the dye in the set time. The rate was slow, but the path is cheap and green.
pmc-10746413:
Birhanu Berhe and co-authors develop in 2023 a tissue culture recipe to multiply an endangered mountain aloe. Aloe monticola survives as a refugee on high ground and needs help to persist. The team grew shoot tips in standard nutrient media spiked with growth regulators at several doses.

Nearly all explants took hold. Media with mid-to-high doses of one regulator plus a rooting partner gave the best shooting, and rooting mixes performed best at similar pairings. Plantlets moved to greenhouse, shade, and open sun in three soils survived at ninety to ninety-eight percent. The protocol offers a conservation tool for the species.
pmc-10746513:
Liu and four co-authors tested icariin in twenty twenty-three on human dental pulp cells under inflammation. Dental pulp is the soft tissue inside a tooth, and its inflammation, called pulpitis, needs treatments that calm swelling and rebuild dentine. Icariin is a plant compound studied for such effects.

The team exposed the cells to a bacterial toxin that triggers inflammation. Icariin lowered key inflammation markers and blocked two signaling cascades that drive them. It also raised genes and proteins tied to dentine formation and blood vessel growth. Treated cells showed more mineral deposits, a sign of hard tissue building. The authors suggest icariin may serve in regenerative pulp therapy, though their tests were in lab dishes only.
pmc-10747513:
Roberto Silva-Velasco and four co-authors pin down which receptors drive blood pressure shifts in rats in a 2023 paper. A stable ADP-like drug can widen or narrow blood vessels. It acts through a family of receptors called P2Y receptors. Which members of that family do the work was unknown.

The team tested 120 rats in four setups, with and without brain control paths. Blocker drugs each shut off one receptor type for fair tests. The fast drop in pressure came from one receptor type alone, P2Y1. The later rise in pressure drew on three receptor types. Those were P2Y1, P2Y12, and P2Y13 acting at the body edge. The work maps drug action for future heart research.
pmc-10747913:
Austin Craig and co-authors prepare radioactive tracers that light up tumours on scans by homing to a protein on cancer-supporting cells, in a 2023 paper. The protein, fibroblast activation protein, marks the scaffolding cells that many tumours recruit. A tracer carrying fluorine-18 can reveal those cells in a PET scan, aiding early detection. The team built two tracer candidates around a sulfur-based exchange trick for attaching the radioactive atom.

Both compounds blocked the target protein strongly in lab tests, at very low doses. The exchange reaction then fitted them with fluorine-18 in a form ready for imaging work. The authors frame the chemistry as a practical route to this tracer family. Such scans could one day map the tumour's support tissue, not just the cancer cells, when doctors plan treatment.
pmc-10748313:
Renate Teterovska and co-authors test wild Latvian plants in 2023 for compounds that fight cell damage. Folk records name five local plants rich in such compounds, used in past care for many ills. The team made extracts with two solvents and dried them for lab work.

Full counts of three compound classes were run, with a fine method naming the parts. One herb and one leaf extract led on flavonoids; oak bark led on tannins and phenolic acids, they report. Two wormwood kin held the least. Acetone pulled more of every class than alcohol did, and scored better on the damage-fighting test. All plants held one shared acid tied to the benefit. Solvent choice, it turns out, shapes the medicine as much as the plant.
pmc-10749313:
Alicja Węgrzyn wrote an editorial in two thousand twenty-three introducing a collection on phage therapy for infections in animals and humans. Phages are viruses that multiply inside bacteria and can kill them. As more bacteria resist antibiotics, this old idea has drawn fresh interest as a possible treatment.

The editorial is candid about the gaps. Despite years of study, phage therapy stays mostly at the lab or experimental stage, and its safety and power at large scale remain in doubt. Many reports used few strains and measured few outcomes. The author calls for fuller studies of how phages and bacteria interact inside real hosts. The piece frames the papers gathered in the collection.
pmc-10749413:
Maryam Alsadat Hejazi and co-authors built bendy brain electrodes from graphene fibers thinner than hairs, in a 2023 study. Electrode arrays that sit in the brain can read and nudge its activity, but stiff metal hurts soft tissue. Graphene brings conductivity, flexibility, and body-friendliness. The team spun graphene fibers ten to fifty micrometers wide, mounted ten of them on a custom circuit board, and coated them for insulation, leaving the tips bare.

Microscope images checked the fiber structure, and electrical tests measured each channel's resistance to signal flow. The spacing between fibers was one hundred fifty micrometers. The method can yield arrays of any fiber size and channel count, the authors say. They pitch the soft arrays as gentler tools for neuroscience and future medical devices, where rigid probes risk damage.
pmc-10750113:
Hitoshi Soyama and co-authors X-ray a swirling bubble cloud inside a Venturi tube in a 2023 study. Cavitation, the birth and collapse of vapor bubbles in fast liquid, powers chemical reactors and water treatment. One form, vortex cavitation, glows faintly as it collapses, and the glow tracks the number and size of its bubbles; everyone assumed those bubbles were tiny spheres.

High-speed X-ray imaging at two great light sources, in Japan and Europe, looked inside the opaque flow directly. The bubbles were not spheres at all but angular, faceted shapes, a geometry that changes how their collapse pressure fields form. The team also clocked the swirl speed at the vortex surface against the classic Rankine vortex model. The finding rewrites the mental picture engineers use when they design for, or against, this useful violence.
pmc-10751313:
Pragya Gupta and a large team of colleagues present SNAPseq, a single-test sequencing assay for the two great inherited blood disorders, beta-thalassemia and sickle cell disease. The standard genetic test reads the beta-globin gene slowly, amplicon by amplicon. Their method amplifies the whole gene at once from a cheek swab or finger-prick blood, no DNA extraction needed.

The assay matched the gold standard completely in validation samples, and an automated pipeline classifies found variants by clinical guidelines and generates reports. Because carrier screening for these disorders matters most where resources are thin, the authors emphasize the test's simplicity and scalability for population programs.
pmc-10751613:
Navid Chamak, Parisa Farrokh, Roohollah Rostami and Fatemeh Salimi hunt soil from decaying plants for bacteria that can eat bisphenol A, a toxic plastics chemical. Soil samples from Damghan, Iran, were raised on rising doses of the chemical until tough strains stood out. The best isolate was named by its gene sequence as Pseudomonas aeruginosa DU2.

Under its best conditions, low dose, alkaline pH, a pinch of salt and ten days, the strain broke down about fifty-three percent of the bisphenol A present. The authors offer rotting-plant soil as a rich hunting ground for such cleaners, and the strain as a base strain whose diet can be tuned further.
pmc-10756913:
Carena Cornelssen and co-authors review sound-wave therapy for seizures that drugs fail to stop. Their 2023 review covers focused ultrasound, which can burn a small spot of brain tissue or gently nudge nerve activity, based on its strength. A third use pops the blood-brain barrier with tiny bubbles so drugs can reach the seizure source.

Work in animals and early human studies both show fewer seizures in some cases, the review reports. Settings such as dose and target choice still need tuning, and trials are ongoing. The appeal is clear: no cuts and no implants. The authors weigh the current proof and map what must be settled before wide clinic use.
pmc-10758613:
Hua Huang, Guowei Cai, and Hongchun Xiang chart a decade of research on chemotherapy and pain in children in a 2023 mapping study. Chemo saves young lives but its pain burden cuts life quality, and the field's hot spots had not been summed up.

More than a thousand papers from 2013 to 2022 feed the map. Output rose across the decade, led by the United States and China. Top journals, authors, and centers are named, with a children's cancer hospital in front. Hot terms center on care and trials. New work leans toward symptom relief and support care for young patients.
pmc-10760413:
Mariana Argel, Carla António, and Jorge Vale present a rare lung-hollowing case of sarcoidosis, the great mimicker, in work from 2023. The disease forms immune clusters across organs and shows in many guises. Hollow cavities in the lung are an uncommon face of it.

A twenty-seven-year-old man from Ukraine came in coughing blood. Scans showed wide thin-walled cavities up to nine centimeters and swollen chest nodes. Two years earlier, a scan had shown a fine nodular pattern along the lung's lymph paths, but he was lost to follow-up. Tissue samples showed giant cells with telltale bodies inside. The case warns that sarcoidosis can hollow lungs while posing as other diseases.
pmc-10761313:
HyunJong Lee, Hoon Myoung, and Soung Min Kim compare the two workhorse immune-suppressing drugs of transplant medicine. Their review was published in twenty twenty-three. Both drugs keep grafts alive but carry lasting side effects, including kidney damage.

Cyclosporine and tacrolimus both block calcineurin, quieting the cytokine signals that drive rejection. Tacrolimus seems to prevent acute rejection better and can rescue grafts failing on cyclosporine; graft survival overall looks similar. The review covers how each works, induction and maintenance use, and switching between them. It also surveys newer drugs that aim to spare the kidney, noting their own trade-offs.
pmc-10764513:
Elizabeth Laferriere and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-three introduction to a special issue on the federal Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program's innovation experiments. Congress has funded the program since two thousand nine. Its cohorts deliberately test new approaches before scaling them.

The article traces how the program's innovation rounds changed with the field's needs. Fifteen innovator projects from the special issue are then synthesized. Shared lessons concern equity, rigorous testing, and moving proven ideas to scale. The piece closes with how the program refined its model for developing adolescent health innovations that hold up under evaluation.
pmc-10772313:
Seema Sinha, Prem Prakash, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It measures cortisol, the stress hormone, in people with hypothyroidism, an underactive thyroid, to probe how the two hormone systems interact.

The thyroid and the adrenal stress axis lean on each other, and cortisol changes may shape how thyroid disease feels and unfolds. At a medical institute in India, the team studied sixty-five patients and sixty-five matched people with healthy thyroids. Blood tests covered cortisol and the main thyroid measures. Cortisol levels correlated clearly with thyroid stimulating hormone and with thyroxine, the chief thyroid hormone. The authors say the pattern supports watching cortisol when judging hypothyroid patients, and may sharpen both diagnosis and treatment planning.
pmc-10780313:
Min-sung Park and co-authors test a carbon fiber and silicon carbide composite built to stay strong at extreme heat. Their 2023 study uses a dense slurry with a very high share of nano-sized silicon carbide powder. A fast sintering method then densifies the material in a few cycles, far quicker than older routes.

The team bent samples inside a furnace under argon gas at temperatures up to 2000 degrees. Strength at the highest heat was well above the room temperature value, which is rare for such materials. The authors discuss why the composite gains strength when hot. Materials like this matter for engines, rockets, and other systems that must bear load at extreme temperatures.
pmc-10784113:
Marco Filetti and co-authors compare first-line targeted drugs for a gene-marked lung cancer in a 2023 network analysis. Tumors with ALK rearrangements answer to a family of kinase blockers, but trials mostly test each against one older drug. Pooling nine trials lets the whole family be ranked.

Second and third generation drugs all delayed progression beyond the older standard. One ranked likeliest best for progression control, while another alone had proven a survival gain so far. Brain spread was best held back by the same leading pair. Side effect burdens varied, with one drug clearly harshest. Two modern drugs emerge as the most promising openers, balancing control and tolerability.
pmc-10790713:
Lindsay Standeven and co-authors study anxiety care for women in a 2023 paper on collaborative care. In that model, primary care staff, care managers, and mental health experts treat patients together. Most past work tested it in general primary care, so its value inside women's health practices was less clear.

The team reviewed records for 219 women at three women's health centers. Anxiety scores fell clearly from entry to the end of care, and longer time in the program linked to larger drops, with a marked gain by ninety days. The study also checked which factors, such as main diagnosis and use of mental health drugs, tracked with better outcomes. Results support the model in this setting.
pmc-10792713:
Mahendra Shrestha, Ajaya Basnet, Rajendra Maharjan, and five colleagues measure cervical virus prevalence in Nepal in this two thousand twenty-three cross-sectional study. Detecting high-risk human papillomavirus DNA helps identify women at risk of cervical cancer. The authors studied women undergoing Pap smear tests in the gynecologic oncology department of a tertiary hospital in Nepal over about five months in twenty twenty-two, using convenience sampling.

Among one hundred ninety-nine women, six, about three percent, carried the virus, a prevalence lower than comparable studies in similar settings. The infected women averaged about thirty-one years old. Typing found HPV sixteen in four of the six infections and HPV eighteen in the other two, the two types most strongly tied to cervical cancer. The authors conclude that even where overall prevalence is low, screening still catches the highest-risk infections in younger women.
pmc-10803413:
Ya-Ning Huang and co-authors study children whose Kawasaki disease shows mainly as jaundice, in a paper whose head is dated 2023. Kawasaki disease inflames blood vessels in children, and a yellowing, liver-led form is unusual. The team reviewed twelve such children at a Taiwan children hospital and forty-two cases reported since 1990.

In their own group, all children had raised liver tests, half had a swollen gallbladder, and most had gut symptoms. Almost all met full criteria for the disease, and a sixth had repeat episodes. All got antibody treatment, but a third did not respond to it. A quarter suffered shock, and more than half developed heart artery problems, though most recovered. Pooled past cases showed the same pattern of higher risk. The authors urge doctors to watch this group closely for shock and heart harm.
pmc-10808313:
Yuxia Chen and co-authors study how mental load affects the stability of older women when they start walking, in work the head dates to 2023. Starting a step is a risky moment for falls, and busy settings demand more attention.

Twenty-three older and twenty-three younger women walked under three conditions: plain start, a light reaction task, and that task plus mental interference. Older women adjusted by prolonging pressure shifts, shortening steps, slowing down, and widening their stance. The busier the mental setting, the lower their stability, above all sideways at step onset.
pmc-10808613:
Adrian Gorecki and co-authors track drug resistance gene variants through a wastewater treatment plant, in this 2023 paper. Treatment plants are known sources of resistant bacteria and their genes, which count as emerging pollutants. Standard checks name the genes present but not their many variants.

The team screened fourteen resistance genes across the plant's stages, then sequenced three genes in depth. Seventy-nine variants were counted, one gene alone holding fifty-two. Some variants rose or fell along the cleaning process, and some may live in new host bacteria. A pool of brand-new variants also turned up. The study argues variant-level tracking sharpens pollution control.
pmc-10808813:
Zhenhua Dong and a team of co-authors test whether gut germs cause peptic ulcers, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. Watch-only studies had hinted at a link, but cause stayed unclear. Their genetic method used germ data from one bank and ulcer data from another.

At a loose gene threshold, some germ groups raised stomach ulcer risk while others lowered it. A longer list of groups shifted duodenal ulcer risk both ways. At the strict threshold, no clear effect survived. The authors read the pattern as suggestive, not proof, and call for more work.
pmc-10811213:
Maria Sereno and co-authors review lung cancer spread to the brain and the role of immunotherapy, in work from 2023. Brain spread is common in lung cancer and worsens outlook sharply. Cancer cells reach the brain through molecular changes that favor nerve tissue.

Immune drugs have lifted survival even when the brain is involved. They enter the central nervous system better than classic chemotherapy does. The review maps how brain deposits form and grow over time. It also weighs how to predict who will respond to immune treatment. Drug pairings that boost brain control get special attention. Clinicians gain a current guide to a hard treatment problem.
pmc-10822913:
Hamdi Messaoudi and five co-authors study warm-up routines in taekwondo in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. Sixteen male athletes tried combinations of a plyometric conditioning activity and music during warm-up. Music varied by who chose it, by tempo, and by whether the genre was a favorite.

Athletes took agility and kicking speed tests under each condition and rated effort, arousal, feeling, and motivation. Self-selected music from a preferred genre, at either tempo, plus the conditioning activity beat the other setups on most measures. Fast self-chosen favorite music also improved feelings and effort ratings after the kick tests. The authors call the pairing an individualized warm-up strategy for taekwondo.
pmc-10827913:
Maria Gavrish and co-authors review how the brain's great bridge of fibers grows in four steps. The review appeared in 2023. The bridge links the two halves of the brain and is the newest such link in milk-fed animals. In humans it holds most of the fibers that cross between halves.

Step one sees a young nerve cell pick a fiber and move to its home layer. Step two sees fibers run toward the mid line in a tight pack. Step three is the cross to the far half. Step four is the reach to a set zone and the growth of links. Each step is steered by many inner and outer cues.
pmc-10828013:
Qingjing Zeng and co-authors fuse two scans into one view to judge liver spots that standard imaging leaves in limbo, in a paper whose head dates it to 2023. Some focal liver lesions look neither clearly benign nor clearly cancerous on MRI scoring, and ordinary ultrasound may miss them entirely. For patients at risk of liver cancer, that uncertainty delays treatment decisions. Fusion imaging overlays the MRI map onto live contrast ultrasound so the same spot can be inspected both ways.

Seventy-one lesions in sixty-three patients were scored by the fused method and by contrast MRI alone. The comparison measures which read gets the diagnosis right more often. Sharper calls on borderline lesions mean fewer missed cancers and fewer needless interventions, a balance hepatology struggles with daily.
pmc-10859413:
Talib Hussain and co-authors test a plant pigment against prostate cancer cells that no longer heed hormones. Their 2023 study deals with aloe-emodin, an anthraquinone, on DU145 cells in dishes and in computer docking. The Wnt and beta-catenin pathway, a growth driver, stood as the suspect route. Doses of the pigment cut cell survival and raised leak markers of cell harm.

Oxygen stress climbed, nuclei broke and shrank, and death switches fired. Mitochondria faded while a death signal rose in the cell fluid. Growth gene reads fell, and docking showed the pigment gripping both pathway targets on par with known blockers.
pmc-10903313:
Akram Sadat Ahmadi and co-authors track how the COVID-19 virus changed across one wave in Tehran in a 2023 study. Full gene reads can map which forms of the virus spread and how they shift. The team read the whole gene set of the virus from fifteen patients.

Samples came from the start, the mid, and the end of the fourth wave in 2021. Gene reads were run on a fast sequencer and set side by side. Shifts that rose or fell across the wave show how the virus adapted as it spread. Health teams gain a local record of a wave that can guide watch for the next one.
pmc-10909113:
Colon cancer is the third most common cancer worldwide, and doctors hunt for tissue markers that warn which patients face a worse course. The authors of a 2023 study stain tumors from 134 patients for two proteins: HHLA2, a newer immune checkpoint molecule, and CD8, a marker of attacking immune cells. They compare the staining with tumor features and with how long patients lived.

High HHLA2 appeared in just over half the cases and tracked with deeper invasion, spread to lymph nodes, higher stage, and later recurrence. On its own it predicted shorter survival. CD8 staining tracked with immune cells inside the tumor and with less spread, but not with survival. The authors name HHLA2 a sign of poor outlook.
pmc-10917113:
Allina Flores-Mendoza, Victor Camacho-Trejo, and Lilia Rizo-Topete present the case of a 39-year-old woman believed to have only one kidney, in a 2023 report. She arrived with two weeks of belly pain, swelling, and painful urination, but no fever. Blood work showed mild anemia and her kidney function was normal, while urine tests pointed to infection and blood in the urine.

A CT urogram overturned the old belief: she had two kidneys, but the right one sat down in the pelvis, swollen by a large stone blocking its outlet. The left kidney showed milder swelling. After two days of antibiotics, doctors removed the stone through a small puncture procedure, and her symptoms cleared fully. The authors discuss misplaced kidneys and their risks.
pmc-10976613:
Przemysław Bąbel and Paweł Ostaszewski weigh neurodiversity acceptance against therapy for autism support, in a viewpoint from 2024. A growing movement reads autism as normal human variety, not a defect to fix. That lens pushes society to adapt settings, like quiet shopping hours, to varied minds.

Therapy built on the same lens can grow independence, creativity, and comfort in daily life. Trouble starts when acceptance hardens into calls to drop therapy altogether, they argue. Dropping help can strand people whose support needs are real and ongoing. The sound path is conscious, responsible choice case by case, they conclude. Respect for variety and honest aid must travel together, not trade places.
pmc-10994613:
Amaar Amir and co-authors review road crash injuries seen at a hospital emergency unit in eastern Saudi Arabia over one year. Road injuries cause death and disability worldwide, and local patterns help guide care and prevention. The team drew records from the hospital system.

Most patients were men, and the largest age group was young adults in their late teens and twenties. About half had some injury, most often cuts and scrapes, with arm fractures the most common break. A small share needed surgery or intensive care, and a few died. Being male and a few other factors were linked with a higher chance of injury.
pmc-11075013:
Finding prostate cancer early means taking tissue samples, and robots now help guide the needle. Akif Erbin, Ufuk Caglar, and Rustu Turkay review studies of robotic systems that fuse MRI scans with live ultrasound and pass the needle through the perineum rather than the rectum. From 343 papers they kept thirteen original studies covering 1,844 patients and two commercial platforms.

Cancer was found in 51 to 74 percent of the men. Clinically significant cancer, the kind that matters most, turned up in 23 to 53 percent of those never diagnosed before. Harm was rare: only two of the 1,844 patients developed urosepsis, the severe infection this route is meant to avoid. Most studies were prospective but none randomized, so the review stops short of proving the robots beat skilled manual work. The authors still judge the technique effective and safe, with strong detection of significant cancer.
pmc-11081113: A 2023 announcement by Christine Neilson invites health science librarians to the CHLA/ABSC conference in Winnipeg, set for June 11 to 14, 2024, at the Hotel Delta Winnipeg. The theme is Disruptive and Diverse, a nod to fresh views and shifting ground in health libraries. A draft program outline was posted, with submissions open online until mid-January 2024. The notice also flags a science bootcamp on the University of Manitoba campus just before the meeting, with a joint reception linking the two events.
pmc-11532313:
The authors develop an imaging method to measure blood flow input at the liver's portal vein for quantitative PET scanning, tested on a phantom. Drug studies in the liver need two input functions, since blood arrives by both the hepatic artery and the portal vein. The portal vein is small, and breathing motion blurs its signal, so measuring it from images is hard. The team builds a custom 3D-printed phantom that mimics the liver and vein.

Their protocol pairs high-resolution magnetic resonance images of the vein with a PET scan and a motion-tracking sequence, while the phantom mimics breathing. Motion data extracted from the scans feeds the reconstruction, yielding nearly motion-free dynamic images. Anatomical images then correct the partial volume effect in the vein's readings. The authors show the setup can deliver portal vein input measurements fit for clinical use.
pmc-11533313:
Xue Li and co-authors test a small peptide that shields eye lens cells from damage, in a 2024 study. Oxidative stress linked to glaucoma speeds the clouding of the lens called cataract. The peptide apelin-13 was tested on human lens cells in dishes. Some cells were stressed with hydrogen peroxide, a standard damage trigger.

Treated cells survived far better than stressed cells left alone. A blocker drug was used to check that the peptide worked through its known receptor. Measures of cell death, energy membranes, and antioxidant reserves all backed the protective story. The peptide kept a key sugar-processing pathway running under stress. That pathway's failure may help drive a severe glaucoma form, the authors suggest. Eye researchers get a candidate shield to test further.
pmc-11533413:
Marianne Cerf and co-authors study how French shoppers see and use the Nutri-Score label, in a 2024 paper. The color-and-letter label grades packaged food at a glance and runs in several European countries. Its scoring formula was about to change, and the team wanted to know what shoppers made of it. They ran six focus groups with 51 adults and shadowed 20 more on real shopping trips, then interviewed them.

Shoppers knew the label but treated it as a backup cue, behind price and habit. They grasped its health aim yet could not say who runs it or how the grade is computed, and that gap bred mistrust. Few had heard media attacks on it, and most welcomed the update. The authors urge a public campaign that explains the math and the label's government backing.
pmc-11535213:
Yingchun Wang and a large team of doctors study prostate cancer markers in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Their patients had hormone-sensitive prostate cancer that had spread widely at first diagnosis. All were treated with newer hormonal drugs. The team asked whether the path of PSA, a blood marker, predicts how patients fare. They reviewed the records of one hundred two patients.

Follow-up lasted about thirty-two months on average. The lowest PSA after treatment, and the PSA density at three months, both carried signal. Patients whose lowest PSA fell to a low level did better. So did those with low PSA density early on. The lack of spread to inner organs also helped. The authors say simple PSA measures can flag which patients need closer watch or stronger care.
pmc-11535513:
Yash Patel and co-authors published a genetics study in 2024 on bright spots in brain white matter and thinning of the brain cortex. These bright spots mark damage in the white matter, which may drive cortex thinning, a hallmark of dementia. The team drew on data from many cohorts and more than fifty thousand people. They asked which genes link the two traits.

The scan found twenty places in the genome tied to the combined trait. Genes near these places act in blood vessel cells and in support cells of the brain. The trait shared genetic links with vessel risk traits and with blood markers of nerve decay. A score built from the results predicted dementia in a large separate sample.
pmc-11536713:
The chemotherapy drug irinotecan often causes diarrhea severe enough to limit treatment, and Deng and co-authors tested a classical Chinese herbal formula as protection. In a double-blind trial across six hospitals, 101 small cell lung cancer patients finished two chemo cycles while taking Shengjiang Xiexin decoction or a placebo. Diarrhea struck 26 percent of the herb group against 52 percent on placebo, and episodes were milder.

The benefit concentrated in patients whose UGT1A1 gene profile flags high risk, where rates were 9 versus 67 percent. Rat experiments tied the effect to calmer inflammatory signals in the gut wall.
pmc-11536913:
Carolina González Abós and five co-authors checked how long waits degrade the tissue removed in robot pancreas surgery, in a study published in 2024. Robot operations run long, and the removed part sits warm in the body, then often cold in storage. That wait can blur the laboratory reading. Sixty specimens were read: open operations, robot operations, and robot operations with cold storage.

Warm wait ran three times as long in robot operations as in open ones. Cold storage ran a mean near thirteen hours. Long surgery, male sex, and cold storage tied to tissue decay in first readings. In joint analysis, cold storage alone stood as the driver, for plain and tumor tissue alike. The decay did not wreck the laboratory call, though. The authors urge fast paths from removal to laboratory.
pmc-11537213:
Michaela Babejová and co-authors make and study nine light-active molecules built as donor-linker-acceptor chains, in this 2024 paper. Such chromophores steer light and charge in solar cells and sensors. Swapping the middle linker or the end groups tunes the energy gap that sets their color and behavior.

Three linkers were tried, drawn from benzene and thiophene rings. Donor ends carried simple or nitrogen-rich groups, while acceptor ends ranged from mild to strongly pulling. Bench tests measured light absorption, glow, and voltage behavior. Computer models matched the measured gaps well. The analysis shows how each swap moves the gap, guiding dye design.
pmc-11538513:
Julia Siguemoto and co-authors searched in 2024 for a stable reference gene for blood tests in people with COVID-19. Such tests measure tiny RNA strands in plasma, and a steady reference is needed for fair reading. No single reference works for all cases, so the team turned to large-scale RNA reading.

They compared patients with healthy volunteers and, in a second run, severe with mild cases. Four candidate strands met strict rules for steady levels. Testing in a group of 125 patients left only one as steady across groups. That strand can serve as a reference for later plasma RNA work in this disease, the authors conclude.
pmc-11539013:
Xiuqi Wang and co-authors test whether a home biofeedback device adds anything to pelvic floor training for women leaking urine after childbirth. Their 2024 trial starts from the standard care: supervised muscle training is the first-line fix for stress incontinence. Whether a pressure-sensing feedback gadget at home boosts it was unproven.

Women with new postpartum leakage at five Chinese hospitals all got three months of supervised training. Half were also given the home device; the rest trained unaided at home. Assessors who scored the outcomes did not know the groups. The main read was a standard incontinence score at three months. Cure and improvement rates, muscle strength, quality of life, confidence, and sticking with the plan were tracked as well.
pmc-11539713:
Fanping Zhu and six co-authors characterize a malaria drug's breakdown product in a 2024 paper. Artemisinin is the world's main malaria drug, and the body transforms it heavily. Whether its main metabolite still fights the parasite was unknown. Liver cell preparations identified the enzymes and the product's structure.

One enzyme family, CYP3A, makes the product, a hydroxylated form. Crystal and spectral analysis pinned its exact shape. Against two malaria strains it worked, but about six times weaker than the parent drug. Blood levels in healthy volunteers were tracked after a standard dose. Exposure ratios suggested the metabolite adds modestly to the cure. The finding completes the drug's pharmacology picture for dosing design.
pmc-11539813:
Yuzhen Wu and co-authors study how a nurse's stress mindset shapes sleep quality in this 2024 paper. Sleep among Chinese nurses is known to be poor, with disorder rates reported near two in three. Health reforms have pushed for better staff mental health and rest.

A stress mindset is the belief that stress is harmful or can be enhancing. The team survey nurses online about mindset, sleep, overload, and anxiety. They test whether overload and anxiety carry the effect from mindset to sleep. A path through those middle steps would suggest clear fixes. Training that reframes stress, plus lighter loads, might help nurses sleep. Hospitals gain when rested staff make fewer errors.
pmc-11545613:
Qi Tian, Siti Maziha Mustapha, and Jie Min study why some students feel satisfied with their studies and others do not, in a paper published in twenty twenty-four. The team focused on undergraduates at local technology universities in China. They linked four things: putting work off, grades, belief in one's own skill, and satisfaction.

Nearly four hundred students from twenty-two schools answered an online survey. Putting work off was common; close to half showed high levels. Delay tied to lower self-belief and lower satisfaction, while better performance tied to higher levels of both. Self-belief also carried part of the effect: delays hurt satisfaction partly by eroding confidence. The model gives schools a lever, since confidence can be trained.
pmc-11547413:
Zhihao Zhao and co-authors test how peanut oil type reshapes gut microbes in rats on a rich diet. Their 2024 study feeds rats a high-fat, high-fructose diet with regular peanut oil, high-oleic peanut oil, or saturated fat. Gene reads and stool chemistry profile the gut response.

Both peanut oils widen microbe diversity versus saturated fat. The high-oleic oil boosts two bacterial groups that make butyrate and acetate, helpful gut fuels. Hundreds of stool markers split the oil groups from the saturated group. Harmful protein fermentation in the colon appears curbed, the main control route the authors propose. The high-oleic group also manages weight and insulin response better. The work links fat choice to gut ecology under a junk-heavy diet.
pmc-11548913:
Caroline dos Santos Costa and co-authors test two quick diet scores in a 2024 Brazilian study. Judging a diet by how processed its foods are is a public health staple, but full recalls are slow and burdensome.

A three minute checklist asks which foods from two lists a person ate yesterday: whole plant foods on one side, ultra processed foods on the other. Each score is a simple count. In a national cohort, both scores were compared with a full day recall done the same day. People in higher score bands ate matching shares of energy from the matching food groups, in a clean straight line. Agreement between score bands and energy shares was substantial for both scores.
pmc-11549913:
Juan Merino-Torres and co-authors weigh the value for money of live glucose sensors against finger-prick checks in Spain. Their 2024 study covers people with type 2 diabetes on daily insulin. Live sensors cut blood sugar markers more and please patients more, but they cost more up front.

A standard diabetes model simulates patients over a lifetime, with costs and health gains discounted yearly. Effect data come from a large United States records study, and prices from Spanish sources. Live sensing yields about nine-tenths of a quality life year more per patient. Lifetime costs run about twenty-three hundred euros higher per patient. Set against the usual Spanish value threshold, the authors assess whether the gain justifies the spend.
pmc-11569613:
Reza Tadayonfar and co-authors map a skin disease, cutaneous leishmaniasis, among Iranian soldiers over five years. The infection, spread by sand flies, is rising worldwide, and Iran is among the worst-hit countries; soldiers are often sent into high-risk areas without prior exposure and with thinner medical cover. Health ministry records gave 2,894 patients between 2018 and 2022, which the team mapped by place, age, lesion site, and disease type.

Cases clustered in central, southern, and western provinces, with the animal-linked form dominating in the worst areas. The team then fitted a standard forecasting model to the monthly counts. Its projections run to the end of 2025 and are meant to guide where prevention and care should be strengthened.
pmc-11570813:
Longguo Zhang and co-authors hunt gene markers that reflect the immune state of neuroblastoma tumors. Neuroblastoma is a childhood cancer whose course varies a lot by tumor traits. The immune scene inside a tumor shapes how it grows and responds to drugs. The team scored immune levels in tumor gene data and split samples into high and low groups.

The groups differed in age and in a key gene status tied to risk. Three learning methods then screened for marker genes that split the groups. Six genes passed all screens, each tied to immune paths and cell types. The authors propose the six as markers of the tumor immune scene. Such markers could help guide treatment choice for each child.
pmc-11572613:
Basavraj Nagoba and co-authors wrote a 2024 editorial on blood markers that may flag severe lung infection in children. The infection is caused by a germ called Mycoplasma pneumoniae, a common cause of chest illness in the young. Knowing early which cases will turn severe can guide care and improve results.

The editorial reviews five markers, among them two interleukins, a clot marker, and an enzyme tied to cell harm. High levels of each marker link strongly to severe cases in the work under review. The authors present the set as a tool kit that helps doctors spot high-risk children early and act in time.
pmc-11574113:
Julian Fernandez and co-authors speed the design of chip-scale cooling devices with machine learning, in a 2024 study. The devices rest on solid-state physics and suit cooling inside integrated chips. Exact modeling couples a quantum method for electrons with the heat equation, but one run takes two days. Their workflow trains a learner on such runs to hunt the best device shapes.

The search space held a vast count of candidate structures. The learner found top designs with prediction errors under a few percent for cooling power and electron temperature. The hunt took about ten seconds once trained. The authors say the flow can widen design searches that brute force cannot touch.
pmc-11575413:
Yanjun Huang and co-authors test whether burning a small spine nerve boosts keyhole disc surgery for back pain, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Ninety-seven patients split into surgery alone or surgery plus the nerve burn. Pain, function, and disability scores ran to six months.

Both groups gained much on all scores after surgery. The paired group beat surgery alone on back pain scores at each check. Leg pain gains did not split the groups.
