Yet the edge fell short of the gap patients can feel, the authors note. The burn may still help as an add-on. Readers get a real but modest boost, plainly sized.
pmc-11576113:
Haotian Guo and four co-authors model the forces on supports that hold a deep building pit through winter in frozen ground, in a 2024 study. In the Changchun area, pits dug in clay-rich soil sit open over winter while the ground freezes. Using room-temperature traits of wet soil misstates the loads, since cold changes the soil’s strength.

The team measured strength in lab tests on unsaturated soil, then built a pit model in simulation software from those values. In its natural state the local clay held a suction of 70 kilopascals, and its cohesion rose as temperature fell. They varied key traits to see which drove stress and bending of the supports. Model results matched field monitoring well, which validates the cold-soil approach.
pmc-11577013:
Loss of bladder control is common in women and rises with age, while a protein called alpha-klotho is known as a marker of healthy aging. Xiaoyan Tang and co-authors asked in 2024 whether blood levels of that protein track the severity of incontinence. They used a United States health survey covering 2,628 women aged forty to seventy-nine.

Women with severe incontinence had clearly lower alpha-klotho levels than women with none, after other factors were taken into account. The type of incontinence did not show a like link. In some subgroups, such as women of normal weight or with heart or kidney disease, the link faded. The authors present the protein as a possible clue to the biology behind worsening symptoms.
pmc-11577113:
Rim Rejaibi and co-authors profile ovarian cancer in a group of Tunisian patients. Their twenty twenty-four paper fills a gap, since most past work focused on Caucasian groups. The team joined tissue signs, gene data, and survival outcomes for epithelial ovarian cancer.

Near two hundred patients were checked for fourteen proteins known to shift in this cancer. Protein levels were matched with copy number changes in the genome. Stage, menopause status, and a DNA repair defect each linked to survival. One gene, ERBB2, showed a tight match between extra copies and high protein levels. Readers get a regional profile that can guide care and further study.
pmc-11577313:
Lutton-Gething and co-authors chart hidden disorder inside a rare-earth framework material, in a 2024 study. The porous crystal soaks up guest molecules in its cages. Fluoride ions sit disordered across key faces of its building units. Guests prefer the large octahedral cage, touching the metal centers. Different guests bend the framework in subtle ways.

Linker rings rotate to set orientations per guest. Two solvent guests lower the crystal's symmetry class. Other guests leave the higher symmetry intact. Swapping solvents switches the structure back and forth. The cage layout itself survives every change. Such flexibility matters for storage and separation uses. Designers must expect order to shift with loading. The study maps exactly where guests sit and what they disturb.
pmc-11577713:
Sesmu Arbous and six co-authors compare three year death rates among intensive care survivors in the Netherlands. Groups are defined by admission cause, sepsis, infection without sepsis, or inflammatory illness without infection. Sepsis is a leading cause of death, and its effects are known to persist for years after discharge.

The matched cohort covers admissions from 2007 to 2019 across 78 Dutch intensive care units in a national registry. Patients were classed by diagnosis within the first day of admission. Only patients discharged alive enter the survival comparison, and each sepsis survivor is matched individually to peers in the other groups. The design separates the long shadow of sepsis itself from the effects of infection or inflammation alone.
pmc-11577913:
Naonori Kumagai and eight co-authors examine kidney tubule function in children and patients newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes during a crisis called ketoacidosis. Their 2024 study notes that the tubules' first segment is known to falter in that crisis. Few studies had checked several of its jobs at once, and the far segment had gone unstudied. Eleven patients were split by whether the crisis was present.

In the crisis group, a marker of proximal tubule strain ran far higher in urine. Blood acidity and phosphate reabsorption dropped too, a pattern of several proximal jobs failing together that resembles a transient Fanconi syndrome. Other markers matched between groups. No signs pointed to failure of the far segment's acid handling. The authors say the pattern supports the current crisis criteria and hints at what drives the temporary tubule trouble.
pmc-11578213:
Norihiro Ohba, Goichi Haraoka, Mayuko Ohba, and Norio Takahashi report methods to fix nose deformities left by cosmetic surgery, in work from 2024. Too much tissue removal can notch the nostril rim, flatten the side of the nose, and blur the crease where nose meets cheek.

The team revised sixteen cases over several years, most of them women. Ear cartilage grafts were the main tool to rebuild shape without a poor color match. A small flap of nearby tissue helped some notches, and two cinching stitches defined the crease. Nearly all flaps survived, with one graft lost to infection.
pmc-11579313:
Chen Yan and colleagues assembled in 2024 a high-quality genome for the Spectacled Fulvetta, a bird found only in China. It is the type species of its genus, a group whose members overlap in range yet look alike, which makes their evolution hard to untangle. A reference genome was needed as a base for such work.

Long-read and chromosome-contact sequencing gave an assembly of about one point two billion bases, with strong continuity and near-complete gene coverage. Its quality matched top vertebrate genome projects. The team annotated close to twenty-four thousand protein-coding genes, most with a known function. The genome is offered as a base for studies of bird evolution and local adaptation.
pmc-11580413:
Giblin-Burnham, Javanmardi, Moeendarbary, and Hoogenboom model atomic force microscopy on soft surfaces in a 2024 paper. The microscope gives detailed surface maps at tiny scales. Most simulations assume hard samples, yet many real samples are soft and dent under the tip.

Finite element models show how measured stiffness drifts from the true material value. Image features depend on tip shape, sample shape, and how deep the tip pushes in. Particles can look up to twice too large or too small. Sharper images do not always mean truer surfaces. Tests on DNA matched the model results. The work gives a frame for reading microscope data on soft matter.
pmc-11582713:
Ana Paula Vargas Garcia and five colleagues present a 2024 study comparing breast tumors in women and dogs under the microscope. The collagen scaffolding around a tumor changes as cancer advances, and those changes carry clues about outlook. Because dogs develop similar mammary cancers naturally, comparing the two species can test whether the clues agree.

The team used multiphoton microscopy on tumor samples from 70 women and 74 dogs across healthy tissue, benign growths, and cancers of rising severity. In both species, cancers showed sparser, straighter, more aligned collagen and denser cell packing than healthy tissue. Tumors with worse outlook had shorter fibers, and in dogs fiber length tracked survival time. The parallel strengthens dogs as a model for human breast cancer.
pmc-11584313:
Elizabeth T Rogawski McQuade and co-authors simulate how diarrhea vaccines could cut antibiotic use in young children, in a research paper from 2024. Vaccines might spare antibiotics by preventing the gut infections that prompt their use. The team drew on a birth cohort from five low-income countries.

Among 1,119 children, over three thousand diarrhea episodes drew antibiotics. Simulations tested nine vaccine plans, single and combined. A Shigella vaccine promised the largest cuts among single vaccines, easing both diarrhea courses and stray exposure of bystander germs. The results give vaccine planners a second benefit to weigh beside illness prevented: slower growth of drug resistance.
pmc-11584813:
Kevin McElroy, David Shin, Matthew Abad-Santos, Eric Monroe, and Jeffrey Chick report early experience with a small catheter system that pulls clots out of veins. Larger devices exist, but this slimmer tool is built for smaller veins, and the team tried it across many clot locations.

Eleven patients with symptomatic vein blockages were treated, with clots in the belly, chest, neck, arm grafts, and legs. One to three passes per patient restored flow in ten of the eleven cases, with very little blood loss. The one failure involved an infected clot in the neck vein, where the team stopped rather than risk spreading the infection. The authors present the series as preliminary experience with the device.
pmc-11585113:
Lin Huang and her thirteen co-authors, publishing in 2024, identify a wheat protein that works against the plant's own defenses. Zinc finger proteins help plants manage stress, but their role in disease was murky. The team found one such protein, TaZFP8-5B, whose levels drop when stripe rust fungus attacks wheat. Lab tests showed it carries a built-in off switch for gene activity.

Silencing the protein's gene made wheat more resistant to stripe rust. Forcing extra production made wheat, and even rice, easier for fungi to infect. The protein partners with a calcium-sensing protein, and silencing that partner weakened resistance instead. Together the pair forms a dial that turns immunity down. The authors offer the module as a new lead for breeding or engineering rust-resistant crops, a pressing need since stripe rust destroys harvests worldwide.
pmc-11585213:
Shuai Tang and six colleagues fed a probiotic yeast to constipated mice and tracked changes in the small gut. Saccharomyces boulardii is a fungal probiotic used for gut complaints, but its small gut actions were unclear. The team made the mice constipated with loperamide. The yeast did not fully restore the stool measures of the animals. It did reshape the mix of microbes in the small gut, toward a mix suited to ease constipation.

Several host genes shifted in telling directions. A water channel gene and a signal that calms swelling rose, while drivers of swelling fell. The machinery for muscle contraction was also turned up, and levels of small cell products changed, among them sugar phosphates. The 2024 study suggests the yeast works through water handling, swelling, and gut motion at once, even when stool measures lag behind.
pmc-11585613:
Quan Chen and co-authors propose MSA-ESRGAN in 2024, a model that enlarges images while keeping them looking real. Super-resolution systems can sharpen a picture yet blur texture or mix subject and background. Their change sits in the part of the network that judges whether an image looks real or made.

That judging part uses a U-Net with attention at several scales, helping it tell subject from background more closely. Trained in the same setup as a known rival for fair comparison, the model was tested on five public image sets. Scores for image quality, signal strength, and structural likeness were higher than older methods, and human judges also rated the results better for texture and realism. A removal test showed the new judging part played a key role.
pmc-11586413:
Choosing between stenting and coiling for an internal carotid artery aneurysm is a standing challenge for surgeons. Jian Pei, Xiang Xu, and Li-Cai Zhao use computational fluid dynamics to compare the two endovascular methods and to find regions at high risk across the cardiac cycle. They test two coiling porosity levels and stent deformation to see how each choice changes blood flow near the aneurysm.

Their results show endovascular treatment works better in small aneurysms than in giant ones. For a giant saccular aneurysm, stenting works well when the parent vessel is fully aligned, so that little blood enters the sac. The study maps how porosity and deformation shift the flow field, giving surgeons a hemodynamic basis for picking a method by aneurysm size and vessel shape.
pmc-11587413:
Manuel Maciel-Saldierna and co-authors measure fear of missing out among Mexican junior high students, and tie it to how they use social media. The Guadalajara study ran during the pandemic's later phase, when screens had swallowed school and social life alike. More than twelve hundred students aged eleven to sixteen, from four schools, completed an adapted fear-of-missing-out scale.

The analysis links scores to sex, age, and the kind and frequency of platform use. Adolescents are the population least able to shrug off the engineered urgency of feeds, and baseline numbers for western Mexico were missing. With a local prevalence in hand, schools and parents can argue from data rather than panic.
pmc-11587613:
Zhenglong Guo and eight co-authors report new gene variants behind an early brain decay disorder in a Chinese family, in a study from 2024. The gene at fault guides a protein that keeps cell iron in balance, and only a few such cases were known.

Gene scans of a baby boy with severe growth and mind delays and pale blood found two new variants, one from each parent. Lab tests showed one variant sped the loss of the iron protein, which threw cell iron off track. Drugs that block protein trash may lift levels again, a lead the authors flag for care research.
pmc-11587713:
Zhu Liu and three co-authors present a 2024 genetics study of Sicista caudata, a small rodent in the birch mouse family. The team read and mapped the animal's complete mitochondrial genome, the small loop of DNA passed down through mothers. Such maps help place a species on the tree of life. The work checks this rodent's spot within the wider jerboa superfamily.

The genome proved to be a circular strand just over sixteen thousand DNA letters long. It holds thirteen protein-coding genes, twenty-two transfer RNA genes, two ribosomal RNA genes, and control parts. Family tree analysis backed the species' placement with full statistical support. The authors present the map as a firm molecular record for future work on this little-studied rodent and its relatives.
pmc-11588313: Jeesoo Choi and Abigail Palmares report a surgery case in 2024. A woman aged 37 had a slow-growing tumor in a central airway of the lung. Her airway branching was unusual, which made the removal harder. Tumors of this kind make up a small share of lung tumors and often grow inside the airway.
pmc-11589813:
Jithender Rallabandi, Smrutiranjan Mohanty, and Indrajit Shown reported a chemistry method in 2024 for editing indole compounds. Indoles are ring compounds with wide use, and adding a carbon chain at one exact site is a valued step. Their method uses a ruthenium catalyst and an ester group to guide the change.

Even though two like sites could react, only the third site was changed, and only once. The selectivity comes from an uncommon six-membered ring formed between the catalyst and the guide group. The authors note simple handling, a broad range of starting materials, and moderate to high yields for the route.
pmc-11590813:
Humphrey Cyprian Karamagi and co-authors map what is known about unequal health care coverage in Africa in a 2024 scoping review. Even as countries push toward care for all, who gets care still splits by place, income, schooling, sex, faith, and other social lines. The team searched eight databases for studies from 2005 to 2022 on services for mothers and children, infections, and long-term diseases.

Studies were kept if they measured gaps in the use of such services in Africa. The team charted each study's setting and the gap lines it used, following a stepwise method with a tested form. Their map shows which gap lines and which services draw the most study, and where proof is thin. The work guides fairer health planning.
pmc-11592413:
Dorofeeva leads a team studying how aplastic anemia blood serum affects marrow stromal cells in a 2024 paper. In this disease the marrow fails and blood cell counts fall. Stromal cells support blood formation, and their growth is slow in patients.

Healthy donor stromal cells grew far less in patient serum than in donor serum. The effect grew with the severity of low platelet counts, and cell death did not explain it. Tests found low levels of a growth factor, PDGF-BB, in patient serum. Adding that factor or donor platelet material restored growth. The authors name this lack as one cause of stromal damage in the disease.
pmc-11592513:
Hepatitis A spreads through contaminated food and water, and how sick it makes you depends heavily on age. Ihsan Hakki Ciftci and co-authors pooled the Turkish evidence in 2024. They gathered fifty-seven studies from 2000 to 2023, sorted into four age bands, each measuring what share carried antibodies from past infection or vaccination.

Antibody rates climbed with age, from about 73 percent in the youngest children to about 91 percent in adults over thirty-five, with an overall estimate of 64.5 percent. The authors credit the national vaccination program begun in 2012 for the rise among the young. But studies disagreed with each other a great deal, and regions differed. They call for region-specific public health strategies and for finer data to judge the vaccine's long-term effect.
pmc-11594713:
Ye-Jin Lee and Chang-Gu Hyun tested whether coumarin derivatives can switch skin pigment production back on. Vitiligo destroys or disables the melanocytes that color skin, leaving white patches. The team screened six variants of 4-methylcoumarin in mouse melanoma cells that model pigment production. Three compounds showed no effect on melanin. Three others stimulated pigment formation, one of them strongly.

The strongest compound, a methoxy-bearing variant, raised melanin and tyrosinase activity dose by dose. Protein analysis showed it also raised the master pigment regulator MITF and two pigment enzymes. The twenty twenty-four study traces the signaling route behind the stimulation. Compounds that safely restart pigmentation could become topical leads for vitiligo, a condition with few effective treatments.
pmc-11595513:
Andrzej Szewczak and Grzegorz Łagód test whether additives can make epoxy glue grip concrete more strongly. Glued joints depend on many factors, and adhesion decides whether a joint can be made and how long it lasts. Epoxy resins are common adhesives whose properties fillers can tune. The team mixed microsilica and carbon nanotubes in amounts set by experiment.

Sound-based mixing with cavitation helped blend the filler evenly through the resin. The team tracked viscosity, surface energy, surface traits, and adhesion. Microscope images showed how each mix looked at small scale. The modified resins reached better values on the measures that govern final grip. The authors say the results can yield stronger, longer-lasting joints when fiber-reinforced polymer strips are glued onto concrete members to strengthen them. The work gives a tested recipe for raising the bond between a common glue and a building material.
pmc-11596813:
Hydrogen sneaks into high-strength steel and makes it crack, and Philipp Hammer and co-authors ask whether copper specks inside the steel can act as traps, in a 2024 study. Copper matters twice over: it is a leftover in recycled steel and a deliberate hardening addition that forms tiny precipitates.

As those precipitates mature, their crystal structure marches from body-centered cubic through an intermediate 9R form to face-centered cubic, and the iron-copper boundary changes with it. Atom-level calculations show hydrogen binding at the boundary strengthens along that march, though it stays modest, about like the trapping at dislocations. Follow-up sums then show the mature cubic precipitates could still lower the risk of one embrittlement mechanism, hydrogen-fed local plasticity. The authors weigh which precipitate stage a steelmaker should aim for.
pmc-11597413:
Carlos A Martin-Blanco and five co-authors study how mayfly nymphs regrow their gills, and what that teaches about insect regeneration. The abdominal gills of Cloeon handle salt balance and gas exchange. After amputation they regrow faster than they first grew, a puzzle worth probing at the molecular level.

Cell counts showed growth sped up evenly across the whole gill, not in one hot zone. Gene activity scans found cell-cycle genes switched on early, plus protein management paths such as neddylation. The team then tested several of these genes in fruit fly wing regeneration and found the same players at work. Regeneration tricks, it seems, are shared widely across insects.
pmc-11598013:
Lina Anaya-Sampayo and co-authors tune printable living gels for building tissue models, in a 2024 study. Three-dimensional bioprinting squeezes cell-laden inks through a nozzle; the ink must flow, set quickly, and not crush its cargo. Their base ink blends seaweed alginate with gelatin, stiffened by a bone-like mineral.

Four recipes varied the mineral content from zero to ten percent. Spectroscopy confirmed the mixes, and flow tests showed the inks thinning under pressure as good printing demands. More mineral raised the consistency and doubled the stiffness recovered after setting. Skin cells riding the richest ink endured shear stress at the nozzle tip within survivable bounds, which the team computed precisely. The work helps labs pick ink recipes that print sharply while keeping cells alive.
pmc-11598913:
Rosalie Fabian and colleagues trace where a cattle herpesvirus actually lives inside its natural host. Bovine gammaherpesvirus 6 is common across European herds yet seems to cause no disease. Knowing its hideouts tests whether it truly is a harmless passenger, as its virus family habits suggest.

The team probed tissues from ten cattle with heavy viral loads, using a stain that lights up one active viral gene. Signal turned up almost nowhere: a few lone lymphocytes in chest lymph nodes, rare lung lining cells, and nothing at all in spleen or tongue. No tissue damage accompanied it. The near silence fits a commensal that keeps its head down.
pmc-11599613:
Kamal Gholipour and five co-authors report a 2024 study of scans that did not need to be done at a district hospital in Iran. Use of medical imaging keeps growing, and some scans add cost and risk with no gain. The team set out to count such scans and find what drives them.

They drew records for patients sent to the imaging unit from March to August 2022. About 28 percent of scans with abnormal results and 21 percent of scans with normal results were judged needless. The rates changed with scan type, age, and sex. Chest X-rays stood out as more often needless than brain CT scans.
pmc-11599713:
Farzam Omidi Moaf and a team of co-authors tested a special concrete under load from three sides. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, deals with two-stage concrete. Past work on this type stuck to load from one or two sides. The team made three mixes, one plain concrete and two of the new type with distinct cement amounts. They then crushed samples under three way load.

The new type, most of all the mix with finer stones, showed stronger shear strength. One peak gain was large over the plain mix. Readers who build with concrete get the first full view of how this type bears three way load. The work fills a clear gap in what was known.
pmc-11599913:
Na Wang and eight colleagues report a metal-free molecular crystal whose electric dipoles twist instead of lining up, in a 2024 paper. Twisted spin textures are famous in magnetism, but their electric cousins are rarely seen because dipoles usually align neatly. The team's organic salt switches between ferroelectric and antiferroelectric phases as conditions change.

Measurements and calculations show neighboring dipoles sit at a 60-degree twist to each other. The phase switch can then be read as a rewriting of the twist sequence along the crystal. The authors frame the result as a new playground for noncollinear polarity, with possible uses in ferroic devices.
pmc-11600613:
Pangolins moving through the illegal wildlife trade may carry coronaviruses with them. Brian Worthington and co-authors examine 89 Sunda pangolin carcasses seized in Hong Kong, mostly in 2018, and test them for signs of virus exposure. They combine virus testing with forensic work on where the animals came from.

Blood tests found one animal clearly positive for antibodies against SARS-related coronaviruses, backed by two test methods. Five more showed a possible positive on one method. Direct genetic screening found no active virus from the target families. The positive animal's genomic data helped trace its origin along trade routes. The authors stress that trafficking itself is the risk: it mixes stressed animals from wide areas. Watching seized wildlife, they argue, is a window on spillover threats.
pmc-11601213:
A large team of researchers finds a new control on a DNA repair enzyme in cancer in a paper from 2024. The enzyme, PARP1, helps fix broken DNA and is a known drug target. Its partner in the study, EZH2, adds small chemical tags to proteins. The team shows EZH2 tags PARP1 directly, and that tagging dials down the enzyme's repair activity.

Tagging also keeps PARP1 from draining a key cell fuel during damage response. It further weakens a growth-driving partnership inside cancer cells. Blocking both proteins at once suppressed prostate cancer growth more than either block alone. The authors propose the pair as a combined drug target. Their work adds a fine-tuning layer to repair control.
pmc-11602113:
Victor Nzengong Juru and co-authors study how an invasive weed changes soil in the Mount Cameroon region in a paper from 2024. The weed, Chromolaena odorata, spreads fast and harms local ecosystems. Its roots leak chemicals that can reshape soil and its microbes.

The team sampled soil at four levels of invasion, from none to heavy, across four sites. They measured soil chemistry, microbe counts, and enzyme activity. At medium invasion, levels of phosphorus, potassium, and iron in root-zone soil rose. Friendly root fungi also shifted with invasion level. The gradient view shows that harm builds step by step. Land managers can use such signs to act early.
pmc-11602913:
Marc Pretze and co-authors describe how to make a radioactive drug, built around lead-212, under strict drug-making rules. The drug targets tumors and pairs with a twin form of lead used for scans, so doctors can plan doses before treatment. Lead-212 may fill a gap between gentler radiation drugs and stronger ones that can harm the kidneys.

The paper walks through a compliant production process for the labeled compound. Careful production matters because the drug decays quickly and must be pure and safe for patients. The authors set out the steps and checks their lab used. Their method supports wider clinical use of this matched pair, where a scan with one form guides therapy with the other.
pmc-11603313:
Meixia Geng and four co-authors map the buried plumbing of the Moon's largest volcanic plain from gravity data. Their 2024 study uses measurements from the GRAIL mission, whose twin craft sensed tiny gravity shifts over Oceanus Procellarum. Density models built from those signals reveal the frozen magma system below the basalt surface.

Long linear magma bodies line the region's western border, with heavy intrusions under the northern and southern Marius Hills. Three narrow, near-flat conduits, 80 to 150 kilometers long, run from near the surface down to about 6 or 7 kilometers deep. Those sheets link the hills to each other and to the border system, marking highways that magma once used to cross the region. The picture makes sideways magma flow a central actor in lunar volcanic history.
pmc-11603813:
Yeabsra Mesfin Seifu, Negussie Deyessa, and Yimer Seid Yimer run a case-control study of weight and gestational diabetes in Addis Ababa antenatal clinics, in a two thousand twenty-four maternal health paper. Both conditions are rising across developing countries.

One hundred fifty-nine women with gestational diabetes were compared with four hundred seventy-seven without, using mid-upper arm circumference for weight status. Obesity nearly tripled the odds of gestational diabetes; overweight alone did not reach significance. Prior caesarean section and low dietary diversity also raised odds, while high physical activity cut them by about seventy-two percent. The authors recommend screening obese pregnant women and counseling on weight, diet diversity, and activity.
pmc-11603913:
Xuefei Pang and colleagues pooled studies in 2024 on laser care for cleft lip scars. Surgery repairs the lip, but scars remain. The best scar treatment is still disputed. The team searched five databases for laser studies. They checked study quality and bias with standard tools. Five studies qualified, with a few hundred subjects in total. Scar scores came from a standard Vancouver scale. The team combined results with care for uneven study designs.

Laser-treated scars scored better than control scars overall. The benefit looked strongest in early treatment stages. Yet confidence in the finding stayed low. Studies disagreed with each other to a very high degree. That spread weakens any firm claim. The authors still judge the laser a useful option. They frame the gain as a tendency needing stronger trials. The review gives surgeons a cautious summary of current proof.
pmc-11604013:
Chen Yongzhong and co-authors probed how a traditional Chinese medicine formula treats heart failure in a 2024 rat study. The jianxin granules are patented for heart failure, but their effects and pathways were not fully known. Protein and metabolite profiling were used to trace the mechanism.

Heart failure was induced in rats by tying a heart artery. Treated rats showed better pumping, less scarring, and healthier cell powerhouses than untreated ones. The formula also eased oxidative stress and cell death signals. Protein and metabolite profiles pointed to pathways the treatment adjusted. Lab tests supported the picture, suggesting the granules protect the failing heart through several routes at once.
pmc-11604713:
Early cell changes on the cervix can grow into cancer if left alone, yet the standard fix cuts away tissue and can harm later births. Yidi Liu and co-authors compare that cut with a light-based cure in a 2024 study from a hospital in China. The light cure uses a cream that makes bad cells react to light, so no tissue is removed.

Records ran from 2012 to 2019, and the team matched thirty pairs of patients with like traits. Full clearing of the changes was close in both groups, as was clearing of the virus that drives most cases. Results held across mild and more marked grades of change. The authors present the light cure as a gentler, repeatable choice that keeps the cervix whole, with results on par with surgery for these patients.
pmc-11604913:
Seiji Ishikawa and colleagues studied in 2024 which factors around anesthesia track with acute kidney injury soon after surgery to remove the esophagus for cancer. Such injury is a known risk of this major operation, but the role of anesthesia choices was unclear. Records covered more than a thousand patients over fourteen years.

About five percent developed kidney injury within seventy-two hours, mostly at a mild stage. Those patients were older and more often had high blood pressure, chronic kidney disease, blood transfusions, and longer anesthesia. Epidural anesthesia was less common among them, and in adjusted analysis it linked to lower risk. No other anesthesia factor, such as inhaled drug choice, showed a clear link.
pmc-11605113:
Paul Richardson and co-authors validate the newest staging system for multiple myeloma in two large trials of relapsed disease. The second revision of the International Staging System folds in a chromosome gain, 1q21, and stacks multiple high-risk features. Their 2024 analysis pools 609 patients from the ICARIA-MM and IKEMA trials, both testing an antibody added to standard doublets.

The revised stages sorted patients by progression-free survival as designed: each higher stage carried a clearly larger risk of early progression than stage one. About a quarter of patients landed in a 'not classified' bucket, a wrinkle the authors report plainly. Adding the antibody lengthened progression-free survival across every stage, roughly halving the hazard. The study is the first validation of the revised system with modern antibody therapy in relapsed myeloma.
pmc-11605813:
Montgomery Dunn and colleagues published a systematic review in 2024. They studied literacy and health in Traveller communities. Gypsies, Roma, and Travellers face poor health outcomes. They are among the most disadvantaged groups in many countries. Literacy rates are often lower than average too. Earlier work focused mostly on health literacy alone. The link between basic literacy and health was unclear. The team searched major databases and grey literature.

Only a small set of studies qualified for review. Just over fifteen studies were analyzed in depth. Four overlapping themes emerged from the findings. Care systems often fail cultural needs of patients. Low literacy can bring shame and disempowerment. Social factors and personal needs interact strongly. Health information needs formats that truly fit readers. The review calls for services designed with communities.
pmc-11606013:
Onat Yetim and co-authors map the two-way traffic between empathy and behavior problems in young teenagers. Two thousand one hundred fifty parents first screened their ten to twelve year olds for symptoms. A final group of one hundred seventy adolescents then completed empathy measures and executive function tests, after a pilot checked the film scenes used to stir feelings.

Working memory and outward behavior problems predicted thinking empathy, while only behavior problems predicted feeling empathy. In reverse, both empathy kinds strongly predicted fewer outward problems, and poor inhibition predicted inner distress. Inner symptoms and empathy showed no link at all. The authors suggest executive training and empathy work could reinforce each other in early adolescence interventions.
pmc-11606213:
Yilun Li, Xiaolu Yang, and Li Ma build a learning model to forecast survival for a recently defined group of breast cancer patients. These tumors show only low levels of the HER2 marker, which puts them between the classic groups and has drawn new drug interest. The team studied 998 women treated at one Chinese hospital from 2017 to 2020, balancing the data and sifting features before training the model.

Their random survival forest beat rival methods, predicting freedom from disease return at one, two, and three years with the best accuracy. Poor outlook tracked with node surgery, family history, advanced stage, and several marker patterns, including a missing hormone receptor and a mutated guard gene. The authors offer the model as an aid to planning care.
pmc-11607313:
Qing Li and co-authors build a vaccine that also helps grow cancer-fighting T cells in mice. Their twenty twenty-four paper uses dendritic cells loaded with tumor material. The aim is adoptive cell transfer, where a patient gets trained immune cells.

Such cells are hard to pull from the body, which limits the treatment. The vaccine sparked a response to new tumor markers in lung cancer mice. It also helped the team grow marker-reactive T cells in a dish. When those cells went back into treated mice, they reached the tumor. More local T cells joined in, and the combined plan fought the cancer better.
pmc-11607513:
Xiaohui Xu and co-authors study how often people at high heart risk eat various foods, and how that tracks with later heart disease. Their 2024 study follows nearly twenty-nine thousand high-risk adults. Outcomes counted heart attacks and strokes together.

Daily egg eating and daily seafood eating each went with lower disease risk in their models, by the trend across intake levels. A prediction chart was built from six body and habit factors plus three foods: fruit, egg, and seafood. The chart sorted future cases from non-cases with fair accuracy in both build and test groups. The authors present it as dietary guidance under a food-as-medicine idea, for people already at high risk.
pmc-11607813:
Kurt Hofmann and colleagues report first clinic use of a new bone matrix in foot fusions, in work from 2024. Foot and ankle fusion needs graft bone, yet a patient's own supply runs short. A next generation matrix claims growing, guiding, and sparking bone traits built in.

Charts of twenty fusion patients treated with the matrix were reviewed back to surgery. No major complications or repeat surgeries appeared across the tracked group. Every patient reached full scan confirmed fusion by twenty-four weeks after surgery. Average fusion time sat near eight and a half weeks in the cohort. Pain, function, and life quality scores all hit meaningful gains by then.
pmc-11607913:
Deep infection after orthopedic trauma surgery can undo a repair and threaten the limb. Huan Liu, Yanan Wang, Hao Xing, Zhengqi Chang, and Junlin Pan pooled 16 studies covering 22,318 patients, of whom 894 developed deep surgical site infections, to find what raises the risk. The combined infection rate was 6.7 percent across the included studies.

Risk was higher for men, current smokers, open injuries, higher body mass index, dirtier wounds, and operations lasting an hour or more, while age showed no clear effect. The authors present the list as guidance for prevention and closer monitoring of high-risk patients after trauma surgery.
pmc-11608213:
Graff and seven co-authors look for warning signs of lung decline in asthma in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Asthma can speed the loss of lung function over the years. The team followed one hundred twenty-five adults from a clinic in Liège. Each was tested again at least five years later. They compared patients whose breathing measure fell fast with those whose held steadier.

Blood and sputum markers were tracked across both visits. A rising blood eosinophil count over time flagged faster decline. So did a sputum signal called IL8. These cheap measures may help doctors spot patients who need stronger control of their asthma. The study is a step toward personal follow-up in a common disease.
pmc-11608313:
Jose Mendoza-Carreño and co-authors build one printed platform that twists white light into a corkscrew, whatever emitter sits on it, in a 2024 paper. Circularly polarised light serves displays, imaging, and communications, but polarising filters waste brightness. Better to make the light source emit twisted light directly. Ordinary emitters are not chiral, so the authors lend them chirality with a patterned surface whose resonances span the whole visible spectrum.

Made by soft nanoimprint lithography, a cheap, scalable stamping method, the platform hosted five different emitters, from quantum dots to perovskite crystals and a polymer. All emerged emitting strongly circularly polarised light. The single design replaces a shelf of narrow-band structures and avoids fragile nanofabrication. The authors pitch it toward integrated light sources that sip power on chips and screens.
pmc-11609313:
Federica Barutta and co-authors tested stem cell rescue in diabetic kidneys in two thousand twenty-four. Diabetes damages podocytes, the cells that filter blood. Their power units fail early in that damage. Neighboring cells can share power units through tiny tubes. Mesenchymal stromal cells are eager donors of such units. Whether they tube-connect to podocytes was unknown.

The team grew podocytes stressed by diabetes-like insults. Stromal cells were then cultured alongside them. Tube formation and power unit transfer were tracked. Injury markers showed whether rescue actually occurred. Diabetic donor cells were compared with healthy ones. Mice with kidney disease received the cells as treatment. Tagged power units revealed transfer inside living tissue.
pmc-11609413:
Liuyi Huang and co-authors study a blood marker for muscle diseases in a 2024 paper. The diseases, called idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, fall into four subgroups. The team asked whether a protein named LGALS3BP can tell the subgroups apart.

They first mined a public gene database and picked LGALS3BP as a candidate marker. They then enrolled 84 patients and 36 healthy controls and measured the protein in blood. Levels fell in a steady order across the disease subgroups and the healthy group. Levels also tracked with clinical features and inflammation markers. The authors present the protein as a helpful aid for sorting these diseases.
pmc-11610313:
Manqing Peng and six co-authors review two immune checkpoints, PSGL-1 and VISTA, in this 2024 paper. Checkpoints are brakes that keep immune responses from attacking the self. Both molecules are common on blood derived cells, including T cells and myeloid cells. VISTA works two ways: on myeloid cells it steers them toward a tolerant state, and on T cells it helps keep them quiet. PSGL-1 binds VISTA and adds its own brake on T cell activation, especially in the acidic setting of tumors.

Together the pair helps tumors hide from immunity. The review covers their structures, expression patterns, and jobs in detail. Blocking them could free the immune system against cancer. The same brakes, strengthened, might calm autoimmune disease or protect transplants. The authors present the pair as a joint target rather than two separate ones.
pmc-11611513:
Theogene Kubahoniyesu and Florence Namalinzi study the timing of first sex among young women in Rwanda in a 2024 paper. Knowing when sexual life begins helps shape health policy for the young, yet Rwanda had little data on the question. The pair drew on a national health survey from 2019 and 2020 and used survival methods to find the median age and its drivers.

More than a third of young women had their first experience before age twenty-five, and a small share before age fifteen, with a median age of eighteen. Older youth, rural living, higher schooling, marriage, and weekly radio listening each went with a later start. The authors suggest that more schooling, stable partnerships, and media access in rural areas could delay first sex.
pmc-11611913:
Xia Wang and co-authors trace how a hormone-blocking drug may lower ovarian cancer risk in women at high inherited risk. The drug, flutamide, blocks male hormone signals, a pathway now tied to this cancer's start. Their 2024 study began with tissue from high-risk women, some treated with the drug and some not, plus tissue from low-risk women for comparison.

Drug treatment brought the tissues' small RNA profile back toward the low-risk pattern, lifting a family called miR-449. In lab cells, the drug raised those same RNAs, and adding copies of them cut levels of two proteins that drive the cancer: the hormone receptor itself and a growth signal receiver. Cancer cells also moved less. The authors say the drug fights the pathway twice over, and may suit prevention for women with low miR-449.
pmc-11612213:
The authors profile individual cells from the left atrium to find signals tied to atrial fibrillation, a rhythm disorder linked to stroke and heart failure. Combining single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing, they sorted the tissue's immune cells into five macrophage groups, three monocyte groups, and others. Communication analysis showed monocytes and one macrophage type sending growth signals to fibroblasts, the cells that lay down scar tissue.

One gene stood out. Amphiregulin was the most strongly raised gene in those immune cells in patients with the disorder, and blood levels of its protein ran higher in people with persistent disease. The authors propose the growth signal pathway as a possible drug target. They also suggest blood amphiregulin could help flag patients whose condition will persist.
pmc-11612513: Li Jian and co-authors report a rare case, in a 2024 paper, in which a fluid-filled sac formed after surgery in front of the sacrum. The patient had a neuroendocrine tumor there that had spread to the liver. Surgeons removed the tumor fully, and the patient also received a targeted drug, sulfatinib, plus heat ablation. The authors warn that poor healing of the wound in this hidden spot, possibly worsened by targeted drugs, can let such cysts form. They urge teams to weigh that risk before operating.
pmc-11612713:
Guo-Heng Jiang and co-authors studied links among three stone and liver diseases in a 2024 paper. Gallstone disease, fatty liver disease, and kidney stone disease may each raise the risk of the others. Past results were mixed, and data from China were thin.

The team ran a multi-centre study of people at health checks in three Chinese cities, plus a review and pooled analysis of past work. Both parts found two-way links among all three diseases, even after adjusting for other factors. A further test judged the pooled proof strong enough to trust. The findings may help doctors spot high-risk patients early.
pmc-11613313:
Ping Sun, Chunyan Zhang, Weisha Wang, and Huagang Ma review how uterine fibroids make the womb lining less ready for pregnancy, in a 2024 article. Fibroids are the most common benign tumors of the female reproductive tract, and even painless ones can lower the chance of conception. Types that press into the cavity clearly hurt outcomes, while the effect of one deep type is still argued.

Beyond simple pressure, fibroids release signaling chemicals, alter blood flow and vessel growth, and change the womb's squeezing motion and inner environment. Faulty signal pathways complete the picture the authors draw. They argue that mapping these routes is the path to better treatment and higher pregnancy rates.
pmc-11613913:
Charlotte Ling and a large team profiled in 2024 muscle tissue from identical twin pairs where only one twin has type 2 diabetes. Because the twins share genes, differences point to environment and gene regulation. They measured three molecular layers in biopsies from twenty pairs: gene activity, small regulatory RNAs, and chemical marks on DNA.

Genes for muscle contraction, fuel burning, and sugar uptake were dialed down in the diabetic twins. Small RNAs targeting many of those pathways were altered too. Chemical marks on DNA differed only slightly. Lab experiments confirmed two small RNAs could blunt insulin signaling in cultured muscle cells. The authors argue that acquired regulation, not DNA sequence, carries much of diabetes-related muscle insulin resistance.
pmc-11614013:
Waleed Al Saadi and four co-authors report a case where wet cupping coincided with fewer pancreas attacks in a man with inherited high triglycerides, in a paper from 2024. The genetic condition floods blood with fat particles and can trigger repeat pancreas inflammation. Cupping is a traditional therapy used in many cultures.

The 34-year-old man was treated at a hospital in Muscat, Oman in 2022 for acute-on-chronic pancreatitis. After cupping joined his regimen, his blood fat levels fell notably at his last visit. Admissions for acute attacks also dropped after cupping began. The authors present the case as a signal needing controlled study, not proof.
pmc-11614513:
Linyuan Fan and co-authors show how a long noncoding RNA helps stem cells turn into bone-forming cells, in a study from 2024. The RNA, EMX2-AS, rises as mesenchymal stem cells mature toward bone. Its partner gene, EMX2, holds that same process back.

Adding more of the RNA sped bone formation in dishes and in mice, while cutting it slowed both. Most of the RNA sits in the cell body outside the nucleus during this switch. It binds EMX2 and blocks its protein from being made, without cutting its message. A known growth pathway, Wnt and beta-catenin, also takes part in the effect. The authors offer the pair as a fresh target for diseases of poor bone growth.
pmc-11614813:
Wei He and co-authors built a deep learning platform in a 2024 study to spot parasite eggs. Worm infections are still common, and the standard check, hunting eggs under a microscope, is slow, tiring, and easy to get wrong. A tireless automated read could speed clinics and cut missed cases.

The team trained a YOLOv4 image model on eggs of human worm species, among them the large roundworm, the whipworm, and the pinworm. The model learns the eggs' shapes from photos and flags them in new slides. Such a platform could bring expert-grade reads to small labs that lack trained staff.
pmc-11615113:
Thyen published in twenty twenty-four a discussion of early preventive services for young children in Germany. These services support families before problems grow severe. Their future depends on firm structures, skilled staff, and family acceptance. Thyen traces the field's roots to the early twentieth century. Evidence from brain science, attachment research, and family studies is gathered. Trauma research and health economics also inform the account.

From that base, requirements for growth are derived. A health-in-all-policies strategy anchors the proposals, with child poverty in focus. Interprofessional learning and inclusive access for all children are stressed. Proof of benefit needs long-term, independent research programs, Thyen argues. Evaluation methods for such complex services exist but need development. The piece sets a development agenda for the German system.
pmc-11616113:
Haiming Wang and eight co-authors pooled trial results on iron given by vein to people with heart failure and low iron, in a review from twenty twenty-four. Past trials disagreed on whether the treatment cuts hospital stays and deaths, and on its safety. The team searched the main medical databases for trials that assigned patients by chance.

Eleven trials with more than six thousand patients met their rules. Iron by vein cut the combined risk of heart failure hospital stays and heart-related death. It also cut hospital stays on their own. Deaths from all causes, though, did not fall in a clear way. Longer treatment courses showed stronger gains, and side effects looked no worse overall.
pmc-11616313:
Xueyan Wang and co-authors search in 2024 for genes that help liver cancer cells survive detachment and dodge the immune system. A cell torn from its matrix should normally die; cancer cells that resist that death can spread. The tissue scaffolding around a tumor also shapes immune attack, which often fades in this cancer.

Joining several omics layers, the team flagged one gene tied to both detachment resistance and immune traits. The gene codes a blood protein best known for dissolving clots. Its signal sorted patients into groups with distinct outlooks. A marker of this kind could help pick who gains from immune therapy. It also points at the scaffold as a drug target in its own right.
pmc-11616413:
Chuan Foo, David Langton, and Francis Thien report repeat asthma treatment cases in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Bronchial thermoplasty uses heat inside the airways to ease severe asthma. The team describes six patients who had the treatment twice because their asthma stayed poorly controlled.

The repeat sessions were well tolerated, with no unexpected problems. One patient showed a mild widened airway area on a scan six months later, but it caused no symptoms. Responses varied widely between patients. Some improved a great deal after the second round, while others did not. The authors say repeat treatment is feasible and may help a chosen few, though benefit is not assured.
pmc-11617113:
Heart rehab works, but which behavior tricks inside app-based rehab do the heavy lifting is unclear. Emma R Douma and co-authors sort the evidence in a 2024 systematic review. Eighty-eight trials with over twenty-five thousand heart patients were gathered from four databases. Each program's behavior techniques were coded from a standard taxonomy. Thirty-one distinct techniques appeared across the set.

Plain instruction on how to perform a behavior showed up in nearly every study. Evidence strength for each technique was graded from strong to absent. Bias checks used a public-health appraisal tool. Digital rehab can widen access, the authors note, which is why its parts matter. The review guides designers toward proven ingredients.
pmc-11617313:
Kerrie Stevenson and fourteen co-authors review what improves maternity care for migrant women in rich countries. Their 2024 systematic review gathers public health, policy, and clinical programs. Migrant mothers and babies face worse birth outcomes than host populations. The team hunted for programs proven to close that gap.

Searches across many databases found twenty-nine studies. Together they held data on over sixteen million women. Care spanned pregnancy, birth, and the first year after. Key outcomes were early birth, birthweight, and showing up for care. Chart-based synthesis compared programs without forcing one pooled number. The review maps which kinds of help carry evidence behind them. Gaps in the map mark where trials should go next.
pmc-11618213:
Stefania Paduano and six co-authors characterize bacterial communities in thermal muds from two spas of an Italian complex by gene sequencing. Peloids form when clay matures in thermo mineral water and gains organic matter from microbes. Their healing reputation may rest on clay, water, and microbes together, yet hard evidence is lacking.

Waters and muds at two, four, and six months of maturation are profiled by 16S amplicon sequencing, which captures cultivable and uncultivable bacteria alike. Peloid communities differ sharply from the waters that made them. Muds from natural clay show greater richness than muds from sterile clay. Sulfur metabolism genera dominate in both spas, as expected for sulfide rich waters. The method gives a baseline for quality control of spa peloids.
pmc-11618313:
Manon Soulier and co-authors test cold plasma as a tool against bile duct cancer cells. Their 2024 paper uses a device that makes plasma with a piezoelectric source, small enough to be portable. Cold plasma can trigger cancer cell death, but its power against this aggressive cancer was little known.

The device can run in two discharge modes, one stronger and one gentler. Both made high levels of reactive species in gas and liquid. Plasma treatment warmed the culture in a gradient pattern, more with the stronger mode. On human cancer cells, effects were local for one mode and even for the other. Treated cells reshaped their inner skeleton and later switched on DNA damage responses. The work maps how this new device acts, a step toward portable cancer tools.
pmc-11618413:
Macarena Siri, Mónica Vázquez-Dávila, Carolina Sotelo Guzman, and Cécile Bidan present a 2024 study of how food supply changes the fabric of bacterial biofilms. A biofilm of gut bacteria builds a shared matrix for strength, and its key beams are amyloid fibers called curli. Whether lean times change the fibers themselves was unknown.

The team grew films on rich and poor media, then measured stiffness and fiber counts. Lean grown films came out stiffer and richer in fibers. Extracted fibers from lean films also held more of the sheet structure linked to strength, and resisted chemical breakdown better. The work links diet like conditions to material design at two scales at once.
pmc-11618813:
Wechsler leads a large team reporting two year results for an asthma biologic, in work from twenty twenty-four. Tezepelumab treats severe, uncontrolled asthma. Trials ask not only whether patients respond, but whether they reach clinical remission: long term disease stability.

Results came from the NAVIGATOR and DESTINATION studies over two years. Proportions of patients who responded, and who reached on treatment remission, were measured in a broad severe asthma population. Remission as a goal changes asthma care from symptom control toward lasting quiet disease. Two year data show whether that ambition is realistic for this drug class.
pmc-11619113:
Renke Luhken and co-authors test whether a mosquito found in Germany can pass on chikungunya virus when the weather is cool, in work from 2024. This mosquito species spreads the virus in warm regions. Its spread into temperate Europe has raised concern about local outbreaks.

Mosquitoes were raised in the lab, fed virus, and kept at steady and shifting temperatures. After two weeks the team checked infection and spread rates. The mosquitoes could carry the virus well, yet they moved far less at low temperatures. That low activity may cut the real risk of spread in cool spells, even when the virus can grow inside them.
pmc-11619213:
Kang Zhao and co-authors compared two ways to open clogged heart arteries in this 2024 study. One uses a balloon coated with a drug that soaks into the vessel wall. The other leaves behind a metal stent that releases drug over time. The patients had fresh blockages in large heart arteries.

Hospital records covered thousands of lesions, then matching narrowed the groups to about seven hundred each. The balloon group needed repeat treatment on the same spot more often over two years. But major bleeding was rarer with balloons, since patients can stop blood thinners sooner. The authors back balloons for patients at high bleeding risk, and stents for most others.
pmc-11619613:
Weak bones are usually confirmed with scans, but deep learning may spot osteoporosis from images already on hand. Amani and co-authors gathered studies that tested such models and pooled their accuracy. From 181 papers found, ten met the bar, and all of them used convolutional networks, with some testing several designs built on known image backbones.

Pooled across studies, the models caught about 86 percent of true cases and cleared about 89 percent of healthy ones, with an overall discrimination score near 0.94. A bias check came back clean. The authors call the showing acceptable and better than older machine learning, while asking for proper clinical trials before routine use. Clinics would gain a second reading tool.
pmc-11619713:
Xia Ren, Zhaoxia Tian, and Hongmei Li study fear of low blood sugar in older adults with diabetes in a paper from 2024. Long illness and many medicines raise the chance of low blood sugar episodes in older patients. Repeated episodes breed fear, which burdens mood and self-care. The team surveyed seventy-eight community patients with standard scales for fear, well-being, and family support.

Low schooling, long disease course, and frequent past episodes raised fear. Prevention education, good well-being, and strong family support lowered it. Family support also carried part of the link between well-being and fear. The authors advise teaching patients and caregivers together. Strengthening family support is presented as a practical lever.
pmc-11623313:
A hands-on therapy that frees tight tissue in the belly wall has eased gut pain in adults, and it may help children too. Anish Rana and nine co-authors test whether such care can be given to children with irritable bowel syndrome at all. Their 2024 study is a first step: a check of feasibility and of how families take to it.

The syndrome brings long belly pain, bloating, and changed toilet habits, and it drags down daily life. Drugs for it are few and often fall short. No past study had tried this massage-style care in children with the syndrome. The team sets out how the sessions run and what counts as a workable, welcome plan. A firm result here would clear the way for a full trial of effect.
pmc-11624113:
Middleton and co-authors explore in 2024 how nurses and allied health staff keep using leadership skills after a postgraduate program. The study used an appreciative inquiry approach in one health district that ran a 12 month program with a regional university. Four group interviews covered 11 staff in all.

Themes grouped the lasting effects into self, others, relationships, and sustained leadership itself. All participants said the program changed how they lead across settings and interactions. The work shows how leadership teaching moves into daily clinical practice, and what helps those habits persist after the course ends.
pmc-11624713:
Shi-Lin Wei and co-authors tested a steroid drug in rats on heart-lung machine support with injured lungs in a 2024 study. Dexamethasone earned its place treating severe COVID-19 lung failure. Venovenous ECMO, which oxygenates blood outside the body, supports the sickest patients with acute respiratory distress, and its use has grown worldwide.

Whether the steroid also helps lungs during ECMO was unknown, and ECMO's circuit itself inflames the body. The rat model lets the team isolate the drug's effect under controlled support. Lung injury scores and inflammation markers answer the question. A benefit would be easy to adopt, since the drug is cheap and familiar to every intensive care team.
pmc-11626413:
Aqel Albutti wrote this solo 2024 study designing a prostate cancer vaccine entirely on a computer. Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men, and current treatments lack precision. The design starts from an enzyme tied to inflammation and tumor growth, and fishes out the fragments of it that immune cells can learn to recognize.

Stitching chosen fragments together produced a multi-part vaccine blueprint. Its gene code scored well for being read by bacteria, a first step toward making it in a lab. Simulated immune responses showed strong signals of the right kind. Docking tests placed the vaccine snugly against immune receptors, and long motion simulations kept the pairing stable. The author stresses these are in silico results, a map for lab work rather than a finished medicine. Still, the construct offers a concrete candidate for testing.
pmc-11626713:
Todd Becker and co-authors poll US rest-home staff on aid-in-dying views and what shapes them. The study appeared in 2024. Talk on the theme runs hot, yet reads sel-dom weigh the work-place frame round views. Near four hundred fifty staff cross four trades took the poll.

Half were docs, with nurses, social hands, and faith hands the rest. Work in a state where the act is law tied to more than twice the odds of aid views. Faith in the home's no-haste rule pulled views the next way. Care-first lean and home-value faith were read the same way. The math let each pull show its own weight.
pmc-11628313:
Xinrui Luo and co-authors mine a national survey for links between womens androgen levels, metabolic syndrome, and heart disease in a 2024 study. Male-pattern hormones in women are suspected metabolic troublemakers, but population proof is patchy. Nutrition survey data from 2013 to 2016 supplied hormone and health measures.

Women with high androgen readings, and those in the top hormone bands generally, carried bigger waists, higher weight, and higher body mass. Regression models then tied the hormone markers to syndrome and disease odds, and survival models to death. The analysis argues androgen checks deserve a place in womens risk workups.
pmc-11630013:
Penpa Yeshe and Fang Li pool past trials in a 2024 meta-analysis on care for advanced cervical cancer that stays in the pelvis. The standard care pairs chemo with radiation at the same time. The pair ask if adding chemo first, with the drugs paclitaxel and cisplatin, helps women live longer and stay free of the disease. They screened the past work and kept eight studies for the pooled sums.

Women who got the added chemo lived longer at two, three, and five years than women who got standard care alone. They also stayed free of the disease longer and had fuller shrinkage of the tumor. Rates of a return of the disease were lower. Side effects such as low blood counts were no worse than with standard care, the pooled data show.
pmc-11630313:
Rachel L Hawkins and co-authors review research on unequal care for adults with inflammatory bowel disease, in a 2024 scoping review. These bowel diseases cannot be cured and need care for life, so gaps in access matter. The team searched three databases for studies published between 2000 and 2023.

Fifty-one studies met their rules. Most dealt with health outcomes, fewer with access to care, and only eight with what care feels like for patients. Race and ethnic gaps were studied most, then income, rural life, and gender. Patients from Black, Asian, and Hispanic groups had worse outcomes in many studies. The authors note whole groups with almost no research, such as gay and trans patients, and call for more work that asks patients directly.
pmc-11631213: Kalyan Kumar Das and Rajdeep Basu report a rare dengue case in a 2024 paper. A man of twenty-six arrived with fever, vomiting, and stomach pain. He went on to develop severe pancreatitis, an uncommon dengue complication. His illness also brought ketoacidosis, a dangerous acid build-up, even without high blood sugar. The authors stress one lesson for clinics in dengue regions. Stomach pain in a dengue patient should prompt checks for acute pancreatitis. Missing it can badly complicate treatment.
pmc-11631713:
Charlotte Brinkmann and co-authors study XopM, a protein that the plant pathogen Xanthomonas injects into host cells to weaken immunity. This bacterium causes spot disease on tomato and pepper and sends in dozens of such effector proteins. XopM's function was unknown and it resembles no other known protein.

They find XopM binds a family of membrane proteins through two copies of a short motif, in a selective way. In plants, XopM helped a harmless bacterium grow and damped an early immune burst. Binding and immune suppression can be separated, but XopM must reach the host membrane system for full effect. The authors propose it targets membranes to blunt early defenses.
pmc-11631913:
Most studies of COVID-19 blood markers focus on patients already in hospital, yet choices about who needs admission happen much earlier. Andrea Alemany and co-authors, in 2024, tested thirty-nine immune and vessel markers in outpatients with mild or moderate illness. Their nested study drew on a trial of convalescent plasma in patients aged fifty and up.

They compared forty-two patients who were admitted within twenty-eight days with forty-two who were not. Nine markers measured in the first week already separated the groups well, and three stood out across both admission and severe disease. One marker best predicted admission, and another best predicted severe illness. The authors say such early tests could help clinics judge risk before symptoms force the issue.
pmc-11632013:
Seven authors, led by Alexander Hermann, lay out in 2024 how their Vienna intensive care unit starts lung bypass support at outside hospitals and then moves the patient. Sending a mobile team to begin the support on site avoids a risky first transfer of a failing patient. But working in a strange setting adds strain to an already hard task.

Their paper walks through a decision tree protocol built for that work. It covers how patients are picked, how the team is organized, and how the transport itself is run. The unit tuned global advice to its own setting, and shares the result as a working model for other centers.
pmc-11632113:
Quinn and co-authors present a navigation aid, published in 2024, that guides blind users by changing shape in the hand. White canes and guide dogs remain the main tools for getting around. Satellite positioning could transform travel for blind people, but screens and voices convey exact directions poorly. The team's device bends its body to point the way in two directions at once. Users hold it and feel where it wants them to go.

Blind and sighted users tried the device against a buzzing-feedback control. Their task was to find virtual targets in space. The shape-changing guide let users locate targets with strong accuracy. Because the guidance is felt, it leaves the ears free for traffic and speech. The authors argue that touch-based direction is the missing link between positioning tech and safe, independent travel.
pmc-11633013:
The authors map expression of a tight junction protein across cancers in a 2024 tissue microarray study. The protein helps seal gaps between cells, and its altered levels are linked to tumor growth. Because disorganized cancer tissue may expose it more than healthy tissue, it is a candidate drug target.

Arrays held nearly fifteen thousand tumor samples across more than one hundred tumor types, plus normal tissue controls. Staining appeared in about two thirds of analyzable tumors, and over half stained strongly. Positivity spanned most tumor categories. Clinical significance by cancer type is analyzed in the full report.
pmc-11634613:
Danyang Li, Haoyi Du, and Na Wu link blood fatty acids to bad outcomes in pregnancy diabetes in a 2024 study. Women with gestational diabetes face higher risks of problems for mother and baby. The team profiled free fatty acids in second trimester blood from one hundred forty four affected women and fifty two healthy pregnant controls.

Fatty acid patterns differed between the groups. One saturated fat, stearic acid, differed between women with normal and adverse outcomes, with a possible tie to fetal sex. Moderate and high levels of that fat were linked to lower odds of bad outcomes. Used alone it predicted outcomes modestly, and combining it with other measures improved prediction. The authors suggest fatty acid profiling could flag high risk pregnancies early.
pmc-11634913:
Hannah Jilani and co-authors linked taste skill to food choice in a 2024 study across eight European countries. The study covered children, teens, and adults living freely at home. It asked whether people who can rank sweet and fat tastes well also eat sweet and fatty foods at distinct rates.

In total, 461 children and 421 teens took part, along with adults, all tested with the same set method. Taste ranks were set against how often each person ate sweet and fatty foods. Past work had rarely joined the two in free-living groups of mixed ages. The findings help show how the senses steer daily diet across the life span.
pmc-11635313:
Ann Sato and colleagues pilot an AI chatbot as a first-pass genetic counselor, in a clinical study from twenty twenty-four. Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk often goes unscreened. Their chatbot checks whether someone meets testing criteria for the BRCA genes. Eleven patients at a cancer center tried it.

Every participant completed the chatbot session unaided. It took about eighteen minutes on average. Most had never used a chatbot before; some had never heard of one. Ten of the eleven participants had cancer themselves. Interviews probed usability and acceptability afterward. The chatbot's criteria judgments were checked against clinical standards. The authors present the tool as feasible for preliminary screening. It could widen access where human counselors are scarce.
pmc-11635513:
Qi Zhang and co-authors develop an alkali-free microemulsion to squeeze more oil from a mature Chinese oilfield block, in a 2024 study. The standard three-part chemical flood works but scales pipes and costs heavily. Replacing the weak base kept the system gentler yet weakened its emulsifying power, so the team compounded surfactants, alcohol, and salt to restore performance.

In lab flow tests the SDBS-based version cut oil viscosity best, reached extremely low oil-water tension, and lifted recovery to about forty-seven percent while dropping water cut. Molecular simulations showed it loosening oil's grip on rock, and field-scale modeling predicted recovery well above water flooding. The authors back it as a cheaper, cleaner flood for the block.
pmc-11636213:
Alana Ayasse and co-authors report a 2024 study of how well air and space sensors catch methane leaks. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, and satellites are fast becoming a main tool to find its sources. Mixing data from many sensors could sharpen the picture, but each sensor's detection odds must be known.

In August 2023, the team timed airborne surveys to overlap with passes of a NASA satellite instrument called EMIT. The shared views let them measure and verify the satellite's detection limits under good conditions. They also built a statistical model to judge whether a silent sensor means a source was truly off. That model helps correct averages for steady sources that sensors miss part of the time. The work supports joint use of airborne and satellite data.
pmc-11637313:
Michiel Vanslambrouck and co-authors read cell forces from microscope images in this 2024 study. Growing embryos are shaped by forces cells make as they pull, divide, and push. Older image methods missed effects like tight spaces and local force spots, so the team built a physics-based model of cell shape.

Their method infers surface pull, glue-like pull between cells, and forces from division and bulges. Applied to early worm embryo images, it tracked force patterns across stages. Laser cuts to cell skins confirmed the predicted pull at the seven-cell stage. The authors offer the method as a non-invasive way to follow force in growing tissue.
pmc-11637513:
Andrew Larkin and co-authors use in 2024 a clever wind test to gauge how traffic fumes affect birth outcomes. Busy roads cluster in poorer areas, which muddies plain comparisons. Instead, the team compared pregnant people who lived on opposite sides of the same busy Texas road, one group mostly downwind of the fumes and one mostly upwind.

Across more than thirty-seven thousand matched pairs, babies born at term to downwind mothers weighed a bit less on average. Living very close downwind showed stronger links, with lower weight and higher odds of very early birth. No links appeared for early birth overall. The steep fall with distance points at traffic fumes themselves.
pmc-11638313:
Uncemented hip stems hold fast when the patient's own bone grips them tightly. Satomi Abe and co-authors review 140 hip replacements using a collared stem, followed for about six years on average. In thirty-two cases, surgeons packed the patient's own ground bone around the stem; the rest form the comparison group.

Bone loss around the stem, called stress shielding, behaved differently between groups. In grafted hips it held steady at about nine percent from year one to year five. In controls it climbed from about fourteen to twenty-nine percent. No stem loosened or needed revision in either group. The 2024 study credits the graft with protecting the bone sleeve.
pmc-11638613:
Dereje Esubalew and co-authors published a 2024 study of poor sleep quality among medical students in Ethiopia who use smartphones at bedtime. Medical students are prone to short sleep as it is. A phone in bed can make it worse. The team set out to measure the problem and name its drivers.

The study drew 354 students at random from three universities. Sleep was scored with a well-known sleep questionnaire, and interviews filled in the rest. The scores were analyzed with statistical tools that weigh many factors at once. More than two in three of the bedtime phone users slept poorly. Poor sleep was tied to six factors: sex, daily coffee, what the phone was used for, how the phone was held, how long it was used, and past ill health. Social media apps led the phone uses, at more than two in five of the group.
pmc-11639113:
Zhen-ni Luo and co-authors examine, in a 2024 survey study, how family health feeds confidence in people living with chronic disease. Self-efficacy, the belief that one can manage one's own care, predicts how well patients cope, and the family is where daily care happens.

More than five thousand Chinese patients answered standard scales on family health, self-belief, felt social support, and health literacy. Healthier families went with stronger self-belief. Felt support carried part of that effect, acting as the bridge. Health literacy changed the strength of the paths, helping some links and not others. The findings suggest programs should treat the family, not just the patient, as the unit of care.
pmc-11639813:
Wang and co-authors pair a microbial gum with common food proteins to steady oil droplets. The gum, sanxan, is a safe, edible polysaccharide made by microbes, with mild gelling and emulsifying powers of its own. Mixed without chemical bonding with casein, pea protein, or soy protein, it forms complex particles meant to coat droplets in Pickering emulsions.

Spectroscopy confirms the partners bind. All three complexes emulsify well, and the pea protein pairing performs best; emulsions held by the complexes also store better than protein alone. The authors say the pairing lifts the proteins' emulsifying strength and gives food makers a new use for this novel gum.
pmc-11640013:
Rawa Jamal Abdul and co-authors measure where the roots of front teeth sit in the jaw bone, in a study published in 2024. They used cone-beam scans of front teeth from one hundred patients in an Iraqi group. The teeth covered upper and lower central and side incisors, plus canines.

For each tooth they classed the root post in the bone and measured bone depth on both sides at three levels. They also noted the tilt of each tooth and compared results by age and sex. Most upper front roots sat toward the cheek side of the bone. Such maps help dentists plan implants and other work where root post and bone depth matter a great deal.
pmc-11640113:
City life changes what birds eat, and that should change the microbes in their guts. Shuai Yan and co-authors compare gut bacteria in Eurasian tree sparrows caught in city and country sites. They took fecal samples from sixty-five adult birds and sequenced twenty of them, choosing males of similar body weight to keep the comparison clean.

City sparrows carried slightly more varied gut microbes, with different dominant groups than country birds. Several bacteria that can cause disease, including Staphylococcus and Helicobacter, were more common in the city group, hinting that city birds both spread microbes and build stronger defenses. The city birds' microbes also leaned toward fat-processing pathways. The authors conclude that habitat shapes the gut community and the body functions it supports.
pmc-11640313:
Kelly Li Lin Wong, Martin Graf, and George Augustine characterize, in a 2024 study, how serotonin quiets a small, richly connected brain structure called the claustrum. Serotonin is a messenger tied to sleep control and to how psychedelic drugs act. The claustrum receives many serotonin bearing fibers, yet how the messenger changes its work was little known.

The team recorded from single projection neurons in mouse brain slices, using electrical measurement, light based release, and drug tests. Serotonin triggered a long lasting outward current in these cells. The current came from potassium ions leaving through a channel opened mainly by one receptor type, 1A. That flow made the cells more negative inside, so they fired less. Light freed serotonin at both the cell body and its branches, and the quieting receptors sat in both places. The net effect is a brake on the claustrum.
pmc-11640513:
Edson Pontes and co-authors stir flower and leaf extracts of a tropical shrub into goat yogurt and track what changes over 28 days, in a 2024 study.
