The plant, Malvaviscus arboreus, is rich in protective compounds. Yogurts carried 1 or 2 percent flower extract or leaf extract, then faced tests for chemistry, texture, flow, and taste.

Both extracts raised antioxidant power, up to about ten units on the test scale, and slowed fat spoilage in storage. They also cut the survival of one starter bacterium, a hint of antimicrobial action. The 2 percent flower version stood out: stronger protection, firmer texture, and less water weeping out by day 28. Tasters liked both flower versions. The team see the flower extract as a promising natural add-in for functional foods.
pmc-11640613:
Nine authors present a cost study from two thousand twenty-four on a drug for a bone marrow disorder. Myelofibrosis often causes anemia, and blood transfusions to treat it burden patients with cost and time. The drug momelotinib was tested against standard care in two large trials, called SIMPLIFY-1 and SIMPLIFY-2.

The authors used the trials' twenty-four-week transfusion data plus cost figures from a United States claims database. They projected how transfusion costs and time would differ on the new drug. Patients were split by whether they needed transfusions at the start, and subgroups by anemia depth and age were checked too.
pmc-11640713:
Inmaculada Criado-Navarro and four co-authors compare ways to dry saffron petals without losing their useful chemistry, in a 2024 study. The petals are a leftover of spice production and spoil fast, yet they hold valued compounds such as flavonols and the pigments called anthocyanins. Drying is the step that decides whether those compounds survive storage.

Three methods faced off: oven heat at two temperatures, freeze-drying, and vacuum evaporation at two temperatures. Extracts from each batch were profiled, turning up twenty-two metabolites. Hot oven drying best preserved rare, precious traces like safranal, the scent compound. Vacuum drying and freeze-drying kept the most flavonoids. The paper gives producers a drying choice matched to which compound they want.
pmc-11640813:
Richard R-C Wang and co-authors explain, in two thousand twenty-four, how two wheat lines cope with salty soil in two different ways. Salt cuts wheat yield, so breeders value lines that can grow in such ground. Both lines came from crosses of lines that each held up fairly well in salt.

The team built four DNA markers to trace a chunk of wild grass chromatin passed into the lines. Tests of salt and leaf sodium then split the lines apart. One parent line kept sodium out of its leaves, and its young passed that trait on. The other parent let sodium in but bore it in its tissue, and both new lines kept that trait. Two clean offspring lines are offered as good stock for future breeding work.
pmc-11640913:
Carrot pomace, the fiber-rich pulp left after carrots are juiced, is usually thrown away. Richards and co-authors mixed it into beef patties at four levels, from none up to four point two percent. They measured composition, acidity, color, cooking yield, and water holding. They checked texture too, and a tasting panel rated each batch.

At three and at four point two percent, the patties held more water and gave higher cooking yields. The strongest mix lost redness and came out softer and less chewy. Tasters rated patties with up to three percent pomace as appealing in look, smell, taste, and overall liking as plain patties. The four point two percent batch scored lower on overall liking and firmness. The authors conclude that up to three percent pomace improves working properties and fiber content without hurting eating quality, turning a waste stream into an ingredient.
pmc-11641013:
Yining Xu and co-authors present a 2024 study on tiny fat-based carriers that nudge gut hormone release. Cells in the gut wall sense food and release hormones such as GLP-1, GIP, and PYY, which help control blood sugar and hunger. The team asked whether common fat ingredients used in drug products can switch those cells on. They tested this in mouse and human gut organoids, small lab-grown gut models.

The fat ingredients did switch on food-sensing switches on the gut cells. Packed into carriers, they raised hormone release from the cells that make these hormones. In mice, changing the fat mix, dose, or size of the carriers changed the strength of the effect. Mice with high blood sugar also responded. The study frames the carriers as a cheap, needle-free way to tune hormones, though all tests so far are in labs and mice.
pmc-11641213:
Yinyin Fu and co-authors map the gene mix of old pagoda trees in northern China in a 2024 study. The tree is prized for its looks, its uses in medicine, and its value to local ecology. The team wanted to know how much variety old trees still hold.

Using 16 DNA markers, they tested 416 old trees from three provinces. The trees held a high level of variety, and most differences lay within single trees rather than between groups. The trees fell into five loose subgroups with much mixing between them. From the full set they built a core group of 104 trees that keeps most of the variety for future care.
pmc-11641313:
Rongbin Zhang and co-authors track how a flavored brine called Xiangzao changes as it ferments for up to four years. The brine is made by letting wine lees ferment on their own, a prized food in China. Four batches, aged one to four years, were compared with tools that read flavor chemicals, germ genes, and small protein pieces.

The one-year batch held the most savory amino acids and savory peptides, while the four-year batch led in acids and fruity notes. Forty-two scent chemicals and hundreds of peptides were named. Certain germs tracked with key scents and with four newly found savory peptides. The study gives makers a map for steering the brine's flavor.
pmc-11641413:
Chiara Bellia and co-authors review in 2024 how well a blood test for one food protein group spots true food allergy. The group turns up in nuts, fruits, and seeds, and can drive strong replies. A firm call needs a food test, so a blood mark would help if it held up.

Fifteen studies with two thousand three hundred ninety five people enter the review. Bias was scored with a set tool for each study. For peanut, hit rates ran low while clear rates ran wide. Nut marks did a bit the same. The team finds the test can back a call, not make it alone.
pmc-11641513:
Patrícia Valentim and co-authors set out the plan for a review of whether digital tools raise health literacy in informal caregivers, in a protocol from 2024. Family and friend caregivers carry much of daily care. Digital health tools could help them find, judge, and use health facts with more skill.

The review will take in trials and other study types on adults who care for someone informally. Searches will cover SCOPUS, Web of Science, CINAHL, PubMed, and gray sources. Two reviewers will screen and grade each study, using named bias tools for each design. The team will pull data on aims, people, methods, and key results. The goal is to guide staff and managers on using digital tools well.
pmc-11641713:
Meng Wei and six co-authors show that the ubiquitin ligase U-Box51 lifts drought tolerance in potato. The ubiquitin system tags proteins for breakdown and steers growth, hormone signals, immunity, and stress response in plants. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

Gene scans flagged the potato version, StPUB51, as a candidate ligase. Its expression was mapped across tissues and under mock drought. Plants bred to overproduce it, and plants with it turned down, were tested for drought strength. Guard enzyme activity and a damage marker were read in leaves under drought. Partner hunts used yeast screens plus light based checks.
pmc-11641813:
Na-Yeon Ha and co-authors build a standard pattern tool for functional dyspepsia in this 2024 paper. Korean traditional medicine sorts indigestion cases into patterns that guide treatment. A shared, tested tool would make those calls more uniform across clinics.

Experts first mined Korean and Chinese studies for common patterns and symptoms. A Delphi survey then rated each item's importance before consensus talks. The draft held six patterns and thirty-eight items, tested on ninety-five patients. Dropping two weak items left thirty-six with strong internal consistency. Scores also lined up well with standard symptom and quality-of-life scales. The authors present the tool as ready for clinical pattern checks.
pmc-11642013:
Karolina Lubecka and co-authors review umbilical and placental tissues for treating jaw joint disorders, published in 2024. These birth-derived materials are rich in healing factors and are being tried in several joint conditions. The review gathered what is known about their use in the temporomandibular joint, especially for pain and mobility.

Seven databases and trial registries were searched. Of the records found, only five studies qualified. They suggested the greatest promise in ankylosis, where the joint stiffens or fuses; a membrane from the placenta showed clear benefit there. Injections of these tissues into the joint helped, but results resembled those of other options such as platelet-rich plasma or steroids. The authors urge larger trials across more patient groups before firm conclusions can be drawn.
pmc-11642113:
Jiri Sobotka and three co-authors test how loading style affects sheet metal curves in a 2024 paper. Stress-strain curves feed the computer models used to design metal forming. Their shape shifts with stress state and loading history, so test conditions must match real use.

The hydraulic bulge test stretches a sheet with fluid pressure under equal two-way stress. The team compared steady pressure rise with a ramp test that holds pressure for ninety-second pauses. Two materials went through both modes. Resulting curves differed by loading path, which matters for the yield rules used in simulations. Careful test design helps factories predict forming outcomes and avoid costly trial runs.
pmc-11642213:
Bartosz Płachno and co-authors examine the wall chemistry of glands on the traps of a carnivorous bladderwort plant. Bladderworts catch small water creatures in bladder traps, and dome-shaped glands dot the trap's outer surface. As those glands mature, the end cell lays down extra wall layers, making the gland a neat model of wall specialization.

Using antibodies that tag specific wall ingredients, the team mapped sugars and structural compounds across the gland's cells. The end cell's first wall held various pectins, while its added layers were rich in cellulose and hemicelluloses. The base cell differed from the stalk and end cells as well. The layered chemistry hints at how the gland's wall is tuned for its job on the trap surface.
pmc-11642313:
Von Lewinski and a team including Quehenberger and Sacherer asked in twenty twenty-four whether dirty air lifts heart attack counts in a low-smog Austrian state. Their list held more than twelve thousand attacks across nine years. Dust and gas levels were matched day by day to attack counts.

No air fact tied to attack counts in the whole group or most ill sub-groups. In smokers, some gas rises tied to fewer attacks that day. Ozone alone tied to more attacks in smokers. The odd smoker split echoes a known paradox, they note.
pmc-11642413:
Salathiel Kendrick-Allwood and co-authors look at the home and money strains facing families of babies at risk of cerebral palsy. Cerebral palsy is a lasting condition affecting movement that is often spotted in infancy. The team screened caregivers at a high-risk infant clinic for unmet social needs, past childhood hardship, and signs of depression and trauma.

Ninety-seven caregivers of children with, or at high risk of, the condition were compared with ninety-seven matched caregivers at the same clinic. Both groups showed high rates of income strain and positive screens for depression and trauma, with no clear gap between them. Food and housing strain and past hardship also looked similar. Every family was linked to local support at the visit, and the authors urge early, broad help for these families.
pmc-11642613:
Researchers model how immune cells are arranged inside melanoma tumors in a paper from 2024. Melanoma is a serious skin cancer, and new immune drugs help some patients but not others. Scans of tumor samples show where cancer cells and immune cells sit before treatment starts. The team built a computer model of those layouts and tuned it with real patient outcomes.

The model shows that clusters of active killer T cells with macrophages help decide the tumor's fate. Worn-out T cells can form a fence that shields the tumor instead. Random chance still matters, but the starting layout carries strong weight. The work may help doctors predict who will respond to immune drugs.
pmc-11642713:
Raimondo and co-authors audit how filgotinib, the newest JAK inhibitor, performs for rheumatoid arthritis outside the polish of clinical trials. The drug selectively blocks JAK1, a signaling switch for the cytokines that drive joint inflammation. Trial patients are selected and closely watched; clinic patients are neither.

The multicenter retrospective study gathered adults treated in routine Italian practice and tracked effectiveness and safety over time. Real-world cohorts include the elderly, those with many illnesses, and those who failed earlier drugs, exactly the people trials under-recruit. Their outcomes tell doctors what to expect when the drug meets ordinary practice, and how it stacks against the crowded shelf of advanced arthritis therapies.
pmc-11642913:
Kun Zhang and co-authors ask whether publishing pollution data spurs green innovation in firms in a 2024 study. City-level disclosure in China since 2008 offers a natural policy test. Green technology upgrades are central to cleaner growth.

Using listed firm data from 2003 to 2020, the team applied a staggered difference method. Disclosure linked to more and better green innovation, and the link survived endogeneity checks. Public pressure, direct controls, and market incentives each carried part of the effect. Gains ran larger in highly marketized and resource-rich places. The authors suggest flexible rules and a mixed governance system to widen the benefit.
pmc-11643613:
Sodium-ion batteries could store grid energy cheaply, since sodium is everywhere, but they need cathodes that work at high voltage without falling apart. Yalong Zheng and co-authors review one candidate family in 2024: iron-based sulfates. These materials offer a stable frame, a tunable structure, and strong voltage thanks to the sulfate group's pull on electrons.

The review covers the family's structures and how sodium moves in and out, then weighs strengths and weaknesses. It surveys tricks used to lift performance and hold the structure together, drawing on work from many countries. The authors aim to guide engineers toward robust sulfate cathodes that can run at room temperature and reach the market.
pmc-11643813:
Yi-Fen Chiang, Ko-Chieh Huang, Mohamed Ali, and Shih-Min Hsia test a grain-based formula against period pain in a randomized trial, in a study from 2024. Primary period pain is common and disrupts daily life, with no pelvic disease behind it. Warm water and like measures give only brief relief.

Sixty-nine women were split by chance into formula and placebo groups of 35 and 34. Pain scores fell in the formula group at the first treatment and at the study end, against both their own start and the placebo group. Reports of dull pain, nausea, swelling, back pain, and cold sweats also eased. Blood markers of inflammation dropped for three of four measures. The authors conclude the Adlay formula helped on both pain and biology.
pmc-11643913:
Darko Vušak and six colleagues present a 2024 chemistry study on how tiny changes in solvent reshape copper compounds. The team combined copper(II) with an amino acid, homoserine, and a flat aromatic partner, phenanthroline, and grew six new crystalline compounds. Merely adjusting how much water or methanol was present during synthesis produced different structures, sometimes two or three from similar mixtures.

X-ray analysis showed the crystals are stitched together by dense hydrogen-bond and stacking networks. Trapped solvent sits in pockets in most compounds and in long channels in two of them, leaving the solids porous. Magnetic measurements by electron spin resonance, tracked from room temperature down to liquid nitrogen cold, profiled the copper centers in each variant.
pmc-11644113:
Cinzia Michenzi, Samuel Myers, and Isabella Chiarotto sift bisphenol A in water kits, its risks for a cyst ill of the egg glands, and clean-up with biochar. Their 2024 review links a foul good that breaks sex gland signs to the most oft-found gland ill in women who can bear young.

The chem good acts like the sex good estrogen and breaks into the gland sign kit. In one set of studies named here, most women checked showed a link that points up twixt dose and the egg gland ill. Its source stays not clear. Biochar is made from waste of life stuff. It came out as a cheap stuff with strong soak-up of foul goods. It hit high take-out grades through rounds of use time and time again. The review weighs how fit biochar is for large-scale clean-up of water from such foul goods.
pmc-11644213:
Seung Min Choi and Chang-Ik Choi review what is known about Ethiopian eggplant in this 2024 paper. The vegetable, Solanum aethiopicum, is one of the five most valued crops in sub-Saharan Africa. It sits alongside tomatoes, onions, peppers, and okra in local diets.

The review covers the plant's nutrition, its plant chemicals, and its effects in the body. The crop holds the three main macronutrients and many compounds tied to health. Studies link it to effects that may help against disease, though much work is still early. Readers get a clear survey of a crop that feeds many people yet stays little known elsewhere. It also notes where more trials in people are still needed.
pmc-11644313:
Rahayu and co-authors build a Kerberos and chain ID check for car webs, VANETs. Car webs feed road facts to hands for route picks and crash curbs. Open air links leave those webs bare to hack threats in use. ID checks thus guard safe, whole talk in such webs in full. Join checks must stay fast to keep that talk safe in flows. Their web stores ID notes in a chain book for key hosts.

Trust hosts and road hosts can read that book in the web. Tests ran in three web forms: rim town, town with one trust host, town with two. Finds show the plan fits more than one web form in runs. It meets ID check, hand-off, and end lag needs in those forms. A spare trust host joins as car counts grow in the web.
pmc-11644413:
Anurupa Goswami and colleagues automate forest timber volume estimation from drone imagery, replacing laborious ground measurement of trunk diameters. Tree crown size, visible from above, relates to growth, wind resistance, and carbon storage. The team built an empirical model linking crown area measured in UAV photographs to stem volume at multiple training and testing sites.

Crown area and volume followed a strong exponential relationship, and applying the model to whole stands from drone images reproduced ground-based totals closely. The authors present the method as a practical fusion of drone sensing with classical forestry, useful for carbon accounting and land-use assessment where walking every tree is impractical.
pmc-11644513:
Sunan Tiptipakorn and four co-authors blend two plant-friendly plastics in a 2024 materials study. One partner is a bio-based resin with strong heat traits; the other, polycaprolactone, is a soft, bendable plastic. Mixing them could yield a material that holds a shape, then returns to its first form on warming, a trick called shape memory.

The team varied the soft partner's chain length and share, then probed bonding, heat behavior, and strength. Signs of hydrogen bonding and shifting softening points showed the two mix in part. More soft partner made blends less brittle but weaker, and only the longest chains gave bendable samples. Rich blends fixed a bent shape well and recovered most of it, which suits smart packaging or medical uses.
pmc-11644613:
Xu Liu and co-authors build a paper-thin light guide for circuit boards in a 2024 paper. Board links must move data fast as chips crowd closer. Their film is a flexible polymer strip a meter long, with standard connectors at its ends.

Tests at a near-infrared wavelength showed a wide bandwidth-length score and low loss over two meters. The film bends like print paper and loses little even at a tight bend radius. Cross-talk between channels stayed very low. A live run sent one hundred gigabits per second on a single lane. The film suits dense boards that need long, fast, compact links.
pmc-11644713:
Umnat Imcharoen and co-authors test steam explosion as a gentler way to draw curcumin from turmeric in a 2024 study. Curcumin, the prized compound in turmeric, usually needs fine grinding, which burns much energy. A steam blast might crack the plant open for less.

Under the microscope, exploded chips showed surface cracks and pits that widened the area open to solvents. Yield reached about three percent of weight, close to the four percent from fine grinding, while using about three quarters less energy. Heavier energy input shrank particles and raised yield in a straight line. Heat and light checks showed the compound itself unchanged and purer.
pmc-11644913:
Francesco Dicandia and co-authors redesign clustered phased arrays to fire several beams at once with wider scan range. Single-pattern elements cap how far beams can steer before gain sags. Their scheme mixes several element patterns and picks among them by aim. A Penrose-style clustering trims the feed points the array needs.

Tests with two and three simultaneous beams show the payoff. Minimum gain rose and peak side lobes fell versus single-pattern clusters. Statistical trials pushed to four and five beams at once. Improvements held across that whole spread. Multiuser and multibeam links are the natural home for the design.
pmc-11645313:
Millán and co-authors survey blood parasites in wild carnivores across Spain, in a 2024 study. The parasites, carried by ticks, can sicken domestic dogs and cats, so knowing their wild hosts matters. The team tested samples gathered over two decades from 244 animals of eleven species.

Badgers were heavily infected, with sixty of eighty-five positive, mostly carrying a badger-type parasite. Eleven of forty-two red foxes carried a fox parasite that also appeared in one badger and a stone marten. Wolves, genets, and pine martens tested negative. Climate mattered too: badger infection rates in Catalonia were lowest in alpine zones. The study pins down the natural hosts of both parasites.
pmc-11645413:
Xuanrong Chen and a large team show that classic androgen response elements act as tumor suppressors in the prostate. The androgen receptor drives normal prostate identity and growth suppressive gene programs. Cancer hijacks the same receptor for oncogenic programs, and whether the normal program can be switched back on was unclear.

A genome wide approach modulates the classic DNA binding sites for the receptor. Turning those sites on promotes differentiation and growth suppressive transcription, and can kill receptor positive cancer cells. Turning them off is tolerated by cancer cells but harms normal prostate cells. Gene signatures from site activity track with better prognosis and luminal tumor types in patients. Reactivating the normal program offers a therapeutic angle.
pmc-11645713:
Manohar Kodavati and Muralidhar Hegde comment on new evidence tying a familiar ALS protein to mitochondrial DNA damage, in a 2024 commentary. Mitochondrial failure runs through ALS, Alzheimer's, and Parkinson's diseases. Damage to the mitochondria's own small genome, and the repair of it, has emerged as a key part of that story.

The commentary discusses the authors' findings on FUS, an RNA and DNA binding protein mutated in some ALS cases. Healthy FUS partners with a mitochondrial ligase to keep mitochondrial DNA intact. Mutant FUS cells carried more mitochondrial DNA damage, directly shown. Restoring repair by expressing a human ligase in mutant models recovered mitochondrial function. The authors read DNA repair as a therapeutic lever for neurodegeneration. Their focus is FUS-linked ALS, but they frame the lesson for the wider family of diseases.
pmc-11646113:
Ayyappa Raja Desingu Rajan and colleagues published a genetics study in 2024 building a zebrafish model of neurofibromatosis type two. The human disorder comes from faults in a tumor suppressor gene. It causes tumors on nerves, in the spine, and in the eyes. A switchable animal model helps researchers test treatments.

The team engineered zebrafish whose matching genes could be knocked out on demand. One gene copy was active everywhere early in development. Switching the genes off early raised cell growth in nerve support cells. Adult fish later developed a range of tumors. Those tumors mirrored the human disease's typical sites. The authors offer the fish for drug screening and driver-gene hunting.
pmc-11646613:
Arnaud Marchant and co-authors report a pregnancy study, published in 2024, on when a common virus passes from mother to unborn child. Cytomegalovirus infection during pregnancy can harm the baby, yet doctors cannot yet predict which infections will cross. The team followed pregnant women with a first time infection and their newborns across several centers, measuring immune responses and virus levels.

Mothers grouped into three clusters with similar starting traits. Virus levels in urine and saliva tended to run higher when the baby was infected. A decision tree model that allows factors to interact flagged antibody levels against one viral protein plus saliva virus load as joint markers. The authors frame the work as a step toward a usable risk test.
pmc-11646713:
Karen Schrijvers and twelve colleagues charted teen health complaints across forty-one countries over three decades. The data came from a long-running school survey of fifteen-year-olds, with nearly half a million teens in all, from nineteen ninety-four to twenty twenty-two. Complaints split into two kinds: mind-based, like low mood and worry, and body-based, like head and back pain. Trend lines were fit for each country, sex, and complaint type.

In most cases, complaints rose over the years. But the shapes of the curves differed. Boys tended toward steady climbs or flat lines. Girls more often showed U-shaped or wavy curves, with dips and fresh rises. Body complaints mostly climbed in straight lines; mind complaints bent more. The twenty twenty-four study warns against one-line claims about teen health: the trend depends on who, where, and what kind of pain.
pmc-11646813:
Goar Egoryan and six colleagues report severe stomach infection by a common virus in a cancer patient on immune therapy, in a twenty twenty-four case paper. The sixty-three-year-old man had advanced skin cancer treated with an immune checkpoint drug for a year plus one shot of an oncolytic virus. He arrived with worsening indigestion, heavy weight loss, and a need for vein feeding.

Scans and biopsies showed the virus, cytomegalovirus, had ulcerated his stomach. Such flare-ups are rare without prior immune-suppressing care. Six weeks of antiviral therapy cleared the infection, and he resumed cancer care on a protective oral drug. The authors flag this risk in patients on immune therapy.
pmc-11646913:
Belamkar, Mounayar, and Clasen report heart protection during lung cancer therapy, in work from twenty twenty-four. Their patient was a man aged eighty-five with advanced lung cancer carrying an EGFR mutation. The targeted drug osimertinib shrank the cancer but appeared to weaken his heart.

After one month he arrived in heart failure with rhythm problems and kidney injury. The drug was held, heart drugs were started, and heart function recovered. When the cancer drug resumed, function fell again, supporting a drug effect. Adding an SGLT2 inhibitor, a heart protective diabetes drug class, is the reported strategy to keep both treatments going.
pmc-11647113:
Michael Shapiro used his 2024 presidential letter to announce new education programs for the American Society for Preventive Cardiology. Writing to members for the second time as president, he frames the offerings as a way to spread core knowledge beyond big training centers. The headline launch is a monthly webinar series on the foundations of cardiovascular prevention.

Each session pairs a thirty-to-forty-minute lecture with live questions. The opening lecture covers coronary calcium testing, given by a leading expert in the field. Over two years the series aims to cover every essential topic in clinical prevention, drawing prominent specialists. Trainees without a home program are the first audience, though all members may join. Shapiro presents the series as both teaching and community building. Further initiatives are teased later in the letter.
pmc-11647213:
Men and women hear nearly alike on basic tests, and a 2024 re-analysis by Dennis McFadden and co-authors puts numbers on the small gaps. The test battery covers nineteen hearing tasks, from telling tones apart to naming sounds, built for studying how listeners differ.

The data came from 340 normal-hearing adults tested earlier, now sorted by sex. Each subtest got an effect size for the sex gap, with a resampling method judging which gaps stand out. Almost all differences proved small. The authors note that body-level measures, such as faint echoes the ear itself emits, show much bigger sex gaps than behavior does. Those hardware gaps, they argue, do not simply travel up the hearing pathway.
pmc-11647413:
Kyeongho Jeon and ten co-authors compared lab tests and live feeding tests for dog food in a 2024 paper. Pet food makers want to know how much of a diet a dog can digest, and lab methods using gut enzymes are cheaper than trials with animals. The question is whether the lab numbers match the real ones at each age of dog.

The team ran lab tests, then fed diets to eighteen beagles split into puppy, adult, and senior groups. Lab values came out higher than live values in most cases. Still, for dry matter and energy, the lab numbers tracked the live ones closely in puppies and adults. The match was much weaker in senior dogs. The results suggest lab testing can stand in for live trials in young and adult dogs, but age matters and older dogs need more care.
pmc-11647813:
Urbanus Mwanzia Ngei and three co-authors optimize power grid add-ons in a 2024 paper. Demand is outgrowing networks, especially in Sub-Saharan Africa, yet new lines are hard to finance and build. Devices that steer power flow on existing lines can raise capacity without new corridors, if they are sized and placed well.

The team targeted three such devices, one that injects voltage support, one that tunes line reactance, and one that does both. Their objective balanced three goals: cut power losses, steady voltages, and hold down operating cost. A hybrid algorithm, part genetic evolution and part improved swarm search, did the tuning. Tested on a standard thirty-three-bus distribution benchmark, the devices were optimized alone and in combination. The authors report the hybrid solver finding placements that improve the network on all three goals. The study speaks to utilities squeezing more from grids they already own.
pmc-11648013:
Georg Bollig, Raymond Voltz, and Erika Zelko report on the Fourth International Last Aid Conference, held in Cologne, Germany, in September 2024. Last Aid courses teach lay people how to care for the dying, much as first aid courses teach them to help in emergencies. Seventy-three people from 16 countries met at a Cologne academy and the university hospital's palliative medicine department.

Talks covered hands-on experience with Last Aid courses and their many formats in different countries. Research on public palliative care education was shared, along with how community care networks are built and kept up. The work of the Last Aid International Research Group, past and future, was presented and debated. Its thread is that end-of-life care is a public skill, not just a clinical one, and that networks of trained citizens can carry part of its weight.
pmc-11648113:
Weimei Shi and four co-authors let machine learning design light emitting molecules, then make them in the lab to check the predictions, in this 2024 study. The molecules use a trick called thermally activated delayed fluorescence, which can turn more electricity into light in organic displays. Good candidates are rare, and hunting them by hand is slow.

A database of model designed candidates supplied the targets, and the team built them with standard coupling chemistry. A battery of tests confirmed the structures and measured how they glow. The solutions showed strong emission and the desired delayed fluorescence. Quantum chemical calculations agreed with the lab readings, which backs the models' judgment. The authors offer the loop of design, synthesis, and testing as a faster route to display materials.
pmc-11648213:
Weijia Huang, Wenzhe Liu, and Xin Wang report the first fossil flower of a parasitic plant family, sealed in Baltic amber, in a 2024 paper. Parasitic plants rot away too fast to fossilize well, leaving their history guesswork. Until now, the family Schoepfiaceae showed only three fossil leaf reports. The new find, from Kaliningrad, Russia, dates to the late Eocene, some thirty-four to thirty-eight million years ago.

The amber holds a corolla of five fused petals with stamens stuck to them, a build pointing to this family. The flower's debut in the macrofossil record tests ideas about the family's evolution. Its Russian home also reshapes guesses about where the family once lived.
pmc-11648913:
Pan and co-authors screen oat varieties for tolerance of low nitrogen during germination and early growth, in a 2024 plant study. Nitrogen fertilizer raises forage yield but costs money and pollutes when overused. Finding oats that thrive on little nitrogen would help sustainable pasture farming. The team measured root, leaf, and enzyme traits in five oat germplasm lines grown with low or normal nitrogen.

Low nitrogen cut root length, leaf nitrogen, and photosynthesis, while stress defenses and protective enzymes rose. The size of each shift varied by variety. Photosynthesis and antioxidant enzyme activity proved the best screening traits. A combined ranking put Qingyongjiu 035 as the most tolerant line and ZNY256 as the least. Breeders gain both marker traits and a ranked shortlist.
pmc-11649113:
Camila Bonfim and a team of co-authors study whether cash transfers cut deaths among psychiatric patients in Brazil in a 2024 paper. People with mental disorders die earlier than others, and Brazil's flagship cash program aids poor families who meet set conditions. The team link social and health records for tens of thousands of people once hospitalized for psychiatric disorders.

Those who got the cash aid after hospital care had lower overall death rates than those who did not, with the clearest drop for natural causes. The gain was stronger in women and younger people. A suicide drop was seen but was not statistically firm. The authors estimate a small share of deaths could have been averted.
pmc-11649713:
Segun Oladele, Iain Gould, and Sandra Varga published this analysis in 2024. It asks whether adding helpful fungi to potato fields and pots actually pays off. These fungi live in plant roots and trade nutrients with the crop, and they are said to lift yields in many plants.

The authors pooled results from 106 separate pot and field studies drawn from thirty-seven papers. On the whole, the fungi improved nearly every plant measure they tracked, from tuber yield to root growth. The one exception was the weight of the plant above ground, which did not change. Potato variety mattered most: some kinds gained far more from the fungi than others. The authors say the right pairing of fungus and variety could make the practice worthwhile on farms.
pmc-11650013:
Westbrook and co-authors report in 2024 on how dissolved nitrogen cycles in the waters of the eastern Canadian Arctic and Baffin Bay, using isotope measures from a summer 2019 survey. Climate change is expected to shift nitrogen inputs there as glaciers melt and frozen ground thaws. Since the easy to use form of nitrogen is scarce in surface waters, the organic form may fuel much of the algae growth.

The team measured amounts and isotope ratios in rivers and sea samples. River nitrate patterns fit a model mixing air borne nitrate with nitrate made from ammonium, minus uptake by algae. Organic nitrogen was low in rivers but varied widely at the sea surface, pointing to active local cycling or distinct sources.
pmc-11651513:
Junlei Bi and eight co-authors use genetics to test whether immune cell types cause gum disease, in this 2024 study. Periodontitis, chronic gum inflammation, destroys the tissue holding teeth. Immune cells are deeply involved, but correlation cannot say which cell types drive the disease and which merely react.

Mendelian randomization borrows genetic variants as natural experiments. The team scanned 731 immune cell subtypes against gum disease data. Several statistical methods guarded against side effects. Significant causal signals emerged for B cells, T-cell maturation stages, and regulatory T cells. Two receptors on myeloid cells, TREM-1 and TREM-2, showed intricate patterns worth deeper study. The authors say the results map causal immune contributors to gum disease, offering targets for prevention research and a base for probing wider body-wide effects.
pmc-11651713:
Cold snaps can stop soybean seeds from sprouting well, which cuts the crop before it starts. Jianguo Xie and co-authors compare a hardy soybean line and a weak one in a 2024 study to find what makes the difference.

The team measured cell stress markers and read gene activity in both lines as seeds sprouted in the cold. The hardy line handled harmful oxygen byproducts better and kept its water balance. Gene groups tied to plant pigments, fatty acids, and a key growth hormone stood out. Network analysis flagged hub genes that may steer the cold response. One candidate gene showed forms linked to better sprouting across many soybean varieties.
pmc-11651913:
Jun Seong Chung, Han Deok Kwak, and Jae Kyun Ju report five cases of large tumors behind the rectum removed by keyhole surgery, in a 2024 Korean case series. Such tumors are rare, grow in a tight space near the tailbone, and often cause vague symptoms. Open removal through the belly or back can be hard on patients.

Between 2017 and 2020, five patients had the tumors taken out through small belly cuts with a camera's help. Operations ran a median of 130 minutes, tumors measured up to 7.5 centimeters, and patients stayed about eight days in hospital. The growths proved to be benign cysts and a fatty tumor. One patient had a wound infection, and no worse problems appeared in short follow-up. The series supports the keyhole route as a gentle, workable option.
pmc-11652113:
Chenjia Jiang and four co-authors report a young girl in China with a very rare immune flaw and a stem cell transplant. The flaw stems from a gene that fixes DNA breaks. It can cause small head size, slow growth, weak immunity, low blood counts, and high cancer risk.

Stem cell transplant is the one cure known for this flaw. It may also cut the long term risk of blood cancers by restoring watchful immune cells. The report adds case detail and a review of past cases. Such rare cases help teams plan care and counsel families.
pmc-11653913:
Janice Du Mont and co-authors built Canada's first research agenda on sexual assault and partner violence against trans people, in work published in 2024. Trans people face high rates of such violence and rarely get the care they need afterward. Research to guide better responses barely exists.

Two surveys went to officials, service providers, researchers, and trans community members. The first gathered proposed questions from more than two hundred people. Twenty cleaned up questions were then scored for answer value, feasibility, impact, and fairness. Every question scored above eighty percent overall. The top item asked how training for students and front line workers can better support trans survivors. The authors offer the agenda to direct future work.
pmc-11654213:
Jiazhen Chen and co-authors report a forty-eight-year-old woman with lung cancer who developed bullous pemphigoid, a blistering skin disease, after treatment with an immune checkpoint drug. Such drugs free the immune system against cancer but can turn it against the skin. Steroids, then stronger immune suppressants, failed to stop new blisters.

Her blood showed high IgE levels, so the team tried omalizumab, an antibody that targets IgE. Within one week the blistering stopped and symptoms eased. Four weeks of treatment brought stable improvement, and four months of follow-up showed no return. Reviewing the few published cases, the authors propose choosing biologic drugs for this condition by the patient's immune profile, including IgE, eosinophils, and cytokine levels.
pmc-11654313:
Arezoo Sarmad and co-authors measure drinking in a western Iranian city and look for traits tied to it. Alcohol use has risen across Iran in recent years, most sharply in poorer areas. Their 2024 survey sampled more than fourteen hundred residents of Ilam city aged over fifteen, picked in clusters.

After adjusting for age and sex, about four percent of residents reported drinking. A degree-level education, cigarette smoking, hookah use, and drug use each went with far higher odds of drinking. Higher wealth went the other way, though weakly. Hookah use and high education were the strongest linked traits by weight. The authors call for prevention work aimed at the groups and habits their data flag.
pmc-11654413:
Alana Ewen and a team of co-authors gather views on a peer-led diabetes program for Black men in Michigan. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Black men face higher rates of type 2 diabetes, and peer support improves outcomes, yet joining and running such programs face real barriers.

The team interviewed eight people tied to the project: researchers, peer leaders, a community partner, and diabetes educators. A chronic disease checklist framed the questions. Themes covered guidelines, personal traits, patient needs, teamwork, resources, and system capacity. The interviews name what helps the program take hold and what blocks it. The authors aim to guide others building peer programs for older Black men with the disease.
pmc-11655613:
Irene Cheah and colleagues scope the harms reported for cannabis products in cancer care. Their scoping review from twenty twenty-four gathers studies across six databases. Patients use cannabis mainly for nausea and cancer pain. Safety reporting, though, is scattered across many study types.

One hundred fifty-two studies met the inclusion rules. Trials formed the largest group, with case reports also common. Gut, liver, and blood cancers dominated the study settings. Nausea control was the leading reason for cannabis use. The review catalogues which adverse events appear and where. Ingredient types and product forms varied widely across studies. Clinicians gain a map of what safety evidence exists.
pmc-11655713:
Emma L Heath and three co-authors review what helps and hinders bone surgeons in using patient-reported outcome data. Their 2024 systematic review collects the qualitative evidence: eight studies from two decades of literature, only one of high methodological quality. The data in question are patients' own scores on pain and function, now gathered by programs worldwide.

Surgeons' barriers were practical and skeptical at once: clumsy logistics, scores that are hard to interpret, and doubt that the numbers matter for real care. The enablers mirror them. Better infrastructure, education on what the scores can do, reporting at group level where patterns are legible, and involving surgeons early when systems are designed all helped engagement. The authors' verdict is measured: the fixes are obvious, but the evidence base is so thin that health systems are mostly guessing, and stronger studies should come before grander rollouts.
pmc-11655913:
Zeinab Aryanian and co-authors profile a rare benign skin tumor in Iranian patients in this 2024 study. The Spitz nevus grows from pigment cells and can mimic melanoma under the microscope, which makes its patterns worth recording. The team reviewed six years of cases at a referral hospital.

Eighty-six patients were found, slightly more women than men, with an average age near sixteen. The upper limbs and the face were the most common sites. Most lesions had been present for one or two years, and no patient carried an underlying disease. Under the microscope the compound type, spanning skin layers, led the list, followed by junctional and dermal forms. The authors present the series as a reference for doctors who must tell this harmless growth from its dangerous look-alike.
pmc-11656113:
Yuanchao Ma and co-authors describe piloting a patient portal that let COVID patients isolate at home without vanishing from care. In Quebec, ninety-five percent of cases were sent home to self-isolate. The Opal portal had patients report symptoms, vital signs, and mental health daily, with clinicians reviewing the stream and stepping in as needed.

Patients and stakeholders helped design the rollout, a mixed methods study of whether engagement improves implementation. The team reports on process, feasibility, fidelity, acceptability, and usability. Remote follow-up built with its users, rather than merely for them, is the model on trial, one future outbreaks and chronic care programs could reuse.
pmc-11656213:
Long Chen and co-authors sharpen a light-driven catalyst made of zinc selenide rods. The rods are laid down by a slanted vapor method. Light catalysts can clean dyes from water, but plain rods work weakly. Their 2024 study treats the rods with sulfur heat, a step called vulcanization. Heat level, time, and rod length were all varied to find the sweet spot.

The best run used mid heat for 45 minutes on rods of a set length. Its light current rose about sevenfold over plain rods. Dye breakdown of Rhodamine B climbed by half. Checks showed the sulfur step forms a zinc sulfide skin. That skin drinks more light and splits charges apart before they can cancel. The recipe is simple and could suit other rod catalysts.
pmc-11656613:
LiLi Ma and co-authors hunt long non-coding RNAs that steer a fiery cell death path in Parkinson disease, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Data from two public brain sets were mined with several learning methods. Two candidate RNAs stood out, and mouse brain tests checked the signals.

Cell death genes shifted in clear ways in the disease data, some up and some down. One candidate, LINC00269, fell sharply in the Parkinson mouse brain, backing its role. Links to four partner genes were also flagged for follow-up. The authors frame the RNA as a lead for new tests and drugs, not a proven cause. Readers get a vetted short list for lab work.
pmc-11656713:
Stacy and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a water-based, light-driven method for making polyacrylonitrile, the precursor of most carbon fiber. About ninety percent of carbon fiber starts from this polymer. Standard production gives broad molecular weight spread and uses toxic solvents. Controlled methods so far reached low conversions and modest chain lengths. Their aqueous photoiniferter process runs in water under light. It achieved high conversion and high molecular weights in their tests.

Kinetics were significantly faster than traditional routes. Control over dispersity, the spread of chain lengths, also improved. Those properties matter for spinning and processing into strong fiber. The method avoids surfactants and harsh organic solvents entirely. The authors claim unprecedented control for this polymer's key traits. Better precursors could raise carbon fiber performance downstream.
pmc-11656813:
Radiation therapy controls many breast tumors, yet some come back, and Kyungmin Kim and co-authors hunted for a cause in 2024. They focused on tiny packets that cells release, which can carry a short RNA strand known as miR-21. Patient data showed that high levels of that strand went with worse survival in those who had radiation.

In lab tests, breast cancer cells hit with a strong dose released more packets, loaded with more of the strand. Those packets made other tumor cells grow, heal wounds, and move faster, and they helped irradiated cells survive. Tumors in mice also grew faster when given the packets. The authors suggest this signal helps explain poor outcomes after radiation.
pmc-11656913:
Vincent Escarrat, Davide Reato, Guillaume Blivet, and four colleagues shine therapeutic light on a multiple sclerosis model in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Photobiomodulation uses infrared wavelengths to stimulate tissue without surgery and has drawn interest for nerve disorders. The team applied daily treatment across the body, back and belly sides, in mice with a model disease that mirrors key multiple sclerosis features. They tracked outcomes with imaging of reporter mice, tissue study, and patch-clamp recordings.

Treatment reduced the animals' movement deficits and proved safe in healthy mice. In the dorsal spinal cord it produced effects against swelling and for nerve protection. Fewer immune cells entered from outside, glial reactivity calmed, and spinal interneurons showed normal excitability in dorsal and ventral areas. The authors conclude the therapy acts body-wide on the model's swelling processes. They propose it as a candidate therapy meriting more study.
pmc-11657113:
Heidy Vera-Peralta and eight co-authors test a measles-based vaccine vector in mice in a 2024 paper. The live measles vaccine has protected people for decades and is now used as a base for new vaccines. The team asks whether it can plant resident memory T cells in key tissues. These cells stay in place in the lungs and liver and react fast to germs.

A single dose made both measles-specific and added-antigen-specific resident cells in lungs and liver. A dose through the nose made more lung cells than other routes. The cells worked when tested, with key types releasing granzyme B and immune signals. Tests on human cells showed the same pull toward tissues. The authors see a path to stronger vaccines.
pmc-11657813:
Tessafa Abrham Ashagrie and co-authors study improved charcoal cookstoves in Ethiopia in this 2024 paper. Better stoves burn cleaner and use less fuel than traditional ones. Yet uptake in the Wereta district has lagged behind hopes.

The team surveyed 308 households with questionnaires and interviews. Income, family size, schooling, and age each shaped whether a home adopted an improved stove. Cooking place and who decides in the home did not show a clear effect. Low awareness and high cost were the top barriers named. The authors urge programs to aim at the traits that matter and to cut cost and knowledge gaps for local families.
pmc-11658413:
Srihari Shankar and co-authors study how an enzyme tags a neuronal protein for disposal, in a 2024 paper. The protein, BNIP-H, helps the cerebellum grow and supports signalling between neurons. The enzyme, CHIP, attaches ubiquitin tags both to BNIP-H and to itself, which controls how much of each is present.

Tagging sites on CHIP itself were mapped, and mutating all nine of them nearly stopped its self-tagging. On BNIP-H, changing four key sites fully blocked its tagging by CHIP. A method that tracks hydrogen exchange suggested a mechanism: the two proteins touch briefly at one end, letting the tagging part of CHIP swing over to mark BNIP-H. After they part, tagged BNIP-H is broken down by the cell disposal system. The authors say the work clarifies roles of both proteins in neuron growth and signalling.
pmc-11659013:
Wenxiu Yuan and co-authors study whether diet and lifestyle balance links to blood levels of cobalt in people with metal implants. Their study appeared in 2024. They used survey data from the United States for 2015 to 2020. A score summed each person's mix of helpful and harmful diet and lifestyle factors. The team then compared scores with cobalt levels in 549 people who had implants.

A higher score from diet alone came with lower cobalt in the blood, once other factors were taken into account. The link differed by age group, and the shape of the link was not a straight line. The authors suggest that what implant patients eat may affect how much metal builds up in the body. They note the study shows a link, not proof of cause, and call for follow-up work.
pmc-11661013:
Fabio Grunspun Pitta leads a team in a 2024 lab validation of a high-sensitivity troponin test on a point-of-care device. Troponin is a heart protein that leaks when heart muscle is hurt. Fast, fine tests of it are the gold standard to rule a heart attack in or out, with a clinical score.

The weak point is time: from blood draw to a result in hand. A bedside device could cut that wait. In a first phase, samples with known troponin values from a big lab assay were read on the small device. The study checks if its calls match the lab's.
pmc-11664413:
Solón Alberto Orlando and a large team published a One Health study in twenty twenty-four on Ecuador's twenty twenty-three leptospirosis outbreak, the first there investigated jointly by physicians and veterinarians. After authorities declared the outbreak in Durán, the team sampled three hundred thirty-five specimens: suspected patients, household contacts, dogs, rats, and water near cases.

Molecular tests found the bacteria's fingerprints in about a quarter of human samples, over two-fifths of dogs, and more than a third of rats. Genetic sequencing characterized the strains. The pilot demonstrates a surveillance template where animal and environmental data are gathered alongside human cases from the start. For a neglected tropical disease spread through animals and water, that integration is the intervention.
pmc-11665213:
Yufan Pu and co-authors built a chart based tool to predict muscle loss risk in stroke patients, in work published in 2024. Stroke and muscle loss are closely linked, but early risk signs were unclear. Data came from a national United States survey over eight years, split into training and test groups.

Eight factors entered the final tool, including sex, body size, waist size, and several blood measures. Women with stroke faced higher risk in their data. The tool separated high and low risk patients with very high accuracy in training and high accuracy in testing. Charts of its predictions matched real outcomes well. The authors offer it as a cheap screen to flag patients early for prevention.
pmc-11665313:
Muluken Tilahun Desbalo and Asregedew Kassa Woldesenbet study how digital building models can guide care of public buildings in Ethiopia, in a 2024 paper. Good data helps owners decide whether to keep, upgrade, or remove a building. In practice, records are often thin or hard to reach, and digital models are rare for older buildings. The authors set out to rank which kinds of data matter most for each choice.

Eleven experts scored the options through a structured survey method that also handles fuzzy judgments. Cost, risk, and business value served as the yardsticks. For keeping a building, data on management ranked first. For upgrading, technical data came first, and for removal it ranked even higher. The authors argue that data plans should be tailored to the choice at hand, not built the same way for every building.
pmc-11665413:
Kayla Osburn and co-authors published a methods study in 2024 on drying dung samples in the field for stress hormone measures. Wildlife stress is tracked through hormone leftovers in feces, but samples must be frozen or dried fast to stay valid. Freeze-drying is hard at remote sites. The team compared it with a food dehydrator and a homemade solar oven across nine species.

Ten fresh samples per species were dried by each method and checked over time. The solar oven matched freeze-drying for all species, from giraffe to leopard. The dehydrator also worked well for the meat-eating species. The authors warn against mixing methods within one study, to keep values comparable.
pmc-11666913:
Gao Zhang, Man He, and their co-authors tested two natural compounds, alone and together, on ovarian function in mice with a hormone disorder. Their 2024 study models polycystic ovary syndrome, which disrupts cycles and fertility. Fifty young female mice were split into five groups: healthy controls, untreated model mice, and model mice given astaxanthin, curcumin, or both.

The team tracked sex hormone levels, cycle patterns, follicle growth, and egg release rates. Markers of oxidative stress and inflammation were also measured. Model mice showed scrambled cycles, cyst like ovaries, off balance hormones and blood fats, and raised stress and inflammation signals. Treatment effects are compared across the groups to judge whether the pair beats each compound alone.
pmc-11667313:
Nyashadzaishe Mafirakureva and co-authors weigh the cost-effectiveness of moving child tuberculosis care into general child health services in Africa. In 2021 over a million children fell ill with TB and more than two hundred thousand died, mostly for want of diagnosis and care. Services usually sit in distant specialist centers, apart from routine child care. A cluster-randomized trial tested bringing TB checks and treatment into local child clinics. Their 2024 paper models what that shift costs against what it gains.

Models stretch trial results over time and across settings. If integrated care finds more cases at fair cost, health ministries gain a strong case for change. The authors speak to planners in high-burden countries weighing scarce funds. Their numbers join clinical proof with budget reality.
pmc-11667613:
Seyyed Hossein Hosseini and Farzam Farahmand ask whether one thigh muscle can be trained alone in a 2024 study. The vastus medialis steadies the kneecap, and its weakness feeds a common pain syndrome. No exercise was proven to hit it selectively. Thirty three women with lateral patellar compression were split into two training groups for eight weeks.

One group trained the target muscle selectively, the other the whole quadriceps. Ultrasound measured muscle size and electrodes its activity before and after. A selective protocol, if it truly works, would sharpen rehabilitation for kneecap pain. The title's skeptical question gets a data based answer either way.
pmc-11668813:
Lei Lei, Yinuo Zhou, Lizhen Ye, and Yanfang Yang followed, in a 2024 China study, how failing senses and weak bodies combine to erode thinking in older adults. They also asked whether an active social life cushions the fall. The data span five survey waves from 2011 to 2020, covering 10,149 adults aged 45 and up.

People were sorted into six body-function groups by sense loss and physical performance. Those with low performance plus both senses impaired scored worst on thinking tests, a gap of 1.63 points. Only one middle group also declined faster over time. Mediation analysis found social participation carried a real share of the effect: active elders lost less ground. The authors argue senior programs should treat social calendars as health equipment, not decoration.
pmc-11669913:
Silvia Polver, Nicole Miller-Viacava, Matthieu Fraticelli, Judit Gervain, and Christian Lorenzi review how babies come to hear the natural world, in this 2024 paper. Speech perception in infancy is well mapped, but the sounds of animals and water are not. The review gathers the few studies that exist into a young field the authors call human auditory ecology.

Newborns already prefer natural water sounds over fake ones, hinting at an old inborn lean. A broad ear for primate calls narrows toward human speech with experience. The authors say genes and exposure braid together in these skills. They call for tests that sound like the real world babies evolved in, with payoffs for hearing care and nature awareness alike.
pmc-11671213:
Chenlin Du and co-authors build a machine learning tool that flags early frailty risk in this 2024 study. Frailty raises risk and lowers life quality in older adults. The stage before it, pre-frailty, can still be reversed, but spotting it is hard.

Data came from a national Chinese aging study with 3,141 adults aged 60 and over who live at home. The team drew 80 features across seven areas of life. A feature-cutting step and a stacked model judged the risk. The model is explainable, so staff can see what drives each flag. Early flags let clinics act while change is still possible.
pmc-11671313:
Caitlin Somerville and six co-authors published a health services study in twenty twenty-four on barriers to interconception care in primary care. Such care between pregnancies could help many women, yet few primary care visits include it. The team asked clinicians, staff, and patients at three Chicago clinics what gets in the way.

Eleven clinicians, fourteen staff, and six patients joined focus groups or interviews. Clinics lacked reliable ways to spot patients who were eligible for this care. Doctors often never learned about a patient's earlier pregnancies, and records were hard to search. Patients, meanwhile, had real needs but were unsure whether to ask their regular doctor or an obstetrician.
pmc-11671513:
Chongwen Wang and co-authors pin down how a long non-coding RNA helps prostate cancer spread to bone. The RNA, called MAFG-DT, does not build proteins but steers other genes, and it was already tied to several cancers. Prostate cancer often travels to bone, its deadliest route. Their 2024 study measures the RNA in patient samples and tests its effect in cells and mice.

Tumors that had reached bone carried far more MAFG-DT, and patients with high levels fared worse. Silencing the RNA slowed cell growth, movement, and invasion, and cut bone spread in the mouse model. The RNA works by soaking up a small RNA that normally restrains two receiver proteins, which switches on the Wnt growth pathway. A partner factor switches MAFG-DT itself on. The authors name the whole chain as a drug target.
pmc-11672013:
Aili Veronica Langford and co-authors survey what clinical guidelines say about stopping medicines, in a 2024 review. Cutting or ending a drug is called deprescribing. It is part of good prescribing, yet its place in guidelines was unclear. The team searched databases, Google, and guideline registries. They covered English-language guidelines from 2012 onward.

Eighty guidelines held three hundred sixteen such recommendations. The wording and format varied a great deal. Most said who should stop a drug, what to stop, and when or why. Fewer than six in ten explained how to stop in detail. In a registry sample, about twenty-nine percent of guidelines held any such advice. The authors conclude the advice is growing but uneven. Clearer, more complete guidance would help clinicians act on it. Patients could then avoid drugs that no longer help them.
pmc-11672313:
Hongmiao Tian and co-authors grow gecko-like sticky pads directly on surfaces, flat or curved. Gecko-inspired adhesives grip through forests of tiny mushroom-shaped posts. The catch: pads are usually made flat, then pressed onto curved parts, where contact is poor and grip collapses. The team instead grows the posts in place using electric control.

Because the posts form right on the target, they meet the surface fully and share stress evenly. On flat surfaces, grown pads matched shop-made ones. On curved surfaces that bend one way, grip rose up to fourfold. On surfaces curving two ways at once, grip rose up to twenty-fivefold. The authors say in-place growth opens robot handling and climbing to the curved world.
pmc-11672413:
Sascha Braun, Ralf Ehricht, and eight co-authors tracked drug-proof germs in Alexandria, Egypt, in work from twenty twenty-four. The germs are gram-negative bacteria that shrug off many drugs, a rising threat in hospitals there. The team paired gene tests with an online map tool to watch these germs spread and change over time.

They studied forty-three samples of one such germ, drawn from Egyptian hospitals over four years. Gene scans found the markers that let the germs beat key drugs, and lab tests checked which drugs still worked. The map tool laid the data out by place and date. The authors say this pairing gives health teams a faster, clearer way to spot outbreaks.
pmc-11672513:
Pengwei Ren and a large team map structural variation in local ducks in Shandong, China, in a 2024 study. Structural variants are large genome changes that shape how duck breeds adapt and differ. Three local breeds are compared. Two tools detect more than twenty-one thousand variants across their genomes.

Most variants sit between genes or inside gene introns, the team reports. Family analysis shows two breeds sit close, while the Wendeng black duck stands apart, likely due to geographic isolation. Notable genes link to nerve growth, cell division, energy use, and breeding traits. The map may guide breed selection and new breed work.
pmc-11672713:
Md Yousuf Ali and three co-authors link gene variants in HSP70 and HSF3 to egg traits in Bangladeshi hilly chickens, in a study from 2024. Heat shock protein 70 helps birds handle heat, and its expression is set by heat shock factor 3. Sequencing and targeted PCR were used to find variants and genotype the birds in this local breed.

Two new variants near HSP70 were tied to egg numbers in a set age window and to egg weight at a later age. Other variants in both genes tracked egg counts at distinct ages. Combined types also linked to maturity age and body weight. The authors say these markers could aid selective breeding for output in warm settings.
pmc-11672813:
Jinjie Hu and co-authors fed plant residue to weaned piglets in a 2024 study of growth and gut health. The residue is what is left after industry extracts artemisinin from a plant, and it still holds nutrients and active compounds. The team tested it as an unusual feed add on. Thirty two piglets, weaned at three weeks old, ate a basic corn and soybean diet or that diet with the residue added at three levels for four weeks.

Piglets on the residue diets showed stronger immune markers in blood, better antioxidant activity, and taller gut lining structures. The middle dose group also grew faster and showed stronger gut barrier gene activity and a healthier gut microbe mix. A dose analysis put the best added level in a band above the middle dose. The authors present the residue as a feed that can support growth and gut health in young pigs.
pmc-11673013:
Velimir Altabas and co-authors surveyed in 2024 the state of pancreas and islet transplantation for type 1 diabetes, where the immune system has destroyed the body's insulin making cells. Transplants can free patients from insulin shots, but they trade that burden for surgery and lifelong immune suppression.

The review compares three routes: a whole pancreas, a sprinkling of insulin making islets, and newer stem cell grown replacements. It tallies how often each frees patients from insulin, and for how long. Infection, bleeding, and rejection shadow the bigger operation most. The authors sort the standing challenges and point to where stem cell products might retire them.
pmc-11673213:
Habing and co-authors track how engineered tissue aids shape healing after severe muscle loss, in a study from 2024. Volumetric muscle loss overwhelms the body's repair program, and blood supply often lags early on. Past work showed that patterned scaffolds can steer blood vessel cells toward healing behavior.

Mice with such an injury received scaffolds loaded with vessel cells, with the collagen fibers either aligned or random. Healing was checked at 2, 7, and 21 days. All groups gained blood vessels and new muscle at like rates. Mice with plain scaffolds lost half their muscle area over the span, while cell-loaded patterned ones kept their mass. The cell constructs also drew more fibrous remodeling near the implant.
pmc-11673713:
Kenneth Meza Monge and co-authors review care for hemorrhagic shock, a top cause of preventable death from bleeding. Their 2024 review covers how the body reacts over time, which blood markers help, and which treatments have proof behind them. Injury type shapes the response, so care must fit the pattern.

Early bleeding control, balanced blood products, and a clot-aiding drug given fast form the core of current care. The immune reaction moves in phases, from wide activation to deep suppression. Many targeted molecular drugs remain in trials. The authors call for better markers, sharper timing, and care matched to each patient. They also flag the hard task of bringing new methods into varied care settings.
pmc-11674313:
Stéphanie Ducrot and Séverine Casalis study how young readers lock onto words in a 2024 paper. Known results say word naming peaks when the eyes land near a word's center. The pair asked whether word parts that carry meaning, called morphemes, steer that early stage in French. They tested second and fourth grade children plus adult readers, shifting where words appeared in view.

Naming was best near the word center for all three groups. Age and word traits, like length and inner structure, shaped the pattern. One test showed word part effects fading as skill grows in children. A second test found that children lean on the spelled look of word parts, while skilled readers use them at a deeper level. The work maps how word part use matures with reading growth.
pmc-11674413:
Carlos Cumplido-Trasmonte and co-authors tested a robotic walking device for children in a 2024 study. The ATLAS 2030 frame helps children who cannot walk on their own take steps. Six children, three with cerebral palsy and three with spinal muscular atrophy, each received eight sessions of robot-assisted gait training.

No serious adverse events occurred. Across sessions, step rhythm, step counts, and six-minute walking distance all rose in both groups. By the end, one therapist could fit the device in under five minutes on average. Children and therapists both rated satisfaction high. The authors conclude the device is safe and practical for these children, a base for larger trials.
pmc-11674613:
Alina Costina Luca and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four summary for pediatricians on physical activity for children with heart disease. Active living lowers body weight and improves life quality. Yet overprotective parents and thin evidence keep many heart-affected children sidelined.

Dozens of studies covering newborns to adolescents were reviewed. The summary sorts which activities suit which congenital heart conditions. Risks like sudden cardiac events frame the guidance. Education in schools about safe activity and against sedentary habits features strongly. The goal is confident, individualized advice instead of blanket bans that harm fitness.
pmc-11674913:
Sorting cells one by one means choosing between looking at them and testing their traits. Behnam Arzhang and co-authors built a flow device that does both at once. Cells drift through a wide channel while a fast camera records their size and shape. At the channel floor, an array of electrodes creates an uneven electric field. Each cell speeds up or slows down based on its response to that field, which reflects its inner state.

By pairing each cell's size from the images with its speed shift, the team could tell live from dead Chinese hamster ovary cells in a mixed sample. Computer simulations linked the speed shift, size, and starting speed to a measure of the cell's electrical response, which tracks its health. Tests with plastic beads confirmed the device reads accurately. The authors say the paired view can sort cell cultures faster than either method alone.
pmc-11675113:
Yurina Otaki and co-authors test augmented reality as a teaching tool for sanitation choices, in this 2024 paper. Pit latrines, the simplest toilets, are common across Asia but leak waste into soil and water. Septic tanks are safer, yet households decide for themselves, so plain awareness matters.

The team surveyed Sri Lankan households that use pit latrines and ran trials in a Japanese lab. Showing risks through augmented reality raised understanding of the health and environmental harm, and people kept that understanding for some time. Enjoying the tool seemed to help the lesson stick. The authors back such tools to speed the move to safer systems.
pmc-11675213:
Feng-Jie Xie and co-authors model output rivalry among cross-border e-commerce supply chains. They split the system into four product-market chains, based on whether the platform shares information and whether goods ship by direct mail or sit in bonded warehouses.

Game theory plus chaos tools let them trace how each chain's output choices push on the others. Steady play holds only while starting output, adjustment speed, and tax rates stay inside set bounds. Past those bounds, the system tips into cycles, then chaos through period doubling. Information gaps between chains change the safe zone. The work gives managers and regulators a map of when rivalry stays orderly.
pmc-11675313:
Alessandra Mazzeo and co-authors argue that opt-in disease plans for farm beasts can lift the far hill zones of Italy. New EU rules sort beast diseases into five bands, from must-wipe to may-watch. Two cattle ills sit in the opt-in band: a herpes cold of cows and a gut waste ill with a mooted link to a human gut ill. Hill farms lose yield to both, yet no law makes them act.

The Molise hills stand as the case ground for the plan. Such zones bleed people and farms yet hold rich food and tour worth. Opt-in plans could cut farm loss, guard food names, and keep herds sound for guests. The plan is tied to EU green and one-health aims in the close.
pmc-11675413:
Kerry Bentley-Hewitt and co-authors test in 2024 a panel of genes tied to stress and defense in baby snapper fish. The first month of life is a make-or-break stage for farmed fish, yet how their stress and immune systems switch on was little known. The team tracked eighteen marker genes in larvae over the first thirty days.

Most genes held steady across the month. A few rose in the first six days and then leveled off, among them genes for energy housekeeping and germ defense. Some genes also swung with the time of day, which warns that sampling hour matters in such studies. The panel now gives farms a tool to test new feeds and conditions.
pmc-11675613:
Çiğdem Yıldırım and colleagues compare gene activity in hepatitis C infected cells against healthy cells, hunting genes that shift in the same way across studies. Hepatitis C can end in cirrhosis or liver cancer, and markers that flag that path are needed. Two public datasets were mined for shared changed genes, then checked for protein links, pathway roles and the small RNAs that target them.

One gene, CXCL10, rose in both datasets, while SCGN and H2BC5 fell. The three proteins did not link to each other directly. CXCL10 sat in hepatitis C and cytokine pathways, and H2BC5 in a cancer pathway. Dozens of small RNAs were predicted to target each gene.
pmc-11675713:
Yu Pan and co-authors hunted for the key switches that guide stem cells as they turn into bone-forming cells, in a 2024 study. These stem cells can become many cell types, and bone growth matters for both care and basic science. Yet the molecules that steer the change over time were only partly known.

The team reworked large public data sets on gene activity, then checked the top candidates in lab tests. Four regulators stood out. Two of them pushed bone formation forward, while the other two held it back. The authors trace how these switches act across the full course of the change, which may aid future bone repair work.
pmc-11675913:
Nick Polson, Fabrizio Ruggeri, Vadim Sokolov, and Éloi Bossé set out a new computing method in 2024 for choosing the act with the highest expected gain. Their method works without needing a full probability density, which can be hard to get. It rests instead on quantiles, a simpler way to describe spread.

A deep neural network learns to produce the needed values from simulated data drawn from the model. The approach only needs the ability to simulate, not a closed-form formula. They show the method on a classic problem of splitting a portfolio, using a rule tied to the Kelly idea. Links to the theory of risk taking are also discussed.
pmc-11676113:
Xi Yuan and co-authors present a 2024 study on raising a tiny wasp used for pest control. The wasp lays its eggs inside the eggs of crop pests, killing them before they hatch. Farms rear it in the eggs of other insects, and the usual hosts have shown problems.

The team tested eggs of a silk moth as a new host. They tracked how heat and time after emergence shaped the moth's lifespan and egg laying. A range of twenty-five to twenty-eight degrees worked best, and eggs needed at least a day to qualify. The wasp attacked the new host eggs in a standard pattern. Wasp-to-egg ratios of one to two and one to three gave the best breeding results.
pmc-11676413:
Xiaomei Xu and Pengfei Gu review the defense systems bacteria use against phages and what industry can do with them in this 2024 paper. Phages, viruses that infect bacteria, have shaped bacterial evolution for eons. Bacteria answered with a wide arsenal of resistance systems. The same phages wreck factory fermentations, causing heavy losses. Borrowing natural defenses could harden production strains. The review sums the known mechanisms one by one.

Recent research progress on each system is covered. Uses range from food making to medicine production. The authors also name the challenges that remain. Resistant hosts must still ferment well, not just survive. The paper is a broad review for microbiologists. It links deep evolution to factory floor problems.
pmc-11676813:
Erina J Young and seven co-authors report a new blood parasite in sea turtles of Western Australia. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Blood parasites of this broad kind are common in reptiles, but none had been logged in sea turtles in a formal way. The find came from routine blood checks in health surveys of two turtle kinds.

Gene tests and a microscope search screen the samples. The parasite shows only in turtles that feed in the area, not in those that nest there. Young green turtles bear most cases. Two gene forms show, close in kin to forms in fresh-water and land turtles. No link to poor health shows, so the parasite looks like a chance find for now.
pmc-11676913:
Yiqiang Deng and six co-workers wrote a 2024 case study on reusing factory wastewater with a fine filter membrane. Water stress and strict rules push firms to recycle their waste water. The team used real waste water from an electronics plant in Suzhou, China. They compared membrane types for cleaning it.
