One membrane won out as the best fit for this waste stream. Its best settings for pressure, heat and flow were pinned down in tests. The cleaned water met the standard for cooling water reuse. Acid washing fixed the clogging that built up on the membrane. The case gives a model for like projects.
pmc-11677013:
Maria Parpori and co-authors compare mood and life quality in women with two long-term ills in a 2024 study. One group had type 2 diabetes alone, and one group had both that disease and breast cancer. In all, one hundred and twenty women in north Greece took part and filled in standard forms.

Women with both ills scored higher on life quality than women with diabetes alone, a result the authors report with care. Retired women scored highest, while women with late-stage cancer scored lowest. In the cancer group, stress and low mood rose and fell with life quality scores, which the study tracks in detail.
pmc-11677213:
Minoru Yamaji and co-authors study light emission from organic crystals in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Naphthalene glows in solution but not as a solid, yet joining aromatic units can switch solid glow on. The team prepared a family of diphenylnaphthalenes and measured their glow in both states.

Most of the compounds emitted similar spectra in solid and solution. One, with phenyl groups at set positions, glowed at longer wavelengths in the solid. Crystal analysis showed that compound packs in a herringbone pattern, while the others stack in columns. The authors discuss how the packing motif shapes the emission, linking structure to light behavior.
pmc-11677313:
Tyler Skeen and co-authors built a family of lab-made compounds around a carbon chain core and tested them against bacteria, in a 2024 study. The design takes its cue from natural products. New antibiotics with fresh ways of killing are badly needed as resistance spreads. The team varied the chain length, the links in the chain, and a key alcohol group, then watched how each change shifted the attack.

Some versions killed certain bacteria well while sparing others, a useful kind of aim. Several also broke up biofilms, the slime cities bacteria build to shield themselves, after they had formed. Wiping out free bacteria and cracking their shelters are the two properties drug hunters want most in this fight. The authors say the map of which shape does what will guide the next round of designs.
pmc-11677513:
Laurian Parmentier, Hannah Vanderstappen, and Geert Haesaert test a kinder mowing style for farm flower margins in a 2024 study. Their three-strip method cuts curved, uneven lines in phases, leaving refuge strips standing. A standard phased mowing served as the control during the third year of trials.

The curved method raised pollinator counts by forty-four percent and natural enemy counts by fifty percent. Rare solitary bees gained most in richness. More plant species bloomed at season edges, and plant-pollinator interactions rose by over half. Readers get a management tweak that turns margins into stronger insect habitat.
pmc-11677613:
ADHD is usually scored as one lump, but its three dimensions, inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, may forecast different troubles. Rapson Gomez and Taylor Brown test that forecast in a 2024 study of Australian adolescents. Parents, teachers, and the adolescents themselves all rated the same young people, 214 rating sets in total.

Structural models asked what each dimension adds beyond the others in predicting emotional symptoms, conduct problems, and peer problems. Impulsivity carried most of the extra weight, especially for conduct problems in teacher ratings. Inattention added a little for emotional symptoms in parent ratings and nothing elsewhere. The patchwork across raters is the point: who you ask changes which dimension matters.
pmc-11677913:
Parkinson's disease affects about ten million people, and no cure exists yet. Hwayoung Lee and co-authors review small-molecule drugs, from classic dopamine routes to new targets. The disease kills dopamine-making cells, so standard care feeds the brain a dopamine precursor plus helpers that protect it on the way in. The review sorts current therapies first. It then turns to targets under study, such as protein clumping, energy failure, and waste clearing inside cells.

Compounds studied between twenty nineteen and twenty twenty-three get special attention as possible future options. Some aim only to ease symptoms, while others hope to slow the disease itself. The survey gives drug hunters a map of where small molecules stand in Parkinson's care.
pmc-11678413:
Eleni Andreou and co-authors surveyed eating habits in Cyprus and Greece in two thousand twenty-four. Mindful eating means paying full attention to food and hunger cues. It has been proposed as a tool against weight gain. Its links to body weight, sleep, and vitamin D were unclear locally. The team studied adults in two yearly cohorts.

Participants filled a tested mindful eating questionnaire. The survey split mindful eating into five sub-traits. Staff recorded weight index, sleep length, and vitamin D levels. Data came from several hundred adults across both years. The authors compared mindful traits with each health measure. Mediterranean adults are little studied in this field. Results may shape diet programs that train attention, not just menus.
pmc-11678513:
Łukasz Sęczyk and co-authors present a 2024 study on how the form of a bearberry preparation changes what the gut can absorb from it. Bearberry is a traditional urinary herb rich in arbutin. The team prepared powdered leaf and dry extracts made with alcohol at six strengths, then ran them through simulated stomach and intestinal digestion. Chemical analysis tracked the main compounds and antioxidant power before and after.

Arbutin survived digestion almost fully, over ninety-five percent accessible in most preparations. Other compounds, total phenolics, and antioxidant activity shifted much more with the preparation and digestion stage. Balancing compound richness against survival, the extract made with forty percent alcohol looked most promising. The authors aim the finding at herbal drug and functional food design. The work shows the delivery form, not just the herb, decides the dose the body sees.
pmc-11678713:
Erika Mooney and co-authors build silver complexes with plant-derived partners in a 2024 chemistry paper. Silver has killed germs since antiquity, and coumarin-based silver compounds showed promise but dissolved poorly. The team attached helper ligands, either a phosphorus compound or a carbene, to help them dissolve and resist light. Structures were confirmed with spectroscopy and, where crystals allowed, X-ray methods.

One carbene version formed a tangled aggregate rather than a neat single complex. Standard dish and dilution assays then measured killing power against disease strains, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Better-behaved silver carriers could matter as drug resistance keeps shrinking the medicine shelf.
pmc-11678813:
Qiaoli Wang and co-authors test in 2024 whether a manganese salt can revive worn out strains of a straw mushroom. Farmed strains of this mushroom lose vigor over time, and manganese supports key protective enzymes in living things.

Adding the salt did little for a fresh strain, but it sped growth and raised yield in two worn strains. One worn strain fruited faster and more, and a badly worn strain grew fruiting bodies again. Enzyme activity tied to defense rose, while harmful oxygen waste fell. The team links the revival to stronger antioxidant defense, and offers the method as support for mushroom farming.
pmc-11679013:
Fabiana Tortora, Antonella Guastaferro, Simona Barbato, Ferdinando Febbraio, and Amelia Cimmino survey sensor-based diagnosis for bladder cancer in this two thousand twenty-four review. Bladder cancer is one of the commonest cancers, yet diagnosis rests on cystoscopy: invasive, costly, and not very sensitive. Diagnosis usually comes late, after blood appears in urine, and population screening is impossible with such a tool. Genetic tests cannot fill the gap because genetic differences between populations blunt their accuracy.

Research hunts universal markers shed in urine, aiming at a test that is non-invasive, quick, cheap, and accurate enough for early diagnosis, follow-up, and eventually screening. The authors discuss the challenges: choosing markers sensitive and specific enough, and building biosensors robust for clinical use. Success would cut mortality and ease the economic burden on health systems. The review maps where biosensing stands and what it must prove before screening programs become realistic.
pmc-11679313:
Chengcheng Feng and co-authors tune a cancer drug's tail to strike a hard trade: hold firm in the blood, yet spill fast at the tumor. The drug rides as a prodrug, a masked form that wakes at the site. Their 2024 study links the drug to fat chains of mixed length through a bond that tumor cues snap. Masked forms clump on their own into nano balls, with no truck.

Long chains hold balls firm but slow the spill. One mid chain hits the sweet spot in their tests. Its balls ride the blood far past a dye mark and pile up in tumors. In mice with breast tumors, that form hits the growth most hard of the set. The work maps tail length as a dial for mask-drug craft.
pmc-11679413:
White spots on teeth can be treated by polishing the surface down or by soaking resin into the lesion. Treetossatep Inna and co-authors compare those two fixes under lab aging. They prepared seventy-eight extracted premolars with artificial white spots, treated them, then cycled some in red wine to test staining and roughness.

Red wine darkened every group; the polished teeth changed color most, then the resin group. Untreated spots stayed the roughest surfaces, while resin-treated teeth came out smoothest. Roughness and color change tracked together moderately. The 2024 study concludes the resin route leaves a smoother, more durable finish, though both treatments still pick up stains.
pmc-11679513:
Mohamed Gomaa and seven co-authors search in 2024 for plant-based compounds that could boost a hormone signal used to treat diabetes and obesity. The target is the GLP-1 receptor, one of the most studied drug targets in this area, yet most current drugs for it are peptides that must be injected.

Working entirely on computers, the team screened natural products for small molecules that attach to the receptor and raise its activity. They ran virtual screening, motion simulations, and safety profiling, and also checked whether known drugs could be reused. The work points to chemical scaffolds that chemists could turn into pills.
pmc-11679813:
Gaetano Pacinella, Anna Maria Ciaccio, and Antonino Tuttolomondo review the links between inflammation, metabolism, and ischemic stroke in a 2024 paper. Stroke is a top cause of death and disability worldwide. Most strokes come from a blocked vessel starving brain tissue of oxygen.

Aging and metabolic risks such as high blood pressure, obesity, and high blood sugar fuel chronic inflammation. That state helps trigger strokes, worsens the damage, and shapes recovery. The review walks through the molecular paths that join the two forces, from vessel walls to immune signals. It also covers clinical effects doctors can act on, aiming to sharpen prevention and care.
pmc-11679913:
Marilena Mangiardi and co-authors follow stroke patients who face both seizures and a risky heart rhythm, in a 2024 study. Stroke is the top cause of new epilepsy in adults, and many survivors also need blood thinners for atrial fibrillation. Pairing a seizure drug with modern thinners raised safety questions that guidelines barely address.

The team tracked 53 such patients on the seizure drug lacosamide plus a modern thinner for two years. A matched group of 53 stroke patients took thinners without having epilepsy. New clot events were nearly identical in the two groups, and seizures grew less frequent and milder in the treated group. No severe drug side effects appeared. The pairing looks safe over the long term.
pmc-11680013:
Jianhua Liu, Kexin Zhang, and Zhongmei Wang propose in 2024 a method to find wavy wear on railway rails from axle box motion data. Wavy rail wear boosts wheel and rail shaking and can damage train and track parts. Finding its place and depth early aids safe upkeep.

The method splits the motion signal into layered parts and drops the most random ones. The part that tracks the raw signal best then gets a time-frequency map that shows where wear sits and its wave length. A filter and a frequency step yield the wear depth. Tests on fake and real rail data confirm the method reads both traits well.
pmc-11680113:
Liancheng Xia and co-authors offer a 2024 review on a small protein and viral infection. The protein, UBL5, is an odd member of its family in shape and role. It steadies the spliceosome, the machine that edits gene messages. It also aids DNA repair and protein refolding. Viruses often hijack those very systems to multiply.

The protein can fight back: it binds a rice virus protein and marks it for destruction. That makes it a bridge between infection and immunity. No prior review had gathered the infection findings, the team says. They sum up what UBL5 does in cells and weigh its likely roles across viral diseases. Better grasp of the protein could aid prevention and treatment, they argue.
pmc-11680213:
A large team in South Korea tested perches for meat chickens on two farms that hold welfare approval. Their 2024 study gave some houses wood perches and left others without them. The team then tracked growth, stress, and health signs in the birds.

Effects on growth were mixed and changed by farm and by week. A stress hormone was lower in the perch group on one farm but not the other. Foot and feather scores did not differ much, though walking scores got better on one farm. Litter was wetter in perch houses on one farm. The team concludes that perches may cut stress but do not lift all outcomes.
pmc-11680313:
Imran Chauhadry, Zulfiqar Bhutta and their co-authors evaluate a community-driven program to cut vaccine gaps in polio high-risk areas of Pakistan in 2024. Immunization saves millions of lives, yet coverage varies sharply by wealth and place.

The program joined community engagement with mobile health camps that offered routine vaccines plus mother and child services across many districts. Surveys before and after covered more than one hundred thousand young children. Full vaccination rose most in the poorest group, and the wealth gap in coverage narrowed. Children who had never received a dose fell across all groups, most steeply among the poorest.
pmc-11680413:
Carolina Barroso and co-authors published a 2024 review on whether vitamins, minerals, and plant compounds in dog food truly support dogs' immune systems. Pet foods increasingly advertise such functional ingredients, riding the trend of treating pets like family. Proof from studies in living dogs, though, is thin. The authors searched two databases for what is actually known.

They found twenty-seven peer-reviewed studies. For vitamins, only two studies showed slight benefits, for vitamins C and E. Research on minerals was sparse, with hints that organic forms of minerals work better. Studies of plant compounds were more encouraging, suggesting calming effects on inflammation and the immune system. The authors conclude the marketing runs well ahead of the evidence. They call for more trials in dogs themselves, so that health claims on pet food rest on fact rather than fashion.
pmc-11683313:
Zarnigar Mussarat Khan and co-authors scope and grade the world's surgical guidelines for inflammatory bowel disease. Many guidelines cover Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis surgery, with unlike quality. A search over 2008 to 2023 found fifteen guidelines, which were scored with the AGREE-S tool made for surgical guidance.

Six guidelines dealt with Crohn's disease alone, five with ulcerative colitis and four with both. Six were purely surgical, while nine mixed medical and surgical advice. Mean quality was fifty-nine percent, with newer guidelines scoring higher. The authors call for joint international guidelines built to the AGREE-S standard, to cut duplication and even out care.
pmc-11683613:
Zhen Sun and co-authors test a stepped wetland system for cleaning lightly polluted surface water in this 2024 study. Such water is a growing concern for environmental protection. Standard treatments are costly and can create second rounds of pollution.

Their built wetland used water hyacinth plants and no added inputs. A sixty-day trial ran in a drainage canal. Lab tests tracked how much contamination the system removed. Gene sequencing showed how microbe communities shifted inside the wetland. The stepped design aims to beat single-stage wetlands on both counts. Low-cost green systems like this suit canals and ponds near farms and towns. Towns can run such systems with local staff and low cost.
pmc-11684013:
Martin Ljubič, Andrej Perdih, and Jure Borišek use computer simulations to study how cell membranes affect an immune receptor, in a paper from 2024. The receptor, a complex of parts called NKG2A, CD94, and HLA-E, helps calm natural killer cells. Its signal depends on how its parts move inside the cell membrane.

The team simulated the full complex, atom by atom, in five membrane mixes. The mixes used different fat types, and one added cholesterol. The inner part of the receptor moved and exposed its signal sites in different ways in each mix. A membrane with strong negative surface charge held the complex close and hid its signal sites from water, which would likely halt signaling. A stiff, gel-like membrane bent and changed exposure as well. The work shows membrane mix is part of the signal story.
pmc-11684513:
James Wester and co-authors explore how breast cancer survivors in Botswana get and stay on hormone pills in 2024. For many cancers these pills, taken for years, cut the risk of return by half. The team spoke with women who had had breast surgery in the past few years. They focused on women whose cancer type calls for the pills.

Women named three main blocks. Doctors gave too little guidance on the pills. Public drug stores often ran out or had strict refill rules. Private stores cost a lot for the pills and for travel. Side effects were not a common cause of stopping. Family support and a woman's own drive helped. The authors call for better talk and a steadier, cheaper supply.
pmc-11685013:
Rheumatoid arthritis destroys joints and brings pain, fever, and fatigue, and a plant-based nanoparticle treatment is tested here in rats. Babar and co-authors made copper oxide particles using root extract of Bistorta amplexicaulis, a plant rich in flavonoids and phenols. They profiled the extract's chemistry, checked the particles' size and charge, and dosed arthritic rats at two levels.

Treated rats showed less joint stiffness and paw swelling, and their spleen and thymus weights fell. Blood counts moved toward normal, and markers of inflammation and joint damage dropped. The extract alone helped, but the particles performed markedly better, the authors conclude.
pmc-11685113:
Lauren Ramsey and co-authors document the second injury hospitals can inflict after a safety incident in a paper from 2024. The first harm is the incident itself: physical, emotional, or financial. Compounded harm comes from how the organization responds afterward. That response is rarely studied.

Forty-two people with lived or professional experience gave interviews. Eighteen were patients or relatives; the rest worked inside response systems. Framework analysis sorted their accounts of what went wrong after things went wrong. Slow, defensive, or silent responses deepened the original wound. The authors propose concrete ways to humanize the process. How a hospital says sorry shapes whether families heal or litigate.
pmc-11685913:
Dong Won Jung and Ji Yun Choi present a case report from 2024 about a rare cause of lasting sinus trouble. Their patient, a fifty-two-year-old man, had a runny nose, blocked nose, and headaches that would not clear. Tests showed a body-wide inflammatory illness in which immune cells gather and form lumps in glands and organs.

The illness had reached his nasal cavity, sinuses, and several glands in the head and neck. The authors pair the case with a review of past reports on this sinus form of the disease. They stress that the condition needs a high level of suspicion to spot, plus care from several kinds of specialists working together.
pmc-11688013:
Lei Wang and co-authors published this 2024 meta-analysis on a nutrition score and survival in lung cancer. The score, called the prognostic nutritional index, blends blood albumin and lymphocyte counts into one number. The team asked whether it forecasts outcomes for patients treated with immune checkpoint drugs.

They searched four databases to August 2023 and pooled 22 studies with 2,550 patients. Patients with low scores had clearly worse progression-free and overall survival than those with high scores. The pattern held across cancer types, first-line and later treatment, and drug combinations. The authors present the cheap blood score as a handy guide for judging who may fare poorly on these drugs.
pmc-11688613:
Jan Willem Van der Laan and Joseph Manuppello introduce a journal collection on cutting animal use in cancer testing, in a 2024 editorial. New drugs must be checked for cancer risk, often in long rat and mouse studies. Those studies use many animals and can cause prolonged distress. Shorter paths would help animals and speed drugs to patients.

Recent guidance lets reviewers weigh all evidence first and skip a rat study when it would add little. Studies in altered mice also cut animal numbers and exposure time. The editorial previews papers that test these ideas, including a twelve-year check of predictions on forty-five compounds. Other articles in the set cover gene-based short tests and planning steps. The editors stress that smart planning starts early in drug design.
pmc-11688913:
Amanda Cheney, John Shean, Erin Bouldin, and Meghan Fadel describe, in a 2024 report, how a peer community helped state health teams turn brain health data into action. The Data for Action Project pairs state teams with a cohort of peers from other states. Together they analyze data on brain health, dementia, and caregiving, then package the results for the audiences who can use them.

The pilot cohort drew in Arkansas, Connecticut, Illinois, and New Jersey. Teams produced estimates for specific places and groups to find who is most at risk, covering risk factors, service use, and family caregivers. Success, participants said, depended on having the data holders in the room and many viewpoints at the table. Eighty-five percent agreed the program improved their department's teamwork on brain health planning. A second cohort followed in 2024.
pmc-11689113:
Ilan Meyer, Lauren Bouton, and Diane Lauderdale survey in a 2024 study what limits daily activity in older LGBT adults. Past work hints this group faces more disability than peers, but the kinds and causes were little known. A national sample can show where support should aim.

Interviews, in person or by video, covered 210 adults age 45 and older across the country. In all, 36% reported at least one limit on their activities. Movement limits led by far, at 72% of those with any limit, with mental health next at 17%. Limits ran higher for those 65 and up, for women, and for lower income adults. Poor self rated health tied strongly to limits, while a chronic disease label alone did not.
pmc-11689213:
Tam Perry and co-authors describe in 2024 how a Detroit housing group plans for emergencies that affect older adults in senior housing. The group has worked since 2013 against displacement of older adults as the city changes.

After the acute phase of the Covid-19 pandemic, the group took stock of lessons from serving seniors in a crisis. The next emergency might hit one building, through a power cut or flood, or many buildings at once. Their work covers better communication, ready made plans, and stronger buildings. They share the plan so other towns can prepare for the needs of a diverse senior population in a crisis.
pmc-11689413:
Michal Engelman and Gina Lee introduce a 2024 symposium on how life-long experiences shape thinking in old age. The talks draw on the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, which has followed a population sample for more than sixty-five years and recently added careful cognitive testing. The exposures under study span schooling, family wealth, job conditions, and family ties.

One talk uses teen IQ scores and fine-grained diagnosis to link early ability and schooling with later dementia. Another ties childhood background and high school life to paths of cognitive change. Sibling data anchor two more talks, on schooling gaps between siblings and on how sibling bonds affect later cognition. A final talk joins gene data with job and pollution exposures. Together, the talks show the power of pairing long surveys with direct testing.
pmc-11689613:
Maki Karakida and Jeffrey Stokes examine how work, race, birthplace, and sleep fit together in older Americans, in this 2024 study. Their data come from the Health and Retirement Study and cover 31,868 adults aged fifty and over, sampled between 2014 and 2020. The pair ask whether working or retired status links to poor sleep in the same way for every group.

Overall, older workers reported more sleep trouble than retirees. The picture changed once race, ethnicity, and birthplace entered the model together. Black adults, both born in the United States and abroad, faced a higher risk of insomnia than white adults born in the country. Some groups of immigrant workers also reported more sleep difficulty than that same reference group. The authors conclude that sleep gaps in later life cannot be read from work status alone; background and birthplace shape the link.
pmc-11689713:
Melanie Stearns, Ashley Curtis, and Christina McCrae present a 2024 study on sleep treatment for a group standard therapy forgets: grandparents raising grandchildren. Ninety-nine such caregivers, average age about fifty-four, reported their sleep and their treatment wishes. Over half met insomnia criteria, typically lying awake about forty-three minutes before sleep came.

Asked what ruins their nights, they named stress, anxiety, family strain, and grandchildren who sleep badly. Most preferred online treatment over in-person or telehealth, and sixty percent chose behavioral therapy over sleeping pills. The authors say insomnia therapy for this group should also target the grandchildren's sleep and the household's stress, and they outline how the standard program should adapt.
pmc-11689913:
Alexander Garbin and Jennifer Stevens-Lapsley introduce a symposium on running mobility programs for older adults over video platforms. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, tools such as Zoom and VA Video Connect have spread through clinics and research. Their 2024 summary covers four projects that share one aim: better mobility for medically complex older adults.

Talks range over a virtual fall prevention trial, remote checks of fall risk factors in veterans, and more. Video delivery widens reach, drops travel needs, and lets staff watch program fidelity from afar. The speakers also flag what can go wrong when complex patients join from home. Rehab researchers get field notes on taking mobility work online.
pmc-11690013:
Katie Cherry and four co-authors study Black women in New Orleans who lived through two crises. Their twenty twenty-four paper covers Hurricane Katrina in two thousand five and the COVID-19 pandemic. All who took part lived in the area at the time of the storm. They filled out a storm form and answered open questions about both events, years apart.

Three themes came from their stories. First came loss of homes, towns, and key life events. Second came faith and growth, as prayer and church helped many cope, though some lost their church home. Third came the sense that COVID was a new, world-wide trauma laid on top of the old one.
pmc-11690113:
In 2019, Medicaid paid nursing homes about 82 cents for every dollar of care the homes reported spending on Medicaid residents. Edward Miller and co-authors break that average down, and the gaps are wide. Roughly 40 percent of homes got 80 cents or less on the dollar, while 8 percent were paid more than their reported costs. Nonprofit homes fared worst, at 76 cents, against 83 at for-profit homes and 80 at government ones. Homes serving mostly Medicaid residents were paid closer to cost than homes where Medicaid was a side line.

Staffing and quality cut the other way: homes with leaner staffing and one-star ratings were paid nearer their costs than richly staffed, five-star homes. The authors present the pattern as a starting point for payment reform debates.
pmc-11690213:
Jennifer Stanley and JohnBosco Chukwuorji introduce a set of papers, in twenty twenty-four, on aging in sub-Saharan Africa. Aging there gets little study, they note, even as the share of older adults grows. The set stresses that local culture shapes late life. Each paper in the set takes up a distinct topic and place.

One paper links support, self-worth, and good aging among Nigerian retirees. One works with older adults in Ghana on activity and place. Others cover disability, end-of-life care, and hidden illness. A shared point is that fear of stigma leads some older Nigerians to hide illness from all but close kin.
pmc-11690313:
Jin You and co-authors study informal care networks and psychological wellbeing among Chinese older adults in a 2024 paper. Population aging raises care burdens, while migration to cities has thinned traditional family care. The team ask who provides care in practice, and how network shape relates to mental health.

Five waves of a national aging study covered nearly twelve thousand care recipients over fifty. Most received care from a spouse, and about half from children or grandchildren. Larger family care networks, especially more children and grandchildren helping, predicted fewer depressive symptoms and higher life satisfaction. More diverse care sources predicted lower satisfaction.
pmc-11690513:
Aderonke Agboji and Shannon Freeman present a 2024 study of an eBook club for older adults in rural northern British Columbia. Apathy can drain drive and joy in late life, and far flung towns offer few group pastimes. A shared reading club, run on e-readers, may fill that gap cheaply.

Twenty eight adults aged 60 to 86, most of them women, joined from three towns. Each got an e-reader stocked to taste, a how to session, and a link to the public library. Groups of at most four met weekly for 45 minutes to an hour, over four to six weeks. About half began with apathy signs. By the end, all of them told of less apathy, plus better mood and more social ties.
pmc-11690713:
Six researchers measure the pace of aging in older Americans in a 2024 paper. The measure tracks how fast the body changes across many systems over time, within each person. Fast aging may flag who will gain most from early action, yet the tool was untested in older groups.

The team used a national retirement study with more than thirteen thousand adults first measured at age forty or more. Nine markers from blood, body tests, and function fed the pace score across a decade. Faster pace went with more thinking loss, new chronic disease, disability, and death. Groups with shorter life spans showed faster pace on average.
pmc-11690813:
Natalie Leland and co-authors study safety for staff who nurse patients at home in a 2024 paper. Home health workers face violence risks alone, far from hospital backup. The team interviewed 102 agency leaders across the country between 2020 and 2022, then twelve frontline staff in 2023 and 2024. A case-study design sorted their accounts into themes.

Leaders contrasted home care's loose safety net with hospital practice, covering gun policies and infection rules, and described spending on escorts and other protection. Staff told of talking down volatile moments in living rooms, judging neighborhood risk, and leaning on agency procedures. The pandemic runs through the accounts as a dividing line. Findings show safety at home is built from policy, money, and street-level judgment together.
pmc-11690913:
Miller, DeMarchis, Michaels, Jaskson, and Dorr report lessons from a learning collaborative on care plans built around the patient rather than the disease. The focus is people living with several chronic conditions at once. Innovators, front-line providers, and implementation experts met across five sessions to swap case studies and hard-won tricks.

Around thirty participants from research networks and a federal agency reviewed promising planning models and named common roadblocks. Group dialogue turned scattered experience into shared knowledge and candidate best practices. The 2024 summary aims the synthesis at policymakers, clinical teams, and system leaders who want to spread person-centered planning. The authors frame the sessions as an accelerator for change.
pmc-11691213:
Andrea Huseth-Zosel, Heather Fuller, and Paul Carson survey vaccine attitudes among older adults in North Dakota in a 2024 study. Older adults face high risk from flu, shingles, pneumonia, and COVID-19. Yet many skip some or all recommended vaccines. The team asked what deters and what might motivate this group.

Surveys were mailed to over nine hundred adults aged sixty-five and up. A subgroup of 132 had missed at least one target vaccine. Reasons differed by vaccine type in the replies. Feeling healthy and not needing shots led for flu and pneumonia vaccines. Side effect worries led for shingles and COVID-19 vaccines. Doctor recommendation topped the list of motivators. More information and free access also raised stated likelihood. The authors frame interventions around those specific levers. Tailoring by vaccine, not a single message, is their advice.
pmc-11691313:
Carma Bylund and co-authors counted how therapists use empathic skills during dignity therapy, a life-story interview that helps dying patients preserve a sense of worth, in a 2024 study. Empathy shapes provider-patient exchanges, yet its use inside this therapy was unmeasured. The team coded 203 session transcripts with older cancer outpatients for four skills: acknowledgement, reflection, validation, and empathic self-disclosure.

Acknowledgement came first, with validation a close second. Usage did not vary by provider's occupation, gender, or the session format. Patients with worse physical function drew more validation and more empathic communication overall, the modeling showed.
pmc-11691513:
Ilja Demuth and four co-authors published a study in 2024 on an epigenetic measure of the pace of aging, called DunedinPACE. The measure reads chemical tags on DNA and estimates how many biological years pass for each calendar year. The researchers asked whether a faster pace predicts metabolic syndrome, a cluster of cardiovascular risk factors.

The study used the Berlin Aging Study II, with 564 adults aged around sixty-eight who did not have metabolic syndrome at the start. About seven years later, 144 of them had developed it. Those with a faster pace of aging at baseline had much higher odds of developing the syndrome later. The association held after accounting for age, sex, other illness, and habits. The authors suggest that the pace measure may help identify people at risk well before the syndrome appears.
pmc-11691913:
Wakui and co-authors test a self-tracking program for family caregivers in Japan, in a 2024 mixed-method study. Caregivers often cannot seek help because time and burden crowd it out. Their program, Care-VIP, lets caregivers log daily care tasks, life activities, and mood. The project began with a survey of 3,256 caregivers, then enrolled 201 of them in a 60-day tracking trial.

About 88 percent of participants finished the program, a high rate for this stressed group. Those who joined tended to work full-time and carry heavier care loads. Written feedback named gains such as more attentive care, spotting problems early, steadier routines, and better awareness of feelings. The authors see self-quantification as a low-cost support for caregivers.
pmc-11692113:
Mooney and Best ask why some people with strong number skills still fail to save for retirement. Two traits are known to help: numeracy, the ability to work with numbers, and future self-continuity, feeling connected to one's older self. The authors test whether the two work together rather than separately.

Using survey data from 798 adults, they found a clear interaction. Among people who had any retirement savings, better numeracy meant bigger savings only for those who felt strongly connected to their future selves. Skilled but disconnected savers did not pull ahead. The authors suggest retirement programs should build that sense of connection, not just teach financial math.
pmc-11692313:
Tooba Umar and four co-authors present a 2024 case study of daily life after brain injury in old age. A traumatic brain injury can leave lasting troubles with memory, mood, and body, and those troubles play out at home. The study followed two pairs, each an older adult with a brain injury and their care partner, and asked both sides how hard daily activities felt.

The pairs rated tasks across health, social life, transport, home life, and leisure. Agreement was rare: the two sides matched only on diet and nutrition in one pair. In one pair the injured person reported more thinking troubles than the partner saw; in the other, the reverse. The authors say such gaps matter, since care plans built on one side's view alone can miss what the other side lives with.
pmc-11692413:
Yuxia Wu, Wanwan Si, and Hong Mi model how China's aging and falling births will reshape community services through 2050, in this 2024 study. Census and family panel data feed micro-simulations of population shifts and service demand over 25 years.

The authors draw on long-term care practice in rich-country groups to propose staged policy steps. Sharp targeting, they argue, comes from clear settings for age mix, health, and care models, plus split service groups. Such design can foster two flows: younger seniors aiding the very old, and grandparents aiding grandchildren. Both flows ease the squeeze on mid-life adults who juggle child and elder care.
pmc-11692513:
Miyeon Jung, Susan Pressler, Dustin Hammers, and Liana Apostolova shared a report in 2024 on how difficult it is to recruit older adults who have both mild cognitive impairment and heart failure. The team was running a pilot study testing cognitive interventions meant to improve cognitive function in this group.

At first, eligibility required an age of sixty-five or older, heart failure confirmed by echocardiography, and mild cognitive impairment defined through a two-step process. In seven months only twelve people enrolled, because many who were screened scored above the cognitive threshold. The team then lowered the age cutoff to fifty-five and dropped the cognitive screening rules. They also began searching health records and calling people at home. In the next seven months, fifty-eight more people enrolled, exceeding the team's goals. Most of those who enrolled did in fact have mild cognitive impairment.
pmc-11692613:
Yeonjung Lee, Cindy Vang, and Youhung Her-Xiong study discrimination and resilience among Asian American older adults in a paper from 2024. Asian elders in the United States have faced many forms of bias. How bias across a lifetime shapes health is still an emerging topic.

Thirty-nine adults took a survey on bias, resilience, and health. Reports covered life before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. Mild perceived discrimination rose after the pandemic began. Resilience also rose during the pandemic years, a surprise pairing. The team reads the results through life course and Asian critical theory lenses. Early data suggest hardship and strength can grow side by side in old age.
pmc-11692713:
Abigail Poe and co-authors present a 2024 conference abstract on how much Hispanic and Latinx dementia caregivers join everyday decisions for the person they care for. The data come from an ongoing daily-life study of these caregivers. Forty-seven caregivers who filled in a decision involvement scale were compared across age bands.

Caregivers reported moderate involvement overall, choosing meals and other daily matters with the person. Age mattered: caregivers in their sixties scored clearly higher than those over seventy. The authors call for work on what else shapes involvement, from culture to context, and how involvement connects with caregiver stress and burden.
pmc-11692813:
Brittany Anderson and co-authors describe how qualitative data are woven together in judging a disaster preparedness program for dementia caregivers, published in 2024. The online program pairs caregivers with trained student volunteers. Together they build a household disaster plan. The plan takes an all-hazards approach. It also guards caregiving tasks during and after one.

Within a hybrid trial, the team studies what helps or hinders the program's rollout. A framework for putting programs into practice guides that work. Three kinds of such evidence are triangulated: observation of sessions, and close attention to how they talk and engage with caregivers about their plans. They surface traits and themes in approach. Those traits led to warmer interactions, deeper talks, and more careful plan building. The authors argue that the blend of methods shows the quality of the rollout, not just outcomes.
pmc-11692913:
Nearly two million Americans on Medicare live with dementia, and their care is spread across a vast, mixed workforce. Donovan Maust and four co-authors charted that workforce in 2024 from 2019 billing records, asking who treats these patients and where.

Over 783,000 distinct clinicians billed for dementia care that year. Offices led the settings, followed by emergency rooms, hospitals, and nursing facilities. Most patients saw a primary care physician, and large shares also saw nurse practitioners or physician assistants. Yet among all clinicians involved, barely two percent were psychiatrists, under two percent neurologists, and only half a percent geriatric specialists. The authors argue coordination plans must start from this real, generalist-heavy map.
pmc-11693113:
Katherine Supiano and Laura Bradbury describe a year-long, state-funded program to raise grief literacy across Utah. Their paper came out in 2024. Grief literacy means being able to sit with someone who is suffering and respond with compassion; older adults face the most loss and the worst bereavement outcomes.

Rather than only funding professional services, the program trained community members to support each other. It reached groups hit hardest by the pandemic: older adults, indigenous people, veterans, and rural communities. Activities included training health providers and first responders, working with faith communities, and engaging citizen groups. The authors present the framework as a way to catch grief early, before isolation and despair compound it.
pmc-11693213:
Tara McMullen, Shari Ling, and Lenise Cummings-Vaughn describe a policy effort on delirium care in a 2024 presentation summary. Delirium is a sudden state of confusion common in older adults, above all in intensive care, where it can affect most patients. It raises the risk of death and lasting loss of function.

The speakers, officials from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, lay out plans for standard screening and checks for delirium. They frame the work inside age-friendly care, which stresses proven steps matched to older patients' needs. The summary also covers quality measures and policy levers that could spread such care in hospitals paid under value-based systems. The aim is better outcomes for patients and for whole groups.
pmc-11693413:
Avalos and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a case report of autoimmune enteritis in an older man with psoriatic arthritis. The condition causes severe diarrhea and malnutrition from immune attack on the gut. It usually appears in infancy, rarely in adults. Their patient, a man in his sixties, developed relentless diarrhea despite many treatments. Antibiotics, gut-slowing drugs, and other standard tries all failed. He eventually needed intravenous feeding to stay nourished.

Scopes showed ulcerations in the upper gut with normal colon appearance. Biopsies showed inflammation and flattened villi matching autoimmune enteritis. Steroids plus a biologic drug, adalimumab, finally brought improvement. After four months he stayed well on the biologic alone. His bowel habits normalized and he ate a normal diet. The case shows the disease can hide behind other autoimmune conditions.
pmc-11697713:
Yiwen Ding and co-authors combine published studies to ask how richer carbon dioxide air affects methane release from land ecosystems, in work from 2024. Extra carbon dioxide stores more carbon in soil, which could feed the microbes that make methane, a strong greenhouse gas.

The meta-analysis pooled 398 datasets from 59 publications across 50 sites. Higher carbon dioxide raised both the abundance of a key methane-making gene and the methane actually emitted. The size of the boost depended on how long the enrichment lasted, the land use, and the soil texture, with these factors interacting. The findings help forecast how land ecosystems will answer a changing climate.
pmc-11700513:
Maham Tahir and Andleeb Raja report a diabetes patient whose emergency visit for anxiety traced back to fat lumps from her own insulin shots, in a case report from 2024. The 28-year-old had type 1 diabetes since age eight and injected insulin about five times daily for a decade. She knew to rotate sites but reused the same belly spots because they hurt less, and stretched each needle for two weeks.

Her control was excellent, with an HbA1c of 6.5 percent. Exam found soft swelling with stretch marks where she injected. The lumps fed body image distress strong enough to trigger panic and repeat emergency visits. The authors stress the mental health side of this physical complication, in a group already prone to mood disorders.
pmc-11700613:
Guilherme Menezes and co-authors present a narrative review, published in 2025, on artificial intelligence in livestock farming. Cameras and sensors already watch animals on modern farms, and the review asks what computer vision and large language models each bring to that work. Dairy farming, the most data rich branch, anchors much of the discussion.

Vision systems identify animals, track behavior and feeding, estimate weight, and flag disease early. Language models promise help merging farm data, trimming it to what matters, and fetching stored knowledge on demand. The authors note language models remain barely tried in animal farming despite that promise. Readers get a map of proven camera uses today and open research room for language tools tomorrow.
pmc-11703413:
Aaron Wong and a team of co-authors asked if genes change how a pain drug works in cancer. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, looked at oxycodone use in people with pain from advanced cancer. Two genes shape how the body breaks down this drug. The team checked dose, blood levels, pain scores, and side effects by gene type.

The study ran at many centers and drew data from visits, forms, and blood tests. In the small group of thirty-three people, gene type did not split drug response. Higher blood levels of a drug by-product went with worse pain control. Readers learn that gene tests may not guide this drug's dose in cancer care.
pmc-11703613:
Urbina and five co-authors report lessons from a European health technology assessment project, in work from twenty twenty-four. Health technology assessment judges the value of new medicines and devices for health systems. Europe adopted a regulation in twenty twenty-one to make its countries cooperate on those judgments.

A two year project, EUnetHTA 21, was commissioned to solve key methods issues and prepare for the new law taking effect. The commentary documents its outcomes in detail. Joint assessments promise less duplicated work for national agencies and faster patient access, if the shared methods are trusted by all member states.
pmc-11704313:
Turki Abu Alfaraj and co-authors review lip reposition surgery for a gummy smile, where too much gum shows when a person smiles. Gum show over three millimeters is often judged unsightly, and causes range widely. Their 2024 review covers how the surgery has changed in recent years.

Causes span late tooth eruption, a lively upper lip, a short lip, excess jaw growth, and gum overgrowth, among others. Each cause needs its own fix, so exams must sort them first. Lip reposition suits people with a mobile lip and mild jaw excess, and it stays gentle and tissue sparing. For mixed causes, it pairs with crown lengthening or gum trims.
pmc-11704613:
Vanessa Pahl and co-authors present a 2024 methods paper on reading bacterial identity and metabolism in a single mass spectrometry shot. Screening engineered strain libraries is slow when identity and chemistry need separate assays. Their trick labels each strain with a tagged ubiquitin protein whose end carries a six-letter amino acid label.

A fast flow-injection instrument weighs the intact protein, reading the barcode, and in the same run measures the cell's small metabolites. Six gene-silenced strains showed both clear tags and the expected metabolic fingerprints of their silenced pathways. A plate holding 132 such tags proved the method scales. The authors pitch one-shot barcoding for metabolic engineering, where thousands of designs compete and their chemistry must be judged fast.
pmc-11707613:
Maciej Tatarczuch wrote a 2024 commentary on the best follow-up therapy for primary central nervous system lymphoma, a brain cancer. The piece discusses a large single-center study of 559 patients treated between 1983 and 2020. The study tracked how consolidation therapy after first treatment shifted over time, away from whole-brain radiation and toward stem cell transplant or gentler chemotherapy.

Radiation controls the disease longer but can damage thinking, especially past age 60. Transplant avoids that harm but is itself hard on older, frailer patients. The commentary weighs the reduced-dose radiation option in the study's title and asks whether it deserves a fresh look. Patients who reached complete response did well long term. Tatarczuch stresses how hard it is to compare gentler regimens when their very definition is fuzzy.
pmc-11707713:
Joana Subtil and colleagues present a 2024 case report of a rare immune crisis hiding a parasitic infection. A twenty-one-year-old woman in Portugal, newly diagnosed with advanced HIV, came to hospital a week after starting antiviral therapy. She had fever, a rash, yellowed skin, and dark urine. Doctors first blamed drug toxicity and stopped her medicines.

Her fever held and her blood counts kept falling despite antibiotics. Blood tests showed very high ferritin and fat levels, a pattern pointing to hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. In that syndrome, the immune system attacks the body's own blood cells. A bone marrow sample then revealed the trigger: visceral leishmaniasis, a parasite spread by sandflies and known in her region. The case warns that this treatable infection can hide behind a dramatic immune syndrome, especially in patients whose immunity is already weak.
pmc-11709413:
Abigail Vogeley and ten co-authors ask if a short health skills test can sharpen a common screen for thought loss in older adults. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The screen in wide use, the MMSE, can miss mild cases or flag healthy people in error. The team paired it with a brief test that asks people to read a food label and answer plain health questions.

Data came from a long study of older adults in Chicago, with three hundred eighty-nine people in this part. Full test scores set who had real thought loss. The screen alone did fair work, but scores rose a lot once the health skills test was added. The authors urge wider use of the pair in front-line care.
pmc-11709613:
Sara Bermudez and co-authors study a growth control pathway in brain immune cells in a 2025 paper on Alzheimer's disease. These cells, called microglia, must switch on protective work when facing the disease protein. A pathway that controls protein making inside cells sits at the center of that switch. The team focused on a brake protein in that pathway and how it changes with short and long exposure to the disease protein.

Short exposure eased the brake, while long exposure raised it again. Removing the brake proteins in mouse microglia boosted cell power units and cut swelling signals and cell death. The team also compared brake levels with swelling markers in patient spinal fluid. Readers learn how protein making control may shape brain immune replies.
pmc-11709713:
Katalina McInerney and co-authors tested which thinking tests best track decline stages in Caribbean Hispanic adults, in this 2025 study. Test norms built on European groups may not fit this population. The sample held 507 older adults of Puerto Rican and Cuban American background.

Delayed story recall was the strongest marker of clinical stage, followed by backward digit span and animal naming. In a smaller subset, a trail-making test emerged as the top marker. Some tests that worked in the full group lost force in the subset. The authors say test choice for this population should rest on local data, not imported norms alone.
pmc-11709813:
David Berron and co-authors present a 2025 conference abstract on memory tests taken at home on mobile devices. Such tests could ease screening for Alzheimer's disease, but they must prove sound without a tester present. The team judged ease of use, validity, and stability in Swedish adults without dementia.

Participants rated the app clear and pleasant, and most preferred it over paper tests. Scores matched standard clinic tests well and tracked with tau scans and brain measures. Baseline memory scores forecast later decline, and adding a blood tau marker improved that forecast. Two sessions averaged together gave good stability.
pmc-11709913:
Edward Robinson and co-authors examine the eyes of people who died with Alzheimer disease or mild memory loss. Their 2025 study rests on a simple fact: the retina is part of the same system as the brain, and it shows some of the same damage. Post-mortem retinas were checked against matched donors with normal minds.

Cell loss was marked in all three layers of the retina, and harmful oxygen byproducts ran about twice as high. The links between nerve cells were cut by half or more in places. Those losses tracked the bad proteins in the eye and, in life, the scores on memory tests. The team ties eye checks to brain health.
pmc-11710013:
One gene variant, APOE4, raises the risk of Alzheimer's disease far more than the common form of the gene. Sarah Philippi and co-authors study, in a 2025 paper, how that variant changes the blood and, through it, the brain. Blood-borne proteins are known to affect memory centers as people age.

The team profiled proteins in blood plasma from people who carry two copies of APOE4 or two of the common form. They found variant-linked shifts in pathways tied to brain function. A mouse arm of the study checked which of those shifts appear in both species. The work aims to explain how body-wide signals shaped by one gene can reach the hippocampus, a key memory region.
pmc-11710313:
Six authors, led by Jingnan Wu, validate in 2025 a three minute game based screening tool for thinking decline in Chinese older adults. The tool runs as a mini program in a chat app and holds three short games: ordering numbers, sorting species, and finding gold. Fast, friendly screening could catch decline early.

Close to five hundred adults aged fifty to eighty nine with memory complaints took the games plus full brain tests, scans, and blood work. Just under half proved to have mild loss or early dementia. The team weighed how well the game scores split the groups, and with what accuracy at each cut point.
pmc-11710413:
Tzung-Jeng Hwang, Cho-Hsiang Yang, and Yi-Ting Lin compare, in a 2025 study, three ways of filling in a checklist for early behavioral change in older adults. Mild behavioral impairment means new, lasting mental symptoms after age fifty. The checklist measures those symptoms, but whose answers count was unclear.

The team recruited 123 patient-and-partner pairs from a university psychiatry clinic. Each side completed the checklist on its own. A researcher then compared the two, clarified disagreements, and made a final rating. Scores from the three routes came out close but not identical. The comparison helps clinics decide whose voice to trust when symptoms are subtle and stakes are high.
pmc-11710513:
Rebecca Solch-Ottaiano and co-authors compare two diets in middle-aged rats in a 2025 study. Human evidence links mid-life eating patterns to later thinking decline. A Mediterranean-style diet seems protective, while a Western diet looks harmful, but the pair had not been tested head-to-head in animals. The team fed rats one diet or the other for about a year.

Thirteen rats ate the Mediterranean diet and seven the Western one, starting at four months old. Maze tests then probed short- and long-term memory. On one maze, scores for correct alternation matched, but the Mediterranean group made more alternations overall. In a water maze, that group also found the platform faster, with the gap growing across days. The pilot backs the human pattern in a controlled model.
pmc-11710713:
Songmi Lee and co-authors published this 2025 study on large DNA changes and Alzheimer's disease. Most gene hunts focus on single-letter changes. Structural variants, which span more than fifty DNA letters, can reshape genes more deeply, yet their role here was unclear. The team used a precise new calling pipeline on a large sequencing project sample.

The data held nearly twelve thousand people, split between patients and controls. The pipeline found tens of thousands of deletions and insertions shared by at least one percent of people. The team focused on variants linked to known risk spots for the disease. They report fifteen deletions and three insertions tied to twelve of those spots. The work adds a missing layer to the genetic map of Alzheimer's.
pmc-11710813:
Hossein Moein Taghavi and a large team of co-authors report, in a 2025 paper, on a smell-related brain area in two diseases. Loss of smell can come early in both Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. The team used a combined MR-PET scan to measure tau, a protein that builds up in Alzheimer's, in the piriform cortex, a key smell area.

They studied 115 people, then set aside some with incomplete data. The groups left were healthy controls with and without amyloid, people with mild memory trouble, and people with Alzheimer's or Parkinson's disease. The scan let them compare tau in the smell area with tau in a nearby memory region, to see whether the pattern sets the two diseases apart.
pmc-11710913:
Zeming Qiu, Long Cheng, Qinyuan Wang, and Zhilong Dong search blood proteins for new drug targets against erectile dysfunction. Current care leaves many men without good options. Their 2024 study used genetic methods that mimic trials, scanning the plasma proteome for proteins that cause or protect against the condition. A second genetic method then sifted the hits for druggable targets.

The scan tied 126 proteins to the condition. Seven targets stood out: one raised risk, while six, among them MDH1 and NQO1, lowered it. The targets clustered in metabolism and redox paths. Docking tests showed candidate drugs bind them well. Lifestyle and disease factors also moved several of the proteins, which hints at prevention routes.
pmc-11711813:
Oscar Calvillo-Arguelles and seven co-authors study heart events and later cancer results in women who had breast cancer, in a 2024 study. The study uses health records from Ontario, Canada. It asks if a heart attack or heart failure after breast cancer changes what comes next.

Records cover more than thirty thousand women. About thirteen hundred had a heart attack or heart failure in the years that followed. Those women faced a much higher risk of death from cancer. They also had more new cancers and more new drug care, which shows why heart health needs close care in this group.
pmc-11712113:
Vaseel and Nalakath Uvais wrote a 2025 study of dementia care through community psychiatry clinics in rural India. Dementia is common, yet many rural patients get little care. The Rythm program, run by a hospital and research center, set up local clinics to bring mental health care closer to home.

Since August 2022, four of eight Rythm clinics have taken dementia cases, and they found twenty nine cases in all. Most patients were women, and most got follow up at home because travel was hard. Trained local volunteers helped find cases early and link people to care. The authors report less strain on caregivers, fewer hospital stays, and more awareness of dementia in these areas.
pmc-11712213:
Michelle Hand and co-authors report focus group findings in 2025 on caring for a loved one with dementia. Caregivers face heavy strain, and keeping social and emotional health matters for both parties. A group digital gaming system was built to prompt movement, thinking, and social contact.

The study drew caregivers of clients at an adult day health center. Their loved ones had mild or moderate memory loss and took part in the gaming sessions. Three focus groups were held to discuss the strain of care and the fit of the game. The paper presents what caregivers said about both topics.
pmc-11712313:
Jeroen Vanbrabant and co-authors develop two blood tests for Alzheimer's markers in a 2025 paper. One tau site in spinal fluid tracks tau imaging closely. Brain-derived tau in blood marks amyloid-linked degeneration better than total tau. Both could stage disease biologically if measurable in plasma.

Prototype assays were built for an automated analyzer platform. Capture antibodies target each marker specifically. Precision within and between runs stayed under fifteen percent variation. Freeze-thaw stability was checked for both assays. Fifty patients and fifty healthy donors supplied test samples. Marker levels fell inside the measuring range for everyone. Patient ranges stretched higher than control ranges. Tiny undiluted plasma volumes sufficed for one assay. The work is prototype-stage validation, not clinical rollout. Staging Alzheimer's from blood draws is the ambition. Larger cohorts must confirm the early performance.
pmc-11712413:
Hannah Burr, Nathan Scott Smith, Wei Zhang, and Chunyu Wang present a 2025 study of a new kind of carbon dot that may block the protein clumps behind Alzheimer's disease. Two proteins, tau and amyloid beta, gather into toxic clumps in the disease. Tiny carbon particles made in the authors' lab had already shown they can slow that gathering.

The new dots blend a dye called Congo red with citric acid in varied ratios. At under twenty nanometers wide, they can cross into the brain and into cells, tests confirmed. The team measured how strongly the dots stop each protein from clumping. Such particles could one day serve as a therapy base.
pmc-11712513:
Lisha Wang and co-authors work on drugs that would destroy the tau protein tangles of Alzheimer's disease rather than merely block them, in a paper published in 2025. The two approved antibody drugs target amyloid, remain controversial, and cannot reach proteins inside neurons. Tau accumulates inside cells, so the team pursues degraders: molecules that tag tau for the cell's own disposal machinery.

Their approach builds proteolysis-targeting chimeras, two-headed molecules that bind tau with one end and the disposal system with the other. Earlier versions were peptides; the field is moving to fully synthetic small molecules that could be taken orally. The team docked known tau binders from a public database into the three-dimensional structure of tau filaments to pick the best starting compounds.
pmc-11712613:
Sandra Machlitt-Northen and a large team of co-authors describe a phase 2 trial of an antibody drug for early Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 paper. The drug aims to raise levels of progranulin, a protein that supports cell cleaning and calms inflammation.

Low progranulin is tied to higher disease risk. A receptor called sortilin drags progranulin down for disposal, and the antibody blocks that receptor. Early studies in healthy volunteers showed the drug was tolerated and raised progranulin in blood and spinal fluid. The new trial, named PROGRESS-AD, enrolls 282 patients with amyloid-confirmed early disease. It is randomized and double-blind, comparing the drug with a placebo on safety and effect.
pmc-11712713:
Patients increasingly ask chatbots about Alzheimer's disease, and a 2025 study asks how good the answers are. Ihsaan Yasin and co-authors put six neurology questions, spanning symptoms and caregiver guidance, to ChatGPT-4, then had two blinded neurologists grade the replies with two standard scoring systems.

Guideline alignment came out moderate, at just over two of seven on the stricter scale, while general quality rated higher, above five of seven. The scores on the two systems moved together. The authors frame the gap plainly: the tool informs at a fair level, but it does not yet speak with a clinician's discipline.
pmc-11712813:
Yara Yakoub and co-authors test whether blood and spinal fluid markers can flag healthy older adults headed for near term cognitive decline. Published in 2025, the study follows 218 unimpaired volunteers from the PREVENT-AD cohort for about five years on average. Plasma amyloid and tau markers were measured while all were still cognitively normal.

Marker positive plasma predicted progression to mild cognitive impairment, and the team repeated the test with spinal fluid and PET scan markers in smaller subgroups. Annual thinking tests tracked who declined. The search matters because brain scans that do this job are costly and scarce, while a blood draw is cheap. The authors frame fluid markers as a practical early warning for trials and clinics alike.
pmc-11712913:
Elisa Calcagno and co-authors describe a 2025 lab study that pairs two kinds of drugs to rescue memory in Alzheimer's disease. One kind switches on enzymes that add chemical tags to the spools DNA wraps around, and the other blocks enzymes that remove those tags. Tag levels fall in the diseased brain, and the pair may restore them better than either drug alone.

The team tested the pair on mouse brain slices harmed by amyloid and in two mouse models of the disease. Doses too weak to help on their own were combined, and the pair was tested on a cell process that underlies memory forming. The study sets up the pair as a joint route worth pursuing.
pmc-11713113:
Madison Musich and co-authors trial elderberry juice for mild memory loss in a 2025 paper. Foods rich in plant guards may cut the risk of decline, yet proof in patients is thin. Elderberry is rich in the same dark pigments as blueberries.

Twenty four patients took elderberry or fake juice three times a day for six months. Mind tests at start, mid, and end gauged memory, speech, and flex of thought. A small sub group gave blood for swelling marks. Early results hint at where gains may lie. The team frame the trial as a first look, not a firm verdict.
pmc-11713313:
Katherine Possin and a large team report long term results for a dementia care program called the Care Ecosystem. The program pairs each person with dementia and their caregiver with a trained navigator by phone, backed by a team of specialists. Past trials covered only 12 months of care.

The extension study follows 456 pairs with high caregiver burden for up to five years or to end of life. Outcomes include quality of life for the person with dementia, plus caregiver depression, confidence, and burden. Hospital and emergency use are also tracked. Results matter for policy because a new Medicare payment model now backs this style of care for wider use.
pmc-11713413:
Abiola Oluwatosin Obisesan and co-authors test probiotics against brain inflammation in a 2025 mouse paper. A bacterial toxin, LPS, is known to inflame the brain, damage neurons, and impair memory. Probiotic bacteria can rebalance the gut and calm immune activity, but their brain-protective power was little tested.

Forty-eight mice received probiotic strains, a standard memory drug, salt water, or the toxin alone, over seven days. Memory was tested with object and maze tasks. Probiotic-treated mice showed lower levels of inflammatory signals and of a damage marker, and higher levels of a protective antioxidant. A growth factor for neurons rose, while markers of inflammatory cell activation and amyloid fell in key brain regions. The authors conclude the strains may shield memory from toxin-driven harm.
pmc-11713513:
Catherine Mummery asks what a true primary prevention trial for Alzheimer's disease would need, in this 2025 paper. Prevention in her sense means treating people before any sign of disease appears. Current trials treat people who already show amyloid or tau, which delays illness rather than preventing it.

Mummery notes that anti-amyloid drugs are prime candidates for such a trial. The hard part is finding healthy people at high risk before pathology starts. That calls for a clear risk sorting plan and markers that predict disease early. She also weighs which drug action to target and the moral questions of treating people who may never fall ill.
pmc-11713613:
Kristin Wildsmith and co-authors report results on the Alzheimer drug lecanemab in a 2025 paper. The drug is an antibody that targets toxic clumps of amyloid, a protein that builds up in the brain. The team asked whether the drug also slows tau, a second protein whose tangles track the disease, using spinal fluid from a large trial called Clarity AD.

They measured a tau fragment in fluid from 167 people with early Alzheimer disease. At the start, this marker matched brain scans of tau tangles more closely than any other fluid test they checked. Tracking the marker over eighteen months let the team judge how the drug affected tau growth tied to amyloid.
pmc-11713713:
Anne Hogue and Daniel Silverman link worsening sleep to falling brain energy use in a 2025 Alzheimer's study. The pair focus on people who carry the APOE4 gene form, a known risk factor. Earlier work by the team showed that people whose sleep got worse also lost memory and brain activity. One rear brain region that fades early in the disease stood out in that work.

The new study draws on more than 2,000 adults from over fifty sites in a national imaging project. Brain scans measured sugar use in forty-seven regions. Thinking tests tracked change over time. Carriers whose sleep worsened showed steeper drops in brain activity than non-carriers. The results tie sleep care to brain health for those at genetic risk.
pmc-11713813:
Thomas Mueggler and co-authors reported this 2025 first-in-human study of a drug aimed at Alzheimer's disease. The drug tweaks an enzyme to cut output of long amyloid pieces that clump in the brain. At the same time, it raises shorter pieces thought to be harmless. Earlier drugs in this class stumbled, so careful early testing matters.

Healthy volunteers took single and rising daily doses, or dummy pills. Blood and spinal fluid were sampled for a day and a half after dosing. Twelve volunteers joined the spinal fluid part, nine on the drug and three on dummy pills. Readings swung widely, which the authors report plainly. The study maps how the drug moves amyloid balance in people, a step toward judging its promise.
pmc-11713913:
Blood tests for Alzheimer disease would be easier if a finger-prick style draw worked as well as a vein draw. Sara Ho and co-authors compared two arm-worn capillary collection devices with standard venipuncture in 2025. Nearly two hundred patients at a Johns Hopkins clinic gave spinal fluid, venous blood, and capillary blood for the study.

Both devices succeeded in most attempts and drew similar volumes of blood. Levels of three markers in capillary blood tracked venous levels closely, with one device matching a bit better on two markers. A fourth marker, tied to tau protein, matched only weakly in all blood samples. The authors conclude that capillary draws can support most of these biomarker tests in clinic use.
pmc-11714013:
Ajay Sood and five co-authors link blood pressure drugs in late life to thinking paths and to brain findings after death, in a 2025 conference paper. High blood pressure raises the risk of thinking loss. Yet how the drugs that treat it shape the brain was not well known.

The study held 4,207 older adults with no dementia at the start, checked each year with thinking tests and drug lists. More than 3,600 used a pressure drug at some point. Users began with higher thinking scores and lost ground more slowly than non users. A subset of 1,880 people died and gave their brains for study. The team matched drug use to plaques, tangles, and vessel harm found there.
pmc-11714313:
Six researchers in Japan study oral frailty inside a dementia prevention trial in a 2025 paper. Weak mouth function tracks poor nutrition in older adults, but no proven program targets the pair. This side analysis of the eighteen month J-MINT trial split participants by a baseline oral frailty score.

Of 531 enrolled, 433 entered the analysis, with a mean age near seventy-four and about half women. The program mixed exercise, nutrition advice, brain training, and vascular care. Outcomes spanned thinking scores, body mass, nutrition ratings, muscle and fat mass, food variety, and appetite. Change in each was compared between program and control arms within the frail and non frail groups, testing who gains most.
pmc-11714513:
Irene Esteban-Cornejo examines in 2025 whether resistance exercise shifts blood markers of Alzheimer disease in healthy older adults. Exercise ranks among the top non-drug hopes for protecting cognition. How it lifts thinking is still unclear, and blood markers may carry part of the answer.

Data come from the AGUEDA trial in Spain, with ninety adults aged sixty-five to eighty who think normally. One arm trains with resistance exercise for twenty-four weeks in a blinded, randomized design. No prior trial has tested exercise effects on these new blood markers. Marker shifts are read against cognitive gains. The study may reveal a blood path through which strength training guards the aging brain.
pmc-11714613:
Núria Guillén and co-authors test whether blood markers forecast thinking decline in Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 study. Spinal fluid and blood markers already help diagnose the disease. Whether they also predict how fast a mind will fade was unsettled.

The team followed 139 people with biologically confirmed disease, testing memory and thinking yearly for up to five years. Two blood markers stood out: patients starting with higher levels of a tau fragment and a glial protein lost ground faster on a standard mental test. A nerve damage marker in blood, and all spinal fluid markers, showed no such link. The authors say simple blood tests may help doctors and families plan, and trials pick patients likelier to decline.
pmc-11714713:
Alcibiades Villarreal and co-authors report biomarker data from older adults in Panama in 2025. Their study profiles people of Hispanic background for signs of Alzheimer disease. Samples cover spinal fluid, blood, and a gene tied to disease risk. Thinking and daily function were also tested for each person.

The group held a few dozen older adults who gave consent and full data. The team links spinal fluid markers with body wide markers in the blood. They also weigh how those markers track thinking scores. Data from this population are rare, so the cohort adds a needed view of how disease signs line up outside the usual study groups.
pmc-11714813:
Diego Szczupak and co-authors chart how the marmoset brain ages in health. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses MRI scans of this small primate, a key model for brain research. Marmosets share traits with humans, such as a large frontal cortex.

A new group, backed by the National Institute on Aging, tracks marmosets from birth through life. Gene-edited animals at risk for Alzheimer disease will be matched with normal aging peers. Here the team maps how each brain region grows and shrinks in healthy animals. That baseline lets later work spot disease change apart from normal aging.
pmc-11715013:
Maha Alshahrani and nine co-authors gathered what is known about models that predict dementia risk in poorer countries, in a 2025 review. Most people with dementia live in low- and middle-income countries, where services and research funds run thin. Models built in rich countries tend to travel badly to those settings.

The team merged findings from three earlier reviews of the whole literature up to 2023. Of more than 50 models worldwide, only seven came from poorer countries: five from China and two from Mexico. The models used standard inputs such as age, schooling, diabetes, and smoking. Their accuracy ranged widely, and none had been tested outside its home data. The authors say local factors such as income, literacy, diet, and pollution belong in the next wave of models.
pmc-11715113:
Fatemeh Seifar and co-authors map protein signatures in Alzheimer disease brains across racial groups. Their twenty twenty-five study answers a skew in the field: most Alzheimer knowledge rests on non-Hispanic White samples. A national partnership built diverse brain data to close that gap.

Protein reads from post-mortem brain tissue were compared across groups. Distinct molecular patterns emerged that past single-group work had blurred. The huge team joins brain banks and analysis centers across the United States. Such maps matter because a drug or test built on one group biology may miss others. The work sets a broader base for diagnosis and treatment design.
pmc-11715213:
Dementia can be fought on two fronts: changing risk factors early, or treating the brain changes once they start. Lynn van Rosmalen and co-authors compared the two fronts in 2025 with a simulation model that followed ten million people. Early prevention was modeled as a year's delay in silent brain change, while later treatment used amyloid-lowering drugs in early disease.

Drug treatment cut years lived with moderate or severe dementia sooner, by about five percent within five years. Risk-factor change paid off more slowly but reached a larger cut, around eight to nine percent, after twenty-five years. The two approaches drew even at nineteen years. Using both together helped, though slightly less than the sum. The authors urge combined, long-term effort.
pmc-11715313:
Jun Li and five co-authors read brain chemicals in folk who kept sharp thought despite heavy brain disease. Such holding up is called cognitive resilience.
