The team used a long study of aging priests, nuns, and lay folk who gave their brains at death. Thought was tested each year of life, and disease load was read after death.

Four hundred eighty-four brains were ground and read for six hundred known chemicals. Seventy-two of them tracked how well thought held up once disease load was set aside. A third of the hits were amino acids and their kin, and a fifth were fats. The hits grouped into six webs, each tied to a job. One web dealt with rust-like harm, one with links between nerve cells, and one with swelling. Lead chemicals in each web may point to new ways to guard thought.
pmc-11715413:
Amirali Vahid, Jafar Zamani, and Hadi Hosseini predict when brain amyloid turns positive, in a study published in 2025. Amyloid plaques build up years before Alzheimer's symptoms, and people whose scans cross from negative to positive face higher risk. The timing and brain pattern of that crossing were unclear.

The team used scans from 446 people who began amyloid-negative in a national Alzheimer's study, followed for about five years on average. Eighty-six crossed to positive in that span. Three survival models learned to estimate each person's crossing time, and checks showed fair accuracy. A ranking method then named the brain regions that carried the most signal. Such forecasts could help select people for prevention trials at the right moment.
pmc-11715613:
Sarah Bauermeister describes how Dementias Platform UK opens vast dementia research records to laboratories around the world. The platform holds data from more than 65 longitudinal cohorts and 3.6 million individuals. The files span clinical records, surveys, brain imaging, and genetic data. Access is free, and the team makes a point of drawing in researchers from low- and middle-income countries, where such data are hard to get.

Use starts with a short online application, and data owners reply in a median of 23 days. The platform also runs low-cost or free training schools and pairs junior staff with senior mentors. So far it counts 428 project requests from 1,038 users in 48 countries. More than 200 guests have joined its training events. Bauermeister argues that fair access and skills, not data alone, will widen who gets to do this research.
pmc-11715813:
Darby Peter and co-authors (2025) ask whether gut microbes carry part of fast food's effect on the brain in Alzheimer's disease. Western diets track with higher dementia risk. They also reshape the gut microbes, which talk to the brain through immune and metabolic channels. The missing link is mediation: do microbes sit on the causal path? The cohort here is cognitively healthy, so any signal precedes symptoms. The team measured fast food intake, gut microbe profiles from stool, and spinal fluid markers of Alzheimer's processes, neuron injury, and glial activation.

A mediation analysis then asks how much of the diet-to-marker link runs through the microbes. The author list spans nutrition, microbe science, and the major Alzheimer's marker laboratories, matching the question's shape. A proven microbial pathway would point to interventions, diet change, or microbial therapy, that could interrupt damage years before memory fails.
pmc-11715913:
James M Roe and co-authors ask whether the slow brain shrinkage of normal adult aging predicts memory decline on its own, apart from Alzheimer's disease, in this 2025 study. Standard models place shrinkage late in a chain that starts with amyloid buildup. Yet the brain regions hit hardest by the disease are also the ones that shrink fastest across a healthy life.

The team pooled repeat scans from three large cohorts, over four thousand scans from about a thousand healthy adults aged thirty to ninety-six. Change in brain structure tracked with change in memory across adulthood. In a smaller group with amyloid scans, the link held even without amyloid present. The results suggest some memory loss in aging follows plain brain change, not hidden disease.
pmc-11716313:
A dangerous pregnancy-linked condition can strike after birth, damaging blood, liver, and kidneys at once. Rita Pinto Medeiros and co-authors review that condition, HELLP syndrome, in 2024, with a focus on its link to a brain syndrome called PRES that swelling can trigger. Their review, prompted by a rare case of their own, searched three medical databases.

They found ten reports of the pairing during pregnancy and seven after birth. Their own patient developed multi-organ trouble, seizures, and stubborn high blood pressure after delivery. Brain imaging revealed the brain syndrome and, unexpectedly, a pituitary problem as well. She recovered fully with care. The authors urge early brain imaging whenever the pregnancy condition is diagnosed, so the brain complication is caught in time.
pmc-11716413:
Ana Montero-Calle and co-authors build electric biosensors to aid early diagnosis of Alzheimer disease in a 2025 paper. Blood signs of the disease could allow cheap, early checks, but they need sound proof. The team targets self-antibodies in blood that past work tied to the disease.

Magnetic beads carry disease-linked protein bits that catch those antibodies from plasma. A tagged second antibody then yields an electric signal on throwaway electrodes. The setup sensed antibodies against several disease-linked targets at once. Such multiplex platforms could one day back blood-based screening, once wider patient tests confirm the marks.
pmc-11716513:
Doris Molina-Henry and co-authors check whether a blood test for Alzheimer's pathology reads the same across racial and ethnic groups. The marker, plasma p-tau217, predicts amyloid buildup on brain scans, but trial data skew toward majority groups. They pooled two preclinical studies with nearly a thousand unimpaired adults, about a hundred from underrepresented groups.

The link between the blood marker and scan values matched across groups. A genetic risk factor did not bend the link in either group. The authors call for bigger samples per subgroup to confirm that the marker travels well.
pmc-11716613:
Hamilton Se-Hwee Oh and Tony Wyss-Coray measured seven thousand proteins in spinal fluid from about two thousand people to find what tracks thinking ability in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 study. The classic protein clumps, amyloid and tau, do not fully explain why some patients decline faster than others. The team looked for stronger correlates across the spectrum from healthy to severe dementia.

Proteins from synapses, the junctions between brain cells, correlated most strongly with impairment. A ratio of two of them, YWHAG to NPTX2, rose steadily with severity and separated resilient from vulnerable patients with the same clump burden. The ratio also climbs with age and rises about twenty-five years before symptoms in inherited forms of the disease.
pmc-11716713:
Hash Brown Taha and three co-authors pool forty-nine studies in 2025 on whether tiny parcels in body fluids can tell dementias apart. Alzheimer's, Lewy body, frontotemporal, Parkinson's, and vascular dementias mimic each other yet differ in cause and treatment. No fluid test now separates them during life.

The parcels, extracellular vesicles shed by cells, carry molecular cargo that may fingerprint each disease. The meta-analysis graded how well vesicle markers separate each disorder from the others and from healthy controls, across fluids from blood to saliva. Plain vesicles outperformed the supposedly brain-enriched ones, with steadier results and less bias, a surprise the authors flag for test designers.
pmc-11716813:
Andrew Hooyman, Kevin Duff, and Sydney Y Schaefer published a study in 2025 on an online thinking test for older adults. Many people cannot reach a clinic for testing, so the team moved a standard speed task onto home computers and touchscreens. Before such a test can be trusted, its scores must hold steady when nothing has changed.

Sixty-eight adults aged fifty-five and older took the symbol-matching task twice, one week apart, without supervision. Scores from the two sessions matched fairly well, though not perfectly. An instruction video and a short practice round helped people settle in. The results support home testing as a workable option, with room to improve steadiness.
pmc-11716913:
Siti Maisarah Mattap and co-authors set out, in this 2025 review, to rank what dementia research should tackle first in Southeast Asia. Most people with dementia live in low- and middle-income countries, yet most studies come from rich nations. The team searched the published work for stated research goals in the region, then compared them with goals set by regional experts at a workshop.

Only two studies, from Malaysia and Vietnam, passed the screen. The workshop group, drawn from six places, ranked twenty members' views into tiers. Top goals were local research skill and data gathering, public awareness, and health policy. Lower tiers covered shared guidelines, fair access, carer support, and digital tools. The ranked list is meant to guide funders and teams toward work that fits local needs.
pmc-11718113:
Usha Shukla, Manoj Kumar, Deepanshu Panchal, and Deepika Doneria compare three drugs added to a local anesthetic in epidural anesthesia for leg surgery. Added drugs can make the block start faster, last longer, and ease pain afterward. Patients were randomly split into three groups, each getting a different addition.

The dexmedetomidine group had the fastest start of both feeling and movement block, and by far the longest block and pain relief. Nalbuphine came next, and clonidine last, though clonidine caused more slow heart rate, low blood pressure, nausea, and vomiting. Sedation was most common with dexmedetomidine but stayed manageable. The authors rank dexmedetomidine first among the three.
pmc-11718513:
Jingjing Zhao and five co-authors review a decade of research on white matter wiring in developmental dyslexia, in a paper from 2024. Dyslexia impairs reading without any lack of intelligence, senses, or schooling. Brain wiring has become a leading place to look for its roots.

The review centers on a French dataset of sixty-four children, half with dyslexia, scanned with diffusion imaging. Three reading pathways recur across studies, and dyslexic readers often show weaker left-side connectivity in the main language tract. The paper also covers how the brain compensates and which thinking skills those wiring gaps explain.
pmc-11722113:
Xiangdong Li and co-authors build a system to predict what tissue type hides in leftover masses after chemotherapy for a testicular cancer type. Their 2024 study joins scan features with blood microRNA levels. A sound forecast can tailor surgery and spare patients needless harm.

Past single-route models did poorly in checks. The new model grows from a simple size measure to rich scan features, then adds precise microRNA inputs. In a forward-looking test set it scored high accuracy. A web tool turns scores and blood levels into quick odds for each tissue type. The authors offer the paired system as a step toward care matched to each patient.
pmc-11724213:
Noora BaniHammad and Raafat Jadah (2024) report a newborn boy whose seizures would not stop, and the drug that finally quieted them. His condition was super-refractory status epilepticus: seizures that persist or return even after a day of anesthetic treatment. Standard drugs failed in sequence, benzodiazepines, phenobarbital, levetiracetam, and a midazolam infusion. Genetic testing found a rare mutation in DDX3X, a gene whose disorders usually affect girls and involve development of the brain.

As a third-line agent the team added lacosamide. The drug works unusually, easing sodium channels into their slow off state rather than slamming them shut. The case describes the infant's response after lacosamide joined the regimen. Single cases cannot prove a treatment, but in a condition where hours of seizing damage the brain, a documented success in a genetic case gives the next team a place to start.
pmc-11725313:
Risa Nakamura and co-authors find the body-weight line above which pregnant patients with diabetes are likelier to need insulin. Gestational diabetes is managed first by diet, but some patients must add insulin, and knowing who is at risk helps planning. Their 2024 study reviews twenty-one patients treated through delivery at one Japanese department between 2013 and 2017.

Seven of the eight patients who needed insulin had a pre-pregnancy body mass index above 23. A statistical cut placed the threshold at 22.5, catching every insulin user while also flagging some who managed without. Patients above the line used insulin significantly more often and showed higher insulin resistance after delivery. Other post-delivery measures, including beta-cell function, did not differ by treatment type. The authors suggest that a simple pre-pregnancy number, well below Western obesity cutoffs, can guide early, closer monitoring in Japanese patients.
pmc-11726913:
Diabetes drugs have been linked to motor neuron disease in past reports, but those reports can mislead. Mengxia Wan and co-authors used gene tools to test cause rather than mere link, in a 2024 study. Their method treats gene variants in drug targets as stand-ins for taking the drug. Data came from large gene studies with over twenty-seven thousand patients with the disease.

One drug class target, tied to a newer sugar-lowering family, tracked with lower disease risk. A classic drug's main target showed no clear link on its own. One part of that drug's action, a cell energy unit, tracked with higher risk instead. Other drug families showed no clear ties. The authors say gene evidence can sort real drug effects from noise.
pmc-11727313:
Mingliang Sun, Jie Yuan, Xiaoyong Li, Dongxiao Liu, and Xinghai Wei design a lightweight way to encrypt images using a slim neural network. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Image protection grows harder as computing and AI spread, and chaos-based methods lose strength when their signals are cut into binary form.

Their scheme trims a known image network to fewer layers while keeping its eye for features. The network makes a key seed from the image itself, so the cipher keys tie to that exact picture. A shifting substitution box further scrambles the pixels. The design aims for high security without heavy computing. It avoids the added complexity of DNA-style ciphers that other teams use.
pmc-11727413:
Daniela Rosca and co-authors compare four risk scores for severe COVID outcomes in patients over seventy-five in a 2024 study. One hundred thirty-one older patients and two hundred twenty-six younger controls entered from two hospitals. Scores were computed at entry and at day five of symptoms. Survival curves and accuracy tests graded each score.

High scores at entry marked sharply lower survival in older patients. One score split survival at twenty-five versus seventy-four percent across its cutoff. By day five, that same score led accuracy among the four. Set cutoffs for all scores showed strong sorting power. Bedside scores can flag fragile older patients early for extra care.
pmc-11727813:
Ana Maria Waaga-Gasser and Thomas Böldicke survey two ways to aim guard cells at hid cancer marks, in a review from 2024. The marks, neoantigens, are fresh protein bits born of growth code flaws. Most sit in the cell, shown on its face in a tray. Stock drugs can not reach in; bred cells and bred binders can.

One road arms a soul's own T cells with a bred reader for the tray. Kin forms swap the reader's head for binder parts, or fuse the two. The next road skips cells: binders that grip the tray from the soup, or sneak in to jam the mark. Both face loss of the mark, tray tricks, mixed growths, and a guard held down. The pair map each form's state and its road to wards.
pmc-11727913:
Alcina Matos Queirós and co-authors survey how nursing home nurses check residents for depression and fall risk, in this 2024 study. The two problems are common in nursing homes and feed into each other, so assessing them together makes sense. The study gathered reported practices and views from nurses in the canton of Vaud, in western Switzerland.

One hundred sixteen nurses answered, most of them women, with an average of about thirteen years of nursing home work. Nearly nine in ten said they judge depression by watching mood and fall risk by asking about past falls. Fewer used validated scales: about three quarters for depression and about three in five for fall risk. Just over half saw depression as a real factor in fall risk. The authors urge wider use of proven tools and better training and policy support for nursing home nurses.
pmc-11728113:
Jiansen Ma and colleagues designed two compact antennas that each work across a very wide range of radio frequencies. The antennas, described in twenty twenty-four, stand in a single line and are meant for ground-based communication that sends signals in all directions. Extra electrical components are loaded onto the poles to widen the working band, and a hat tops one pole. Because real components change behavior with frequency, the team modeled them as varying with frequency rather than fixed, which gives more honest simulations.

With tuned load values, one antenna covers a low to mid frequency span and the other covers a higher span, both with acceptable signal reflection. Fast simulation methods let the team sweep the wide bands quickly. The authors present the pair as promising for vehicles, broadcasting, and other land-based radio uses.
pmc-11728413:
Zhihang Pan and co-authors test an open-source control system for ultra-precision machine axes, in work published in 2024. EtherCAT is a fast communication bus used in computer-controlled machine tools. High-end controllers with the master function built in are common, but the open-source IgH master had rarely been tried on ultra-precision machines.

The team turned a personal computer into a bus controller running the open master. They designed a motion interpolation method and a way to process tool-path code so the master gets accurate real-time data. Precision air-bearing axes and servo drives served as the controlled devices. Tests covered single-axis moves and two axes moving together in lines and circles. The controller drove the axes through ultra-precision motion well, showing the open route can meet the strict demands.
pmc-11728613:
Ana Pereira and co-authors review ways to raise vaccine uptake among older adults in a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis. Vaccines prevent millions of deaths each year, yet many older people still miss their shots. The team searched two large databases for trials of any method aimed at adults aged sixty and older. They pooled the results to compare which methods worked best.

Twenty studies passed the screen, most of them on flu shots. Teaching-based methods, such as clear talks and print guides, raised uptake the most among the methods with firm data. Advice from a doctor showed a large but less firm effect. Letter-based methods helped only a little. The authors note that free shots and age may also matter, and that more trials are needed.
pmc-11728813:
Iftikhar Khan and co-authors tune spray drying to make inhaled powders that carry drugs to the lungs, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. The powders start as fat-based carriers that form tiny bubbles once wet. Heat, air flow, and feed rate were varied for three sugar carriers to find the best settings.

Three plain powders gave high yields, small grain size, and low water content. When the best settings were used with a model asthma drug, the mannitol powder won on yield, grain size, and trapped drug. It also sent the most drug into the fine mist that reaches deep lung. Readers get practical settings for making such powders at larger scale.
pmc-11728913:
Vittoriana Crisera and three co-authors review how Saudi Arabia builds and uses clinical practice guidelines in a 2024 article. Guidelines give doctors shared, evidence-based steps for care, with the aim of better results and fairer treatment. They sit at the heart of the country's current plan to reform its health system.

The authors walk through how topics are picked, evidence is gathered, and guidelines are written and shared. A national center checks and publishes the stronger ones. They also name weak spots: conflicts of interest, missing voices at the table, uneven methods, and little follow-up after release. Their fixes include firm resources, building guidelines into electronic health records, and a culture that values proven care. Digital tools, they argue, will shape the next stage of the reform.
pmc-11736513:
Armağan Ütük and co-authors test bee venom against a pet fungus in a 2024 lab paper. The fungus causes ringworm-like skin disease in cats and dogs and spreads to people. Many samples now resist standard antifungal drugs. Bee venom kills microbes in other settings, so the team tried it on fungus samples taken from sick animals.

Four standard drugs were tested beside the venom across a range of doses. Every sample resisted two of the drugs outright, and only one drug worked well on all of them. Venom stopped the fungus at higher doses than the best drug needed. The gap matters, but a natural product that works at all on resistant samples earns further study.
pmc-11738113:
Adahra P Beso and co-authors report a rare case where lung cancer spread to a far-off bone in the lower leg. A sixty-year-old woman came in with cough and breathlessness, plus pain and swelling in her left leg. Spread of cancer to the hands or feet is very rare and usually a bad sign.

Scans first suggested two separate cancers, one in the lung and one in the leg. Tissue tests and marker stains settled the matter: the leg tumor was lung cancer that had traveled. The authors note lung cancer is the most common source of such distant bone spread. They stress that doctors should suspect it early, since quick, correct diagnosis shapes how the patient is treated.
pmc-11754013:
Reyhani-Ardabili, Fathi, and Ghafouri-Fard review CRISPR gene editing for modeling Gaucher disease in a 2024 paper. The disorder comes from faults in a gene for an enzyme that breaks down fatty material. Its forms range from lethal at birth to symptom-free.

Existing targeted therapies and stem cell transplants help, but success is limited. CRISPR tools raise hope for better treatment of metabolic disorders like this one. Editing also helps reveal the molecular steps behind the disease. The review covers both uses: building models that show how the disorder unfolds, and paths toward therapy. The authors weigh promise against the field's early stage.
pmc-11759113:
Dragan Jankovic and co-authors model blood flow in face pain in a 2023 study. The pain, among the worst known, comes when a vessel presses a face nerve. Surgery lifts the vessel off, but how flow in that vessel shifts after the lift was not known.

The team read scans from a small set of patients, most of them older women, before and after surgery. Flow sums gave stress marks on the vessel wall at each stage. The top arm vessel was the most common culprit. Such maps may show which flow traits track with pain that stays or fades. Brain surgeons gain a flow view of a nerve cure.
pmc-11759313:
Keisuke Yamamoto and Hirofumi Hashimoto test whether not knowing helps people stay generous, in a 2025 web experiment. In the dictator game, one player splits a sum and may simply avoid learning how much the other side needs. Past work found that the chance to stay ignorant cuts giving.

The pair reshaped the game so the other player faces a loss, a setup meant to stir empathy. Two hundred Japanese adults played online. The loss twist changed nothing: giving and strategic ignorance ran at their usual rates. Even told of the other's loss, players used ignorance as cover to give less, as if it excused them.
pmc-11760413:
Sindy Nelwan and four co-authors test the accuracy of digital mouth scans for children with mixed dentition in a 2024 study. Mixed dentition is the stage when baby and adult teeth share the mouth. Scanners that build a 3D model of the teeth have changed dental work fast, but their truth at this stage was in doubt.

Dozens of children were scanned with a named scanner and also had classic plaster models made from molds. Arch widths were read the same way on both forms. The team then set the two sets of measures side by side, to judge how close the scan comes to the cast.
pmc-11772413:
Coulter and Prather test one brain nook's part in how hen finches hold song picks in this twenty twenty-four study. Hens pick mates by song, and their rank of songs guides that choice. Two ear-brain sites feed this nook, which hints it helps judge song worth.

Inside, hens heard set songs and showed their picks in act tests. When the nook was stilled by a cut, song ranks lost their firm hold. Hens still heard the songs, yet their pick order swung from test to test. The team reads the nook as a hub where ear paths meet to set worth. That hub may lock a pick in place while court acts play out.
pmc-11773813:
Andrea Fuentes-Terrón and co-authors review enzymes that set up proteins for destruction through the N-degron pathway in plants. Their paper, reported in 2024, deals with the cysteine and arginine branch of that pathway.

This branch controls proteins that start with methionine followed by cysteine, once the methionine is cut and the cysteine is oxidized. Targets include factors that drive responses to low oxygen, and proteins tied to developmental hypoxia. Two enzyme groups control their start: methionine aminopeptidases and plant cysteine oxidases. The review covers what these enzymes bind and how well they act, since those traits decide which proteins are degraded and when.
pmc-11774713:
Yitian Lang and co-authors weigh the cost of adding a new drug to breast cancer care, in a study published in 2024. The drug, capivasertib, is added to an older hormone drug for advanced cancer that feeds on hormones. Trial results showed the pair fights the cancer well. The question here is whether the gain is worth the price for health payers.

The team built a model of how patients fare over time on each plan. For the United States, the added health gain came at a very high cost per year of good life. Checks from many angles gave the same answer, and a test case for China agreed. At the current price, the authors judge the pair poor value for money.
pmc-11775013:
Wang and co-authors introduce a journal research topic on how animal pathogens interact with the cells they infect, and on new ways to detect animal diseases. Infections are among the biggest threats to livestock farming, and understanding exactly how a germ enters and spreads inside host cells guides the design of drugs, vaccines, and antibody treatments.

The editorial explains why current diagnostic tests still suffer from low sensitivity, inaccuracy, and slow results, and why many animal vaccines remain weak or unsafe. The collection gathers twenty studies across three themes: immune mechanisms of infection, new diagnostic technology, and novel vaccines. The editors present it as groundwork for faster outbreak detection and better disease control on farms.
pmc-11782013:
Yue Yao and co-authors describe three patients with cutaneous pseudolymphoma, a skin condition where reactive growth of lymph tissue looks like skin lymphoma under the microscope and in the clinic. Causes vary widely, and in many patients no cause is ever found. Lab findings alone can only suggest the diagnosis.

The three cases differed in cause, appearance, and treatment. The authors stress that confirming the condition takes clinical details, further tests, and follow-up over time, not just a biopsy. Because the condition can mimic a true cancer yet behaves differently, treatment should target the cause where one is known, and patients need long-term watching. The series aims to help clinicians keep this imitator in mind.
pmc-11786213:
Abbas Andishmand and co-authors reviewed lung clot cases in central Iran in two thousand twenty-four. A pulmonary embolism blocks arteries in the lungs. It can kill quickly if missed or severe. The team gathered cases from one medical center. They profiled symptoms, treatment, and outcomes. Follow-up stretched to about two years median.

Just over one hundred patients were analyzed. Breathlessness was by far the commonest symptom. Chest pain appeared in about half the cases. Most clots were classed as non-massive in severity. Survival analysis hunted predictors of death. Age emerged among the independent predictors. Local outcome data help regional hospitals plan care. The study anchors Iranian evidence on this emergency.
pmc-11790413:
Yuxiang Huang and six co-authors wrote this review on liver cancer care. The catalog lists the review under 2025, while the text itself is dated 2024. The topic is natural killer cells, immune cells that watch the liver for threats. In liver tumors, these cells wear out and lose their killing power.

Worn-out killer cells show fewer attack switches and more brake switches, such as PD-1, TIM-3, and LAG-3. The review weighs plans that block several brakes at once to revive the cells. Early lab studies suggest such combined blocks can restore killing and help drugs work better. The authors present this pairing as a fresh path for treating a cancer that now kills many patients each year.
pmc-11793113:
Chronic diseases like high blood pressure and diabetes are rising fast in poorer countries, yet they draw little global funding. Semira Abdelmenan and co-authors measure the burden in this 2024 survey of adults in a tracked district of Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

About one adult in nine reported at least one chronic condition. Blood pressure led, followed by diabetes. Older age, no schooling, being formerly married, and greater wealth all came with higher reported rates. The authors call for wider early screening and care in city settings, arguing that the capital's figures show these diseases are now a major public health task for Ethiopia.
pmc-11795313:
A large team of researchers surveyed people who work on rare diseases in Türkiye for this study, published in 2024. Rare and undiagnosed diseases are hard to treat because each one affects few people and tests are scarce. The team wanted to hear from the professionals themselves about what blocks their work.

The online survey drew 363 replies from researchers, health workers, and people who do both jobs. Replies pointed to the same barriers: patients must be sent to special centers, costs are high, key tests are hard to get, and research support is weak. Small patient groups also make studies hard to run. The authors call for more funding, better tracking systems, and a clear national plan for rare diseases.
pmc-11811113:
Le Tong, Lin Tang, Bangli Tang, and Jianna Zhang published a meta-analysis, with the head dated 2024, on stem cell sources for healing diabetic foot ulcers. These wounds drive much suffering and cost. Twenty-four studies with over thirteen hundred patients were pooled, comparing cells from blood, fat, cord, bone, and other sources against usual care.

Every source raised the odds of healing. Blood-derived cells ranked highest, followed by fat and cord cells, though only the cord group's edge cleared statistical doubt and its studies varied widely. Bias checks trimmed the pooled benefit, which stayed positive. The authors call stem cell therapy promising for ulcer care while urging cleaner trials.
pmc-11825813:
Patrick Greiss and co-authors test how scent compounds from cannabis affect lung immune cells, in work from twenty twenty-four. The compounds, called terpenes, give the plant its aroma and may calm swelling. The target cells guard the lungs against germs, so any change in their work matters.

The team exposed a mouse lung cell line to two store bought terpene mixes, with and without a bacterial trigger. The mixes did not change swelling signal output. Cells did take up coated beads more, but germ uptake stayed the same. Adding THC, the main active compound, changed little. The authors conclude that terpenes have minimal impact on these lung cells.
pmc-11833313:
Guanjian Chen and seven co-authors build an AI model to spot blood vessels near the stomach during cancer surgery. Their paper is dated two thousand twenty-five in the pack, while its text head says the year before. The surgery removes the stomach in part and clears lymph nodes, a key step for advanced stomach cancer. Skill in finding vessels varies by surgeon, which can affect safety.

Their model learns from still images cut from surgery videos, then is tested on full live videos. It finds arteries and veins with high scores for precision and match. Hard views with blood or smoke lower its scores, while views from obese patients stay good. The tool may cut stray bleeding in surgery.
pmc-11847613:
Anil Kumar Tomar and co-authors hunted blood protein markers of breast cancer in Indian women in a 2024 study. Cancer patterns in India differ by age, risk, and outcome, and deaths stay high, so early screening tools are badly needed. The team compared the full protein mix in patients' blood with that of healthy controls.

Several proteins split the groups cleanly. Four ran higher in patients and three ran lower, and one lead protein was confirmed by a second method. The shifts grew step by step from early cancer to spread disease for two of the proteins. The authors name these proteins as candidate markers for future tests and drug targets. They call for deeper work on what each protein does in the disease.
pmc-11879413:
Maude Lavallée and eleven co-authors document a near-total failure to report serious drug harms in a Canadian hospital, in this 2024 paper. Serious adverse events must be reported to Health Canada, and since 2019 a law named for a young victim, Vanessa's Law, has required hospitals to file them. Whether the law changed practice was unknown.

The team reviewed 500 patient records from a Quebec heart and lung institute, spanning 2018 to 2021, in four yearly cohorts. Patients took a median of eighteen drug products, and reviewers counted 302 serious events in total. The share reported to Health Canada was zero percent, both before and after the law took effect. The authors raise a red flag: a reporting duty that staff barely know cannot protect patients, and they call for urgent fixes.
pmc-11888613:
B Keerthana, M Janani Moorthy, R Sarvesh, and Vinoth Thangam tested a scan method for tumors at the back of the brain, in a 2024 study. Tumors in this rear lower area are hard to tell apart on plain scans. The method, diffusion-weighted imaging, tracks water movement in tissue and often marks tumors brightly. The team ran a forward-looking study on patients with suspected tumors there.

Twenty patients were scanned on a standard machine with the method included. Most tumors appeared in patients aged sixty-one to seventy, and men outnumbered women. One tumor type, medulloblastoma, was the most common found. The scan method scored high on both finding tumors and ruling them out. The authors back it as an aid to diagnosis and planning.
pmc-11932713:
William L Harryman and co-authors warn that mid-grade prostate tumors can hide killers. Their 2024 paper focuses on intermediate risk prostate cancer, most of it managed with surveillance, radiation, or surgery, and on two subtypes buried inside that label: cribriform architecture and intraductal carcinoma.

Both subtypes carry more metastasis, recurrence, and death, yet biopsy misses them up to half the time, and even guided sampling catches barely half. Finding either one can disqualify a man from surveillance. The authors argue the field needs sharper detection, from molecular study of the subtypes to AI-read pathology and live microscopy of surgical tissue. Matching each hidden subtype to its best treatment, they say, could stop quiet tumors from becoming high-risk disease.
pmc-11975513:
Zicong Wang and a team of co-authors map a research field in a bibliometric study from two thousand twenty-four. Long noncoding RNAs help drive diseases of blood vessel growth, from cancer to diabetic eye disease. The authors charted fifteen years of work on these RNAs in such diseases.

They analyzed one thousand five hundred sixteen papers published from two thousand twelve to two thousand twenty-two. Output rose steadily and peaked in two thousand twenty-one. China led in volume, the United States in influence, and one Chinese university topped the institutional list. Burst keywords pointed to fresh fronts such as vascular remodeling and pulmonary arterial hypertension. The authors say these hotspots mark where the field is heading.
pmc-12007513:
Moritz Koster and co-authors found this 2023 cultural split already present in one-year-old brains. Adults in Western cultures attend to focal objects; East Asian adults weight the background more. Whether that tuning starts in infancy was unknown. The team recorded brain waves from thirty-five Viennese and thirty-six Kyoto infants while objects and backgrounds flickered at different rates, letting the signals be separated.

Viennese babies showed a stronger object signal; Kyoto babies a stronger background signal. In a play session, Viennese mothers also pointed out objects more than Kyoto mothers did. The authors trace part of the split to these everyday interactions. Culture, it seems, starts tuning the eyes before a child can talk.
pmc-12022613:
Kopiczko and co-authors test a blood fat as a sign of fatty liver in children in a 2024 study. Fifty-seven children with obesity were checked with a scan that weighs liver fat. Blood levels of three related fats were read, plus two enzyme gauges built from their ratios. A lean reference group gave a base line.

The fat called DGLA ran higher in children with obesity than in the reference group. Its level and one enzyme gauge rose with liver fat content. As a test for liver fat, DGLA scored fairly well. The authors propose DGLA as a needle-only sign that could spare children scans, and link the fat pattern to how the disease forms.
pmc-12068013:
Victoria Shvetsova and co-authors study two additives in a fast-setting blended cement: sodium citrate and a PCE plasticizer. The binder mixes Portland cement with a tenth calcium aluminate cement, giving quick set and high early heat. Each additive alone is known, but their combined and sequenced use was unmapped.

Their 2024 study tracks heat flow, phase makeup, microstructure, and the strength of fine concrete as the additives enter together or in turn. Citrate reshaped the new crystal phases and slowed the main silicate's hydration several fold, while speeding other clinker parts early on. Timing the plasticizer against the citrate changed the outcome again. The results guide mix designers who need speed without losing control of the cure.
pmc-12182013:
Hunter and a large team set out a study protocol on city environments and brain health in twenty twenty-four. Keeping the mind sharp in later life is a global priority. Activity and supportive neighbourhoods may delay dementia. How the urban exposome acts through the body is poorly understood.

The study recruits older adults from Northern Ireland ageing cohorts. Each wave aims for four hundred people aged sixty-five and over. Wrist devices track movement, and GPS units track location. Those data link to cognitive tests, mood scales, and blood based molecular data. Maps of the built and natural environment complete the picture. Analysis will use causal and mediation methods to trace pathways.
pmc-12323813:
So Hyun Kang, Jihoo Kim, and their co-authors present a 2024 method to sharpen MRI scans that are taken with only part of the usual data. Partial scans are faster, but filling in the missing part well is hard. Their method joins a classic phase based rule with a newer deep learning trick that needs no training data at all.

The trick rests on the idea that a fresh, untrained network can itself capture the shape of good images while it rebuilds one. The team tested the combined method on three data sets, including a public brain and knee set and a low field scanner set. Image quality beat older methods, with error cut by factors from about 1.15 to 2.5. Faster scans with clean images could widen MRI access.
pmc-12581013:
Tomohide Kubo and three co-authors study sleep and tiredness in shift-working nurses in Japan, in this twenty twenty-four paper. Sleep at night restores the body more than sleep by day. Nurses who work nights lose many chances for night sleep, and the cost to their energy was unclear.

More than five hundred nurses logged their sleep daily for one month, right after waking. The team grouped them by how many nights in the month they could sleep at night, from few to almost all. They then compared tiredness and related outcomes across the groups. The study tests the idea of anchor night sleep and may guide roster planning.
pmc-12659613:
A scorpion sting can do more than burn: its venom sometimes reaches the heart's electrical system. Mohammad Javad Zibaeenezhad and co-authors report in 2025 a 56-year-old Iranian man stung by a yellow scorpion who arrived dizzy, fainting, and with a dangerously slow pulse. His electrocardiogram showed complete heart block — the atria and ventricles beating independently — and blood tests pointed to heart muscle injury.

Temporary pacing through a vein steadied him while fluids, atropine, and monitoring supported recovery. His heart's pumping function was reduced but its structure was intact. The block ultimately resolved with a permanent pacemaker in place, and he went home stable. The authors urge emergency teams in scorpion country to watch the heart rhythm from the first hour, since this rare complication turns deadly without pacing.
pmc-12660713:
Qiang Zheng and co-authors build a column that cleans acid mine drainage with steel slag, in a research paper from 2025. Mine drainage carries sulfate and heavy metals that harm water and health. The team fills a lab column with coarse sand and carbon steel slag in varied mixes, and tests which mix cleans best.

One mix with a fifth slag removed almost all iron, manganese, and zinc, and most sulfate. Surface tests show metals stuck as exchanged ions, hydroxides, and mixed deposits. Sulfate sat in calcium and iron compounds. Most metals lodged in the top layer at the best mix. The work offers a low-cost use for steel waste.
pmc-12662913:
Refugees arrive in the United States carrying high rates of hypertension, and whether they understand the condition may decide whether they control it. Abeer Alharthi and co-authors study that link among Iraqi and Syrian refugees in a 2025 paper. Ninety-five patients at a San Diego health center answered an Arabic survey on knowledge, attitudes, and practices.

Participants then measured their blood pressure at home with digital cuffs, several days a week for a month. Control was judged by cardiology guidelines against the averaged home readings. Statistical models tied each level of survey score to the chance of control. The sample averaged near fifty-nine years old, and most were unemployed. The authors aim the results at fairer hypertension care for resettled refugees.
pmc-12663113:
Hossein Ghahvehchian, Golshan Latifi, and Masoud Aghsaei Fard measure eye surface nerves in children with a genetic tumor condition, in a 2025 study. The condition can grow tumors along the optic path, and the cornea's tiny nerves may mirror nerve health. A microscope that images living tissue makes the nerves visible without a biopsy.

Thirteen eyes of seven affected children were compared with ten eyes of six healthy children. Two software tools, one guided and one automatic, measured nerve length, density, and branching. The affected eyes showed longer and denser nerves on key measures, a surprise direction. Agreement between the tools was also checked. If confirmed, the eye's surface could offer a painless window on this condition in children.
pmc-12663213:
Agata Trzcinska and co-authors test how boosting self-esteem affects materialism in preschoolers in a 2025 experimental study. The team asked whether feeling able and accepted makes young children want things less, and whether mind reading skill matters.

Over two hundred Polish preschoolers took part, after a pilot check proved the esteem boost worked. Esteem was raised in skill and social acceptance areas. The boost cut materialistic leanings, but only in children with well-developed theory of mind. Those children can model what others think and feel. The findings back early esteem work as a guard against materialism, with gains tied to social cognition growth.
pmc-12663313:
Jingwei Xu and co-authors test high-pressure abrasive water jets for cutting reinforced concrete in a 2025 study. Such jets could help tunnel boring machines break through concrete strengthened with glass fiber polymer bars. How the jet cuts the bars and the concrete together was not well studied.

The experiments clarify how each material is removed during cutting. The team describes itself as presenting the first full experimental analysis of this coupled cutting. Tunnel builders get data on a method that could cut composite reinforcement without the wear and sparks of mechanical tools.
pmc-12663413:
Adithya Venkatachalam, Umadevi Seerengasamy, and Abraham Sudharson Ponraj present a 2025 framework that designs a key chip part on its own. The part, called a multiply-accumulate unit, does repeated multiply-and-add steps. Such units sit at the heart of fast signal work, from image filters and sound to neural networks, where speed and low energy use both matter.

Their system uses a Python script to write hardware code that can be built as a chip. Users can set the bit width and the number of cycles. The design pairs a grouped multiplier with a fast adder to raise speed and cut energy use. The team checked the code with pro tools and ran it through synthesis and layout steps to show it can scale for high-end computing tasks.
pmc-12664213:
Chih-Hsueh Lin and co-authors studied drugs that may be unfit for older adults at a rural hospital in Taiwan, in a 2025 paper. Such drugs can do more harm than good in old age, yet rural areas have fewer resources and little past study. The team used two screening lists, one built for Taiwan and one from the United States, to count how often these drugs were given.

Records covered a full year and 8,234 older outpatients. About 58 percent got at least one flagged drug by either list. A second study within the study then compared drug exposure in the month before a hospital stay with exposure in three earlier windows. Recent exposure tied to higher odds of urgent admission.
pmc-12669913:
Zhao and co-authors follow more than 15,000 rural Chinese adults for ten years to measure what long-term dirty air does to hearts and brains. Most earlier evidence came from cities; rural exposure patterns differ. The cohort spans three sites with contrasting levels of fine particle pollution, tracked from 2013 to 2023 for heart attacks, strokes, and related events. Statistical models linked each person's average exposure to their outcomes.

Every small rise in fine particles — one microgram per cubic meter — came with about five percent higher risk of cardiovascular disease overall. The rises were steeper for specific events: seven percent for ischemic stroke, eight for coronary heart disease, and ten for brain bleeding. The highest-exposure quarter faced clearly more risk than the lowest, and older residents were hit hardest. The authors argue that air quality policy is heart policy, in the countryside as much as in the city.
pmc-12680613:
Tarik Saleh and co-authors test the strength of a steel part that sat in a nuclear test reactor in 2025. The steel is a type used for parts that face high radiation doses. The part was a duct from a fuel test set. Light from the core gave it very high doses near the middle and low doses at the top.

Small samples were cut along the duct's height. They were pulled in tests at room heat, mild heat, and near their in-core heat. Heat had a larger effect on strength than dose did. Below a set heat, radiation made the steel harder as heat fell. Above that heat, changes were small. The team links the pattern to flaws inside the steel.
pmc-12682913:
Paula Pavia and six co-authors hunt for reasons the standard drug fails a third of Colombian soldiers treated for cutaneous leishmaniasis, a skin disease spread by sandflies. They followed one hundred twenty-eight soldiers treated with meglumine antimoniate in 2018 and 2019. Records covered patients, lesions, and the parasite species involved, mapped by region. Some parasites from failed cases faced the drug again in the lab.

About sixty-eight percent were cured, leaving failure near thirty-two percent. Failure clustered with earlier infections, earlier use of the same drug, swollen lymph nodes, and certain lesion types and sizes. Infections picked up in the Orinoquía and Pacific regions also failed more often. One parasite species dominated in the east and Amazon, another spread widely. Lab tests found no drug resistance, so the authors point to patient and exposure factors and urge closer monitoring of high-risk soldiers.
pmc-12683813:
Seyoung Park and five co-authors measure size differences between male and female Yellow-browed Buntings, a small songbird. Their study came out in 2025. Knowing a bird's sex in the field helps explain why males and females migrate on different schedules.

The team caught first-year birds at a stopover island in South Korea and confirmed each bird's sex with a genetic test. Wing length differed most between the sexes, with tail length next. A simple rule based on wing length alone sorted the birds correctly in almost all test cases. Field workers can now sex this species quickly, without sending samples to a laboratory.
pmc-12686313:
Nanotechnology carried much of the fight against COVID-19, from masks to the vaccines themselves. Mamo Dikamu and co-authors survey that record in this 2025 review, sorting the tools by the health world's three-part plan: prevent, detect, treat. Tiny fibers and metal particles strengthened masks and disinfectant coatings during the outbreak.

Gold and magnetic particles powered fast tests, joined by quantum dots and smart sensors. Lipid nanoparticles delivered the mRNA vaccines, while other carriers aimed drugs at infected tissue. The review also names hurdles: safety rules, scale-up, and proof in patients still lag the lab work. The authors close by asking how these tools can be kept ready for the next virus.
pmc-12687513:
Inusah and three co-authors measured wealth gaps in malaria prevention during pregnancy across West Africa in twenty twenty-five. Pregnant women should receive at least three doses of a preventive antimalarial to cut anemia and poor birth outcomes. Coverage varies widely, and equity is a stated global goal.

Using household survey data from fifteen countries between twenty fifteen and twenty twenty-one, the team applied a World Health Organization equity toolkit. Coverage ranged from eleven percent in Mauritania to fifty-eight percent in Burkina Faso. Richest women were far ahead in Guinea, Togo, and Benin. Paradoxically, the poorest quintiles led in Liberia, Nigeria, and Sierra Leone, showing near-equitable access there. The authors call for equity-driven strategies to lift coverage among poorer women elsewhere.
pmc-12691213: Sasha Shafikhani closes a journal research collection, in a 2025 editorial, on how the immune system and bacterial infection shape each other. The piece is a brief closing editorial rather than a research report. Its opening stakes the theme plainly: bacterial infections remain a persistent and evolving threat to human health worldwide. As the final word on the collection, it frames the gathered work on immunopathogenesis, the study of how immune responses drive and respond to bacterial disease.
pmc-12693213:
Yanhui Jiao, Xiaoqian Wang, Zisheng Tang, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It reports a way to grow thin sheets of a vanadium-bearing crystal, V-WSe2, a material prized for future light-based electronics.

Such two-dimensional crystals are hard to grow evenly. The team used a vapor method at normal air pressure, adding halide salts to help the process along. The salts lowered the temperature at which a key ingredient evaporates, giving better control and cleaner crystals. Of the three salts tried, potassium iodide allowed the lowest growth temperature. The team also varied how much vanadium went in. More vanadium narrowed the material's energy gap and shifted its light response. The study lays out knobs growers can turn to tune the material for devices.
pmc-12693613:
Li Ting Lee and co-authors published this 2025 study on germ-fighting peptides from a freshwater fish. The climbing perch makes peptides in its skin mucus that can kill bacteria. Earlier work found two such peptides, and one, AtMP2, also fought cancer cells in tests. The team asked whether tuned versions of AtMP2 could kill germs even better.

They used a guided change process to breed new variants on the computer, then scored them with three prediction tools. Two variants were made and tested in the lab. Both beat the original against the Gram-positive germ group. At a set dose, both also proved safe for the human and animal cell lines tested. The work points toward new germ-fighting drugs drawn from fish defenses.
pmc-12694413:
Viktor Klimov and co-authors coat pine wood with a varnish blend that sheds water so well the drops bead at extreme angles, in a 2025 paper. The base is epoxy varnish, tough but only mildly water-resistant. Into it they mix tailored copolymers carrying fluorine-bearing side chains, which migrate to the surface and lower its energy. The result keeps the wood's natural grain visible while reaching superhydrophobic behavior, with contact angles up to 155 degrees.

How the coating is applied shapes its micro-texture and thus its repellency, a link the team demonstrates directly. After sixty days underwater, coated wood absorbed less than a third as much water as wood in plain varnish. Six months in the tropical climate of South Vietnam left both the repellency and the wood's looks intact. The authors propose the blend for outdoor wood that must survive wet climates.
pmc-12696213:
Drugs used against head and neck cancers can harm healthy tissue, including the glands that make saliva and the cells that build blood. Raneem Obeid and four co-authors tested in 2025 whether mango peel extract could shield those tissues in rats. Sixty male rats were split into groups that got the drugs alone, the extract alone, both, or neither, over three weeks.

Rats on both kept more weight than rats on the drugs alone, and their blood cell counts fell less. Under the microscope their saliva glands showed less scarring and milder cell damage. The extract did not undo the drugs' drop in blood sugar. The authors read the results as early support for the extract as a helper treatment.
pmc-12698513:
Pingping Xiao and five co-authors reported an adult whose immune storm paired a gene flaw with a herpes flare, in a case report published in 2025. The storm, called HLH, floods the body with immune activity and can kill. Hers came at age 43, with a month of fever and liver faults. Blood counts fell across lines, iron stores soared, and the marrow held scavenger cells.

Gene tests found a half flaw, one altered copy, in a known HLH gene. The flare of a common herpes virus, type 6B, matched the time she fell ill. Earlier case reports show such half flaws turn up in adults with the storm, often next to a microbial trigger. Full care left her alive and well. The authors urge gene checks in adult cases, with or without a microbe.
pmc-12699813:
Holmes and co-authors lay out a trial plan testing ultrasound in children with blunt belly trauma. Bleeding from inner belly injuries is a top cause of trauma death in children. The FAST scan is a quick bedside ultrasound that looks for free fluid after injury.

The randomised trial enrolls children who are stable despite their injuries. It tests if adding FAST to usual care changes outcomes, scan use, or hospital stays. A clear protocol matters because past results on FAST in children have been mixed. The trial aims to settle when the scan truly helps.
pmc-12699913:
Gang Wang and colleagues mapped in 2025 the expansin gene family in pecan, a plant gene group that loosens cell walls so cells can grow. Expansins shape plant growth and stress response, but pecan's set was unknown. The team scanned the pecan genome and tracked gene activity across tissues, stress, and fruit drop.

They found thirty-nine expansin genes on fourteen chromosomes, in four subfamilies, with many duplicated pairs that likely grew the family. Promoter regions held elements tied to hormones, growth, and stress. Most genes were active in select tissues, and some reacted strongly to stress from living and non-living sources. Many switched on in fruit that stayed on the tree, hinting at roles in fruit retention.
pmc-12700513:
Alaa Abd-Alrazaq and a large team of co-authors weigh the hype around artificial intelligence in clinical care against daily reality. AI could improve decisions, smooth workflows, and lift patient outcomes. Yet the authors argue the gains stay limited by linked technological, human, and ethical barriers. They call for a holistic, systems-based approach that treats these barriers as connected, not separate.

Named obstacles include limited explainability, algorithmic bias, poor interoperability, and weak validation. Human hurdles include resistance to change and thin clinician training, while legal worries cover liability, privacy, and consent. Their fixes include shared global rules, co-design with clinicians and patients, and more clinician education.
pmc-12703013:
Ghedak Ansari and co-authors study pain around surgery for obstructive sleep apnea, in this 2025 paper. The team reviewed more than two thousand adults who had throat or jaw surgery for the condition in one health system between 2009 and 2017. They tracked prior pain diagnoses, depression, and pain drug prescriptions before and after surgery.

About a third of patients had a pain diagnosis before surgery, and two in five already had an opioid prescription. After surgery, nearly all patients received opioids, most often after soft tissue surgery. The authors warn that this group starts with high pain and mood burdens, which raises the risk of drug problems.
pmc-12703113:
Gholamreza Shamsaei and three co-authors test sound scans for fast diagnosis of a nerve attack disease in a 2025 study. Guillain-Barré syndrome strikes nerves fast, but wire tests can read normal in the first days, which delays care. Sound scans offer a no needle way to size nerves at the bedside, and the team asked if swollen nerves show up early.

They enrolled seventy five patients within two weeks of onset and seventy five matched healthy peers at a hospital in Ahvaz, Iran. All got wire tests plus scans of the arm nerves. Every scan width and wire measure split the groups with clear gaps. Patient nerves ran wider at the measured sites. The authors back scans as an early aid beside wire tests.
pmc-12703413:
An expert panel of the European Food Safety Authority weighs whether fish eggs can smuggle three salmon viruses into disease-free waters, in a 2025 assessment. The viruses cause hemorrhagic septicemia, a blood-forming tissue necrosis, and salmon anemia, all devastating to farms and wild stocks. Countries free of them guard their borders, but fertilized eggs and gametes cross those borders for breeding.

The panel found no proof that any of the three viruses passes truly inside the egg from parent to offspring. Surface contamination, though, cannot be excluded. If exporters follow the draft international code, including testing each broodfish at stripping, the median chance of introduction with a shipment of eggs is well under one percent. The assessment gives regulators numbers to set import conditions on, instead of fear or habit.
pmc-12703713:
Alistair Thorpe and co-authors test whether a simple leaflet can change how older adults view antibiotics for bacteria in the urine. Bacteria can sit in the urine with no symptoms, a state called asymptomatic bacteriuria. Treating it as an infection wastes antibiotics and can harm patients over sixty-five.

Their 2025 study is an online survey experiment with adults in that age group. Each person read a scenario about a positive urine test before surgery, then got a leaflet or not, along with varied advice from a surgeon. The main outcome was comfort with skipping antibiotics when they are not needed. The study also tracked false beliefs and knowledge about the condition.
pmc-12704113:
Jasemin Todri, Enkeleda Gjini, and Orges Lena test four pain scales in Albania in a 2025 paper. Pain strength is the main measure in low back pain trials, and a sound scale is key to picking care. The four scales use a line, numbers, faces, and a short survey form.

Two hundred people with low back pain at one regional center took all four scales at their first visit. They rated worst, average, least, and current pain over the past week. The scales agreed strongly with each other in every domain. Math checks showed all four tap one shared trait, which supports using any of them in this group.
pmc-12704913:
Fei Xu and colleagues followed middle-aged and older adults across China in a nationwide study published in two thousand twenty-five. They asked whether staying socially and intellectually active changes how frailty develops over time. Seven years of survey data were sorted into distinct frailty paths using a standard frailty index.

Three frailty trajectories emerged, from steadier health to worsening weakness. More frequent social and thinking activities linked to safer paths, with effects varying by age, sex, and whether people lived in town or countryside. Health planners gain long-term evidence that clubs, games, and learning are not extras; they track with slower decline.
pmc-12706013:
Ferdinard Oshionebo and colleagues simulate car radiators cooled by ternary hybrid nanofluids, mixes of three nanoparticle kinds in a base coolant. Nanofluids already beat plain coolants, and particle mixes and shapes can push further. Eight blends of metals and oxides, among them iron-copper-silver and silver with two oxides, were run through a ruffled-fin radiator model.

More particles meant better heat flow and cooler outlet fluid. The best blend cut engine outlet temperature by 44.6 percent. A combined performance index slipped by about six to twelve percent, though, with plain oxides slipping least. The study maps the gain and the trade-off for radiator design.
pmc-12706213:
Angela Chen and co-authors lay out a pilot trial for women who had gestational diabetes and now face high type 2 diabetes risk. Their 2025 protocol runs in Australian referral hospitals. Lifetime risk after pregnancy diabetes reaches about sixty percent, most of it landing within a decade.

The factorial design crosses drug therapy with activity monitoring. One arm takes metformin alone; another adds a GLP-1 drug. Activity trackers support behavior change in the parallel arm. Feasibility and acceptability are the pilot goals, since neither drug path has solid postpartum safety data yet. Lifestyle programs work but struggle to roll out, the authors note. The pilot will show whether drug plus tracker support can be delivered and tolerated in new mothers.
pmc-12707013:
Seven researchers led by Susanna C. Larsson used gene data to test whether drinking alcohol causes cancer. Their study, published in twenty twenty-five, applied a method that uses gene variants linked to drinking as a stand-in for drinking itself. Data came from four large biobanks and from cancer research groups, covering twenty types of cancer.

The team found no link between gene-predicted drinking and cancer overall. They did find signs of higher risk for head and neck, food pipe, and bowel cancers. Evidence for liver cancer was mixed, and none appeared for breast cancer. Some cancers, such as kidney cancer, showed lower risk instead. The authors note weak spots in the method and urge care in reading the results.
pmc-12707113:
Marina Arkkukangas and four co-authors translate a fear-of-falling questionnaire into Swedish and test how well it works, in a research paper from 2025. Fear of falling is a real health issue for older adults, yet the mental side of fall risk is often missed. No Swedish version of this standard questionnaire existed.

The team translated both the fifteen-item and six-item forms and checked them with experts and older adults. The long form's model could not be tested cleanly. The short form held up better: its two scales, covering harm outcomes and degree of threat, showed fair to good reliability. The authors recommend the short Swedish form for use in early fall prevention.
pmc-12709813:
Andrea Blažinović, Jelena Popić, and Stipe Radoš report a case meant to put a rare diagnosis on the emergency room's radar. A 67-year-old Croatian man came in with three days of belly pain spread all over, nausea, acid rising, and vomiting. Scans showed his small intestine had telescoped into itself, one loop sliding inside the next, a condition called intussusception that mostly strikes children.

Blood tests showed infection signs and odd red cell shapes, and plain X-rays showed a blocked small bowel. A CT scan gave the answer, with the classic target and kidney signs of loop within loop in the ileum. Surgeons removed the trapped section and joined the ends, and lab study of the tissue confirmed the diagnosis. The patient recovered and went home within days. The authors stress fast imaging when adults show this pattern.
pmc-12710913:
Evan Hutchison and co-authors study how a gut receptor shapes cholesterol in male mice in a 2025 paper. High blood cholesterol drives artery disease, and dietary fiber helps partly because gut bacteria ferment it into short-chain fatty acids. Those acids are sensed by receptors such as GPR41.

Mice lacking this receptor showed changes in gut microbes and bile acids. A cholesterol uptake gene in the small intestine was also expressed less, and high cholesterol was softened. The pathway links fiber, microbes, and a single receptor to a major heart disease risk factor.
pmc-12711913:
Joanna Moncrieff and Mark Horowitz set out in 2025 how people can be helped off antipsychotic drugs, and when they should be. The default in psychosis care is lifelong treatment after several episodes, with a stop allowed for some after one. The authors press on that consensus from several sides.

Not everyone who stops relapses, they note. Stopping trials may overstate drug protection because withdrawal itself can trigger the relapse counted against the patient. The drugs' long side-effect ledger also weighs in. Recent trials using slow tapering give mixed news: relapse risk is real, yet social functioning can improve over time. No reliable traits mark who can stop safely, the review concedes. Readers get a careful clinical argument: if, when, and how, with the uncertainty kept in view.
pmc-12712013:
Zupeng Liu, Zhao Liu, Xia Lei, Yujue Yang, and Titao Jing published this study in 2025. It builds a stretchable light-emitting device that turns on at unusually low voltage. Such glowing skins are wanted for wearable displays, but most need strong, high-frequency power that wearables cannot easily supply.

The trick is a clear gel with a very high dielectric constant, used as the emitting layer's matrix: the gel concentrates the electric field, so less voltage does the same work. The device lit at just thirteen volts and shone brightly at modest settings, while stretching to six times its length. Colored electrodes let the team show yellow, green, and red without complex structures. They assembled a small display that updated in real time. The authors present the gel route as a practical step toward soft, low-power luminous devices.
pmc-12714713:
Javier Diez-Sierra and co-authors publish a global dataset that outlines cities and their rural rings for climate study, in a 2025 paper. Knowing where a city ends and its countryside begins is step one for judging urban climate change. The set draws on regional climate model runs, both worldwide and European, at two grid sizes.

A set of large cities stands in for megacities across regions. The authors also share a Python workflow that others can extend to more cities and models, with tools for measuring the urban heat island effect. The data and code sit in public archives. The authors call it the first global model based city and countryside database of its kind.
pmc-12715313:
Timo Sachsenberg and co-authors take stock of a fast-moving field in this 2025 article. Their subject is the computing side of mass spectrometry, a lab method that weighs molecules to learn what a sample holds. The method now serves studies of proteins, fats, sugars, and many small molecules in cells.

New machines, new ways of gathering data, and machine learning have changed what the software must do. The authors list open problems: merging data from many labs, judging how sure a match is, searching huge public stores, joining data across molecule types, and guarding patient privacy. They also urge training so more scientists can use learning tools well, and they note the role of a community group that links experts.
pmc-12715913:
Kangning Wang and co-authors review whether curcumin, the yellow compound in turmeric, could treat eye disease. The compound fights oxidation, inflammation, microbes, and unwanted vessel growth, and it protects nerves, all prized in eye care. Earlier reviews treated the body in general. This one gathers the eye-specific record across diseases of the front and back of the eye, from macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy to cataracts and dry eye.

Pooling the last five years of animal and clinical studies, the authors find real promise across that list. The obstacles are practical: dose, delivery form, and long-term safety all remain unsettled. Lab success has not yet become a clinic routine. The authors call for trials that settle those basics so curcumin's eye benefits can be judged fairly.
pmc-12716313:
Nana Yao and Bo Huang review how viruses cause human cancer in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. About thirteen percent of the world's tumors trace to pathogens. Viruses account for roughly 2.2 million new cancer cases each year.

Nine confirmed carcinogenic viruses headline the review, from hepatitis B and C to papillomavirus and Epstein-Barr virus. Several others, not formally designated, are closely tied to tumors as well. DNA and RNA tumor viruses work through different mechanisms. The authors walk through each virus, the cancers it causes, and how it transforms cells. Comparative analysis ties the mechanisms together. The review is a map of viral oncogenesis for researchers entering the field.
pmc-12716413:
Bing Hu and co-authors study what drives young people in China to cut down on sugar, a habit that has become a youth-led movement. Too much sugar feeds obesity and diabetes, and social media now shapes how the young think about health. The team extends a standard behavior model that runs from stimulus, through the person, to response.

Their version adds a cultural factor the authors call face, the concern for social standing. A national web survey tests how social media exposure shapes health awareness and conformity, and how face concern and online health skill change those paths. The model aims to explain why sugar cutting spreads as a social trend, not just a private choice.
pmc-12716513:
Chen, Huang, and Cheng study how air pollution, inhaler choice, and flare-ups of chronic lung disease interact in one Taiwanese hospital's records from 2016 to 2024. Pollution is known to worsen COPD, while the pressurized inhalers many patients use release greenhouse gases. The team linked visit records with local pollution data and estimated the carbon cost of each inhaler type. They modeled how drug choices and dirty air each related to flare-up rates.

Higher fine-particle pollution tracked with more flare-ups, while triple therapy tracked with fewer. Heavy use of rescue inhalers signaled poorer control. When greener inhaler types rose in 2020 and 2021, hospital stays and emissions both fell. A later swing back to pressurized inhalers coincided with more flare-ups and a bigger footprint. The authors argue that prescribing can serve lungs and climate at once, if the greener devices are chosen when they fit the patient.
pmc-12717213:
Xiaoxu Li and co-authors watched crystal plates slide into order in two thousand twenty-five. Some crystals grow by snapping small pieces together. The pieces must align before they fuse. How uniform stacks form was the open puzzle. Their mineral plates settled into staggered rows. A steady sideways slide guided each plate home.

Microscopy and X-ray scattering revealed the superlattice. Liquid-cell imaging caught the sliding live. Plates slowed as overlaps grew during approach. The stagger angle stayed uniform across the crystal. Forces inside the gaps set the final registry. The pathway explains mesocrystal architecture broadly. Materials makers may steer growth by guiding slides.
pmc-12717313:
Masato Saito and six co-authors report a lab study, published in twenty twenty-five, on a drug called KHK2455 in mice with skin tumors. The drug blocks an enzyme that helps tumors grow by breaking down a key amino acid. Alone, the drug lowered the waste product of that process but did not shrink the tumors.

Paired with a second treatment that blocks a brake on immune cells, the drug worked much better than that treatment alone. The two treatments acted on different arms of the immune system. One woke up helper T cells, while the other raised the number of killer cells and other first-line defenders. Together they turned on both arms at once, a result that may guide future paired treatment plans.
pmc-12717713:
Mengmeng Pu and co-authors trace how a long non-coding RNA weakens insulin cells in type 2 diabetes. Blood from ninety-five patients and eighty-three healthy people was compared. The RNA, NBR2, ran high in patients while its target microRNA ran low. NBR2 levels sorted patients from controls with strong accuracy scores.

In rat insulin cells, silencing NBR2 revived cell life and insulin output. Death rates, inflammation markers, and oxidative damage all fell. Shielding the target microRNA partly undid those rescues. That flip confirms the pair works as one axis. NBR2 thus stands as both a marker and a possible drug lever.
pmc-12717813:
Cells lining blood vessels age early inside artery plaques, and one enzyme's rise may mark that aging. Meng-Ting Jiang and co-authors tracked the enzyme, SULF1, in this 2025 study. Vessel-wall aging feeds plaque growth, the core of atherosclerosis. Data came from single-cell reads of plaque cores and nearby healthy tissue.

Bulk gene data from early and late plaques narrowed the suspect list. SULF1 stood out and was checked in mice prone to plaques and in human artery cells stressed with oxidized fat. Silencing the gene, protein blots, and aging stains all tested its role. A marker tied to vessel aging could guide drugs that keep arteries young. The multi-layer data design strengthens the claim.
pmc-12718113:
Japan's Food Safety Commission assessed whether feeding cattle-derived meat-and-bone meal to chickens, pigs, and non-ruminants risks human BSE, the prion disease behind mad cow outbreaks. The agriculture ministry had asked for the review. The commission found that, as long as safeguards hold, prions are highly unlikely to build up in the animal parts used for this feed. Leakage of the meal into cattle feed is negligible while the ban on feeding it to ruminants is obeyed.

Oral transmission of the prions to chickens and pigs is unlikely, on accumulated scientific evidence. The commission judged the risk of human infection through these foods to be highly unlikely, with negligible adverse health effects expected. The conclusion is conditional: it rests on the mitigation measures staying in force and being followed. The document is a regulatory risk assessment, written to support feed policy in Japan.
pmc-12718313:
Ran Xue and co-authors test a two-in-one immune drug added to standard chemotherapy for advanced pancreatic cancer. Their 2025 trial report covers a fusion protein that blocks the PD-L1 checkpoint while also trapping TGF-beta, a signal tumors use to hide. Fifty-six patients with advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma received it with the standard two-drug chemotherapy backbone.

About a third of patients saw their tumors shrink, and typical survival reached roughly ten months in a disease where gains are hard won. Serious treatment side effects hit just under half the patients, led by lowered white cell counts. Patients whose tumors carried more PD-L1 responded markedly better, with survival nearly doubled in that small subgroup. Marker changes during treatment also tracked outcomes. The authors call the combination promising and manageable, and they sketch which patients benefit most.
pmc-12719613:
Bekahegn Girma and co-authors pool studies on sleep quality in patients with long term illness in Ethiopia, in a review from 2025. People with lasting body or mind illness sleep poorly more often, but pooled proof for Ethiopia was scarce.

Just over half of such patients slept poorly, the pool found. Risk rose with age, female sex, drug and drink use, and other illness at the same time. Weak social backing, poor sleep habits, anxiety, and low mood also tied to poor sleep. The authors urge counsel against substance use and care that treats sleep as part of illness care.
pmc-12721113:
Mahnoor Shafi and co-authors present a 2025 case where augmented reality guided spine hardware around a large sacral tumor. A 61-year-old man with chronic back and leg pain carried a solitary plasmacytoma that had eaten into the sacrum and squeezed the canal. Such tumors usually answer to radiation, but his spine was giving way.

Through small incisions, the team placed lumbopelvic fixation with dual screws under AR guidance, sparing him the infection and wound risks of open surgery. Radiation followed on schedule. Five months on, hardware held, erosion was unchanged, and pain eased. The authors offer the case as proof that AR guidance suits fragile oncologic spines. Small wounds also speed the road to radiation.
pmc-12722013:
Wenrui Linghu and five co-authors adapt an eye questionnaire for Chinese children with uveitis and test whether it measures well, in this 2025 paper. Uveitis, inflammation inside the eye, can badly damage a child's sight and daily life. The Pediatric Eye Questionnaire was built in English to capture that burden from children and parents alike.

The team translated the teen version into Chinese and studied 347 children with uveitis, 154 younger and 193 older, each with a parent. A Rasch analysis, which checks whether items form one clean scale, confirmed each domain measured a single trait. Answer categories ordered properly, precision was adequate, and items targeted the children well.
