Two forms had one slightly misfitting item, and a few items behaved a bit differently for boys and girls. The authors judge the Chinese version valid for clinic and research use.
pmc-12722313:
Raghda Eldesouki, Omar Tarek, and Hassan Morsi build a survival model for ovarian cancer in a 2025 study. The cancer splits into kinds with wide gaps in outlook. The team drew on a large cancer atlas with 2,427 patients of two main kinds. Gene data stood for 1,011 of them. Four machine learning models trained on clinic and gene facts to guess two-year survival.

One model, a support vector machine, best caught the death class, which the team prized most. A boost model scored high on the broad grade but missed more deaths. Weight checks named key genes, among them WT1, MUC16, and MYC, plus age at first find. Gene tests showed cell cycle and growth paths hot in worse cases. Change maps split by cancer kind. The authors frame the model as a step toward care shaped per patient.
pmc-12723013:
Lohani and three co-authors make the case for pocket eye-track gear in museum halls in this twenty twenty-five paper. Eye tracks can show where guests look, moment by moment, as they move through a show. That live proof is still rare in loose, out-of-school learn spots like science halls.

Inside, the team uses a climate change show as its worked case. Guest gaze data can flag which boards pull eyes and which get skipped at a glance. Those facts can then guide board layout, text size, and flow through the hall. The authors also flag cost, fit, and data load as bars to wide use of the gear.
pmc-12723313:
Hirotaka Yamagata and co-authors examined, in a 2025 study, whether guideline training for psychiatrists changes how outpatients with depression are treated. A national project called EGUIDE had already lifted care for hospital patients. Its reach into clinic care, where most depression is treated, was untested.

The study followed 255 outpatients at seven sites who had a first diagnosis of major depression and at least six months of care. Drug choices at six months were compared between patients of trained and untrained psychiatrists. Checks covered how often severity was graded, how often a single antidepressant stood alone, and use of sedative drugs. Dose levels of the main drug classes were also weighed. The work tests if classroom learning turns into changed prescriptions.
pmc-12723813:
Replacing a narrowed aortic valve through a catheter, rather than open surgery, is now offered to patients across the risk range. Arif Khokhar, Jonathan Curio, Matthew Hammond-Haley, Matti Adam, and Neil Ruparelia reviewed in 2025 how to pick among the many valve devices on offer. Devices differ in frame design, materials, and leaflet setup, and those differences matter in specific anatomies.

The review works through hard cases: small valve rings, coronary disease, patients who will live long with the device, risk of needing a pacemaker, and leaking native valves. For each case it weighs which design traits help or hurt. The authors aim to match device to patient as use expands to younger groups.
pmc-12723913:
Kasali and coauthors adapt a scale for dental student views on online learning. The shift online in the pandemic showed a need for sound scales. A scale for medical students existed and could be adapted. The team retuned it for dental students and tested it.

The study held 181 dental students in one cross-section. Factor tests checked if the scale items group well. Fit scores gauged how well the model matched responses. Trust checks used split halves and item links. Scores showed the adapted scale is stable and valid. Schools can use it to gauge online learning views.
pmc-12724013:
Hudu and co-authors study a fungus that harms maize seed in Ghana and lowers seedling growth. Fusarium verticillioides is a common maize pathogen, yet its effects on local varieties were poorly known. The team isolated fungi from seed of the Bihilifa variety. Using shape traits and a gene marker, they confirmed three isolates of the fungus.

All three isolates cut seed germination and root growth in lab assays. They also changed the chemical profile of the young plants. The results show that seed-borne infection can weaken crops before they even reach the field. The work gives Ghanaian growers and seed testers a clearer picture of the risk this fungus poses.
pmc-12724213:
Yuting Wang and co-authors reply to a letter in a 2025 journal exchange on fake acupuncture in sleep trials. Trials of acupuncture for insomnia need a sham form, a fake version, so patients cannot tell which group they are in. Critics had questioned whether one sham form, a noninvasive type, is truly inert. The reply defends the team's past pooled study of such trials.

The authors note that ethics rules shape these trials. Both the sham group and the control group get usual care on top of the sham needles. So a tie between the two groups does not mean the sham works as therapy. It means the sham adds little on its own, which is what a good sham should do. They grant that few head-to-head studies exist so far.
pmc-12727813:
Yesenia Alvarado-Campos and four co-authors track an endangered Mexican butterfly whose life dances to the rains. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Baronia brevicornis is an ancient lineage found only in Mexico, and adults emerge when the wet season starts.

Seven mating seasons of monitoring showed more males than females. Color forms and wing sizes shifted between years. Pupae could wait one or two years underground; skipping water the first year delayed emergence, but two-year waits cut success. Modeling pointed to accumulated rainfall, not heat, as the trigger for sightings. A sweet spot of rain seems to time emergence to host plant growth. Long waits carry fitness costs the authors weigh.
pmc-12728213:
Mazhar Syed and co-authors present a 2025 study on greener ways to firm up soft clay soil. Weak clay damages light buildings and costs billions each year. Classic stabilizers work but carry a heavy footprint. The team treated clay with banana fiber and a geopolymer made from waste ash and alkaline fluids. Mix ratios were varied across many tests.

Treated soil gained a great deal in strength in compression, shear, and penetration tests. Higher shares of a fine silica additive gave the lowest void ratio. Tiny structure and heat tests tracked the changes inside the soil. A learning model then predicted strength from the mix with high accuracy. The work links soil mechanics with microstructure in one frame.
pmc-12728413:
Zeyi Cheng, Zibo Lin, and Hong Xu report a rare case in which draining fluid from around the heart caused the very emergency it aimed to prevent. The patient was a man aged sixty-five with chest tightness and a large build up of fluid around the heart. He had a long history of kidney failure on dialysis and diabetes.

Soon after the drain was placed, his blood pressure fell and the fluid ran bright red. Surgeons found active bleeding where the tube pierced a small artery near the heart, and they stitched the point closed. A bone plate from an old fracture forced an unusual cut below the breastbone. The man left hospital on day six, well. The case warns teams to hunt the drain path when bleeding starts.
pmc-12729013:
Ramil Kohkaew and co-authors study cross-breeding between two fig trees in this 2025 paper. The trees have opposed tastes: one favors riverbanks, and the other favors drier open ground. Fig trees depend on tiny wasps that usually stick to one species, so how species borders hold or break is a puzzle.

Fruiting periods overlap in Thailand's rainy season, which may let wasps move between the species. Trees thought to be hybrids had traits between the parents, but larger leaves. Gene tests confirmed their hybrid state and showed mixing with parent species. The hybrids grew mainly in river areas. Their seed traits were poorly suited to water spread, so they likely need fruit-eating animals to spread their seeds.
pmc-12729213:
Jia Hua Low and co-authors review how core values in family medicine shift across regions in a 2025 scoping review. Family doctors share broad principles worldwide, yet each health system reads those principles through local needs. The team gathered studies from many countries to trace common threads and local turns.

Twenty one studies made the cut. Care centered on the person, continuity, broad scope, and coordination stood out everywhere. Rich regions stressed relationship care and advocacy, while lower resource areas stressed access and hands on skill. Newer values have emerged, such as care for the planet and comfort with complexity. The authors urge value frameworks that join global insight with local ground.
pmc-12729313:
Ruihang Zhang and co-authors build a forecast model for heart disease rates in a 2025 paper. Ischaemic heart disease is the world's top killer, and planners need to know where rates head next. Plain statistics miss curved patterns, while deep networks can be hard to explain to clinicians.

Their model mixes a swarm-tuned memory network with a multi-scale attention step. It trained on world disease data from 1990 to 2021, split by age and sex into twenty-four groups. Error scores beat a classic statistics model by a wide margin. An explanation tool showed which age and sex groups drove each forecast, and which parts of the network carried the main trend.
pmc-12729513:
Ruth Manzanares-Fernandez and co-authors weigh a common way to manage free-roaming cats on islands, in a 2025 paper set in the Canary Islands. The method traps, neuters, and returns cats, but new regional rules bar it in and near protected areas under a national animal welfare law. The team asks what those limits mean over time.

They combine a review of the multi-level rules with computer models of cat numbers over twenty years. At low rates of neutering, the models show fast growth toward a high cap. Only a high rate, kept up year after year, brings numbers down across island settings. The authors argue that what counts is the rate that can in fact be reached, and they urge steady high coverage with safeguards in sensitive areas.
pmc-12729713:
Geir Fagerjord Lorem and six colleagues follow a Norwegian town's residents to see whether a lifetime of stressful events predicts heart attacks and earlier death, in a 2025 study. Stress is a known heart risk, but its lifelong tally is rarely measured.

Over twenty-one thousand adults from the Tromsø study were tracked across decades. People reporting four or more major life events had non-fatal heart attacks nearly four years earlier, on average, and deaths over a decade sooner. Each added event raised risk step by step, even after standard heart factors were counted. The authors urge preventive cardiology to screen for lifetime stress, not just current strain.
pmc-12729813:
Marriage between kin is an old custom in Yemen, shared by two in five couples or more, and it raises the odds of gene-linked ills in children. Mansour Mehdi, Naif Ali, and Radfan Saleh survey that custom in the Radfan districts in 2025. Their net caught 1,065 households, picked at random.

The kin-marriage rate stood at 57.46 percent, far higher in the countryside than in towns. Wives with a university degree were far less likely to be in a kin match. Kin couples faced higher odds of lost pregnancies and other ill outcomes than non-kin couples. The survey joins forms with clinic records where they exist. Its aim is a clear count of risk for health planners, in a place where data are scarce.
pmc-12730013:
Michael Tekle and co-authors compared blood markers in young Brazilian adults with type 1 diabetes and in healthy peers, in a 2025 study. Long-term high blood sugar harms cells and may upset a growth-factor system tied to heart risk. The team wanted to see how those markers differ early in adult life.

The study covered 129 patients and 95 controls of about the same age. Patients had lower levels of one growth factor and higher levels of its binding partner, plus a riskier fat profile in blood. Patients with tighter sugar control looked closer to healthy controls. Stress-related markers ran high in patients, which the authors read as the body trying to adapt. No clear link appeared between the stress markers and the growth system.
pmc-12730113:
Enrico Baraldi and co-authors describe in this 2025 paper how a Swedish alliance turned sixty causes of antibiotic shortage into ten chosen fixes. Shortages endanger patients, raise costs, and feed drug resistance. The platform, Platinea, gathers drug firms, hospitals, and agencies; through expert calls, workshops, and ranked voting, it sorted the causes and matched each with policy moves.

The ten fixes include bigger stockpiles, central coordination, joined IT systems, higher unit prices, yearly fixed payments, and Nordic joint buying and making. The paper lays out a six-step method, from open brainstorming to cause-solution matching, and offers it to other countries facing the same squeeze. Sweden's drug supply debate gains a worked example.
pmc-12730413:
Jovana Kocić and co-authors present a 2025 study on trace elements in precancerous cervical tissue. Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia is a graded set of early lesions that can advance to cancer if missed. The team's earlier work found element shifts in patients' blood, so they moved to the tissue itself for a sharper signal.

They measured sixteen elements in lesion samples from 60 patients with mid- and high-grade lesions. Healthy tissue from the same patients served as the control. A plasma mass spectrometry method gave precise levels for each element. Lesion tissue held more of several needed elements, including chromium, cobalt, selenium, and molybdenum. It also held more of the toxic elements beryllium, nickel, and cadmium. The pattern may help flag risky lesions.
pmc-12730513:
Axel Bachoux and co-authors grow silver nanoparticles inside a medical silicone to make an antibacterial coating, in a study published in 2025. Silver kills bacteria, but heavy doses also harm human cells, so balance matters. Their trick uses the silicone's own chemistry: a solvent swells the polymer, silver ions drift in, and built-in silane groups reduce them to metal on the spot. The result is an even spread of ten-nanometer particles through the material, tinting it yellow.

Staining tests showed no apparent harm to human gum cells. Under the microscope, fewer Escherichia coli bacteria stuck to the coated surface, hinting at an anti-adhesive antibacterial effect. The authors call the method cheap and simple. Next they want the particles' release profile, which decides long-term safety for light-therapy devices and other gear.
pmc-12730613:
Kaitlyn Smith and co-authors test a gene regulating drug against Ewing sarcoma in cells and animals, in a study from 2025. This aggressive cancer, mostly of children and young adults, badly needs better treatments. A family of enzymes that loosen DNA packing helps drive the tumor, and blocking them is a promising line of attack.

Several blocking drugs were screened against tumor cell lines, and one, romidepsin, came out strongest. Protein tests showed it switched off machinery for cell division and DNA repair. In dishes it also boosted the effect of standard chemotherapy drugs. The team then moved the tests into living models, alone and beside standard care. The results build a case for trying the drug in patients.
pmc-12731213:
Ayfer Bakır and co-authors compare HPV infection in infertile and fertile women in Türkiye. Human papillomavirus is among the most common sexually spread infections, yet its link to infertility is unsettled. Their 2025 study tested cervical samples from two hundred women in each group, screening for twenty-eight virus types.

The virus turned up in a smaller share of infertile women than fertile women, a gap too small to claim as real. Types 82 and 16 led among infertile women, while 45 and 16 led among fertile women. Single-type infections were more common in the infertile group. Vaccination status and cell test results were tracked beside the virus data. Fertility clinics get local numbers rather than guesses about a suspected cause.
pmc-12731713:
Poor sleep is one of the most common burdens for women who survive breast or gynecological cancer. Silvia Martella and co-authors review the evidence on insomnia in this group, with a focus on hormones. Poor sleep is about three times more common in survivors than in the general public. In breast cancer survivors it may reach sixty-two percent. The review traces causes from inflammation and stress systems to treatment effects and distress.

Hormone disruption sits at the center, since many treatments force an early menopause. Hot flashes, mood change, and sexual problems then feed sleepless nights. The authors argue that sleep care belongs in standard survivor care. They map what is known and where studies are still thin.
pmc-12731913:
Ruiling Zhong and Claire Richardson review the cell's waste hubs in aging nerve cells in a 2025 paper. Those hubs, called lysosomes, shred worn parts and spent clumps, recycle the bits, and send growth signals. Nerve cells live long, stretch far, and burn much fuel, so their hubs bear a heavy, lasting load.

How hub power is kept up with age, and where it fails in sound nerve cells, was little mapped next to the vast work on brain ills. The review sums what is known of hub flow in youth and age. It also flags the hard parts of gauging hub work in live cells.
pmc-12732713:
Martin Alewijn and co-authors grade the health risk hiding inside food fraud cases in Europe, in a 2025 study. Food fraud is often read as a money crime: cheap goods passed off as fine ones. Yet faked food can carry real hazards. The team pooled three streams of cases: union fraud reports, journal write-ups, and Dutch crime files.

About one in three fraud cases held a notable safety risk. Within the risky set, one fraud type ruled: food laundering, where banned or dirty stock is slipped back into the legal chain. That route carried the most risk of all. Crooks, the authors say, often knowingly shrug off safety rules. They urge labs to hunt not just doctored goods but laundered ones, and food law to treat fraud as a safety threat in its own right.
pmc-12732913: Marko Tarle edits a 2025 special issue on how head and neck cancers arise and how they are treated. Head and neck cancers rank among the most common cancers worldwide and carry a heavy global health burden. The issue gathers work on causes, growth, and care for these diseases, giving clinicians and researchers a focused set of current studies in one place.
pmc-12733213:
Inclisiran is a newer drug that lowers blood cholesterol, and Alexandra Maștaleru and a team of co-authors pool the published studies asking whether it is worth its price. Heart and artery disease still causes about forty percent of deaths worldwide, and mixing several drugs can cut cholesterol far more than one drug alone, yet risk remains for many patients. The review gathers studies that report health gains in quality-adjusted life years alongside costs.

The value of the drug turned out to depend heavily on place: local prices, patient risk, and health system capacity all shifted the answer. It looked worthwhile in richer settings and for high-risk patients, but not for broad first-line prevention. The authors urge risk-based targeting and price talks.
pmc-12733413:
Stefka Dzhokova and co-authors uncover a new job for a protein that rearranges the packaging of DNA in mammal cells. The protein, Srcap, is best known for placing a variant building block into the DNA spools at gene start sites, which affects which genes switch on. Whether it also shapes how DNA copies itself was unknown. The team lowered the protein's levels in human cells and watched the copying process.

Copying slowed by about a quarter, and fewer copying sites fired across the genome. A stress marker tied to stalled copying piled up, and the variant block the protein installs became scarcer on the DNA. Fine imaging showed sparser, weaker copying clusters. Gene activity data added that many copying genes switch down without the protein. The authors conclude Srcap keeps copying efficient in two ways, through DNA organization and through keeping the copying machinery's genes on.
pmc-12733713:
Lihong Yang and co-authors published this remote sensing study in 2025. Mapping lakes and rivers from satellite images guides water protection and planning. General image models often fail when a new satellite or region changes how scenes look. The team built DASAM, an adaptation of the Segment Anything Model tuned for water. Its core addition is a training module that aligns features between plain images and style-shifted copies. That teaches the model to ignore surface style and keep the water signal.

Two further parts sharpen the details and add scene context. On a Chinese GF-2 satellite dataset, DASAM beat existing methods. It also held up on two outside datasets, from other sensors and regions, without any labels from those domains. The authors present it as a step toward large-scale water monitoring that works across the varied imagery satellites produce.
pmc-12734113:
Xiao and eight co-authors catalog an enzyme gene family in a rice pest, in work from twenty twenty-five. The rice leaf roller is a major migratory pest of rice. Its GMC oxidoreductase enzymes serve many body processes, but the family had never been systematically mapped in this species.

Fifty-four family genes were identified and analyzed. The team also tested how the genes respond to spinetoram, an insecticide used against the pest. Gene responses to the drug may reveal detox routes that drive resistance. A full family map is basic groundwork for smarter, more targeted pest control.
pmc-12734213:
Panagiotis Cherouveim and co-authors present a 2025 review comparing pregnancy outcomes after insemination versus in-vitro fertilization. Assisted reproduction overall carries extra risks for mothers and babies. Whether the treatment strength itself, beyond infertility, drives those risks is the open question.

Original studies comparing the two conception routes were pooled, on single pregnancies without donor sperm. For mothers, differences were mostly absent but reported in patchy ways. For babies, results were reported more evenly across studies. Comparing gentler against stronger treatment helps split the burden of infertility from the footprint of the treatment itself.
pmc-12734313:
Milos Babic and seven co-authors report the first human use of a very strong, very brief burn to fix a stubborn heart rhythm fault. Their twenty twenty-five case report deals with AVNRT, a fast heartbeat loop in the heart's relay node. Standard ablation had already failed twice for this patient, and drugs had not held it either.

The patient was a sixty-one-year-old woman. With a mapping system guiding the catheter, the team gave several bursts of ninety watts for four seconds each at the slow pathway. A brief heart block appeared and cleared on its own. At six months she stayed free of the rhythm fault. The team offers the method as an option for refractory cases.
pmc-12734413:
Ho Seung Lee and eleven co-authors study fluid leaks during a common bile duct endoscopy and test a device that catches them, in a 2025 paper. Fluid escaping the scope's biopsy port slows the procedure and risks contamination. The team measured leaks in 183 patients.

Harder procedures leaked far more than simple ones. Long procedures and frequent flushing of the bowel predicted heavy leakage. Plastic bile stents and cancer diagnoses also raised the odds. The catcher gathered an average of 11 milliliters per procedure. It both measured and contained the fluid. The authors say wider validation is needed before routine use.
pmc-12734513:
Jingru Li and three co-authors design a new patterned material that can bend in unusual ways and block shaking waves, in a 2025 study. The base pattern is a honeycomb with walls that fold inward, which makes the sheet widen when stretched. The team repeats that pattern at smaller and smaller scales, a trick called a fractal design. They test three levels of the design in computer models.

The models track how much the sheet widens when pulled and where waves of each pitch stop or pass. By tuning the scale ratio and wall shapes, the team could move the blocked bands and change how strong the widening effect is. The work aims at parts that must both bear load and cut noise or shaking. It offers a base for such dual-use designs in machines and buildings.
pmc-12734813:
Xu Pei and co-authors tested whether hammering the surface of a printed titanium alloy with laser shocks makes it last longer under repeated load. The alloy is used in aircraft parts, and parts built by melting powder layer by layer can crack early from fatigue. Laser shock treatment presses the surface and leaves it in a helpful state of compression.

Samples received zero, one, or two rounds of treatment, then faced repeated pulling and pushing until they broke. One round more than doubled fatigue life, and two rounds did slightly better still. Microscope views of the breaks, stress measures, and hardness tests explain why. The treatment hardens and compresses the surface, slowing crack growth in printed parts.
pmc-12734913:
Ziyue Wang, Weikang Fang, and Yichen Yang tackle schedule repair in factories that package tiny wafer chips. Their paper appeared in 2025. Such workshops face small batches of many chip types, and daily life brings breakdowns, rush orders, and changed orders. Each event wrecks the standing plan. The team set up a math model of the problem and a rolling method that re-plans in short windows as events arrive.

Their solver blends two search ideas. One copies how fireflies drift toward brighter mates, to evolve good schedules. The other varies the search neighborhood, to escape dead ends. Tests against rival solvers and on real workshop cases showed the blend holds up well. The authors offer it as a practical way to keep precision packaging lines on plan.
pmc-12735013:
Shoaib Ahsan and co-authors test, in a 2025 study, membranes that mix a rubbery polymer with two-metal crystal sponges to separate carbon dioxide from nitrogen. The polymer alone passes gas easily but sorts poorly. Crystal fillers can sharpen the sorting.

Three filler variants paired nickel with copper, cobalt, or zinc inside the same framework family. Membranes were cast from solution and checked by microscopy and diffraction. Even at one percent loading, the nickel-copper version let far more carbon dioxide through. Tests with single gases charted the gains. Better membranes matter wherever exhaust gas must shed its carbon before release.
pmc-12735313:
Bacteria that calm the mind sound like science fiction, yet psychobiotics, probiotic strains with mental health effects, are a serious research front. Guillermo Roberto Jiménez-Pareyón and co-authors review the field in 2025 where brain degeneration meets psychiatry.

The gut-brain axis links intestinal microbes to inflammation, oxidative stress, and the signaling chemicals of mood and memory. Animal and human studies are weighed for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, depression, and anxiety, with attention to biomarkers and quality of life. Newer angles include precision strains matched to a patient, microbe-drug teamwork, and overlap with metabolic disease. The authors are candid about the translation gap: strain choice, standard methods, and trial design all need tightening before clinics can prescribe with confidence.
pmc-12735513:
Daniil Bogachikhin and four co-authors wrote this 2025 review on making metal nanoparticles with living chemistry instead of harsh chemicals. Metal nanoparticles serve in catalysts, electronics, drugs, and advanced materials. Plants, plant extracts, bacteria, and even the insides of living cells can turn metal salts into particles, which fits the aims of green chemistry.

The review walks through ways to make particles from precious and base metals with the reducing agents and enzymes that plants and bacteria supply. It also covers a newer route: letting living cells do the reduction in place, which grows hybrid materials that mix the living and the made. The authors weigh what these routes offer for cheap, clean production and where the science still needs work.
pmc-12735913:
Rong Yang and co-authors trace the gene tale of plague germs took from wild rats in Yunnan in 2022. Three wild plague flares ran that year; nine germ strains were took and read whole. Their 2025 study sets those reads next to a wide bank of past strains from world stores. All nine sit in one limb of the plague tree, with old strains from the same wild focus.

One strain hugs past kin from its own town; the bulk form a fresh knot with old home strains. Small script shifts split the new from the old: a few point swaps and small cuts, some in germ-work genes. One swap hits an iron-grip gene tied to germ strength. Home-born plague thus holds its limb while it drifts in fine steps.
pmc-12736013:
Tatsuya Matsusaki and eleven co-authors tested a probiotic strain in fat-fed mice in a 2025 study. Obesity is rising worldwide, and friendly gut bacteria are one hoped-for line of defense. The team used a mild obesity model, where mice gain fat and early metabolic trouble without much weight change.

For eight weeks, mice on a fatty diet got the bacterial strain or no supplement. Treated mice stored less fat around their organs and grew smaller fat cells. Genes tied to fat handling and inflammation in fat tissue shifted toward a healthier pattern, and early liver fat lessened. Gene reading of gut contents showed the strain reshaped the gut community, holding down bacteria linked to inflammation. The authors say the strain may help prevent early metabolic decline, at least in mice.
pmc-12736513:
A Siberian herb in the plantain family has long been used for belly pain, colds, and snake bite. Zhi-Ying Wang and co-authors hunt in 2025 for the gene that makes one of its scent compounds. They read the herb's full set of gene copies and sifted them for scent making genes.

From more than one hundred thousand gene reads, the team found a short list of twelve scent gene picks. One, when cloned and tested, turned a stock compound into nerolidol, a scent used in care goods and scent craft. It could also make a second scent from a shorter stock, though plant tests showed nerolidol alone. Paired with a boost gene, yields rose a lot. The find opens a plant cell route to the scent.
pmc-12737013:
Antonio Ivanov and co-authors review how Europe's drug agency handled repurposed medicines during the COVID-19 pandemic. Repurposing an approved drug for a new disease skips years of safety work, a precious shortcut in a crisis. Their 2025 field study reads the agency's public assessment reports for products cleared against the virus.

Eight products won the COVID indication. Three of them — remdesivir, tocilizumab, and anakinra — arrived by repurposing. The reports show how much data each route demanded, shaped by where the drug sat in its life cycle. The authors draw lessons for the next emergency, when speed and proof must again be traded. Regulators get a case file on crisis flexibility done in the open.
pmc-12737313:
Jian Wu and three co-authors improve indoor position tracking with ultra wideband radio in a 2025 paper. In workshops, walls and machines block the direct path between tags and anchors, which ruins accuracy. Their base method times signals both ways between nodes to fix distance.

First they trim the message exchange, saving energy and time at each node. Then an adaptive Kalman filter judges how much each blocked signal should be trusted and adjusts its weight on the fly. Bad readings get filtered out before they can pull the position off course. Tests in both still and moving setups showed clear gains in accuracy. The authors present the method for factories that need fast, precise tracking of tools and goods.
pmc-12737513:
dos Santos and co-authors sweep breath germ tales and the rise of wide gene hunts. Breath ills stay a top cause of sick and death round the world. Weak hosts bear the brunt: kids, old hosts, and guard-low hosts. Stock tools, like germ grow and set PCR sets, miss many cases. Vast germ range drives that miss in set test frames. Wide gene hunts read all germs in a bit with no aim list.

That hunt can catch known and new germs in one pass. The sweep stresses its worth in hard cases for such ills. Guard-low hosts, where stock tools fail most, lead that stress. Chief germs in breath ills get their own care in the sweep. Strong and weak points of the hunt way both get weighed. Its role in gene track work caps the sweep text.
pmc-12737613: Tang reflected on pandemic teamwork in this editorial from twenty twenty-five. During COVID-19, he led three special journal issues built around questions practitioners and researchers kept raising. The first asked how ordinary diagnostic services could be maintained while a pandemic raged. The piece frames the issues as a record of sharing and collaboration under pressure. It presents those shared problem lists as the starting point for lessons the field should carry forward.
pmc-12737713:
Yang and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-five on quercetin, a plant compound, against a pig virus. The virus causes heavy losses in swine herds worldwide. In cell tests, quercetin blocks the virus from copying itself. It works by tuning autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning process. Formation of cleaning sacs is curbed while their fusion for disposal is aided. A named signaling pathway carries this effect, the team show. Blocking that pathway's flow matches the antiviral result.

The authors propose quercetin as a candidate antiviral for pig farms. Pathway control of autophagy is the named mechanism. Further animal work would be needed to confirm farm value.
pmc-12738713:
Yingxue Xu and co-authors built a pathology foundation model that learns from slides, expert reports, and gene data together, in a study published in 2025. Most models read only images or image captions, and zoom into small patches, missing the whole slide. Their model, mSTAR, trains on over twenty-six thousand slide-level bundles across thirty-two cancer types, holding more than one hundred sixteen million patch images. Whole-slide context from all three sources is injected into each patch's representation.

Across ninety-seven oncology benchmark tasks, mSTAR beat prior state-of-the-art models. The biggest gains came in molecular prediction and tasks mixing data types. The authors conclude that fusing modalities teaches more than simply scaling image data. They offer the model as a base for slide-level cancer analysis that sees tissue, text, and genes at once.
pmc-12739113: A malaria vaccine made of weakened parasites, given by mosquito bite, protects some volunteers in full, and blood clues may explain who. Tanisha Robinson and co-authors studied volunteers in controlled malaria cases after such immunization. They checked immune cells in the blood and how blood cells answered parasite matter in a dish. Two signals stood out with protection. One was interferon-gamma release on meeting the parasite. The other was interleukin-4 release after the vaccine, joined by a certain T cell pattern.
pmc-12742113:
Cam Bowie, Anthony Costello, and Karl Friston model the worth of face coverings in the UK epidemic in a 2025 paper. The value of masks in the pandemic stayed disputed for years. Dynamic causal modelling can test spread and intervention claims. The team fit one such model to UK outbreak data.

The model merged spread dynamics with behavior and vaccine data. Mask use cut transmission by about five percent in adults. The cut was smaller in children and near zero in younger adults. That modest cut still translated into huge mortality gains. The model credits masks with saving about 102,000 lives. That equals roughly half the deaths in the study window.
pmc-12742213:
Sima Soltanpour and co-authors assemble, in a 2025 paper, a fully automated pipeline that prepares animal brain scans for analysis, ending the hand-tuning that slows preclinical imaging. Functional scans of small animals arrive noisy, low in resolution, and geometrically unlike the atlases they must be matched to. Their pipeline chains three learned modules: a generative network that denoises, a transformer that strips the skull, and a new registration network that warps each brain onto the atlas.

The registration module, a multi-stage Swin transformer widened with dilated convolutions, reads misalignment at both the local and global scale, which is where earlier methods slipped. Across several preclinical data sets it aligned brains more accurately, by the standard overlap score, than the leading alternatives. The authors frame the pipeline as robustness work: each stage answers a failure mode the data actually present.
pmc-12742313:
Spine surgery hurts afterward, and opioids remain the blunt default. Joseph Delaney and co-authors review a slower, local answer in a 2025 paper: a long-acting numbing drug delivered in a plane block beside the spine.

The block bathes spinal nerves where they exit, using ultrasound guidance, but the standard drug wears off fast. The liposomal form leaks its payload gradually as its fat bubbles break down, stretching relief. In early uses, from children's scoliosis surgery to lumbar fusion, opioid use fell by thirty to fifty percent against controls. Hospital stays shortened by up to a third in some series. The review weighs this promise against the still-thin trial record.
pmc-12743113:
Daxin Chen and co-authors study liensinine, a compound that can ease vascular remodeling in hypertension. Their 2025 paper deals with aortic stiffening, a main risk factor for cardiovascular events in hypertension.

Past work showed liensinine helps, but its mechanism was unclear. In hypertensive mice, it lowered blood pressure and pulse wave velocity and reduced aortic wall thickness. Protein tests showed it raised expression of GPX4, a guard against ferroptosis. The team traces its benefit to a ferroptosis-related TLR4 inflammatory pathway. Blocking that path of inflammation and cell death may be a way to protect blood vessels early in hypertension.
pmc-12744913:
Hanane Aksim and co-authors report a gut illness that looked exactly like appendicitis. A seventy-six-year-old man arrived with five days of severe pain in the lower right belly. The true cause was diverticulitis of the ileum, a rare inflammation of a small pouch in the small intestine. Such pouches are common in the colon but rare this far up the gut.

Scans, rather than symptoms, pinned down the diagnosis. The team treated the man by the same rules used for the common colon form of the disease, and he recovered. The authors warn that the condition's rarity and vague signs invite delay, and delay can turn deadly if the pouch bursts. Their case argues for imaging early when belly pain does not fit the usual script.
pmc-12745313:
Taena Hanson and co-authors link saliva DNA methylation to brain white matter volume in children in this 2025 paper. White matter carries signals between brain regions, and its growth shapes cognition. Chemical marks on DNA may help regulate that growth. The data come from a national child health study called ECHO.

The sample held 205 children from infancy to age 15. Saliva marks at sites in white matter related genes predicted brain volume. Thousands of sites changed their link with age, and effects ran strongest in early childhood. Saliva marks matched brain tissue marks closely in their checks. A spit sample may thus track brain development without a scan. Stage aware reading is key, since the same mark means different things at different ages.
pmc-12745413:
Kui Zhong and eight co-authors published this review in 2025. It profiles LINC01410, a long non-coding RNA: a gene that makes no protein yet steers many that do. Found on chromosome 9, it has emerged as a multi-tool player in cancer biology.

Across tumor types, the RNA is overproduced and pushes growth through several famous pathways, including PTEN/AKT, Notch, and NF-kappaB. It also tunes metabolism, encouraging sugar burning and fat droplet storage, and shapes the tumor's surroundings through exosome messages between cells. The same molecule flips sign outside cancer: in preeclampsia and diabetic kidney disease its levels fall, hinting at context-dependent jobs. The authors argue this breadth makes it a promising biomarker for diagnosis and a candidate drug target. They caution that most evidence is still laboratory-based, and clinical translation needs targeted delivery methods that do not yet exist.
pmc-12747813:
Yogesh S and co-authors grade the first full undergraduate medical conference held at Madras Medical College. Their 2025 paper reports feedback from MIRACLE 2025, a meeting built to mix classroom learning with hands-on exposure. The medicine workshop drew 40 students, 24 of whom returned detailed surveys, and four large plenary talks drew about 200 raters each.

Ratings ran strongly positive. Content coverage, interactivity, and audiovisual quality scored highest, while time management lagged. Open comments praised approachable faculty and asked for longer, more practical sessions. Plenary talks earned top marks from most raters across both days. The authors conclude that student-run conferences can bridge theory and clinical practice, and that structured feedback should steer the next edition.
pmc-12748213:
Yalan Hu and co-authors present a self correcting graph retrieval system for liver medicine decision support in a 2025 paper. Clinical knowledge grows fast, and language models can hallucinate. Standard retrieval systems also struggle to use complex medical knowledge structures, such as verified knowledge graphs.

Their framework runs a retrieve, evaluate, refine loop. Agents generate graph searches, validate them semantically, and improve them step by step to build an accurate context for the answer. On a custom set of clinical questions, the system beat strong baselines on faithfulness, context recall, and answer relevance, with scores above nine tenths.
pmc-12748613:
Márton Szabados and a team of co-authors adapt a quality-of-life questionnaire for Hungarian teenagers with cancer. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. As survival improves, how young patients feel and function matters more, and Hungary lacked a validated version of the tool.

Ninety-two patients, half in treatment and half at least a year past it, plus forty-six healthy peers, completed the form. The translation followed standard cross-cultural guides. Scores proved steady and matched a known children's quality-of-life scale well. Patients scored lower than healthy peers. Those in treatment scored no worse than those past it. Bone, soft tissue, and brain tumor patients fared worst. Supportive parents tracked with better scores.
pmc-12748713:
Bahare Jafarsalehi, Sahar Boozari, and Giti Torkaman test a tool-based soft tissue therapy plus exercise for knee osteoarthritis, in work published in 2025. The disease wears down the knee joint and often makes leg muscles overwork during walking. The therapy uses hand tools to press and release soft tissue.

Thirty patients with moderate disease were split between real therapy plus exercise and a sham therapy plus exercise, over four sessions in two weeks. Muscle activity during walking fell after treatment in the real group for several muscles, while it rose in the sham group. Fast walking raised muscle activity in everyone. Pain, strength, and self-rated disability also improved. The authors suggest the therapy may help muscles work more efficiently during gait.
pmc-12748913:
Ting Fan and co-authors analyse drug resistance and risk factors for a hardy yeast infection in a Chinese hospital, in a 2025 study. Candida auris spreads in hospitals and resists many drugs. Records covered new yeast finds from early 2022 to early 2025.

New cases of this yeast rose steadily over the period. Resistance to a front-line drug topped seventy-seven percent, while resistance to a stronger drug stayed low. Infected patients stayed in hospital longer and died at higher rates than patients with other yeasts. Intensive care stays, high blood pressure, weakened immunity, and in-dwelling devices each raised risk. The authors urge strict infection control and watchfulness for resistant strains.
pmc-12749413:
Abdallah Barakat and co-authors test bone char, a phosphorus-rich charcoal made from bones, as fertilizer for spinach in chalky sandy soil, in a 2025 pot study. Such soils lock phosphorus away from plants. Twelve treatments mixed bone char with sulfur or humic acid, tried acid-treated char, and compared rock phosphate.

Every treatment freed more phosphorus than the untreated soil. The strongest mix, modified bone char plus humic acid, raised available phosphorus from 11.6 to 26.1 milligrams per kilogram. Spinach shoots grew heavier under most mixes, with bone char plus humic acid on top for fresh weight. Weighing cost, the authors favor bone char with sulfur as the practical best buy.
pmc-12749813:
Md Tanjil Sarker and co-authors build a smart power plan for a large hospital in Kuala Lumpur in a 2025 study. Hospitals need power at all times for patient safety, yet they use huge amounts of energy. The team aimed to cut waste and grid reliance while keeping key wards safe during faults.

They mapped the site, with its 1,500 beds and vast floor area, device by device. Smart forecasting and learning algorithms then planned solar use, upkeep, and cooling. In simulation, roof solar met most daily demand, cooling energy fell by more than a tenth, and total efficiency rose by a quarter. Unplanned downtime also fell sharply. The plan offers a model for other large care sites.
pmc-12750313:
Kuo Li and five colleagues quantify how breathing blurs a precision radiation technique for liver tumors. Lattice radiotherapy deliberately creates a peak-and-valley dose pattern inside the tumor, expecting the valleys to drive immune and bystander effects. Using 4D scans from twenty-four patients, the team simulated delivered dose under real respiratory motion.

Average motion was about 8.6 millimeters, mostly up-and-down. Vertex peak doses dropped substantially, and the valley-to-peak ratio rose in every direction, worst along the breathing axis, climbing sharply once motion passed eight millimeters. Low-dose spill also grew. The authors conclude motion management is not optional for liver lattice therapy if its signature dose pattern is to survive delivery.
pmc-12750613:
Wei Wei and co-authors study a gene-editing enzyme that seems to worsen cartilage cell injury in osteoarthritis. The enzyme, METTL3, tags RNA with a chemical mark that changes how genes act. Osteoarthritis is common and rising, yet its drivers stay murky. Their 2025 paper treats human cartilage cell lines with an inflammatory signal to mimic the disease in a dish.

The team tracks cell survival, death, inflammation, and oxidative stress under this setup. Their results point to METTL3 raising levels of CTSB, a protein-cutting enzyme, and through it deepening the injury. Blocking that chain is the implied test for a future therapy. Joint researchers get a named pathway linking RNA marks to cartilage damage.
pmc-12750813:
Leila Barati, Narges Lashkarbolouk, Somayeh Ghorbani, and Lobat Shahkar review in 2025 how children with COVID-19 fared on the antiviral drug remdesivir. Their study looked back at records from a hospital in Iran. All the patients were under eighteen, admitted with severe breathing trouble between early 2021 and late 2022, and treated under the national protocol.

Ages ran from twenty-five days to seventeen years, with a median of ten. Fifteen children needed intensive care, and half of those had failure to thrive. Body weight mattered: heavier children over ten showed abnormal chest scans far more often. The drug was well tolerated overall. No child had to stop it, and liver and kidney tests showed no real harm, apart from mild, brief rises in liver enzymes in some. The authors call for forward-looking studies to pin down the drug's role in children.
pmc-12751413:
David Lukacsovich and a large team hunt DNA marks that mirror a heart health score and speak to dementia risk. The score, Life's Essential 8, sums diet, activity, sleep, and body gauges. Low scores track with higher dementia risk. Their 2025 study scans the epigenome of 273 stroke-free Hispanic adults from a Manhattan cohort. Methylation, the chemical dimming of DNA, was read on a dense chip.

Marks tied to the score were mapped gene by gene and in stretches. The team cross-reads them against gene activity, gene variants, and past dementia finds. Brain-to-blood echoes are checked too. The hope is a blood test that reads lifestyle's fingerprint. Such a gauge could flag risk long before symptoms.
pmc-12751513:
Shi-Rui Jia, Chao-Hong Deng, Aziguli Yimamu, and Jing Liu identify risk factors for blood clots after ovarian cancer surgery in a 2025 study. Vein clots are a common, dangerous complication that lengthens hospital stays and raises death risk. Knowing who is at risk allows targeted prevention.

The retrospective study compared patients who developed clots after surgery with a larger group who did not, all confirmed by imaging. Every patient received scheduled ultrasound screening in the first weeks, with deeper scans when findings were suspicious, so silent clots were not missed. Clinical and surgical factors were compared between groups.
pmc-12752913:
Jamaal Green, Brian Glass, Jordan Purdy, and Dyann Daley lay out a 2025 plan to aim child protection services where they do the most good. Child abuse and neglect harm health, schooling, and life chances. The plan works with one partner region and repeats in cycles as needs shift.

First, a mapping method learns from past cases and traits of the built setting to flag blocks at high risk. Those areas get more services, such as home visits, child care aid, and parent support. Then a what if model tests how moving services would change outcomes. The aim is to place each service where the model says it helps most.
pmc-12753413:
Raya Amin and co-authors pool evidence on cell power units in Wilson disease in a 2025 review. The genetic disease traps copper in the body, above all in the liver. Mitochondria, the cell's power plants, seem especially open to copper harm.

Thirteen human and animal studies met their rules. Copper inside liver mitochondria ran far above normal, and their inner structure looked abnormal. Stress markers rose, while energy output and key respiratory steps fell, more so in older or symptomatic cases. DNA copies inside mitochondria dropped too. Some flaws appeared before symptoms, hinting that power unit harm is an early driver of the disease.
pmc-12753613:
Xinmeng Wu and co-authors report, in a 2025 paper, five cases of a rare and aggressive cancer that grows on the sheath around nerves. Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors are soft tissue sarcomas with few treatment options and a poor outlook. About half of cases link to a genetic condition called neurofibromatosis type one. The authors reviewed patients treated at a hospital in Henan, China, over five years, and set their cases beside the wider literature.

The five patients ranged in age from twenty to sixty-four, and four had surgery. Outcomes varied widely: one patient died of complications within a year, while others were still alive several years later. One case carried the linked gene mutation, and one patient whose tumor could not be removed still survived on drug treatment alone. The authors offer the series as practical experience for a tumor most doctors rarely see.
pmc-12753813:
Alicja Stanisławska and eight co-authors studied how print angle affects rust resistance in a 3D-printed medical alloy, in twenty twenty-five. The alloy, a cobalt-chrome mix, was printed by laser powder bed fusion at angles from zero to ninety degrees. The team read the metal's defect patterns with microscopy and X-ray methods, then tested rust behavior in a salt solution like body fluid.

The ninety-degree sample resisted rust best. It held the fewest dislocations, the least lattice strain, and the richest chrome oxide skin, with that oxide making over sixty percent of its surface film. Low-angle samples carried more strain and less protective films. The authors say the print-induced defect pattern drives rust behavior. Tuning print angle could thus lift durability without coatings or extra alloying.
pmc-12754013:
Alessandro De Santis and co-authors study soil bacteria from dumped-waste sites in southern Italy that can tolerate and remove heavy metals, in work from 2025. Illegal dumping loads soils with metals that linger and harm soil life. Local bacteria that already cope with metals could help clean such sites.

The team took one hundred isolates from twelve spoiled soils and screened them under five metals. Lead strains removed over sixty-five percent of four metals and up to ninety percent of lead in lab tests. They also grew under salt, acid, and cold stress. Gene checks placed the strains in known soil groups. The authors present them as candidates for cleanup work.
pmc-12755013:
Jing Cheng, Wenjun Dai, Sixuan Chen, Lidan Wang, and Ren Chen study health power across income levels in Anhui, China, in a 2025 paper. Health gaps by social rank stay wide, and giving people more say and skill over their health may narrow them. How that power spreads by rank was not well known.

A survey in five cities drew 1,364 people by targeted sampling across three rank groups. Chronic disease ran at 24.1% in the low group, 15.1% in the mid group, and 14.0% in the high group. Health reading skill also lagged in the low group on both cut lines used. High reading skill linked to less chronic disease in the low and mid groups. It also linked to better self rated health in all groups.
pmc-12756313:
Axel Broman, Megan Havers, Roman Sattarov, and Thomas Laurell present a faster way to fish specific tiny parcels out of blood plasma. Their 2025 paper works with extracellular vesicles, small bubbles that cells shed, carrying proteins that can signal disease. Vesicles vary widely, and isolating one subgroup can reveal markers from a specific cell type.

Their method joins sound-based trapping with antibody-coated beads on an automated platform. In eight minutes, from a droplet of plasma, it yields two fractions: sound-trapped vesicles and those bound to beads targeting one surface marker. Protein profiling showed the bead fraction was enriched for that marker, beating a ninety-minute manual method.
pmc-12756813:
Enzo Borazo and co-authors build glowing, germ-fighting nanotubes in a 2025 paper. Titanate nanotubes are cheap and stable, and loading them with europium ions adds red light emission plus stronger antibacterial action. Two versions were made: a simple ion-coated tube and a dressed-up version with organic light-harvesting partners.

The dressed version soaked up more ultraviolet light and killed bacteria across a wider zone in dish tests. The plain version also fought both a staph and a colon bacterium. Light checks confirmed the classic red europium glow. Readers get a dual-use material for medical coatings and imaging.
pmc-12756913:
Jungang Zhang and nine co-authors line up nanowires for see-through shield films in a 2025 paper. Wires at the nano scale could make fine gear, yet no sound way stood to place them just so on soft films, which stalls firm, large builds. Their way uses an electric grip at a surface edge.

The grip slides and turns wires across a wide span of angles on thin films. A fast laser pass then welds wire joints with no touch, which lifts both flow and light traits. Shield films that stay clear can now be built wire by wire.
pmc-12764513:
Chaoyi Shi and seven co-authors test whether taking more photos during a stomach scope exam raises the catch rate for early upper gut cancer. The scope exam is a standard screen for such tumors, yet quality marks are not well set. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Records covered a huge pool of people scoped at two hospitals across six years, for screening or for symptoms. Cases were split into low, mid, and high photo count bands. Early cancer was proven by tissue tests. Catch rates were clearly higher in the high photo group than in the other bands. The team also hunts for other traits tied to a catch.
pmc-12765013:
Angelica Casotto and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-five methods paper on mapping how lab-grown neuron networks organize in space. Networks form as single neurons wire into circuits. Studying thousands of spread-out cells by hand is impractical.

Their pipeline pairs high-content confocal imaging with automatic analysis. Thousands of neurons in one well can be measured at once. Networks from three mouse brain regions were compared as a demonstration. Fine details like nucleus size and the number and length of axon starting segments were extracted. The workflow suits drug and disease studies using mouse or human stem-cell neurons.
pmc-12765313:
Damla Bilgin Avsar and Ahmet Atila Ertan test what shapes the accuracy of digital scans for dental implants, in a 2025 lab study. A digital impression must line up near-perfectly, or the false tooth will not fit. The team printed an upper jaw model with two implant posts at set spots. Scan bodies sat on the posts in three forms: plain, built up, and trimmed down.

Each form was scanned ten times with a mouth scanner. Two software suites then aligned the scans against a reference model. One suite, Medit Link, strayed less than the other, Exocad, on both shift and tilt. Plain scan bodies beat both altered forms. Post position in the jaw also swayed the scores. The authors say smart alignment software can cut misfits before a crown is ever made.
pmc-12766113:
Wanni Li and six co-authors report an unusually placed lupus rash in a 2025 case paper. Subacute cutaneous lupus causes sun-sensitive, ring-shaped, scaly patches and belongs to the autoimmune lupus family. This patient's plaque sat on the left chin, an uncommon spot that led to repeated misdiagnosis.

Three lenses settled the question: dermoscopy of the skin surface, confocal microscopy imaging the skin in place, and a biopsy. Together they confirmed the diagnosis where single looks had failed. Treatment combined steroids with immune-modulating drugs. By the nineteen-week follow-up, the lesion had regressed markedly. The authors argue the two non-invasive imaging tools together cut diagnostic errors and let clinicians monitor treatment in real time, sparing patients repeated biopsies. Rare presentations, the case suggests, are where imaging combinations earn their keep.
pmc-12767013:
Siqi Guo and co-authors tracked changes in the choroid, the blood-rich layer at the back of the eye, after a combined eye surgery. The patients had cataracts and a form of glaucoma where the eye's drainage angle is too narrow. The operation removed the cloudy lens and freed the stuck drainage tissue.

The study covered seventy-nine eyes from fifty-four patients, checked before surgery and at times over six months. The choroid first grew thicker after surgery, then thinned back to its starting level. Pressure in the eye dropped in the first week and stayed lower. Changes in choroid thickness tracked changes in the eyes' focusing error after surgery, while other measures did not. The authors say this link may help explain why vision prescriptions shift after this operation. Knowing the pattern could help surgeons warn patients about changes in their glasses after surgery.
pmc-12768413:
Kirsty McGee and co-authors test a hopeful idea: that calming the immune system's long war against herpesviruses could free up defenses for other threats. These viruses never leave, and the effort to hold them down grows with age. An antiviral drug, valaciclovir, can suppress the viruses themselves, so the team asked whether it also shrinks the immune response aimed at them.

Donors over 65 took one of three doses, up to four grams a day, for six months, with blood and quality-of-life checks over a year. The drug changed neither the size nor the character of the antibody and cell responses to two herpesviruses, cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus. Physical and mental quality of life stayed flat as well. The authors conclude that, at this dose and length, the approach does not ease the immune burden in this age group.
pmc-12768613:
Oresta Piniazhko and co-authors test horizon scanning for fresh health tools in Ukraine, with HIV care as the case, in a 2025 report. Horizon scanning hunts new tools early so a health system can plan for them. The team used a European tool kit and a ranking tool on trial, patent, and group sources.

Three tools made the cut: a hand-held tester for drug levels, a smart model that flags patients at risk of quitting care, and a text note service for people with HIV. Each one backs steady drug use, which cuts failure and drug strain. All three sit at the market stage, so Ukraine could take them up soon, the team says.
pmc-12768713:
Nyantara Wickramasekera builds a personal decision aid for ulcerative colitis care, in a 2025 conference abstract. Patients with this gut disease face a hard pick among drugs and surgery, each mixing gains, harms, and family-planning weight. Stock decision aids treat all patients alike. The new aid learns each patient's own trade-offs through a choice game played online.

Three hundred patients weighed paired care profiles and picked the one they would take. Math models turned those picks into scores for what matters most to each person. The aid then shows those scores and names a best-match care path, all inside a live web app. Early word from patients is warm, and fuller user testing is under way. Wickramasekera frames the tool as a step toward choices that fit the person, not the average.
pmc-12768813:
Everton Macêdo Silva and four co-authors wrote a 2025 study on what public health spending does for the economy of Brazil. Health care is a large part of the national economy, and public care also shifts income toward poorer homes. The team set out to measure how far one round of health spending spreads through other parts of the economy.

The team built a model from the national accounts for the year 2021, tracing cash flows between sectors. They found that a one percent rise in government health spending lifted national output by 1.61 percent. That gain beat the average gain from other government spending. Much of the boost came from the extra jobs the spending supports. The results suggest that health budgets aid both public health and family income.
pmc-12770313:
Tien-Wei Hsu and co-authors pull together trials of AVATAR therapy, a treatment for voices heard by people with psychosis that drugs have failed to quiet. In the therapy, the person faces a digital figure that speaks as the voice does, with help from a therapist.

The review found six trials with 675 people in all. The therapy cut the severity of the voices next to control care, and it eased the broader set of positive symptoms too. The team also check quality of life, mood, and whether gains held after care stopped. Drop out rates were part of the check for how well the care is borne.
pmc-12772613:
Nancy Jecker and Roger Chung draw on Confucian thought to argue for a more humble global bioethics, in a paper from 2025. Bioethics now works across borders, where values clash. The field's leading views grew in rich Western settings and carry those marks. The authors center the virtue of li, a blend of ritual care, propriety, and respect in daily conduct.

From li they draw calls for tolerance, cultural humility, and fair hearing for all knowledge traditions. They charge that the field gives Western views too much credit and Eastern views too little. Case fields include abortion policy, AI rules, and climate duties. Views of personhood in robots, unborn life, and nature show the East-West split at work. They close with a call for many worlds of value to stand side by side.
pmc-12774913:
Peiyang Wei and a team of co-authors build an expert system to tune deep learning forecasters, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Forecast accuracy hinges on training settings, and hand tuning is slow. Their system, HOES, blends six evolution-style optimizers into one team.

Three devices steer the team: sharing for wide search, memory for keeping the best, and punishment for dropping weak tactics. Six public datasets covered traffic, weather, power, and home energy. On solar power, the tuned model cut two error measures by about a quarter and a third. Gains in accuracy and speed held across the board.
pmc-12775513:
Nitrate washing off farms and out of factories pollutes water and threatens health, and charcoal-like biochar can pull it back out. Laleh Divband Hafshejani and Mehri Saeidinia ask when in the making of rapeseed biochar aluminum should be added. They try adding it before charring, after charring, and after charring with a second bake, then compare the three products.

The after-charring version won on nearly every count: more surface area, even pores, and more of the surface groups that grab nitrate. It kept about three quarters of its power after five rounds of use and washing. A random forest model predicted removal best among the learning methods tried. The authors stress that the order of steps in making biochar matters as much as the recipe.
pmc-12775613:
Matthew Lindsey and co-authors present a 2025 journal article on failed spinal fusion in patients with Parkinson's disease. Failed fusion, called pseudoarthrosis, is the top reason for repeat spine surgery, and Parkinson's brings posture problems that strain fusions. The team reviewed adults with the disease who had thoracolumbar fusion at one center from 2017 to 2022.

Of 59 patients, about 27 percent failed to fuse. Failure tracked with screw loosening and with higher death rates at ninety days and one year. Tremor, low bone density scores, wheelchair use, and trauma as the surgery reason all raised the risk. Disease duration and drug use showed no link.
pmc-12775713:
Nicolas Girard and co-authors pool trial proof on immune drugs for lung cancer in a 2025 review. Non-small cell lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer, with higher death rates in Asia. Checkpoint drugs work, but whether they work alike in Asian and non-Asian patients was unclear.

The team gathered multiregional randomized trials that split results by Asian subgroup. Drug alone and drug paired with chemotherapy or a second immune agent were weighed across first and later treatment lines. Survival and progression ratios anchor the comparisons. The pooled read aims to guide line-by-line choices for both populations.
pmc-12776213:
Meredith Nuo Zhang, Hongcun Bao, and Xiang Ji build a prognostic signature from palmitoylation-related genes for head and neck cancer, published in 2025. Palmitoylation is a reversible lipid modification that guides protein movement and signaling, and it has been linked to several cancers. Its role in this aggressive, varied cancer was largely unexplored.

Using cancer atlas and public data sets as training and validation cohorts, the team curated thousands of related genes and found hundreds that differed in tumors. Statistical selection narrowed these to an eight-gene risk model. They combined the risk score with clinical factors in a prediction chart. Survival curves, accuracy analyses, immune profiling, and drug sensitivity tests were used to judge the model's clinical value for sorting patients by risk.
pmc-12777313:
Xin Jiang and five co-authors hunt for genes shared by obesity and autoimmune disease in this twenty twenty-five study. The two kinds of illness often occur together, but their shared gene roots were not fully mapped. The team worked with people of European ancestry.

They merged genome scan data for obesity and seventeen autoimmune diseases. New methods measured how far the gene patterns overlapped and flagged spots on the genome that seem to drive both. Follow-up checks tied the spots to genes and tissues and ranked likely drug targets. The shared map may explain the pairing and point to treatments that help both.
pmc-12780413:
Ahmed K Awad, Mahmoud Alshneikat, and Faisal G Bakaeen review heart bypass surgery in bodies whose shape makes it risky, in a 2025 paper. Bypass grafting is the most common heart surgery, but a stiff, chalky main artery, poor spare vessels, or a chest opened before can wreck the standard plan. The review gathers the latest proof and expert craft for such cases.

Scans before surgery drive the plan, the authors stress. A chalky aorta may call for no-touch methods, an arm entry point, or full cooling and aorta swap. Weak graft stuff can be met with chained grafts or vessel cleaning. A torn artery wall often heals best without surgery, while big artery bulges need repair. Skill and flexible plans close the review's advice.
pmc-12780613:
Udaikumar and a team of co-authors review the evidence on fruquintinib, a drug for colorectal cancer that has spread and stopped responding to earlier treatments. The drug blocks receptors that help tumors grow new blood vessels. The review asks how well it works and how safe it is, alone and with immune therapy drugs.

Fifteen studies were gathered, and twelve of them, covering 3,703 patients, were combined in a meta-analysis. Fruquintinib lengthened both time without growth and overall survival compared with placebo, while side effects were common, most often high blood pressure and hand-foot skin reactions. The authors conclude the drug is a useful later-line option, with combination benefits still unproven.
pmc-12780813:
Ana Vila-Concejo and co-authors show that reef grooves move coral rubble ashore during cyclones in this 2025 paper. Reef islands survive only if new sediment arrives from the forereef. Spurs and grooves are ridge and channel patterns fringing most reefs. They were known to shed wave energy and carry sediment offshore.

Field evidence now shows the grooves also run in reverse during storms. Cyclone waves push broken coral through the channels onto the reef flat. That delivery feeds island building and rubble ecosystems. Without it, islands would starve as seas rise and storms chew their edges. Reef shape is thus part of island defense. Protecting groove systems protects the land behind them.
pmc-12784013:
A stiffened ligament down the back of the neck can squeeze the spinal cord, and surgeons argue over how to relieve it. John Chi writes a 2025 commentary on a multicenter study of one such choice: keeping the bone arches in a reshaped form, or removing them and fusing the spine. The study followed 349 patients for at least two years.

The sorting tool was the flexion K-line, a line drawn on bent-neck images that may or may not cross the hardened ligament. Patients whose line crossed it had more hunched alignment and recovered less well after surgery. Within that harder group, the study compared the two operations head to head. Chi walks through the stakes: the calcified ligament can stick to the cord's covering, making any approach risky. The commentary weighs what the K-line can and cannot decide for the surgeon.
pmc-12784613:
Mine Topcu and Ozcan Aygun published this study in 2025. It links health literacy to patient activation among people with high blood pressure in Turkey. Activation means the drive and skill to manage one's own care. The team surveyed 425 patients at a family health center. They used standard scales for literacy and activation, plus a background form. Interviews were done face to face.

Nearly half the patients had insufficient health literacy, and only about a third reached adequate levels. Activation spread across four levels, with most patients in the top two. The link was clear at the extremes: top-level activated patients showed adequate literacy far more often than the least activated. The authors recommend building literacy to strengthen self-management. For a lifelong condition like hypertension, an engaged patient is part of the treatment.
pmc-12784813:
Naia Seminario and co-authors study bladder recovery after major surgery for early cervical cancer in this 2025 paper. Removing the uterus widely can disturb the nerves that help the bladder empty, leaving urine behind. The team measured how long recovery took, what raised the risk of slow recovery, and whether an early reading could guide care.

They reviewed sixty-seven patients treated with two grades of surgery. The wider operation clearly slowed recovery: its patients took a median of two and a half days to empty well, against one day for the narrower grade. At discharge about a fifth still needed a catheter. The team proposes a simple plan: narrow-grade patients can skip a voiding trial, while wider-grade patients with a high day-one reading should keep the catheter longer.
pmc-12785013:
Mingfei Xu and co-authors identify a cholesterol making enzyme as a driver of breast cancer in a 2025 paper. Faulty cholesterol handling is a known mark of this cancer, but the key molecules were unclear. The team combined genetic evidence, database screens, lab tests, and patient data.

The enzyme, DHCR24, was high in tumors and linked to worse outcomes, above all in two subtypes. Oddly, lowering it in one cell line made those cells act more malignant. The team resolves that puzzle by showing the enzyme acts through the tumor's immune setting rather than through the cancer cells alone. Lowering it also shifted two other genes. They propose the enzyme as a drug target on the cholesterol and immune axis.
pmc-12785313:
Jia-Xin Yang and six co-authors analyse goldenrod essential oil and its antifungal action against mulberry sclerotinia disease, in work from 2025. The fungus behind the disease is a major threat to mulberry trees, and chemical sprays bring residue, pollution and resistance problems. Oils were drawn from flowers, leaves and stems, and their chemistry was profiled by GC-MS.

Flower oil gave the highest yield and the strongest fungal block in lab tests. Two compounds, alpha-pinene and myrcene, tracked antifungal strength most closely. Gene and cell tests show the oil breaks cell walls and membranes, leaks cell contents and drives oxidative stress that damages DNA. The authors offer the oil as a green pesticide base.
pmc-12785913:
Mateusz Kowalczyk and five co-authors reviewed the cellular basis of new depression treatments, from ketamine to brain stimulation, in a paper published in 2025. Depression touches more than 300 million people and raises the risk of self-harm. Its roots braid genes, stress, inflammation in the brain, and worn cell links. Standard mood drugs work on one set of signaling systems and often fall short.

New treatments hit other systems: the fast signal network, the calming network, and the drive network. Named forms span ketamine relatives, a cough drug pair, and hormone-based pills. Non-drug methods add magnetic pulses, mild current, and light applied to the skull. The team ties each treatment's cell actions to the roots of the disease. They aim at precise, matched, multi-way care.
pmc-12786013:
Helen Hayeso and four co-authors present a network that fuses three image types to diagnose colorectal cancer in this 2025 paper. Most medical AI reads one image kind and cannot explain itself, two habits that slow clinical use. Their system, IDF-Net, takes endoscopy photos, CT scans, and tissue slides, each through its own encoder. A two stage gating system weighs the inputs, and cross attention mixes them. Five fold validation gave accuracy near ninety-two percent and an area score near 0.99.

Heat maps from the model lined up with expert marked lesions. Contribution scores showed which image type drove each case's call. Removing parts proved each piece earned its place. The system also works when CT is missing, matching how clinics actually stage patients. The authors present interpretability as a feature to engineer, not a hope.
pmc-12786613:
Burcu Dogan and co-authors check heart risk in people with ankylosing spondylitis, a long-term joint disease that raises heart risk through steady inflammation. They compared 24 patients with 24 healthy adults, using two standard risk scores and blood levels of Klotho, a protein tied to slower aging and blood vessel health.

Klotho levels did not differ clearly between patients and healthy adults, nor across risk groups. One warning sign did stand out: in the high-risk score group, a fat-based index of vessel risk was raised at 0.42, and patients with active disease showed the same pattern. The authors read this as a sign of higher heart event risk in the patient group. They call for larger studies on Klotho and on the finer classes of blood fats in this disease.
pmc-12786913:
Dora Wynchank and co-authors present a 2025 narrative review on women with ADHD and the menstrual cycle. The question is how hormone swings across the cycle affect thinking in this group. The disorder already strains attention and working memory. Dopamine signalling sits at its core. Clinicians increasingly hear that symptoms flare at certain cycle phases, enough to blunt treatment, but the evidence had not been drawn together.

Searching a major medical database for work from 2015 to 2025, the authors gathered studies of attention, executive function, working memory, and impulse control across cycle phases. The studies covered women with and without ADHD. The review weighs how strongly hormones move each skill, a step toward cycle-aware dosing and support.
pmc-12787013:
Ten doctors in Romania study blocked presentation in colon cancer in a 2025 paper. Metabolic illness is tied to colon cancer growth, but its link to emergency blockage at diagnosis was murky. The cohort held 677 consecutive surgical patients with proven colon cancer.

About thirty-five percent arrived with partial or full obstruction. In adjusted models, each added year of age raised obstruction odds slightly, while the sheer count of other illnesses and inflammation markers did not. Diabetes, oddly, linked to lower odds of severe presentation. Stay length in hospital tied only to other factors in the final model. The authors argue age, not metabolic load, flags the risky presentation.
pmc-12787513:
Adrian Odriozola and co-authors published a review in 2025 joining thyroid, gut microbes, and mitochondria into one axis for exercise science. Exercise demands tight coordination among hormone, microbial, and energy systems to keep metabolism stable. The review gathers evidence across fields on how this axis works during training. It covers sharp, chronic, and overload phases of training.

Signals run both ways: microbe products tune thyroid enzyme action and energy building, while thyroid hormones shape gut movement and microbe balance. Under excess load or poor fueling, the axis tips into a reversible low-hormone pattern. The authors frame this state as dynamic recalibration and back tailored recovery plans for athletes.
pmc-12788013:
Six authors led by Madina Mussalimova review a class of plastics that carry both plus and minus charges on one chain. Such mixed-charge chains, called polyampholytes, can be tuned by charge balance, water uptake, and chain shape.
