That tune range suits them for parts in batteries, capacitors, solar cells, and fuel cells. The review sorts the class into three types and maps how each type is built and where it fits.

Tables in the review set side by side the flow, balance, and toughness scores of each type. In lithium and zinc batteries, these chains free ions, even out fields, and curb spiky metal growth. In capacitors, gels of this class still work when bent or frozen. In solar cells, thin layers lift charge flow. Design rules close the review for device builders.
pmc-12788513:
Fatty liver disease quietly shadows obesity worldwide, and insulin resistance is thought to tie the two together. Janak Nayak and co-authors screened in 2025 two hundred forty obese adults at a tertiary care center, scanning their livers with ultrasound and measuring fasting glucose, insulin, and blood fats. A standard index turned those numbers into an insulin resistance score.

Fatty liver showed up in sixty-three percent of the patients. Those affected were heavier, carried wider waists, and scored far higher on insulin resistance, and the score climbed in step with the liver's fat grade. The authors urge early screening and targeted lifestyle or drug intervention for obese patients.
pmc-12788713:
Sharvari Mairal and co-authors review in 2025 how well AI judges a hard call in braces care: whether to pull teeth. The choice shapes a whole treatment plan, so errors matter. The team searched six sources to June 2024 for studies that tested AI models on this call.

Eleven studies made the cut, from 361 records found. Nine scored over half on an AI quality list, the review notes, which counts as fair method. Yet a bias tool found some risk in every study, most in how patients were picked and how the gold answer was set. Neural nets and sorter models led the field. The verdict is careful: the tools look able, but biased tests mean clinics should not trust them blind yet.
pmc-12794313:
Ionel Popa and Ronen Berkovich review force based memory in proteins in 2025. Pulling forces act as switches inside cells, flipping protein parts between states. Those flips can store a record of past pulls, a kind of molecular memory. The review centers on one switch: the flip of a proline link in the protein chain.

That flip is reversible and settles into graded states rather than simple on or off. Models and experiments show it can hold memory over long spans. The authors link the mechanism to design of smart materials. Force aware matter could serve tissue repair and soft robotics.
pmc-12800013:
Matthew Hunt, Tinglong Dai and Michael Abràmoff test whether general-purpose AI chatbots can screen diabetic eye disease, in this 2025 Europe PMC paper. Autonomous AI for diabetic eye exams is heavily validated, yet little used, while off-the-shelf generative models are being tried in clinics without such proof. Four commercial models graded retinal images from a public dataset against a strong reference standard.

The best model reached a discrimination score well below that of retina specialists and below regulatory endpoints for medical devices; one model's score could not even be computed. The authors conclude consumer AI is not ready for this task, and sketch a possible future route: task-specific licensing by state medical boards.
pmc-12800113:
Jian Li, Qilong Shi, Shanchang Xu, Kangxin Sun, and Yue Liu monitored stress inside a huge underground wall while it was being built, in a 2025 paper. Diaphragm walls brace deep excavations, here for a bridge anchorage, and their forces shift at every construction stage. Steel bar sensors corrode and lag, so the team used bars of fiber-reinforced polymer with optical fibers embedded, sensing strain themselves. Data flowed wirelessly to a cloud platform during the Shiziyang Bridge project.

Readings traced the wall's changing state stage by stage. Early on, shallow layers pulled in tension while deep layers pressed in compression, driven by digging and falling groundwater. Later, as the liner, base slab, and backfill were added, upper stresses eased and lower ones flipped. Peak stresses stayed within safe bounds. The authors conclude self-sensing bars can watch such walls in real time with high reliability.
pmc-12800313:
Beshir Awol and co-authors work out in 2025 the quantum behavior of light trapped with a three level atom in a leaky cavity. The set up is a staple of quantum optics: a single cavity mode talks to an atom with three energy levels. The cavity sits open to a vacuum bath, and a steady coherent beam drives the whole system.

With the bath's noise kept in the math, the authors track how the light's two quadrature components behave. Both showed squeezing, a quantum narrowing of noise below the vacuum floor in one component. Stronger driving could offset the blur from the atom's random photon loss, keeping the squeezing intact. At high drive the effect no longer cared about that loss at all. Photon counts also skewed toward even numbers, a signature the authors detail. Squeezed light is a resource for sensing and quantum technology.
pmc-12800613:
Liam Crowley, Cian Williams, and others put out a moth genome sequence in 2025. The Mottled Grey is a geometer moth. Its genome was assembled from one moth. Two haplotypes were built during the build. Chromosome-level framing worked for one haplotype.

Most of that haplotype formed thirty-one chromosomes. The Z sex chromosome came with it. Total length passed five hundred million bases. The mitochondrial genome was also assembled. Work sat inside the Darwin Tree of Life project. That project reads British and Irish species. Standard genomes support broad wildlife research. Genome notes like this aid species naming.
pmc-12801813:
Erynne Sjoblom, Stephanie Montesanti, and Barbara Verstraeten set out a plan for a scoping review in this 2025 protocol paper. The review will study how health and well-being are measured for Indigenous people from before conception through early childhood.

The authors note that most current measures rest on Western medical models that miss Indigenous views of health and family ties, and focus on disease over strength. Their review will search world academic and grey sources for studies in Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and the United States. Each step will be guided by Indigenous values and community input, so the results can support fairer measures.
pmc-12801913:
Kristina Gottberg and three co-authors ask people with multiple sclerosis how daily life feels on modern disease-modifying drugs, in a 2025 interview study. These treatments can slow the disease, and their medical effects and side effects are well cataloged. The patient’s everyday view of taking them for years was much less studied.

Eight patients on different drug types gave in-depth interviews. Three themes emerged: expectations fulfilled when set against harsher past treatments, a constant need to manage side effects and logistics, and the ongoing weight of staying on therapy. The accounts show treatment burden as a daily reality, not a footnote. Clinicians who hear it can support adherence with more than leaflets and lab schedules.
pmc-12804513:
Sundas Javed and co-authors profile proteins and chemistry in blood plasma from people with Lesch-Nyhan disease, a very rare inherited disorder, in a 2025 study. The disease stems from a missing enzyme in a recycling pathway, causing uric acid buildup plus severe movement and behavior problems that the acid alone cannot explain. Twenty-nine affected people took part, most with the classic form.

Theirs is the first plasma protein study of its kind in this disease, paired with routine chemistry and inflammation markers. The authors suggest blood protein patterns could track how the disease progresses and how treatments work. They hope the approach points to therapies beyond the recycling pathway, where patient needs remain unmet.
pmc-12804713:
Zilong Li, Anders Albrechtsen, and Robert Davies present a 2025 tool that fills gaps in gene data from raw reads. Cheap and sound gene typing is key to modern gene science and health risk checks. Their tool, called QUILT2, uses huge panels of known gene patterns to guess the missing parts of a new sample.

The tool works with short reads, long reads, linked reads, and even old DNA from past remains. It can also split the genes of a mother and her unborn child from a blood draw, with no surgery. Tests on a large British panel show sharp results for the mother and fair results for the child.
pmc-12805713:
Chloe Docherty and co-authors ask facilitators how an impaired-driving program works in person versus by video call. Their 2025 study covers an Ontario program that drivers attend after an offence, built to cut repeat offending. The program had been in-person only until the pandemic forced it online.

The team interviewed ten facilitators who had run the shorter workshop both ways. Facilitators said online delivery improved access and let providers fit more participants in. The interviews also surfaced drawbacks of the video format and ideas to improve it. Hearing from the people who run the sessions adds a practical angle that attendance numbers alone cannot give. The findings can guide programs now choosing how to deliver remedial education.
pmc-12807913:
Wang and Zhang published in twenty twenty-six a case report of Lemierre's syndrome diagnosed quickly by gene sequencing. The syndrome is a rare, dangerous infection that starts in the throat. It is often caused by a Fusobacterium species invading throat tissue. Standard bacterial culture can confirm it, but culture is slow and can miss cases.

Metagenomic sequencing reads all DNA in a sample to name the culprit. In their patient, that method identified the infection rapidly and accurately. The authors present sequencing as a valuable supplement for such infections. Fast, precise identification can steer treatment before the disease turns fatal.
pmc-12808113:
Syphilis is rising again worldwide, and a vaccine piece built from one bacterial protein may train the right immune arm. Yinbo Jiang and co-authors tested a short epitope from that protein in two delivery forms. One used mRNA packed in fat particles, the other a carrier protein. Mice given either form mounted strong helper T cell responses. Only the mRNA form also raised killer T cell markers.

Rabbits challenged with the syphilis bacterium fared better with both forms. The protein form prevented ulcers completely, while the mRNA form cut them sharply. Bacterial loads and blood test titers fell in both groups. Cell-based epitope vaccines, the authors argue, deserve a place in syphilis prevention plans.
pmc-12810113:
Chetna Malhotra and a large team build and pilot a phone app ecosystem for people caring for family members with dementia, in a study from 2025. Caregivers carry heavy stress, and generic apps rarely fit their personal situation. A theory-driven, tailored design was the aim.

The app bundles personal assessments with matched advice, a chatbot, location tracking, peer support, a helpline, telemedicine, and self-care content. Caregiver interviews shaped development before two pilot rounds. Usability scores rose across rounds and passed the standard benchmark, and the second pilot scored near the top of a mobile health scale. Caregivers praised the dementia guidance and well-being content.
pmc-12813013:
Adina Yuetikuer explores in this 2025 study how empathy moves online crowds during a health crisis. The case is a storm on China's Weibo platform after a doctor's suicide. Topic modeling and sentiment tools sorted posts into four arenas: care disputes, cyberbullying and platform duty, media replay, and official probes.

Four kinds of empathy surfaced in comments: for the profession, for institutions, for the culture, and geared to action. Each carried its own emotional tone and spark to act, and women engaged with more empathy than men. The author frames digital empathy as a layered engine that platforms can steer toward constructive response. Each post became a small act of care.
pmc-12813113:
Shizhuang Zhu and co-authors run a randomized controlled trial of patches put on acupoints, for postherpetic neuralgia. That is pain that goes on after shingles. Their 2025 trial takes in patients whose pain pattern fits a set diagnosis in the traditional form.

One hundred thirty-four patients were put by chance in a group with real patches or a group with placebo patches. The patches went on more than one acupoint, with standard health education too. Care joined patches that cut swelling and pain with patches of herbal powder. Points took in the navel and sites of pain. Results took in scores for pain, scores for the traditional syndrome, quality of sleep, and surveys of health in broad terms. Blood measures took in inflammatory factors, groups of immune cells, and neurotransmitters. Some who took part dropped out from each group in the trial. The team reports that fact.
pmc-12815513:
Alicia M Gonzalez, Elizabeth Keating, and Aimee Moulin set out a seven-step plan in twenty twenty-five. Their aim is to help staff in emergency rooms break down blocks to care. Many people who come to an emergency room say they have no other place to get care. That gap is worst where basic care is hard to find.

The plan grows out of work led since twenty eighteen by the Bridge Center at the Public Health Institute. That work has spread to hundreds of hospitals in more than forty-five states. Steps in the plan have been used for drug use care, sexual health care, and harm reduction work. Readers get a tested way to start change in their own hospital.
pmc-12815713:
Mansour and eight co-authors test how nutrient limits shape a nitrogen-fixing ocean microbe's response to warming, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The microbe Crocosphaera supplies usable nitrogen to ocean food webs. Oceans are warming and growing more nutrient-poor in many regions. The team runs full temperature curves under iron-limited, phosphorus-limited, and rich conditions.

Nitrogen fixation suffers more than carbon fixation under both limits. Iron-limited cultures thrive at higher heat and share optima with rich cultures. Phosphorus-limited cultures favor cooler water with a narrower optimum. Extreme heat or cold erases the limit effect at curve ends. Phosphorus-poor regions like the North Atlantic look most vulnerable to warming.
pmc-12815913:
Dandan Tian and five co-authors present in 2025 a spatial fluorescence barcode for detecting many nucleic acid targets with a single color of light. Standard multiplex tests lean on many colors, which collide spectrally and cap how many targets fit. Their platform encodes targets by the layout of DNA-coated beads instead of by color.

Targets trigger strand swaps on the beads, and built-in enzymes reset the probes so they can be reused. The team detected pathogen sequences in infected blood and cancer-linked microRNAs in tissue. Layout-based encoding scales without new dyes, and resetting probes cuts the cost of repeat assays. Simpler, reusable barcodes could widen multiplex testing in clinics that cannot afford complex optics.
pmc-12816313:
Ziqiu Zhuang and Xue Li studied AI-aided music making in two thousand twenty-five. College students created music together with generative AI support. Creative learning is a hot area for AI tools. How AI shapes music creativity was little understood. The team measured several facets of student creativity. Interest, confidence, and self-guided learning were all tracked.

More than four hundred Chinese university students took part. The design mixed experiments with survey modeling. AI support raised creative interest clearly. It also lifted students' belief in their creative skill. Self-regulated learning improved alongside those gains. Perceived creative competence rose as well. The authors trace paths between these effects. Music teachers can use the findings to plan AI activities.
pmc-12816613:
Pablo Ruiz and co-authors validate a blood score for liver transplant rejection in this 2025 study. Rejection is normally confirmed by biopsy, an invasive step. A score built from two small RNAs and one immune signal had shown promise earlier, and this team tested it on fresh patients.

One hundred fifty-one recipients were followed through their first year, with biopsies when liver tests strayed. Forty developed rejection. Blood levels of the small RNAs mirrored their levels inside the liver during rejection, rising several-fold. The old score predicted and diagnosed rejection with very high accuracy in the new cohort. Extra markers added nothing. The authors back the score for noninvasive monitoring.
pmc-12816713:
Aris Widayati, Ingenida Hadning, and Erna Tri Wulandari survey herbal medicine use among people with high blood pressure or diabetes in Yogyakarta, Indonesia. Plant remedies are common in chronic care, and the state backs their place in the health system under a 2023 law. Their 2025 study questioned patients with one of the two conditions, leaving out those with extra illnesses. It recorded who used herbal products alongside prescribed drugs, and what traits tracked with that choice.

Knowing who mixes remedies with prescriptions matters, since some plants change how drugs act. The authors aim the results at pharmacists and clinics that counsel these patients. The study adds local data for a national policy that is still taking shape. It also flags where safety advice is most needed.
pmc-12817513:
Wenbin Ding and six co-authors compare two fixation systems for hip neck fractures in young patients in this 2025 study. Seventy patients treated between 2018 and 2023 received either a femoral neck system or hollow screws. Hip function scores formed the main outcome.

Final hip scores did not differ between the groups. The newer system healed fractures about two weeks faster and allowed full weight-bearing roughly seven weeks earlier. It also needed fewer X-ray checks and left less neck shortening. Fixation failure was rarer with it as well. Other measures and complication rates matched. The authors credit the system's stronger stability for the smoother recovery course.
pmc-12817813:
For people with the most severe obesity, picking the right weight-loss operation is still unsettled. Mostafa Mohammed Saad Mahran and co-authors pool the evidence on one-anastomosis gastric bypass in this 2025 review, covering seventeen studies and more than twenty-two hundred patients with very high body mass.

By two years, patients had shed about two-thirds of their excess weight. Diabetes cleared in roughly four of five patients and high blood pressure in a similar share. New reflux appeared in a small minority. The authors call the operation a valuable option for this group, while noting that long-term data are still missing.
pmc-12819313:
Yuwei Zhou and co-authors compare three ways to judge thyroid nodules in a study published in 2025. Ultrasound scoring, stiffness imaging, and AI assistance all promise discrimination. Nodule size may change which method wins. The head-to-head evidence was thin before this work.

Over one hundred nodules in ninety patients were analyzed prospectively. Each nodule received all three evaluations. Size split the set at one centimeter. In larger nodules, the AI system performed excellently. The scoring system also performed well there. A stiffness measure topped the accuracy table alone. Combining AI with scoring matched adding stiffness too. Subcentimeter nodules degraded every method's performance. Sensitivity and specificity were reported per size group. The authors guide method choice by nodule size. Small nodules remain the diagnostic frontier.
pmc-12819413:
Shakti Singh and colleagues tested a next-generation vaccine against Candida fungi in 2025. Candida species cause surface and deep invasive infections, and drug resistance is growing, including in a newly emerged resistant species. The candidate vaccine combines two fungal surface proteins produced in the laboratory, aiming for broad and lasting protection.

In mouse work the vaccine protected against bloodstream-spread infection by the main Candida species and by the resistant relative, and against mouth and throat type infection as well. It did not block antifungal drugs, and vaccine plus drug together trended toward better survival than either alone, though that gap was not statistically firm. Durable immunity is the promise highlighted.
pmc-12819713:
Daryl Yang and a large team show how land form and plant traits shape where two tall shrub kinds grow in low-Arctic tundra. Their study, from two thousand twenty-five, joins sensed maps with field reads.

Shrubs spread across the tundra, and that shifts how land and air trade heat and gas. Yet which shrub grows where was hard to read at wide scale. The team read two shrub groups, kin of alder and of willow. Land form proved a key hold on both, and made patchy but foretold maps of their spread. Trait reads in the field helped part the two. The work aids counts of how the far north greens.
pmc-12819913:
Sardar Ali and five co-authors review two therapies for peripheral nerve injury in a paper from 2025. Cut or crushed nerves regrow slowly, and surgery often leaves weak recovery. Electric stimulation speeds regrowth and re-coating of nerve fibers, while platelet-rich plasma, drawn from the patient's own blood, delivers growth factors that calm inflammation and support repair cells.

Used alone, each helps only in part. Lab evidence suggests the pair work better together: stimulation primes the injury site and plasma sustains support. The authors call for standard doses and settings, trials in patients, and blends with biomaterials and smart stimulation systems.
pmc-12820113:
Calum Murie, Mario Lebrato, Livia Gavard, and Simon Oliver report a 2025 study of sharks and rays on reefs in southern Mozambique. Few studies ask whether the mix of fish and coral on a reef shapes which sharks and rays show up. The team set out to test that link.

A remote video station was placed on each of four reefs once a month for a year, giving 140 hours of film. After each visit, a swim survey measured coral cover along a fixed strip. Math maps then compared reefs by fish and coral traits and by the sharks and rays seen. Coral mix tracked most with reef depth, and the shallow reef stood apart with less coral cover.
pmc-12821813:
Tulsi Ram Bhandari and co-authors wrote a 2025 report on a school nutrition program for teenage girls in rural Nepal. Adolescence is a window of fast growth when poor diet does lasting harm. Anemia affects nearly a quarter of young people worldwide. The program teaches nutrition through the theory of planned behavior, which links attitudes and intentions to action.

The trial covered 200 girls in grades seven to nine at 19 public schools, all with low iron stores. Schools were assigned at random: nine schools got the program, with 103 girls, and ten served as controls, with 97 girls. The team tracked diet behavior, health knowledge, and nutrition status. The report details how the program was designed and run. It offers a model for school health work in low-resource settings.
pmc-12822013:
Yuanru Liu and co-authors build a tiny reactor to treat gouty arthritis, a painful joint illness. Their 2025 paper deals with crystals that deposit in joints. The crystals trigger fierce swelling and growing tissue damage. Two enzymes used together have shown promise, but delivery has been poor. One enzyme breaks down the crystals. The other clears a harmful by product.

The reactor is an emulsion that holds both enzymes at the boundary between oil and water. That placement lets intermediates pass fast between them. Sugar tags on the droplets target swollen immune cells. A drug in the oil core cuts oxidative stress and swelling. One injection into the joint shifted immune cells to a healing type in mice. Swelling signals fell, and joint damage was reversed.
pmc-12822113:
Chinyere Okeke, Uchenna Ezenwaka, Obinna Onwujekwe, and Bassey Ebenso map what helps and what blocks health care in urban slums of southeast Nigeria. Slums grow fast and unplanned, leaving clinics thin on the ground. The team surveyed four slums in two cities, interviewing over one thousand caregivers and two hundred fifty providers, formal and informal.

Poverty topped the barriers: four in five people said they could not pay for care. Missing drugs in public facilities and high treatment costs followed. Providers blamed poor medicine quality and weak supervision. Statistical checks tied service provision to facility type and worker training, and use of care to employment. Residents asked for free or subsidized care and better training for informal providers. The authors urge slum-specific investment to close the gap.
pmc-12822913:
Morteza Oshagh, Masoud Davoudian, and Majid Kazem adapt a dental feedback questionnaire for Iran in a 2025 study. The Dental Patient Questionnaire captures how patients judge their care, from being put at ease to understanding the treatment plan, and it reflects trust and satisfaction. No validated Persian version existed, so the team translated it and checked it carefully.

Back-translation guarded the wording, and 228 patients at Tehran dental offices answered the final form. Expert review kept all twenty-three items, each passing the content checks, and a sampling adequacy index came out very high. Factor analyses then tested whether the questions group as intended, and agreement statistics checked steadiness over repeats. The authors deliver an instrument clinics can use for quality work.
pmc-12826813:
Austin Solak and co-authors argue that AI literacy for doctors should start at the bedside, through grassroots and reflective teaching, published in 2025. The piece opens with a junior resident facing an AI-generated diagnosis in a hospital workflow. Without training in how to judge the model's reliability or bias, the resident hesitates over a treatment that could harm if the output is wrong.

AI tools are now common in clinical care, yet students enter residency without tools to evaluate them safely. Bias is a core concern: tools trained on narrow data can underperform for some groups and deepen existing gaps in care. The authors call for training rooted in real clinical encounters and reflection, rather than abstract lectures alone, so new doctors can integrate these tools with critical judgment.
pmc-12827513:
Pengfei She, Bingqin Qin, Kening Lin, and Di Zhang test an old drug against a hardy germ in a study printed in 2025. The germ, a staph type, shrugs off a front-line drug class, and new cures are in short supply. The drug they test is an old cure for other germs, now tried on a fresh target.

Lab tests set the dose that stops and kills the germ in dish growth. The team also probed how fast the germ learns to resist, and how low doses bend its films, spread, and red-cell harm. The drug works by breaking the germ's inner power flow, a new route for an old pill.
pmc-12829213:
Mistrust of hospitals runs deep in communities shaped by racism and neglect, and San Francisco's Pregnancy Village tries to rebuild it by pairing the health system with neighborhood organizations. Odiase and co-authors evaluated the model with surveys of 116 pregnant or postpartum people and family members, plus eighteen interviews. Trust was scored on a standard scale and explored in open answers.

Trust in the Village ran high, at 85.9 of 100 on average, though it dipped among Latine participants, those with a prior early birth, and those facing food insecurity. Interviews credited the community groups with whole-person, responsive care, while the health system drew mixed views colored by past racism. Most participants still backed the system's role in the Village. The authors conclude that steady, community-guided teamwork is what makes such a bridge hold.
pmc-12830913:
Daily rhythms of sleep and activity matter in mental illness, but measuring them outside the lab is hard. Loran Knol and co-authors propose reading those rhythms from smartphones in a 2025 paper. Phones are carried everywhere and record behavior passively, so patterns can be gathered without wristbands or diaries.

Their framework turns phone data into estimates of daily rhythm. As a test, they predict sleep duration from the dynamics of typing alone. They also track how the rhythm's phase shifts when people cross time zones. Data came from a clinical outpatient group and from a year-long collection in everyday life. The authors present the method as a way to study rhythms at a scale clinics cannot reach, while asking nothing extra of the people measured.
pmc-12831313:
Kanokkan Nakasuwan and five co-authors check whether child cancer survivors still carry protection from the measles, mumps, and rubella shot after drug therapy, in a study from 2025. Cancer drugs weaken the body guards, which can erase shot gains.

Fifty four survivors, all shot at least once before their illness, were tested a few years after therapy ended. Four in five lacked cover for at least one of the three germs, with measles loss the most common. Loss of measles cover grew with time since therapy. The authors back routine repeat shots after therapy, above all where blood tests are scarce.
pmc-12835013:
Poornima Seralathan and A Shirly Edward built a learning system in 2025 to spot stress in rice crops early, using satellite and phone images. Standard plant health indices are fixed formulas that can miss early signs of trouble and do not adapt to a crop.

Their system lets a learning agent build the index itself, choosing band mixes that best flag stress in rice. It pairs satellite views with phone photos from the field, a first for this kind of work. In tests on real rice fields in Tamil Nadu and on shared data sets, it reached about eighty-nine percent accuracy. It beat fixed indices by up to twelve percent and flagged stress ten to fourteen days before symptoms showed.
pmc-12835113:
Satish Kumar and co-authors published this materials study in 2025. Magnesium alloys are light but wear quickly. Stirring hard ceramic particles into the surface can toughen them. The team used friction stir processing to embed titanium carbide particles into AZ31 magnesium at five, ten, and fifteen percent by volume. They then rubbed the composites under varied loads and speeds to measure wear, and checked grain structure and hardness.

The fifteen-percent composite performed best. Its grains shrank from about sixty micrometers to eight, and hardness nearly doubled, from 62 to 116 on the Vickers scale. Five machine learning models were trained to predict wear from load, speed, and particle content. A gradient boosting model proved almost exact, matching measurements within experimental error. The authors offer the combined recipe, physical processing plus learned prediction, as a template for designing wear-resistant lightweight parts.
pmc-12836813:
Renee Colucci and co-authors audit side findings in a veterans' lung cancer screening program, in a 2025 paper. Chest scans meant to catch lung cancer often reveal other issues, from heart to thyroid findings. Programs lack a standard way to flag which ones matter and tell doctors and patients.

The team reviewed scans from VA Boston taken between August 2023 and April 2024, skipping scans with likely cancer. Of 495 patients, 444 scans stayed in the study. They compared what the scan reader marked as significant, using a special code, against what the screening team judged significant. The paper also offers a standard report form with suggested next steps for doctors and patients. Better flagging could cut both missed risks and needless worry.
pmc-12836913:
Nipat Bock Pichayayothin, Wanachaporn Pipattanawong, and Natacha Phoolcharoen survey what Thai gynecologic cancer patients and their families know about advance directives. These documents state the care a person wants at the end of life. The study ran at a large Bangkok hospital.

Just over two hundred people took part, split between patients and family members. More than sixty percent of each group had never heard of advance directives, and test scores on the topic were low. Many wrongly equated the documents with euthanasia. Most said they would prefer a natural death, yet very few had signed anything. Feeling informed was the one factor that predicted plans to prepare a directive.
pmc-12837013:
Roughgarden sets mate pick lore gainst a social pick frame in this twenty twenty-five piece. The old frame casts sex as a fight for mates won by guile. Its tale leans on bad genes, strife, and force in her read.

Inside, she finds fault lines in the old frame's logic and fact base. Her new frame casts sex as work to land young, not win mates. Talk, team work, and task shares drive that frame's core acts. Each frame springs from its own world view of wild life. The piece asks peers to weigh both frames on proof, not habit.
pmc-12837113:
Tibor Rák and co-authors (2025) create the first Hungarian version of a standard questionnaire measuring use of complementary and alternative medicine. The questionnaire asks what therapies people use, from herbs to healers. It exists in several languages, but not Hungarian, even as interest in it grows in Hungary. Without a tested local version, surveys miscount use and policy flies blind. The team translated the form with a strict forward-backward process.

Language experts rendered it into Hungarian. Others translated it back, catching drift, and a panel settled the final wording. The final text was piloted with healthy health-care workers from eye departments, people without eye disease, who rated its clarity and cultural fit. The pilot checked that questions about treatments make sense in Hungarian daily life. A tested tool now lets Hungarian teams count alternative medicine use comparably with other countries.
pmc-12837613:
Cinnamon may soothe the gut-liver conversation gone wrong in lupus, in a 2025 mouse study by Georges Maalouly, Tarek Itani, and Nassim Fares. Lupus is a multi-front autoimmune disease, and leaky gut and altered microbes are increasingly blamed for feeding it.

Female mice were split into five groups: healthy controls with and without cinnamon, and lupus mice untreated, treated after disease onset, or dosed before and after. Lupus was raised by painting an immune-stimulating cream on the ear three times weekly for six weeks. Cinnamon was fed daily by mouth. Stool sequencing tracked the gut microbes, while tissue tests measured bacterial leakage and liver inflammation and cell death. Cinnamon nudged the microbial balance back toward normal in treated lupus mice.
pmc-12838013:
Girma Mamo Zegene, Tadele Shiwito Ango, Getachew Mesfin Bambo, Seid Tiku Mereta, and Seblework Mekonen wrote a 2025 review on drug-resistant Escherichia coli in Ethiopia. This common gut bacterium can cause serious illness, and strains that shrug off antibiotics are a growing threat to people and farm animals. Data in Ethiopia were scattered, so the team pooled what exists.

From more than seventeen hundred papers screened, fifteen studies fit their rules. About twenty-nine percent of samples carried the bacterium. Resistance was found in about fifty-six percent of human samples and forty percent of animal samples. Resistance to some older drugs ran above ninety percent. The review argues for a stronger national system to track resistance in one shared way.
pmc-12838413:
Paolo Gennari, Daniel Schlund, József Mészáros, and Atanas Ignatov survey parents in a German state on the HPV vaccine, in work from 2025. The vaccine is advised for all children in Germany, yet uptake lags, above all in boys. Parents decide for young teens, so their views drive the rates.

The survey drew 406 parents of children aged nine to fourteen. Mothers knew more about the virus than fathers and were more willing to vaccinate. Parents of daughters feared the linked diseases more than parents of sons, though willingness did not split by child sex. The team also weighed which offers might move unsure parents. Results aim to guide outreach that speaks to fathers and to parents of boys.
pmc-12840313:
Ilaria Galliano and co-authors track ancient viral genes as fat stem cells turn into cartilage cells in a 2025 study. Human genomes carry scraps of old retroviruses, called HERVs, whose activity is policed by epigenetic regulators. Stem cells from fat can become cartilage, a path of interest for joint repair.

The team measured three HERV families, two regulator genes, and three stemness genes during the change. Cartilage formation was confirmed by a marker gene and staining. No HERV family changed significantly, though two trended downward. One regulator dropped clearly, and one stemness gene fell as well. In mature cells, one HERV family's activity moved opposite to one regulator and with the other. The pattern hints at family-specific wiring.
pmc-12842713:
Six authors wrote a review in two thousand twenty-five on lung scarring that can follow COVID-19. The infection can leave interstitial lung disease as its major long-term complication, with progressive scarring and falling lung function. The review updates what is known from research and clinical guidelines since two thousand twenty.

Diagnosis rests on history, examination, lung function tests, and chest imaging, with biopsy used in some cases to pin down the pattern. The review describes lasting symptoms and scan findings in post-COVID disease. It also covers how the scarring arises from the initial infection and what may influence its course.
pmc-12843313:
Ziwen Zhao and five co-authors survey, in a 2025 study, the helpful fungi that live on maize roots in the salty soils of northern Xinjiang, China. These fungi trade nutrients with the plant and help roots take up more from poor soil. The team sampled the soil around maize roots in four areas to map which fungi live there and what shapes their mix.

Gene sequencing and spore study found eleven genera, with Glomus by far the most common. Soil nitrogen, potassium, and an enzyme measure best explained the mix. From the spores, they grew three strains and tested them on maize in pots. One strain clearly boosted plant growth, root growth, and uptake of phosphorus and potassium, which marks it as a candidate farm aid.
pmc-12844213:
Ayushman Ramola, Amit Kumar Shakya, Nezah Balal, and Arik Bergman present a 2025 design study of a fiber sensor for early cancer marks. The sensor is a glass fiber with a near-D cross shape, coated with gold and a clear polymer. Light in the fiber stirs a wave on the gold that shifts as cells of unlike bend traits sit near. Computer sims tuned the gold depth and air hole sizes for the sharpest response.

Too thick a gold coat dulled the sense and bled light. The tuned build read bend shifts with very fine steps on a breast cancer cell line. On-paper sensors let engineers spend sims, not glass, while hunting the best shape. Early cancer spotting is the long prize.
pmc-12845113:
Sahoo, Pandey, and Pattnaik review a cell defense switch that can help or hurt during virus infection in 2025. The switch turns on shield genes that fight chemical stress. That shield aids host defense and virus killing. Yet some viruses bend the same path to ease their own growth.

The review sorts both roles across RNA and DNA viruses. It lays out the tricks each side uses. Drug ideas that target the switch are weighed with care. The authors stress that timing and context rule the outcome. A blanket boost or block could backfire. Fine tuned control is the goal for future antiviral work.
pmc-12846613:
Dengue has spread across Paraná in southern Brazil since 1995, with the worst outbreaks in the west and north. Magda Clara Vieira da Costa-Ribeiro and co-authors evaluated a mass vaccination campaign run in 30 municipalities of the state. Their interrupted time series study covered 15 years of official records. They modeled case rates while adjusting for population, weather, and outbreak patterns at each site.

At full coverage, the campaign was estimated to cut dengue incidence by 18.7 percent. At the three-dose coverage actually reached, the cut was 8.2 percent, and it would rise to 17 percent at 90 percent coverage. Smaller municipalities gained most because they vaccinated a larger share of residents. The authors present the campaign as a real brake on dengue trends.
pmc-12847713:
Jin-Lei Wu and co-authors shrink light-routing devices on photonic chips by speeding up a usually slow process. Topological pumping moves light along a chip in a way that resists defects, but it demands very slow, gentle changes, which forces large devices. The team wanted the same protection in a fraction of the space.

Their approach applies repeated shortcut transformations, called superadiabatic steps, built around a gap-mode design. On a working chip, the device moved light as designed while taking up twenty times less room than standard pumping designs. It also halved the size of the best rival acceleration schemes. The device worked across a wide band of wavelengths, from red into the near-infrared. It can also be woven into larger waveguide circuits. The authors present the method as a general framework for compact topological transport.
pmc-12847813:
Root-knot nematodes are tiny worms that invade potato roots and form galls, draining the crop. Sapinder Bali, Mirosław Sobczak, Hao Peng, and Cynthia Gleason studied a potato gene in 2025 that helps roots lay down callose, a sugar wall material used in defense. The gene, GSL05, is switched on when roots sense attack signals, and the team silenced it to see what would change.

Plants with the gene silenced made less callose, and more young worms got in and formed galls. Yet those worms produced no extra eggs, because their feeding sites inside the root were misshapen. Callose thus both blocks entry and shapes the feeding cells worms need, a dual role the authors say matters for breeding resistant crops.
pmc-12847913:
Paithoon Sonthon and co-authors study what helps drinkers in Thailand give up alcohol for a full three months. Their 2025 paper looks at a national drive tied to Buddhist Lent, which has lost some of its pull in recent years. The team wanted to learn why some people finish the stretch with no drinks at all.

They pooled survey data from 5,898 current drinkers across three rounds, in 2015, 2018, and 2021. Seeing the drive's ads and messages was linked to full success, as were older age and drinking less often before the drive. The authors tie the recent slide in success to weaker reach of the messages, more frequent drinking, and the strain of the 2021 period.
pmc-12849113:
Gram and five co-authors asked in twenty twenty-five whether smoke breathed as a child at home lifts breast cancer risk in later life. The group held more than twenty-four thousand women who never smoked, across many races. Their child smoke hours were told in mid-life forms, with cancers tracked by state lists.

In near eight years of checks, seven hundred nine breast cancers arose. Any child smoke tied to a risk near a fifth higher than none. More hours per day and more years both pushed the risk up. The step-wise rise held across nine other risk facts. Child smoke may be a real cause, they argue.
pmc-12849313:
Falciola and co-authors use AI language models to map a century of research on neurosyphilis, in a 2025 study. Neurosyphilis, a late effect of syphilis on the nervous system, is hard to diagnose and its literature is scattered. The team searched five databases for records up to the end of 2024. A small language model sorted the papers into 23 research fields, and network tools traced how the fields connect over time.

Of 14,934 records found, 4,646 met the study rules. The AI sorting proved highly repeatable, agreeing with itself almost perfectly. Research clusters shifted from tight, single-field groups toward larger mixed networks over the century. Time series analysis linked publication swings to major clinical and technical milestones. The study offers a template for mapping other neglected topics.
pmc-12849413:
Ji-Kang Chen and Chaoyue Wu test how family hardship shapes teen depression and aggressive behavior in mainland China. Published in 2025, the study extends the family stress model to cover long term care needs, a factor rarely tested in Asian settings. Data came from a national education panel with 9,433 student parent pairs across 112 schools, followed over two waves.

Economic hardship at the first wave did not predict teen outcomes directly at the second. It worked indirectly, through parental conflict early on and then the parent child relationship later. Long term care needs did predict later teen depression directly. The authors also examine how the paths differ for boys and girls, using structural equation models.
pmc-12849613:
Food companies shape what nations eat, and a 2025 study by Carmen Klinger and co-authors adapts a scorecard to grade them where hunger and obesity strike together. Many poorer countries carry that double burden: undernutrition beside overweight and diet-driven disease.

An existing tool grades firms on their promises and practices around obesity and healthy diets. To make it fit double-burden countries, the team ran a Delphi process, asking experts in rounds to pick the best practice markers worth keeping. Those markers can then benchmark both global and local firms. The authors aim to give watchdogs and governments a fair ruler for holding the industry to account.
pmc-12852813:
Panjavarnam, Kanimozhi, Rahmath Nisha and Dharini wrote a 2025 paper on placing web-connected services on edge computers. Edge sites have limited power and space, while apps need varied resources. Good placement must weigh load, delay, energy and speed at once. The team built a search method with a bird-inspired twist.

Their method borrows ideas from vulture search and from quantum-style coding of options. A fitness score blends load balance, energy, delay and speed. Test runs beat base methods on each of those counts by a clear margin. Stats checks backed the gains. The authors aim the tool at 5G-era edge networks.
pmc-12852913:
Borecki, Mucha, Niżański, and Partyka tested freezing mixtures for African penguin semen in twenty twenty-five. Frozen semen banks support breeding of this endangered species. Two protectants were compared: dimethylformamide, which enters cells, alone, versus a lower dose combined with trehalose, a sugar that protects from outside the cell.

After thawing, the groups traded strengths. The standard mixture gave higher total motility and better mitochondrial energy status. The trehalose mixture produced better movement quality measures, less cell-death-like change, less damage to the sperm cap, and less DNA fragmentation. Viability was maintained under both. The authors conclude the protectants influence different sperm traits, and trehalose's targeted protection could matter for fertilization even without raising total motility. Such differences must be mapped species by species, they note.
pmc-12853813:
Meng Jia, Yi-Dan Guo, Peng-Peng Ye, Xiao-Ling Zhou, and Yang Luo present a 2025 study of kidney injury after a liver shunt procedure in patients with advanced cirrhosis. The shunt relieves dangerous pressure in the liver's blood flow. Kidney injury after the procedure is common and raises death risk, yet its drivers in this group were not fully mapped.

The team reviewed records of 384 patients who got the shunt. Injury was judged by an international kidney guideline. Statistical models, first simple and then adjusted, sorted which traits raised the odds of injury. They also tested how injury linked with death from any cause during follow up.
pmc-12853913:
Feng-Yi Wang and co-authors review wearable biofeedback devices for walking training after stroke in a 2025 analysis of trials. Stroke often impairs gait, balance, and mobility, cutting independence and raising fall risk. Wearable devices give real time feedback during training, aiming to improve motor recovery.

The review searched many databases through September twenty twenty four for randomized trials. It compared wearable feedback training with general gait training or other controls. Outcomes covered gait speed, balance, functional mobility, and daily living activities. The authors pool the trial evidence to guide clinical practice and future research design.
pmc-12856013:
A protein complex called the NLRP3 inflammasome fans inflammation in the brain, and blocking it could help in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and stroke, yet no approved drug targets it. Sami Alzarea screened plant compounds against it by computer in 2025, chaining several methods together. Machine learning models trained on known active and inactive compounds first fished out candidates from a plant library.

Docking tests then ranked how snugly the survivors fit the target's engine region, and stability simulations checked the best fits over time. Energy calculations and an electron-level analysis singled out one compound as the most promising, with a second close behind. Alzarea presents both as starting scaffolds for selective blockers, pending lab proof.
pmc-12858713:
Dazhou Li, Guihui Tong, and Wenqing Huang used in 2025 single-cell data to split the support cells around stomach tumors into subtypes with different outlooks. These fibroblasts shape tumor growth and immune response. Drawing gene sets from thirteen single-cell datasets, the team scored large tumor cohorts and found two subtypes.

One subtype meant poor survival, more suppressive immune cells, and weaker predicted response to immunotherapy. The other fared better. A drug called dasatinib was flagged as a candidate for the worse subtype. A five-gene model predicted outcomes consistently across datasets. Lab tests confirmed one model gene is switched on in these fibroblasts and helps cancer cells invade.
pmc-12859913:
Esmée Vaes and co-authors use a change lab to ask patients and clinicians where primary care diagnosis should go next. Their 2025 study notes that fresh tools aim to improve how family doctors reach a diagnosis, yet those who live the process are rarely asked. Two groups of patients, family doctors, and specialists met four times each over four months. Clashes of view were used as fuel for learning, under a theory that maps clashing work systems.

Joint work named tensions inside and between the systems that touch diagnosis. One clash: faster, wider testing in primary care can strain time and trust. Another: partners in the chain hold split aims and drives. The groups turned those clashes into new directions.
pmc-12860013:
Gökhan Varlı and four co-authors test two plant compounds against pancreatic cancer grown in mice, in this 2025 study. The cancer is among the deadliest, resisting standard drugs, while quercetin and curcumin are known for gentle, cancer fighting properties. Thirty-four mice carrying human tumor grafts were split into six groups for a month of treatment.

The compound pair, given by mouth or injection, held tumor growth about forty percent below untreated controls, matching the standard drug cisplatin alone. Pairing the compounds with cisplatin did better still, and dead tissue inside tumors grew. A group dosed before tumors were planted tested prevention. The authors read the results as evidence that the plant pair can support chemotherapy against a stubborn cancer, pending human trials.
pmc-12860113:
Herbal medicines are widely used in Tanzania, yet almost no harm reports about them reach the global safety database from Africa. Alambo Mssusa and three co-authors surveyed 380 healthcare professionals across five Tanzanian regions in a 2025 study, testing what they know and do about drug safety reporting. Most scored low on knowledge of the reporting system and of herbal harms.

Attitudes were warm: nearly nine in ten favored reporting. Practice lagged far behind, with under a quarter ever filing a report, and fewer than a fifth of those reports concerned herbal products. The authors say training and simpler pathways must close the gap between goodwill and action.
pmc-12860313:
Ahmed Bin Salem, Faisal Muzian, and Hussam Kutub report repeated migration of a brain shunt's lower catheter in an obese woman with a high-grade brain tumour. Their 2025 case report covers a rare but important cause of shunt failure.

The sixty-three-year-old needed an emergency shunt for blocked fluid flow from her tumour. Two weeks later, painless abdominal swelling showed the catheter had slipped into the abdominal wall. Surgeons repositioned it, but within a month it migrated again with abdominal fullness. A second revision lengthened and firmly fixed the shunt, working through dense internal adhesions. The authors blame obesity, repeat revisions, and raised abdominal pressure, urging awareness of these predisposing factors.
pmc-12866113:
Rui Liu and co-authors look back at surgery records in 2025 to link low blood pressure during surgery to kidney injury in older patients. The study covers non heart surgery under general anesthesia.

More than ten thousand patients aged sixty and older were included. Kidney injury struck just under three percent overall, and the rate rose with age, reaching near five percent in the eighties group. The link between the lowest pressure during surgery and injury was not a straight line. Both the depth of the drop and the lowest level reached mattered. The authors hunt for harm thresholds that could guide care for the oldest patients.
pmc-12866313:
Ye and six co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a score chart that predicts survival after surgery for a rare tumor. The tumor grows in the pancreas and starts in hormone-linked cells. Surgery is the main care, yet results after surgery stay mixed. The team checked blood signs tied to swelling and nutrition in one hundred two patients. They sought which signs best predict who lives longer. They built a chart that blends the top signs with tumor stage.

Three signs, two blood ratios and one nutrition score, stood out as firm predictors. The chart split patients into low and high risk groups cleanly. Its accuracy held across three, five, and ten year horizons in their checks. The authors admit the study is small and from one center. They offer the chart as a guide for care after surgery.
pmc-12866413:
Pietro Santocchi, Annamaria Agnes, and Alberto Biondi review gentler stomach cancer surgery in this 2025 survey. Standard surgery removes much of the stomach, hurting nutrition and life quality. East Asian centers, which catch the cancer early more often, widely use function-keeping variants that spare the stomach's outlet or top.

In well-picked early cases, survival matches standard surgery, the review finds. Drawbacks like food stasis and reflux have spurred new joinery tricks. Western uptake lags for want of early cases, training, and guideline backing. Rising care centralization revives interest, the authors say, and even advanced cases may gain short-term benefits.
pmc-12867013:
Van Schaik and co-authors ran this 2025 pilot study on the hidden effort of daily tasks after leg amputation. People who lose a lower limb often have less stamina, while daily activities demand more of them. That squeeze can shrink participation and quality of life. Rehab goals need real numbers on how hard tasks like stairs truly are.

Six adults with one-sided amputations took part, with an average age of 59. They first did a full exercise test, then performed five standard tasks, from a six-minute walk to climbing stairs. A portable device tracked their oxygen use during each task. The pilot also tested whether a recovery-based method, using extra oxygen burned after effort, can size up short tasks. Feasibility was the main goal.
pmc-12868713:
Gaia Griguolo and a large team of co-authors wrote this 2025 study on the immune life inside a common class of breast cancer. These cancers carry hormone receptors but lack a second marker, and they are usually classed as immunologically cold. Yet adding immune drugs to chemo has raised cure rates in high-risk cases, so the team asked which tumors are in fact immune-active.

Gene data came from two trials of pre-surgery treatment, covering 109 tumors. A standard typing scheme put most in the two luminal groups, but about eighteen percent typed as basal-like. Those basal-like tumors held far more immune cells and showed much stronger immune gene signals, plus higher levels of the very targets the immune drugs strike. No such gap split the two luminal groups. The authors say this subgroup may gain most from immune drug mixes.
pmc-12872613:
Yunzhan Li and co-authors expose a weakness of pancreatic cancer in a 2025 study. The tumor's surroundings starve it of cystine, an amino acid vital for defense against oxidative damage. Cells that adapt to that starvation, the team finds, grow faster by boosting a side route of sugar metabolism.

That route feeds building blocks for DNA and fats, while fat storage droplets shield the cells from fat toxicity. A drug screen spots an existing drug that blocks fat assembly, slowing adapted tumors and boosting chemotherapy. The authors present the fat pathway as a targetable flaw created by the tumor's own adaptation.
pmc-12909213:
Myoung-Jin Yoo and co-authors study early thyroid hormone changes in preterm infants and later brain development, in a research paper from 2025. Thyroid hormones drive brain growth in late pregnancy and early life. Preterm birth disrupts the control axis, causing patterns that standard newborn screening can miss, yet those patterns may forecast development at age two.

More than two hundred infants born at or before thirty-two weeks had thyroid tests in the first weeks and near discharge. Development was assessed at two years with a standard scale, and brain scans measured network traits. Infants were grouped by hormone level at each time point. The study links hormone paths to impairment risk and scan traits.
pmc-12913713:
Loan Phung Bich Tran and co-authors assessed, in a 2025 study, rabies vaccination coverage and pet owner behavior in a Vietnamese district during a mass campaign. Rabies still kills in Vietnam, and control rests on vaccinating dogs and cats and on owners who act early. The survey covered eleven communes of Duc Hue District in early 2024.

Households answered both a general survey and a structured questionnaire on knowledge, attitudes, and practice. Mapping and statistics software handled the data. Regression hunted for traits tied to owners who vaccinate without prompting. Grouping methods then sorted owners into behavior classes from their answer patterns. The aim is practical: aim campaign effort at the owner types least likely to vaccinate, rather than blanketing everyone alike.
pmc-12927213:
Xue Ren and co-authors pool the trials on a protective film used to prevent radiation skin damage in cancer patients. The film, Mepitel, is laid over skin in the treatment field. The team searched six databases to August 2024 and gathered 27 controlled studies with 2,313 patients, checking each for bias with a standard tool.

The film cut the odds of radiation dermatitis sharply, with an odds ratio of 0.28 against control care. The benefit held across cancers, from nasopharyngeal and breast tumors to mixed groups. Moderate and severe skin grades also fell steeply, with odds ratios of 0.26, 0.19, and 0.10 for grades two, three, and four. Damage severity scores dropped as well. The authors conclude the film prevents and softens radiation skin injury.
pmc-12932613:
Agnieszka Filipek and Edyta Czepielewska review plants of the olive family as sources of artery-protecting compounds, in a study published in 2025. Artery clogging grows from inflammation, oxidative stress, and lipid imbalance. Olive compounds lead the evidence: oleuropein and oleocanthal calm inflammation, hydroxytyrosol fights oxidation, and several others help move cholesterol out of artery walls.

Animal studies show strong protection across these compounds. Human proof, though, mostly covers polyphenol-rich olive oil as a food, not purified chemicals or the family's other species. The authors map the pathways each compound touches and call for proper trials before any of them can be prescribed. They also note that dose and formulation will decide whether lab promise survives contact with patients.
pmc-12951013:
Five authors measure urinary schistosomiasis in women in Eswatini in this 2025 study. The water borne parasite disease is endemic in much of Africa, yet data on women of reproductive age, who face added risks, are scarce.

At one health center, 360 women aged twenty to forty-nine who came for cervical cancer screening gave urine samples and answered questions on water contact and background. Infection, defined by parasite eggs in the sample, was found in about eleven percent. Women older than the median age of twenty-six had over twice the odds of infection, while secondary schooling was linked to lower odds. The study maps who most needs testing and prevention.
pmc-13037613:
Mst Aesha, Md Sheikh Sadi, Md Emtiaj Alam, Takashi Tanida, and Md Royhan Gofur published a study in 2025 on growth of the epididymis in Bangladeshi sheep. The epididymis is the duct where sperm mature, and ram fertility depends on its growth. The local Barind breed's timeline was undocumented. The team examined twenty-one lambs at seven ages, from newborn to seven months.

Growth was slow for the first month, then rapid. By puberty the duct was over five times longer and fifty times heavier than at birth, and sperm first appeared in its channel at seven months. The tail region developed first and long carried the tallest lining and widest tube, a lead that flipped for lining height at seven months. Regional timing, the authors show, is the story.
pmc-13058613:
Marit Hidding and co-authors ask what moves self-esteem up or down after a first episode of psychosis has passed. They studied people in remission three to six months after that first episode, measuring symptoms, self-stigma, childhood experiences, social support, and reactions to medication. Cross-sectional data covered 299 people, and 238 were followed for six months to watch self-esteem change.

At one point in time, low self-esteem travelled with worse symptoms, more self-stigma and childhood hardship, less support, and poorer personal recovery. The follow-up held a surprise: higher early stigma, emotional abuse, and dislike of medication predicted later gains in self-esteem. Meanwhile, easing symptoms and stigma, better reactions to medication, and growing support also lifted it. The authors argue early programs should work on these levers while expecting some counterintuitive paths.
pmc-13081413:
Sogol Tavanaeian and co-authors hunt pancreatic cancer in mouth and gut microbes, hoping to catch a killer early. Pancreatic cancer kills reliably, with five-year survival near twelve percent, largely because it is found late and its signs are vague. Certain bacteria have been tied to its risk. Their 2025 paper builds machine learning models reading clinical and microbial clues together.

The data were small: twenty patients and twenty controls. Five classifiers were tested under cross-checking repeated two hundred times, with penalties to keep the models honest. Age alone separated the groups almost perfectly, and a ratio between two gut bacteria separated them completely in this sample. Models joining age to that ratio scored at the top of the scale. The authors package them as nomograms clinicians could use, while the cohort warns how far the proof has to travel.
pmc-13088613:
Welhenge leads a team that tests three chest pain risk scores in Sri Lanka. Their pilot study from twenty twenty-six is set at a single center. The HEART score is wide used to sort chest pain risk.

Two other scores, GRACE and TIMI, guide outlook in heart syndromes. Data came from a small group of chest pain patients. Each patient got all three scores worked out in full. The team checked how well HEART flags acute heart syndrome. It also checked big heart events in the weeks after. Accuracy was set next to the other two scores.
pmc-13092813:
Rachel Poutre and co-authors compared five-year outcomes of hip arthroscopy in patients who also had lower-spine problems against matched patients without them. Hip and spine conditions can amplify each other's symptoms, raising doubts about operating on the hip first. The study matched thirty-eight patients in each group, all treated for hip labral tears, and tracked patient-reported outcome scores plus revision and hip-replacement rates.

The spine group reported worse function at baseline and at every follow-up point out to five years. Yet they improved by similar or larger amounts, and they reached meaningful improvement at similar rates. Revision and replacement rates did not differ between groups. pmc-13098513:

pmc-13176313:

pmc-13176813:

pmc-13177813:

pmc-13177913:

pmc-13181913:
