Both ways cut pain in most tests, but scores still split. Age, drug use at the same time, and test form may drive the split.
pmc-13200513:
Tine Østergaard and co-authors studied survival and relapse in Danish patients with thymic epithelial tumors, in a 2026 paper. These rare tumors grow in the chest gland called the thymus. The group covers thymoma, thymic carcinoma, and a neuroendocrine type. The team wanted better risk groups for death and relapse.

The cohort held 282 patients diagnosed from 2015 through 2020, with follow-up records. Data covered the disease, other illnesses, relapse, and survival. Models in R tested which traits at diagnosis predicted later outcomes. Mean age at diagnosis was in the mid-sixties. Results can guide how closely each patient is watched after treatment. They also support fair, evidence-based care plans.
pmc-13203413:
Qingshan Ma and co-authors review heat stress in dairy cattle in a 2026 paper. Heat is one of the costliest weather threats to milk output worldwide. It cuts yield, harms milk quality, and damages the udder at the cell level.

A heat index marks where harm begins, and the limit differs by breed. At the gene level, heat switches on protective heat shock genes while switching off milk protein and fat genes. The review traces those paths and the breeding signs of heat tolerance. Farmers and breeders get a combined view of management and genetics for a warming world.
pmc-13203813:
Seven researchers review antimicrobial peptides from fish in a 2026 paper. These small proteins are part of the natural immune kit of fish and kill germs broadly with low toxicity. Fish farms lose much stock to disease, and drug resistance makes new tools urgent.

The review covers peptide classes, where they sit in the body, and how they kill germs. It also covers how to extract or build them in the lab. Uses span disease prevention on farms, food preservation, and standing in for antibiotics. Stability in the field, production cost, and rules for use remain open hurdles, the authors note.
pmc-13204013:
Hui Chen, Zhenya Wang, Shikai Zhang, and Ligang Yao present an engineering paper, published in 2026, on a soft robotic hand with four fingers. Soft hands handle fragile and oddly shaped objects well. Many designs fix the fingers in one layout, though, so they grip poorly when object size changes a lot.

Their hand pairs soft air-driven fingers with a stiff base that can move all fingers in or out together before a grip starts. A math model links the base movement, finger bending, and the space the hand can reach. In tests, matching the finger spacing to the object's size gave steadier grips and a wider range of sizes than a fixed layout. The authors say reshaping the hand itself is a simple way to make soft hands more flexible.
pmc-13204613:
Yubing Lv and eight co-authors build a sensor for two Alzheimer's related chemicals in a 2026 paper. The compounds, called NADH and glutamate, both figure in the disease's development, so measuring traces of them in blood could aid research. The team synthesized a layered framework material and loaded it with cobalt, then fixed it onto a printed electrode.

The cobalt framework sped up NADH oxidation strongly, and adding an enzyme let the same platform read glutamate through a linked reaction. Detection ranges were wide and limits very low, down to nanomolar levels for NADH. Tests in human serum showed the sensor picks up trace amounts reliably. The authors offer it as a tool for Alzheimer's pathology studies.
pmc-13204813:
Pantelidis and co-authors review AI tools that spot a hidden heart rhythm fault in a 2026 paper. The fault, atrial fibrillation, raises stroke risk, yet silent bursts escape notice. AI can read a normal-looking heart trace and find faint signs of the fault. The review weighs results from short traces, day-long monitors, and worn patches.

Deep learning on ten-second traces sorted people with the fault with high scores, beating standard risk scores. Patch and monitor tools also beat the scores for finding hidden cases or near-term bursts. Some tools even flag an attack hours ahead. Most studies so far look backward at old data, though. The authors call for live trials before routine use.
pmc-13206313:
Flores-López and co-authors test indirubin, a plant pigment, against the gut parasite Giardia lamblia, in a 2026 paper. Standard drugs against the parasite face growing resistance, so new attack routes are wanted. The team watched how the compound hit two of the parasite's metabolic enzymes.

Indirubin cut the growth and survival of the parasite's feeding stage and directly blocked both enzymes, triosephosphate isomerase and aldose reductase, hitting the parasite versions harder than the human ones. A toxic byproduct then built up, damage spread through the cell, and the parasites died. The authors back the compound as a lead for new giardia drugs.
pmc-13207013:
Lide Arana and co-authors review in 2026 how tiny fat-based carriers could help beat drug-resistant fungal infections. Fungi are learning to shrug off the few drugs that can kill them, and new drugs are slow to arrive. The carriers wrap a drug in a small bubble or bead of fat.

The review covers four kinds of carriers, from simple fat bubbles to newer lipid particles. These carriers can slip into the sticky films fungi grow in, and they can push drugs past the pumps fungi use to throw drugs out. They also help the body take up the drug and can cut side effects. The authors see them as a strong tool for hard-to-treat fungal disease.
pmc-13207413:
Ding Li and co-authors published this study in 2026. It tests a plant compound, 25R-inokosterone, from the herb Achyranthes bidentata, against Parkinson's disease signs. The work pairs cell experiments with computer modeling. In cells, the compound switched on a defense path centered on Nrf2 and its partner HO-1. That path guards cells against oxidative stress, a driver of neuron loss in Parkinson's.

At the same time, two other players linked to the disease turned down: MAOB and GSK-3β. The modeling checked how the compound might bind its targets. The authors read the pattern as mainly protective through the defense path, with the two turn-downs in support. The study is early-stage, in dishes and in silico only. It frames the compound as a candidate worth testing in animals next.
pmc-13207613:
Andreea Stefan-Hodorogea and co-authors map the gene faults in childhood leukemia in a 2026 study of ninety-six young patients. This cancer is the most common one in children, and gene tests now guide how doctors judge risk. The team combined classic chromosome tests with modern gene sequencing.

Two clusters of faults stood out: one around RAS pathway genes, one around a gene fusion called ETV6::RUNX1. Some faults, such as loss of the IKZF1 gene, tracked with worse two-year outcomes. Others, like the fusion above and extra chromosomes, tracked with better early response. RAS pathway faults tied to how patients answered the first phase of treatment. Such maps help doctors sort children into risk groups.
pmc-13208213:
Seounghun Lee, Jiho Park, Juyeon Kim, and Yeojung Kim study how needle path affects a neck injection for nerve pain. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The shot puts steroid near the spine in the neck, through a path that is seen as safer than a side route. How the dye spreads may hint at how the drug will act.

They sort past cases by whether the needle leaned inward or outward. The outward path gave far more wide dye spread toward the nerve exit. It also gave more pain relief two weeks later. In checks that held other factors fixed, needle path stayed tied to relief. Dye spread alone did not.
pmc-13208613:
People over sixty-five with moderate-to-severe psoriasis are often left out of drug trials, so Vanda Bondare-Ansberga and Aleksandra Grigorjeva reviewed treatment records at one center from 2019 to 2025. The study covers 38 patients on biologic drugs and asks how often therapy was switched, and why.

Fifteen patients, 39.5 percent, switched biologics, mostly because the drug had stopped working, not side effects. Switching came on average 325 days after starting the standard first-line drug. Patients with psoriatic arthritis switched less often than those without it, while overall illness burden showed no link to switching. Serious events such as infections and heart problems did occur in this older group. The authors conclude that biologic therapy was generally well tolerated, and that loss of effect, not other illness, drives most changes.
pmc-13209013:
Yuriy Vasil'ev and co-authors study the layered support tissue of the face, called the SMAS, where it reaches the forehead. Surgeons rely on this layer for face lifts, but its form in the forehead was unclear and terms for it clashed. Their 2026 study used tissue samples from body donors.

The team took full depth samples from five face and neck zones in 30 donors and stained them in several ways. Known SMAS types held up in cheek, jaw, and neck zones. On the forehead they found two new stacked forms, proposed as added types. One is marked by a spread of nerves and vessels. Counts of gaps and nerve depth back the split.
pmc-13210213:
Georgi Vasilev, Sonya Ivanova, and Ivan Milanov argue that multiple sclerosis should be understood as a spectrum rather than three split kinds, in a two thousand twenty-six survey. The classic labels, relapsing-remitting, second progressive, and primary progressive, still guide treatment choices.

Disability often builds up without relapses, a pattern named progression independent of relapse activity. The review weaves that concept along with smouldering-linked worsening and the brain's shrinking nerve reserve. Second progressive disease becomes simply clear built-up progression; primary progressive becomes progression visible early because reserve is low. The authors push for earlier spotting of progression and treatments aimed at its biology, not just relapses.
pmc-13210413:
Elda Villasenor-Tapia and three co-authors review new treatments in 2026 for a common liver disease tied to excess fat and metabolic problems. The disease can progress from fat buildup to inflammation, scarring, and in some cases liver cancer. Current care rests mostly on lifestyle change, with limited long term success.

The review covers several drug classes that improve metabolic measures and reduce liver fat, though their effect on scarring is still unclear. It also covers gene based therapies and tiny particle delivery systems that may target drugs more precisely. Most of these newer options are still in early testing. The authors call for stronger trials and shared standards before wide use.
pmc-13211013:
Alicja Wiora and Józef Wiora test cheap carbon dioxide sensors meant to fly on drones for air quality checks. Their 2026 study puts the sensors in a controlled chamber and grades them like measuring instruments. Drone surveys can reach places fixed stations cannot, but low-cost sensors bend under weather, and the team wanted hard numbers on how much.

One probe proved strongly swayed by temperature, shifting about seventeen parts per million per degree. Near freezing it reported absurdly low values far below the global background. Humidity and electromagnetic noise barely mattered, and readings matched whether taken in flight, after landing, or in the lab. The results tell drone teams which errors to correct and which to ignore.
pmc-13211313:
Reading a molecule's structure from its magnetic spectra is expert work, and a 2026 study by Chao Han automates it with vision transformers. The research article introduces NMRViT, which takes raw one- and two-dimensional NMR spectrum images directly, instead of hand-picked peak lists, and predicts the molecular structure end to end.

Training ran on a large simulated spectral library before testing on real experimental benchmarks. Moving from simulation to the laboratory left a clear performance gap, but fine-tuning on a handful of real spectra shrank it substantially in the authors' experiments. A final re-ranking step, scoring candidates against expected chemical shifts, lifted accuracy in both settings.
pmc-13211513:
Lama Alzamil charts measles in Saudi Arabia across a decade in a 2026 study. The country pairs high vaccine coverage with two complicating facts: vast pilgrimages that gather the world in one place, and a large expatriate workforce. COVID-19 shook routine immunization everywhere, and Alzamil asks how measles incidence, coverage, and burden shifted from 2015 to 2024.

Using World Health Organization data and the Saudi health ministry's yearly books, the study splits the decade into three eras: before the pandemic, the disruption years, and the rebound since. Cases are mapped by region, age, and nationality, and set against figures for the Gulf, the wider region, and the world. The result is a full picture of where measles pressed hardest and how coverage held or slipped, a base for planning the next catch-up campaigns.
pmc-13212613:
Yu Liu and colleagues describe in 2026 a light-based treatment for precancerous lesions affecting both the cervix and vagina at once. Surgery for such combined lesions can distort anatomy and affect sexual function, so an organ-sparing option would be valuable.

Eight women received an injected light-sensitive drug, followed days later by red laser light aimed at the lesions. Three to six months on, six women had complete responses after one session. The remaining two cleared after a second light session or heat treatments. With so few patients, the authors present the approach as feasible and worth larger study rather than proven.
pmc-13213713:
Yididia Desta Langena and co-authors compare in 2026 how well mothers in southern Ethiopia feed babies aged six to twenty-three months, contrasting a rural district with a nearby town. The first two years set growth trajectories, and poor weaning foods raise infection and death risks.

Interviews with 565 mothers found good complementary feeding in a quarter of urban families but only about an eighth of rural ones. A mother's knowledge predicted good practice in both settings. Food insecurity mattered rurally, while the child's age and postnatal care visits mattered in town. The authors urge nutrition teaching woven into routine mother and child health services, with rural outreach prioritised.
pmc-13213813:
How warm an office feels changes how people work and feel, but studies often track only one signal at a time. Puneet Tomar and nine co-authors release a dataset in 2026 that records many signals together. Twenty-four healthy adults each worked through a set nine-part office routine twice, once in a cooler room and once in a warmer room, under tight temperature control.

Brain waves, skin signals, and skin temperature were recorded alongside room conditions and surveys of how each phase felt. Webcam checks added context. The authors share the raw recordings so others can study comfort, focus, and recovery across activities and temperatures.
pmc-13214313:
Johannes Kornhuber and co-authors run a 2026 trial in Germany comparing two group therapies for depression against usual care. One programme helps patients identify what matters to them, schedule meaningful activities, and follow through, while the other pairs psychotherapy with indoor climbing.

One hundred twenty-eight adults were randomised across ten weekly two-hour sessions, then followed for a year. Both new therapies cut depression scores more than usual care right after treatment, with moderate effect sizes. The scheduling therapy also produced clearly higher remission rates than usual care. Response rates favoured both new options, adherence was good, and side effects were minimal, supporting group formats that widen access to treatment.
pmc-13214913:
Wan-Chun Su and co-authors check whether brain and behavior measures hold steady across posture shifts. Their 2026 paper uses light-based brain imaging during a dual task: keeping balance while holding back wrong answers. Eighteen healthy adults sat, stood, and stood heel-to-toe, with tasks of rising difficulty. Scans were repeated after a sit-to-stand bout.

At low loads, brain activity rose with task demand in frontal and sensor zones. At high loads, the pattern flipped. Behavior scores ranged from shaky to rock steady on repeat. Brain measures were less steady still after posture change. The authors read the load flip as shared mental resources running dry. They warn studies to log posture when reading such data.
pmc-13215413:
Xiuchuan He and colleagues published a 2026 meta-analysis on whether mindfulness delivered through virtual reality eases depression and anxiety. The authors pooled randomized trials to test the approach and to see which conditions make it work better.

Fifteen trials with 864 participants met the criteria, and the combined results showed clear symptom reductions. Effects were largest in older adults and in studies run in Eastern regions, and sessions of thirty minutes or less performed well. Both fully immersive and partly immersive formats helped. The authors present virtual reality mindfulness as a useful add-on treatment while calling for longer, stronger trials.
pmc-13215513:
Hasan Yalim Akin and colleagues published a 2026 genetics study of COVID-19 severity, testing whether two inherited immune systems interact. One involves KIR genes that guide natural killer cells; the other involves OAS gene variants inherited from Neanderthals.

The team genotyped 175 unvaccinated patients whose illness ranged from symptom-free to severe. People lacking both the protective KIR motif and the Neanderthal OAS variants were more likely to develop symptoms and severe disease, with the combined pattern classifying outcomes at roughly three-quarters accuracy. Age, male sex, and variants in two other genes added risk, while blood group A looked protective. The authors call for confirmation in larger, more varied cohorts.
pmc-13216113:
Owen Hibberd and co-authors present a 2026 observational study testing how well exhaled carbon dioxide readings stand in for blood levels in seriously injured patients before hospital. Air ambulance teams use the breath reading to guide ventilation, especially after head injury.

The team studied 53 adults who had an arterial line placed at the scene by a UK helicopter service between 2015 and 2023 and were flown to a major trauma centre. In four out of five patients the gap between blood and breath values exceeded the accepted range. The breath reading also placed over two-thirds of patients in the wrong carbon dioxide category. The authors conclude the breath measure is not a reliable substitute in this setting.
pmc-13216213:
Nuo Chen and co-authors present a 2026 imaging study pinpointing where radiation physically breaks mouse sperm. Radiation is known to cut sperm counts and movement, but the damaged structures had stayed blurry at the nanoscale.

The team combined four imaging methods, including synchrotron X-ray techniques that view sperm close to their natural state. After a single radiation dose, the clearest injury was fracture of the annulus. That ring joins the sperm's midpiece to its tail, and it was damaged together with the fibrous sheath that stiffens the tail. A sheath protein called AKAP4 dropped in step with the damage. The authors offer the platform as a general way to inspect nanoscale injury in complex cells.
pmc-13216613:
Arthur Neuberger and co-authors present a 2026 structural study of how spermine, a natural molecule present in every cell, plugs the calcium channel TRPV6. The channel feeds calcium into the body and is overactive in several cancers, so its natural brakes are of drug-design interest.

Cell experiments showed spermine blocking the channel in a voltage-dependent way. Cryo-electron microscopy then caught spermine sitting inside the open pore, stretched along its axis through the central cavity and selectivity filter. Mutations and simulations confirmed the main binding site in the filter and suggested spermine passes two further, temporary sites on its way in. The authors offer the stepwise blocking mechanism as a template for designing TRPV6 inhibitors.
pmc-13216713:
Julianna L. Barbaro and co-authors present a 2026 case report and literature review of a Wilms tumour growing outside the kidney, in the soft tissue beside a newborn's spine. Such extrarenal tumours are vanishingly rare and can only be identified under the microscope.

The mass was spotted on prenatal ultrasound at twenty weeks, beside the lower spine, while both kidneys looked normal. Removed days after birth, it showed the classic three-part Wilms pattern of blastemal, stromal, and primitive epithelial tissue. Counting their case, the authors find sixteen reports of spinal or paraspinal tumours of this kind. Surgery followed by chemotherapy is the usual approach, and they call for a standardized regimen and wider awareness of the diagnosis.
pmc-13217513:
Yuan Wang and co-authors lay out a long-term safety study of a silver clip used for permanent birth control. Their 2026 protocol notes that the clip method is common yet barely studied for body-wide effects. Ten hospitals will recruit women who had silver clip or silk tie sterilization, or who use condoms, and now need surgery for benign conditions.

Follow-up runs a full year after surgery, with visits at one day, one month, six months, and twelve. Blood tests track silver levels, inflammation signals, and clotting measures over time. Tissue findings and pelvic scarring from the surgery join the comparison. The authors hope the data will guide safety monitoring and future contraceptive advice for women and policymakers.
pmc-13217713:
Drug hunting needs predictions for many properties at once: will a molecule heal, harm, dissolve, or stick to its target? Vladislav Mun and Siamac Fazli build one model for the whole panel in a 2026 paper, fusing readers for molecule strings and protein strings into a single transformer. The shared brain serves more than six hundred eighty prediction tasks.

Across thirteen public benchmarks the model matched the best poison detectors and set new marks for physical property prediction, while staying competitive on drug-target strength. Sharing parts across tasks keeps it small and quick, and new tasks bolt on as fresh heads. The design replaces a shelf of single-purpose models.
pmc-13217913:
Laila I. Sakhnini and colleagues present a 2026 computational study on predicting when therapeutic antibodies will bind to things they should not. Such non-specific binding can undermine a drug candidate, so developers want an early warning from the antibody's amino acid sequence alone. The team tested two routes to that prediction.

One route used embeddings from protein language models, which capture sequence context. The other used a set of plain physical descriptors that humans can read directly. Models were trained on published human and mouse antibody data and checked against three public datasets. The heavy chain, especially its third hypervariable loop, carried most of the predictive signal, and the best model reached about 71 percent accuracy in cross-validation. The isoelectric point stood out among the physical descriptors, and combining both approaches made the scores more reliable for early screening.
pmc-13218113:
A large team led by Keyvan Razazi describes a rare, deadly kidney infection in intensive care patients. The infection rots kidney tissue and fills it with gas. The team gathered cases from forty-eight French intensive care units over twenty years: 109 adults in all. Most were women, most had diabetes, and three quarters were overweight. Nearly three quarters arrived in septic shock.

Care began with antibiotics or drainage in about half the cases. A share of patients had the kidney removed, early or after some days. The paper sets out the profiles, the care paths, and what kidney removal meant for outcome, in a disease where proof has been thin.
pmc-13219313:
The mitral valve, guarding the heart's left side, fails in millions of people, and its failure weaves together tissue change, inflammation, and inherited risk. Shilin Jin and co-authors review a decade of omics research on the disease in 2026. They sort findings by layer: genes, gene-control marks, gene activity, proteins, and small molecules, plus studies that merge the layers.

The review centers on mitral valve prolapse and its spongy, myxomatous form. Each layer has yielded candidate markers and hints at mechanism. The authors look ahead to combining layers into multi-omics pictures, hoping for sharper diagnosis and treatments aimed at the valve's biology rather than its symptoms alone.
pmc-13219813:
Xiaoqian Lan, Hongyan Zhuang, and Pengfei Li report a negative result on a prescribing workaround for antipsychotic side effects in a 2026 study. The antipsychotic amisulpride raises prolactin, a hormone whose excess can disrupt periods, fertility, and bone health. Clinicians add aripiprazole, a drug with an opposite grip on the dopamine system, hoping it will pull prolactin back down, but proof for amisulpride specifically was missing.

Reviewing records from a psychiatric hospital between 2022 and 2025, the team compared prolactin levels in the week before patients started add-on aripiprazole with levels a week after. The average change was small and insignificant, and splitting the patients by sex or diagnosis changed nothing. Removing any patient from the analysis, one at a time, never altered the conclusion, so no outlier was driving the result. Until evidence arrives, the authors advise caution about expecting this combination to rescue patients from prolactin elevation.
pmc-13219913:
Lin and co-authors validate a risk score meant to predict failure after keyhole surgery to stabilize a dislocating shoulder. The Pittsburgh Instability Tool weighs factors like loose joints, young age, near track bone lesions, and repeat episodes before surgery. Their 2026 study reviews 120 patients aged fourteen to forty treated at one center from 2021 to 2023, with or without an added filling procedure.

Failure meant the shoulder slipped again or needed another operation. Patients were split into low, moderate, high, and extreme risk bands by score. The study tests whether the band predicts short term failure, and whether the added procedure moves a patient into a safer band. The work aims to match surgical choices to each patient's measured risk.
pmc-13221113:
Jinghui Zhai and co-authors test a ginseng compound alongside cisplatin in a 2026 lung cancer study. Cisplatin works well against tumors, yet it harms kidneys and tumors often resist it. Ginsenoside Rg3, drawn from ginseng, has shown anticancer effects and possible protection for healthy tissue.

In cell and mouse experiments, the pairing killed more lung cancer cells and slowed tumor growth better than either agent alone. Rg3 also eased kidney injury by calming an inflammatory complex through the SIRT1 pathway, an effect reversed when SIRT1 was blocked. Transporter changes may explain both kidney protection and reduced drug resistance. The compound looks promising as a chemotherapy partner.
pmc-13221513:
Nisith Kumar and colleagues convene patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy to rank what matters in treatment, in a 2026 multinational advisory board study. The disease stiffens the heart as misfolded protein builds up, often ending in heart failure. Thirteen patients from five countries completed a pre-meeting survey, then discussed priorities together.

Tiredness and fatigue bothered participants most among side effects, while injection site pain bothered them least. Lowering death risk ranked as the top benefit, though quality of life and time for enjoyed activities mattered deeply too. Once-daily pills were the preferred format on average. Preferences varied between individuals, which the authors say trial designers and prescribers should respect.
pmc-13222013:
Chunhong Shi and co-authors interview family caregivers of people in hospital with HIV/AIDS in Hunan, China, in a 2026 interview study. Seventeen caregivers, aged twenty-two to seventy-four, spoke in depth between August 2024 and January 2025 at a hospital infectious disease ward. Family members carry most caregiving duties in China, yet their hospital experiences were little studied.

Three themes emerged. Caregivers described personal growth, stronger family bonds, and new resilience alongside the strain. They advocated for mental-health support, better HIV education, easier access, respectful care, and financial relief. Views on death mixed anticipatory grief with wishes for a dignified end. The authors recommend structured family-centered support.
pmc-13222213:
Nina Hadzimustafic, Tyler Safran, and Joshua Vorstenbosch comment on a bibliometric review of capsular contracture research, in a 2026 piece. Contracture, a tightening scar shell around breast implants, remains common and poorly understood. The reviewed analysis counted 2,065 English articles and mapped growth, leading countries, institutions, journals, and cited authors over the past decade.

Hot keywords included biofilm, contamination, dermal matrices, and implant placement, pointing at current theories for prevention. The commentators praise the map of collaboration gaps, yet note a sting: the highest-impact studies rest largely on low-level evidence. They call for randomized trials and systematic reviews to firm up guidance on reducing contracture.
pmc-13222513:
Miroslav Zashev and Nevrie Niyazi report two cases of Buschke–Lowenstein tumour, a giant wart-like growth around the anus, in a 2026 surgical report. The lesion links to human papillomavirus types 6 and 11 and grows aggressively in place despite benign cells. Both patients had large circumferential growths that had enlarged progressively.

Wide local excision removed the tumours, and bilateral V-Y advancement flaps closed the extensive defects. Tissue checks confirmed giant condyloma with no dysplasia or invasive cancer. Recovery was uneventful, with no early recurrence during follow-up. Complete excision with sound margins plus planned reconstruction is the authors' central message for these extensive lesions.
pmc-13222613:
Keyuan Fang and Xiaoxiao Ding write a 2026 letter about a study linking the Prognostic Nutritional Index with death risk and severity in sleep apnea. The index combines lymphocyte counts and serum albumin into one number. Fang and Ding value the work, yet warn that acute infections can distort both halves of the score in opposite directions depending on severity and timing.

Albumin also reflects inflammation more than nutrition, guidelines now caution, so infected participants could skew the index away from baseline status. The letter further flags competing risks: with far more non-cardiovascular than cardiovascular deaths during follow-up, standard survival models may misstate the cardiovascular link. Cleaner participant selection is their main request.
pmc-13222913:
Johan Gustafsson and co-authors improve digital patient models used to test nuclear medicine imaging accuracy, in a 2026 simulation study. Three body phantoms received tumors copied from real patient scans, placed at realistic sites, and set moving with breathing. Activity levels were drawn from patient distributions, and organs such as liver and spleen got uneven internal patterns.

Full models looked much more like real patients than standard spherical-lesion versions. Estimated tumor activity ran more negatively biased in the realistic models for both PET and SPECT imaging, showing that motion and background texture change the errors researchers must expect. Realistic phantoms, the authors conclude, give fairer tests of correction methods.
pmc-13223013:
Andrew Maust and co-authors test food safety in non alcoholic beer in a 2026 study. Removing alcohol also removes a key barrier that stops germ growth. The team asked whether acid level, fizz, and added preservatives could jointly keep five harmful bacteria in check.

They mixed the bacteria into a model beer under eighteen treatment blends and tracked counts for sixty days. Low acid proved the strongest single factor, and strong fizz curbed two of the bacteria. Hop acids added control of one bacteria group. Some blends cut counts below detection, while mild blends let germs grow. The results show that recipe choices decide whether alcohol free beer stays safe on the shelf.
pmc-13223513:
Ben Murphy and two co-authors report a young rugby player who tore the knee tendons of both legs in one play. Both-side tears of the patellar tendon are rare, most in sick or drug-weakened tendons. Their patient was a fit 33-year-old man with no such risks on his chart. A pop in both knees left him with pain and no leg lift on either side.

Hand checks found a gap on the right only, and swelling blurred the left read. Bedside sound scans backed tears on both sides, with a ward scan sealing the left call. The right tendon was sewn at once; the left followed once proof firmed. Both tendons looked worn at the cut, which points to slow wear from repeat small knocks. Braced rehab closed the tale.
pmc-13225513:
Chunxiu Tan and co-authors look for signs that predict renewed bleeding after a liver shunt procedure, in a study from 2026. The procedure, known by the short name TIPS, lowers pressure in liver veins for patients with severe liver scarring. It is used when veins in the food pipe bleed, a dangerous event.

The study followed just over two hundred patients treated at one center over three years. Renewed bleeding was split into early cases, within six weeks, and late cases, after two years. Early cases were few, and higher blood sugar before the procedure linked to lower early risk. Late bleeding was more common. Being male and having an infection before the procedure raised the late risk. The findings may help doctors grade risk around the procedure.
pmc-13226713:
Mohamed Zaki Khedr and colleagues investigate a 2026 geological survey of Egypt's black sands, beach deposits rich in heavy minerals along the Mediterranean coast and in southern Sinai. Samples from six sites underwent mineral separation, microscopy, chemical analysis, and, for Sinai, remote sensing. The goal was to trace where the sands came from and what they might be worth.

Coastal sands proved to be recycled sediments delivered mainly by the Nile and reworked by waves, while Sinai deposits were first-cycle material from local drainage and wind. Valuable heavy minerals averaged higher shares on the coast and included ilmenite, magnetite, zircon, and rutile. Rare-earth elements concentrated in the mineral monazite. Early reserve estimates favour the coast, though some Sinai pockets are locally richer.
pmc-13229113:
Tejas Athni and co-authors review twenty years of invasive fungal sinusitis in patients with blood cancers at a large United States hospital system. The infection races through the sinuses and kills often. Records from 2005 to 2024 found thirty-one proven cases, most in people with a fast-growing marrow cancer on strong chemotherapy.

One mold genus caused the most cases, with others close behind. Nearly all patients got a classic antifungal drug, and most had sinus surgery through the nose. Dead tissue and thickened lining were common sights on exam and scans. Still, about seven in ten patients died by the study's end, with typical survival of about a hundred days.
pmc-13230313:
Meltem Kaya and colleagues trial in 2026 expiratory muscle training, which strengthens the muscles used to breathe out, in children with asthma. Thirty stable children aged eight to eighteen joined the single-blind randomized trial. One group added daily breathing-out exercises to home chest physiotherapy for eight weeks, while the comparison group used almost no resistance.

Lung measures improved clearly only in the training group, including forced vital capacity and airflow in one second. Strength of breathing-out muscles also rose only there, while cough strength and walking distance improved in both groups with larger gains in the training group. Asthma control scores rose in both groups and rose more with training. The add-on looks safe and helpful alongside standard home care.
pmc-13231013:
Chengcheng Zhang and colleagues compare in 2026 industrial ways to dry cabbage while keeping quality and nutrition high. Hot air alone, microwave alone, and a combined method were tested at production scale. The combined treatment led on color, firmness, and how well the dried leaves soaked water back up.

Combined drying also kept more green pigment, amino acids, plant phenols, and antioxidant strength than single methods. Nearly one hundred scent compounds were found, and the combined method widened both their range and their total amount over plain hot air. Chemical profiling showed heat methods released more of certain plant compounds than freeze drying did. For factories, pairing microwave with hot air looks like a strong default choice.
pmc-13231413:
Moždiak and four co-authors make a fresh set of iridium compounds and test what they can do in this twenty twenty-six paper. The compounds pair the rare metal with a ring-shaped partner that holds an oxygen arm. Heat can strip a small group off that arm and change the whole build.

Inside, the stripped forms serve as starts for larger builds that join iridium with zinc and with ruthenium too. The stripped forms can also snap a class of carbon bonds and swap in new oxygen-linked groups. A side swap at the metal bond showed up as well and was traced in depth. The work maps new routes to mixed-metal builds.
pmc-13232013:
Ugonna Mbaekwe and co-authors review in 2026 the two edged role of iron control in the repair of the lung's air sac lining. The oxygen rich lung needs tight iron balance, yet this side of lung health draws little attention. Loss of that balance has been tied to many sudden and long term lung diseases in recent years.

The review sets out how the air sac lining takes in, stores, and moves iron, and how slips in that system stall repair after injury. It then weighs new treatments that aim to restore balance, boost repair, and slow disease. Readers get a full account of iron as both a needed nutrient and a source of damage in the lung.
pmc-13232613:
Roddy M Grieves and colleagues ask in 2026 whether the brain maps of rats hug the ground surface when land rises and falls. Place cells in the hippocampus fire at set spots and anchor the mental map of a space. Rats foraged over flat and ridged floors while the team recorded those cells.

Firing zones stretched along the terrain contours, like paint following the hills rather than the open air above them. That stretching ran against the direction the rats preferred to move, which rules out a simple movement echo. A third of the cells repeated their firing zone on every ridge in the set. A boundary-based model reproduced the pattern, tying map shape to the lay of the land.
pmc-13233013:
Yongbo Yang and colleagues published a 2026 prospective cohort study on alcohol drinking and esophageal cancer risk across age groups in China. The country carries more than 40 percent of the world's new cases of this cancer. Data came from the China Kadoorie Biobank, which followed 489,664 adults aged 30 to 79 enrolled between 2004 and 2008.

Cancer rates rose with drinking frequency in every age group under 70. The relative risk tied to weekly drinking was strongest in the youngest group and eased steadily with age, even while absolute rates climbed sharply into the early fifties. Adjusted hazard ratios for weekly drinkers fell from just over four in the youngest band to about one and a half in the early seventies. The pattern points to age shaping how alcohol affects risk.
pmc-13233513:
Mengna Xu and colleagues published a 2026 modeling study mapping where the invasive plant Nicotiana glauca could spread. Tree tobacco harms farms and wild ecosystems, so early warning maps help managers act before it establishes. The team fed known locations and climate variables into the MaxEnt model and projected suitable areas under past climate and future scenarios for 2061 to 2080.

Four climate measures mattered most, including the hottest month's temperature and the daily temperature range. Suitable territory already spans large parts of the Americas, Africa, Europe, Asia, and Oceania, with the highest threat in southern regions. Future scenarios enlarged the total threatened area and shifted its center. The authors offer the maps as a planning reference for prevention programs.
pmc-13234213:
Sanches, Cucci, and de Nadai present a case report, published in 2026, on an odd complication of a hormone-releasing contraceptive device. The device sits inside the womb and prevents pregnancy for years. Its removal threads should hang through the neck of the womb, ready for a doctor to grasp. A 42-year-old woman came in for a routine check with no symptoms. The threads were seen poking through the front wall of the cervix instead.

A three-dimensional ultrasound scan showed the device itself sat correctly inside the womb. Only the threads had taken a wrong path through the tissue. Under local numbing and scan guidance, doctors cut the exposed thread segment and removed the device with forceps. The patient had no problems afterward. The case shows that misplaced threads do not always mean a misplaced device. A scan check can spare the patient needless alarm and surgery.
pmc-13234613:
Levothyroxine is the standard hormone replacement for an underactive thyroid, but some patients still feel unwell on it, and use of a second hormone, liothyronine, has been growing. Fredric Hedberg and co-authors used Swedish national registers to ask whether starting liothyronine is linked to later psychiatric illness. They followed more than one hundred eighty thousand adults with autoimmune hypothyroidism who had no earlier psychiatric problems. They compared those who added the second hormone with those who stayed on the standard drug alone.

About three percent of the cohort started liothyronine during follow up. Those patients faced a notably higher risk of new psychiatric problems overall, with similar rises for mood and anxiety conditions and for psychotic illness. The authors are careful about cause: the pattern could reflect an effect of the drug, or it could mean that patients who seek the extra treatment were already more vulnerable.
pmc-13234713:
Wen Hu and a large team reported in 2026 on an engineered antibody aimed at many filoviruses, the group that includes Ebola and Marburg viruses. These viruses kill a high share of infected people, and outbreaks are hard to predict. The antibody carries a fused hormone-like piece meant to help it reach a hidden viral target inside cells. A related body receptor, though, interfered with that strategy.

Changing one building block in the fused piece, at position twenty-seven, reduced the unwanted receptor engagement. That single change strengthened virus neutralization across the filovirus family in their tests. The work targets a conserved site that the virus needs for entering cells through an internal receptor. Broad protection matters because the next outbreak species cannot be known in advance. The authors present the tuned antibody as a candidate for wider filovirus therapy.
pmc-13234813:
Chirag Lodha and Eric Basile report severe failure of both heart ventricles in a thirty-three-year-old man. Their 2026 case report follows a patient with known weak heart muscle and high blood pressure who arrived with worsening breathlessness and chest pain.

Standard ultrasound suggested his pumping fraction matched earlier tests, but cardiac MRI showed far worse function in both ventricles. Multiple specialist teams optimised his guideline-directed drug therapy during the week-long stay, adjusting several medicines and adding new ones. A heart catheter procedure guided management, and a wearable defibrillator bridged him toward an implanted device. Severe sleep apnoea was found and treated with airway pressure. He went home stable, with transplant evaluation planned.
pmc-13235213:
Shiyu Zhuo and seven co-authors present a 2026 study pinning down the gene behind a wheat line's strong mildew resistance. Powdery mildew is a major wheat disease, and breeders need resistance genes with markers they can track. The line YZ16 resisted most tested strains of the fungus as a seedling and stayed resistant as an adult plant in the field. Crosses showed a single dominant gene was responsible.

Gene-hunting by pooled sequencing placed the gene at the tip of chromosome 2A. Fine mapping showed it travels perfectly with a marker for the known resistance gene Pm4. Sequencing proved the protein matches known Pm4 variants, so YZ16 carries that gene in a new source line. Two splice forms of the gene shifted after infection. Across two seasons the line's yield traits held up. The authors offer YZ16 as a donor for breeding, trackable by the marker.
pmc-13236513:
Yanghong Ou, Lili Wang, Hongguang Qu, and Yingmei Jia reported in 2026 two different tumours growing side by side in one adrenal gland. A 49-year-old woman had endured three years of intermittent limb weakness before imaging found the mass. Scans showed a well-defined right adrenal lump with two visibly distinct components. Detailed reconstruction placed a cortical adenoma in the outer portion and a blood-vessel tumour in the inner portion.

Each component displayed its own characteristic pattern on computed tomography and magnetic resonance images. Pathology confirmed the two tumours met at a sharp border marked by a fibrous band, without mixing. Collision tumours of the adrenal are rare and can mislead staging when one part is mistaken for spread. Recognizing the separate imaging signatures can guide correct management before surgery. The authors advise considering a collision tumour whenever one part of a lesion looks atypical.
pmc-13236613:
Dustin Sherriff and co-authors validated in 2026 a questionnaire that maps what adults value in life, including how sleep fits among those values. More than four hundred fifty United States adults completed the new inventory online alongside an established sleep valuation measure. Statistical modelling tested the structure of the questionnaire and its links to demographics and sleep attitudes. Sleep value remains little studied inside wider value systems, the authors note.

Five value domains emerged, covering health, fundamental human values, status, accomplishment, and community. Reliability was high for every domain in the sample tested. Sleep sat inside the health domain alongside mental and physical health at its core. Older respondents valued health and fundamental values more strongly than younger respondents did. People who appreciated sleep most also rated the health domain highest among the profiles.
pmc-13236913:
Xuefang Liu and co-authors reported in 2026 a child with West syndrome, a severe infant epilepsy, whose cause proved to be a new variant in the ARFGEF2 gene. The gene guides brain cell movement before birth, and faults in it cause clusters of misplaced gray matter plus a small head. Only slightly more than 20 such cases were known worldwide.

Exome sequencing found the child carried two copies of a splice-site change never reported before. A laboratory minigene test confirmed the change makes the gene skip a whole segment, producing a shortened, broken protein. The work adds one more entry to the gene's known fault list. It also gives families and doctors firmer ground for diagnosis and counseling.
pmc-13237013: Shuya Li and team issued a correction in 2026 to their Scientific Reports study comparing natural and artificial musk. The notice is a correction only, with no new study content. It rewrites one abstract sentence so artificial musk is credited with anti-inflammatory activity. It also swaps a named supplier for a plain description and deletes a sentence about a preservative in the artificial product. The original article has been corrected.
pmc-13237113:
Gmelin and colleagues run a genome-wide study of short repeating DNA stretches in Alzheimer's disease. Most such studies scan single letter changes and skip these repeats, called short tandem repeats, though repeats can switch genes on or off. The team tested repeats across the genomes of about a third of a million people in the UK Biobank.

Their group included a few thousand Alzheimer's cases, many more people classed by family history as likely cases, and a large control group. Repeats were read both from gene-chip guesses and from full genome sequencing. Hits from this overlooked layer of DNA could reveal fresh mechanisms behind a disease that still lacks a clear genetic story.
pmc-13239413:
Leanne Burton and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review about peer support after miscarriage, meaning help from people who have lived through the same loss. Guidelines say little about protecting parents' mental health after such a loss, so services need evidence on what helps support reach families.

The reviewers searched nine databases plus grey literature in June 2025 and gathered nine qualitative or mixed studies. Shared recognition emerged as a strong draw, since peers validate grief that others may dismiss. Group dynamics such as modelling coping and guiding mourning helped people take part. Exclusion from ordinary support, timing, and access shaped whether programmes actually got used.
pmc-13239713:
Le Chen and colleagues sequence the complete chloroplast genome of a high mountain wetland plant in a 2026 genomics paper. Caltha scaposa grows in the Himalayas and Hengduan Mountains, and its genetic blueprint helps settle where the species sits within its plant family.

The circular genome follows the typical four-part structure and carries 132 genes, including eighty-seven that code for proteins. Comparing it with nine relatives showed shifting boundaries in the repeated regions, with this species holding the shortest repeats. Family tree analysis placed the plant as sister to a group containing Anemone and Pulsatilla. Highly variable spacer regions offer markers for future population studies.
pmc-13240013:
Fang-Tzu Chang, Yi-Ying Chen, and Fu-Yu Lin link raised pressure inside the skull to a blood disorder in a 2026 case report. Pseudotumor cerebri syndrome mimics a brain tumour through high pressure and swollen optic discs, yet scans show no mass, so clinicians hunt for secondary causes that targeted treatment can fix.

Their patient also had essential thrombocythemia, a marrow disorder that keeps platelet counts high and raises clotting risk. Symptoms eased notably once antiplatelet and platelet-lowering therapy began, suggesting the blood disorder helped drive the pressure problem. The authors propose this association deserves recognition when pressure cases are worked up.
pmc-13240113:
Kamrul-Hasan and co-authors weigh new gut-hormone drugs for weight loss in adults without diabetes, in work published in 2026. The drugs copy amylin, a hormone that helps curb hunger. The team pooled six trials with more than four thousand adults and ranked each drug and dose against dummy care and older drugs.

High doses of amycretin cut body weight the most, by near a quarter on average. Two other new drugs came next, and both beat two older standard drugs. Gut side effects, such as nausea and vomiting, were more common at high doses. The authors call the proof thin and early, and they ask for larger trials.
pmc-13240213:
Varshini Krishnamoorthy and colleagues turn wheat bran proteins into vegan mayonnaise in a 2026 food study. Mayonnaise normally relies on egg yolk to hold oil and water together, and plant proteins from milling waste offer a sustainable stand-in for shoppers avoiding eggs.

The team separated bran protein into albumin, globulin, and glutelin fractions and built an emulsion with each. The albumin version matched the egg control on acidity and stability, and it even resisted flow more strongly at rest. All vegan versions flowed with the same shear-thinning pattern as real mayonnaise, though their colour ran brownish. Thickness behaviour fitted a standard flow model well.
pmc-13240813:
Sahaana Rajagopalan, Brian Dulmovits, Matthew Devine, and Christopher Thom map high platelet counts in hospitalized infants in this 2026 paper. Very high counts can trigger costly tests and blood thinners, yet their causes in newborns were poorly charted. The team studied over twenty thousand infants in two intensive care units.

About three percent of the infants had high platelet counts, and eight percent of preterm infants did. Extreme counts were rare, and far lower than at a comparison unit. High counts tracked with signs of inflammation and with relative anemia, but not with clots or bleeding. Low vitamin D also tracked with higher counts, while thyroid and liver measures did not. The authors say the pattern should calm responses to most cases.
pmc-13241013:
Alejandro Feito and co-authors publish a 2026 simulation study on making PARP inhibitor drugs more selective. These cancer drugs exploit faulty DNA repair in tumors. Trouble comes because most of them also hit a close relative protein, causing blood-related side effects.

The researchers compared four drugs, two selective for PARP1 and two not, using detailed molecular simulations. Their calculations closely matched lab measures of binding preference. Contact mapping showed that networks of tyrosine residues and charged interactions hold the drugs in place together, not single contacts alone. Trimming the pocket piece by piece cut binding sharply. The results give drug designers a map for building safer, more targeted inhibitors.
pmc-13241413:
Ng's team at Flinders University compared telehealth use between Australians with and without cancer. National Patient Experience Surveys from 2022 to 2024 supplied the data. Respondents numbered over two thousand with cancer and 45 thousand without. Logistic models mapped who used telehealth and what followed.

Thirty-eight percent of cancer respondents had used telehealth, against 26 percent of others. Mental health conditions raised use in both groups, while being uninsured or less educated lowered it. Cancer patients using telehealth reported the poorest health and most hospital contact, reflecting greater need. Over ninety percent of users rated the service positively.
pmc-13241513:
Elkhoriby and colleagues at Mansoura University fed plant additives to two strains of Japanese quail and tracked growth and gene activity. Three hundred young female quails entered the trial, split evenly between brown and white strains. Each strain received a plain control diet or drinking water dosed with frankincense or lemon balm extract. The feeding period lasted twenty-eight days.

Responses depended strongly on strain, a clear interaction between genetics and treatment. Frankincense at both tested levels suited the brown strain best. For white quails, the lower frankincense level and the stronger lemon balm dose worked best. Treated birds gained weight more efficiently and switched on growth and antioxidant genes while quieting a muscle-limiting gene.
pmc-13241713:
Jiaxin Yang and co-authors describe a 2026 protocol for testing salt and alkali tolerance in young maize plants. Salty and alkaline soils limit maize output worldwide, and the two stresses injure plants differently. Their assay separates the two while keeping conditions steady.

Seeds germinate in sand beds dosed with prepared stress solutions, given separately or combined. The stable sand setup keeps moisture and stress levels even without daily watering. Researchers then measure several seedling traits and rank varieties with a combined scoring method. The protocol supports large, repeatable screening of maize collections at an early growth stage. Breeders can use it to find lines suited to damaged soils.
pmc-13242113:
Neven and colleagues in Antwerp correct their systematic review of recessive congenital methemoglobinemia, a rare inherited blood disorder. The review catalogued reported cases and their CYB5R3 gene variants. Two production errors slipped into the printed version. An author's name was also printed incorrectly.

Tables 2 and 3 had been switched, sending readers to the wrong tables from three spots. Table 2 covers diagnostic tests and therapy; Table 3 lists the unique gene variants. The garbled byline is fixed to Marije Meuwissen. Treatment details in the review stand: most documented patients got vitamin C, some with methylene blue. The original article has been updated accordingly.
pmc-13242513:
Mona Hegazy and co-authors tested a diabetes drug as a partner for the standard treatment of schistosomiasis in mice. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. Praziquantel kills the Schistosoma mansoni worms, but liver damage from the infection often persists, so helpers are needed. Infected mice received dapagliflozin alone or combined with praziquantel, and the team counted worms and eggs and examined liver tissue under the microscope.

The combination clearly outperformed the untreated course of infection. Worm burden and liver egg load fell, more of the remaining eggs were mature or dead, and the granulomas that scar the liver grew fewer and smaller. Protective liver chemicals rose, and a marker of programmed cell death increased as well. Used alone, dapagliflozin also showed benefit, though the pairing looked strongest. The authors propose it as a convenient add-on that targets inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell death together.
pmc-13242813:
Li Chen and co-authors present a 2026 study from an Acute Care for Elders unit, testing what best predicts short-term recovery of daily function in older adults in hospital. Standard geriatric assessment leans on a cumulative illness count. The authors argue the main acute diagnosis better captures the stress of the current illness.

Just over two hundred patients aged sixty-five and above were followed from admission to discharge. Models using the principal diagnosis explained recovery better than the comorbidity count model. Sorting measures also improved when it entered. Certain illness groups, including endocrine and respiratory diseases, predicted recovery strongly, while the illness index did not. The authors recommend adding the main diagnosis into routine geriatric assessment.
pmc-13243013:
Kai Xia and co-authors present a 2026 re-evaluation of the lying-down test for a positional vertigo type arising from the horizontal ear canal. The standard roll test can be uncomfortable and its eye movement patterns vary. Lying flat offers a simpler, gentler check, but its reported accuracy has been inconsistent.

Records covered just over two hundred confirmed cases, all later cured by repositioning treatment. The test was positive in about three fifths of patients, and when positive it named the correct side almost always. Positive patients needed fewer diagnostic steps. Stronger and faster eye responses on the first roll marked the positive group. Older age independently predicted a positive test in the loose-particle subtype. The authors recommend routine use beside the standard test.
pmc-13244513:
Yue Xi and colleagues built a prediction model for metabolic syndrome in women around menopause, centered on a simple body shape measure. Their study appeared in Annals of Medicine in 2026. The body roundness index, computed from height and waist, estimates visceral fat better than weight alone. Models were trained on United States survey data from 2007 to 2020, checked in a Chinese hospital cohort, and extended with a ten-year follow-up.

A neural network won the cross-sectional contest, scoring about 0.85 on internal testing and 0.88 externally, with sound calibration. Importance ranking put body roundness at the very top of sixteen predictors, ahead of liver enzymes and blood cell measures. Adding how roundness and lab values drift over years sharpened the long-term forecasts further. The authors offer the tool for screening in clinics where a tape measure is always available. Catching the syndrome early is the prize.
pmc-13245513:
Jeff J McIntyre, Gina Bartes, and Raquel Peck write from the patient side of chronic liver disease in a 2026 commentary. People with liver disease move through scattered entry points, from primary care to emergency rooms to specialty clinics. Too often no clear next step or steady coordination follows them.

Effective tools already exist: hepatitis C can be cured, alcohol harm can be cut by proven policies, and fatty liver disease can be caught early. Outcomes still lag because systems stay split across liver, hormone, heart, and addiction services. The authors argue that patient voice must shape design, not decorate it. Joined-up care, they say, would close the gap between what is possible and what happens.
pmc-13246613:
Yongxiu Liu and co-authors weigh vitamin D as an add-on for asthma in a 2026 umbrella review. Vitamin D helps steer immunity and airway defense, so it might ease asthma. Single reviews disagreed, so the team graded the reviews themselves.

Twenty-one systematic reviews and meta-analyses met the rules, though they reused many of the same trials. Vitamin D went with fewer asthma attacks across the pool. Gains in daily control, lung function, and inflammation markers were weak or mixed. No rise in side effects appeared. Much of the proof rated low in certainty, so the authors urge care and better-targeted trials.
pmc-13246713:
Turgut Karaköse and co-authors pool hundreds of studies on emotional intelligence, digital addiction, and student mental health in 2026. Students lean on digital tools heavily, and overuse can harm mental health. Emotional skill and resilience may buffer that harm.

The team joined correlations from 257 studies in one structural model. Emotional intelligence linked to mental health both directly and through two middle paths. Digital addiction carried one path toward worse health, while resilience carried another toward better health. Rival models were also tested to check the fit. The joined picture gives universities clearer levers: grow emotional skill and resilience while curbing digital overuse.
pmc-13247313:
Yaikhan and co-authors analyzed the genomes of a notorious hospital pathogen at global scale in this 2026 Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal study. Acinetobacter baumannii resists many antibiotics, and its resistance genes often travel on mobile DNA such as plasmids and insertion sequences. The team assembled ten and a half thousand quality genomes and asked whether resistance load tracks the mobile element load within each bacterial lineage.

A few lineages dominated the collection. Genome-wide, resistance burden correlated only modestly with insertion-sequence counts and plasmid variety, and a stricter count of genuinely acquired resistance told a similar story. Mobile-element features differed sharply between lineages, while virulence gene profiles stayed comparatively uniform. The authors argue resistance in this pathogen must be understood lineage by lineage, not as one global pattern.
pmc-13247713:
Daniele Pinton and co-authors share a fine-grain data set on a dammed Florida lake in a 2026 paper. The lake, fed by farm runoff and cut off from full tides, piles up dead plant matter. A robot boat ran four survey days in spring 2023 with sound gear for depth and a probe for water health.

Thousands of points map depth and bed height along the lake's ten kilometres. The probe logged warmth, salt, oxygen, sourness, cloud, and green pigment at each pass. Clean maps come with the set. The data can tune flow models and guide gate use against overgrowth.
pmc-13247813:
Fernando Pereira and five co-authors report a striking pancreatic cancer case from 2026. A woman of seventy-two had a tumor in the head of her pancreas that surgeons could not remove, a stage with grim odds. Alongside standard chemotherapy, she received an implant of radioactive phosphorus particles that deliver radiation from inside the tumor while sparing nearby tissue.

Her tumor first shrank partly on chemotherapy, then grew during a justified pause, and steadied after the particles were placed at the end of her fourth cycle. No harm from the device or procedure appeared. Months later the surgical team judged removal possible, and a major operation cleared the tumor. Fifty months after diagnosis, and forty-two after surgery, she remains alive with no sign of disease. The authors offer the case as a sign the implant can help convert hopeless tumors into operable ones.
pmc-13247913:
Havers, Fazel, and Smuk mapped how childhood maltreatment and teenage emotional problems intersect across social positions in England, in this 2026 Epidemiology and Psychiatric Sciences study. Average group comparisons hide combined disadvantage. So the team used a multilevel intersectional method on the OxWell 2023 survey. Nearly twenty thousand students aged eleven to sixteen were sorted into one hundred eighty strata. The strata combined gender, ethnicity, poverty, school year, and school deprivation.

Maltreatment's damage was pervasive yet uneven across those strata. Most inequality in emotional problems reflected simply additive social patterning, each disadvantage stacking. But non-additive intersectional effects appeared too, and they were stronger among maltreated adolescents. The authors argue for trauma-informed, equity-focused policy that looks at combinations of disadvantage. Teenagers carrying several disadvantages at once bear distinctive, not merely summed, psychological costs.
pmc-13248113:
Cezar and colleagues built a scoring system for pig diseases in the United States, reported in 2026. Veterinary labs confirm many infections in tissue samples, yet no single ranking showed which causes were most active. The team combined years of records from the Iowa State University diagnostic laboratory into one index.

They analyzed nearly sixty thousand tissue cases covering eighty-one causes, from bacteria and viruses to parasites. The index stayed stable across years, with PRRS virus and Streptococcus suis scoring highest most often. Two less familiar viruses rose over time. The authors offer the index, shown on an interactive dashboard, as a planning tool for disease control.
pmc-13248313:
Carl Ekstrand and co-authors compare two antibiotic pairings in dogs in a 2026 pharmacology study. Both pair trimethoprim with a sulfa drug, yet one uses sulfadiazine and the other sulfamethoxazole. The classic dose ratio was set for human blood levels, which may not suit dogs.

Beagles got each pairing by vein and by mouth in a crossover plan, plus trimethoprim alone once. Absorption by mouth ran high for all three drugs. Trimethoprim cleared far faster than either sulfa partner, and the sulfa drugs lingered at differing lengths. Binding to blood proteins also differed by drug. Free drug ratios in blood matched the target only briefly.
pmc-13248713: Alejandro Cruz-Soto and co-authors report the draft genome of a salt-loving bacterium in work from 2026. The strain of Virgibacillus salarius was isolated from water at the San Juan Hypersaline Lagoon in Chihuahua, Mexico. The species draws interest for enzymes that work in salty conditions. The paper presents the draft whole-genome sequence and its annotation.
pmc-13249113:
Roh, Yoon, and Oh tested a sleep chatbot built around questions rather than instructions, reported in 2026. Digital therapy for insomnia teaches proven habits, yet users often drop out because the programs lecture instead of listening. Their SleepPathfinder chatbot asks Socratic questions, then lets users decide their own next step, in a four-stage conversation.

A one-session pilot with forty-five users rated the system usable and credible. In a five-day comparison with thirty users, the questioning style softened how threatening users found their sleep problems and nudged feelings of choice upward. Deeper personal storytelling, not the sheer number of questions, tracked with changed thinking. The authors propose the layer as a companion to standard digital therapy.
pmc-13249713:
Alperen Aksakal and colleagues report a 2026 lung study of young smokers who feel perfectly healthy. Standard breathing tests can look normal early in smoking, even while the smallest airways are already changing, so the team used a gentler sound-wave test that is more sensitive to those airways.

University students who smoked were compared with never-smokers before and after a six-minute walk test. Both groups had similar standard test results, but smokers showed higher airway resistance and stiffer small airways. Smokers also walked less far and had lower oxygen levels in their leg muscles. The authors say the sound-wave test could flag early smoking harm sooner.
pmc-13250213:
Tuyisenge and colleagues reflect on a six-year partnership that worked to improve care for mothers and newborns in Rwanda. Their 2026 BMJ Paediatrics Open paper describes work by British and Rwandan pediatric bodies with UNICEF and Rwanda's health ministry. From 2017 to 2023, the program ran across many hospitals and selected health centers.

The authors report measurable gains in care quality and patient outcomes over the program years. Even so, preventable newborn deaths persisted, which they link to deeper system limits and community-level health factors. They argue that the numbers are only part of the program's value. Working side by side for years also revealed the structural reasons good clinical steps sometimes fail to become reliable care.
pmc-13250613:
Zhongzheng Zhang and three colleagues present a 2026 revision of Iris series Tenuifoliae, a group of irises spread across Central and East Asia. About ten species were recognized, but their boundaries and relationships stayed unclear from appearance alone. The team combined full chloroplast genome sequences with plant morphology to settle the group's structure.

Their analysis split the series into three well-supported branches and confirmed where the group sits inside the wider iris genus. One branch is marked by a flipped segment in a specific region of its chloroplast genome, a rare structural clue. The authors also name three species new to science, all collected in central-western China. The work gives growers and conservationists a firmer map of a group adapted to dry country.
pmc-13252313:
Ruchi Vashisht, Umesh Kumar, Ashish Kumar Kakkar, and three colleagues test chilled irrigation for root canal pain in this two thousand twenty-six randomized, double-blinded trial. Pain after root canal treatment remains a key concern. The trial enrolled one hundred eight patients with painful apical periodontitis in molar teeth, all treated in a single visit. Four irrigation groups compared room-heat against chilled sodium hypochlorite, and room-heat against chilled neem extract, a plant choice.

Pain was scored on a visual scale at twenty-four hours, forty-eight hours, and seven days. Chilled irrigants produced clearly lower pain at the first two time points than their room-heat matches. Neem extract performed about as well as chilled sodium hypochlorite. The authors conclude chilled neem extract is a biocompatible irrigant for cutting pain after treatment, pairing cooling with a natural product patients may prefer over bleach.
pmc-13253113:
Thierry Landre and co-authors (2026) pool real-world evidence on a first treatment choice in advanced lung cancer. For metastatic non-small cell lung cancer with high PD-L1, at least fifty percent, two strategies open the fight. One is an immune checkpoint drug alone. The other adds chemotherapy to the same class of drug. Trials suggested similar overall survival, but trial patients are selected; routine clinics treat older, sicker, more varied people. The authors gathered retrospective studies that compared the two strategies in such real populations.

Following standard guidelines, they combined overall survival as the main outcome. Progression-free survival and response rates came alongside. The question is practical: if survival ties, the gentler single-drug route spares patients chemo's toxicity, unless subgroups do better with both. Real-world pooling cannot replace a trial, but it can show whether trial results survive contact with ordinary oncology practice.
pmc-13253213:
Trichinella worms coil into muscle from undercooked meat, and once there they are hard to kill with current drugs. Xiaoyan Yu and co-authors screen thirty plant extracts for a better weapon in a 2026 study. An ethanol extract of the pearly everlasting plant won the screen outright.

At a modest dose the extract killed every muscle larva in the dish within seventy-two hours, in clear dose-dependent fashion. In infected mice it cut the larval burden by up to about sixty percent and softened the muscle damage and inflammation. Chemical profiling found organic acids and flavonoids at the top of the ingredient list. Deeper tests pointed to wrecked worm mitochondria as the mechanism, with host tissue protected at the same time.
pmc-13253713:

pmc-13254113:

pmc-13254813:
Abrham Tesfaye Habteyes and co-authors gather Ethiopia's scattered evidence on a rare group of pregnancy growth disorders, in this 2026 review. These growths burden mothers, yet national numbers were undefined. Local studies sat apart in journals and records.

pmc-13255213:

pmc-13255713:

pmc-13256313:

pmc-13256613:

pmc-13256813:

pmc-13257913:

pmc-13258013:

pmc-13258713:

pmc-13260013:

pmc-13260213:

pmc-13260713:
Maria Margarida Teixeira and colleagues charted in 2026 the real-world cost in Portugal of treating locally advanced head and neck cancer. pmc-13260813:

pmc-13261713:

pmc-13262613:

pmc-13262713:

pmc-13263013:

pmc-13263213:

pmc-13263613:

pmc-13263713:

pmc-13270413:

pmc-13270913:

pmc-13272013:

pmc-13272213:

pmc-13272913:

pmc-13273013:

pmc-13273213:

pmc-13274513:

pmc-13274913:
Nadine Domnik and colleagues present a 2026 journal article on building a phone app that shows rehabilitation patients their own health data in plain form. Rehab clinics collect many test results that rarely reach patients in an understandable way. pmc-13275513:

Better precision, they argue, tells managers where monitoring pays off.
pmc-13275613:
Agata Burzawa, Katarzyna Potera, and Aleksandra Walczyńska present a 2026 journal article testing whether diet changes how tiny animals shrink as temperatures rise. pmc-13276313:
Kai Li and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on cleaning cadmium from rice paddy soil with charred rice husks. The oxidant-treated char held the most acid groups and trapped cadmium best at low to moderate pollution. The alkali-treated char, strongly alkaline, stabilized soil best under severe pollution. Both also shifted soil humus, the dark organic matter tied to fertility. The authors map which char suits which contamination level.
pmc-13276413:

Patients with both fare worse, but how the species affect each other was unclear.

The authors say the species occupy separate niches yet still influence each other.
pmc-13276513:

pmc-13276713:
Szymon Andrusiów and colleagues examine gut and spinal fluid microbes in a nerve disease called CIDP, in a 2026 study. Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy damages the insulation around nerves through immune attack. Its triggers are unknown and no confirmed biomarker exists.

pmc-13276813:
Yueying Zhang and colleagues wrote a 2026 study linking plant-based diets to throat tissue microbes and disease in China. They studied 236 people having upper gut screening in Linzhou, an area with high rates of esophageal cancer, meaning cancer of the food pipe. Food surveys sorted diets by how healthful the plant foods were.

Healthful plant diets were tied to less severe esophageal disease, while unhealthful plant diets were tied to worse disease. Swabs from the throat lining showed different microbe patterns for each diet type. Adding diet and microbe data improved risk grouping a little beyond basic factors. The authors treat the link as a lead for screening, not proof that diet caused the changes.
pmc-13277113:
Chon-Kit Chou and colleagues review immune receptors that control regulatory T cells in a 2026 article. Regulatory T cells can calm both, yet growing stable batches for therapy is difficult.

The review walks through eight members of the TNF receptor superfamily found on these cells. Switching on TNFR2 or DR3 may expand the cells while sparing the graft's anti-leukaemia power. pmc-13277213:

Lactate and the SOFA organ score were the most reliable guides overall. Lactate best predicted death within one month, and SOFA also predicted ward and intensive care admission. pmc-13277413:
Yong Soo Jang leads the panel behind part three of the 2025 Korean resuscitation guidelines, published in 2026. The section sets adult basic life support steps for lay rescuers and professionals alike. Early action before hospital care largely decides whether a collapsed person survives.

Trained rescuers willing to give breaths should use standard CPR with ventilations included. Untrained or unwilling rescuers should give compression-only CPR instead. pmc-13277613:
Seong-Hyeon Cho leads a 2026 study of augmented reality glasses that help people who cannot tell some colors apart. Color vision deficiency, often red-green confusion, has no cure. Tests confirmed selective light coupling, and demonstrations placed overlays on target objects only. Wearable, targeted help of this kind proved feasible in principle.
pmc-13277713:
Isaac Zablah leads a 2026 letter responding to a review of large language models in health care. The letter praises the review's coverage of clinical uses and ethics, but says computing performance needs more attention, above all in low-resource settings.

Top models also need large amounts of graphics memory that many hospitals, especially in poorer countries, lack. Serving hundreds of users at once adds further strain. They urge work on shrinking and trimming models so they can run on local devices.
pmc-13278813:
Yan Zhou leads a 2026 modeling study of climate change and hydropower effects on endangered plateau fishes in the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau region of China. pmc-13279013:

pmc-13279313:

pmc-13279713:

pmc-13280313:

pmc-13280413:

pmc-13282013:

pmc-13282213:

pmc-13282413:

pmc-13283013:

pmc-13283413:

pmc-13284113:

pmc-13284213:

pmc-13284313:

pmc-13284413:

pmc-13284813:

pmc-13285013:

pmc-13285713:

pmc-13285913:

pmc-13286013:

pmc-13286213:

pmc-13286513:

pmc-13287013:

pmc-13287213:

pmc-13287413:

pmc-13288713:

pmc-13288813:

pmc-13289013:

pmc-13289113:

pmc-13289313:

pmc-13290713:

pmc-13290913:

pmc-13291013:

pmc-13291113:

pmc-13292313:

pmc-13292513:

pmc-13293513:

pmc-13294113:

pmc-13294313:

pmc-13294413:

pmc-13294513:

pmc-13295713:

pmc-13296213:

pmc-13296413:

pmc-13296513:

pmc-13299213:

pmc-13300213:

pmc-13301413:

pmc-13301513:

pmc-13301913:

pmc-13306613:

pmc-13307413:

pmc-13307913:

pmc-13308313:

pmc-13308713:

pmc-13309413:

pmc-13310613:

pmc-13310813:

pmc-13311013:

pmc-13311113:

pmc-13311213:

pmc-13311813:

pmc-13311913:

pmc-13312013:

pmc-13312913:

pmc-13314113:

pmc-13314413:

pmc-13315513:

pmc-13315613:

pmc-13316213:

pmc-13317313:

pmc-13319713:

pmc-13321013:

pmc-13323813:

pmc-13325913:

pmc-13326313:

pmc-13327613:

pmc-13327713:

pmc-13328413:

pmc-13328713:

pmc-13329513:
