pmc-13330413:
Bhawani Shankar Verma and team mapped virulence genes among Enterococcus isolates from Central India. Their 2026 study took 106 enterococcal isolates from patients at Index Medical College Hospital in Indore between December 2021 and August 2024. It tested for cytolysin, surface protein, and gelatinase genes by RT-PCR. Enterococci, once known mainly for heart, urinary tract, and belly infections, now raise serious concern through rising antibiotic resistance genes.

The surface protein gene esp proved most common at 74.53%, then cytolysin at 55.66% and gelatinase at 45.28% of those tested. Enterococcus faecalis carried virulence genes more often than Enterococcus avium. Resistance was high to erythromycin, penicillin, chloramphenicol, and tetracycline, while most isolates stayed sensitive to linezolid and vancomycin. The team says they show strong disease-causing power, with high virulence gene rates and varied resistance patterns that muddy treatment choices.
pmc-13330613:
Sabrina Schneider and a large team arm a cancer-killing virus with a fiery cell death protein in a 2026 study. Gasdermin E can flip quiet cell death into loud, immune-stirring pyroptosis, but many tumours silence it. The team built a chimeric vesicular stomatitis virus that carries full gasdermin E into tumour cells.

The armed virus kept its growth pace yet killed with higher potency in lab tests, the authors report. Death shifted toward pyroptosis and tumour cells grew more visible to immunity. In mice, tumour control improved, survival lengthened, and dendritic cells plus killer T cells grew more active inside tumours. Pairing viral killing with loud death may widen therapy reach.
pmc-13330913:
Duval Donoso and colleagues report a rhenium complex built on a brominated pyrazole-pyridazine ligand in a 2026 article. Such ligands grip metals well, stay flat, and suit light-based uses, yet the bromo form had no solved structure before. The team reacted the ligand with a rhenium carbonyl chloride in hot toluene.

The product formed in a yield of 48 percent in the reported synthesis. Crystals held one dimethylformamide solvent molecule per complex, tied by hydrogen bonding to the ligand frame. The rhenium centre sits in an octahedral layout with three carbonyls on one face. Related metal cases are rare in the literature, the authors note. The structure anchors future light and catalysis work.
pmc-13331113:
Obidimma Ezezika and a large team set out a 2026 protocol for comparing COVID-19 vaccine uptake across 12 African countries. Uptake gaps across the region are wide, yet local drivers at service, system, and political levels are poorly mapped. Countries span Angola to Uganda and will be grouped by high, moderate, or low uptake.

Number data will come from global sources on health, economy, and governance. Talk data will come from expert interviews in all countries except Angola, where ethics delay means public reports and literature will stand in for now. Pair and trio country contrasts aim to show what helps or blocks uptake. Lessons should guide fairer pandemic planning.
pmc-13331213:
Kolos Kalman Nagy and colleagues audit head and neck vessel scans in emergency trauma care in a 2026 study. Scans hunt blunt injury to brain-feeding vessels at a level 1 trauma centre. Charts covered visits from January 2021 to December 2023 for patients over age 16 with blunt injury who received such imaging.

In total, 643 patients met the entry rules. A large share, 74.2 percent in the reported yield, had negative scans, and low yield tied strongly to skipping the modified Denver screening rules at triage. Transfer status and trauma level showed no clear link to yield. Most patients with true action-worthy findings had met the screening rules. Tighter rule use could cut radiation and delays.
pmc-13331713:
Mengyuan Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 endoscopy case involving a 74-year-old woman who had part of her colon removed for cancer three years earlier. A check found a flat spreading tumor, about 4 by 3 cm, growing inside a blind loop left by her surgery, a spot that is hard to reach and see.

The team cut around the growth and lifted it with injected fluid. They finished the removal underwater, adding an internal traction clip where the tissue base was firmly stuck. The two-hour procedure took the full wall thickness at one point, and the gap was closed with clips in a folded pattern. Tissue study showed an adenoma with early cancer change and clear margins, and she went home on day three without needing more surgery.
pmc-13332013:
Vahdat Barkhordari and three colleagues test irrigation designs for alfalfa in a dry corner of Iran, in a 2026 field study. Water scarcity threatens forage production across semi-arid regions, and alfalfa is thirsty. The two-year trial in Jiroft compared flood irrigation with two buried drip systems, each at four water levels from full requirement down to seventy percent.

Buried drip pipe gave the best water use efficiency overall. Flood irrigation at full water still produced the heaviest forage, fresh and dry. At the seventy percent level, the buried pipe system improved feed quality: more protein and soluble carbohydrate, more protective proline and antioxidant activity, and less fiber. Cutting water to seventy percent raised efficiency and quality markers across all systems. The authors recommend buried drip at deficit levels where water, not land, is the binding constraint.
pmc-13332213:
A small randomised trial from India, reported in 2026 by Chandrani Khatri and co-authors, tests two drug plans for gall bladder cancer that has spread or cannot be cut out. Sixty patients were split into two arms. One arm got two drugs, gemcitabine and cisplatin, and the other got those two plus a third drug.

The three-drug plan shrank tumours in far more patients than the two-drug plan. Time before the cancer grew again was also longer, at a median of about seven and a half months against about four and a half. Severe side effects did not rise with the added drug. The authors present the triplet as a promising option, while the small size of the trial calls for larger tests to confirm the gain.
pmc-13333313:
Natalia Cediel-Becerra and co-authors developed a framework in 2026 to grade how well One Health tools handle gender equality and social inclusion. One Health, which treats human, animal, and ecosystem health as one problem, preaches equity at policy level. Yet its everyday assessment and planning tools largely ignore gender and social difference.

Their OH GESI framework scores tools along a ladder: ignoring inequality, noticing it, responding to it, and finally transforming the root causes and structural barriers behind it. Applied to tools inventoried by the One Health High Level Expert Panel, the framework exposed major shortfalls while marking exactly where each tool could improve. The authors aim the guidance at tool builders, users, and stakeholders. They align practice with the equity promises of the One Health Joint Plan of Action and urge intersectional analysis inside real programs.
pmc-13333413:
Omar Alqaisi and colleagues surveyed bone surgery patients in Amman in a 2026 study linking how pain care feels, how well patients sleep, and how satisfied they end up. Pain after orthopedic surgery is near-universal, and the three-way relationship among these experiences is tangled.

The descriptive study enrolled 125 patients at two government hospitals, using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and a pain treatment satisfaction scale. Overall satisfaction with pain management landed at moderate, averaging 3.23 on its subscale: pain relief itself was rated kindly, while doctor-patient interaction was flagged as the weak spot. Lower income and more dependents went with lower satisfaction. Older age, higher body mass index, and longer stays went with worse sleep, with BMI correlating strongly with poor sleep scores at r = 0.72. The authors call for personal care plans, timely medication checks, and better conversations between doctors and patients.
pmc-13333513:
Muhammad N. Aslam and colleagues pilot a mineral supplement for leaky gut in ulcerative colitis in a 2026 open-label trial. Aquamin, an extract of red marine algae rich in calcium and minerals, had already raised gut barrier proteins in colon tissue, and the team tested whether that translated into tighter intestines.

Eight patients with mild or remitting colitis and eight healthy controls took Aquamin capsules supplying 800 mg of calcium daily for 90 days. They drank a mannitol solution before and after, so urine levels could reveal how much sugar leaked through the gut wall. At baseline the patients leaked 54 percent more mannitol in the first two hours than controls. After supplementation their leakage dropped by a quarter to two-fifths across collection windows, with total excretion down 29 percent, and no serious side effects appeared. The authors call the result preliminary support for a barrier therapy and want a larger trial.
pmc-13333613:
Working from hospital records, Juan Yu and co-authors examined how laparoscopic surgery for ovarian cysts affects later ovarian reserve in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Their review covered 150 patients treated for cysts on one ovary.

Hormone measures were compared before surgery and at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months afterward. AMH levels fell and FSH levels rose at every check, showing reduced reserve after surgery. Drops were largest for cysts of 7 centimeters or more and for bleeding stopped with electrocoagulation rather than stitches. Among 86 patients hoping to conceive, the pregnancy rate reached 59.3 percent during follow-up. Large cysts, endometriotic cysts, and electrocoagulation stood out as risk factors surgeons should weigh when planning care.
pmc-13333813:
Shima Yazdanpanah and Yaghoub Fathipour feed a guardian mite through ten generations in a 2026 study. The predator mite Neoseiulus cucumeris is mass-reared to hunt pest mites and thrips in greenhouses. Its stand-in prey eats cheap pantry mixes, and enriching the menu might breed hardier hunters.

Six diets, from plain bran to blends with yeast and dog food, were compared. Enriched diets stretched lifespan and egg laying without changing the growth rate. Then came the marathon: ten generations on the two best blends. One blend left females laying more and multiplying faster by generation ten; the other shortened their lives. Menu choice echoes across mite generations.
pmc-13334013:
Guowei Ma and co-authors tackle water bursting through coal mine floors above a pressurized limestone aquifer in a 2026 case study. The Weibei mine works narrow strips of coal, and its floor must hold back confined water below. Rebuilding the whole aquifer seal from the surface costs too much, and scattered short holes leave gaps.

Their answer is continuous grouting from underground through long directional boreholes aimed at the water-blocking layer. Theory, simulation, and field readings together trace how mining cracks the floor and where the grout must go. Sandstone pore maps explain the seepage paths. Site results support the cheaper, unbroken shield.
pmc-13334813:
Kristie L Ebi and co-authors gave a 2026 working group report for the ADVANTAGE project, mapping how climate and environmental change cross into health across the whole life course. The report takes an ecological view, weighing genes and health status alongside diet, social conditions, and physical surroundings.

Stage by stage, from before birth to old age, the authors link weather exposures such as heat stress, humidity, and poor air quality to undernutrition, overnutrition, micronutrient gaps, and priority diseases. At-risk groups get close attention where physiology makes them sensitive. Rather than a single study, the document gathers felt impacts and future risks, then names knowledge gaps and research priorities for the project's diet and adaptation agenda.
pmc-13335513:
Yu Xia and co-authors reviewed stem cell therapy for stroke in a 2026 article covering mechanisms, clinical translation, and what comes next. Clot-busting treatments help only within narrow time windows, leaving many survivors with lasting deficits that restorative therapy might address.

The review gathers evidence on mesenchymal and neural stem cells mainly, noting the field's shift from expecting transplanted cells to replace dead tissue toward having them reshape the post-stroke environment. Human trials so far show dependable safety but inconsistent benefit. A central obstacle is that most transplanted cells die quickly. The authors discuss cell-free options such as extracellular vesicles and bioengineering tricks to harden cells, and argue standardization is the gate to real clinical impact.
pmc-13335913:
Linsha Ma and co-authors mined a rat retrovirus for a better prime editing enzyme in a 2026 genome engineering study. Prime editors write precise DNA changes without cutting both strands, but their power depends heavily on the reverse transcriptase they carry, and good ones are scarce.

Screening 558 candidates surfaced 19 active new enzymes, with a Rattus norvegicus retroviral enzyme, RERV-RT, the strongest. Structure-guided engineering plus deep mutational scanning produced an optimized variant, enRERV-RT. Editors built on it beat the standard M-MLV enzyme by 1.20-fold across mammalian and plant cells, reaching 1.88-fold at stubborn loci, and handled multiplex edits of functional genes. A high-throughput testing platform, TRAP-seq-PE, let the team compare performance across many mutation types systematically.
pmc-13336413:
Zifeng Wu and co-authors showed that swallowed microplastics hasten Alzheimer's-like decline in mice by wrecking gut microbes in a 2026 brain study. The particles fill the food chain, but their brain effects were unknown.

Long oral exposure to 2-micrometer polystyrene particles in 5XFAD Alzheimer's-model mice worsened memory, amyloid buildup, brain inflammation, and synaptic loss, and stalled cellular cleanup. The plastics breached the gut barrier and grew a taurine-eating pathobiont, Bilophila, while holding back taurine-making commensals, leaving a body-wide taurine deficit that foretold the brain damage. Wiping out or swapping microbes proved the effect runs through the microbiota. Restoring taurine calmed microglia, restarted cleanup, and rescued memory, and human ADNI plasma data backed the taurine link.
pmc-13336513:
Yujin Ahn and co-authors created a wound dressing that blasts biofilms apart with tiny bubbles in a 2026 study. Treatment-resistant wounds harbor mixed-species biofilms armored in polymer slime, and even new nanoparticle, phage, and enzyme approaches struggle to clear settled mats.

The dressing, called µBLAST, layers manganese dioxide-doped diatom silica under a cellulose mesh that releases hydrogen peroxide. Catalytic oxygen bubbles form inside the biofilm and burst there, tearing the viscoelastic matrix at the tissue interface while peroxide keeps working. The confined disruption dislodges mature, antibiotic-resistant mixed biofilms that drugs alone cannot shift. Pairing physical demolition with chemical attack offers a route for chronic wounds stuck in inflammation and pain.
pmc-13336913:
Haoxuan Wu and a large team teach a swallowable camera capsule to steer itself through the stomach in a 2026 study. Capsule endoscopy is painless, yet unguided capsules miss patches of lining and navigation tricks rarely transfer between patients. Their learning system follows anatomical landmarks, fusing edge, contour, and depth cues into compact coordinates instead of raw video.

In simulations across eight patient-derived stomach models, coverage topped 97% within 50 s for the method. It beat three standard learning agents on coverage and consistency. In lab scans outside the body, mean coverage hit 87% across five scans with procedure time cut by 53% versus expert manual control in the reported setup. Cheaper, steadier autonomy could widen capsule screening.
pmc-13337413:
Xinmiao Hong leads a 2026 team linking earlier menopause to heart disease and death using national survey data plus a hospital cohort. Women with natural menopause in the NHANES database were grouped by menopause age. Those reaching menopause before 40 years faced more cardiovascular disease and higher overall and cardiovascular death risks than women with menopause at 50–51 years in the comparison.

Each one-year drop in menopause age added about 3% to disease prevalence and overall mortality risk, and 4% to cardiovascular mortality risk, in the dose-response analysis. Blood cholesterol measures, blood pressure, and blood sugar partly carried the effect in mediation models. The hospital cohort backed the pattern, tying early menopause to metabolic drift worth monitoring.
pmc-13337713:
Jonathan Diener leads a 2026 trial of a phone app meant to prevent falls in nursing homes. The BeSt Age App guides staff to give personal exercise sessions to residents. Lasting use depends on whether staff and residents accept the tool and find it workable.

Eleven homes in Southern Germany joined a 12-week cluster trial, with 37 employees and 137 residents. Staff rated ease of use, usefulness, experience, and intent to keep using the app. Residents rated motivation and their own intent to continue. Statistical models linked usefulness and usability to continued use, showing what homes must get right for digital fall prevention to stick.
pmc-13337913:
Jianfeng Huang and co-authors describe three rare uterine mesothelial cysts in a 2026 case report. These benign, fluid-filled growths arise from surface lining cells and usually appear in the belly lining. In the uterus they are uncommon and often missed or mistaken for other disease.

Cases treated at Minda Hospital over ten years are detailed, with a review of prior reports alongside. All three patients had scope exploration and did well afterward as reported. No shared standard for diagnosis or treatment exists yet. By laying out symptoms, imaging, and surgical handling, the report aims to help gynecologists recognize the condition sooner.
pmc-13338013:
Wuyu Huang, Sihang Wang, and Pei Li present a deep learning frame for football tactics in this 2026 paper. Instead of reading raw video, the system models structured tracking data. Two modules split the work by scale.

One module, a transformer, encodes player motion with role and zone awareness. The other scans match segments for recurring tactical motifs using contrastive learning. On benchmark sets the pair improved event forecasting, path prediction, and motif grouping over prior methods. Attention maps and tactic timelines make the output readable for analysts. The authors pitch the tools for coaching staffs as well.
pmc-13338213:
Gülşah Saç and co-authors turn an invasive fish into biodiesel in a 2026 study. Gibel carp harms ecosystems where it spreads, so using its oil offers both control and value. Lipase enzyme fixed onto magnetic nanogels served as the reusable catalyst.

Conditions were tuned for enzyme amount, methanol to oil ratio, and temperature. Best output came at 4000 units of lipase with a 5 to 1 ratio at 55 degrees in the reported optimization. Yield reached 97.45 percent under those settings. The catalyst kept at least half yield across 13 reuse cycles, presenting a first case for this fish as biodiesel feedstock.
pmc-13338313:
Maryam Kohsari and colleagues studied gene variants and cardiometabolic disease in 2026 among 509 Kurdish people in Iran. Variants in the antioxidant genes Nrf2 and NQO1 may shape risk for hypertension and type 2 diabetes, but evidence in this population was thin. Genotypes were typed by PCR, diets were surveyed, and health markers were compared across genetic groups.

Carriers of recessive variants showed higher biochemical, oxidative stress, and body measures. Cox models linked homozygous recessive genotypes to much higher hypertension risk over time, with a hazard ratio of 2.82, and linked combined variants to higher diabetes risk. The findings suggest genetic screening could refine prevention in this community, pending replication in larger cohorts.
pmc-13338413:
Xuqiu Cheng and co-authors link blood nutrients and metals to disability in older Chinese adults in this 2026 paper. The study covered nearly four thousand people aged sixty and up. It measured seven metals plus folate and vitamin D in blood. Disability meant trouble with daily tasks such as dressing and bathing.

Higher folate and vitamin D each came with lower odds of disability, rising in a steady dose pattern. Cobalt and strontium showed U-shaped links instead. When the team modeled all nine exposures together, the mix leaned protective. Folate and vitamin D drove most of that effect. The authors back broad nutrition plans over single-supplement fixes for keeping older adults able.
pmc-13338813:
Yan Ting Woo and colleagues weighed two front routes to chest spine surgery in 2026, small cut versus wide open cut. Files from adults treated at Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham from 2016 to 2021 were read, with harms and pain after surgery as main outcomes. Days in hospital, days in intensive care, blood loss, drain time, and op time were also tracked.

A small cut may mean less pain and a faster return home, but only if safety and access to the spine hold up. The head to head test helps spine surgeons and patients weigh a gentler route against the wide view of open surgery for varied chest spine problems.
pmc-13339013:
Vegar Stubberud and co-authors print water-repellent surfaces copied from a floating fern in a 2026 study. Salvinia molesta leaves trap air with hair-like structures that mix water-loving tips and water-shy sides. Copying that shape has been hard with standard methods.

Two-photon printing built the tiny hairs directly at high resolution in a single material. Varied print settings and tip shapes tested how geometry alone steers wetting. Printed surfaces reached contact angles above 135 degrees and held a water surface over 0.47 mm in the reported measures. Shape alone overcame the base material's natural wetting, aiding repellent and drag-cutting designs.
pmc-13340013:
Kanade Fujiwara, Tomoyuki Makino, and Toru Hamamoto measure sugar breakdown by single microbes in man-made soil in a 2026 study. Real soil mixes too many forces to credit one species. Two bacteria, Bacillus subtilis and Streptomyces cinnamoneus, grew alone and together for 14 days.

Bacillus breathed fast and high, while Streptomyces breathed slowly and lower as reported. Together, total breathing matched the Bacillus-alone level and tracked its share of DNA. Streptomyces instead cut soil acidity sharply despite low breathing. Man-made soil thus separates who burns carbon from who changes soil chemistry, clarifying microbe roles in the carbon cycle.
pmc-13340213:
Coastal bacteria living on particles carry richer plasmid loads than their free-floating neighbors, according to a 2026 metagenomic study by Zhendu Mao and colleagues. Working in the Pearl River Estuary and Daya Bay in South China, the team compared particle-attached and free-living fractions across a pollution gradient.

Plasmids in the attached fraction proved more varied, more often transferable, and packed with genes suited to life on particles. Modeling pointed to biofilm-forming genes as the main route by which lifestyle shaped plasmid variety. As pollution rose, so did plasmid diversity and the share of antibiotic and metal resistance genes, a pattern with clear weight for tracking resistance spread in coastal waters.
pmc-13340713:
Metal wear from hip replacements produced large inflammatory masses in two women, reported by Ahmad Hammad and colleagues in 2026. Patient A, 58, had her hip replaced 16 years earlier and came in with a deep vein thrombosis; scans revealed a huge pelvic pseudotumor pressing on vessels.

She improved after two-stage revision surgery and walked again. Patient B, 81, had severe metallosis with a broken socket wall, and damage plus infection made reimplantation impossible, so surgeons removed hardware, used vacuum wound care, and gave long antibiotics. The contrast shows how metal debris disease ranges from fixable to joint-destroying.
pmc-13340813:
Vector control modeled on the immune system outperformed the standard approach in a 2026 cluster-randomized trial in Arequipa, Peru, led by Michael Z. Levy. Sixty health-facility districts, averaging 2,271 households each, were split between an adaptive immune-style arm and a conventional military-style campaign against Chagas disease vectors.

By the planned March 2023 interim look, the immune arm had found and confirmed 23 infested households spread over 10 separate foci. The conventional arm found only 5, all in one focus. The adaptive arm spent more effort confirming each find, yet its detection rate per person-day was far higher, with a rate ratio of 3.66 reported.
pmc-13341213:
Eun Jung Koh reviews digital twins in two thousand twenty-six as the working layer of precision medicine in children's brain surgery. Precision care promises treatment tuned to each child, but surgeons struggle to turn complex data into individual decisions. A digital twin links a real patient's data to a living computer model that updates as new data arrive.

The framework has five parts: the patient, the data link, the in-silico model, the clinician interface, and time synchronization. Models range from physics-based simulations to AI to hybrids. Koh organizes uses by clinical question across epilepsy surgery, brain tumors, blood vessel disease, hydrocephalus, and skull shape disorders. A staged path runs from prototypes through retrospective and prospective checks into learning health systems, with governance and audit throughout.
pmc-13341413:
Shaohong Yu and colleagues mapped weight and joint disease in 2026 across many data banks, hunting weight cutoffs for sharp prevention. The study joined Global Burden of Disease 2021, NHANES 2007 to 2018, and gene wide data. Additive models drew the weight to joint disease curve with adjustment for confounders, while split models hunted cutoff effects.

From 1990 to 2021, age standardised joint disease rates and disability years were highest in high development regions, and rates rose in a curved way with weight. Gene based tests gauged causal effects on joint disease subtypes. Cutoffs from the work could sharpen weight based prevention for joint disease.
pmc-13341513:
Knocking out a master gene in nerve cells reshapes their electrical behavior, in a 2026 study by Silvia Cardani and colleagues. PHOX2B directs autonomic nervous system development, and its mutations cause neuroblastoma and a syndrome of failed breathing control, yet its target genes remain partly unknown.

Using CRISPR in IMR32 neuroblastoma cells, the team combined expression, binding, electrical, and imaging analyses. The knockout cells matured more in form yet fired oddly, with shifted resting voltage and weaker calcium responses. PHOX2B proved to repress ion channel genes including KCNQ5, SCN3A, and RYR2 directly. Checks in stem-cell-derived neurons from patients supported the developmental relevance.
pmc-13341613:
Plague bacteria reach the brain in a mouse model, in a 2026 study by Brian A. Smith and a large team. Plague meningitis complicates 6 to 11% of human cases yet had never been described in animal models of the pneumonic form, so mice were exposed to aerosolized Yersinia pestis CO92.

Bacteria appeared in brain homogenates by day 2 after challenge, and inflammatory signals such as IL-6 rose in brain tissue. Microscopy in mouse tissue, cross-checked against primate sections, supported central nervous system involvement. Characterizing how lung plague seeds the brain could inform treatment of one of its deadliest complications.
pmc-13342213:
Kerstin Uvnäs-Moberg and Maria Petersson review, in 2026, how the hormone oxytocin is released and what it does, with close attention to touch, social contact, and closeness. The authors draw on clinical evidence about gentle stroking and skin contact and the calm, social, and healing responses that follow.

The review sets out a two-step account in which light touch and later firmer contact activate different skin nerves that signal brain centers where oxytocin is made. Released oxytocin then supports social bonding, lowers stress, pain, and fear, and aids growth and repair. The authors also discuss birth, breastfeeding, parent-infant skin contact, and the harms that follow when close contact is lacking.
pmc-13342513:
Neri Berman and co-authors show that past quakes carry hints about how big the next one will be in a 2026 study. Standard forecasts treat quake size as a fresh draw each time, blind to history. The team built a neural net that reads the place, time, and size of past quakes and deals out odds for the next size.

On lists from three quake zones, the net beat the standard size law by a small but steady edge. The edge held after tricks to rule out sensor quirks. Catalogs thus hold more signal than the field assumed, the team says, and hazard work can use it.
pmc-13342813:
Meng Li and co-authors set out a 2026 protocol for a multicenter randomized trial on fixing femoral neck fractures with three cannulated screws. Freehand placement leans on repeated X-ray shots and can lack precision, so the trial tests an intelligent navigation system against the standard freehand method.

The plan enrolls 300 adults across centers, half in each group, with 12 months of follow-up after surgery. The main outcome is how many fluoroscopy images surgery needs, with healing, hip scores, blood loss, and caregiver burden also tracked. Enrollment began in June 2024 and runs to October 2026. A clear win could set a standard protocol for guided fracture repair.
pmc-13343913:
Anders Orskov Rotevatn and six co-authors measure short-chain fatty acids in the blood of patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a long-term lung disease that narrows the airways. Their study came out in 2026. These fatty acids are produced mostly by gut microbes and can influence the immune system.

Eight fatty acids were measured with precise laboratory methods in patients and controls. One, called formate, was clearly lower in patients with the disease. Two others were lower in patients with the most severe airway obstruction, and one of those also tracked with frequent flare-ups. Another fatty acid rose with symptom burden. No consistent links appeared for the emphysema or allergy-linked forms of the disease. The authors urge more work on mechanisms, including the often overlooked formate.
pmc-13344013:
Chongfa Tang and co-authors show that a frontline antiviral signal can backfire during chlamydia infection in 2026. Type I interferon alone did nothing to genital epithelial cells, yet paired with Chlamydia trachomatis it fired inflammation far beyond what the bacterium triggered by itself, a synergy with tissue-damaging potential.

The team traced the effect to interferon raising levels of Toll-like receptor 3, a sensor that detects leftover viral-style RNA inside infected cells. Silencing or deleting that receptor killed the synergy, while blocking AKT, mTOR, or ERK signaling also dampened it. Downstream cascades through MAPK and AP-1 completed the chain. Calming these pathways could limit the overinflammation some patients suffer.
pmc-13346113:
Jamil E G Faccin and co-authors report six feeding trials, published in 2026. That test how much soybean meal can be added to corn-based diets for pigs at nursery, grower, and finishing stages. Groups ranged from small nursery pigs near 10 kg to finishers over 100 kg, with meal levels varied widely across trials.

Higher meal levels lowered feed intake and daily gain in the youngest nursery pigs, while pigs starting near 13.5 kg were less affected in the same kind of comparison. Grower pigs on corn diets gained faster with more meal, but that gain vanished when distillers grains were included. Late finishers showed no clear change in growth or carcass traits.
pmc-13347013:
Jin-Seok Lee and co-authors identify a plant compound, tomentosin, as a candidate drug for depression that resists the standard drug fluoxetine. Their 2026 study starts from the role of brain immune cells in hard-to-treat depression. Overactive inflammasomes in microglia drive a fiery cell death called pyroptosis, which the team targeted.

A network screen of more than one hundred seventy thousand plant compounds singled out tomentosin, which reaches the brain well. In mice unmoved by fluoxetine, the compound eased depressive behavior and calmed microglia in a frontal brain region. It blocked the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway, and its effect vanished in mice missing a key pathway gene. The authors propose it as a targeted new option.
pmc-13347713:
Nokuthula Mbele, Zanine Moyce, and David Bishop explore how mothers felt after caesarean birth in Durban public hospitals, in a qualitative study from 2026. Interviews with 100 women at two government hospitals covered pain control, emotional support, and staff talk, with themes drawn from guided conversations plus short background questionnaires.

Seventy-seven women said they were satisfied overall, and only one voiced clear dissatisfaction, with good outcomes, solid pain relief, and a warm ward mood lifting scores most. Yet only a third would choose the operation again, and thin pre-surgery briefing, language gaps, low say in choices. Weak feeding or emotional support dragged feelings down, a split the authors call complex.
pmc-13348013:
Graham Little and co-authors present an automated method that segments deep grey matter structures using only diffusion tensor brain images, without the structural scans many clinical protocols lack. Their 2026 study deforms three-dimensional models to fit boundaries visible in diffusion maps, targeting five structures including the thalamus, striatum, and hippocampus.

Against standard structural segmentation in a test-retest sample, agreement was strong for half the ten side-specific structures. It was weak for the globus pallidus, amygdala, and right hippocampus. On inspection, though, the new method looked more accurate, and it gave smaller volumes throughout. Applied to a lifespan cohort of 357 people aged five to ninety, the diffusion measures followed distinct curves: diffusivity fell then rose after the early thirties, while directional measures varied by structure. The authors note these microstructural trajectories differ from volume trajectories, and offer the tool for large studies of deep grey matter microstructure.
pmc-13348413:
Solomon Maina and Leonard Tesoriero sequence a lettuce virus found in stored garlic, in an announcement from 2026. Isolate LY came from a garlic plant gathered in Yanco, New South Wales, in 1980 and kept in a herbarium since. Dried leaf RNA was read and rebuilt to give the full coding genome for lettuce necrotic yellows virus, a serious lettuce disease spread by aphids.

Gene order matched the family pattern, and the isolate shared 97.8 percent identity with a New Zealand isolate against 81.28 percent for another Australian isolate in the reported matches. Finding a lettuce virus hiding in garlic stock stresses quarantine checks on imported garlic breeding material.
pmc-13348613:
Thi Duc Thai and co-authors review the growing toolbox for engineering a methane-eating bacterium, in this 2026 paper. The strain DH-1 turns methane, a potent greenhouse gas, into useful chemicals. Reliable gene tools are the price of admission for that promise.

Recent work cracked the cell's defenses against foreign DNA and built plasmid-free genome editing with a penetrating enzyme. A dial-a-level promoter set and a small RNA platform now tune genes up and down. The review also covers evolution in the lab, mixed cultures, and systems models. Together the methods make the strain a workable factory chassis.
pmc-13348713:

pmc-13348813:

pmc-13350013:

pmc-13351013:

pmc-13352113:

pmc-13352413:

pmc-13352513:

pmc-13352813:

pmc-13352913:

pmc-13354113:

pmc-13354313:

pmc-13354413:

pmc-13354813:

pmc-13355213:

pmc-13356613:

pmc-13357113:

pmc-13359413:

pmc-13359513:

pmc-13360213:

pmc-13360613:

pmc-13360713:

pmc-13360913:

pmc-13361113:

pmc-13361213:

pmc-13361613:

pmc-13362213:

pmc-13362313:

pmc-13362513:

pmc-13362813:

pmc-13364213:

pmc-13364513:

pmc-13364713:

pmc-13365413:

pmc-13371013:

pmc-13371813:

pmc-13374313:

pmc-13375113:

pmc-13376213:

pmc-13377413:

pmc-13383913:

pmc-13384213:
Karol Steckiewicz argued in a 2026 letter that small studies in intensive care should not be dismissed on size alone. The letter asks readers to judge size against the question asked.
pmc-13385513:

pmc-13385813:

pmc-13385913:

pmc-13386013:

pmc-13386713:

pmc-13387713:

pmc-13389613:

pmc-13389813:
Habtamu Alemayehu and colleagues survey, in 2026, what horse and donkey owners in South Gondar Zone, northwest Ethiopia, know and do about internal parasites. These worms are a major drag on working equid health and output worldwide.

The region depends heavily on working equines.
pmc-13390013:

pmc-13390913:

pmc-13392813:

Efficacy needed no fresh check for a renewal.

pmc-13394513:

pmc-13394813:

pmc-13395913:

pmc-13396413:

pmc-13397513:

pmc-13397713:

pmc-13398713:

pmc-13399013:

pmc-13399113:

pmc-13399313:

pmc-13399513:

pmc-13399613:

pmc-13399713:

pmc-13400013:

pmc-13400413:

pmc-13400613:

pmc-13400713:

pmc-13401013:

pmc-13401213:

pmc-13402013:

pmc-13402213:
Takahiro Asano and co-authors follow a 79-year-old man on the blood thinner edoxaban whose left adrenal mass kept growing until it looked like adrenal cancer. pmc-13402313:
Sheela S Sinharoy and a large trial team ask whether cleaner cooking changes blood hemoglobin in pregnant women, using the HAPIN randomized trial across Guatemala, Peru, India, and Rwanda. pmc-13402713:

pmc-13402813:

pmc-13403213:
Joan Hansen and colleagues interview Danish women about the psychosexual fallout of testing positive for high-risk human papillomavirus in cervical screening. pmc-13404113:

pmc-13404413:

pmc-13404613:
Federica Fogliazza and colleagues review gene therapy for beta-haemoglobin disorders in a 2026 narrative survey. pmc-13404713:

pmc-13404913:

pmc-13405113:

pmc-13405313:

pmc-13407613:

pmc-13407713:

pmc-13407813:

pmc-13408013:

pmc-13408113:

pmc-13408613:

pmc-13408713:

pmc-13408813:

pmc-13409613:

pmc-13410413:

pmc-13410613:

pmc-13410713:

Vaccine side effects stayed mild, mostly brief skin irritation at the injection site. Among those assessed, about 94 percent saw tumors respond. Two years on, about a fifth remained free of progression, a figure the team calls promising for such an aggressive disease.
pmc-13410913:

pmc-13412013:

pmc-13412113:

pmc-13412313:

pmc-13414313:

pmc-13417713:

pmc-13418513:

pmc-13419413:

pmc-13420313:

pmc-13421113:

pmc-13421313:

pmc-13421713:

pmc-13421913:

pmc-13422313:

pmc-13422813:

pmc-13423313:

pmc-13423813:

pmc-13423913:

pmc-13424313:

Surface-type species grew scarcer toward the deep zones and tracked food availability at small scales. Cave specialists instead tracked moisture at the cave scale and, at small scales, simply distance from the entrance, favoring deep buffered spots. Because each cave held a distinct community, the authors argue that licensing cannot treat one cave as a substitute for another.
pmc-13424413:
Taeko Saito, Natsumi Shimizu, and Li Yao conduct an umbrella review, a review of reviews, on non-drug treatments for older adults living with dementia. The team searched five databases to February 2025. They sought systematic reviews covering agitation, mood, anxiety, cognition, and quality of life. They then graded the reviews' own quality and checked how much their underlying trials overlapped.

Twelve reviews covering 147 randomised trials qualified, with very slight overlap between them. Non-drug approaches gave small but consistent relief: agitation, depression, and anxiety scores all improved by roughly a fifth to a quarter of a standard unit. Every review carried at least one weakness, so the authors present the benefits as real but modestly evidenced.
pmc-13424513:
Souhaila Akir and five colleagues report a rare complication of liver hydatid disease. In their patient, a parasitic cyst invaded the portal vein. The 56-year-old man had earlier surgery for the same condition. Hydatid disease, spread by Echinococcus parasites, is common across North Africa and the Mediterranean, and the liver is its usual home, but blood-vessel invasion is exceptional.

Imaging told the story: a cyst in liver segment IV had opened into the portal vein, seeding daughter cysts along the vein and its branches and blocking flow. Collateral vessels had formed the corkscrew pattern of a portal cavernoma, and Doppler scans showed no flow in the main vein. The case mimicked ordinary vein thrombosis, a trap the authors flag for clinicians in endemic regions.
pmc-13424613:
Divyansh Sinha and six colleagues pilot a study linking worn teeth, jaw muscle stiffness, and pain in people with and without head and neck pain. The pain group showed greater average tooth wear than controls. Correlation checks then connected wear severity with the tone, stiffness, and elasticity of muscles including the masseter, temporalis, and pterygoids. pmc-13425713:
Wananit Wimuttisuk and colleagues studied how Vibrio infection changes fat-based signaling in shrimp gut tissue in a 2026 experiment. Acute hepatopancreatic necrosis disease, driven by Vibrio parahaemolyticus carrying PirA and PirB toxin genes, kills farmed shrimp in large numbers. Farm teams lose stock fast when this germ hits, so facts on how the gut reacts in the first day can guide quick steps to limit loss.
pmc-13426313:
Tung-Yun Wu and colleagues combined a stomach acid drug with an antibody fragment to treat type 1 diabetes in mice in a 2026 study. Their regimen paired omeprazole, intended to spur new islet formation, with a non-Fc-binding anti-CD3 fragment to calm autoimmune T cells.

Diabetes was triggered in susceptible NOD mice with cyclophosphamide, and treatment after high blood sugar began was tracked by glucose readings, T cell profiling, and beta cell function tests. Dual action on regeneration and immunity is the strategy under test.
pmc-13426413:

Blocking that jam could restore the alarm in infected cells.
pmc-13426713:
Adwan and colleagues report two 2026 cases of vallecular cysts, rare fluid-filled sacs at the base of the tongue that can block an infant's airway. The first baby, a 54-day-old boy, arrived with breathing distress, noisy inhaling, choking episodes, and bluish spells that had worsened since his first week of life.

The second child, a one-year-old boy, had chronic snoring, mouth breathing, and feeding trouble, with imaging showing a neat round lesion at the tongue base. Surgeons opened and drained his cyst in a procedure called marsupialization, and his symptoms resolved completely. The authors urge considering this diagnosis in infants with persistent noisy breathing.
pmc-13426813:
Jordan Wight, Helene Schulz, and Logan Banadyga report cross-reactive antibodies to Bundibugyo virus in ferrets given an Ebola vaccine in a 2026 study. The work matters because the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared a Bundibugyo virus outbreak on 15 May 2026 in Ituri Province, initially reporting 246 suspected cases and 65 deaths. pmc-13426913:
Godfrey Nattoh and colleagues watched the first hours of dengue virus infection inside mosquito guts, using a new signal-boosting detection method. Dengue spreads to people through Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, and the gut is the first barrier the virus must cross.

The new method proved far more sensitive than the standard antibody test and spotted virus as early as six hours after infection. Only a handful of virus particles started each gut infection, showing a severe early bottleneck for the virus. That narrow start can reshape the virus population and its fitness for later spread. Nattoh argues these early events are a promising target for new ways to block transmission.
pmc-13427313:
Narvai reviewed in 2026 the history of Brazil's national oral health surveys, known as the SB Brasil project, and drew lessons for the planned 2030 edition. These surveys steer dental policy in the public health system. Editions ran from 1986 to 2023, each making choices about what to measure and whom to sample.

The essay questions those choices, including which measures were kept or dropped, such as an index for badly damaged teeth with exposed pulp. Narvai argues that judging measures only by clinical interest warps the survey, since policy and fairness questions also deserve space. Training examiners to score teeth the same way remains hard even with standard methods. The author concludes that the 2030 round can build on a rich stock of Brazilian experience in oral health counting, if it heeds these warnings.
pmc-13427413:
Yehui Fu and coauthors tested whether carbon trading pushes firms toward energy-saving innovation in a 2026 study of Chinese listed manufacturers. Using 3.09 million patent texts from 2008 to 2023, the team applied a large language model to identify energy-saving technological innovation at firm level, a narrower target than general green patenting. Staggered difference-in-differences estimation then measured the trading scheme's effect as regions adopted it at different times.

Trading significantly promoted energy-saving innovation, robust across checks, through higher carbon-risk exposure, substitution between subsidies and market incentives, and correction of market inefficiencies. Effects ran stronger in firms with lower pollution baselines in the mechanism analysis. Firm by firm counts, built from a vast pile of filed claims to new goods, give the test a scale few polls of plant chiefs could hope to match.
pmc-13427813:
Laura Bandini and colleagues pool studies on vitamin D in pregnancy and later autism and attention-deficit diagnoses in children. Both conditions mix genes and surroundings, and the biology linking a mother's vitamin D to child brain development stays unclear.

Fifteen studies qualified, with 8 on autism, 5 on attention deficit, and 2 on both, searched to February 2026. High versus low maternal vitamin D lined up with lower risk, at a ratio of 0.91 for autism and 0.90 for attention deficit, with a dose-response pool across the full range. Parents and clinicians get a careful link, not proof that supplements prevent either condition.
pmc-13427913:
Tufan Agah Kartum and co-authors dissect, in a 2026 anatomy study, the layered tissues that complicate a wide skull-base approach. The cranio-orbito-zygomatic approach swings open bone around the eye and cheek to reach deep targets. Its wide exposure endangers branches of the facial nerve that cross the temple layers. The team performed the approach on 10 cadavers, studying both sides of each head.

They traced how scalp layers, the temporal fascia, and nerve branches relate at each step. Facial nerve branches run in a defined layer between the galea, the scalp's tough sheet, and the temporal fascia. Following one fascia layer downward opened a natural plane toward the cheek prominence without crossing the nerves. Skull-base surgeons gain a clearer map for protecting facial movement during a demanding exposure.
pmc-13428313:
Lilian Almeida Nascimento Rabêlo and colleagues test, in a 2026 dental materials study, how a year in water changes two filling resins. Semidirect restorations are built outside the mouth and given extra hardening, often in an autoclave, before fitting. One resin held special glass fillers that can release helpful minerals; the other was a standard nanohybrid resin. Forty-eight discs were made, half with the extra hardening step, and all were stored in distilled water for twelve months.

The mineral-filler resin changed color more over the year than the standard resin. Extra hardening made no difference to color change in either material. Surface roughness rose in every group after storage, again regardless of hardening. Microscope checks matched those results. Dentists choosing materials for visible restorations get a caution about long-term shade drift with the mineral type.
pmc-13428813:
Peter Rhodes writes an essay on medicine and crowd madness, using the COVID years as context for a wider warning. Individual judgment, he argues, is fragile, and people can be swept into a shared thought window by mass narrative or by the certainty of a totalised mind.

Loss of the self to the group can run from small group-think to literal crowds and on to global propaganda and technocratic control. Milgram's obedience tests and Hannah Arendt's phrase about the banality of evil frame the risk, with the bureaucrat as a new kind of wrongdoer. Readers get a polemic that asks science, too, to check its own crowds.
pmc-13429113:
Hamza Abedallaa, Zuheir Al-Shehabi, and Nader Abedallaa review, in a 2026 study, eighteen years of testicular cancer care at one Syrian hospital. Testicular cancer is the commonest cancer in males aged 15 to 39 and among the most curable. The Latakia center's records covered 318 patients from its opening in 2007 through late 2025. The team sorted tumors by type and stage and checked risk features used to plan treatment after surgery.

Median age at diagnosis was 32 years. Germ cell tumors dominated, split almost evenly between seminoma and non-seminoma forms, with mixed tumors the largest single subgroup. Most patients arrived at stage I, the earliest stage, though seminomas presented early more often. Risk features such as vessel invasion were tallied for each group. The pattern matches global reports, and the authors call for more regional research from Syria and the Middle East.
pmc-13429313:
Dennis Kool and seven co-authors published a 2026 study of what changes for patients once small fiber neuropathy is finally diagnosed. The condition damages the smallest nerves, causing pain, lower quality of life, and high costs. Earlier work measured the burden only before diagnosis. This team surveyed 84 patients at a Dutch expert center, before diagnosis and again three to six months after it was confirmed. They tracked care use, family costs, work losses, pain, and quality of life.

Total costs, pain, and quality of life did not budge after diagnosis. Patients did visit specialists less, spent less on those visits, and felt their health was better understood. The authors conclude that a clear diagnosis alone does not lighten the burden. Better symptom care and support must follow the diagnosis for patients to gain.
pmc-13430413:
Asta Nyvang Rank and colleagues surveyed orthodontic specialists in Denmark and Sweden for a 2026 study on judging when braces are needed and when care should start. Nearly 500 certified specialists received a 20-item survey built around nine patient cases. Each case came with photos, head drawings, and notes on how the teeth meet.

Replies from 219 specialists showed clear gaps between regions and between the two countries. Danish replies lined up more closely, which the authors link to shared national guidance. Swedish replies spread more widely. Digital referral tools were more common in Sweden, yet their use went with more choices to watch a case rather than judge need at once. The findings point to uneven practice even among trained experts.
pmc-13430913:
Fanfan Cao and colleagues set out a systematic-review protocol on acceptance and commitment therapy for weight stigma. Such stigma brings negative attitudes and stereotypes, linked to body-image distress, eating disorders, depression, anxiety, self-harm, and suicidal thoughts.

Acceptance and commitment therapy, a third-wave talking therapy, aims to build psychological flexibility and values-led action, and it shows promise against stigma. Yet evidence stays limited and fragmented, often missing stigma's many dimensions. This protocol plans a synthesis of how well the therapy cuts stigma and improves related mental health, giving therapists a clearer evidence verdict.
pmc-13431013:
Ketfi and Ben Saad compare two yardsticks for lung function tests in healthy Algerian adults. Spirometry grades breathing against reference equations. The Global Lung Function Initiative replaced its 2012 race specific equations with race neutral ones in 2023, to remove race as a medical input. Their 2026 study runs both equation sets over 488 healthy adults aged 18 to 85 who passed breathing tests. It compares the labels each set assigns.

The two yardsticks agreed on a normal label for about nine in ten people, so the headline barely moved. Under the surface, percent predicted values for the two main volumes ran several points higher under the neutral equations. Abnormal labels shifted too. More people were classed as obstructive, fewer as restrictive or non specific. Isolated low first second volume vanished as a class. Broad comparability, with real reclassification at the margins, is the fair summary for this population.
pmc-13431613:
Cinzia Auriti and co-authors reviewed the trials of spotting a common womb infection in 2026, centered on cytomegalovirus and its risks in pregnancy. The virus spreads widely, sleeps for life in the body, and can wake or strike again. A first infection during pregnancy carries the highest risk of passing to the unborn child.

Effects on children range from no signs at all to grave body-wide illness, slow growth of mind skills, and hearing loss. The review stresses fast checks for the mother, care in telling first bouts from fresh ones, and joined checks before and after birth, from scans to hearing tests. Drugs against the virus now exist for pregnancy and infancy, which sharpens the case for early flags. Wide screening of newborns earns a close look as a way to catch missed cases.
pmc-13431713:
Estella Castillon and colleagues describe three people whose patchy light skin follows Blaschko lines, tied to new post-conception ACTB gene variants. ACTB faults already link to several conditions, including a constitutional gain-of-function syndrome and somatic variants in birthmarks and muscle hamartomas.

Deep gene sequencing of skin biopsies from affected areas found the same missense variant, Arg335His, in two people, previously seen in a fetus in constitutional form. The third person carried a new insertion-deletion variant. Two of the three also showed neurodevelopmental features. The report widens the ACTB disease spectrum, showing that variants acquired after conception can paint skin in lines and affect the brain.
pmc-13432813:
Yongshu Wu and co-authors deleted a sensing gene in 2026 from a food-borne germ that sickens people, then watched how the loss cut both toughness and attack skill. The gene sits in a two-part alarm system that reads stress cues from the world around the cell. Germs without it grew poorly in acid, alkali, and salt strain.

The crippled strain also fared worse under strong acid, metal strain, and harsh oxygen strain, while a restored copy healed most gaps. Inside host cells, the strain broke in less well and moved more slowly. In mice, it filled liver and spleen more weakly and killed later. Gene voice reads under acid showed stress genes lit in odd patterns without the sensor. The authors cast the sensor as a twin pillar of survival and harm.
pmc-13433313:
Ben Langford, Jonathan Williams, and Jérôme Casas warn that dirty air garbles insect scent talk unevenly in a 2026 study. Insects court and alarm by airborne chemicals, and pollution eats those signals at rates set by each chemical's build.

Alarm scents are small, light, and simple, so they stay airborne about as long in dirty air as clean. Sex scents are bigger and stickier, and night pollution slashes their range, partly by soaking them into particles. That soaking may also shield them from decay. The upshot: mating channels suffer most, a subtle route by which smog reshapes insect life.
pmc-13433413:
Marko Balan and colleagues develop climate-conscious recommendations for critical care in Canada, under the Choosing Wisely banner. The climate crisis is framed as the largest health threat of the twenty-first century, and critical care's footprint can shrink if clinicians have safe guidance.

A national multidisciplinary working group refined a recommendation list between November 2023 and May 2024, drawing on content experts and literature review. A three-stage anonymous voting process selected and polished the final list. Clinicians and managers get evidence-based steps to cut intensive-care emissions without compromising patient safety.
pmc-13435913:
Charles W Tran and a large team pool blood tumor markers from more than 2,300 lung cancer patients in 2026. Six tumor proteins plus one swelling marker were read at start and at six weeks. Five trials of immune therapy mixes supply the data.

A learning model blends marker levels from both time points to rank survival risk. Its accuracy held in both squamous and non squamous test sets. One marker, CYFRA, carried the most weight in both lung types. Marker math matched costlier DNA blood tests in prior work. Cheap blood panels may guide care when DNA tests lag or fail.
pmc-13436013:
Fiona Lynch's team asked Australians living with rare or undiagnosed genetic conditions in 2026 what they think of automating genomic reanalysis. Re-reading old genome data against new knowledge can yield diagnoses, yet manual reanalysis is slow and rarely routine, so cases that could now be solved stay unsolved. Automated reanalysis could widen access, but worries about transparency, bias, data security, and trust had not been studied with affected people.

Twenty-three Australians in seven online focus groups voiced strong support for automation, while raising conditions around openness, accountability, and control of their data. Genomics services get a user-grounded mandate with guardrails: automate to find answers faster, but show the reasoning and protect trust. Policy makers should weigh these views before scaling automation.
pmc-13436213:
Kate Stoeckle and coauthors follow leukemia patients whose guts carry resistant germs into chemotherapy in 2026. The study enrolls 159 patients getting strong induction therapy with no preventive antibiotics. Stool checks at chemo start sorted patients by germ carriage.

Fifteen patients carried ESBL type germs, and seventeen carried AmpC type germs. Three of the ESBL carriers grew the same germ in blood during low white cell counts. Just one non carrier did so, a stark gap. AmpC carriage showed no such risk lift. Gut screening may flag who needs closer watch or tailored cover.
pmc-13436813:
Zuhal Mohmand's team surveyed young adults in 2026 on sedation during endoscopy after moving from pediatric to adult bowel care. Sedation habits differ between child and adult units, and that shift may color how patients with childhood-onset inflammatory bowel disease experience scopes. Deep sedation was far more common in pediatric care, and adult scopes brought lower sedation satisfaction plus more pain and discomfort, while anxiety and preparedness ratings did not differ. Patients cited thin communication and perceived low empathy as barriers, with education and compassion as helps. Transition teams get a clear prompt: explain adult sedation plainly and early.
pmc-13437813:
Jukka Sivonen and colleagues studied how feeling unable to afford adequate energy shapes Finnish views on climate action. Their 2026 study drew on a representative 2023 survey of 5,909 people and modeled support for fossil fuel taxes and two gentler climate nudges.

Higher felt energy poverty came with lower support for climate measures across the board. The authors split the harm of being left behind into two kinds. The sting of exclusion flows from the felt condition itself, whatever the meter says. Pure money harm from nudges, by contrast, lands more on people objectively poor in energy terms. Either way, climate policy ignoring energy hardship risks losing the very households it most needs onside. They advise pairing carbon measures with visible relief and honest messaging about who pays.
pmc-13438313:
Ahmed Hadj Hassen and colleagues reviewed research and gray sources on moving through airports with a disability. Their 2026 scoping review reads the airport journey from curb to gate through five lenses: whether help exists, can be reached, is acceptable, is affordable, and truly works in practice.

Across the studies, access arrived in pieces. Ramps, lifts, and desks existed yet often failed to join into a usable whole, leaving travelers dependent on booked assistance. Needs beyond mobility drew the least attention, above all invisible disabilities such as cognitive or sensory ones staff cannot see. The authors insist compliance checklists are the wrong finish line: access is a living quality of the trip. Their map is meant to push airports from providing features toward guaranteeing a journey holding together.
pmc-13438813:

Their 2026 study starts from a fused metallacycle with a three-membered ring and ends at a charged six-membered metal ring.

Radical-trapping tests and modeling pointed to electrophilic attack followed by elimination, a familiar substitution pathway pushed somewhere new. The authors frame the switch as proof aromatic frameworks can be re-cut, and a practical route into compounds otherwise hard to make. For chemists, a controlled reshaping reaction is a new kind of tool: edit the frame, not just the fittings.
pmc-13439013:

Coeliac disease demands a strict gluten-free diet. Yet gluten-free staples cost one and a half to two times their ordinary versions, and many Canadian households with an affected child report food insecurity. Their 2026 study drew on fifty-nine parent-child pairs from a wider survey, with open-ended interviews.

Cost dominated: more than ninety percent named high prices, and nearly as many blamed absent food policy. Their policy asks were concrete: child tax credits led, backed by school nutrition education and official recognition of coeliac disease as a disability. The authors frame gluten-free food as medicine priced like a luxury. Their take-away: families have already drafted the agenda; what is missing is adoption and funding.
pmc-13439313:

Patients received the pentaspline, balloon-in-basket, or lattice-tip catheter, with blood tests before and 24 hours after the procedure. Only the pentaspline system caused significant depletion of haptoglobin, a protein that mops up free haemoglobin, and only that group saw acute kidney injury, in 4.9 percent of cases. The authors conclude catheter design drives these differences.
pmc-13440313:

One gene helps anchor protein making machinery inside the cell. Another starts the building of new proteins. The third helps fold proteins under stress. Past work showed silencing can cut aphid lifespan and offspring counts. This study checks whether these three targets do the same. The method feeds or delivers matching RNA pieces to the insects. Results could point to precise, species specific pest control.
pmc-13440713:
van de Wetering and Lee interviewed 11 Dutch teen climate activists aged 14 to 18. Through growth science, they sought to learn what young people get out of striking for the climate. Three themes fell out of the interviews. They were held online between September 2022 and 2023, with six female, two male, one non-binary, and two undisclosed teens. Activism was driven by wanting to build a just world. Accounts spanned solidarity with future generations and the Global South. It also worked as the teens' own choice, helping them explore and express who they are during the teen years. Finally, activism created a felt bond with some others, though not all. The authors suggest backing such involvement, since it channels teen growth needs well.
pmc-13442613:

Unaligned variants ran weaker and more brittle. Composite engineers get a threading method that reinforces the weak direction without sacrificing in-plane performance.
pmc-13444213:
Azahara Rodríguez-Luna and co-authors review whether natural compounds can shield skin from visible light, the part of sunlight ordinary sunscreens barely block. Their 2026 systematic review gathers lab and clinical studies of natural agents against visible-light damage: oxidative stress, inflammation, unwanted pigmentation, and photoaging, which fall hardest on darker skin.

In laboratory studies the compounds blunted oxidation, calmed inflammation, and interrupted pigmentation pathways. In human studies, formulations with natural agents improved redness and pigmentation outcomes after light exposure. The studies varied too much in doses and measures to pool numerically, and the authors say so. For photoprotection, the review marks a frontier: as the ultraviolet problem found its answer in filters, the visible problem may find part of its answer in antioxidants worn on the skin.
pmc-13445713:

They found wide isoform switching along the way. The switches mostly came from genes starting or ending at different points, not from splicing changes. They also ran apart from rises or falls in total gene output. Genes for the heart's pumping parts and ion channels were prime targets. The authors frame isoform switching as its own layer of control in heart development.
pmc-13446313:

Such variants may explain part of the missing-cause group with protein S deficiency. The authors argue that diagnostic testing should extend into this intron, and that non-coding regulation deserves a routine place in the workup of inherited clotting disorders.
pmc-13446413:

Comparing people, the predicted link failed: those who framed more beliefs as chances were not more humble overall, in either sample. Comparing beliefs within the same person, the link appeared. Political and moral beliefs a person held as probabilities came with a humbler stance toward those very beliefs, even after allowing for how extreme the beliefs were. Framing may thus soften single beliefs without marking a humbler character, a hint that teaching chance based framing could cool hard disputes.
pmc-13447113:

Most single factors opened chromatin in only a small share of cells at a time. Added together, though, the binding of many factors set how often an enhancer switched on. Tests on hundreds of enhancers placed at a new genome spot showed the helper protein p300 was needed for full activation.
pmc-13447413:

Official writing presents the model as building responsibility, participation and inclusion, with women workers gaining new public visibility. Whether daily life matches that picture remains unverified, since no fieldwork tested lived experience. The authors call for on-the-ground research into how households and workers actually experience the system.
pmc-13447813:

He received two 28-day cycles of albendazole separated by a 14-day break, to reduce recurrence risk after surgery.
pmc-13448113:

pmc-13450413:

pmc-13450613:

pmc-13451213:

pmc-13451813:

pmc-13451913:

pmc-13453013:

pmc-13453713:
Reiko Kanno and others told of a three-button heart fix in 2026, for valve-sparing root swap in giant cell arteritis. This artery disease hits mid and large tubes, and root widening with a left main heart tube bulge is most rare. A plain one-button fix was ruled out once the bulge was cut away.

pmc-13454113:
Kang Li and five co-authors map two decades of research joining childhood obesity with precocious puberty, the early onset of puberty. pmc-13454313:
Damico, Mathus, and Demchenko tackle a core problem in sugar chemistry in 2026: steering new bonds between sugars to face the right way. pmc-13455313:

pmc-13455613:

pmc-13457813:

pmc-13458713:

pmc-13458913:

pmc-13459113:

pmc-13459213:

pmc-13462513:

pmc-13466513:

pmc-13466813:

pmc-13467113:

pmc-13467513:

pmc-13467913:

pmc-13468113:

pmc-13468813:

pmc-13469613:

pmc-13470213:
