Twenty-two genes tied to the healthy pattern emerged, and a network pass named three hubs, HADHA, ACOX1, and GOT2, all linked to fat burning and cell energy. Tests in mice, rat heart cells, and human tissue agreed: the three ran high in healthy thickening and low in harmful thickening. Human diseased heart muscle confirmed the drop. The authors say the trio marks a metabolic fingerprint that may one day help doctors tell the two growth kinds apart.
pmc-13499013:
Kumar and colleagues profiled proteins inside vesicles shed into blood by certain brain cell types, aiming at earlier spotting of Alzheimer's disease, in a 2026 biomarker study. Standard blood tests cannot tell which brain cells a signal came from and miss scarce proteins. The team collected vesicles from neurons, astrocytes, microglia, and three other brain cell types from people with normal cognition, mild impairment, or Alzheimer's-related dementia.

Kumar measured 122 proteins spanning Alzheimer's changes, degeneration, and inflammation with a sequencing-based assay. Each cell type's vesicles carried a distinct pattern. Mild impairment already showed early shifts in protective, inflammatory, and vascular markers in vesicles from neurons, microglia, and the myelin-making oligodendrocytes. Full dementia showed broader change across many vesicle types, with tau and amyloid signals, inflammation, vessel problems, and synaptic loss. The authors argue the blood platform can surface changes across many cell types long before dementia, supporting biomarker discovery.
pmc-13499113:
Ono and colleagues look for early signs that can show who may one day stop leukemia drugs safely. Their patients have chronic myeloid leukemia, a slow blood cancer driven by one faulty gene fusion. All got newer second-round kinase blockers, drugs that switch off that faulty signal.

The team drew on a trial with more than four hundred patients. A very deep fall in cancer gene levels by six months stood out as the key early sign. Patients who hit that mark had a strong chance of deep lasting control by three years. Such control is the gate for a safe trial stop of the drug. Six-month blood tests can thus sort patients early for stop plans.
pmc-13499713:
Sacco and colleagues test whether a body's electrical properties can help forensic doctors estimate time of death, a stubborn problem once the first day has passed. Bioelectrical impedance analysis, a bedside technique that passes a tiny current through tissue, is routine in living patients but barely explored after death. Their 2026 pilot study measured 29 cadavers at times ranging from under two hours to about eight days after death, repeating measurements after autopsy in ten cases.

One derived value, the phase angle, rose moderately and consistently with time since death, while raw resistance and overall impedance tracked time poorly. The relationship curved: electrical change ran fast in the early hours and flattened later, matching the known biology of membrane breakdown and ion shifts. Body size showed no link to time estimates. With heavy scatter remaining between cases, the authors present the method strictly as exploratory, needing far larger studies before courtroom use.
pmc-13500713:
Negin Hashemi and colleagues coat in 2026 toxic but useful quantum dots with plant extracts to tame them for medicine. Cadmium sulfide dots can image and target tumours, yet bare dots damage healthy cells and burst red blood cells. Extracts of two plants, a Persian hogweed and an oak gall, were used to coat the dots in an eco-friendly synthesis. Instruments confirmed the particles' size, surface charge, and structure before cell and blood safety tests.

Plant coating shifted the surface charge in a direction suggesting better stability in the reported measurements. Bare dots proved substantially toxic and blood-damaging, while the hogweed-coated dots achieved the highest cell survival and the least red cell rupture. Oak gall coating protected moderately yet slightly increased blood rupture in the assays, a mixed result. Green coatings clearly can soften quantum dot toxicity, though each plant recipe needs its own safety vetting.
pmc-13500813:
Sungho Park leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 imaging study that tests a faster form of 4D flow MRI for measuring turbulence in the aorta. Four-dimensional flow MRI records blood movement through a volume over time, and turbulent kinetic energy quantifies energy lost to swirling flow. The team scanned healthy volunteers and patients with aortic stenosis, a narrowed aortic valve, using both a conventional method and a compressed sensing version that reconstructs images from far fewer measurements.

In patients, the two methods agreed closely: peak total turbulent energy differed by about 5.0 percent in the ascending aorta and 7.4 percent across the whole aorta, neither difference reaching significance. In healthy participants, the fast method read much higher values, roughly double in the ascending aorta and triple across the whole region. The authors attribute that gap to the very low turbulence levels in healthy aortas.
pmc-13501613:
Xu Shi and co-authors test whether HIRA loss is a must in a rare kidney cancer in a 2026 study. Fumarate hydratase deficient renal cancer is fierce and driven by fumarate buildup. Mouse work had cast loss of the histone chaperone Hira as the spark that turns such cells malignant.

In human tumors from many centers, HIRA loss was common but not universal, present in about three quarters of cases. Loss did not track with patient outcomes. Gene programs split by HIRA state: lost tumors ran MYC and mTORC1 paths, kept tumors Wnt and Notch. Human disease takes two roads.
pmc-13501713:
Shuncheng He and Wooyeol Lee present a 2026 methods paper arguing that therapy trials should judge not only whether average symptoms fall, but whether a patient's day-to-day instability changes too. Mood and symptoms swing within a person, and a treatment might steady those swings without moving the mean much. Their framework extends dynamic structural equation modelling, a technique for intensive longitudinal data, by letting each person's residual variance depend on which trial arm they were assigned to. Instability itself becomes a treatment outcome that can be estimated directly.

An empirical case illustrates the approach, showing the model estimating separate treatment effects for the experimental and control groups. Monte Carlo simulations then stress-tested the method under varied conditions, and parameter recovery stayed accurate with stable estimates throughout. The authors position the framework as a flexible extension of randomized trial analysis for the era of phone-collected symptom data.
pmc-13501813:
Saleh Molla and co-authors track Canadian life satisfaction across twelve years spanning the pandemic, in work from twenty twenty-six. A community cohort founded years before COVID supplies the data. Four survey waves bracket the outbreak and its aftermath. Satisfaction odds are compared before, during, and after the crisis. Social traits, distress, and money stressors are tested as correlates.

Satisfaction odds fall during the pandemic and stay low afterward. No rebound appears by the twenty twenty-four wave. Singles and middle-aged adults report lower satisfaction odds. Psychological distress drags satisfaction down in the same models. Income stress and earlier hardship also predict later dissatisfaction. The pandemic's wellbeing scar had not healed by twenty twenty-four.
pmc-13502013:
Thomas Laval and others build a glowing marker mouse to watch fat-eating, the self-eating breakdown of lipid droplets, in artery clogging. In 2026, the study tags perilipin 2 with Rosella, an acid-touchy sensor, creating Rosella-PLIN2 mice, then tests fat-eating in human eater cells, grown foam cells, and an artery clogging model. Lipid droplets steer lipid balance, and odd shifts drive energy disease.

Clog-causing fat carriers and cell cleanup starters spurred fat-eating, while aimed tying compounds cleared droplets only where wanted. In vessels, the marker showed a shortage in vessel smooth muscle foam cells versus eater cells, with TREM2-marked eater cells showing high lipid and low flux. Boosting fat-eating offers a new healing angle for plaque biology.
pmc-13502913:
Daniel Elakpa and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of what helps or hinders blackfly control for river blindness in Sub-Saharan Africa. The disease spreads by blackfly bite and stays a major public health load in the region. The review pulls together proof on the drivers of control program success.

Four databases were searched for studies from 2000 to early 2025. Two reviewers screened the hits with a shared tool, and quality was graded with a standard checklist. Seventeen studies made the cut. Cash limits topped the barrier list, since larvicide programs cost much to start and keep up. Village methods such as clearing trailing plants were cheap but needed steady local commitment. Poor larvicide use and resistance also cut gains.
pmc-13503013:
Karla Andrade de Oliveira, Ashley Cardona, and Mirela Ponduchi report a 2026 orthopaedic case stacking rarity on rarity. A 57-year-old man presented with pain in both knees, and MRI showed both quadriceps tendons ruptured. The injury accounts for under three percent of such ruptures because the tendon normally withstands force. Such tears usually need a weakness, from kidney disease or diabetes to long steroid use. Surgical repair of both sides followed, the route back to walking.

His recovery went well, then both repaired knees developed septic arthritis, a joint infection that strikes a single joint and can dissolve cartilage within days if missed. Bilateral infection after bilateral tendon repair is so uncommon that no published incidence exists. Care demanded aggressive treatment of the site infections to protect the joints. The authors use the case to argue for monitoring, since a missed diagnosis means lasting joint damage.
pmc-13503913:
Wilayat Khan and three colleagues outline retinal lesions with help from written clinical prompts, in a 2026 paper. Most lesion-spotting models read images alone, so their cues may not match what doctors mean by a lesion. They also need costly hand-drawn masks for each new data set.

The new pipeline aligns image traits with text traits drawn from prompts that state clinical facts about each lesion type. One round of training sets that alignment. After that, the network can mark lesions in fresh data sets with no new mask training. Tests on six public data sets beat prior best methods, with overlap gains up to about 8 points. The authors frame the design as a way to cut labeling cost in eye care.
pmc-13504213:
Tayeb Weisi and three colleagues test zinc oxide nanoparticles as a feed additive for young common carp, in a 2026 study. Zinc is vital for fish growth and immune work, yet plain feed sources are poorly absorbed. Tiny zinc particles may deliver the mineral more effectively.

Three hundred young carp were split across twelve tanks and fed four diets for sixty days, from no added particles up to the highest dose. The middle dose gave the best weight, length, and feed use, plus the highest survival. Blood counts, hemoglobin, and defense markers in blood and skin mucus peaked there too. The top dose raised stress-linked white cells, a warning sign. The authors back the middle dose for farm use, with care at higher levels.
pmc-13504813:
Jiang Li leads a team using genetics to ask whether gut-hormone drug targets slow aging, in a 2026 study. Drugs that mimic two gut hormones now treat diabetes and obesity, with known heart and kidney gains. Their effect on aging itself was untested in trials.

The team used gene variants that stand in for turning each hormone path up or down, then checked four aging measures in large data sets. Sugar lowering through the GIP path linked to less frailty, slower measured aging, longer chromosome caps, and higher odds of long life. Weight lowering through the same path helped frailty and longevity. The GLP-1 path linked mainly to longevity through sugar effects. Combined paths looked much like the GIP path alone.
pmc-13506113:
Atul Goel and colleagues present ninety-nine patients with type 3 Klippel-Feil anomaly, a condition where neck vertebrae at and below the third cervical level are fused together. Patients treated between 2004 and 2024 ranged from four to fifty-four years old and all had weakness and sensory problems alongside neck pain and stiffness. Many also carried linked findings such as Chiari formation, a fluid-filled cord cavity, or an atlas fused to the skull.

Every patient received fixation of the top two vertebrae, with no bone removal at any level. Follow-up stretched from three months to nearly sixteen years, and clinical improvement appeared in all patients. The authors argue the fusions and related changes are protective responses to chronic instability at the atlantoaxial joint, not primary defects. On that reading, stabilising that joint can reverse changes long treated as fixed and deliver life-changing gains.
pmc-13507013:
Toni Martin, Howard A Young, and Enitome E Bafor ask, in 2026 mouse work, whether the ovary itself can reshape T cells that enter it. They tracked a rare T cell type that lacks both CD4 and CD8 surface helpers, called double-negative cells. Labeled cells moved from the spleen into the ovary, and many gained CD8 within four days.

Ovary cells alone could drive that gain in lab dishes. Gene data pointed to IL-7, a growth signal made by ovary support cells. Cells without the IL-7 receptor gained CD8 poorly, and mice lacking that signal showed a shifted ovary cell balance. Local cues, not just cell sorting, appear to set ovary T cell traits.
pmc-13507113:
Jia-Yang Cai leads a 2026 team that uncovers a non-enzymatic role for NANS, a sugar-making enzyme, in hormone-sensitive breast cancer. This common cancer type often stops responding to hormone therapy and to CDK4/6 blocker drugs. Tumors with high NANS levels grew faster and resisted both drug types, and patients fared worse.

NANS protected another protein, LATS2, by recruiting a cleanup blocker called USP7, which kept LATS2 from being destroyed. Stable LATS2 then raised hormone receptor and CDK4 levels through a growth pathway. Restoring LATS2 partly revived growth and resistance after NANS loss, in dishes and in mice. Patient samples supported the same chain, which marks NANS as a drug target.
pmc-13507213:
Jeffrey A Lackmann leads a 2026 field study in Costa Rica on whether coffee farms spill leaf fungi into neighboring forest. Dense coffee plantings can amplify fungi, and forest plants related to coffee may catch them more easily. Surveys, air spore traps, and DNA barcoding ran along lines crossing the farm and forest border.

Leaf spot rates fell with distance into forest for coffee relatives, but not for unrelated plants. A dominant coffee leaf fungal order and nineteen coffee-linked types faded in step. Ninety-three coffee-linked fungal types sat at higher modeled levels on forest relatives than on other hosts. Crop borders may quietly reshape forest understory health through relatedness.
pmc-13507513:
Ebenezer Afrifa-Yamoah and co-authors predict new hypertension in Australian men with machine learning in this 2026 paper. Data come from the Ten to Men cohort, linking surveys with drug and health service records. The sample held 13,519 men free of high blood pressure in 2014. New cases over ten years were read from antihypertensive dispensing.

Twenty five baseline features fed four learning models. About 9.7 percent of men developed hypertension in the window. All models scored near 0.77 on discrimination, with XGBoost at the top by a hair. Flexible tree methods barely beat plain logistic regression. Calibration and threshold behavior were reported with intervals. Linked routine data can flag men for early blood pressure checks.
pmc-13508013:
Norihito Oshima leads a team of eleven authors studying Japanese schoolchildren who care for ill family members, focusing on how the burden differs when the illness is mental. Young carers research has grown, but few studies separate recipients' conditions. Eight hundred sixty junior and senior high school students completed surveys of caring activities and psychological difficulties.

About nine percent qualified as young carers. Regression showed that caring for someone with a mental health problem specifically predicted heavier burden and more emotional symptoms. Follow-up analyses detailed the activity and difficulty patterns in that group. The authors argue support services should treat mental-health caregiving households as a distinct, higher-need category rather than folding them into generic carer programs.
pmc-13508213:
Yong Chen and five co-authors test how soon before a stomach camera exam older patients can safely drink water, in 2026 work. Long water bans before the exam leave patients thirsty and uneasy. The study enrolled 252 middle-aged and older patients having the exam without sedation at a cancer hospital in Shaanxi, China. Patients were assigned at random to drink a glass of warm water six, two, or one hour before the exam. Staff scored discomfort, leftover stomach fluid, and how clear the view was.

Patients who drank later reported less thirst, dry mouth, nausea, and weakness than those who waited six hours. View clarity and leftover fluid rates held up in both later-drinking groups, with no choking events. The one-hour group, though, showed a worrying drift toward more leftover fluid. The authors recommend drinking two hours before the exam as the best balance of comfort and safety.
pmc-13508313:
Hilal Boynuyogun and Ezgi Atik compare in 2026 two ways to fix a mild bite fault in teenagers. In Class II Division 2 cases the upper teeth tilt inward and the bite runs deep. Sixteen patients wore light elastic bands early in treatment, fifteen wore a fixed spring appliance, both with self-ligating braces.

Head films before and after showed the fixed appliance moved the lower jaw measure more, while the elastic group gained more vertical change. Both pushed front teeth outward alike. The appliance group reported more pain in the first day, the elastic group more comfort overall. Both routes fixed the molar fit in the same time.
pmc-13508413:
Kristine Sørensen and four co-authors track seven years of ambulance urgency and real patient severity in North Denmark, in 2026 work. Ambulance demand is rising across Western countries, and it is unclear whether callers are sicker or simply quicker to call. Records covered 202,746 adult patients assigned an ambulance from 2017 to 2023. Dispatch urgency was graded A for most urgent or B for less urgent. Severity on scene was scored from vital signs with an early warning tool.

The share graded A slipped from 62 to 59 percent, while B rose in step. True critical illness stayed a steady share within each grade. Raw counts of critical patients still climbed each quarter, driven by rising total volume. Patients also grew older and carried more severe illness over the period. The authors read the pattern as more calls overall rather than looser grading, with real need growing alongside demand.
pmc-13509513:
Pasecinic and colleagues synthesised in 2026 the evidence on prostate cancer grade changing between biopsy and surgery. Grade Group discordance affects a quarter to half of men with localised disease and steers choices about surveillance and nerve-sparing surgery. Thirty-seven primary studies and eight earlier reviews were included, with bias and certainty ratings applied.

Agreement between biopsy and final grade ranged from forty-four to about seventy percent across studies. Upgrading ranged widely, from fourteen to sixty-seven percent, and downgrading from five to twenty-six percent. The lowest biopsy grade carried the highest upgrading risk, at fifty-five to sixty-seven percent. Four predictors earned moderate certainty: MRI scan category, biopsy approach, a PET scan uptake value, and PSA density. The authors say knowing migration risk can sharpen counselling before surgery.
pmc-13510213:
Kammermeier and five co-authors report antibodies found in breast milk in a neuroimmune case, in work from twenty twenty-six. MOG antibody associated disease attacks the myelin sheath of nerves and may follow infections. Whether the antibody passes from blood into breast milk was unreported.

Their patient was a lactating woman aged thirty-eight with severe disease after enterovirus gut infection. She was still breastfeeding at presentation. Detailed clinical and lab work documented the antibody in her milk. The finding raises questions about infant exposure that clinicians had no data to answer before, though it does not by itself prove harm.
pmc-13511113:
Anza Memon and eight co-authors study, in 2026 work, how brain regions link up in people with multiple sclerosis who feel deep fatigue. Thinking troubles in this illness are now tied to shifts in brain networks. A fast brain-reading tool can track those links at rest and during tasks.

In their small trial, patients at rest showed weaker links between the brain's two halves in some wave bands, yet stronger links in a few front and back zones. During a speed task, the same patients drew more on those zones, as if to make up for loss. A review of past studies in the field backed the pattern. The team says such links could serve as marks of network change.
pmc-13511913:
Zhaoyu Zhu and colleagues built FracPINN, a neural network with built-in physics rules, to predict how quantum walks spread under memory-carrying noise. Quantum walks model particles whose paths interfere, and noisy surroundings can slow or speed their spread in odd ways.

The model blends a sequence-learning network with a solver for fractional spread equations, the maths of memory-driven transport. On 3,709 held-out simulations, it beat plain data-driven rivals, cutting average error by 5.3 percent overall. Gains were largest, 13.5 percent, in the slow-spreading regime where memory effects dominate, while other regimes stayed accurate. Once trained, it answers in a fraction of a millisecond instead of seconds of simulation, Zhu reports.
pmc-13512413:
Nie and colleagues analysed in 2026 the genetic variation of a pig virus protein across strains circulating in China. PRRSV-2, the dominant type of a costly swine reproductive and respiratory virus, keeps evolving by mutation and mixing. Its NSP1 protein helps regulate the immune system, but its variation was not fully charted. The team analysed 425 complete NSP1 sequences and charted forty-eight representative strains in detail.

Strains shared as little as about eighty percent of their NSP1 letters, showing wide diversity. Among all sequences, 290 amino-acid sites varied while ninety-three stayed completely conserved. Lineage 8 dominated the set, with over three hundred sequences, while lineage 3 had only four. Seven sites showed strong signs of positive selection, evolution favouring change, supported by three methods.
pmc-13514413:
Sachin Khanduri heads a ten-author team examining, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, whether two simple vessel measures track how severe coronary artery disease looks on CT angiography. The measures are the coronary calcium score and the thickness of the neck artery's inner wall, measured by ultrasound. Seventy-five symptomatic patients at one tertiary centre received both alongside detailed CT scoring of their coronary narrowing.

Calcium scores lined up very strongly with both CT severity scores used, and neck artery thickness showed a moderate to strong link with the same scores. Patients with heavier calcium and thicker neck walls consistently carried more complex disease. Khanduri and colleagues argue that pairing these low-burden measures can help clinicians decide who needs advanced imaging and how tightly to manage prevention. The study covers one centre at one point in time, so it shows association rather than cause.
pmc-13515413:
Jiahui Zhang and colleagues report a kidney study, published in 2026. It asks why acute kidney injury sometimes turns chronic. The work focuses on failed-repair proximal tubule cells. This is a stuck healing state in the kidney's main filter tubing. The team asked whether these cells share a chemical signature. The signature would centre on purine metabolism.

The team combined sixteen mouse data sets. Human kidney cell data were included. Genetic analysis and patient blood samples were also used. The samples came from over two thousand patients. Uric acid and one related compound stood out. They were the only signals conserved across injury models. They peaked during the transition window. The failed-repair cells showed a matching pattern. It was a four-part pattern of purine pathway changes. It appeared in both acute and chronic disease.
pmc-13515513:
Tolga Kunak, Aysegül Ülgen Kunak, and İbrahim Başarıcı examine a blood fat called Lp(a) in people with high blood pressure. Their 2026 study asks if high Lp(a) links to organ damage from that pressure. They focus on plaque in the neck artery and on whether blood pressure dips at night as it should. Past data on these links were thin.

The study covered 80 adults who did not have diabetes. Those with high Lp(a) had plaque far more often and were more apt to lack the night dip. After checks for age, sex, and other risks, both links held. No clear links showed for heart wall growth, eye damage, or kidney measures.
pmc-13515713:
Yuanyu Yu and colleagues redesigned a tiny ultrasound chip, called a CMUT, to push out much stronger sound for medical imaging. Their design pairs a collapse working mode with a grooved membrane, then tunes the groove by smart search.

A plate-bending model first estimated the best groove position, narrowing the space the search had to explore. Tuning groove position, depth, and width together beat tuning them one by one, reaching 72.34 kilopascals of output pressure. Against a plain membrane, the tuned design more than doubled output pressure and lifted the pressure-bandwidth product by about 29 percent. Repeat runs varied by only 0.052 percent in output, Yu notes, showing the search lands on the same design reliably.
pmc-13515913:
Kairat Davletov leads a multicenter team reporting in 2026 how common poor sleep is among heart disease patients in Kazakhstan, and what travels with it. Sleep is now counted among the core measures of heart health, yet data from Central Asia have been scarce.

Nearly four hundred patients, assessed six to twenty-four months after a coronary event, completed a standard sleep questionnaire. About thirty-seven percent slept poorly. Anxiety was the only factor tied to poor sleep across the whole group once other traits were accounted for. Patterns split by sex: anxiety and lower schooling mattered most in women, while retirement and low activity mattered in men. The authors urge routine sleep and mood screening in cardiac follow-up care.
pmc-13516013:
Shakiba Rahimi and colleagues tested whether dietitian-led feeding plans shorten intensive care stays for critically ill patients in Tehran. The trial compared personal plans from dietitians against usual feeding directed by physicians alone.

The study covered 107 patients at two centres who were expected to stay at least five days. After adjustment, the dietitian group left intensive care about 2.5 days sooner than the control group. Nutrition risk scores also improved more in that group on two standard screening tools. New infections hit 7.7 percent of the dietitian group against 38.2 percent of controls, and pressure sores were rarer too. Death rates at 28 days did not differ, so Rahimi calls for randomised trials to confirm the gains.
pmc-13517713:
Wang and colleagues tested in 2026 a cheap clay extract as the calcium source for trapping arsenic with bacterial mineral-making. Microbially induced carbonate precipitation uses bacteria to form calcite that locks up pollutants, but pure calcium chemicals are costly. The team screened natural minerals and chose Baiyin attapulgite clay, richest in calcium with fewest toxic impurities.

In twenty-day water tests, the clay extract roughly doubled arsenic removal versus standard calcium chloride. Removal peaked at about two-thirds of the arsenic for both strains, far above blank controls near one-fifth. In thirty-day soil tests, clay plus bacteria cut the most available arsenic fraction from 0.115 to about 0.03 milligrams per kilogram. The authors present attapulgite extract as a low-cost, sustainable calcium source for large-scale cleanup.
pmc-13518413: Isabel Okeke, Alfonso Munoz, and Castellano report, in a 2026 short paper, a new protein partnership in the machinery that starts protein synthesis. The initiator CERES interacts with the RNA helicase RH37. More than that, CERES bridges the pair: it is what brings RH37 together with eIF4E, a core initiation factor. A three way complex of this kind hints at how cells coordinate the unwinding of RNA messages with the start of their translation.
pmc-13518713:
Caroline M Stüven and seven colleagues study photodynamic therapy for central serous chorioretinopathy in a large 2026 real-world cohort. In that condition, fluid collects under the retina and blurs vision. Light-activated drug therapy is a standard choice when fluid persists, yet doctors know little about which patients respond best or whether waiting hurts results.

Their review covered 115 patients treated at one center. Retinal thickness fell clearly after therapy, fluid cleared fully in 51.3 percent of eyes, and vision improved slightly. About 30 percent of eyes saw the fluid return, while repeat therapy helped again. Waiting longer before treatment linked to a weaker thickness response, supporting earlier action.
pmc-13518813:
Bingxiang Wu, Pengcheng Yang, Yiming He, and Huayang Liang propose a 2026 hybrid model for short-term electricity price forecasting. Good forecasts help markets run and grids stay reliable, yet prices depend on long time patterns plus network connections that most models handle separately. Training mixed data streams together can also create conflicting updates.

Their framework joins a Transformer encoder for time patterns, a graph neural network for network structure, and a gradient surgery method that calms training conflicts. Market records from PJM were fused with simulated sensor data from an IEEE 39-bus grid. Across five runs the fused model posted the lowest average error, with tighter uncertainty than the strongest rival baseline.
pmc-13519013:
Sunghwa Kang and five colleagues compute the best possible single-shot detection limits in 2026 for quantum illumination, a sensing trick that uses entangled light to spot a faint target in noise. Textbook intuition says maximally entangled many-part states should win. Their analysis of three- and four-part systems, spanning qubits up to four-level qudits, says otherwise.

The optimal recipe combines one maximally entangled pair with the rest, because entanglement among the signal parts themselves hurts performance. Multi-part states still beat the classic two-qubit benchmark in several cases. Quantum correlations explained the advantage except for the four-ququart case, which broke the pattern. Kang and co-authors supply exact limits against which real devices can be judged.
pmc-13519413:
Ghazala Khurshid and colleagues tested whether adding stem cells to bone grafts helps dental implants bond more firmly. Published in 2026, the trial split sixty patients at random into two groups, with one group receiving stem cells plus graft and the other graft alone, then followed both for six months. Firm bonding between living bone and implant, called osseointegration, decides whether an implant lasts, especially where bone quality is poor.

The stem-cell group showed higher implant stability scores, greater bone volume gain, and denser new bone than the graft-only group. Every implant survived in the stem-cell group, against a survival rate just under 97 percent in the control group. The authors present stem cells as a promising aid to implant healing, while the small size and short follow-up argue for larger trials. Readers get a compact, hopeful result with its limits in plain view.
pmc-13520113:
David Muhmann and co-authors study outcomes in a rare inherited muscle weakness tied to one gene, in work from 2026. The gene builds part of the receptor that nerves use to trigger muscles. Faults cause weakness from birth, but the range of severity was poorly mapped.

Records covered nine patients from specialist centers, all confirmed by gene testing. Most carried two different faulty copies, and one carried the same fault twice. Onset ranged from birth in most cases to the teen years in two. Eye signs, above all drooping lids, were common. Three patients were followed for over twenty years. The long records help doctors counsel families on what to expect.
pmc-13520313:
Tingjuan Huang and colleagues report in 2026 a targeted delivery system for acute liver injury using tiny vesicles shed by stem cells. Plain vesicles spread widely in the liver, so the team adds vitamin A to steer them toward stellate cells that drive scarring, carrying a gene called REDD1.

Lab tests showed stronger uptake by activated stellate cells, while animal tests showed better liver build-up. Treatment quieted stellate cell activity, lowered inflammation and cell death, and improved liver function and scarring measures. The design pairs a natural targeting trick with gene delivery, offering a template for more precise liver medicines.
pmc-13520713:
Gwyndolin M. Vail and colleagues argue in 2026 for course plans that honour student culture from the design stage. The aim is to keep more underrepresented students in science degrees. Past work coached teachers on delivery. Course blueprints got far less focus.

Good design values what students already know. Good design also links content with lived life. Real issues such as racial health gaps in the pandemic can build science identity. A new 2024 course at a mostly Black college tackles myths about race, genes and AI. Built-in support also cuts the load on each teacher in class.
pmc-13521813:
Older patients carrying diabetes, high blood pressure, and obesity at once eat under many rules. Svetlana Plyassovskaya and co-authors check what actually reaches their blood, in a 2026 study from Central Kazakhstan. Three hundred fifty-one adults aged sixty to ninety reported their diets and gave fasting blood samples.

Shortfalls were everywhere. Potassium, calcium, and vitamin C intakes sat near a third of the national reference values, while sodium ran about double, worse in men. The study's focus is sex: the same nutrient can track differently with glucose, cholesterol, kidney markers, and triglycerides in men and women. In men, total and saturated fat intake already showed links to blood markers in the visible results. The authors argue diet advice for this group should be written separately for men and women, not averaged.
pmc-13522113:
Yuansheng Huang and co-authors map how city growth heats the land in Zhejiang Province, China, in this 2026 study. Replacing fields and forests with pavement traps heat, but which land swaps matter most was unclear. The team combined land-cover maps with summer surface temperature and greenness data across two decades.

Built-up land grew by well over double, mostly by swallowing cropland. Average summer surface heat rose about two degrees, and the hottest readings rose far more. Fresh pavement warmed most and carried the highest heat exposure, while steady forest warmed least. Across cities, more new pavement meant more heat risk, and greener land meant less warming. The authors back green-blue planning in new districts.
pmc-13522213:
Marc Garbey and five co-authors tested ways to read emotion in ALS patients in a 2026 study. The disease weakens muscles and speech, so how a patient feels can be hard to judge, yet it guides personal care. The team asked whether voice analysis could measure emotional response without contact.

They studied twenty-eight patient visits, using clinician ratings, standard function and breathing scores, and features of recorded speech. Patients were classed as matching their physical state, muted, or excessive in expressed concern. Large language models asked to rate concern proved unreliable without expert oversight. Stated concern also clashed with breathing measures. Voice itself carried signal: muted responders sounded loud and sharp with little roughness, while excessive responders sounded the reverse. The authors say voice markers may one day support, not replace, clinical judgment.
pmc-13522513:
Mingguang Cui and seven colleagues published this 2026 synthetic biology study introducing VIPbodies, nanobodies, tiny antibodies, fitted with viral protease switches. Controlling a protein's binding activity, rather than its amount or location, has been a standing challenge. Each VIPbody carries a self-cleaving viral protease that keeps snipping the nanobody apart until an antiviral drug blocks the protease, letting the intact nanobody fold and grab its target.

Starting from prototypes against a red glowing protein, the team built versions answering to different protease-drug pairs, each working alone inside the same cell. Wired into gene circuits, the nanobodies gave drug-tunable gene expression and performed all six canonical Boolean logic operations, the building blocks of cell logic. They also steered cell death both ways, triggering two distinct death programmes through caspase coupling. The authors present VIPbodies as a compact, programmable framework for chemogenetic control of protein function and cell fate.
pmc-13522613:
Anqi Li and colleagues report a materials study, published in 2026. It covers 3D printing of chiral luminous materials. These glow with circularly polarised light. The twist of the light can be controlled. Keeping the twisted order intact during fast printing was a barrier. Curing usually disrupts how layers line up.

The team used a new curing method at the layer boundary. Each layer set within twenty seconds. The printed forms gave off twisted light in all directions. The twist effect was strong. Fine detail reached ten microns. The glow could even flip its handedness. This depended on the light setup or on the growth direction.
pmc-13523213:
Ying Tan and colleagues map the care journey of older patients with chronic lung disease in a 2026 qualitative study. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease care is often fragmented and focused on crises rather than long-term needs. In-depth interviews with older patients were analyzed thematically and assembled into a journey map spanning screening, diagnosis, hospital care, and home rehabilitation.

Themes covered management tasks, emotional experience, and pain points at each stage. Patients struggled to recognize early symptoms, carried ongoing burdens of symptom control, and faced barriers to lung rehabilitation, weak support, nutrition knowledge gaps, and worry about physical activity. The authors argue for a shift from episodic care to continuous support that combines digital tools, self-management education, and community resources across the whole pathway.
pmc-13523513:
Chunyan Zhao and colleagues map, in a 2026 data-driven review, the worldwide landscape of clinical trials for pulmonary fibrosis treatment. Pulmonary fibrosis covers chronic lung diseases where scarring impairs breathing and can end in respiratory failure. Knowing where trials cluster, and what they test, guides future strategy.

Searching a pharma intelligence database produced 1,203 interventional trials. Activity grew in three stages, with a surge in 2020, and concentrated in the United States with 316 trials and China with 285, while only 128 were multinational. Two established drugs still dominated, nintedanib in 94 trials and pirfenidone in 88. Endpoints focused on safety and on forced vital capacity, a breathing measure. The disease range widened beyond idiopathic disease, and the authors call for more collaboration and precision grouping.
pmc-13524613:
Munshi and colleagues studied in 2026 the protein Gα13, a signal relay inside cells, in pancreatitis, the painful inflammation of the pancreas. Samples from people with acute and chronic pancreatitis showed lower levels of this protein. The team then triggered pancreatitis in mice with a standard drug, comparing normal mice with mice whose pancreas lacked the protein, and added rapamycin, a drug that blocks the growth pathway mTOR.

Munshi found that mice without the pancreatic protein suffered worse injury to the enzyme-making acinar cells in both acute and chronic disease. Inflammation rose only mildly, and only in the chronic form. Loss of the protein also raised mTOR signalling. Rapamycin softened the acute injury in these mice but made chronic disease worse, a split result. The authors conclude Gα13 normally protects the pancreas, and mTOR blockade helps only in the acute setting.
pmc-13525813:
Heat therapy can kill liver cancer cells, but the cells fight back by making heat shock proteins, and the light used to warm them does not reach deep. Yuqing Zhu and co-authors built a combined treatment to beat both limits, reported in 2026. Their system joins gold nanorods, which turn light into heat, with a peptide-drug part packed in a microgel that homes to tumors.

An enzyme common in tumors triggers the drug release, and the system also targets the cell's power plants. In cell tests and in mice with liver tumors, the combined system plus laser light suppressed tumors most strongly, lowered the key heat shock protein, and damaged the power plants. Safety checks looked good, and the authors offer the design as a smarter way to deliver cancer drugs.
pmc-13525913:
Lew and co-authors describe technology for measuring blood chemistry continuously during dialysis. Their 2026 paper addresses a practical gap: dialysis prescriptions could be tailored moment by moment if clinicians knew a patient's electrolytes and acid-base status in real time. Point-of-care devices using small whole-blood samples already return sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, urea, gases, and more within minutes.

The authors outline a setup that draws samples from the dialysis arterial line. It runs them on a point-of-care device installed in the machine itself. Results reach the clinician promptly for prescription adjustments. Derived measures such as the anion gap could flag problems like diabetic ketoacidosis or alcohol poisoning mid-session. They also flag pitfalls honestly: whole blood values differ from serum values, and arterial samples differ from venous ones, so readings must be interpreted with the sampling route in mind.
pmc-13526313:
Awang and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of massive biliary ascariasis, infestation of the bile ducts by the roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides, in a 73-year-old woman. The disease is common in tropical Southeast Asia, where warm climate, poor sanitation, and farm work sustain transmission. Worms wandering from the gut can block the bile ducts and mimic gallstone colic. Her ultrasound showed the worms in the ducts, a recurrence after earlier endoscopic clearance despite prior gallbladder removal.

Treatment used endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, a scope procedure that both confirms and clears duct blockage, and the team extracted fourteen worms. Anti-worm medicine after clearance is standard to kill gut worms and prevent recurrence. The authors note that such a heavy burden, especially in an elderly patient after gallbladder surgery, is rarely documented. They review imaging choices from ultrasound first to MR and CT when the picture is unclear.
pmc-13526713:
Christian Michelitsch and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-six clinical study asking whether four screws suffice to fix upper arm bone fractures with locking plates. These shoulder-end fractures are common and prone to collapse or screw problems. Minimally invasive guides often allow only four screws in the bone head.

Over one hundred consecutive patients were grouped by screw count. Function was scored with a standard shoulder measure. X-ray checks tracked angle holding, screw penetration, and bone death. Outcomes at about eighteen months were comparable between the four-screw and more-screw groups. The simpler fixation appears adequate.
pmc-13527613:
Urszula Radzikowska and others comment, in a 2026 editorial, on new evidence that glutamine breakdown acts as a metabolic checkpoint for protective immunity against tuberculosis. The discussed study found the enzyme GLS1, which starts glutaminolysis, raised in blood cells from patients with active tuberculosis and rising further after bacterial stimulation.

Blocking the enzyme in that study weakened the Th1 and Th17 helper T-cell responses that defend against the bacterium. It also cut energy production and let bacteria survive better inside macrophages. The effect was traced to histone marks maintained by a GLS1-derived metabolite and reversible with supplements. The editorialists stress context. The same checkpoint drives harmful responses in autoimmune disease, where blocking helps, yet sustains protective responses in tuberculosis, where blocking harms, shaping how future GLS1 drugs should be judged.
pmc-13527913:
Mohd Rashid Khan and seven colleagues present a 2026 systematic review of basket and umbrella trials in children's precision medicine. In a basket trial, one targeted drug is tested across several diseases sharing a genetic marker; an umbrella trial tests several drugs within one disease, split by marker. Such designs suit rare childhood conditions where patient numbers are small.

Searching three databases produced 1,867 records, of which 28 studies met the criteria for the final review, and topic modeling of 76 articles mapped the field's main themes. Basket designs appeared more often than umbrella designs, especially in early cancer and rare-disease work. The authors find these trials can speed drug development, provided statistical planning is careful and regulators are involved early.
pmc-13528113:
Kidney cancer of the clear cell kind ends very differently for different patients, and Zhenduo Yu and co-authors build a survival score from blood inflammation and tumor features. Their 2026 study pools more than sixteen hundred surgical patients from several centers across fifteen years. A shrinking selection method kept twelve candidate clues.

Five stood on their own: tumor grade, dead tissue inside the tumor, platelet count, whether the cancer had returned or spread, and one combined inflammation index. Folded into a chart, they sorted patients into risk groups with clearly different survival, and the chart's accuracy held up on held-back patients. The tool aims to guide follow-up intensity.
pmc-13528713:
Shots guard adults from flu, lung germs, and Covid, yet take up runs low in many lands. Gamze Şanlıdağ İşbilen and co-authors survey take up in Türkiye in a 2026 study. Their form went to adults of all ages and asked about shots, health, and grounds for a no.

Near three in ten had a flu shot, and near all had a Covid shot. The old and the long ill led the flu and lung shot counts. Health staff also took flu shots more oft. The top ground for a flu no was a sense that the shot was not needed. For Covid, plain no wish and fear of side harm led. The team urges more teaching and talk on shots.
pmc-13528813:
Rhoubi Asmae and colleagues report a 2026 hospital laboratory study from Oujda, Morocco, on iron stores and blood sugar control in diabetes. The team reviewed records for 1,412 patients who had both serum ferritin, a marker of body iron, and HbA1c, a measure of average blood sugar, tested during 2023.

Ferritin showed no link with HbA1c in the 214 patients with type 1 diabetes. In the 1,198 patients with type 2 diabetes, the link was strongly positive, and ferritin rose steadily as sugar control worsened. Because the study looked at one point in time, the authors note it cannot prove ferritin changes cause poor control, and they call for follow-up studies over time.
pmc-13528913:
Peyton Carpen and Matthew Greenblatt comment in 2026 on a study linking diet fats to bone growing where it should not. Such stray bone can follow trauma or burns and leaves pain and stiff joints, with no good drug care yet.

The study they discuss found that fatness raised the risk, but the driver was not extra calories. A class of fats common in western diets piled up at the young stray bone site. There the fats fed a signal that pushed cells toward bone making. Carpen and Greenblatt back diet change or drugs aimed at that signal as paths to cut the risk.
pmc-13529113:
Wang and colleagues reported a 2026 case in which fever after stroke turned out to be caused by the antibiotic rather than by a new infection. A 45-year-old woman with a brain infarction complicated by pneumonia linked to her stroke received piperacillin-tazobactam. During treatment she developed high fevers while her neutrophils, infection-fighting white blood cells, kept falling.

Wang describes a search for infectious and other causes pointed to drug fever combined with agranulocytosis. A drug-reaction scoring scale rated the link as probable. Agranulocytosis is a near-absence of neutrophils, and her lowest count fell to critically low levels. Stopping the antibiotic and giving a growth factor that boosts white cell production, plus adjusting other antimicrobials, resolved the fever and restored her counts. There was no recurrence over a year of follow-up. The authors urge blood monitoring during long courses of this antibiotic.
pmc-13529613:
Leonard Knoedler and eight colleagues mine United States hospital data on chin surgery outcomes in a 2026 study. The database covered inpatient genioplasty from 2000 to 2022. It held 485 admissions, with a mean age near thirty-two. Just over half the patients were women. Most had private insurance and lived in richer areas.

Complications appeared in about ten percent of stays. Older patients suffered them at about fifteen percent, versus six percent in younger ones. Bone-cutting chin surgery made up about sixty-four percent of cases. It cost more, lasted longer in hospital, and drew more complications than soft methods. Long stays tracked with complications in both subgroups. Lower-income patients stayed longer despite similar complication rates. The authors flag fairness gaps and call for larger prospective work.
pmc-13529713:
Poonyaporn Poolborwornrak and three colleagues build a two-step cleanup for microplastics in lab wastewater in a 2026 study. Polyethylene bits from 0.15 to 1 millimeter were the target. Step one used clumping chemicals to gather the bits. Three clumpers were tried, with chitosan as a helper. Step two passed the water through a simple sand column.

Clumping worked best at neutral pH. One agent, PAC, cleared about seventy-seven percent of the finest bits alone. Alum and iron chloride trailed. Coupling clumping with sand at a slow flow changed the game. Total removal hit 99.93 percent in the best run. The authors pitch the pairing as cheap and scalable. Real wastewater, with mixed plastics and dirt, is the next test.
pmc-13529813:
Zoo animals live with human-made noise, from visitor chatter to events and machinery, and keepers want to know what that noise does to welfare. Tamara Kruse and Mark Flint survey the research in this 2026 scoping review. They searched widely and sorted what has actually been tested in zoological settings.

From an opening pool of 1,608 papers, thirty-one studies formed the core set, nearly all published since 2014. Mammals drew most of the work, above all primates, with birds next and reptiles rare. Heightened watchfulness was the behavior recorded most often. Thirteen papers suspected a negative effect on welfare, while the rest found none, could not tell, or did not judge welfare directly. Common advice included teaching visitors, adding sound barriers, and giving animals a quieter place to retreat to.
pmc-13530113:
Meng Cao and colleagues reviewed double emulsions that carry both water-loving and fat-loving nutrients for athletes. Published in 2026, the review covers water-in-oil-in-water droplets, which nest one water phase inside oil inside water, allowing two cargo types in one vehicle. Demand for tailored sports nutrition keeps growing as athletes seek performance, muscle, and recovery gains.

The review explains how cargo releases, why these droplets break down, and how to stabilize them, then surveys preparation methods and fabrication techniques. Sports uses center on supplements that deliver bioactive compounds in stable, functional forms. Future work points toward athlete-specific designs with better stability and targeted release. Readers get a design guide for a promising but finicky delivery format.
pmc-13530213:
Fengmin Xu, Zhenting He, and Qianqian Li search in 2026 for a gene signal that tracks inflammatory bowel disease activity without invasive testing. The illness mixes disturbed gut metabolism with a disordered immune setting. Machine learning sifted genes tied to a form of regulated cell death shaped by metabolism.

Three genes survived strict checks across separate patient groups and rose together during active disease phases. Single-cell data placed each gene in distinct gut cell types, from immune to lining to support cells. The trio links metabolism, immune entry, and cell death, offering a candidate signature for sorting patients.
pmc-13530413:
Hye-Ji Han, Hyun Mee Ryu, and a large team ask if pre pregnancy exercise cuts two forms of pregnancy diabetes in Korea, in work from 2026. One form is held by diet alone, while the other needs insulin shots. Past work rarely split the two forms when it judged exercise gains.

More than three thousand women were tracked from before birth through after birth. Muscle build exercise before pregnancy cut risk of the diet form by about half. More days of such work cut risk still more. No clear cut showed for the insulin form. Pre birth muscle work may thus guard moms in a set way.
pmc-13531113:
Shun Kawamura and seven co-authors tested in 2026 whether a sleep drug can shield the testes of rats from a cancer drug's harm. The cancer drug, cisplatin, can impair sperm and hormone output, and few guards exist. The sleep drug acts on melatonin receptors and is known to protect organs from swelling and cell death. Thirty-two young male rats were split into four groups for a week of dosing.

Cisplatin alone damaged the sperm-making tubes, cut sperm count and movement, and lowered testosterone. Adding the sleep drug softened each of those harms and eased tissue damage. Gene activity for hormone making recovered in part, while death and swelling signals fell. The authors propose the drug as a candidate for guarding fertility during chemotherapy.
pmc-13531213:
Florin-Leontin Lazar and co-authors describe in 2026 a stent-sparing strategy for a frail woman with disease in all three coronary arteries. The 76-year-old arrived with a heart attack pattern short of full blockage, plus a hard calcified branch junction and one fully closed artery. Shock struck when a side branch closed mid-procedure.

Drug-coated balloons reopened both branches without new stents after careful preparation that included shock-wave calcium cracking. A later session opened the closed artery with a mixed balloon and single-stent plan. One-year imaging showed healthy vessel widening, favoring minimal metal in frail patients.
pmc-13531713:
Ovie Martin Albert and Alexander Arthur compare fatal drug harms across rich countries from 2015 to 2023, in a 2026 review. Death counts have risen in many places, yet each nation counts cases in its own way, so raw league tables can mislead.

The pair lined up public data from the USA, Canada, England and Wales, and Europe. US deaths rose fast through 2022, then dipped a bit, while deaths in England and Wales kept climbing. In Canada, deaths tied to three or more drugs rose from 20 percent in 2018 to 42 percent in 2023. How deaths get logged, by event date or by filing date, also shifts the trend lines. Care during release from prison stood out as a weak link.
pmc-13531813:
Shizuka Kudo, Tomoko Kodama, and Yuri Sasaki map social drivers of older adult suicide across Japanese medical regions in a 2026 ecological study. About 40 percent of Japanese suicide deaths in 2020 involved people aged 60 and over. Public data on income, living arrangements, work, habits, and illness were set against regional suicide rates.

Among men, rates rose with high blood pressure, smoking, daily drinking, living alone, and older-worker employment. Among women, rates fell where more mental health professionals practiced and where taxpayer income ran higher. The split pattern argues for prevention plans fitted to local conditions and to each sex.
pmc-13531913:
Donald A Redelmeier, C Mark Cheung, and Akash M Patel test in 2026 whether gut protein leakage explains low blood protein after heart surgery. Low albumin after major surgery is common and ominous, yet its cause stays murky. Thirty-eight consecutive cardiac surgery patients gave paired blood and stool samples for a clearance test of a marker protein.

Low albumin appeared in about 82 percent after surgery. The leakage test flagged protein-losing gut in about 39 percent. Every positive leakage result came with low albumin, giving perfect positive prediction in this small group, while sensitivity stayed near half. Leakage may explain some cases only.
pmc-13534213:
Sofia Solari-Hernandez and colleagues review in 2026 immune problems in Down syndrome, a condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21. Clinically, people face higher risk of severe lung infections and weaker, shorter vaccine responses. Studies report more hospital care and deaths plus faster fading of antibody levels after vaccines. Readers gain a frame for tailoring prevention and vaccine plans for this group.
pmc-13534413:
Jeong-Hyun Ryu and colleagues test in 2026 how dose changes the effects of zinc oxide nanoparticles on bone-forming cells. The lowest strength boosted cell growth, survival, and bone gene activity, with more enzyme action and mineral build-up. The highest strength harmed cells clearly and showed strong toxicity. Readers learn that low doses may support bone repair while high doses must be avoided in material design.
pmc-13534613:
Jinning Liu and colleagues study in 2026 how to find and protect critical nodes in layered networks that link hospitals, water supply, and power supply. Two ranking methods together flagged both central nodes and unstable nodes as high risk for spreading failure. Protecting just a small set of flagged nodes curbed early cascade spread in tests. Managers gain a focused protection plan for linked infrastructure under stress.
pmc-13534713:
Jennifer M Mongiovi and colleagues study in 2026 whether contraceptive history shapes immune cell patterns inside ovarian tumours. Non-hormonal devices create local inflammation in the uterus, while pills suppress ovulation, and both link to ovarian cancer risk in unlike ways. High-grade serous tumours held the highest shares of T cells overall. Ever using a device linked modestly to more killer T cells in tumours, while pill use for a year or more linked to fewer. Device use also linked to more exhausted T cells in some subgroups.
pmc-13535413:
W Jared Brewer and co-authors hunt for markers of outlook in papillary kidney cancer in a 2026 study. This form is the second most common kidney cancer in adults. After surgery, doctors judge risk from tumor size, node spread, and grade, since no molecular marker is in routine use.

The team built a grid of tumor samples and nearby normal tissue, then mapped proteins in place across them. Patterns tied to later return of the cancer could sharpen those judgments. Such markers would help decide who needs close watch or extra treatment after surgery, and who can safely be spared both.
pmc-13536513:
Suzanne Butler wrote a 2026 theory article arguing that poverty should be understood as a story unfolding over a life, not a fixed state. Research on poverty swings between two poles. One side blames structures and scarce resources. The other blames personal behavior. Butler argues both sides make the same mistake about human agency, treating it as either missing or a matter of morals.

Drawing on feminist sociology, life-course research, and narrative methods, the article offers a new frame: poverty as biography in motion. Lives in poverty move in patterned ways, with turbulence, stalling, and fragile gains. Feelings are central in this account: emotion is the channel through which hard conditions are lived and choices are made. Agency becomes situated, shared, and shaped by feeling over time. The author offers this grammar to explain why poverty endures and why change is often fragile.
pmc-13536613:
Mengtong Sun and colleagues track in 2026 whether insulin resistance scores predict combined heart and metabolic disease in people with fatty liver disease. Over 109,000 UK Biobank adults with fatty liver but no such disease at entry were followed for near sixteen years. Nine scores built from blood sugar, fats, and body measures were compared.

Higher scores on all nine meant higher risk of combined disease later. Scores mixing waist and height or body mass led the list for risk and added small gains to standard prediction. Blood markers for inflammation and organ strain explained part of the links seen.
pmc-13537813:
Shaban Sinnokrot and co-authors measure how worn out nursing students in Jordan feel by online learning, and how that weariness links to mental workload, in a 2026 paper. The team sent an online questionnaire to undergraduate nursing students at public and private universities in the spring of 2025. Standard scales gauged digital fatigue, the exhaustion of constant screen work, and the several kinds of cognitive load that study imposes.

Five hundred thirty-seven students replied, reporting fairly high fatigue and load. One kind of load, the kind imposed by poor teaching design rather than by the subject itself, showed the strongest crowding at the top of the scale. Digital fatigue tracked that load even after accounting for age, grades, and other factors. Study year, university type, and daily hours on devices also mattered. The authors point at course design as the lever teachers control most directly.
pmc-13538413:
Zhuming Bi and co-authors present a digital twin case for judging remaining life of used storage racks in a 2026 study aimed at small and medium firms. Virtual copies can guide reuse decisions, yet real benefit cases for smaller firms stay scarce. Four selected racks were modeled digitally and tested under worst-case loads for safety margins. Changing loads in design studies then showed how safety margins respond, supporting reuse and recycling choices.

Models supplied managers with evidence-based safety factors for each rack under harsh loading. Load sweeps clarified which racks tolerate heavier reuse and which need limits or retirement. The authors frame the assistive project as proof that twin methods can deliver practical sustainability gains beyond large firms, linking longer resource life to leaner manufacturing.
pmc-13538713:
Max Falkenberg and co-authors call for a fairer global science of political polarization in a 2026 paper. A globally relevant, interdisciplinary understanding is still missing, and the authors argue for renewed effort to build one.

They sort findings into insights that hold across countries, effects unique to specific contexts, and gaps in the literature. Closing those gaps needs research beyond wealthy democracies. The paper is a roadmap for funders and scholars who want polarization science that travels.
pmc-13539713:
Hyein Shin and Woohyeon Kim split health literacy into components and link each to health behaviors among South Korean adults in a 2026 survey study. Higher active engagement raised odds of regular activity and weight control attempts. Compliance orientation lowered activity odds yet raised current drinking odds. pmc-13540213:
Marta Szulik, Luis Hortells, and Manuel Rosa-Garrido wrote a 2026 editorial opening a special issue on epigenetics in heart health and disease. Gene sequence alone cannot explain how the heart grows, adapts, ages, and fails. Chemical marks on DNA and its packaging form a flexible control layer.

The collected studies treat these marks as one connected system, not lone events. Multi layer data hunts in one paper found a new driver of stress related heart thickening, then proved it in cells. Other pieces map methylation shifts in failure. The editors argue the field has moved from describing marks to finding drug targets among them.
pmc-13540913:
Mohammad Heidarzadeh and co-authors catalogue what blocks well-run regional care for mothers and newborns in this 2026 review. In many places it works unevenly, and the reasons are scattered across the literature.

Clinical surprises and unsafe transfers came first, then distance and poverty, cultural resistance, and strain on local doctors' standing. Money rules that reward rivalry, weak transport, and thin infrastructure in poor regions rounded out the list. The authors offer the map to planners as a checklist for reform. Fixes, they argue, must be systemic and shaped to each setting.
pmc-13541213:
Jay Fox and Jeffery Martens survey automated biomedical laboratories and chart how ordinary research centers could adopt them. Two decades of growth lead from single liquid handlers to cloud labs and self-driving systems that propose their own tests.

The review proposes levels of autonomy to sort the field, then judges which classes fit shared core facilities. Standardized preparation and screening workcells, they argue, adapt most readily. Their roadmap aims to spread automation's speed beyond elite centers, into the shared resources most scientists actually use.
pmc-13541913:
Ling Wang leads a 2026 five-year prospective study linking CT-measured changes in muscle and fat to declining strength and mobility in older adults. Muscle performance change sits at the heart of sarcopenia, the age-related wasting that leads to frailty.

One hundred twenty neighbourhood volunteers had CT scans, grip strength, and a timed stand-and-walk test at entry and again five years later. Muscle size and density shrank across back, pelvis, and thigh compartments, while fat grew more in women. In women each unit of front-thigh muscle loss tracked with weaker grip and slower walking. In men, one deep trunk muscle's density behaved in the opposite, protective direction.
pmc-13542013:
Nicholas Streicher and Hermela Wubet present a study the catalog lists under 2026. A rare gene disease makes a transport protein fold wrong and clog nerves and heart. All carried disease codes for both the amyloid condition and nerve damage, plus a confirmed gene variant. One variant dominates this patient group.

Each case was graded by how strongly the records backed the nerve diagnosis. Treatment with protein stabilizers and gene silencers was then checked against that grade. Weak documentation may steer real treatment choices, which is the worry. Nerve clinics get a caution on coding habits: a code is not proof. Tighter exams before labeling could spare patients wrong paths and focus costly gene drugs where nerve harm is firm.
pmc-13542413:
Jiahui Chu and co-authors review sound as a tool to move tiny things in a 2026 paper. Sound waves can push, hold, and sort grains and cells with no touch at all, and they pass deep into fluids and flesh with ease.

The review first lays out how sound is made and how it presses on matter, then sorts the gear that shapes the sound field. Work has used the push to trap, carry, group, sort, and lay out targets in neat ranks. A fast-growing branch builds tiny swimmers that sound drives, some by their odd shape, some by bursts of bubbles or sharp edges that hum. Swarms of such swimmers can move as one and steer. The authors chart the gains and the blocks for use in care, in new materials, and in fine making.
pmc-13542613:
Tahseen Ahmed and fifteen co-authors connect a gene switch to childhood glaucoma in a 2026 paper. Congenital glaucoma deforms the eye before birth and blinds without treatment. The WT1 variants clustered in a region that exports the protein from the nucleus. In fish embryos, suppressing wt1 together with pax6 disrupted eye formation. pmc-13543413:

Among 266 cases, most children were under age two and just over half were male. The team reviews what form was eaten, where it happened, and who owned the product. They test whether poverty of the home area links to social work input, child protection reports, and safe discharge plans. The aim is fair and even care for all families after such events.
pmc-13543613:

Modeled death at 30 days ran near 27 percent under usual care. Score-guided plans cut that rate by about six to seven points across three cut rules. The team calls the gains a lead for real trials, not a rule for bedside use yet.
pmc-13543913:
Manman Xu and co-authors build a tiny drug-like catalyst in 2026 that attacks tumors on two fronts at once. Tumors fend off attack by burning food to soak up harm. A drug that only stirs that harm often falls short, since the tumor keeps its food lines open.
