The blend rests on a high-mix base that boosts the act. Lab results back the paired strike. Cancer teams gain a design that starves and strikes in one pass.
pmc-13544113:
Emanuel Heil and co-authors study sex differences in a freezing-balloon treatment for a faulty heart rhythm in a 2026 paper. The rhythm fault, atrial fibrillation, is more common in men, but women bear worse symptoms and more return of the fault after treatment. Body shape differences may explain part of that gap.

The team reviewed more than two thousand first-time patients at six German hospitals. All got the same fixed-size freezing balloon to seal off the lung veins. They compared how the freeze doses landed in men and women and how often the fault returned. Equal tools may not mean equal treatment.
pmc-13544613:
Ahmet Akcan reviewed recent human research in two thousand twenty-six on microbes in the airways and gut of people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Lung function tests alone do not explain flare-ups, steady inflammation, or why treatments help some patients more than others. Microbe studies promised answers but often disagree.

Results swing with sampling site, contamination control, sequencing choices, and medicines patients take, all reviewed in detail. Lower airway variety and dominance by normally resident but harmful microbes appear repeatedly. Effects of antibiotics and inhaled steroids on these communities are also covered. Lung doctors gain a guide to reading a noisy field with care.
pmc-13545213:
Jamil Hallak and AH Abdul Hafez presented a 2026 planning model for rebuilding waste services in Idlib Governorate in northwest Syria, a region recovering from conflict. Their mathematical model chooses where to place transfer stations, treatment plants, waste-to-energy facilities, and landfills while weighing cost, carbon emissions, and two kinds of risk. Formal local data were scarce, so the case drew on field information, geographic analysis, and judgments from eleven experts.

The preferred design opened three transfer stations, two treatment facilities, one energy plant, and two landfills, producing a large yearly electricity output. Carbon taxes, subsidies, and permit trading mainly shifted costs rather than the network itself. Readers get a template for infrastructure planning where records and institutions are thin.
pmc-13546713:
Hypatia Thobejane, Tlou Grace Manyelo, and Busisiwe Gunya fed Creole goats leaf meal from the Muni tree in 2026 to see whether a local plant feed can help control gut worms. Sixteen yearling male goats were assigned diets containing none of the leaf meal or three rising shares, up to 30 percent, for 42 days. Worm egg counts in dung were measured at the end.

Results were mixed across parasite types. One worm genus was absent at the middle dose yet appeared more at higher doses, while whipworm eggs and coccidian cysts fell as leaf meal rose. The authors read the pattern as enough promise to justify further work on the tree as a natural supplement, given that commercial dewormers are costly and resistance is growing.
pmc-13546813:
Yang Hu, Qiao Liu, and Xuyang Lu compare microbes living on glaciers in a 2026 study. The debris that covers some glaciers hosts rich life despite cold, thin air, and scarce food. Warming now threatens these little-known communities. The team sampled five debris-covered glaciers in two ranges of the southeast Tibetan Plateau.

Gene reading named the bacteria and fungi in the debris. A few families dominated each group, showing that specialist communities do form on glacier surfaces. Debris from one range held notably less varied bacteria, likely filtered by soil acidity and carbon levels. Fungal variety differed little between ranges. The study maps how place and chemistry shape life on melting ice.
pmc-13546913:
Ehsan Ahmadifar and co-authors present a 2026 study on feeding farmed carp a germ-fighting peptide wrapped in tiny carriers. The peptide, a natural defense molecule, breaks down easily, which limits its use in feed. Wrapping it in nano-scale shells could protect it and raise its effect.

Young carp were fed for eight weeks on a plain diet, a diet with the plain peptide, or diets with the peptide in one of two carriers. The fish were then exposed to a harmful bacterium. Growth, blood measures, and immune responses were tracked before and after the challenge. The trial tests whether wrapping makes the peptide a stronger shield for farmed fish.
pmc-13547213:
Doudou Cao, Enrico R. Crema, and Emma Pomeroy analyzed in 2026 body measurements from more than 90,000 adults in 213 groups across China to untangle what shapes human body form in one country. Their statistical models weighed climate, altitude, town versus countryside living, language group, and time period against height, weight, sitting height, and body breadth.

Bodies grew larger over recent decades, especially heavier, in step with economic development and city living. Northern groups stayed taller and heavier than southern ones, and men and women responded in similar ways. Rainfall, rather than temperature, was the strongest climate link, possibly acting through food production and disease. Highland and northeastern groups broke the general patterns, hinting at altitude adaptation and population history.
pmc-13547413:
Megan E Parker and a multinational team evaluated in 2026 crackers fortified with crickets and black soldier fly larvae as school snacks in Madagascar, where children often lack protein and iron. Laboratory checks cleared the snacks on germs and heavy metals and found solid nutrition, with protein near twelve to fourteen grams per hundred grams plus useful iron and zinc. The real test was whether children would eat them.

Among 187 schoolchildren, about four in five ate at least eighty percent of their portion, and nearly nine in ten chose the insect crackers over a plain control when offered both. Savory versions beat sweet ones. Caregivers in focus groups spoke positively and reported fuller, more energetic children. The authors present insect snacks as acceptable and safe.
pmc-13548013:
Jae-woo Lee reviews in 2026 how to ease cancer pain in bone for patients in hospice and end of life care. Bone spread is common in myeloma, breast, and prostate cancers. It brings steady pain, pain on movement, breaks, cord pressure, and high blood calcium.

Care starts with careful checks that split steady pain from movement pain. Plans follow the world pain ladder, yet many hospice patients need strong opioids early, dose rotation, and rescue doses. Added drugs, bone drugs, and team care all play a part. The review centers on comfort and low burden, in line with each patient's goals and the idea of total pain.
pmc-13548213:
Ibrahim Alghamdi and co-authors lay out in 2026 a study plan to test whether two blood markers, added to clinical signs, can sort stroke types fast at the hospital door. Telling a brain bleed from a blocked large vessel early is key to good care. One marker rises in bleeds, the other links to large vessel blocks, and both can be measured with a bedside test.

The study will enroll at least 257 patients with suspected stroke within six hours of onset at two United Kingdom centers. Blood and clinical data are taken on arrival, and final diagnoses are recorded before discharge. The team will build models and report how well they separate the two stroke types from other causes.
pmc-13548713:
Jian Zhou and colleagues hunt in the blood for a T cell type that foreshadows success of combined chemotherapy and immunotherapy in advanced lung cancer, in a 2026 study. The patients came from a phase two trial of first-line treatment for non-small cell lung cancer. The team profiled their blood immune cells with multicolor flow methods. On samples from eight patients they layered single-cell gene and receptor sequencing.

A late-differentiated killer T cell marked by missing CD28 and carrying KLRG1 stood out: patients starting with more of these cells, and keeping them during treatment, fared better. Far from being exhausted leftovers, the cells had expanded in clones and could feed the tumor with fresh fighters. A zinc-linked pathway governed the subset, and adding zinc in mice strengthened treatment. The authors propose a convenient blood test and a possible zinc pairing.
pmc-13549313:
Yunyan Wang, Li Hong, Ping Wang, and Zhi Cheng reply to a letter critiquing their trial of perineural esketamine for pain relief after total knee replacement. The critics raised questions about methods, statistics, outcome reporting, and how the drug might work. The authors answer each point in turn.

They explain that mismatched wording about pain score timings across sections came from editing errors during revision, not from any change to the pre-set protocol. Corrections have been made to the text. They also clarify their handling of repeated testing and their reading of the drug's mechanism. Response letters like this one form part of the trial's public record.
pmc-13549913:
Avishikta Banerjee and co-authors review whether vibrating root-canal sealer into place with ultrasound beats older placement tricks. A good sealer layer in root canal work must creep into tiny side tubes, coat the walls, and leave few voids. The team gathered lab studies from 2000 onward under standard review rules; ten qualified, six with poolable numbers.

Ultrasound-assisted placement drove sealer far deeper into the wall tubes and covered much more of the canal wall. Lab reports also favored ultrasound for surface fit, fewer voids, and stronger bonding when pushed. The catch is that every study was in vitro, on extracted teeth, and results varied wildly between labs. The authors refuse to claim clinical superiority. They call for trials in real patients before dentists change their routine.
pmc-13551013:
Yukun Zhang and co-authors scan brains in two postures in a 2026 study. Cerebral small vessel disease alters the brain's resting activity, but scans are almost always done lying down. Standing changes blood flow and may reveal faults a flat scan hides. The team compared patients and healthy controls in both upright and supine positions.

Forty-one patients and thirty controls underwent scans in each posture. Local synchrony of activity, called regional homogeneity, shifted with posture across wide brain areas. Upright, patients showed higher synchrony in a frontal control region than controls, and that excess tracked with worse thinking scores and heavier disease burden. Posture itself becomes a variable future brain studies may need to respect.
pmc-13551513:
Eren Demir published a 2026 paper presenting a decision support tool meant to make hospital planning usable by managers and clinicians, not only modeling experts. Hospitals must balance rising demand against limited beds and staff, and existing tools often cover only parts of a system. The tool runs a discrete event simulation, a computer model of patient flow, spanning specialties and their connections with 360 input parameters.

Scenarios for 2023 to 2027 produced activity levels, bed and clinic needs, theatre use, and financial effects. One scenario, a virtual ward where patients are monitored at home, cut backlogs and eased resource strain from 113 percent to 80 percent in the reported run. Demir presents the adaptable tool as a way to test changes before committing resources.
pmc-13551713:
Jinhuo Wang, leading eight colleagues, published a 2026 laboratory study of whether salvaged blood can be safely returned during liver cancer surgery. Machines that collect, wash, and return a patient's own blood save donor blood, yet might also return cancer cells. Blood from twenty patients was sampled at three stages: from the surgical field, after salvage processing, and after an added leukocyte depletion filter.

Cancer cells appeared in most samples at every stage, though counts fell significantly after processing in the reported comparisons. After three weeks of culture, cancer cell clusters grew only from untreated field samples, and none were detected after filtration. The authors read the combined process as stripping salvaged blood of viable tumor cells.
pmc-13552013:
Raghavendra Kembhavi, Jojin Chitten, and Siddharath Parameshwar report a rare combined knee and leg injury, in work from 2026. A crash broke the shin bone and tore two key knee supports at their anchor points. Such a mix is very rare and easy to miss at first check.

Their patient was a 25-year-old man hurt in a road crash. The shin break was open and was fixed at once with a rod inside the bone. Later, scope surgery fixed the rear knee ligament with strong threads tied to screws already in place. The side ligament complex was also repaired. The report warns that missed knee damage can leave lasting wobble and harm.
pmc-13552113:
In a 2026 study, Flor Torres-Juarez and ten colleagues examined a tuberculosis bacterium enzyme that appears to restrain the microbe's own virulence. Protein kinase F had poorly defined roles, though cell work tied it to limiting inflammasome activation. The team infected mice with a mutant strain lacking the kinase gene, comparing lung bacterial growth, inflammation, and survival against normal and restored strains.

The mutant made far more of a pro-virulence surface lipid and grew dramatically more in mouse lungs by late infection in the reported counts, with heavier lung inflammation alongside. The effect persisted in mice lacking the inflammasome sensor, ruling out that pathway as the explanation. Highly susceptible mice also died sooner with the mutant, leading the authors to cast the kinase as a brake on virulence through lipid suppression.
pmc-13552313:
Ecaterina Vasenina and co-authors test amino acid supplements for calf recovery after hard exercise in a 2026 trial. Lengthening-style contractions damage muscle, leaving soreness and swelling for days. Essential amino acids fuel muscle building, so they might speed repair.

Thirty-six active young men were split into supplement, placebo, and no-treatment groups. All performed a punishing calf routine, then recovered for seventy-two hours while soreness, pain thresholds, and calf size were tracked. Damage signs appeared as expected. The supplement group reported less soreness at twenty-four hours than the placebo group, and their calf swelling settled back to normal by seventy-two hours while the placebo group's stayed up. Tendon thickness did not respond. The authors call the benefit modest.
pmc-13553113:
Tadas Kargelis, Zhen K Lam, and David Mangan present a 2026 journal article on pitfalls in measuring dietary fiber. Official methods split fiber by chain length using liquid chromatography, and the border between two chain classes decides the count. The team ran 74 carbohydrate standards through five column setups and scored how correctly each sorted them.

One column brand, doubled in series, sorted best. The sugar alcohol maltitol caused trouble: alone it could be fenced out, but baked with starch it spawned an extra peak that inflated fiber readings by up to eight percent. The authors give column guidance and warn labs about the sweetener artifact.
pmc-13553313:
van den Bulck and co-authors seek pro pact on what helps old hosts curb drink. Drink strain in old age needs care plans built to fit that stage. The team asked pros to pact on parts that work and how they work. Parts split by how grave the drink strain runs in each host. A three-round Delphi poll ran in the Netherlands for the pact. Round one held 20 pros from care, search, law, and life past.

Rounds two and three held 18 pros each in the poll. Pros scored 85 parts for worth and fit in the first rounds. Ways the parts work got scored for probe force as well. Round three ranked 40 parts and 39 ways that won pact. Top parts met age-tied needs and the drink-smoke pair at once. Talk style and a warm, keen ear ranked high too.
pmc-13553713:
Temesgen Assefa Gelaw and eight co-authors review how microbes help crops survive a changing climate, in this 2026 paper. Heat, drought, salt, and pests press farms worldwide, and yields suffer. Plants, though, host partner microbes on roots and leaves that can buffer stress, a resource farming has barely tapped.

The review explains the partnership's machinery: microbes make plant hormones, tame damaging oxygen species, and switch on plant immune defenses. Roots leak sugars and signals that feed and steer their partners, and microbes talk back with their own signals. New gene-scale tools now reveal candidate genes for hardier crops. The authors look ahead to designed microbe mixes, built with AI and synthetic biology, that could keep yields up while easing chemical use and guarding soil health.
pmc-13553813:
People play games to escape, and escaping can soothe or can slide into disorder. One part is how easily one disengages from the game; the other is how easily one re-engages with daily activities. They test the measure in two studies of active gamers.

Across both samples, a smoother return went with better mood, satisfied needs, and more vitality after play, and with fewer gaming disorder symptoms, beyond the effect of escape motives alone. Easy disengagement was the strongest guard against disorder, while easy re-engagement tracked vitality and life satisfaction. The authors argue for judging escapist play dynamically, by how the session ends, not just by why it began.
pmc-13554313:
CT scans of heart arteries sometimes understate a narrowing, and in the ambiguous fifty-to-seventy percent band that error can cancel a needed procedure. Yu Xie, Chengzhuo Wang, Xuzhe Wang, Wenyu Wang, and Ruifeng Liu study when the understatement strikes in this 2026 paper, comparing scan readings against catheter measurements in two hundred and sixteen patients. Sixty-three had been understated.

The suspect is calcium: artery calcification distorts the scan's view. The team quantifies the full range of calcium scores against understatement risk, hunting thresholds that sort patients by danger and other clinical signs that sharpen the scan's verdict. The relationship they chase is not a straight line: both light and heavy calcium may mislead in different ways, forming a U. The goal is practical: know when a moderate scan reading deserves the catheter anyway.
pmc-13554413:
Xin Sun and co-authors map the stiffness of eye tissue in three dimensions over time, in a 2026 study. Ultrasound shear wave imaging measures how fast vibrations cross tissue, which reveals stiffness. The probe's panels fire in turn through a multiplexer, and a swept-cross scan fills the gaps between panels. Tests used wire and point targets, chicken tissue, and a live rabbit cornea. pmc-13554713:
Bucur Maria and co-authors rank ways to prevent diabetes in a 2026 analysis of 378 trials. About one in ten people worldwide has prediabetes, a state where blood sugar runs high but not yet at diabetes level. Many drugs and lifestyle plans claim to stop the slide, but their rank order was unclear.

The team used a network method that compares all options at once, even those never tested head to head. Trials in adults with prediabetes and any plan aimed at blood sugar were eligible. A clear ranking helps doctors and patients pick a plan with the best proof, not just the loudest claims.
pmc-13554913:
Trevor T Lovell, Jennifer Ogrin, and Ahmad Elashery report a grapefruit clash that weakened a heart drug's safety in a 2026 case report. Their fifty-seven-year-old patient took mavacamten for a thickened, obstructed heart muscle. Over months the drug eased the obstruction while pumping strength held steady. Then he began drinking grapefruit energy drinks daily.

About two months later his pumping strength had slipped to a reduced range. Grapefruit blocks a liver enzyme that clears the drug, so levels likely climbed too high. Stopping both the drug and the drinks restored his heart strength. Restarting the drug alone, without grapefruit, caused no repeat fall. The authors warn that hidden diet clashes can push this narrow-window drug into harm.
pmc-13555513:

Clinicians described what helped, what hindered, and what should change.

Flexible referrals, outreach-friendly structures, and chances to build skills eased the work. Clinicians valued that the service catches young people who fall outside other programmes' intake rules. Heavy demand strained workloads, and the care model felt unsettled in its early phase. Suggestions included co-design with local communities, a more flexible model, and staff with cultural awareness and specific skills.
pmc-13555813:
Dochka Tzoneva Tobova and co-authors report a woman aged sixty-one whose recovery from general anesthesia was badly delayed by an undiagnosed enzyme fault. She had elective surgery to fix a crushed vertebra. The fault, hereditary pseudocholinesterase deficiency, slows the breakdown of muscle relaxant drugs such as succinylcholine, so breathing can stop for far longer than planned.

Such patients need machine breathing and sedation until muscle strength returns and the tube can come out safely. Early spotting of long blockade after anesthesia is key to avoid harm, the authors stress. The case also sets out how anesthesia should be planned once this rare genetic condition is known.
pmc-13556013:
Cajal-Retzius neurons appear early in the developing cortex, secrete the signal that layers the brain, and then mostly vanish. Federico De Rosa and co-authors ask whether they merely signal or actually join the young network. Tracing their wiring and watching activity in mouse cortex, they find dense calming inputs onto these cells in the first days of life, yet many fire spontaneously, in step with their neighbors.

Their chloride balance keeps the calming transmitter excitatory, and blocking its transporter spared cells from dying in culture. Switching the cells on with light raised the whole network's excitability. Their brief career, it seems, helps tune the circuits that outlive them.
pmc-13556113:
Jeevan Toor and Jossee Lavoie scanned reports of racism in health care for Inuit in a 2026 paper. Race has no basis in science, yet racism still shapes who gets care and how, for Indigenous peoples around the world and for Inuit in Canada. Community members had raised clear worries about unfair treatment in clinics and hospitals.

No past work had gathered current Inuit accounts of racism in care in one place. The pair searched the record for such accounts and sorted what they found. Their scan gives scholars, policy makers, and Inuit groups a shared base. From it, steps to make care fair can be planned and checked.
pmc-13556413:

Half received active stimulation and half a sham version, without knowing which. On the main symptom scale, the share of time spent in response did not differ between groups. pmc-13556513:
Kida reviews how the hippocampus handles a fear memory once it is called back. This 2026 conference paper starts from a known twist: recall is not passive, since a recalled memory turns soft and must be restabilized. That restabilizing, called reconsolidation, can strengthen or update the memory.

In fear training, recall can also start extinction, a new safety memory that competes with the old fear. Which trace wins decides the fate of the memory. Comparing the cell and molecule signs of both paths in the hippocampus, the study finds they pull in opposite ways there. Kida argues those signs govern the switch between the two paths.
pmc-13556613:

Readers learn whether a nose-delivered factor can tune the very neurons that standard mood drugs target.
pmc-13556713:
B Pedraz Petrozzi and a large team search for markers of ketamine response in 2026. Thirty-six adults with treatment-resistant depression received six ketamine infusions. The course ran over three weeks.

Blood measures came from the kynurenine pathway, a route tied to inflammation. The team checked levels before treatment and tracked them over time. Mood was scored with a standard depression scale. The aim was to see whether starting levels predict who responds. Changes during care were also tied to outcomes. Readers learn how a blood panel might one day guide personal ketamine care.
pmc-13556813:

Fear circuits link the amygdala, hippocampus, and prefrontal cortex. In the stress disorder, fear memories grow too strong and too broad. The team used animal work to find which structures drive the mood side. Emotional and motivational circuits are the likely bridge. Readers learn how fear learning might tip a stressed brain into depression.
pmc-13557013:
Nguyen-Ha and co-authors computed a 2026 theoretical study of aluminium clusters doped with a boron triangle, spanning cluster sizes from three to twenty-one atoms in three charge states. Density functional theory, a standard quantum chemistry method, mapped the lowest energy shapes. The clusters grow around a stable three boron unit while aluminium atoms accumulate around it.

At thirteen aluminium atoms the boron unit moves from outside to inside the cluster, Nguyen-Ha found. At eighteen aluminiums the boron triangle straightens into a line for neutral and positive clusters, but negative clusters keep the triangle because that charged unit is exceptionally stable. Adding boron improved the stability of the aluminium frameworks in every charge state studied. Certain magic sizes grabbed extra electrons almost as eagerly as halogen atoms do, earning quasi-halogen behaviour.
pmc-13557613:
Salah Kassab and co-authors test whether AI can help set pass marks for medical exams. Their 2026 study uses the Angoff method, where judges guess how a borderline student would score on each item. The method needs many expert judges, and the judgment is hard to make well.

Mean cut scores from the two groups were nearly equal, with no clear gap. Checks on consistency gave mid-level trust for the faculty panel. The work adds early proof on AI help for exam standards.
pmc-13557713:
Yifei Ge and five colleagues published a methods study in two thousand twenty-six on finding cause-and-effect order in dense body data. Molecules rise and fall over time, and earlier changes may drive later ones. Sparse sampling and noisy links make that order hard to read.

Their tool, lagCI, scans the full lagged correlation pattern between signals rather than a single offset. A quality score then filters out flimsy links. On wearable data it recovered the known link from activity to heart rate, with person-specific delays. On frequent human multi-omics sampling it built a web of over one hundred fifty-seven thousand predicted links. Known hormone and immune cross-talk reappeared. The tool ships as a free software package.
pmc-13557813:
Jiu Kim and co-authors explore how nursing students who never lived with grandparents view older adults. Their 2026 study uses photovoice, a method where people take photos and talk about what the images mean. Nine students from two universities join five sessions of talks and photo work. The team sorts dozens of photos and stories into themes about age bias and distance from older people.

Three themes emerge from the talks. One shows confusion and fixed views inside a fast-changing society. A second shows distance built from rule-breaking scenes and the social isolation of older adults. A third shows mixed feelings shaped by daily life, welfare systems, and culture. Warm views sit beside stereotypes in the same students. The study urges more contact across ages in nurse training.
pmc-13558313:
Alexandra Villalpando-Solórzano and five colleagues pooled in 2026 studies testing whether one gene variant raises blood levels of the HIV drug efavirenz. Five studies with 373 patients who had both HIV and tuberculosis qualified. People with two copies of the variant form carried clearly higher drug levels than either of the other groups, while those two groups barely differed from each other. Higher levels were not directly tied to side effects in the pooled data, yet the authors support genetic testing to fine-tune dose and lower toxicity risk.
pmc-13558613:
Jack Lee Smith, Christina Antoniou, and Ruaridh Alexander released in 2026 a Python tool, stratapy, that draws geological layer logs from simple text or spreadsheet input. The package ships standard rock pattern fills, a curated symbol library, automatic alignment with the geological time column, and slots for samples and notes. Panels can be joined into correlated multi-log figures for complex systems. The authors aim to standardise log illustration across research and industry, and to modernise a daily Earth science workflow.
pmc-13558713:
Sreekanth Rallapalli and Weiwei Jiang assembled in 2026 a cyberthreat detector that lets three nature-inspired search algorithms tune a sequence-learning network in turn. Formal paired tests confirmed the gains were statistically solid rather than lucky runs. The authors judge the hybrid fit for near-real-time defence, with one clear caveat. The benchmarks are archived traffic. Live networks must validate the system before anyone trusts it at the perimeter.
pmc-13558913:
Zhao and six co-authors traced in twenty twenty-six how the rabies virus blocks an iron-led cell death to copy it-self in host cells. That death, called ferroptosis, can slow virus spread when it runs free. The virus core protein lifts a fat-build-ing gene that seeds oil drops in the cell.

Those drops trap free fats, which strips a fat tag from a guard protein named CYB5R1. Un-tagged, that guard is eaten by the cell's own clean-up path. With the guard gone, two death paths close and the virus thrives. Block-ing the fat gene re-stored the guard and slowed the virus in their tests.
pmc-13559213:
Robyn McCarthy and five co-authors review school based studies of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder in a 2026 paper. The review covered twenty nine studies from five databases. Most used active case finding, where teams test and assess children directly. Definitions, tools, and diagnostic rules differed widely across studies. Reports often skipped non participation rates and community involvement. Most exposure checks relied on mothers reporting their own drinking. The authors call for standard methods to make future counts comparable.
pmc-13559513:
Søren S Olesen and colleagues chart the natural course of recurrent acute pancreatitis using Danish national registries. Recurrence meant a new hospital episode at least ninety days after the previous one. The team modeled how risk changes as episodes pile up.

pmc-13559713:
Lachaise, Collard, and Anstett study which flowers draw pollinators in blackcurrant fields. Farms often sow flower strips or leave wild blooms to help bees. Small and large bees rose with the count of wild blooms. Hoverflies rose instead with sown flowers. Small bees thinned out toward the middle of rows. Pollinators on bushes tracked pollinators in the next row, not flower counts. The authors say sown and wild flowers play split, matching roles.
pmc-13559813:
Simmi Patel and Rana Naous wrote a 2026 teaching case for medical students about a tumor type that grows in the gut wall. The case is made up, not a real patient record, and it follows set national goals for pathology teaching. It opens with an older woman who comes to an emergency room with sudden, severe belly pain.

From that scene, the case walks students through how such tumors start, how they look under the scope, and how they are classed. It also covers the gene changes that drive gut cancers more broadly. Students must weigh test results and predict how the illness may act. The format helps schools teach gut tumor topics in a shared, tested way.
pmc-13560113:
Xuanming Hu, Meilin Wen, and Shunfang Liu compare exercise formats for blood sugar control in type 2 diabetes through a network meta-analysis. Their 2026 study pooled sixteen randomized trials with 744 participants, searched across four databases to October 2025. Moderate continuous training faced two interval styles: short bursts of sixty seconds or less, and long intervals of two minutes or more.

All three exercise types lowered glycated hemoglobin and fasting glucose compared with no exercise. Long intervals produced the largest drops and ranked first for both outcomes in the ranking analysis. Long intervals also beat moderate continuous training on glycated hemoglobin in the main analysis, though that edge faded in a sensitivity check removing one trial. Fasting glucose showed no clear differences among the active formats. Insulin resistance improved markedly only under long intervals. The authors present long-interval training as the leading option, on modest evidence.
pmc-13560213:
Chen Liu, Jiali Zhang, and Liu Yang use unsupervised machine learning to sort high-risk newborns into hearing-risk phenotypes. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 447 babies in a neonatal unit, clustering demographic, perinatal, and diagnostic data by a medoid method suited to mixed data types. A decision tree then translated the clusters into bedside rules.

Four phenotypes appeared. Term babies with jaundice failed hearing screening least often, at 20.5 percent of their group in the reported rates. Preterm boys with respiratory illness failed most, at nearly half. Preterm girls sat between, and term babies with respiratory or infectious problems scored moderately. Simple rules emerged, such as boys under a stated birth weight failing at very high rates. Network analysis showed respiratory illness, infection, and prematurity forming a tangled core, while jaundice stood apart. The authors argue pattern-based sorting complements single-factor thinking.
pmc-13560313:
Children with many severe injuries at once need care shaped to their smaller bodies, and head injury usually drives the outcome. An eight-author team reviewed all such cases, defined by a high injury score, treated at a university hospital in Bonn between 2023 and 2025. Thirty-two children qualified, with a median age of thirteen and a half.

Traffic accidents caused three quarters of the cases, and head trauma led the injury list, including skull fractures in about a third. Nearly half the children needed surgery, the typical intensive care stay was three days, and complications struck about one in six. No child died in hospital, and most went straight home. Injury scores did not track length of stay in this small group. The authors stress head injury as the main burden and report encouraging outcomes at a specialist center.
pmc-13561013:
Oscar Werner, Alban-Elouen Baruteau, and a large French team lay out the CATAMARAN study, which follows babies born with severe heart defects to catch early signs of slow development. Heart surgery in the first months of life saves these children, yet a third to a half score low on early development tests.

The study enrolls 150 unborn babies with the diagnosis, at eight French centers, and tracks them to six months of age. It banks blood, placenta, and stool samples, scans, and parent surveys on stress and food. A case-control look inside the cohort will hunt for genes and other traits that set some babies back. France has no tested care path for this risk, the authors note.
pmc-13561313:
Salsabela Razaq and Saleema Allana lay out a plan to map what is known about fairness in digital health for immigrants in Canada and the United States, in a 2026 protocol. Immigrants form a large share of the population yet face uneven access to app- and portal-based care. The scoping review will chart the research on those gaps.

The protocol follows a classic five-stage scoping framework and is registered openly on the Open Science Framework. The authors expect the map to expose concrete barriers, from language and cost to trust and digital skills. Health planners can then use the picture to design services that reach immigrant patients more fairly.
pmc-13561813:
Om Kolthoum Sallem and co-authors report a difficult celiac disease case from 2026 in a 56-year-old Tunisian woman. Her illness had become type two refractory celiac disease, a rare pre-cancerous form that no longer responds to a gluten-free diet. She arrived severely malnourished at thirty-four kilograms, wheelchair dependent, with up to twenty stools a day.

Scans found no lymphoma, but gut biopsies showed total villus flattening and a large share of abnormal immune cells. Feeding by vein, then by tube, plus a targeted steroid in open capsules, slowly restored her. By six months she had gained twenty-six kilograms and her blood protein had normalized, though biopsies still showed flat villi and the abnormal cells. Recovery and gut healing can part ways.
pmc-13562313:
Diana Vossen, Xenofon Baraliakos, and Maria Polyzou test how well chatbots advise women with joint and muscle diseases on pregnancy. Expert care on family planning helps both mother and child, but such clinics are not open to all. Their 2026 study asks four well known chatbots fifty-four questions on pregnancy, birth, and feeding a baby.

Ten experts from Europe scored more than two thousand answers for safety, accuracy, and depth. All four chatbots scored high on safety. Two of them led on accuracy, while one gave the fullest answers and one lagged on depth. The experts often disagreed with each other, though. The authors say the tools can help with routine care but cannot stand in for expert judgment.
pmc-13562413:
Samia Karkoutly and co-authors find a switch that links two fasting processes in the liver in a 2026 study. When animals fast, the liver must dump nitrogen through the urea cycle while also making new glucose. FoxO transcription factors, proteins that switch genes on, were known to run fasting metabolism, and the team shows they directly control a urea cycle enzyme gene called Ass1.

Cutting FoxO in the livers of fasted mice lowered the enzyme, dropped blood sugar, and shifted urea cycle amino acids, even without a second factor once thought required. Silencing the enzyme copied those effects, while restoring it rescued glucose output in liver cells. A DNA enhancer with a FoxO binding site, active during fasting, seals the mechanism.
pmc-13562513:
Anita Csizmarik and thirteen colleagues hunt for a blood signal that warns when a prostate cancer drug is about to fail. Enzalutamide, a hormone-blocking drug, extends life in advanced prostate cancer, yet many tumours resist it from the start. No test currently guides that choice. The 2026 team first grew prostate cancer cell pairs, one sensitive and one resistant to the drug, and compared their genes and DNA. Three candidates emerged, among them a stretch called UCA1 and the androgen receptor gene.

The researchers then counted copies of each candidate in cell-free DNA from patients' blood serum. Groups covered 20 men on enzalutamide, 20 on a related drug, and 40 on chemotherapy. Extra UCA1 copies went with shorter survival on enzalutamide, while extra receptor copies mattered for the related drug only. The authors suggest a simple blood count could help doctors pick the right drug sooner.
pmc-13562613:
Yasmeen A. S. H. Hameed and seven colleagues spin a triple-duty nanofibre membrane that pulls toxic mercury from water and shows biological activity. The 2026 membrane blends a tough plastic, PVDF, with chitosan from natural sources and a layered aluminium-copper mineral. A battery of imaging and surface tools confirmed the blend and revealed a porous mat rich in chemical groups that grip metal ions. Batch tests varied dose, acidity, and contact time to find the best uptake conditions.

At the sweet spot, mildly acidic water and 100 minutes of contact, each gram of membrane held about 423 milligrams of mercury. Uptake followed a chemical-binding pattern and absorbed heat as it ran. Beyond cleanup, the mat killed breast and liver cancer cells in a dose-dependent way and mopped up free radicals. The authors pitch the material for water purification first, with medical uses as a longer-term prospect.
pmc-13562713:
Xianhuan Luo and six colleagues model how much strain a glued-on fibre sensor feels when the structure beneath it stretches. Fibre Bragg grating sensors watch wind turbine blades for damage, prized for small size and immunity to electrical noise. The catch sits in the glue: the adhesive layer between blade and fibre absorbs part of the strain, so readings understate it. Their 2026 paper builds a model for the end-bonded layout, where the sensor is fixed at its ends.

The model spells out how the glue's stiffness, its Poisson behaviour, and its thickness drain transfer efficiency, along with the sensor's gauge length. Finite element simulations, a stress test, then checked the formulas. Both routes agreed on the governing patterns. The authors offer the model as a design guide: choose glue and geometry on paper, and the sensor on the blade reports strain more faithfully.
pmc-13562813:
A land's great moon aim seeks to weave smart help in the home and ward, fed by a stream of body reads. Hiroto Shimizu follows that weave in a 2026 study from inside the land's sense AI drive. His field work tracks how the drive casts flesh and gear as one tight pair, with help that fades in the back ground.

The drive hits snags where data must join, where say so is sought, and where the body is safe. Shimizu traces side winds: body data that flows to trade, and old gaps that the drive may widen. The drive has since been cut by a shift in state aims. Shimizu, the sole author, holds the cut drive a live mark of how such webs are made and unmade.
pmc-13562913:
Tran, Vo, and Nguyen report the case of a young man whose missing antibody system nearly killed him after a year without replacement therapy, in this 2026 case report. His condition, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, leaves the body unable to make antibodies, so regular immunoglobulin infusions are lifesaving. Cost had forced a twelve month gap.

He arrived with fever, cough, chest pain, and low oxygen, and scans showed two lung lobes consolidated. Blood and airway tests found two bacterial species at once. Antibiotics alone improved his counts but not his fever or breathing after five days. One infusion of immunoglobulin turned the case within two days. He went home on day fourteen and resumed monthly therapy. The authors stress that antibiotics cannot substitute for the missing protection.
pmc-13563113:
Yanhua Lu, Meng Yu, Jinghe Zhou, and Yang Yang study in 2026 why thick, raised scars form after burns. They focus on a tiny bit of RNA in blood and skin cells that helps set how genes act. Blood tests showed less of this RNA in burn patients than in healthy people, and still less in those who went on to form thick scars.

In lab tests, skin cells hurt by heat also held less of the RNA. When the team raised its level, the cells grew and moved less and made less scar protein. The RNA works by binding a gene called MEOX2 and holding it down, and raising that gene undid the effect. Low levels of the RNA may flag who will scar, and it may serve as a target to stop thick scars.
pmc-13563913:
Leyao Qian and colleagues describe laboratory and feeding trials, published in 2026, of a blended plant extract tested in the fish Acrossocheilus fasciatus. The mixture combined four plant sources and was first checked for its ability to stop Streptococcus agalactiae, a bacterium that harms farmed fish.

A dose mixed into feed at a low rate gave the best survival after bacterial challenge and caused no harm to growth. Treated fish showed healthier liver and gut tissue and a gut microbe mix with more helpful bacteria and fewer harmful types. Fish farmers and researchers get a candidate alternative to antibiotics, with dose and safety details spelled out.
pmc-13564213:
Pulsed field ablation treats a racing heart with short electric pulses instead of heat, and its use is spreading to new targets in the heart's upper chambers. Takigawa and co-authors asked what those pulses do to pacemakers and defibrillators already implanted in a patient. In a pig study, thirteen animals received modern device systems and seven of them then had ablation at several sites, including directly over exposed defibrillator coils.

Ablation in the left atrium, away from device parts, caused no critical failures, though a few settings drifted slightly. In the right atrium and the big vein nearby, disturbances and one dislodged lead traced mostly to the catheter bumping the leads, not the pulses. Pulses over the bare coils changed local readings without breaking the devices, and a leadless pacemaker and a skin-level defibrillator stayed steady. The lesson: the risk depends on where and how the energy lands.
pmc-13565813:
Boris Burnjakovic and co-authors review how long-term pain, poor sleep, and mental health feed each other in this 2026 paper. The three often occur together and form a cycle that harms daily life. The review joins brain, immune, and hormone facts into one frame for the cycle.

Pain grows more sharp as the nervous system becomes over-reactive, helped by immune cells in the brain. Poor sleep raises swelling in the body and upsets daily rhythms. Shifts in brain chemicals and stress hormones add to anxiety and low mood. The authors suggest that treatments aimed at shared paths, such as swelling and brain cell activity, may help all three problems at once.
pmc-13565913:
Iuliia Golovynska and nine co-authors shine near-infrared light on poisoned brain cells to test whether it rescues their power plants, in a 2026 study. Alzheimer disease is increasingly seen as a failure of mitochondria, the cell’s energy hubs, which fragment and falter. Light treatment at gentle doses had protected brain cells in animal models, but whether fixing the mitochondrial web is required for that rescue was unknown.

The team bathed mouse hippocampal neurons in the amyloid protein that marks the disease, then irradiated them with 808-nanometer light at a set dose. Shape maps of the mitochondrial network, plus readings of reactive oxygen, energy currency, and membrane voltage, showed whether the light restored normal function. Proof of mechanism matters before shining light into human trials.
pmc-13566213:
A sudden inflamed pancreas can turn severe, and emergency doctors need fast ways to spot the patients at risk. Ömer Damar and Mahmut Yaman test a blood-based score in this 2026 study of acute pancreatitis. The score, built from routine blood counts of three cell types, is checked against a standard five-part score used for the same job.

The study covers 523 adults treated at one hospital between 2020 and 2025. About nine percent developed severe disease. The blood score ran far higher in severe cases than in mild ones, and both scores predicted severe disease, intensive care, and death on their own. Joined together, they forecast severe disease and death better than either alone. The authors say the cheap blood score adds real value at admission.
pmc-13566513:
Yusuke Inoue and co-authors study why patients stop a vessel-relaxing drug after brain aneurysm bleeding. Their twenty twenty-six registry study uses a national Japanese database on subarachnoid hemorrhage outcomes. Clazosentan cuts the vessel spasm that often follows such bleeds, and it has been used in Japan since twenty twenty-two.

The drug also brings body-wide side effects that can force a stop. The team sorted which clinical traits link to stopping the drug. They also probed how stopping relates to discharge state and six-month outcomes. Many centers feed the registry, so the pattern is broad. The work helps teams weigh who can stay on a useful but taxing drug.
pmc-13566613:
Quynh Luong and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, a small antibody form that cuts viral RNA, as a shield against flu. Flu spreads fast and shifts its form, so drugs can lose their grip. The protein, 3D8 scFv, breaks both DNA and RNA of viruses and has shown wide antiviral force. The team first traced where the drug goes in mice by route and dose. Nose doses piled up in the lung; vein doses spread through the whole body, lung in the mix.

They then set two paths against a mouse flu strain. In one, the drug was given after infection. In the other, mouse cells made the drug on their own before infection. That built-in path saved all the mice, at 100 percent life. The dosed path saved a third. The gap makes a strong case for built-in guards.
pmc-13567113:
Anton Bahtiar and colleagues test a tropical tree's leaves against bone loss, in a 2026 study. Osteoporosis thins bones and raises fracture risk, especially when estrogen falls after menopause. The tree, Artocarpus integer, holds plant compounds with known biological effects, but its bone potential was unexplored. The team combined chemical profiling, computer network analysis, and rat experiments.

Fine chemical scans identified several active compounds in the leaves, including genistein and apigenin. Network analysis linked them to targets and pathways involved in bone building and breakdown. Rats that had their ovaries removed, a standard model of menopause, then received the extract. The researchers tracked weight, blood markers, and calcium in thigh bones, plus gene activity tied to bone growth. Their results support the extract as a candidate for protecting bone when estrogen is low.
pmc-13567613:
Roza Shayakhmetova and co-authors studied nickel recovery from rock in two thousand twenty-six. Laterite ores are a major source of nickel for steel and batteries. Dissolving the ore yields a mix of metals in liquid form. Pulling nickel out alone is hard because sister metals crowd in. The team tested two sponge-like resins that grab nickel by chemical hooks.

Both resins picked nickel over cobalt and magnesium in lab tests. The team measured how fast and how much each resin could hold. They also tested cleaning the resins so they could work again. Checks on the ore used X-ray and microscope tools. The results feed a draft plant flow for ore processing. Cleaner recovery could cut waste in nickel supply chains.
pmc-13567813:
Live shopping streams increasingly star AI hosts, and how human they seem can move viewers to buy on impulse. Jingqi Huang and Wasim Ahmad test that mechanism with scenario experiments built on a stimulus-organism-response frame. They vary two cues: how human the host looks, and how socially it chats.

Both cues fed impulse buying through two inner states, cognitive trust and emotional arousal. The chat cues outperformed the visual ones at building both states. The pattern held roughly steady across genders, but shifted with product involvement and prior AI experience. The 2026 study advises stream designers to invest in conversation before cosmetics.
pmc-13568113:
Zoran Šverko and co-authors seek EEG markers that separate two dementias from healthy aging in a 2026 study. Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia can look alike early on, which delays the right care. Brain wave recordings are cheap and widely available, a good base for a sorting test.

Recordings from eighty-eight people were analyzed for spectral traits and directed links between brain areas. A ratio of slow to mid waves stood out as the top marker, above all in frontal areas. The team also projects how a light therapy case might shift the markers. A validated EEG test could aid clinics without scanners.
pmc-13568513:
Ho Cheung William Li and co-authors ran a 2026 trial of digital health coaching for emergency department patients. Diseases driven by behavior, such as tobacco use, heavy drinking, poor diet, and inactivity, are the world's leading killers. An emergency visit can be a wake-up moment when patients are open to change.

Patients leaving the department were assigned by chance to usual care or to a digitally boosted health program. The digital arm added phone-based support to standard promotion advice. The trial measured whether patients quit their risk behaviors over follow-up. A positive result would give busy emergency departments a light-touch tool that keeps working after the patient goes home.
pmc-13569313:
Shuai Yuan and colleagues write, in a 2026 letter reporting a nationwide Swedish cohort study, about fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems. Their question is whether it raises the risk of peripheral artery disease in step with liver severity. Biopsy records from twenty-eight pathology departments were linked to national registers covering care, medicines, and deaths.

Adults with biopsy-proven fatty liver were followed from their biopsy or first matching diagnosis code, with other liver diseases and alcohol misuse excluded. The design lets risk be graded across tissue severity stages rather than treating fatty liver as one uniform condition. Clinicians watching heart and vessel risk in liver patients get population-scale evidence organized by how advanced the liver changes are.
pmc-13569813:
Boyin Li and eleven co-authors report a compound from a fungus that defeats drug resistance in lung cancer. The standard targeted drug for this cancer often stops working as tumors adapt. The compound, a small molecule drawn from a fungus that lives inside plants, was tested on resistant cancer cells and in mice carrying resistant tumors. It slowed the growth of the resistant cells and shrank tumors in the animals.

The compound works by triggering ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron and fat damage. It binds directly to an enzyme that normally protects cell fats, and marks that enzyme for destruction. With the guard gone, fat damage builds and the cancer cells die. Blocking the same enzyme by other means had similar effects, which supports the claim that it is the key target. The authors propose the compound as a candidate drug for resistant lung cancer.
pmc-13570013:
Multiple myeloma is the second most common blood cancer, and adding an antibody drug to standard triplets has raised hopes for new patients. The search covered four sources up to April 2026 and gathered seven randomized trials. The main measures were time before the disease progressed and whether any trace of disease remained. The team also split results by the genetic risk grade of the cancer. Evidence quality was graded with a standard framework, which helps readers judge how much trust the pooled numbers deserve.
pmc-13570213:
Junzhe He and co-authors review in 2026 how pain tied to cancer and the growth of cancer drive each other. Pain is common in cancer and can hint at how the ill will run. The authors stress that pain is not just a side sign that sits still.

Growing tumors cause pain by wrecking tissue and by shifts in nerves, blood, and the space near the tumor. In turn, pain signals, stress paths, and brain hubs can feed tumor growth and spread. The review also flags open fights, such as the mixed role of sense nerves and the risk that strong pain drugs may help tumors. Care teams get a case for treating pain as part of the ill itself.
pmc-13570313:
Hehuan Zhu and co-authors study how colon tumors display identity markers to the immune system in a 2026 paper. Tumors use surface proteins called HLA to show fragments of themselves to immune cells. Losing those proteins can help a tumor hide. The team asked how the full set of these proteins, old and newer types alike, relates to immune attack and patient outcome.

In two hundred eighty tumors, high levels of the classic proteins and dense immune cell entry each linked to longer survival. Loss of the classic proteins was more common in advanced tumors and in one genetic subtype. Among the newer proteins, only one linked to better outcomes. Combining protein patterns with cell density split tumors into three immune types with distinct outlooks. The authors say the combined view could guide immune therapy choices.
pmc-13570413:
Colin Lee and co-authors measure tooth decay activity in caregivers of preschool children in a 2026 study. Caregivers shape a child's daily oral care, and their own decay activity may track with the child's. The study enrolled more than two hundred fifty primary caregivers and tested both caregiver and child with a commercial decay activity kit.

About one in three caregivers scored high on the activity test. Caregivers of children with high scores were far more likely to score high themselves. After adjustment, high activity linked to a high past decay count, frequent snacking, being a grandparent caregiver, and the child's high score. The authors frame decay control as a family level task.
pmc-13570513:
Five authors, led by Susann Arnell, report how Swedish mental health staff experienced a new home-care service in this 2026 study. More adults need psychiatric care, and clinics are stretched. The response under study is SPOT: mobile specialist psychiatric nursing teams that visit patients at home, backing up both outpatient and hospital care.

Little was known about how staff would take to the model. The team ran focus groups and interviews with eleven professionals: nurses, psychiatric aides on the home teams, and psychiatrists who advised them. Their accounts cover the early phase of the rollout, its promise and its friction. An open, data-driven analysis sorted the themes. The study gives planners a ground-level view of what helps a mobile team take root in an established care system.
pmc-13570613:
Muneeba Iqbal and Abdullah Iftikhar wrote a letter in 2026 raising methodological concerns about a study of vision-related quality of life in Portuguese patients with uveitis, an eye inflammation. Data on this population are scarce, so the study drew interest. The letter writers argue its design limits what it can show.

Their first concern is the online questionnaire format, which left diagnoses self-reported with no clinical check, inviting bias and possible misclassification. They dispute the claim that recruitment through patient groups made verification likely. Their second concern is a stark sex imbalance between the patient and control groups, which could distort comparisons. They urge the authors to state these limits plainly.
pmc-13570913:
Musa İşnas's team tested wormwood leaf extracts, plain and nano, against diabetes damage in rats, in a 2026 study. Diabetes drives oxidant stress that injures liver, kidney, and pancreas, and plant extracts are candidates for easing that harm. The team induced diabetes in 48 female rats and gave ethanolic lyophilised or nano Artemisia haussknechtii extracts at two doses for 21 days.

Diabetic rats showed persistent high glucose, weight loss, abnormal fats, and suppressed oxidant defences, all of which improved dose-dependently with treatment. The high-dose nanoparticle form performed best, normalising insulin, HbA1c, and C-peptide markers and markedly sparing tissue damage. The authors present the plant, especially in nano form, as a promising complement against diabetes-related oxidant injury.
pmc-13571113:
Luisa Semmler and a large international team report on diabetes arising within mitochondrial diseases, using records from the GENOMIT registry across Germany, Austria, and Italy. Their cohort study came out in 2026. Mitochondria produce the cell's energy, and inherited faults in them can damage many organs, including the insulin system.

Of nearly two thousand four hundred patients with confirmed mitochondrial disease, about one in eight had diabetes. It appeared across many genetic variants, but one variant stood out sharply, with about half of its carriers affected and a tenfold risk increase. Half of the diabetic patients used insulin, and the common drug metformin was widely used and usually tolerated. The authors argue that diabetes risk in these diseases depends strongly on genotype, and that blanket avoidance of metformin is not justified.
pmc-13571313:
Thanai Pongdee and co-authors describe treatment patterns and burden for a rare blood disorder in the United States in a 2026 study. Hypereosinophilic syndrome involves lasting high counts of a white cell type that damages organs. Steroid pills have long been the main treatment for its two main subtypes, but long use brings toxicity, and newer biologic drugs still leave gaps.

Using linked health records and claims, the team followed one hundred ten patients for up to two years. On average nearly three organ systems were involved at the start. Half the patients had no treatment within two years, and steroids were the most used therapy. Fewer than forty percent reached full remission. Among new cases, years often passed between the first high cell count and diagnosis. The authors call for earlier detection and better options.
pmc-13571613:
Kenan Calisir and Mohamed Kadiye chart the causes of adult blindness at a major eye center in Somalia. Their twenty twenty-six study reviews records from Mogadishu for the full year twenty twenty-five. All patients were sixteen or older.

The pair pulled age, sex, which eye or eyes were blind, and the clinical cause for each case. They then weighed how age and sex linked to the main causes. Trauma stood out as a heavy source of lost sight in this group. The results give Somali eye care a hard count of who goes blind and why, a base for prevention work.
pmc-13571713:
Laura Maté Miguel and Pablo Pazos Lama report, in a 2026 case written in Spanish, a 62-year-old man in intensive care after an ischemic stroke. His central venous catheter tore the innominate vein, a large vein behind the upper chest. The line had been placed under ultrasound through the left subclavian vein, and the first chest film looked reassuring.

Two days later he became unstable, with kidney failure, fluid around both lungs, and fluid squeezing the heart. CT imaging with contrast sent through the catheter itself showed the tear leaking into the chest cavity, and a vein study confirmed it. The catheter was removed in an operating room with a blocking balloon ready, no new leak appeared, and recovery went well. The authors stress imaging when decline has no clear cause.
pmc-13572013:
Lymphoma in the chest moves as the patient breathes, which blurs the aim of proton therapy.
