Patients held their breath with help from nasal high-flow air, while an optical surface scanner watched the chest and gated the beam within a three-millimeter window.

Across 187 treatment fractions, breath holds stayed steady within a millimeter, and the beam's center drifted by less than three millimeters during delivery. A session took about forty-four minutes at first and grew shorter as patients gained practice. Only one plan in the whole group needed adaptation. Shifts between sessions ran slightly larger than shifts within one, so the authors suggest pairing bone alignment with soft-tissue checks. They judge the method feasible, with stable holds and acceptable times.
pmc-13572313:
Wan and colleagues fed two probiotic strains to heavy finishing pigs in 2026 to compare how each shapes fat, inflammation, and meat quality. Two hundred eighty-eight pigs were split into three diet groups for forty-two days: plain feed, or feed with one of two Lactobacillus strains, given daily. Probiotics are marketed to trim fat, but strains are often lumped together despite different habits.

Both strains lowered stress hormone and inflammation signals in blood, raised a calming immune factor, and cut saturated fat in the loin muscle. The second strain went further on fat: thinner backfat, more lean meat, and smaller fat cells, through a metabolic switch pathway the team measured. The first strain instead improved the meat itself, making it more tender with less internal fat. The authors say producers should pick strains by goal.
pmc-13572413:
Szymon Plewa, with five colleagues, presents a 2026 lab method for measuring amino acids tied to proline use in skin cells. Proline helps build collagen and plays a part in wound healing and swelling. Sound measures of proline and its partner compounds are needed to study those paths.

The method pairs liquid chromatography, which sorts compounds in a fluid stream, with a precise mass detector. The team checked the method for straight-line response, range, repeat results, accuracy, and stability, and all checks passed. It then measured the target amino acids in lysates of HaCaT cells, a lab skin cell line, with success. The authors note that the setup can add more compounds later. It can also extend to other complex samples from living tissue.
pmc-13572713:
Kazuhito Murakami and others tested a traditional Japanese herbal remedy in two thousand twenty-six. The remedy is called Goreisan. They studied brain support cells called astrocytes. These cells carry a water channel named AQP4. That channel can amplify inflammation signals in the brain. The team asked whether the herbal mixture calms those signals.

Cell tests triggered inflammation with two different stimulants. The remedy lowered production of many inflammatory messengers. A mouse model of brain inflammation showed similar calming effects. The group also tested single herbal ingredients separately. Brain researchers gain a candidate treatment lead. Human proof remains far away.
pmc-13573413:
Aurélien Cornil, with five colleagues, presents a 2026 umbrella review of what drives protective behaviour in pandemics. Masks, hand hygiene, and distancing saved lives in COVID-19, and future crises will need the same habits. The team gathered past reviews to sort the factors that help or hinder those habits.

From 86 records, 11 reviews met the bar, covering COVID-19 plus flu, SARS, MERS, and Ebola. Factors fell in three bands: who people are, what they think and trust, and the world around them. Trust in credible sources, belief that steps work, and clear multi-channel messages helped. False claims, conspiracy beliefs, and lack of supplies blocked action. Age, gender, and schooling cut both ways across habits. The authors urge tailored, honest messaging and fair access to supplies.
pmc-13573713:
What a fly larva tastes can echo into its adult choices, at least for one bitter compound. Vaibhav Menon and co-authors raise fruit fly larvae on food dosed with papaverine in a 2026 study. As adults, those flies avoided the bitter alkaloid less than their naive peers did.

The effect was specific: other bitter chemicals still repelled the adults, and their preferences among bitter tastes otherwise stayed put. Larval bitter taste neurons, their projection targets in the brain, and a memory-linked enzyme all contributed to the change. The authors read the result as development writing a narrow, compound-specific note into the adult feeding system. Early diet, in flies at least, tunes later taste behavior with surprising precision.
pmc-13574313:
Alex Lancaster and co-authors track sleep around hip and knee replacement surgery and test whether melatonin helps. Poor sleep slows healing and raises pain, and worn joints plus surgery both wreck it. Their 2026 randomized study split 48 replacement patients: 23 took melatonin for seven weeks around surgery, and 25 took a placebo. Daily forms recorded sleep and opioid use for up to three months.

Sleep was poor before surgery in nearly all. Hip patients on melatonin slept more hours than the placebo group, yet their sleep quality scores did not improve. Knee patients showed no gain at all. Scores rose with time in both joints: knees passed their starting point by two weeks, while hips took three months to get back. The team calls melatonin a weak aid here.
pmc-13574513:
Lunavath and colleagues report in 2026 a cross-sectional study of gum health and oral health-related quality of life in postmenopausal women. In this group, estrogen loss is suspected of accelerating periodontal breakdown and so denting daily comfort and function.

The team examined 266 women attending a tertiary government hospital. They charted bleeding, pocket depth, and attachment loss tooth by tooth, and scored quality of life with the fourteen-item oral health impact questionnaire. The average numbers of teeth with bleeding, and of teeth with pockets and attachment loss, were significantly associated with the quality-of-life score. The correlations themselves were weak. More teeth showing bleeding tracked with slightly lower impact scores in some domains, while more teeth with pockets and attachment loss tracked with slightly worse scores overall in this sample.
pmc-13574713:
Gabriele Russo and co-authors read tooth enamel isotopes to rebuild past ecology in the Levant in 2026. The region was a land bridge for early human spread out of Africa. Local conditions on the central coast were poorly known. Enamel from eight plant eating species came from three sites in Lebanon. The span covers about three hundred thousand years.

Carbon and oxygen marks in the enamel track plants, water, and season heat. The coast kept a steady Mediterranean season pattern the whole span. Summer to winter gaps barely changed across ice ages. Woodlands of one plant type and wet, mixed habitats held firm. The authors call the coast a stable refuge. That steadiness likely aided repeated human stays and spread.
pmc-13574813:
Benjamin Lefranc, with twelve colleagues, reports a 2026 find of a new chemical twist in frog skin peptides. Frog secretions brim with small protective peptides, often reshaped after the cell builds them. Two peptides from the giant gladiator treefrog carried a reshaping never before confirmed in any backboned animal.

Mass and magnetic tools read the pair's makeup, and lab-made copies confirmed the read. Their head unit was a ring-shaped form of the amino acid tryptophan, built by a classic ring-closing reaction. Computer models pegged that unit as the spot where electrons move most freely, a hint at redox work. In radical-mopping tests, the reshaped peptides scored lower than their plain kin. The find widens the known menu of natural peptide edits and shows how inventive frog skin chemistry runs.
pmc-13575113:
Ileana Quiñones and colleagues shared a large brain-imaging resource for studying how minds that speak many languages handle language. Language use relies on a known left-brain network, but how it varies from person to person, above all across lives lived in two or more tongues, remains little studied. Their 2026 data paper presents NEUROLINGUA, MRI scans from 725 healthy adults aged 18 to 82 in a Basque-Spanish setting, plus language history and test scores.

In the scanner, people did hear-and-read tasks plus number tasks, allowing side-by-side checks across senses. Early checks tied brain structure to social background and thinking, and showed the functional scans pinpoint the language network as expected. The authors offer the set as a top resource for studying how language networks bend to fit varied language lives.
pmc-13575213:
Ruiyi Shen and co-authors propose a way to sense clear-air turbulence with terahertz beams in a 2026 paper. Clear-air turbulence endangers flights yet evades weather radar. Optical sensors fail in severe cases and suffer when beams drift out of line. Their beams carry orbital angular momentum, a twist in the wavefront.

Turbulence scrambles the twist modes in a pattern tied to air structure. A derived model maps that crosstalk to a standard turbulence strength measure. Lab tests and simulations confirm the link. The method stays sound where optical tools saturate and shrugs off misalignment far better. It can also locate the main turbulent clusters.
pmc-13575313:
Jaegeun Cho and colleagues studied 231,386 Korean adults in the 2024 Community Health Survey to test whether an inflammation-related lifestyle score tracks with quality of life. The score combined smoking, drinking, physical activity, and body mass index into one measure. Quality of life was rated with a five-dimension health questionnaire, and depressive symptoms were checked with a nine-item mood scale.

Higher lifestyle scores lined up with poorer quality of life after other health and demographic factors were taken into account. That link was clearly stronger among people with depressive symptoms than among people without them. The results suggest that daily habits and mood should be weighed together when health workers try to understand why quality of life differs across a population.
pmc-13575613:
Oana Raluca Radbea and co-authors survey in this 2026 study how Romanian medical students view artificial intelligence in their training. At one large medical university, 374 students across all six years answered a checked questionnaire in May 2026. Nearly all had used AI tools, and about three in five used them often or daily.

Students praised AI most for saving time in lookups and for easing hard concepts. Senior students felt the time gains more than juniors. A warm overall attitude strongly predicted faith in AI's clinical worth. Worries about accuracy and over-reliance persist, so the authors call for structured AI literacy teaching and clear school rules. Other schools in the region face the same choice.
pmc-13576113:
Barak Levit and four co-authors survey how well Israeli doctors know head injury guidance in a 2026 paper. Guidelines for mild traumatic brain injury have sharpened worldwide over the past decade, aiming to prevent re-injury and long recoveries. Israel had never been audited on them.

Sixty-eight hospital physicians in emergency and trauma care answered a thirty-item questionnaire. Nine in ten recognized headline symptoms like headache and dizziness, but only forty to sixty percent spotted neck pain, sleep problems, balance trouble, or light and noise sensitivity. Half knew the international guidelines, yet far fewer acted on key steps. About a third gave return-to-sport instructions, a third covered return to school or work, and a fifth handed out standard discharge sheets. The gap between knowing and doing is the paper's story. The authors call for better dissemination and tools that make the guidance the default.
pmc-13576213:
Tong Wang, Weiwei He, Scout Fronhofer and colleagues mapped the shapes of three simple single-stranded RNAs in solution in 2026. They combined small-angle X-ray scattering with molecular dynamics simulations to build refined structural ensembles for thirty-unit strands of poly-A, poly-C and poly-U.

Clear differences emerged. Poly-A was the most compact and helical, poly-U was mostly a loose coil, and poly-C sat in between as a moderately structured but highly varied strand. Circular dichroism and melting tests backed up the ensembles. Knowing how each base sequence folds on its own helps explain how larger RNAs are recognised by other molecules.
pmc-13576413:
Clara García-Carro and co-authors follow a new kidney drug out of its trials and into Spanish hospital corridors, in this 2026 real-world study. Sparsentan cut protein leakage impressively in randomized trials of IgA nephropathy, the commonest glomerular disease. Whether the effect survives contact with ordinary practice, and ordinary patients, was unmeasured beyond the short term.

The multicenter review covers 41 biopsy-proven patients who started the drug outside any trial. Median age was forty-two; kidneys were already impaired, with median filtration at 44, and nearly all patients also took an SGLT2 inhibitor. Urine protein began at a median of 1,163 milligrams a day. Three months in, it had fallen to 772, a median drop of 44 percent, and just over half the patients passed the responder bar of halving their proteinuria. Six- and twelve-month data test whether the early win endures.
pmc-13576713:
Emily Schwartz and eight co-authors report early United States use of low dose radiation for worn joints in a 2026 study. The treatment is old in parts of Europe but new in local clinics. Their clinic gave it for joint arthritis outside the spine and tracked pain, function, and pain pill use in the first patients treated.

Thirty patients with fifty five joints got three gray in six small doses. Mean pain fell from about eight to about three and a half on a ten point scale at first check. A global score showed gains in ninety two percent of joints. Near a quarter of patients cut pain pills, and none had to raise them. All finished care with no sharp side effects, and the authors back formal trials.
pmc-13576813:
Sarah A Sacco leads a 2026 study feeding cell cultures with acids from the cell's own energy cycle to control acidity in drug-making reactors. Chinese hamster ovary cells dominate production of therapeutic proteins. Three cycle acids, malic, succinic, and alpha-ketoglutaric, replaced the usual carbon dioxide bubbling in two industrial antibody-making cell lines.

Carbon tracing showed deep rewiring of central metabolism under every acid feed, with clear differences between the two lines. Fed cultures ran the energy cycle harder, leaned less on glucose, and spilled less lactate. The alpha-ketoglutaric feed split the lines on nitrogen handling: one made more glutamine and cleared ammonia, the other stockpiled glutamate instead. Antibody output per cell rose later in the runs. The authors back acid feeding as a combined acidity and metabolism lever.
pmc-13577013:
Il-Rae Cho and colleagues mapped which part of the H-1 parvovirus outer shell lets the virus enter human cancer cells. H-1 parvovirus already kills HeLa cells in the laboratory, while the closely related Kilham rat virus does not. By building hybrid viruses that swapped segments of the VP2 shell protein, the team narrowed the key region step by step.

A minimum stretch from amino acid 208 to 435 set infectivity, yet it could not sustain infection on its own. Two further segments, plus variable regions named VR4b and VR8, were also required. Hybrids carrying all of these pieces infected human lung and pancreatic cancer cells, pointing to precise shell regions that could guide future cancer-targeting virus designs.
pmc-13577213:
Iipumbu and eleven co-authors map how drug resistant TB reshapes households in Namibia in a 2026 study. Family setups in southern Africa shift often, yet how the disease bends those setups was little known. The team sat with one hundred nineteen patients across three regions for deep talks, drawing kin, friend, and village maps with each.

Eleven household patterns emerged from the talks. Fourteen patients saw their household change after diagnosis: some moved near clinics, some reshuffled to pool care, some split to cut exposure fears, and some merged to save money. Each shift remade who sleeps near whom, and so who shares air with the patient. The authors say contact hunts should treat households as moving targets, not fixed lists.
pmc-13577513:
Jaeeun Yoo studies why some lupus patients make antibodies against donated red blood cells, in a 2026 analysis. Such alloimmunization is a real risk for patients who receive transfusions, and its triggers in humans are poorly known. In mice, type I interferon signaling drives the process. Lupus keeps that same signaling switched on, and lupus patients show high rates of the complication. Yoo mined three public gene data sets covering 150 lupus patients.

In all three sets, interferon scores ran higher in lupus blood than in healthy blood. Patients with strong interferon signals showed gene programs tied to alloimmunization and to antibody-making cells. The two scores moved together in every set, while a related helper-cell program showed no link. Yoo names the interferon score a candidate warning marker for transfusion risk.
pmc-13577613:
Imbusch and co-authors survey in 2026 the state of automated outbreak detection across the European Union and the United Kingdom. Automatic systems can flag outbreaks early and speed public health action, yet national use was little documented. Data came from a survey sent to 25 countries, an expert workshop, and follow ups during 2023 and 2024.

Twenty one countries answered. A third had working systems, a fifth planned them, and near half joined a pilot project. All surveyed countries said they act on detected signals in some form. The study maps demand, system prerequisites, and the barriers institutes face when putting such detection in place.
pmc-13577813:
Tina Rosland and co-authors compare death risk after womb surgery by self report versus hospital records in Norway in 2026. Removal of the womb or both ovaries may affect later death risk. Past studies lean on self report, which can bias results. The team links a large population cohort to death, cancer, and hospital records.

More than thirty seven thousand women were followed to late 2020. Hospital records linked womb removal to a lower death hazard. Self report for the same surgery showed no link at all. Ovary removal showed a like split between sources. Early ovary removal, before age fifty, did link to higher death risk in hospital data. Source choice may explain past mixed results.
pmc-13578213:
Jakub Kufel and colleagues describe a 2026 machine learning tool that finds breathing tubes on chest X-rays of adults. A tube placed for a ventilator must sit at the right depth, and doctors judge that by the gap between the tube tip and the carina, the point where the windpipe splits. Reading that gap by hand takes time in busy intensive care units.

Six doctors marked tubes and windpipes on close to four thousand X-rays to train the model, which paints both structures on each scan. On outside test scans its outlines matched the doctors well, and its gap readings missed the true value by a few millimeters on average. The authors see the tool as support for staff, not a stand-in for them.
pmc-13578413:
Batool Zarei, Sepideh Elyasi, and Gholamreza Karimi reviewed compounds that may shield patients from the harms of a major heart rhythm drug, in a 2026 paper. The drug works well, but long use can damage lungs, liver, kidneys, thyroid, and fertility. The team searched four databases through July 2025 for cell, animal, and human studies of protective add-ons. Thirty-five reports made the cut, with set tools used to rate bias in each kind of study.

Nearly all proof was preclinical: one human report, and no randomized trial at all. Lung models led the set. One vitamin had the widest backing across studies. Plant and nutrient compounds such as curcumin and milk thistle extract also recurred. Protection ran through a shared set of paths: less fat oxidation, calmer swelling signals, and guarded cell powerhouses. The authors judge the case plausible but not clinical, and call for human trials.
pmc-13578613:
Xiao-Chen Liu led a team of thirteen that studied, in two thousand twenty-six, a grave gut ill of newborn babes. The ill is necrotising enterocolitis, in short NEC. In it, gut tissue dies. Why it starts is not fully known, and doctors lack firm early signs to spot it in time.

The team joined many ways to read tissue at once: proteins in bulk and by place, and the RNA of single cells. They checked finds with stains, blood tests, and a mouse form of the ill. One theme ran through the reads. Gut lining cells took on traits of deep cells, a shift known as the epithelial-mesenchymal transition. In mice, a drug that blocks that shift eased gut harm and death. Four proteins stood out as tissue signs. One, ANXA2, was high in blood too, with a score of 0.944 for spotting the ill.
pmc-13578913:
Joshua David and co-authors test if amyloid build up in the brain tracks thinking decline over eight years. Their paper from 2026 uses the Dallas Lifespan Brain Study. More and more work hints that amyloid is not the sole early driver of decline in Alzheimer disease.

Data came from forty eight people, split into two groups of twenty four by amyloid status. The groups were matched by age and sex. Thinking was tracked across memory for events, working memory, speed, and reasoning. A link with amyloid group showed for reasoning but not for the other three fields as a whole. Broad decline over the eight years took place in both groups.
pmc-13579313:
Wang and a team of colleagues tested a new kidney-protective compound in twenty twenty-six. Severe acute kidney injury often heals badly, leaving scarring that becomes chronic kidney disease. A repair program in tubule cells can turn maladaptive, driven by oxidative stress and an iron-linked cell death called ferroptosis. A master switch, Nrf2, normally defends cells against both.

Mice lacking Nrf2 developed worse scarring and more stress and death markers after blood-flow injury. The compound 6K frees Nrf2 from its keeper protein, Keap1. Treated mice kept better kidney function, showed less oxidative damage and ferroptosis, and shifted repair genes toward healthy patterns. In human kidney cells, 6K restored a key protective enzyme and cut lipid damage. Fibrosis also slowed in a second injury model. The authors propose 6K as a kidney-targeted drug candidate.
pmc-13579413:
Alexandra Régia Dantas Brigido and co-authors review abnormal heart rhythms after organ transplantation, in this 2026 Europe PMC paper. Atrial tachyarrhythmias, including fibrillation and flutter, follow patterns that depend on the organ and on time since surgery. Early cases stem mainly from surgical stress, inflammation and shifts in fluids and metabolism.

Thoracic transplants carry the highest burden. In heart recipients, late rhythm problems often trace to surgical technique and can signal rejection or vessel disease in the graft. In liver recipients, fibrillation links to advanced disease and worse outcomes. Across organs, these rhythms lengthen hospital stays and raise clot, death and graft loss risks. Care needs careful drug interaction checks and, increasingly, ablation.
pmc-13579613:
Rafael, Garcia, and Subtil grade built wetlands by reliability, not just average cleanup, in a 2026 study. Planted wetland systems treat home sewage at low cost. Claims of toughness often rest on mean removal rates, ignoring swing. The team applied a reliability score to thirty-four systems drawn from past reports, judged against Brazilian discharge and reuse lines.

Mean removal was strong for most pollutants. Once swing was priced in at a strict odds target, fewer systems stayed safely under the lines. Nitrogen and phosphorus lagged under both views. Scores varied widely within each design type, so no design owns one score. The authors urge designers to plan for swing, not means.
pmc-13579713:
Yuhang Wu and colleagues weigh which early pregnancy risks drive low birth weight in central China, and how many cases could be prevented, in a 2026 study. More than thirty four thousand pregnant women were followed from 2013 to 2019, split into those with and without pregnancy diabetes. Six changeable risks were scored from the first months, from older mother age to missed folic acid.

Five risks mattered in each group, with one swap: secondhand smoke in the diabetes group and alcohol in the other. Low education carried the largest preventable share in both groups, ahead of low body weight and older age. In total about a fifth of low weight births in the diabetes group and a third in the other group traced to the five risks. Tailored early care is the authors' prescription.
pmc-13579913:
Li Guo and colleagues test whether a stiffness reading from ultrasound can flag moderate to severe chronic kidney disease, in a 2026 study. One hundred fifty two patients across all five disease stages had standard scans plus shear wave readings, which time tiny ripples through tissue to gauge firmness. A combined scoring sheet that folds in size, layer thickness, and brightness was also computed for each kidney.

The stiffness of the outer kidney layer sorted stage three and beyond with strong accuracy. It rarely cried wolf, which makes it handy for ruling disease in, yet it missed about a third of cases, so a soft reading cannot rule disease out. The combined score sorted nearly as well. The authors back the pair for staging help in clinic, with the miss rate as the caveat.
pmc-13580013:
Zi-Ren Zhou and co-authors report a scope method to release stiff hip muscles, in work from 2026. Severe tightening of the buttock muscles can block squatting and leg crossing. Open surgery frees the muscle but causes wide tissue damage and slow recovery.

The new method frees a ring of tissue around the hip bone knob, an area sparse in nerves and muscle. Records cover patients treated from late 2019 to late 2022. All showed clear pre-surgery signs such as blocked squatting or a snapping hip. Surgeons checked release quality by scope view and by moving the hip during surgery. The series weighs pain, function, and return to activity after the gentler approach.
pmc-13580113:
Miguel Sanchez-Marin, Marco Giulini, and Alexandre Bonvin compared methods in 2026 for predicting how nanobodies bind their targets. Nanobodies are tiny binding proteins with antibody-like grip, prized for therapy and diagnosis. Their shape is hard to predict when bound, in part because their key loop takes many forms and evolution gives few clues.

The team benchmarked leading machine learning methods for nanobody shape prediction. They also tested docking workflows that use physics and known facts to guide the fit, feeding them varied starting shapes and levels of prior data. From the tests they propose an ensemble docking pipeline that improves on single runs. Readers get a practical ranking of tools for a hard modeling case, plus a workflow that blends AI guesses with guided docking.
pmc-13580413:
Dicky C Pelupessy and seven co-authors present a 2026 school-based study of suicidal behavior among teens in Depok City, Indonesia. Such behavior is rising worldwide, yet studies from poorer countries and city settings are few. The team drew on an online school climate survey at two public junior high schools.

Of 446 students, about 7 percent said they had ever had suicidal thoughts, plans, or attempts, and most were female. Four factors predicted the behavior: being female, time spent with family, exposure to physical assault, and truancy. Ties with parents, school support, and contact with antisocial acts were also weighed. The authors call for programs shaped to local teen traits, and they add rare data from an urban setting in the Global South.
pmc-13580613:
Yi Yang, Furen Dai, and co-authors review pair use of a fat diet and germ adds for an ovary ill, in work from 2026. The ill mixes sugar fight, male scent flood, and gut germ skew. Gut germ tales tie those threads in one axis of cause talk.

The fat diet cuts carbs, lifts burn bits, and eases sugar fight in tales. It may thin good gut germs as a side cost in some runs. Germ adds may patch that cost and calm body fire at once. No lot trial yet tests the pair in sick folks head on. Pair gains stay a tale to prove in wards.
pmc-13581013:
Valeria Teso and co-authors report litter found deep in an Argentine submarine canyon in this 2026 survey. A remote vehicle explored the Mar del Plata canyon in the southwestern Atlantic. Deep seas face growing human pressure, yet litter maps still have large gaps.

Canyons can act as channels that carry litter down and as zones where it piles up. The survey recorded what litter lay on the deep floor and how it met local life. Such records show that waste reaches places far out of sight. They also give managers a base line for the region. Future surveys can track whether the load grows or falls.
pmc-13581413:
Jennifer Acevedo and co-authors report a rash puzzle in a liver transplant patient in a 2026 case report. The 55-year-old woman kept getting what looked like skin infection in her legs. Care teams read it as cellulitis, a true germ infection of the skin. Over 11 months she went to hospital ten times and took many germ drugs, with no lasting gain.

Tests for germs, fungi, and slow germs all came back clear. A skin sample showed swelling around vessels and sweat glands, with no germ or vessel harm. That mix points to a drug rash that mimics infection, a form called pseudocellulitis. The team suspect tacrolimus, a key transplant drug, since the rash began after the transplant and flared while she took it. They note other drugs she took cloud the proof.
pmc-13581513:
Jieying Li and co-authors report the care of a man with a severe tooth-based infection of the face and jaw, in a 2026 case report. The patient also lived with HIV and syphilis and a badly weakened immune system, a mix that makes such infections hard to control. He arrived a week after a molar was pulled, with swelling, jaw stiffness, and trouble breathing.

Scans showed gas-forming abscesses across several face spaces, and his immune cell count was very low. Doctors opened his airway through the neck and drained the abscesses at once. Care then combined bacteria drugs in sequence, penicillin for syphilis, early HIV treatment, and preventive drugs. He left the hospital on day 25, and at four months the infection had not returned and his immune count had risen a great deal.
pmc-13581713:
Mariana Oliveira and five co-authors show that diabetes turns a fungal infection fatal in mice. The fungus Sporothrix brasiliensis causes sporotrichosis, which is usually limited. The team builds a type 1 diabetes mouse model and compares infected diabetic mice with infected controls with normal blood sugar.

Diabetic mice develop progressive ulcerative lesions and spread of fungus to lymph nodes, liver, and brain, with full mortality. Blood signals show high levels of three inflammatory proteins and low counts of a key T cell type in the spleen. Immune cells from diabetic hosts first bind yeast strongly, then fail fast, a sign of exhaustion. Liver markers suggest a late stage block in cellular cleanup. The model maps how diabetes weakens antifungal defense.
pmc-13581813:
Five authors, led by YuQing Bi, studied a Chinese breathing practice in this 2026 paper. The practice, LiuZiJue, uses set sounds and breath patterns and is a form of qigong. The team asked what a single session does right away to executive control, the brain's power to focus and resist distraction.

Twenty healthy young adults took part in a randomized crossover study. Each person did both the breathing practice and a control rest with eyes closed. The team measured Stroop task scores, brain blood signals with near-infrared light, resting brain scans, and brain responses to magnetic pulses. The practice cut Stroop reaction time against both baseline and control, with no loss of accuracy. Brain readings showed matching shifts in activity and connections. The study maps quick brain changes from one short session.
pmc-13582013:
Jiunn Wang and ten co-authors evaluate the cost utility of NeuroSAFE guided robotic prostate surgery against standard surgery in the United Kingdom. Robotic removal of the prostate is a standard cure for localized cancer but risks erectile dysfunction and incontinence. The NeuroSAFE technique checks tissue during surgery to spare nerves while avoiding positive margins.

A within trial economic evaluation runs alongside a blinded multicenter randomized trial over twelve months. Men with non metastatic cancer, good baseline erectile function, and no prior treatment qualify. Costs are counted from health service and societal perspectives. Quality adjusted life years come from a standard questionnaire, and cost effectiveness ratios plus net monetary benefit are estimated with bootstrapped uncertainty.
pmc-13582513:
Shu Chen and co-authors ask what makes art and design teachers willing to use AI in class. Standard adoption models stress ease and usefulness. In creative fields, worries about originality and skill loss may matter as much. The team surveyed over a hundred teachers and talked with a smaller group in depth.

Several classic paths held: ease fed usefulness, and usefulness and attitude fed intent. One path flipped sign, with ease linked to worse attitude. Readiness of resources helped ease but not usefulness. Talks surfaced fears of shortcuts, copy theft, and weak rules. The authors say adoption in creative teaching turns on craft values, not just function.
pmc-13583113:
Li and co-authors report in 2026 a medium entropy alloy that gains both strength and ductility from an ordered phase change under strain. Ordered aluminide materials are light and strong but tear poorly at room temperature, since their lattices limit dislocation motion. Lowering phase stability while keeping order was their design lever.

Tuning aluminum content made the B2 matrix metastable. Under tension it slips on set planes and transforms to a new ordered phase by an unusual path. The alloy reached about seven percent elongation and 1.1 gigapascals of tensile strength. Its strength per density beat most reported light B2 materials. Controlled metastability is the transferable lesson.
pmc-13583313:
Hospital accreditation badges hang in lobbies everywhere, yet nobody publishes how the badge is actually computed. Arjavi Patel, Bhavinkumar Parmar, and Sankalp Sagar scoped the literature across two decades. Of nearly three thousand records, twenty-seven sources qualified for close reading.

The silence was the finding. No source examined how standards are weighted, how scores are added up, or where pass thresholds are set. Only six looked at transparency beyond the pass-fail label. Most treated accreditation as a simple compliance exercise and flagged weak causal methods. Seventy percent still described the badge as a reputation signal. The authors call the hidden scoring architecture the field's blind spot.
pmc-13583513:
Nicola Colucci and co-authors demonstrate a milk fat test that exposes bile leaks during liver surgery, in a 2026 video report. Leaks after liver removal cause much suffering, above all after big resections. The team injected a white lipid emulsion backward through the bile duct stump during a keyhole extended left liver removal for spread bowel cancer.

The white fluid welled out at one small leak near a staple line, which was sealed on the spot. The patient healed without any leak or fluid pocket, and later scans stayed clean. The authors praise the test's simplicity and contrast, with the video as the teaching core.
pmc-13583913:
Jinming Bai and six co-authors review how artificial intelligence can link the full path of cancer drug discovery. In most work each AI tool is used for one step alone. The review instead treats drug work as four linked stages, from finding a target to testing drug response and resistance.

The authors propose a design, test, and refine loop that spans all four stages. In that loop, AI predictions guide lab tests, and test results then improve the next round of design. They stress that AI should guide lab and clinical judgment, not replace it. Weak training data, tumor diversity, and poor transfer to new cases remain key limits that need strong checks in more complex models.
pmc-13584313:
Anita Słupska and co-authors give practical guidance on short courses of ketamine for stubborn depression, in a paper from 2026. Ketamine and its cousin esketamine can lift mood fast when other drugs fail. The nasal form of esketamine has an official label in many places. Most other forms, like oral or under-skin doses, are used off-label.

The review sorts the forms by strength of proof. Under-skin dosing has the firmest trial base among the non-vein routes. Oral dosing has thin but real support, mostly from small trials. Home-mixed nasal sprays rest on the weakest ground. For all forms, the authors urge tight protocols: screening, watched dosing, and measured follow-up. Treatment should stay brief and sit inside a wider care plan. Misuse risk must be weighed for each patient.
pmc-13584513:
Lorena Sampaio and thirteen co-authors present a 2026 study on fast-dissolving oral films made from plant polymers. Such films melt on the tongue and ease dosing for people who struggle with pills. The team blended galactomannan, extracted from a tropical plant, with corn or arrowroot starch in varying shares. They then measured how the recipe changed the films' structure, strength, and dissolving behavior.

Starch type steered the mechanics: corn starch made films more flexible, arrowroot made them stiffer, likely through differing starch composition. The films came out uniform, clear, and near neutral in surface acidity. Spectroscopy pointed to hydrogen bonding between the polymers as the glue behind the changes. A blend of seventy-five percent galactomannan with twenty-five percent corn starch balanced strength, flexibility, and fast disintegration best. The authors pitch the blends as sustainable bases for oral film products.
pmc-13585213:
Two drugs paired as first care for a hard lung cancer form are tested by Xiaojun Yang and co-authors in work dated 2026. The cancer carries a growth switch flaw plus extra flaws in genes like TP53. Such extra flaws speed drug failure, so one drug alone fades fast. Thirty-eight patients across sites took the pair, with blood tests before and after.

Tumors shrank in near three of four patients, and all held at least steady. Mid time before spread ran near twenty-nine months. Harsh side effects hit under a fifth of patients, with no drug deaths. The pair looks strong and safe enough to test more.
pmc-13585513:
Deepak Kumar Vaishnav and co-authors reviewed out-of-pocket medicine costs for chronic patients in India in a 2026 paper. People with long-term disease must buy drugs for years, and those costs fall heavily on households. The team pooled past studies to size the burden and see how it varies.

Thirty studies entered the review and eleven the pooled analysis. Average yearly medicine spending per chronic patient came to a stated pooled figure, with wide variation across studies. About half of patients paid something for medicines. Drugs made up a large share of total care costs, more in outpatient than inpatient care. Diabetes estimates were pooled separately, also with wide variation.

pmc-13603913:

pmc-13604113:

pmc-13605813:

pmc-13606413:

pmc-13606813:

pmc-13607113:

pmc-13607613:

pmc-13607713:

pmc-13608013:

pmc-13608113:

pmc-13608413:

pmc-13608913:

pmc-13609113:

pmc-13609313:

pmc-13609413:

pmc-13609513:

pmc-13609613:

pmc-13610013:

pmc-13610113:

pmc-13610313:

pmc-13611313:

pmc-13613413:

pmc-13616713:

Aurore A. Perrault and four colleagues test whether sleeping on a gently rocking bed helps people who sleep badly, extending the team's earlier success with good sleepers. Sixteen young adults who struggled to fall or stay asleep, and whose recorded sleep confirmed the problem. They spent an adjustment night in the laboratory, then one night on a bed rocking slowly sideways. A second night used the same bed held still, with memory tested each night.

The rocking night fragmented sleep less: participants spent less time awake and in light sleep, objective sleep efficiency rose, and they rated their sleep better. Brain recordings showed the rocking motion entraining sleep rhythms, boosting fast spindles and slow oscillations during deep sleep, replicating the effect seen in good sleepers. Memory consolidation did not improve. The authors offer this as early evidence that rocking could serve as an add-on for some chronic insomnia.
pmc-13619213:
Xiaoxuan Wang and co-authors look for risk factors for bleeding inside a stroke after clot-busting treatment in a 2026 paper. The drug tenecteplase can reopen blocked brain arteries, but the damaged tissue sometimes bleeds afterward, a change called hemorrhagic transformation. The team reviewed treated patients at one center between 2022 and 2025, all with follow-up brain imaging.

Of close to two hundred patients, about sixteen percent developed the bleeding, split between milder staining and fuller blood pockets. Older age, worse stroke severity at arrival, a lower early scan score, and higher blood pressure went with the bleeding. Two blood measures, a clotting ratio and a clot-breakdown product, also ran higher in those who bled. The authors warn their model rests on few events and may overfit, so the findings are leads for larger studies, not settled rules.
pmc-13619413:
Na Lu, Hongping Gong, Hualin Yan, and Yu Liu reported a rare case in 2026. A parasitic cyst grew in the breast of a woman from an area where the disease is common. The disease, cystic echinococcosis, is caused by a tapeworm larva and usually settles in the liver or lungs. Breast involvement is extremely rare, so it can be mistaken for a tumor.

The patient, a Tibetan woman aged 50 years, felt a lump in her left breast. Ultrasound showed a mixed-echo nodule with a folded pattern the authors call the cerebral gyrus sign, after the folds of the brain. MRI added detail, and tissue tests after surgery confirmed the parasitic cyst. Readers get a named imaging clue that may help doctors suspect this rare cause before surgery.
pmc-13619513:
Ashoke Mitra and co-authors compare migraine treatments in a 2026 systematic review and network analysis of trials. Many drug options exist for acute migraine, but common over-the-counter choices are rarely tested directly against newer prescription drugs. The therapy under study pairs an antihistamine and caffeine combination with ibuprofen.

Because head-to-head trials are scarce, the team combined randomized trials into a network that allows indirect comparison across treatments. Rivals included lasmiditan and the newer CGRP-blocking drugs ubrogepant and rimegepant. The results help adults with episodic migraine and their doctors judge whether a cheap shelf option can match newer prescription drugs.
pmc-13619713:
Demir and colleagues follow in twenty twenty-six hip replacement patients for at least ten years to check wear in a vitamin E blended plastic socket liner. Wear of the plastic cup is a main driver of loosening, the top reason hips get redone. The vitamin blend aims to resist the chemical ageing that weakens older plastics, but long-term proof was thin.

Automated software matched implant models to X-rays, measuring wear and cup angles without observer bias. Wear rates fell between year five and year ten and stayed far below levels tied to bone damage. Cup tilt held steady, though a forward angle crept up slowly. The authors call the liner's decade performance favourable and ask for head-to-head studies.
pmc-13620113:
Panagiotis Poulis and four colleagues investigated a side effect of the chemical tweak that made COVID-19 mRNA vaccines practical. The modified building block, called m1Psi in the study, calms immune alarms and stabilizes the message. Earlier work hinted it can also make ribosomes slip and read the message in the wrong frame. The team measured that slipping with glowing reporter genes in cells, a rebuilt translation system, and single-molecule microscopy.

Slipping rose on one short sequence pattern where the reading machinery paused. At that pause the modified block weakened the grip between message and transfer RNA and nudged the transfer RNA into a slip-prone shape. Swapping the pattern for two nearby alternatives erased the effect entirely. The authors say vaccine designers can keep the useful modification while simply avoiding the risky sequence when they optimize the code.
pmc-13620213:
Moby Solangi and four colleagues report what four decades of tracking say about dolphin lifespans in Mississippi Sound. In 1982, fifty bottlenose dolphins there were freeze-branded during a health study and followed by their marks. Later photo-identification surveys, which recognize dolphins by fin shapes, kept watch over the same population.

Ten of the branded dolphins were still being seen between 2011 and 2026. Seven of the survivors are now over thirty years old, and one is confirmed at forty-seven, a striking age for the species. Two of the living dolphins show long-term loyalty to the same home waters. Because mark tracking has limits, the authors caution that ages and fidelity need continued checking. They urge keeping the surveys going, since these dolphins also serve as sentinels for the health of the whole sound.
pmc-13620813:
Si-Yu Ma and five colleagues describe two new species of wood-inhabiting fungi found in a tropical rainforest national park on China's Hainan Island. Fungal diversity in the tropics remains poorly mapped, and these fungi belong to Biscogniauxia, a genus of carbon-crust fungi that live on bark and wood. The team combined close study of spore and fruiting body shapes with family trees built from three gene regions.

One new species, named for Diaoluo Mountain, shows flat fruiting crusts and spores with a bold straight germ slit running nearly the spore's length. The second, named for the Jianfeng range, carries tube-shaped spore chambers and spores with a faint slit plus a small opaque appendage on one side. Gene trees confirmed both stand apart from known relatives. The paper adds full descriptions, illustrations, and an identification key for the whole genus.
pmc-13621213:
Wang and colleagues review in twenty twenty-six an advanced brain scan method for judging fine damage after stroke. Standard scans show where a stroke hit and whether it bled, but they miss tiny structural change and repair in early tissue. The newer method, a form of magnetic scanning, measures how water moves along nerve fibres to gauge their density and spread.

The review covers the method's basis, its uses in both blocked-vessel and bleeding strokes, and its limits. One striking use is spotting changes in mood pathways after stroke. About one in three survivors faces depression, and the method may flag those at risk better than older measures. The authors map next steps to bring it into routine care.
pmc-13621813:
Mary Leick and three co-authors review records of liver transplant patients who switched to everolimus, a drug used to lower reliance on older immune-suppressing medicines that can harm the kidneys. The question was whether the timing of the switch changes kidney outcomes. Patients at one academic medical centre were grouped by how soon after transplant the switch happened.

Eighty patients were included. Those switched within six months showed kidney gains that held at one month and at twelve months after the change. A later group gained at one month but not at twelve, and the latest group gained at neither point. The trade-off was rejection, proven by tissue sampling, which was most common in the earliest group. The authors conclude that early switching protects kidneys best but needs care because rejection risk runs high.
pmc-13622913:
Vasileios Sotirios Akrivos and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review that hunts for spin in studies comparing two versions of the Latarjet operation for shoulders that keep dislocating. Spin means presenting results in a slanted way that makes one method look better than the data support. The operation moves a piece of bone to stabilise the joint, open or through small scopes.

The reviewers screened comparative studies from the last twenty years and checked each one against a spin classification system. Four in five of the twenty-five studies showed at least one form of spin. Selective reporting was the most common problem, followed by missing discussion of limits and claims of differences that were never tested statistically. Studies judged weaker in design carried more spin per paper. Funding and declared conflicts made no difference. The authors warn readers to check the numbers behind claims in this surgical debate.
pmc-13623013:
Alessio Maione and a large surgical team compare kneecap ligament repair results in patients whose knee anatomy sits at the borderline of normal. The medial patellofemoral ligament holds the kneecap in its groove, and rebuilding it can stop repeated dislocations. Surgeons debate whether patients with slightly abnormal bone shapes need extra bone surgery on top of the ligament repair.

The team reviewed fifty-one patients, covering fifty-five knees treated between 2013 and 2023, and split them into standard and borderline anatomy groups. After an average follow-up of nearly eight years, both groups improved strongly on pain and function scores. Final scores and redislocation rates were much the same in the two groups, and stacking several borderline features did not worsen results. The authors conclude that ligament repair alone serves well-chosen borderline patients, and bone procedures should wait for clearly abnormal anatomy.
pmc-13623713:
Zijian Liu and co-authors rank Chinese herbal formulas used beside mecobalamin for diabetic nerve damage in the feet and hands. The formulas aim to move blood and open the collateral channels, and trials suggest they lift nerve conduction and ease symptoms. No trial, though, has pitted the formulas against each other.

Their 2026 review sweeps six databases for randomized trials that add a formula to mecobalamin against the drug alone. Outcomes run from a clinical nerve score to motor and sensory conduction speeds in two nerves, plus side effects. A Bayesian network model pools direct and indirect proof and ranks the field. The verdict aims to guide add-on choices in type two diabetes care.
pmc-13623913:
Johanna Pirchner and co-authors studied how to make a yeast host secrete very small peptides, in a 2026 paper. Small peptides are a growing class of medical drugs, but making them by chemistry has limits, so microbe factories draw interest. The yeast they used is a workhorse for secreted proteins, yet peptides under a set size slip through poorly and are hard to detect.

The team used a tiny tagged peptide of 23 building blocks as its test case. They varied chain length and the signal that sends a peptide out of the cell, and boosted parts of the export machinery. A random mutation screen found new genes that sway secretion. The tricks then carried to three other peptides.
pmc-13624013:
Yusuke Matsui and a large engineering-medical team published a 2026 test of a robot that drills needles into bone under CT guidance. Placing biopsy and treatment needles into bone by hand is slow and exposes staff to radiation. Their remote-controlled robot adds a rotating drill plus force feedback that adjusts pushing speed as resistance changes.

The team attempted insertions into the spine, pelvis, and thigh bones of three pigs, six tries per site. Every insertion succeeded. Angle errors between plan and final needle stayed tiny, well under a degree in most planes, with the thigh bone the least exact. Insertion times ran from about twenty seconds in spine and pelvis to about a minute in the dense thigh bone. No adverse events occurred. The authors call the system feasible and accurate in animals, a step toward human trials.
pmc-13624313:
Kayoung Han and colleagues show that star-shaped brain support cells, astrocytes, step in to manage blood flow only when sensory demand lasts. Brief stimulation draws a standard response, but the brain needs a gear for sustained activity, and the study compares five-second against twenty-second stimulation in animals using optical imaging and microscopy.

Long stimulation, not short, switched on a relay inside astrocytes: a water channel let the cell swell, and the swelling opened a calcium gate. The calcium then triggered release of a signalling molecule, D-serine, through a second channel. That signal boosted neuron activity and blood volume, and it set the resting tightness of brain arteries. Removing any relay part in mice broke the long-stimulus response while sparing the short response, and supplying the missing signal molecule restored it. The work assigns astrocytes a duration-sensing role in matching blood supply to demand.
pmc-13624913:
Suwasin Udomkarnjananun and co-authors set a national standard for anti rejection drugs after kidney transplant in a 2026 guideline from Thailand's transplant society. No full world consensus had been refreshed since 2009, leaving clinics to improvise.

The guideline spans induction, upkeep dosing, drug level checks, and rejection care. It bends the science to local genes and budgets, with cost cutting routes like generic drugs and helper drugs that stretch each dose. Special chapters cover fasting, pregnancy, and cancer settings. The society offer it as a working model for other middle income health systems.
pmc-13625613:
Roselin Mohandas and co-authors surveyed adults with type 2 diabetes in Puducherry, India, in a study published in 2026, asking how many keep their blood sugar under poor control and why. Uncontrolled diabetes is a major cause of early death through its complications.

The team visited 340 adults at home who had lived with the disease for at least six months. About sixty-four percent had poor control by the standard blood test. Age, place of residence, alcohol use, and how steadily people took their treatment were all linked to poor control. Once other factors were taken into account, irregular treatment stood out as the one clear driver, with a very large effect.
pmc-13626213:
Karina Bursch and co-authors analyze missense variants in the EHMT1 gene that cause Kleefstra syndrome, a congenital neurodevelopmental disorder. Their 2026 paper focuses on the ankyrin repeat domain of this lysine methyltransferase.

EHMT1 writes and reads histone methylation marks that repress transcription. Its ankyrin repeat domain recognizes a key histone mark and interacts with other epigenetic regulators. Nearly half of the missense variants there are still classed as variants of unknown significance. The team used multi-tiered structural genomics at atomic resolution to predict how 56 syndrome-linked variants alter the domain's structure and function. Such deep phenotyping can help classify variants.
pmc-13626313:
Ayaka Tajiri and six colleagues, publishing in 2026, refine a cheaper way to forecast how antibody drugs behave in human blood. Developers usually scale up doses from cynomolgus monkeys, whose cost keeps rising, so this team used common marmosets, far smaller primates. Two arthritis and bowel drugs, golimumab and ustekinumab, were given four times each, and size-based scaling math, averaged with three earlier antibodies, predicted the human curves.

Ustekinumab's human profile was matched excellently, while golimumab's fade rate came out slightly off. Immune reactions against the human drugs were tiny or brief, clearing a key worry about repeat dosing. The authors settle on provisional scaling values and present marmosets as a workable stand-in for early pharmacokinetic work.
pmc-13626713:
Yang and co-authors identify a ginseng compound that stunts the roots of neighboring plants, a chemical warfare effect called allelopathy. Ginseng plants are rich in such compounds, but the inner workings of the effect were murky. Their 2026 study isolates the compound, zingibroside R1, and tests it on ginseng roots and on a small model plant.

The compound blocked side root growth in ginseng and main root growth in the model plant. Tracking markers showed it jams the transport of auxin, the hormone that steers root growth, and tests with blockers and mutants backed that reading. It also switched off genes that maintain root tip stem cells. Stress chemistry rose in parallel, upsetting the plant's cleanup systems. The authors frame the result as a full mechanism for this root war.
pmc-13627013:
Seven veterinarians report long-term control of a lymphatic growth disorder in a dog in a case report from 2026. The disorder forms soft cystic masses that are hard to remove fully, since borders blur into normal tissue. The patient was a small mixed-breed dog with recurring masses near the groin. Surgery at another hospital and steroid treatment had failed to stop regrowth.

After wide surgery at the authors' hospital, the masses returned quickly. Repeated injections of minocycline into the cysts then shrank or stabilized them. More than five hundred days later the dog stayed active with good gait. Gene tests found no known driver mutation. The authors propose the injections as a gentle option for hard cases.
pmc-13627113:
Kim and colleagues use a Korean cohort to ask whether alcohol's link to liver cancer grows with age. Hepatocellular carcinoma, the liver cancer, is an established cost of heavy drinking, but age specific risk was murky. Their 2026 study follows 3.9 million adults who had a health exam in 2009. It records drinking level and cancer cases over a median of more than eleven years. The analysis splits into twenty year age bands.

Twenty thousand people developed liver cancer in follow up. A dose trend, rising risk with rising intake, reached clear levels only at sixty and over. Heavy drinking raised risk in both the forty to fifty nine band and the sixty plus band. The raise was far larger in the older group, near half again the risk of non drinkers there. Prevention talks, the authors suggest, should press hardest on middle aged and older heavy drinkers.
pmc-13627413:
Zhen Xue and three co-authors hunted for factors that keep patients stuck in the recovery room after anesthesia, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Long stays slow bed turnover, raise costs, and frustrate patients and surgeons. The team reviewed more than sixty-nine thousand adults who woke up in the unit after general anesthesia over two years.

Two hundred ten patients stayed past two hours and were matched with controls. Emergency surgery, major surgery, past stroke-related disease, more blood loss, and longer operations each raised the odds of a long stay. A higher blood level of a nutrition-linked protein before surgery went with lower risk. The team built a chart tool that sorts patients by risk with good accuracy, but they note it needs testing at other hospitals first.
pmc-13627713:
Ring-shaped protein complexes that hug DNA organize whole chromosomes, yet watching one work has been nearly impossible. Kenichi Umeda and three co-authors film the Smc5/6 complex directly with high-speed atomic force microscopy, at detail fine enough to see its parts move on DNA.

At rest the complex sits in a narrow I shape with its arms aligned. When ATP binds, it opens into an O-shaped ring and grips DNA at its head domains. Burning the ATP traps the DNA inside the ring and slides it toward the hinge. The complex also bridged two DNA stretches at once and stabilized twisted DNA, compacting it. The authors say the footage shows how one ring switches between binding modes. The study appears in 2026.
pmc-13628313:
Hannah Gordon and a large team check whether a diabetes drug taken in pregnancy is tied to slower child development at school entry, in work dated 2026. Metformin is prescribed more and more often in pregnancy. In animals it shapes early brain growth, but whether that matters in children was unknown.

Birth records from 2009 to 2020 were linked to a national census of child development taken in the first school year, at ages four to six. Exposure meant a metformin prescription filled during pregnancy. Children were rated for vulnerability across development domains. The huge linked cohort lets small risks show, or lets families be reassured by their absence.
pmc-13628613:
Catherine Mollart and co-authors published this 2026 study on a puzzling carbon material used in battery anodes. The material, called OSPC-1, can be made by two routes, and one test method backed a simple picture of its framework. Yet its NMR spectra, which probe atomic structure, did not fit that picture at all.

The team shows that a dense, tightly interwoven structure explains the spectra for both forms of the material. They also find signs of a second, open structure that likely holds the pores. Both shapes must be counted when judging how the material conducts and stores ions. That fuller picture should guide the design of better battery carbons.
pmc-13628913:
Zhilin Hu and twelve colleagues asked why a usually mild childhood leukaemia sometimes turns risky. The danger comes when a second mutation is present. Their 2026 study concerns leukaemia carrying the AML1-ETO fusion. It asks what a matching KIT mutation in exon 17 does to outlook and drug response.

The team mined a database of 957 child patients. The exon 17 mutation largely wiped out the fusion type's survival edge. Tests on marrow samples from sixteen patients in Shenzhen hinted at broad drug resistance. Standard chemotherapy drugs seemed to fail against it. Gene activity pointed to one gene, SOCS1, switched up in the resistant pattern. The authors argue for finer risk grouping by KIT profile. They also urge study of the linked signalling axis as a treatment target.
pmc-13629213:
Ayushya Ajmani and four co-authors report a severe case of a painful skin disease in unusual places, in this 2026 article. The disease, hidradenitis suppurativa, causes repeated lumps, abscesses, and tunnels under the skin, usually in the armpits and groin. In this patient, sores also spread to areas outside those folds, a pattern doctors call ectopic. Her disease was at the most severe stage and covered more than a tenth of her body.

The first-choice biologic drug for the disease did not control her symptoms. Doctors then switched her to a related drug at a higher dose, which did help. The case stands out because widespread disease of this kind, in both usual and unusual sites, had not been reported before. It offers guidance for the hard cases where the standard drug fails.
pmc-13629313:
Jenny Blythe tracks how London's betting shops, arcades, and bingo halls shifted across five years, and where they ended up. She used the national regulator's register for all 32 boroughs, matched with a standard score of local deprivation.

The city lost a few dozen sites in all, down from 1,516 to 1,478. But the drop hid a tilt. The poorest quarter of boroughs gained five sites while the richest quarter lost eleven. The link between poverty and site counts grew stronger over the period. Blythe argues that current rules let gambling cluster where harm bites hardest, and urges reform that weighs local need.
pmc-13629413:
Marcus Brady and Rachel Crespo-Otero benchmark the computer methods used to simulate what a propeller-shaped molecule does after absorbing light. The molecule, a three-bladed rotor, mostly wastes the energy as motion rather than glowing, and simulation results depend heavily on which electronic-structure theory drives the calculation.

Running surface-hopping dynamics under several methods, the pair mapped the crossing points where the molecule drops between energy states. One method relaxed the molecule far faster than the others, and the preferred crossing point was consistent across approaches, though a second crossing changed character between theory levels. A spin-flip method produced the richest outcomes, including a bicyclic product. The study questions how far push-button excited-state tools can be trusted for photochemistry.
pmc-13629813:
Lijun Sun and five colleagues compared the two home dialysis methods for people whose kidneys have failed, asking which better preserves the kidney function patients still have. Their single-centre retrospective study followed fifty-three Chinese patients starting treatment, nineteen on the automated overnight method and thirty-four on the manual daytime method.

Both groups began with similar remaining function and urine output. By six months the automated group's residual function had fallen significantly further, and its yearly rate of decline was clearly faster. Statistical modelling tied the automated method itself, plus higher starting function, to quicker loss. The authors advise weighing this trade-off when choosing a starting modality, since lingering kidney function strongly shapes dialysis patients' health.
pmc-13630113:
Anna Dankers and nine colleagues catalogued the yardsticks hospitals used to run and judge their services during COVID-19. Their review screened five databases. It sought European inpatient studies from 2020 to late 2024. It then pulled out every distinct yardstick in use.

Ninety-four studies yielded 459 separate yardsticks. They grouped into six families, from health outcomes to access times. The same measure often carried unlike definitions across hospitals. Like ideas also hid under unlike names. That made comparison treacherous. Most studies used the yardsticks to compare pandemic care with the time before. Few blended health and logistics views. The authors offer the catalogue as groundwork. Standard, crisis-ready hospital dashboards could grow from it.
pmc-13630413:
Supriya Das and co-authors broke down Kraft lignin in 2026 with nothing but sound blasted water droplets, in a single step of about twenty minutes. Lignin, the tough glue of wood, is a rich raw material, but turning it into useful chemicals usually needs harsh heat or catalysts and gives poor yields.

Their droplets carried both the lignin and an oil phase, shaken by ultrasound. More than half of the lignin turned into one small product, a molecule built from altered plant units joined to a ring core. Tests of the product showed it can give and take electrons, a trait prized for energy storage. The droplets both cut carbon bonds and added nitrogen groups.
pmc-13630513:
Kawano and Hagio split apart the roles of direction practice and position practice in learning brand-new movements in twenty twenty-six. De novo motor learning means building a sensorimotor map from scratch. Many solutions could work, so the task is open. Which kinds of practice shape a sharp map was not clear.

Twenty-five people learned a made-up joystick-to-cursor mapping. They practiced under setups stressing target position, movement direction, or both, kept apart. Direction practice cut early errors in movement direction. A lack of position practice, by contrast, raised final position errors. Using both gave no simple added gain. In its place, end point accuracy tracked how well direction-based and position-based outputs lined up in the loose control space. The authors say sharp new maps rest on lining up the two kinds of practice, not piling up either alone.
pmc-13630613:
Lucas da Costa and co-authors test, in a 2026 rat study, whether sodium nitrite can lower a harmful compound in a model of preeclampsia. The pregnancy disorder brings high blood pressure and vessel damage. A compound called ADMA blocks the enzyme that makes nitric oxide, a vessel-relaxing gas, and runs high in the disorder.

Pregnant rats were split into healthy and low-flow placenta groups, each with and without nitrite in their diet. The dose ran at 15 milligrams per kilogram daily from mid-pregnancy. The team then measured circulating ADMA and vessel function. Nitrite can turn into nitric oxide when oxygen is scarce, exactly the placenta's condition. The title reports the hoped-for drop in ADMA.
pmc-13631013:
Rajib Dasgupta, Shreya Pujari, and Purnamita Dasgupta argue for care with oral rehydration salts in child heat care in a 2026 paper. Heat action plans name ORS a key shield for children. ORS saves lives in diarrheal dehydration across the world. Its use in heat stress raises fresh questions, though.

Most heat plans stay silent on mixing and dosing details. Reviews show low know-how on correct preparation among workers. The authors insist only the WHO formula should be used. Plans should give age and weight dosing, per UNICEF advice. India's many languages call for pictorial, multilingual mixing guides. Frontline workers need training to give ORS correctly.
pmc-13631313:
Outammassine Abdelkrim and ten colleagues publish a global atlas of the Asian bush mosquito. Their study appeared in 2026. Aedes japonicus invades readily and thrives in varied containers of water. It can carry dengue, Zika, West Nile, and several other viruses. Yet it draws a fraction of the attention given to its famous cousins.

The team gathered three quarters of a century of sightings, from 1950 to 2025. They mined journals, national surveys, and biodiversity stores. Each record was cleaned and geolocated through strict quality control. The result is 4,618 verified points. It is the first dedicated global store for the species. The authors offer it as working infrastructure. Distribution mapping, invasion tracking, and disease risk assessment can all build on it.
pmc-13631613:
Limberger and team compared two mood measures in twenty twenty-six. Both measures are used in daily-life diary studies. Phone diaries ask people about feelings many times a day. Scales must stay short yet still be sound at each moment. The team studied a clinic group and a larger public group. Both filled in a mood questionnaire and a good-bad feelings scale.

Checks covered score spread, soundness, and modeling assumptions. In the public group, most scales behaved very well. The bad-feelings scale skewed badly, with many floor-level scores. In the clinic group, the good-feelings scale flipped to weak. The mood questionnaire spread well in both groups. The team says such scales need careful choice. Reporting how they behave should be routine in diary research.
pmc-13631713:
Francesca M Cohn and seven colleagues present a lab method for telling apart six look-alike coral species in French Polynesia. These Pocillopora corals build reefs across the Indo-Pacific, yet their shapes vary so much that eyes alone cannot name them reliably. Genetic naming usually needs sequencing, which costs money and needs facilities that field teams may lack. Their method uses DNA cutting patterns instead.

The protocol works on two known marker regions, one from mitochondria and one from a histone gene. Cutting the DNA with chosen enzymes gives each species its own pattern of fragment sizes. In blind checks done both on computer predictions and in the lab, the method named every species correctly. Because the test is cheap and fast, similar protocols could help reef surveys, conservation work, and restoration projects in other regions.
pmc-13631913:
Ming Qu and co-authors map the cell programs that run follicle choice in laying hens, in a 2026 study. Each cycle, a few ovarian follicles are picked to mature while the rest stall. The granulosa cells that wrap each egg drive that choice.

The team fused single cell gene reads with bulk data, open chromatin maps, contact maps, and trait genetics. About sixty-three thousand cells fell into eighteen fine states under four broad programs, from early growth to hormone making. Trajectories ran from early states toward the chosen hormone state. Three genes topped a scoring scheme as candidates for the switch. The atlas gives breeders and biologists a shared frame.
pmc-13633213:
Srija Nuguri and co-authors count medication mistakes at home serious enough to land people in hospital. Their study appeared in 2026. They mined United States poison center records from 2000 to 2024. In that span, 115,071 dosing errors outside health facilities were tied to a hospital admission. Most happened at home, involved one drug, and affected women and adults over 49 most often.

About 39 percent of patients needed critical care, and over half had serious outcomes, including 745 deaths. Heart drugs, painkillers, and antidepressants were the most common culprits. The rate per million people nearly tripled across the period, rising fastest in adults over 69. The authors call for safer packaging, clearer labels, and support for older patients managing many drugs.
pmc-13634013:
Khan and co-authors test in a 2026 study an AI overlay that paints the anatomy in live brain surgery video, pixel by pixel. The trial, the first in people, used pituitary surgery as its test case. Such surgery is high stakes, with a steep learning curve, and old guidance tools break the flow.

The model ran on a local box for speed, with no cloud link. The team judged whether it worked in the room, how staff found it, and how patients fared, using set frameworks for early AI trials. Recordings were also reviewed blind after the fact to check quality.
pmc-13635213:
Yige Cao and eleven colleagues published this 2026 study testing whether yeast-derived particles can strengthen the tuberculosis vaccine. The BCG vaccine protects children well but guards adults unevenly against lung tuberculosis. The team added whole beta-glucan particles, fiber pieces from fungal cell walls that wake up immune cells. In dishes, the particles sharpened macrophages, the cells that first meet the vaccine bacteria, improving how they swallowed, digested, and displayed bacterial parts to T cells.

The effect ran through a known sensing pathway in those cells. Breaking that pathway erased the gains and weakened T cell responses. In mice, giving the particles at a separate site from the vaccine worked best and calmed early lung inflammation. The pairing strengthened memory T cell responses and improved control of a tuberculosis challenge while reducing lung damage. The authors propose the particles as a vaccine helper worth developing further.
pmc-13636613:
Peter J. Halfmann and six colleagues published this 2026 study building nanoparticle vaccines against the coronaviruses behind many common colds. Two endemic viruses, OC43 and HKU1, spread widely through airways and can hit older and immune-weakened people hard. Their spike proteins keep evolving, and a large animal reservoir adds spillover risk. The team mounted spike proteins from three virus versions onto nanoparticles and also made a two-in-one version pairing two of them.

Vaccinated mice produced strong spike-targeting antibodies. The antibodies reached across to matched virus relatives, a hopeful sign for breadth. The paired vaccine matched the single versions against each of its targets, losing nothing by combining. The authors frame the work as groundwork for vaccines against this whole virus family. A future universal cold vaccine is the distant prize, and knowing the antibody landscape of these spikes is a needed early step.
pmc-13637713:
Christopher Barrington-Leigh questions whether the spread of life satisfaction scores in a country truly measures how unequal that society is. Scholars have used that spread as a catch-all gauge of inequality. Countries with higher average scores tend to show a narrower spread, which some read as proof the spread itself matters for welfare.

Barrington-Leigh names a further flaw: many people round their answer to a few focal values, such as nought, five, or ten, on the zero-to-ten scale. This habit warps the spread in a fixed direction. He works out how large the warp can be and checks survey data for its size. At common rounding rates, the warp could reach half the range seen across countries. The critique warns against reading deep meaning into a warped gauge.
pmc-13638313:
Lahousse and co-authors examine a quiet problem in lung research: health records do not use the same words for the same breathing outcomes. One clinic may record an event with one label while another clinic picks a different label. That mismatch makes it hard to pool records and trust what pooled studies find.

Records from daily care cover far more people, yet their value drops when key terms shift from place to place. The paper calls for common wording so that record-based studies of lung disease can be compared and combined with more trust.
pmc-13638713:
Niangmei Cheng and seven colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study on why liver cancer can stop responding to the drug lenvatinib. That drug is a first-line treatment for liver cancer that cannot be removed by surgery, but resistance often develops over time.

Cells carrying that change survived lenvatinib better in dishes and in mouse tumors, partly because the altered protein raised Bcl-2, a protein that blocks cell death, and lowered BAX. The work names one route to resistance that future drugs might try to close.
pmc-13639013:
Teerachai Amnuaylojaroen and one colleague present MSEA-Daily, a 2026 climate dataset for mainland Southeast Asia. The dataset gives daily rain and temperature values on a four-kilometer grid for Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam across the years 1981 to 2014.

The builders blended monthly TerraClimate values with daily patterns from satellite rain data and a weather reanalysis, then checked results against seventy-seven weather stations. Temperature matched station records closely, while heavy rainfall extremes were understated somewhat. The dataset reproduces monsoon timing and El Niño patterns, supporting farm planning, water modeling, and studies of climate extremes in the region.
pmc-13641213:
Egbring and co-authors study how eye refraction skews widefield vessel measures in a Caucasian population. OCT angiography maps retinal and choroidal blood flow without dye injections. Past work showed refraction, the eye's focusing profile, shifts these metrics in the central fundus, which can distort patient readings.

The team used widefield swept-source OCTA to cover a broader retinal area. They aimed to set normative reference values for vessel metrics, split by refraction level. Such norms help doctors tell true disease change from simple optics. Widefield ranges are vital as these scans enter routine eye care.
pmc-13643313:
Henriette Zeidler and co-authors present a 2026 study of how young children help their peers across six cultures. Helping is a core part of human social life, yet cross culture tests of child helping are rare, and most past work used adult child pairs. Peer help matters more in many settings.
