The steps earlier resolutions required had still not been carried out. It asks the Secretary-General, as a matter of urgency, to survey how the four General Armistice Agreements are being enforced. He is to arrange measures with the parties. Those include withdrawal of forces from the lines and full freedom of movement for United Nations observers. He is to report back within one month.

Siam, the country now called Thailand, applied to join the newborn United Nations in 1946. It had never been colonized, but the war had left its status tangled. A dispute with France over border territory had to be settled first. The Council noted that its members unanimously approved the application.

Resolution 13 then recommends Siam's admission to the General Assembly. The Assembly admitted Siam in December 1946. It was among the UN's earliest new members. The country's later name change to Thailand did not affect the seat. This short text preserves the formal step by which a Southeast Asian kingdom joined the postwar order at its very start.

Resolution 1313, adopted on 4 August 2000, extends the UN mission in Sierra Leone while admitting the peace there has broken down. Rebels of the Revolutionary United Front had attacked and detained UNAMSIL peacekeepers that spring, breaking the Lomé Peace Agreement. The Council praised the mission and its commander for pushing back against the threat.

The mandate was extended only until 8 September 2000. The Council judged that the rebels' widespread and serious breaches since May had destroyed the cooperative climate the agreement assumed. Until security allowed progress toward a settlement, it said, the mission's structure, strength, resources, and mandate all needed beefing up, and it signaled its intent to order that strengthening next.

Resolution 1413 is a UN Security Council extension of the Afghanistan security force, adopted unanimously on 23 May 2002 under Chapter VII. The International Security Assistance Force, created after the Taliban's fall to protect Kabul and the interim Afghan government, had been led by Britain, and Turkey had offered to take command.

The resolution extends the force's authorization for six months beyond 20 June 2002 and authorizes participating states to take all necessary measures to fulfill its mandate. It thanks Britain for organizing and leading the force and welcomes Turkey's offer to assume the lead. The force it kept in being later expanded nationwide under NATO.

Three months of cover for the Sahara mission came from this spare text of 2003. On 28 October, the Council adopted Resolution 1513 without dissent. It recalls the Council's past Sahara texts. One stands out: Resolution 1495 of July 2003. That text backed the envoy's peace plan as the best path for the territory.

One step does the work here. MINURSO's mandate runs to 31 January 2004. A report from the Secretary-General is due before that term ends. The bridge kept the mission in place while replies to the plan hung fire. The Polisario Front had accepted the plan by then. Morocco had not, and the gap stayed open.

Names, not laws, fill this Council text on the Yugoslavia court. On 26 July 2005, it adopted Resolution 1613. The court, built by Resolution 827 in 1993, used stand-in judges to widen its trial capacity. Candidates reached the Council through the Secretary-General. The Assembly then elects the judges from the Council's list.

The text sends thirty-five names to the Assembly. The nominees come from many states, from Pakistan and Nigeria to Canada. Latvia and Jamaica are on the list as well. Such staffing steps were routine work for the Council. They kept the court's rooms staffed through its busiest trial years. Each name had to pass the Assembly vote to serve.

Another year of scrutiny for Sudan's sanctions began with Resolution 1713. It was adopted on 29 September 2006. A Darfur peace deal existed, but key rebel groups had refused to sign. Violence and impunity were getting worse. Aid workers faced growing danger. The expert panel's final report had landed that August.

Members extended the panel until 29 September 2007. A fifth expert was added to strengthen it. The panel owed an interim report within ninety days. A midterm briefing was set for 29 March 2007. Non-signers were urged to join the Darfur agreement at once. Signers were told to honor it. All parties had to halt attacks on civilians.

Negotiations over Western Sahara gained rare momentum in 2007 and 2008. Morocco offered an autonomy plan in April 2007. The Polisario Front tabled its own proposal a day earlier. Four rounds of direct talks followed. Resolution 1813, adopted on 30 April 2008, tried to keep that process alive after the Secretary-General's latest report.

MINURSO, the UN mission in the territory, was extended until 30 April 2009. Members demanded respect for the ceasefire agreements. They told both parties to negotiate in good faith, without preconditions. Realism and compromise were called essential. The text also backed family visits between separated relatives, by air and possibly by land. Money from member states was sought for such confidence-building steps.

In March 2010 the future of the United Nations Mission in the Central African Republic and Chad, known as MINURCAT, was still unsettled. Chad's government and the United Nations were still discussing what should happen to the mission. Resolution 1913 simply extended the mandate until 15 May 2010, on the same terms as before. The Council said the situation in the region remained a threat to international peace and security. The short extension kept the mission in place while the talks went on.

Cast out by Malaysia in August 1965, Singapore stood alone. The rich port city had not sought the split. It had to build a state from scratch, fast. A bid for a UN seat came at once. Resolution 213 passed with no dissent on 20 September 1965.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Singapore. The Assembly did so the next day. Lee Kuan Yew led the new state. Few gave the small isle much hope then. It had no farms, no oil, and a port as its chief wealth. Time proved the doubters wrong. The seat was a first shield for a weak new state. This one-line text is the legal start of Singapore's life among nations.

Few Council demands are as short, or as blunt, as this one of 1972. On 28 February, it adopted Resolution 313 without dissent. Israel had struck into Lebanon by ground and air. The raids answered guerrilla attacks from across the border. Lebanon brought the matter before the Council.

One sentence carries the whole text. Israel must halt and shun all ground and air action against Lebanon at once. All its forces must leave Lebanese soil. The brevity is itself the message. Most Middle East texts balance calls on both sides. This one speaks to a single party, in command voice, with no softening clauses at all.

Vietnam had been shut out of the UN for years by vetoes. The war ended in 1975 with the land made one. Saigon fell, and a single state took shape. Its bid for a seat had been blocked in 1976 by the United States. In 1977 the mood had changed. Resolution 413 passed by common consent on 20 July 1977.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit the Socialist Republic of Viet Nam. The Assembly did so that fall. Hanoi took the seat with no foe at the gate this time. The vote closed a long tale. The UN had split the land's fate in the 1950s. War and cold rivalry kept a seat out of reach for a full age. Now the one state took its place.

Yugoslavia was breaking apart in fighting in the autumn of 1991. The federal army faced forces in Croatia and Slovenia. Cease-fire deals signed that September were already breaking down, and the loss of life was heavy. Yugoslavia itself had welcomed a meeting of the Council. Resolution 713 was adopted on 25 September 1991.

The Council praised the peace efforts of the European Community and of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. Then, acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, it ordered a general and complete arms embargo. All states had to stop deliveries of weapons and military equipment to Yugoslavia at once. The embargo would last until the Council decided otherwise. It was meant to help establish peace and stability in the country. The Council kept the matter on its agenda until a peaceful solution was achieved.
un-un-res-second-report-of-the-secretary:
Early 2000 finds the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone still finding its feet, and the second report of the Secretary-General, document S/2000/13, takes stock. UNAMSIL had taken over from the observer team under the Lomé peace deal. Its troops were spread thin across a tense country.

The report covers deployment, disarmament of fighters, and talks with rebel leaders. It notes slow progress and lists the risks that could wreck the peace. Read with the later reports, it shows a mission walking a narrow line before the crisis that nearly destroyed it.
us-amendment-13:
The Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution was ratified in December 1865, eight months after the Civil War ended. Congress had passed it in January, and Abraham Lincoln signed the proposal before his death. Emancipation had come by war proclamation; the amendment wrote abolition into the nation's supreme law.

Its first section declares that neither slavery nor involuntary servitude shall exist in the United States, except as punishment for a crime. The second gives Congress power to enforce the ban by law. Four million enslaved people gained legal freedom by its words, though the fight for real freedom had only begun. The charter of freedom for those four million souls was bought at the cost of over six hundred thousand war dead. It remains the first of the three Reconstruction amendments.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s18-13:
Section 18.13 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers the withdrawal or correction of filed documents. It sits in Part 18, on the preparation and sending of documents in general. Part (a) states the rule for a document filed for public inspection with the Office of the Federal Register but not yet published. Such a document may be pulled from publication or corrected by the agency that sent it.

Small fixes and withdrawals may be made by a letter sent in good time. The letter must be signed by a duly cleared agent of the agency. Large fixes may call for the agency to pull the document in full, as the text goes on to state. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s601-13:
Section 601.13 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets out the marks of Commission acts that fit an environmental assessment. It sits in Part 601, on the carrying out of the National Environmental Policy Act by the National Capital Planning Commission. Part (a) states what an assessment is in that scheme. It is a concise document with facts and analysis enough for a key call.

That call is whether the Executive Director should issue a finding of no significant impact or prepare an impact statement. Part (b) lists the marks of acts that as a rule need an assessment. The first marks named are harm to environmental quality that is minor but likely real, as the list goes on. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s602-13:
Section 602.13 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets the fees for freedom of information requests handled by the National Capital Planning Commission. It sits in the commission's part on how it answers requests for its records.

Fees follow the guidelines of the Office of Management and Budget. For charging, the commission sorts requesters into three groups: commercial users, schools and news media and nonprofit science bodies, and everyone else. Search fees are not charged to the school, science, and media group. Other requesters pay search fees based on staff time, figured in quarter hours from average federal pay plus a share for benefits. A requester who owes fees may ask for a waiver under a later section.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s603-13:
Section 603.13 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations deals with calls for the use of Records. It sits in Part 603, the Privacy Act rules of the National Capital Planning Commission. A man or woman who seeks the use of Records about that same man or woman must use a set path. The call can be made in the flesh at the place of work of the Commission. It can also be made in writing to the Privacy Act Officer of the Commission.

Calls in the flesh are by a set time with the Privacy Act Officer, and on a work day in the set hours of work. Calls by post are to go to the Privacy Act Officer at the address of the Commission on its web site.
uslaw-usc-t1-s113: Section 113 of Title 1 of the United States Code deals with proof of laws. Three kinds of print count as sound proof of the laws they hold. The first is the laws and treaties set printed by Little and Brown. The second is the slip form of the laws of the land. The third is the series of treaties and other world acts. All may be used as proof in courts of law across the land.
uslaw-usc-t1-s213: Section 213 of Title 1 of the United States Code authorizes an appropriation for preparing and editing supplements to the Code of Laws. It sits in Chapter 3 of Title 1, on the Code of Laws of the United States and its supplements, current through Public Law 119-134. The whole provision is one sentence. For preparation and editing, a yearly appropriation of 6,500 dollars is authorized. The money is to carry out the purposes of sections 202 and 203 of the same title.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1313:
Section 1313 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers rights under the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 for congressional staff. It sits in Chapter 24 of that title, the Congressional Accountability Act, in the part that extends rights to such staff. Part (a) takes up fair labor standards in general terms.

The rights and shields named are those set up by named parts of the 1938 Act. The parts cited are parts of section 6, section 7, section 12(c), and section 18D of that Act, as found in Title 29. The section thus brings those wage and hour shields to the staff it covers. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1413:
Section 1413 of Title 2 of the United States Code is headed Privileges and immunities and sits in the Congressional Accountability Act. It is found in Chapter 24 of Title 2, in the subchapter on administrative and judicial dispute steps. The version here is current through Public Law 119-134.

The text guards named rights against being read as given up. Taking part in proceedings under sections 1405, 1407, and 1408 of the title does not count as a waiver of sovereign immunity for any other purpose. Nor does it waive the privileges of a Senator or a Member of the House under the speech or debate clause of the Constitution. It also leaves untouched any power of either House under the Constitution, including the power over its own records and information.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1513:
Section 1513 of Title 2 records Senate findings on the shifting of costs between levels of government. The Senate finds that Congress should be concerned about shifting costs from the Federal level to State and local authorities. It should be equally concerned about the growing tendency of States to shift costs to local governments.

Cost shifting of that kind, the findings say, has often forced local governments to act. They raise property taxes or cut services that are sometimes essential. Higher local taxes and cuts in services then threaten home ownership in safe communities. The section states a sense of the Senate as well. The Federal Government should not shift certain costs to the States. And States should end the practice of shifting costs downward. The section sits in Chapter 25 of Title 2, the Unfunded Mandates Reform chapter.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1613:
Section 1613 of Title 2 of the United States Code bars gifts from lobbyists. It sits in the chapter on telling Congress of lobbying work. A covered person may not give a gift to a branch official. Travel for such an official is barred on the same terms in the text.

The bar holds when the giver knows the gift may not be taken. The test of what may be taken sits in the rules of each house. House rules bind House officials, and Senate rules bind Senate ones. The next part names the persons held by the bar in full. They are lobbyists on the roll or bound to be on it. Groups that hire lobbyists and are on the roll are named too. Staff listed as lobbyists for such a group complete the class.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1813: Section 1813 of Title 2 of the United States Code is a one line rule on the outside of the Capitol building. It sits in the chapter on the Architect of the Capitol, in the part on general powers and duties. From July 7, 1884, on, it is the duty of the Architect to clean the exterior of the Capitol and to keep it in proper order. The text as hosted is the full section, and it states that single charge with no added terms or limits.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2013:
Section 2013 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets up a revolving fund for the House gymnasium. It sits in Chapter 30 of that title, on the operation of the Capitol complex, in the part on the House. The section creates the fund in the Treasury of the United States. The Architect of the Capitol is to deposit sums in the fund.

The sums are those the Architect takes in as gym dues or assessments. They come from Members of the House and from other persons allowed to use the gym. The sums so deposited are open for use by the Architect for the gym. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2213:
Section 2213 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets the general duties of the Chief Executive Officer of the Capitol Visitor Center. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the chapter on that visitor center. Its subchapter covers the center's own office. The hosted text is current in twenty twenty six.

Except where the chapter provides otherwise, the Chief Executive Officer is responsible for the center, the text states. That duty covers operation, management, and budget preparation and execution. Facilities, services, and activities of the center all fall under that charge. The section thus gives one officer clear ownership of how millions of Capitol visitors are received.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4313:
Section 4313 of Title 2 gives a House committee power over members' allowances. Subject to a provision of law named in the text, the Committee on House Oversight may act by order of the committee. By such an order it may fix and adjust the amounts of House allowances.

The power reaches terms and conditions as well. It also reaches other matters relating to those allowances. The section sits in Chapter 43 of Title 2, on congressional committees. It falls in the subchapter for the House of Representatives. The hosted text is the Code as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel, current through Public Law 119-134. In plain terms, the section lodges the purse strings for House office funds in a named committee, acting formally by order rather than by fresh statute each time.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4713: Section 4713 of Title 2 of the United States Code sits in the congressional ethics chapter, in the part for the House. It orders reporting of payments made to witnesses by the House committee then called the Committee on Standards of Official Conduct. Information on payments for attending as a witness in a closed session during a Congress must be reported. The deadline is the second semiannual report in the Congress that follows.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4913:
Section 4913 of Title 2 of the United States Code gives the Page Board power to make regulations for House pages. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the chapter on congressional pages, in the House subchapter. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. It is a single sentence grant of rulemaking power.

The Page Board shall have authority to prescribe such regulations as may be needed, the text states. Those regulations carry out the linked sections on the page program. Schooling, service, and supervision of teenage pages in the House are the matters at stake. A short grant gives the board room to run a residential student program in detail.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5513:
Section 5513 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets up an account for the House of Representatives. It sits in Chapter 55, on House officers, in a general part of the chapter. The account is set up in the Treasury of the United States. Its name is the House of Representatives Modernization Initiatives Account. A second clause deals with the use of the funds in the account. The House is to use those funds to carry out plans to make its work new in form.

Those plans include plans to push the skill of the way the House is run. They also include plans to spread the use of new tools of work in the offices of the House. A third clause deals with the span of the funds.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6113: Section 6113 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers staff hired by the President pro tempore of the Senate. It sits in Chapter 61 of that title, on Senate leadership. From 1 October 1979, the President pro tempore is cleared to appoint such staff as he deems fit. He is also cleared to fix the pay of those staff. A proviso caps the gross pay of such staff. It may not pass 123,000 dollars in each fiscal year.
uslaw-usc-t2-s613: Section 613 of Title 2 of the United States Code lets the Congressional Budget Office set up senior level posts. The Director may create such posts and fix their pay to meet key needs of the office. Those needs may be in science, tech, skilled, or leader work. The yearly pay for such a post may not top the rate for level two of the Executive Schedule. The section is stated to apply from fiscal year 2017 and each year after.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6313:
Section 6313 of Title 2 of the United States Code creates a single account for Senators' staff and office costs. Before 1988 those costs were split among separate funding lines. This section gathers them into one pot inside the Senate's contingent fund.

The account is named the Senators' Official Personnel and Office Expense Account. The short name used in the section is the Senators' Account. It took effect on January 1, 1988. The account funds all items, activities, and expenses of a covered kind. Covered items are those funded just before that date under the older lines the text names. One account thus pays the people and the offices of every Senator. The merger lets each office manage its people and its expenses as a single budget.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6513:
Section 6513 of Title 2 of the United States Code caps Senate daily travel costs. The cap hits funds granted under the head of Contingent Expenses of the Senate. It first held for sums granted on and after the 27th of June 1956. Daily and living costs may not pass the rates a named panel sets.

That panel is the Committee on Rules and Administration of the Senate. It may set higher rates for travel past the mainland of the nation. Pay back on a real cost basis is also let by the text. That path is capped at the daily rate the panel sets for home travel. The section does not reach the travel costs of Senators and their own staff.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6613: Section 6613 of Title 2 of the United States Code lets the Secretary of the Senate advance funds to the Sergeant at Arms for special costs. It sits in the part on the general powers and duties of that Senate office. From July 31, 1958, on, the Secretary may, at his own choice, make such an advance. The sums must be those needed to meet any out of the way costs of the Senate. No advance may top 4,000 dollars. The hosted text is the full section in one sentence.
vidyabhusana-nyaya-sutras-1913:
Logic in India begins with the Nyaya Sutras of Gotama, translated complete into English by Satis Chandra Vidyabhusana in 1913. The volume, eighth in the Sacred Books of the Hindus series, holds the founding text of the Nyaya school. Its subject is right reasoning: how we know, how we prove, and how we argue fairly.

Short sutras lay out kinds of proof, the parts of a syllogism, and the traps of bad debate. Every later Indian school of thought had to answer Nyaya's standards. For students of logic beyond the West, no shelf starts earlier than this one.
webster-unabridged-dictionary-1913:
The 1913 edition of Webster's Unabridged Dictionary was the standard desk dictionary of the English-speaking world for a century. It descends from Noah Webster's great American dictionary, expanded by generations of editors. Every headword, definition, root, and pronunciation is given in full.

Entries run from common words to rare scientific and literary terms, with examples of use. The book's size was its promise: nothing a reader met in print should be missing. Libraries, schools, and newspaper offices kept it close at hand. As a snapshot of English in 1913, it remains a rich quarry for writers and historians.
wharton-custom-of-the-country-1913:
Edith Wharton published The Custom of the Country in 1913, her most savage look at American money and marriage. Wharton wrote it while her own marriage was collapsing. Her heroine, Undine Spragg, came from a small midwestern town with rich parents and unlimited ambition.

Undine climbs through a string of husbands: a gentle New York heir, a French marquis, and a railroad magnate. Each marriage buys her a higher social floor, and each bores her once she owns it. Divorce, in Wharton's account, is simply the custom of the country for women like Undine. The novel is funny, cold, and prophetic about celebrity culture. Many readers rank it as Wharton's finest satire.
witches-apprehended-examined-executed-16:
Bedford gives this 1613 pamphlet its case: witches taken, questioned, and put to death. Witches Apprehended, Examined and Executed pairs the trial report with a guide to finding witches. The two parts sit side by side, court record first and plain advice after.

The guide tells readers what marks, acts, and signs should raise alarm in their own towns. That pairing is the point of the print, and it was a shrewd one. Trial news taught fear, and the guide taught readers how to act on it. The pamphlet shows charge and belief feeding each other in Jacobean England.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol13:
Liverpool printed Volume XIII of the Journal of Discourses in 1871, well into the set's second decade of publication. The stenographic pages hold sermons by Brigham Young, his counsellors, the Twelve Apostles, and other leading speakers. By now the Journal was a fixture: the way spoken teaching became lasting print for the Saints everywhere.

Readers find doctrine taught with the confidence of a church no longer fighting for its ground. Daily counsel still threads through the talks, since the speakers governed towns as well as souls. Volume XIII adds its full share to the year-by-year record of nineteenth-century Mormon teaching.
